running_heads.spectemus, & nomen Dei timeatur ab ortu: let us behold, and let the name of God be feared from rising to setting in the whole earth.
running_heads.rarum aftruat, & armorum ftudiis antepon: let him assert it as rare, and place it before the pursuits of arms, since these arts, arising from God himself, lead man back to God. Let him be called Lord of Hosts, but he is the begetter of wisdom from all eternity.
running_heads.Conclus. Per Apostrophum desinat in admi: Conclusion. Through apostrophe let him end in admiration of Moses, as of a man who had no equal; and from there let him turn to the commendation of obedience to the Law written by him.
running_heads.Hatterius Agrippa Senator illos retinend: Hatterius Agrippa, a senator, judges that they should be retained.

units.la: Magnifice, Nobilissimi, Amplissimi Consultissimi, Prudentissimi Viri, Patroni & Autores Optimi.
units.tr: Magnificent, noble, most distinguished, most learned and most prudent gentlemen, patrons and best of authors.

units.la: Recens Vobis absq; dubio est memoria Cl: Hipstedii, Viri, cùm de universo orbe Erudito, tam de Illustri Schola la Patria meritissimi. Atque utinam, quæ nobis scripta mortalitatis lex est, non intervenissęt laboribus & studiis ejus, quibus noctes diesque bene merēri de Erudita Juventute solebat. Neque enim tantum ex obitu B. Viri vulnus sentirent publicæ privatæque doctrinæ. Cùm verò in senectutem eámque afflictam admodum ex annorum gravitate devolveretur, non videbatur quidquam instare propinquius, quàm ut planè ex mortalium rebus mox eximeretur. Cui beati discessus voto cùm annueret ante anni circiter quadrantem benignissimus Deus, fuit non immerito princeps eorum, qui ad ipsum adtinebant, cura, ne immortalitate digna ingenii Hipstediani monumenta, hactenus per modestiam Autoris intra privatos cancellos latitantia, vel omninò perirent vel à tineis arroderentur. Initium itaque edendorum operum ab dispositionibus oratoriis facere mihi lilibuit, quibus exercere vim eruditio-nis suæ vel in primis B. Viro visum est. Non enim ingratos istiusmodi labores inutilesve studiis juventutis oratoriis existimabam.
units.tr: You will certainly still remember, gentlemen, the most distinguished Hipsted, who deserved so well of the whole learned world and of this illustrious school of our homeland. Would that the law of mortality, which is written for all of us, had not come upon his labours and studies, by which he used to deserve well of the learned youth night and day. For the wound of the blessed man's death would be felt not only by public but also by private learning. But when he was sinking into old age, and a very infirm one by reason of the burden of his years, nothing seemed nearer at hand than that he should soon be wholly removed from mortal affairs. When, about a quarter of a year before, the most gracious God granted this wish for a blessed departure, it was not undeservedly the chief concern of those who belonged to him that the monuments of Hipsted's genius, worthy of immortality, which until then had lain hidden within private bounds through the author's modesty, should either altogether perish or be gnawed by moths. So I chose to begin the publication of his works with the oratorical dispositions, by which the blessed man thought it best to exercise the power of his learning. For I did not think labours of this kind were unwelcome or useless to the oratorical studies of young people.

units.la: Eos vero cur vestris, Amplissimi Viri, dedicatos voluerim nominibus, cum aliis ea me impulit causa, quod Cl. Hipstedium omni favoris genere, dum viveret, prosequi, & benignè de ejus infracta licèt laboribusque impari valetudine sentire nunquam cessastis, meq; præterea, omni humanitate, dum scholasticis laboribus vacare licebat, fovere studuistis. Quorum beneficiorum memoriæ ut hoc qualecunque monumentum exstruerem, à me jure quodam efflagitare videbatur animi mei ingenuitas: exoraturus cæteraDeum Optimum, ut vos Reip. patriæ atque Illustris Gymnasii saluti & emolumento in multos annos superstites esse jubeat, omnipræque praeterea coelestis gratiae rore perfundere dignetur. Accipite ergo serena fronte hoc debitae meae observantiae testimonium & favete porro illi, qui est eritque.
units.tr: As for why I wished to dedicate these works to you, most distinguished gentlemen, the reason that impelled me, among others, is this: the illustrious Hipsted, while he lived, was never ceased to be favoured by you in every kind of goodwill, and you never stopped thinking kindly of him, though his health was unequal to his infirm and laborious life; and besides, you were willing to cherish me with every courtesy while I was able to devote myself to scholastic labours. The frankness of my mind seemed to require of me, as a kind of right, that I raise this memorial, however modest, to the remembrance of those benefits. I shall also beseech the Best and Greatest God to grant that you may survive for many years for the safety and advantage of the fatherland and the illustrious Gymnasium, and to deign to drench you with the dew of heavenly grace in every respect. Accept therefore with a serene countenance this testimony of my due respect, and continue to favour him who is and will be yours.

units.tr: EUPHEMISM. To the posthumous rhetorical-practical work, most skilfully edited by the most distinguished Mr. JOHANN HIPSTED, a most meritorious professor for many years, and written by the very reverend Mr. GERHARD MEIER, S.S. Theol. D., formerly professor of mathematics and now a most faithful minister at St. Stephen's. Dedicated by DIDER. SAGITTARIUS, professor of pedagogy and librarian.

units.la: MOrtuus es nuper, sed non es mortuus omnis, HIPSTEDI, tua enim vivit pia fama superstes, Cum virtute fides, labor indefessus agendo: Vivus solerti cum dexteritate docebas, Atque doces vitâ functus disponere, cujus Prima fuit semper dicendo gloria: nam cùm Sit facilis prudens inventio, teste Secundo, & Eloquium natura juvet, disponere verè est Solius artis opus. Sic cum virtute triumphat Ars, labor, atque fides: jure hinc post funera vivis! Et Tu, male labore Tuo, MEIERE, quòd aptè Eruis è latebris, olim quæ condidit AUTOR! Sic decet indagare Locos, Studiosa Juventus, Sic inventa licet dextrè disponere, ut a, tum Eloquium (decus id summum) comitetur utrumque: Ut laus atque decus Nostrum comitatur utrumque!
units.tr: You have died lately, Hipsted, yet you are not wholly dead, for your devout fame survives you. Faith joined with virtue, and tireless labour in your work: while alive you taught with skilful dexterity, and now that you have departed you still teach to arrange, whose first glory was always in speaking. For although invention is easy for the prudent, as Secundus attests, and nature aids eloquence, to arrange truly is the work of art alone. Thus art triumphs together with virtue, labour and faith; rightly, then, you live on after your funeral! And you, Meier, rightly draw out by your labour what the Author once hid in its hiding places! Thus it befits studious youth to search out the topics, and thus, once found, to arrange them skilfully, so that eloquence (that highest ornament) accompanies both: so that both our praise and our glory accompany us!

units.la: Viri, dum viveret, Celeberrimi in omni Eruditione, Sui quondam Præceptoris ad ultimam Memoriam suspiciendi.
units.tr: Of a man most celebrated for all learning while he lived, to be remembered to the last by his former pupil.

units.la: Post Mortem quoque spirat Abel; mirabile dictu! Exanimis loquitur: Sic Sacra Scripta docent. Hæc Fidei Vox est, sunt hæc quoque Sanguinis ora; Dum Caro fit Pulvis, non cineratur Amor. Sic etiam Hipstedii vivit post Funera Virtus, Cujus inexhausti Pectus Amoris erat. Sic tacet & loquitur, sic spirat mortuus Idem; Crede mihi, Eventum Ligna Futura dabunt.
units.tr: Even after death Abel still speaks; wonderful to say! Though lifeless, he speaks, as the Sacred Scriptures teach. This is the voice of faith, and these are the mouths of the blood. While the flesh turns to dust, love is not reduced to ashes. So too the virtue of Hipsted lives on after his funeral, he whose breast was a well of inexhaustible love. Thus the same man is silent and yet speaks, and though dead still breathes. Believe me, the wood of the future will yield the outcome.

units.la: DISPOSITIONES ORATORIÆ, In Genere Didascalico.
units.tr: Oratorical Dispositions, In the Didactic Genre.

units.la: I. DE FELICITATE SCELERUM ET SERA NUMINIS VINDICTA.
units.tr: I. ON THE PROSPERITY OF THE WICKED AND THE SLOW VENGEANCE OF GOD.

units.la: Exord. 1. Meritò dicit David Pf. 73. propemodum declinaf-sent pedes mei, tantùm non effusi sunt gressus mei, cùm æmu-larer insanos, prosperitatem improborum viderem.
units.tr: Exord. 1. Rightly David says in Psalm 73: "My feet had almost gone; my steps had nearly slipped, when I envied the mad, seeing the prosperity of the wicked."

units.la: 2. Rationem subjiciat à dissimili proborum & improborum hìc sæpe conditione. Exemplo Davidis & Pompei in comparatione Saulis & Cæsaris.
units.tr: 2. Let him give the reason from the frequent dissimilarity between the condition of the good and that of the wicked. By the example of David and Pompey, compared with Saul and Caesar.

units.la: 3. Illustretur dissimili, eleganti scilicet ordine, qui in reliqua natura tota observatur: at solæ res humanæ perperam & te-merè fluere videntur: Hinc factum ut in profanitatem & A-theismum multi & olim, & adhuc prolapsi sint. Ipse David etiam fluctuare coeperit.
units.tr: 3. Let him illustrate it by the dissimilarity, namely by the elegant order that is observed in all the rest of nature, whereas human affairs alone seem to flow at random and by chance. Hence it has come about that many, both in former times and still now, have fallen into profanity and atheism. David himself also began to waver.

units.la: Propositio: Haud inutile itaque futurum, si secuti magnum Plutar-chum rationes serae Numinis vindictae & infidae scelerum felicita-tis inquiramus; quò in adversis patientes, in secundis modesti simus.
units.tr: Proposition: It will therefore not be useless, if, following the great Plutarch, we inquire into the reasons for God's late vengeance and the faithless happiness of crimes, so that we may be patient in adversity and modest in prosperity.

units.la: Tractatio:
units.tr: Treatment:

units.la: I. Exponat Dei patientiam in tolerandis impiis longo tempore: eamque illustret. 1. exemplis, v.g. Caini, primi orbis, & populi Judaici; itemque diversorum regnorum, urbium, tyranno-rum, ut Pharaonis, Nebucadnezaris, Philippi Macedonis, Dio-nysii Siculi, Juliani, &c.
units.tr: I. Let him set out God's patience in tolerating the impious for a long time, and let him illustrate it: 1. by examples, for instance that of Cain, the first of the world, and of the Jewish people; likewise those of various kingdoms, cities and tyrants, such as Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Philip of Macedon, Dionysius of Sicily, Julian, etc.

units.la: 2. Consequenti: videlicet hinc fieri, ut casu fluere omnia, non à providentia regi multis videantur.
units.tr: 2. Consequently, that it is thus brought about that all things seem to many to flow by chance and not to be governed by providence.

units.la: II. Opponat rationes huius divinae longanimitatis; praemissa prolepsi de difficili arcanorum Dei consiliorum scrutatione; cum nec legis latorum semper rationes in promptu sint: multo minus Dei; cui optime notum tempus vindictae. Nihilominus tamen rationes ipsius in differendis poenis investigandas. Itaque
units.tr: II. Let him set out the reasons for this divine long-suffering, after first raising the objection of how hard it is to search out the hidden counsels of God, since the reasons of lawgivers are not always at hand, much less God's, to whom the time of vengeance is best known. Nevertheless, his reasons for deferring punishments are to be investigated. Accordingly:

units.la: 1. Ratio est, Quia Deus est fons omnis virtutis, cuius exemplum imitari debent mortales. Itaq; praebere etiam nobis vult exemplum longanimitatis. Quae virtus commendetur tanquam ardua & necessaria mortalibus maxime principibus & judicibus. Illustretur exemplo Dei in tolerandis Sodomitis & Pharaone.
units.tr: 1. The first reason is that God is the fountain of all virtue, whose example mortals ought to imitate. Therefore he also wishes to offer us an example of long-suffering. This virtue is to be commended as difficult and necessary for mortals, especially for princes and judges. Let it be illustrated by God's example in tolerating the Sodomites and Pharaoh.

units.la: 2. Ratio est. Quia Deus non delectatur poena, sed differens poenam exspectat poenitentiam. Hinc ipse futuri praescius, sepe rescindit illico, quos cernit insanabiles; contra differt poenam illorum, per quos adhuc boni aliquid vult efficere. Ita per Cainum, per Esavum produci debuit magna soboles, per Dionysium ordinari Sicilia, per Periandrum Appollonia, Anactorium Leucadia aliaque Graeciae Insulae excoli debuerunt. Vid: Plut.
units.tr: 2. The second reason is that God takes no delight in punishment, but, by deferring punishment, waits for repentance. Hence he, who foreknows the future, often at once cuts off those whom he sees to be incurable; on the other hand, he defers the punishment of those through whom he still wishes to bring about some good. Thus through Cain and through Esau a great offspring was to be produced; through Dionysius Sicily was to be set in order; through Periander Apollonia, Anactorium, Leucas and other islands of Greece were to be cultivated. See Plutarch.

units.la: 3. Ratio est. Quia Deus utitur malis tanquam carnificibus & exsecutoribus justitiae suae, non secus ac leonibus, lupis, ursis, aliisque noxiis animantibus ad poenam hominum, exemplo Phalaridis apud Agrigentinos. Syllae apud Romanos. Ita Saul datur in ira Judaeis. Ita pestiferae herbae propter medicinam excoluntur.
units.tr: 3. The third reason is that God uses the wicked as executioners and agents of his justice, just as he uses lions, wolves, bears and other harmful animals for the punishment of men. Example: Phalaris among the Agrigentines; Sulla among the Romans. Thus Saul was given to the Jews in anger. Thus poisonous herbs are cultivated for the sake of medicine.

units.la: 4. Ratio est. Quia malitia conjunctam semper habet poenam, videlicet rodentem conscientiam; cujus vis explicetur ex Seneca & Parad: Ciceronis. Comoediam igitur ludunt tantum improbi; crucem interim impositam habent humeris, haeret lateri lethalis arundo; cicutam & venenum Sardonium hauserunt, hamum deglutiverunt certo puniendi suo loco & tempore. Deus videt venire diem ejus. Ps. 37. Hinc Bessus parricida ab hirundinibus exprobrari sibi dixit patricidium.
units.tr: 4. The fourth reason is that wickedness always has punishment joined to it, namely a gnawing conscience; its force is to be explained from Seneca and from Cicero's Paradoxes. The wicked, therefore, play at comedy only; meanwhile they carry the cross laid on their shoulders, the deadly arrow sticks in their side; they have drunk hemlock and Sardonian poison, they have swallowed the hook, to be punished in its proper place and time. God sees his day coming. Ps. 37. Hence the parricide Bessus said that swallows reproached him for his patricide.

units.la: 5. Rat. est: Quia haec vita nil nisi momentum est Deo, cujus usuram facile indulget filiis seculi: exemplo divitis epulonis. Quis invideat vinum incarceratis & ad mortem damnatis? Talis conditio impiorum est. Eccles: 12. Lætare juvenis.
units.tr: 5. The reason is this: this life is nothing but a moment to God, whose interest he easily allows to the children of this age; the example is the rich man who feasted. Who would envy wine to men shut in prison and condemned to death? Such is the condition of the wicked. Eccles. 12. Rejoice, young man.

units.la: 6. Ratio est. Quia Deus sæpe differt pœnam in senectam, item in liberos & nepotes, donec completa iniquitas, exemplo Cananitarum, & domus Achabi. Ita Branchidarum urbem evertit Alex. M. ob proditionem templi Milesii factam ab ipsorum majoribus. Vide Plut. Illustretur prolepsi: Videlicet injustum hoc videri. Resp. Non semper, ita feloniæ culpa punitur in tota stirpe. 2. Posteris assignantur illustria facta majorum. Ergo & scelera 3. Deus hominem considerat ut stirpem, cui vel benedicit, vel maledicit sæpe. Hinc abjecta ad servitutem Ismaelis & Esavi progenies; uti morbi parentum sæpe adhærent liberis. Idem homo sæpe in senectute luit peccata juventutis; corporis pars una peccat, aliam plectitur. Bello decimatione punitur civitas, exercitus. Si hoc in corpore politico; quanto magis in iis, qui ex eodem semine nati. 4. Requirere hoc justitiam Dei, ne peccata maneant impunita.
units.tr: 6. The reason is that God often defers punishment until old age, and likewise to children and grandchildren, until iniquity is complete; the example is the Canaanites and the house of Ahab. Thus Alexander the Great overthrew the city of the Branchidae because of the betrayal of the temple of Miletus made by their ancestors. See Plutarch. Let it be illustrated by an objection: namely, that this seems unjust. Answer: not always; thus the guilt of a felony is punished in the whole stock. 2. Illustrious deeds of ancestors are assigned to posterity; therefore crimes too. 3. God regards man as a stock, which he often either blesses or curses. Hence the offspring of Ishmael and Esau were cast down into servitude; just as the diseases of parents often cling to children. The same man often pays in old age for the sins of youth; one part of the body sins, another is punished. A city or an army is punished by decimation in war. If this holds in the body politic, how much more in those who have been born of the same seed. 4. God's justice requires this, lest sins remain unpunished.

units.la: 7. Ratio est. Quia Deus punit peccata post hanc vitam. Hoc ostendatur cognitum fuisse gentibus, quæ varia supplicio-rum genera apud inferos commentæ sunt. Plutarchum, cum afferre aperte noluit, per somnium revelatum Thespesio in exstasi, narrare. 2. Clare revelatum populo Dei, præcipue in V. Test. vid. Es. 16. & 66. & in N. Test. passim vermis eorum non moritur. Item Matth. 24.
units.tr: 7. The reason is that God punishes sins after this life. Let it be shown that this was known to the Gentiles, who devised various kinds of punishments in the underworld. Plutarch, since he was unwilling to state it openly, relates it as revealed to Thespesius in a dream, in an ecstasy. 2. It was clearly revealed to the people of God, especially in the Old Testament; see Isa. 16 and 66, and in the New Testament passim: their worm does not die. Likewise Matt. 24.

units.la: 8. Rat. est quam solæ sacræ literæ suppeditant. Videlicet Deum sic exercere suos. 1. in patientia; 2. in fide promissionis. 3. in spe vitæ melioris. vid. Ps. 37. & 73.
units.tr: 8. The reason is one that Holy Scripture alone supplies, namely that God thus exercises his people: 1. in patience; 2. in faith in the promise; 3. in hope of a better life. See Ps. 37 and 73.

units.la: Conclusio. Refutet atheos, qui felicitate impiorum securi redditi, dicunt in corde suo, non est Deus. Qui oculum fecit, annon videat? &c. ex Ps. 115.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him refute the atheists, who, made secure by the happiness of the wicked, say in their heart, There is no God. He who made the eye, shall he not see? etc., from Ps. 115.

units.la: 2. Hortetur impios, ne securi reddantur Dei longanimitate, quia ad pœnitentiam illos vocat. Rom. 1.
units.tr: 2. Let him exhort the impious not to become secure through God's long-suffering, because he calls them to repentance. Rom. 1.

units.la: 3. Consoletur pios ad constantiam in passione; suo tempore afore Deum vindicem ipsorum.
units.tr: 3. Let him console the godly to constancy in suffering, since God will be their avenger in his own time.

units.la: II. DE POLITIARUM ET POLITICES ORTU ET PROPAGATIONE.
units.tr: II. OF THE ORIGIN AND SPREAD OF STATES AND POLITY.

units.la: Exord. à politiarum præstantia ac necessitate.
units.tr: Exordium: from the excellence and necessity of states.

units.la: I. Nihil excellentius in mundo, religione & politico regimine.
units.tr: I. Nothing in the world is more excellent than religion and civil government.

units.la: II. Ratio: per illam cœli, per hoc mundi & societatis politicæ civis quis efficitur, quo nihil majus.
units.tr: II. The reason: through religion a man becomes a citizen of heaven, and through civil government a citizen of the world and of political society; nothing is greater than these.

units.la: III. Expolitio rationis, ab humanæ naturæ corruptione & perversitate; qua ex optimo pessimum omnium animalium effectus est homo, extorris cœlo, & ineptus ad societatem. Quod ostende per hypotyposin hominis integri & corrupti.
units.tr: III. An elaboration of this reasoning, from the corruption and perversity of human nature, by which man, from the best of animals, has become the worst of all, exiled from heaven and unfit for society. Show this by a sketch of man in his integrity and in his corruption.

units.la: IV, Solam huic malo succurrere religionem & disciplinam politicam, præsertim qua mores ad virtutem & societatem formantur,
units.tr: IV. Only religion and civil discipline, especially that by which morals are formed to virtue and to society, can bring help against this evil.

units.la: Propos it. Missa igitur in præsens religione, quia altioris originis, politiarum & polices ortum & propogationem te indagaturum. Fiat stipulatio attentionis.
units.tr: Proposition: Religion being therefore set aside for the present, since it is of higher origin, I will examine with you the origin and spread of polities and of politics. Let attention be pledged.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. Ortum arcessat à Deo; à quo omne bonum, Hic 1. Rejice sententiam illorum, qui hominum inventum putant, qui revelationes Dea Egeriæ finxerunt; altiores esse radices politiarum. 2. Deum ostende autorem, qui a. naturæ insreverit & conservaverit principia practica; ut quemadmodum ratio præest affectibus; ita prudentiores præsint in civitate. vid. Cic. & Plat. de L. L. Hinc Dei ductu constitutas œconomias sub primis Patriarchis, sub Melchisedecho, Josepho. b. per Moisen Remp. optimam formaverit & sanctissimis legibus ordinaverit. Expone hic Reip. Judaicæ sub diversis regiminis formis constitutionem, & Lex Forensis per Moisen à Deo tradita laudetur per inductionem quandam generalem. Hanc excoluere successores, Josua, Judices, Reges, qui juxta legem hanc Remp. constituerunt; juvarunt prophetæ. Hinc manasse salubria omnia instituta ad Assyrios & Persus doce.
units.tr: I. Let the origin be traced to God, from whom comes every good. Here: 1. Reject the opinion of those who think that polities were a human invention, and who feigned revelations from the goddess Egeria; the roots of polities are deeper. 2. Show God as the author, who implanted and preserved in nature the practical principles, so that just as reason rules the passions, so the wiser should rule in the state (see Cicero and Plato, on the laws). Hence the economies established under God's guidance under the first Patriarchs, under Melchizedek, and under Joseph. b. Through Moses he shaped an excellent commonwealth and ordered it with most holy laws. Here set out the constitution of the Jewish commonwealth under its various forms of government, and praise the civil law given by God through Moses by a certain general induction. Its successors, Joshua, the Judges and the Kings, who established the commonwealth according to this law, cultivated it; the prophets gave help. From here, show that all the wholesome institutions passed on to the Assyrians and Persians.

units.la: II. Progressum ostende sub Persis, ad quos postmodum summum impeImperium translatum. Horum instituta circa regiam institutionem describit Plato de Rep. Erudiebantur 1. In sapientia. 2. justitia, 3. temperantia, 4. fortitudine, a peritissimis. Vid. Xenoph. Cyropæd. lib. 1.
units.tr: II. Show the progress under the Persians, to whom the supreme rule was afterwards transferred. Plato, in the Republic, describes their institutions concerning the education of kings. They were trained 1. in wisdom, 2. in justice, 3. in temperance, 4. in courage, by the most skilled teachers. See Xenophon, Cyropaedia, book 1.

units.la: III. Ulteriorem perlustra propagationem sub Græcis, ubi florere cœpere liberæ resp. & doctrina politica. Ostendatur præcipue in Civitate Atheniensi & Lacedæmoniensi disciplina & legislatoribus illustribus. Præcipue hic ostendat Doctores Politices Atheniensiū. Primus Socrates fuit, qui civitatibus philosophiam intulit. Secutus hunc fuit Plato; vide libros ipsius de Rep. ubi proximè accedit ad Mosen. Tertius fuit Aristoteles, qui secus atque Plato, Deum in sua rep. oblitus est, de cætero prudens. Secuti sunt Xenocrates, Speusippus & præcipue Theophrastus, vid. Laërt.
units.tr: III. Trace the further spread under the Greeks, where free commonwealths and political learning began to flourish. Show this especially in the states of Athens and Sparta, with their discipline and their famous lawgivers. Here especially show the teachers of politics at Athens. The first was Socrates, who brought philosophy into the cities. Plato followed him; see his books on the Republic, where he comes nearest to Moses. The third was Aristotle, who, unlike Plato, forgot God in his commonwealth and was otherwise prudent. Xenocrates, Speusippus and above all Theophrastus followed; see Laertius.

units.la: IV. in Italia propagavit politiam & politicam Pythagoras, ejusq; discipuli: reliquiæ doctrinæ ipsorum passim videntur apud Laërtium &c. Hinc ad Romanos manavit doctrina politica, qui præxi ipsos Græcos superarunt. Vide Liv. ab initio & Val. Max. lib. 1. Vide & instituta primorum Regum, Consulum, Cæsaris & Augusti. Hinc Leges Romanas in XII. tabulis. & interpretibus contemplare. Hinc præceptis tradidit Cicero politicam lib. de Legg. Fiat comparatio memoratorum Legislatorum: Moses & Plato plurima de Deo, Aristoteles nihil, Cicero populi gusto accommodata.
units.tr: IV. Pythagoras and his disciples spread polity and politics in Italy; remnants of their teaching are found here and there in Laertius, etc. From here political learning passed to the Romans, who surpassed the Greeks themselves in practice. See Livy from the beginning and Valerius Maximus, book 1. See also the institutions of the first kings, consuls, Caesar and Augustus. From here consider the Roman laws in the Twelve Tables and their interpreters. From here Cicero handed down politics in precepts in his book On the Laws. Let a comparison be made of the lawgivers mentioned: Moses and Plato said very much about God; Aristotle nothing; Cicero adapted things to the taste of the people.

units.la: V. Passim hinc exstitere Doctores politici, in Legistas degenerantes, vide Pomponium de Orig. juris. Inde corruptio in Remp:
units.tr: V. From here teachers of politics arose on all sides, but they degenerated into lawyers; see Pomponius, On the Origin of Law. From this came corruption in the commonwealth.

units.la: VI. Justinianus Imperator restituit doctrinam politicam, & omissa diu in politicis divina humanis rursus conjunxit, non è scholæ latebis, sed ex medio imperii culmine politicam proponens. Secuti interpretes, Bartolus, Baldus, Jason, qui jura publica privatis junxerunt. Bartolus de regimine civitatum pueriliter licet conscripsit. Carolus Magnus arctiori vinculo sacra humanis junxit, Carolus IV. per auream bullam imperium formavit dexterrimè & stabili vinculo ex tribus quasi formis temperavit.
units.tr: VI. The Emperor Justinian restored political learning, and, having long left aside the divine things joined with the human in politics, he joined them again, setting forth politics not from the hiding places of the schools but from the very height of empire. Commentators followed: Bartolus, Baldus, Jason, who joined public law to private. Bartolus wrote on the government of cities, though somewhat childishly. Charlemagne joined sacred things to human with a closer bond. Charles IV formed the empire by the Golden Bull, most skilfully tempering it with a stable bond out of three forms, as it were.

units.la: Confutatio redarguat ex dictis illos,
units.tr: Refutation: let it refute from what has been said those who

units.la: 1. Qui politiæ administrationem ejusque disciplinam fidei adversam esse putant, uti sunt Anabaptistæ.
units.tr: 1. think that the administration of polity and its discipline are hostile to faith, as the Anabaptists do;

units.la: 2. Qui rem facilem & cuivis notam illam putant, adeoque præmaturo ambitu Remp. petunt.
units.tr: 2. think this matter easy and known to anyone, and so seek the commonwealth with premature ambition;

units.la: 3. Qui cum Machiavello aliisque pseudo-politicis vafritie ac dolis politicam, rem sanctissimam, inquinant.
units.tr: 3. with Machiavelli and other pseudo-politicians, defile politics, a most holy matter, with craft and deceit.

units.la: Conclus. Recollectis breviter argumentis 1. hortetur ad gratam providentiæ Divinæ recognitionem, quod politias constituit & salutaribus præceptis conservavit, nosq; in Rep. Christiana præsertim vivere velit. 2. Hortetur ad studium politicum, expuriffimis præsertim antiquorum fontibus hauriendum.
units.tr: Conclusion: Having briefly recalled the arguments: 1. let it urge a grateful acknowledgment of divine providence, which established commonwealths and preserved them by wholesome precepts, and which wishes us to live especially in the Christian commonwealth. 2. Let it urge the study of politics, to be drawn above all from the purest sources of the ancients.

units.la: III. TRACTATIO CHRIÆ.
units.tr: III. Treatment of the Chria.

units.la: Isocr. ad Demon. Σοφία μόνη των κτημάτων ἀθάνατον. Sola sapientia ex omnibus possessionibus immortale bonum est.
units.tr: Isocrates to Demonicus: Wisdom alone, of all possessions, is an immortal good. [Σοφία μόνη τῶν κτημάτων ἀθάνατον]

units.la: Oco exordii breviter commendetur lectio autorum: & in specie laudetur Isocrates, tum ob styli suavitatem, tum ob rerum ac sententiarum præstantiam. Inter alias referatur & brevi paraphrasi illustretur hæc sententia.
units.tr: In the exordium, the reading of authors is briefly commended, and Isocrates is especially praised both for the sweetness of his style and for the excellence of his matter and sentiments. Among other things, this saying is cited and briefly explained by a paraphrase.

units.la: Loco propositionis: verissimè hoc ab ipso dictum esse breviter testatur oftensururum pace auditorum.
units.tr: In place of the proposition, he briefly testifies that it was said most truly by him, and, with the audience's permission, will show it.

units.la: Loco confirmationis adferantur rationes.
units.tr: In place of the confirmation, reasons are offered.

units.la: I. à causa, quia animi bonum est sapientia. Uti igitur animus immortalis est, ita etiam bonum ejus. Maximè quia sapientia vera non ab homine, sed a Deo est, fonte omnis sapientiæ æterno: & æternos producit fructus, virtutem & famam.
units.tr: I. From the cause: because wisdom is a good of the soul. Therefore, just as the soul is immortal, so too is its good. Above all, because true wisdom comes not from man but from God, the eternal fount of all wisdom, and it produces eternal fruits, virtue and fame.

units.la: II. A contrario, seu diversis aliis bonis, vid. divitiis, voluptatibus, honoribus, quæ incerta & fugacia: Probetur breviter, experientiâ, exemplis, testimoniis.
units.tr: II. From the contrary, or from the other goods, namely riches, pleasures and honours, which are uncertain and fleeting. This is briefly proved by experience, examples and testimonies.

units.la: III. A simili, defumto a luce solis, quæ ingenita & perpetua est, lunæ contra mutuatitia & instabilis: ita sapientia animæ lumen. Ostendatur tamen etiam dissimilitudo: videlicet etiam ipsum solis lumen cessabit, at sapientia perpetua est.
units.tr: III. From a likeness, taken from the light of the sun, which is innate and perpetual, whereas the light of the moon is borrowed and unstable; so wisdom is the light of the soul. Yet the dissimilarity should also be shown: namely, that even the light of the sun will one day cease, but wisdom is perpetual.

units.la: IV. Ab exemplo sapientum ex gentibus & viris sanctiss. v. g. Bi-antis, Solomonis.
units.tr: IV. From the example of wise men among the Gentiles and of most holy men, for instance Bias and Solomon.

units.la: IV. A testimoniis sacris videlicet Prov. 8. & profanis. Concluf. Ex repetita propositione inferat adhortationem ad sapien—tiam, tum precibus, tum labore acquirendam.
units.tr: IV. From the sacred testimonies, namely Prov. 8, and from profane ones. Conclusion: from the repeated proposition he draws an exhortation to wisdom, to be acquired both by prayer and by labour.

units.la: IV. CHRIA.
units.tr: IV. CHRIA.

units.la: Curt. Nihil tam alte natura constituit quo virtus non possit eniti.
units.tr: Curt. Nothing has nature established so high that virtue cannot strive toward it.

units.la: Xord. Commendat dictum, ab autore Curtio, historico dignissimo & sententioso: ex quibus non postrema haec, quae repetenda & paraphrasi illustranda.
units.tr: Xord. The saying is commended: it comes from the author Curtius, a most worthy and sententious historian, from whose works this is not the least notable saying, and it is to be repeated and illustrated by paraphrase.

units.la: Propos. Hujus veritatem evincendam esse.
units.tr: Propos. Its truth is to be proved.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: I. A causa. 1. quia virtus originis & naturae caelestis est, reliqua vero omnia terrena, caduca, fragilia sunt. 2. Insuper in animo hominis sedem habet, qui mundi corporalis limitibus non continetur: multo minus virtus, quae animi perfectio.
units.tr: I. From the cause. (1) Because virtue is of heavenly origin and nature, whereas all other things are earthly, perishable and frail. (2) Moreover, it has its seat in the mind of man, which is not contained within the limits of the corporeal world; much less virtue, which is the perfection of the mind.

units.la: II. A contrario: vitio & animi vilitate; qua ad omnia ineptus homo redditur.
units.tr: II. From the contrary: from vice and baseness of spirit, by which man is rendered unfit for everything.

units.la: III. A simili, videlicet ab igne, qui non paleas tantum populatur, sed non cessat dum summa superarit aedium turriumque fastigia.
units.tr: III. From a likeness, namely from fire, which does not merely consume chaff but does not cease until it has risen over the summits of houses and towers.

units.la: IV. Ab exemplis illorum, qui coelorum altitudinem, marium profunditatem, siderum cursum, metallorum venas invenerunt. Deinde illorum, qui urbes, nationes, regna subegerunt, ut Alexandri, Romanorum.
units.tr: IV. From the examples of those who discovered the height of the heavens, the depth of the seas, the course of the stars, the veins of metals; then of those who subdued cities, nations and kingdoms, such as Alexander and the Romans.

units.la: V. A testimonio: Labor omnia vincit &c.
units.tr: V. From testimony: Labour conquers all things, etc.

units.la: Concluf. Verissime dictum a Curtio: inde ad studium virtutis cohortetur.
units.tr: Concl. Curtius has said most truly; hence he exhorts to the pursuit of virtue.

units.la: V. CHRIA REFUTANDA.
units.tr: V. A CHRIA TO BE REFUTED.

units.la: Ovid. Diciqve beatus ante obitum nemo, supremaque funera debet.
units.tr: Let no one be called happy before his death, and he must wait for his funeral rites.

units.la: Loco Exordii laudetur quidem autor, qvod doctus, qvod poeta; sed notetur simul animi festivitas & judicium minus solidum: unde & haec sententia, paraphrasi illustranda, & autori Soloni assignanda.
units.tr: In the Exordium the author may be praised, indeed, as learned and as a poet; but at the same time his cheerfulness of spirit and his rather unsound judgment should be noted. Hence this saying is to be illustrated by paraphrase and assigned to Solon.

units.la: Propos. Non recte dictum esse, licet multos habuerit adstipulatores. vid. Arist. 1. Eth. c. 10. & interpretes.
units.tr: Proposition. That it was not rightly said, although it has had many supporters. See Arist. 1. Eth. c. 10 and the commentators.

units.la: I. A cauConfutetur.
units.tr: I. From the cause: It is refuted.

units.la: I. A causa felicitatis, quae virtus est, cujus constantia praedicetur, etiam in omnium jactura.
units.tr: I. From the cause of happiness, which is virtue, whose constancy is praised even in the loss of all things.

units.la: II. A contraria infelicitate: quae in hac vita urget facinorosos etiam in media fortunae externae indulgentia. Vide Cic. in Parad:
units.tr: II. From the contrary unhappiness, which in this life afflicts the wicked even in the midst of external prosperity. See Cic. in Paradoxa.

units.la: III. A simili; sole qui lucidus dicitur, licet ob interpositionem lunae eclipsin quandoque patiatur, ita & felix, licet adversam aliquando fortunam sentiat, illam non posse turbare animum virtute munitum.
units.tr: III. From a likeness: the sun is called bright, though on account of the interposition of the moon it sometimes suffers an eclipse; so too the happy man, though he sometimes experiences adverse fortune, cannot disturb a mind fortified by virtue.

units.la: IV. Ab exemplo illorum, qui pro religione, pro patria patiuntur, ut martyres, Horatii, Reguli.
units.tr: IV. From the example of those who suffer for religion or for their country, such as the martyrs, the Horatii, and Regulus.

units.la: V. A Testimonio.
units.tr: V. From testimony.

units.la: Concluf. Male dici: ante obitum nemo beatus: Virtutem felicem reddere.
units.tr: Conclusion: It is wrongly said that no one is happy before death; virtue makes a person happy.

units.la: VI. CHRIA REFUTANDA.
units.tr: VI. A CHRIA TO BE REFUTED.

units.la: Juvenal, O cives, cives quaerenda pecunia primo est, Virtus post nummos.
units.tr: Juvenal: "O citizens, money must be sought first of all; virtue comes after money."

units.la: Loco exordii laudentur poetae, & in specie Juvenalis. Addatur cautio, multa ipsos non ex suo sensu, sed per mimesin dixisse: qualiter etiam hoc dictum sit, cujus sensum paraphrasi proponendum.
units.tr: In the place of the introduction the poets are to be praised, and Juvenal in particular. A caution should be added: the poets often said many things not from their own opinion but by way of imitation (mimesis); and so in this saying too the sense must be set out by paraphrase.

units.la: Propof. Pessime dictum esse.
units.tr: Proposition: that the saying is very badly put.

units.la: Confutatio.
units.tr: Refutation.

units.la: I. A Causa: quia opes instabiles & causa insolentiae, luxus, exitii multis. Ergo in iis non collocandum summum bonum.
units.tr: I. From the cause: because wealth is unstable, and is a cause of arrogance, luxury and ruin to many. Therefore the chief good is not to be placed in it.

units.la: II. A contraria inopia, quae non obstat, quo minus quis beatus sit: imo quae multis calcar fuit ad virtutem & felicitatem. Quomodo igitur divitiae tanquam summum bonum quaerendae?
units.tr: II. From the contrary, poverty, which does not stand in the way of a man being happy; indeed, to many it has been a spur to virtue and happiness. How then is wealth to be sought as the chief good?

units.la: III. A simili, uti viatoris, qui nimiis sarcinis se onerat, ineptus est ad iter; ita qui nimia opum cura.
units.tr: III. From a comparison: as a traveller who loads himself with too many burdens is unfit for the journey, so one who has too great a care for riches...

units.la: IV. Ab Exemplis divitum vitiosorum, inopum virtuosorum.
units.tr: IV. From the examples of wicked rich men and virtuous poor men.

units.la: V. A Testimoniis.
units.tr: V. From testimonies.

units.la: Concluf. Cavendum, ne cum vulgo erremus in constitutione summi boni. Fiat adhortatio ad quaerendum verum bonum.
units.tr: Conclusion: we must take care not to err with the common crowd in fixing the chief good. An exhortation should be made to seek the true good.

units.la: VII. SENTENTIA SENECÆ.
units.tr: VII. THE SAYING OF SENECA.

units.la: Sapientis animus supra lunam est, semper ibi serenum.
units.tr: The mind of the wise man is above the moon; there it is always clear.

units.la: Xord. A commendatione proverbiorum & sententiarum quòd veluti gemmulæ sint, in quibus tota linguæ ac sapientiæ vis inclusa. Applicetur ad hypothesin; & sensus exponatur paraphrasi.
units.tr: Exordium: On the commendation of proverbs and maxims, that they are like little gems, in which the whole force of language and wisdom is enclosed. Let it be applied to the hypothesis, and the sense be explained by paraphrase.

units.la: Propos̃it. Veritatem dicti breviter evincendam esse.
units.tr: Proposition: The truth of the saying is to be shown briefly.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. A causa: quia sapientia domat affectus, qui mentem obnubilant & turbant: Amplif. inductione præcipuorum affectuum, quorum vis ostendatur.
units.tr: I. From the cause: because wisdom subdues the passions, which cloud and disturb the mind. Amplification: by an induction of the principal passions, whose force is shown.

units.la: II. A contraria insipientia, cujus perversitas & perturbatio per hypotyposin hominis bardi & bruti explicetur.
units.tr: II. From the contrary, folly, whose perversity and disturbance is explained by a description of the foolish and brutish man.

units.la: III. A simili, ab aere nubibus & ventis turbido, cui similis animus hominis inculti; huic opponatur purus æter super lunæ orbitam: cui similis animus sapientis.
units.tr: III. From a likeness: from the air, turbid with clouds and winds, to which the mind of the uneducated man is like. Set against this the pure ether above the orbit of the moon, to which the mind of the wise man is like.

units.la: IV. Ab exemplis Socratis, Platonis.
units.tr: IV. From the examples of Socrates and Plato.

units.la: V. A Testimoniis.
units.tr: V. From testimonies.

units.la: Conclus. Hortetur ad sapientiam & subactionem affectuum, unde animi tranquillitas.
units.tr: Conclusion: it exhorts to wisdom and to the subduing of the passions, whence comes tranquillity of mind.

units.la: VIII. TRACTATIO LEGIS LYCURGI.
units.tr: VIII. A DISCUSSION OF THE LAW OF LYCURGUS.

units.la: Juniores in patrias leges ne inquirant.
units.tr: Younger men should not inquire into the laws of their country.

units.la: Exordii loco commendetur Lycurgus tum a prudentia, tum à legibus salutaribus, quibus Spartam, quibus deinceps Cretam Insulam formarit. In specie referatur lex ejusque sensus applicetur, quòd noluerit leges patrias sub censuram vocari à Junioribus.
units.tr: As an introduction, Lycurgus is to be commended both for his prudence and for the salutary laws by which he shaped Sparta and afterward the island of Crete. Specifically, the law is to be cited and its meaning applied: that he did not want the laws of the fatherland to be called into question by the younger men.

units.la: Propos. Approbetur hæc lex tanquam æquissima.
units.tr: Proposition. This law is to be approved as most equitable.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. A Causa Legis, necessaria scil. legum autoritate: quæ evilescit, si quorumvis judicio obnoxiæ sint. Exegesis à curiositate juniorum, quæ libenter carpit, quæ non capit. Illustretur opposita autoautoritate Legislatorum: quæ a nemine subditorum disputari debet, si leges salvæ esse debeant. Conclusio. Ergo rectè lata lex hæc.
units.tr: I. From the cause of the law, namely the necessary authority of laws, which is weakened if they are subject to the judgment of anyone at all. Explanation: from the curiosity of the young, which readily carps at what it does not understand. Let the opposing authority of the lawgivers be illustrated: it ought not to be disputed by any of the subjects, if laws are to remain intact. Conclusion. Therefore this law was rightly enacted.

units.la: 2. Ab exemplo Dei summi legislatoris; qui obedientiam exegit à populo suo, non censuram. Hujus gerere vices in terris legislatores & magistratus.
units.tr: 2. From the example of God, the supreme lawgiver, who required obedience from his people, not criticism. Lawgivers and magistrates bear his office on earth.

units.la: Confutatio.
units.tr: Refutation.

units.la: Objectionum. 1. Legem omnem niti debere ratione; quam utique inquirere licet. Resp. a. Licet, sed ad stabiliendam, non ad labefactandam legis autoritatem. b. Non à junioribus, qui fundamenta Reip. nondum intelligunt. 2. Subditos non obligari ad cæcam obedientiam. Resp. Nec hanc exigi hac lege: sed imperari modestiam, ne privati sibi arrogent illud, quod magistratus est.
units.tr: Of the objections. 1. Every law ought to rest on reason, and reason may certainly be inquired into. Reply: (a) It is permitted, but to establish the authority of the law, not to undermine it. (b) Not by the young, who do not yet understand the foundations of the commonwealth. 2. Subjects are not bound to blind obedience. Reply: This law does not demand such obedience; it enjoins only modesty, lest private persons arrogate to themselves what belongs to the magistrate.

units.la: Conclusio. Laudet legem hanc, & subditos, maximè juniores, hortetur ad obedientiam legibus præstandam.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him commend this law, and exhort the subjects, especially the younger ones, to render obedience to the laws.

units.la: IX. EXAMEN LEGIS LYCURGI, QUA MERCATURAM ET PEREGRINATIONEM PROHIBUIT.
units.tr: IX. An Examination of the Law of Lycurgus, by Which He Forbade Trade and Foreign Travel.

units.la: Exordium. Laudet legislatores gentiles, inter cæteros Solonem & Lycurgum, verùm notet in illis omnibus commune vitium erroris humani, quod etiam Lycurgo usu venerit in multis suis legibus. Ut in specie in lege, qua mercaturam & peregrinationes prohibuit.
units.tr: Exordium. Let him praise the pagan lawgivers, among the rest Solon and Lycurgus; but let him note in all of them the common fault of human error, which also befell Lycurgus in many of his laws. Specifically, in the law by which he forbade trade and journeys abroad.

units.la: Propos. Minimè probandam esse legem hanc; id quod evincendum.
units.tr: Proposition. That this law is by no means to be approved; which is to be demonstrated.

units.la: Tractatio. Nullam idoneam legis hujus esse rationem. 1. Hic ostendat primò animam legis rationem esse. Deinde hujus legis nullam esse rationem. Nam si dicat, luxum invehi per communicationem cum peregrinis. Resp. Fieri hoc per accidens; prohibenda esse vitia, non tollendam rem per se licitam. Urge Lycurgum per instantiam, eodem jure tollendam esse omnem societatem, usum vini &c. quod absurdum.
units.tr: Treatment. That there is no sound rationale for this law. 1. Here he should show, first, what the soul of the law's rationale is; then that this law has no rationale at all. For if someone says that luxury is introduced through communication with foreigners: the reply is that this happens only incidentally; vices are to be forbidden, not a thing that is lawful in itself to be abolished. Press Lycurgus with an instance: by the same right every society would have to be abolished, the use of wine, and so on, which is absurd.

units.la: 2. Sufficere quamlibet terram alendis incolis & formandis moribus. Resp. Miseram esse vitam, si ad necessitatem semper reducta sit; Deum junxisse populos per necessitatem.
units.tr: 2. It is said that any land is sufficient to feed its inhabitants and form their morals. Reply: it would be a wretched life if it were always reduced to necessity; God has joined peoples together through necessity.

units.la: II. Proferat rationes in contrarium. Videlicet.
units.tr: II. Let him set out the reasons to the contrary. Namely:

units.la: 1. Mercaturam utilem. a. in apportandis & exportandis rebus necessariis & superfluis. Amplificetur expositione indigentiæ locorum, quæ aliunde supplenda. b. augendo ærario. c. in occupanda hominum industria.
units.tr: 1. Trade is useful: a. in bringing in and sending out both necessary and superfluous goods. This is to be amplified by an explanation of the needs of places, which must be supplied from elsewhere. b. by increasing the public treasury. c. in employing people's industry.

units.la: 2. Peregrinationem utilem esse. a. moribus formandis, b. ad discendam politicam & leges. Probetur exemplis: verbi gratia Romanorum, qui Athenis petierint Leges. c. ad cognoscendam Dei potentiam & sapientiam. Illustretur oppositione hominis, qui peregrinatus est, & qui nunquam egressus est limen patrium.
units.tr: 2. Foreign travel is useful: a. for forming morals; b. for learning politics and the laws. This is to be proved by examples, for instance that of the Romans, who sought laws at Athens. c. for knowing the power and wisdom of God. This is to be illustrated by contrasting the man who has travelled abroad with the man who never went beyond his native threshold.

units.la: Conclusio. Minimè igitur probandam hanc legem; cum monela, ut caute imitemur instituta aliorum. Solam legem Dei sanctam & perfectam esse.
units.tr: Conclusion. Therefore this law is by no means to be approved; with the warning that we should imitate the institutions of others with caution. Only the law of God is holy and perfect.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Chria examinans illud Cæsaris.
units.tr: A chria examining that saying of Caesar's.

units.la: SI VIOLANDUM EST JUS, REGNANDI GRATIA VIOLANDUM EST, IN CÆTERIS PIETATEM COLAS.
units.tr: IF RIGHT MUST BE VIOLATED, IT MUST BE VIOLATED FOR THE SAKE OF RULING; IN OTHER THINGS, CULTIVATE PIETY.

units.la: Affirmative.
units.tr: Affirmative.

units.la: A. Proponatur dictum cum brevi commendatione Autoris, paraphrasi, & approbatione.
units.tr: A. The saying is to be put forward, with a brief commendation of its author, a paraphrase, and an approval.

units.la: B. Adducantur rationes ex consideratione consequentis, imperii scil. ac dignitatis; cujus tantus splendor est.
units.tr: B. Reasons are to be adduced from the consequence, namely of the rule and its dignity, whose splendour is so great.

units.la: I. A causa, quæ est a. Deus, qui hunc veluti radium suæ gloriæ homini communicavit. Expoliatur descriptione imperii Dei in mundum superum, inferum; & communicatione cum homine, quoad mundum inferiorem ipsumque hominem. b. Eminentia virtutum omnis generis, quibus fit ut homo hominī veluti Deus præmineat ac imperet. Illustretur hypotypos hominis excellentis & abjecti ac neglecti.
units.tr: I. From the cause, which is (a) God, who imparted this as it were a ray of his glory to man. It is embellished by a description of God's rule over the upper and lower world, and by his communication with man, as regards the lower world and man himself. (b) The eminence of virtues of every kind, by which it comes about that man excels and commands other men as if he were a god. Let the portrait of the excellent man, and of the abject and neglected man, be set forth to illustrate this.

units.la: II. Ab effectis imperii; uti sunt a. autoritas & imperandi & licentius vivendi, quo nihil dulcius. b. Honor, amplificetur distributione: videlicet in patria, extra illam; in vita, post vitam. Illustretur contrario. c. opes; illustretur similí à capite, quò omnis vis spirituum, & stomacho, quò omnes cibi deferuntur. d. Abblanditio omnium etiam inimicorum.
units.tr: II. From the effects of rule: (a) authority, both to command and to live more freely, than which nothing is sweeter. (b) Honour, which is amplified by its distribution: namely in one's homeland and outside it, in life and after life. Let it be illustrated by the contrary. (c) Wealth; let it be illustrated by a likeness: from the head, to which all the power of the spirits is sent, and from the stomach, to which all food is carried. (d) The flattery of all, even of enemies.

units.la: III. A Contrario vita privata; ubi omnia superiora secus se habent.
units.tr: III. From the contrary, private life, where all the higher things are otherwise.

units.la: IV. A Simili, Sole, qui exortus non modò omnem reliquorum astrorum obfuscat gloriam; verùm & ita perstringit oculos, ut alia objecta penitus non, aut luce colorata videant. Ita imperii fulgor &c. A Minori, auri splendor, divitiarum amor, ita mentem sæpe occupant, ut alia omnia susque deque habeant <bl>φιλαςγυροι</bl>. Multò magis imperium.
units.tr: IV. From a likeness, the Sun, which, when it rises, not only obscures the glory of all the other stars but so dazzles the eyes that people see other objects not at all, or only tinged with its light. So the splendour of rule, etc. From the lesser, the splendour of gold: the love of riches so often occupies the mind that it holds everything else of no account, <bl>φιλαςγυροι</bl> [lovers of silver]. Much more so rule.

units.la: V. Ab Exemplis, Testimoniis.
units.tr: V. From examples and testimonies.

units.la: VI. Concludatur approbatione effati Cæsaris.
units.tr: VI. The conclusion is drawn by approval of the saying of Caesar.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: IDEM THEMA NEGATIVE.
units.tr: THE SAME THESIS, NEGATIVE.

units.la: A. Accessus per comparationem generalem dictorum factorumque magnatum. Non omnia quæ à magnis dicuntur, illico oracula sunt, uti nec facta ipsorum semper miracula. Ita minimè approbandum illud Cæsarris. Si violandum est jus Reip. &c.
units.tr: A. Access through a general comparison of the sayings and deeds of great men. Not everything that great men say is at once an oracle, just as their deeds are not always miracles. Thus that saying of Caesar's, "If the law of the commonwealth must be violated, etc.," is by no means to be approved.

units.la: B. Rationes ex consideratione antecedentis & consequentis simul, videlicet. violare jus & imperium.
units.tr: B. Reasons drawn from considering the antecedent and the consequent together, namely: "to violate law and rule."

units.la: I. A natura justitiæ inviolabili. Quod probatur.
units.tr: I. From the inviolable nature of justice. This is proved as follows.

units.la: A causa efficiente justitiæ Deo, qui illam lege sancivit & menti ceu perpetuam regulam actionum impressit. Illustretur comparatione minorum, cum statuto regis aut Reip.
units.tr: The efficient cause of justice is God, who sanctioned it by law and impressed it on the mind as a perpetual rule of action. Let this be illustrated by comparison with lesser things, such as a statute of a king or of the commonwealth.

units.la: A fine justitiæ, qui est præservare omnia à violatione. Amplificetur hoc inductione summorum, infimorum magistratuum, subditorum, ipsiusque adeo sceptri, coronæ, corporum, bonorum, quæ non nisi jure conservantur ac justitia. Turpe igitur violare illud propter imperium, propter quod institutum est imperium.
units.tr: The end of justice is to preserve all things from violation. Let this be amplified by induction from the highest and lowest magistrates, the subjects, and indeed the sceptre, the crown, the persons, and the goods, all of which are preserved only by law and justice. It is therefore base to violate justice for the sake of rule, since rule was instituted for the sake of justice.

units.la: II. A distributione juris: Est enim jus divinum, humanum: & hoc rursum, naturale, gentium, civile. Nulla species violari potest sine scelere: Ostendatur per inductionem.
units.tr: II. From the division of law. There is divine law and human law, and the latter again is natural, of nations, or civil. No kind of law can be violated without wickedness. Let this be shown by induction.

units.la: III. A natura imperii, quæ apparet Ex fine ejusdem, videlicet conservatione humanæ societatis per administrationem justitiæ. Illustretur 1. a causa efficiente imperiorum secundaria: vid. fiducia justitiæ ac integritatis quæ fecit ut certis personis imperium deferretur. Probetur testimoniis Justini aliorumque. 2. Inductione functionum imperialium, quæ omnes huc tendunt. IV. A Natura injustitiæ, quæ est causa destruens imperiorum præcipua. Hoc probetur exemplis, dictis.
units.tr: III. From the nature of rule, which appears from its end, namely the preservation of human society through the administration of justice. Let this be illustrated, first, from the secondary efficient cause of rulers, that is, the trust in justice and integrity which caused rule to be committed to certain persons; let it be proved by the testimonies of Justin and others. Second, by induction from the functions of rulers, all of which aim at this end. IV. From the nature of injustice, which is the chief destructive cause of empires. Let this be proved by examples and sayings.

units.la: V. A Comparatione
units.tr: V. From comparison.

units.la: a. Similium: a gangrena, phtisi, intemperantia, quæ vastant sanitatem; ita & injustitia regum.
units.tr: a. With like things: as gangrene, phthisis and intemperance lay waste health, so does the injustice of kings.

units.la: b. Minorum, si eodem autore Cæsare, nulla res est ob quam violare jus debemus; quanto minus pro imperio: quippe quod viri cordati etiam detrectarunt, & quod ob justitiæ administrationem institutum est.
units.tr: b. With lesser things: if, on Caesar's own authority, there is no cause for which we ought to violate law, then much less for the sake of rule, which men of sound judgement have even refused, and which was instituted for the administration of justice.

units.la: VI. Conclusio improbet dictum Cæsaris, & ad saniora hortetur.
units.tr: VI. The conclusion should reject Caesar's saying and exhort to saner counsels.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Plin. in panegyr. NEC PROVOCES BELLA, NEC TIMEAS.
units.tr: Pliny, in the Panegyric: "Do not provoke wars, and do not fear them."

units.la: 1. Assertive pro parte priore. Affectus intendatur, metus belli.
units.tr: 1. Assertive, for the first part. The emotion is to be heightened: fear of war.

units.la: A. Præmissa commendatione Autoris, approbetur dictum, & brevi illustretur paraphrasi, in specie laudetur pars prior.
units.tr: A. After a commendation of the author, the saying is approved and briefly illustrated by a paraphrase; the first part is especially praised.

units.la: B. Afferantur rationes assertionis.
units.tr: B. Reasons for the assertion are to be given.

units.la: I. A causa: Quia dubia est belli alea, ubi nec temere spes concipienda, aut desponcendus animus; Prob. 1. Ratione, quia omnia ex fortuna pendent 2. Experientia & exemplo unoatque altero, ut Annibalis, Xerxis.
units.tr: I. From the cause: because the outcome of war is uncertain, so that hope should not be rashly conceived nor courage given up. It is proved (1) by reason, because all things depend on fortune; (2) by experience and example, one or two, such as Hannibal and Xerxes.

units.la: II. Ab effectis belli, quæ illustrentur comparatione cum effectis victoriæ, ut pateat majus semper periculum metuendum ex bello, quam concipiendam spem ex victoria.
units.tr: II. From the effects of war, illustrated by comparison with the effects of victory, so that it is clear that a greater danger is always to be feared from war than hope is to be conceived from victory.

units.la: III. A contraria temeritate ac arrogantia, quæ plerumque maximorum malorum causæ. Probetur 1. ratione: quia judicium obnubilant, affectus turbant, unde turbida & inauspicata consilia, tristes eventus. 2. Exemplo Xerxis temere moventis contra Græciam; Sennacheribi, superbe minitantis Hierosolymis.
units.tr: III. From the opposite, rashness and arrogance, which are very often the causes of the greatest evils. It is proved (1) by reason: because they cloud judgment and disturb the emotions, whence come turbid and ill-omened counsels and sad outcomes; (2) by the example of Xerxes, who rashly moved against Greece, and of Sennacherib, who proudly threatened Jerusalem.

units.la: IV. A comparatis, 1. minoribus, processibus, pugnis, rixis, quibus prudens non temere se miscet. 2. Simili a brutis, quæ non temere certamina ineunt, nisi aut fame, aut necessitate compulsa.
units.tr: IV. From comparisons: (1) with lesser things, such as brawls, fights and quarrels, into which a prudent man does not rashly throw himself; (2) with a similar case from brute animals, which do not rashly begin contests unless driven by hunger or necessity.

units.la: V. Ab exemplis Joasi regis Israelitarum: qui Amasiam superbe & sine causa bellum inferentem, dehortatus est ab armis. 2. Chron. 14.
units.tr: V. From the example of Joash, king of Israel, who dissuaded Amaziah from arms when he waged war proudly and without cause. (2) Chron. 14.

units.la: VI. TeVI. A testimoniis. C. Conclusio approbans effatum Plinii & a temerariis armis dehortans.
units.tr: VI. From testimonies. C. The conclusion, approving Pliny's saying and dissuading from rash arms.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Assertivè pro parte secunda. Affectus intendatur, siducia.
units.tr: Assertively for the second part: that the affect be strengthened, confidence.

units.la: A. Acceslus: injuriam fieri Autori, cum dicta ipsius mutilatè accipiuntur. Dehortari quidem Plinium a bellis temerariis, at eundem & cohortari ad necessaria, quod ex sensu verborum patet, quæ posteriora verba æque atque priora observatu digna.
units.tr: A. An objection: injury is done to the Author when his words are taken in a mutilated way. Plinius does indeed dissuade from rash wars, but he also exhorts to necessary ones, as is clear from the sense of the words; the latter words are just as worthy of observation as the former.

units.la: B. Hoc probetur.
units.tr: B. Let this be proved.

units.la: I. A causa. incidere enim sæpe tempora, ut arma ab ipsis legibus porrigi videantur. Amplificetur per inductionem causarum belli, uti sunt violenta invasio, recuperatio ablatorum, sames Regni & Reip.
units.tr: I. From the cause. For times often arise when arms seem to be offered by the very laws themselves. Let this be amplified by an induction of the causes of war, such as violent invasion, the recovery of what has been taken away, and the hunger of the kingdom and commonwealth.

units.la: II. Ab effecto belli, pace & incolumitate Reipubl: Illustretur comparatione cum malis & cladibus, quas secum trahit bellum, hæcce temporalia, illam perpetuam esse. Digressiuncula in laudem pacis armis acquisitam, quæ stabilior illâ, quam veluti gratuito quis habet.
units.tr: II. From the effect of war, peace and the safety of the commonwealth. Let it be illustrated by comparison with the evils and calamities that war brings in its train: these are temporary, whereas peace is perpetual. A short digression in praise of peace won by arms, which is more stable than that which one has as if freely given.

units.la: III. A contrario: nimia meticulositate, quæ principi & Reipubl. probrosa & damnosa fit. Illustretur ab effectis, hinc enim crescere animos hostibus, etiam alioquin imbecillibus.
units.tr: III. From the contrary: excessive timidity, which becomes disgraceful and harmful to the prince and the commonwealth. Let it be illustrated from its effects: for hence the spirits of enemies grow, even of those otherwise weak.

units.la: IV. A comparatis. Qui injurias suffert, lites metuit, omnium præda est, in vita privata: jam quod lites inter privatos, hoc bella esse inter respublicas. Bruta animantia etiam imbecillia cubilia sua, aviculæ nidos, omnia vitam ac esse tuentur.
units.tr: IV. From comparisons. He who suffers injuries fears lawsuits and is everyone's prey in private life; now as lawsuits are between private persons, so wars are between commonwealths. Even brute animals, even the weak ones, defend their lairs, little birds their nests; all things guard their life and their being.

units.la: V. Ab Exemplo Græcorum, qui duce Pausania exiguis copiis Xerxis exercitum suderunt; Romanorum, qui toties ab Annibale cæsi, animum non desponderunt.
units.tr: V. From the example of the Greeks, who under the leadership of Pausanias defeated the army of Xerxes with small forces; and of the Romans, who, though so often slaughtered by Hannibal, did not lose heart.

units.la: VI. A testimoniis & adagiis.
units.tr: VI. From testimonies and proverbs.

units.la: C. Conclusio utramque partem effati approbans, & ad fiduciam cohortans.
units.tr: C. Conclusion approving both parts of the saying, and exhorting to confidence.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: INTERPRETATIO LEGIS REGIÆ ex 1. Sam.8. v.11. & seqq. Qua adstruitur fuisse Legem illam jus aliquod à Rege sibi arrogatum & usurpatum.
units.tr: THE INTERPRETATION OF THE ROYAL LAW, from 1 Sam. 8. v. 11 and following, in which it is maintained that this law was a certain right arrogated and usurped by the king for himself.

units.la: A. Exordium. Salutares quidem sunt leges, at noxia interpretum contorsio legem flectentium pro lubitu, imò pravos principum mores pro lege accipientium. Idem hic usu venit.
units.tr: A. Introduction. Laws are indeed salutary, but the harmful twisting of them by interpreters, who bend the law as they please, or even take the depraved customs of princes for law, is a fault. The same thing happens here.

units.la: B, Propositio. De cujus sensu proinde disquirendum.
units.tr: B. Proposition. Therefore its meaning must be investigated.

units.la: C. Expositio: hic,
units.tr: C. Exposition, in which:

units.la: I. Repetatur lex ex 1. Sam. 8. v. 11. & seqq.
units.tr: I. The law is to be repeated from 1 Sam. 8. v. 11 and following.

units.la: II. Per brevem & analyticam interpretationem ostendatur ejus sensus & rigor, & discrepantes de illa interpretum theologorum & politicorum sententiæ; quæ eò tandem recidunt, quòd alii Legem regni statuant divinitus approbatam; alii jus aliquod à Rege sibi arrogatum & usurpatum.
units.tr: II. Its meaning and force are to be shown by a brief and analytical interpretation, along with the differing opinions of theologians and political writers about it. These come down in the end to this: some hold that the law of the kingdom was approved by God, while others hold that it was a certain right arrogated and usurped by the king for himself.

units.la: D. Confirmatio adstruat sententiam posteriorem, nempe Legem Regiam esse jus aliquod à Rege sibi arrogatum & usurpatum.
units.tr: D. Confirmation, to establish the latter opinion, namely that the royal law was a certain right arrogated and usurped by the king.

units.la: a. a Nomine, quia non dicitur Lex, sed judicium seu ratio & consuetudo regis dominaturi.
units.tr: a. From the name: it is not called a law but a judgment, or the custom and claim of a king who is going to rule.

units.la: b. a causa hujus legis, importuna populi postulatio quæ fuit ac indignatio: non consilium Samuelis, non gratia Dei. Probetur α quia Samuel gravissime dehortatus est populum ab hoc propósito. β. Deus ipse dicit se rejectum a populo, ne ipse imperet. γ. Quia apud Hoseam Deus dicit, se dedisse ipsis Regem in ira sua.
units.tr: b. From the cause of this law: the importunate demand of the people, which was born of discontent and indignation, not the counsel of Samuel or the grace of God. This is proved: α, because Samuel most earnestly dissuaded the people from this purpose; β, because God himself says that he had been rejected by the people, so that he should not rule over them; γ, because in Hosea God says that he gave them a king in his anger.

units.la: c. Ab effecto: exercitio ejus, quia operatura erat quiritationem populi & aversionem precum ipsius. Hoc autem non solet consequi observantiam præceptorum Dei: quod probatur promissionibus contrariis.
units.tr: c. From the effect, namely its exercise, since it was going to produce the murmuring of the people and the turning away of their prayers. This, however, does not usually follow from the observance of God's precepts, as is shown by the contrary promises.

units.la: d. a diversa praxi: quia ipsi Reges eo jure non potuerunt nec ausi fuerunt semper eo uti. Probetur exemplis Rehabeami, a quo discessere 10. tribus, cum onus minitaretur; & Achabi, qui non nisi per mendacia uxoris potiri potuit vinea Naboti.
units.tr: d. From the different practice: because the kings themselves could not, and did not dare, always to use that right. Let it be proved by the examples of Rehoboam, from whom ten tribes fell away when he threatened a heavier burden, and of Ahab, who could gain Naboth's vineyard only through his wife's lies.

units.la: e.
units.tr: e.

units.la: A forma ipsa legis hujus; quæ fuit conformitas cum reliquis gentibus, quod Judæi quidem intellexerunt tantùm de autoritate regis in judiciis & bellis: verùm Deus in vindictam prædixit etiam de violentia & rapinis: Jam Deus populum suum dissimillimum in omnibus voluit esse reliquis gentibus. Ergo hæc non est Dei lex, sed comminatio.
units.tr: From the very form of this law, which was a conformity with the other nations. The Jews indeed understood it only of the king's authority in judgments and wars, but God foretold in punishment that it would also involve violence and plunder. Now God wanted his people to be wholly unlike the other nations in all things. Therefore this is not the law of God but a warning.

units.la: A dissonantia à vera lege Regia, quæ ostendatur collatione hujus legis & Deut.17.
units.tr: From its disagreement with the true royal law, which is shown by comparing this law with Deut. 17.

units.la: Vindicetur ab objectionibus.
units.tr: It is defended against objections.

units.la: Jus dicitur regis. Resp. Non divinitus approbatum, à Rege usurpandum, à Deo non impediendum.
units.tr: It is said to be the king's right. Reply: it was not approved by God, it was to be assumed by the king, and it was not to be hindered by God.

units.la: Dicitur hoc jus conforme omnium gentium juri; Ergo saltem juris gentium est adeoque à Deo; Resp. juris gentium est, quoad Δικαιολογίαν & πρατηγωγίαν; non quoad violentiam, uti ab adulatoribus regum illud allegari solet.
units.tr: It is said that this right agrees with the law of all nations; therefore it is at least a law of nations, and so from God. Reply: it is a law of nations as regards the pleading of right [δικαιολογίαν] and the conduct of affairs [πρατηγωγίαν], but not as regards violence, which is the point that flatterers of kings usually allege.

units.la: Dicitur quod Deus non audiat clamantes contra hoc jus. Ergo jus est, non oppressio. Resp. Imò vero pœna est, quam intempestiva populus flagitatione sibi accersiverat.
units.tr: It is said that God does not hear those who cry out against this right. Therefore it is a right, not an oppression. Reply: indeed it is rather a punishment, which the people had brought upon themselves by their ill-timed demand.

units.la: Conclusio. quæ genuinam legis sententiam repetat, Reges à violentia, populum à pruritu novitatis dehortetur & ad præsentium amorem cohortetur.
units.tr: Conclusion: which restates the genuine sense of the law, warns kings against violence, and exhorts the people to love of the present state, away from the itch for novelty.

units.la: XV. INTERPRETATIO EJUSDEM LEGIS REGIÆ, QUA ADSTRUITUR FUISSE LEGEM REGNI DIVINITUS TRADITAM ET APPROBATAM.
units.tr: XV. THE INTERPRETATION OF THIS SAME ROYAL LAW, BY WHICH IT IS SHOWN THAT THE LAW OF THE KINGDOM WAS DIVINELY DELIVERED AND APPROVED.

units.la: Exordium, à sententia Aristotelis: In Legibus salus est Reipubl. Probetur.
units.tr: Introduction, from the saying of Aristotle: "In laws lies the safety of the commonwealth." Let this be proved.

units.la: à causa: malitia hominum, quæ illustretur à comparatis, quæ tanta sit ut vix legibus contineri queat, nedum sine iis.
units.tr: From the cause: the wickedness of men, to be illustrated by comparisons, which is so great that it can scarcely be restrained by laws, let alone without them.

units.la: Exemplo ipsius Dei, qui Remp. Judaicam exemplar reliquarum Legibus ipse disposuit. Inter illas maximè memorabilis & vexata est, quam de ipso rege publicavit.
units.tr: By the example of God himself, who arranged the Jewish commonwealth by laws as the model for the rest. Among these the most memorable and the most disputed is the one he promulgated concerning the king himself.

units.la: Disquirendum ergo de ejus genuino sensu contra antecessorem.
units.tr: Its genuine sense must therefore be investigated, against the opinion of his predecessors.

units.la: Repetatur lex ex 1.Sam.8. v.11. & seqq.
units.tr: Let the law be repeated from 1 Sam. 8, v. 11 and following.

units.la: Expositio, hic
units.tr: Exposition, here.

units.la: I. Repetatur Lex ex 1.Sam.8. v.11. & seqq.
units.tr: I. Let the law be repeated from 1Sam.8. v.11. and following.

units.la: II. Ostendatur ejus autor & ferendæ occasio, senium Samuelis, & iniquitas filiorum Samuelis, postulatio populi, cui hoc jus integrum videatur relictum Deut.17. v.15.
units.tr: II. Let its author and the occasion for enacting it be shown: the old age of Samuel, the wickedness of Samuel's sons, and the demand of the people, to which this right seems to have been left entire, Deut. 17 v. 15.

units.la: Sententia, scilicet quod regi tradat absolutam potestatem, populum obliget ad puram obedientiam,
units.tr: The sense, namely that it gives the king absolute power and binds the people to unqualified obedience.

units.la: Interpretum Theologorum & Politicorum circa hanc legis sententiam divortium: dum alii jus statuunt aliquod a Rege sibi arrogatum & usurpatum; alii Legem Regni divinitus traditam & approbatam.
units.tr: Theologians and political writers are divided over this sense of the law: some hold that it is a right claimed and usurped by the king for himself; others hold that it is the law of the kingdom, divinely delivered and approved.

units.la: III. Eligatur sententia posterior & astruatur,
units.tr: III. The latter opinion is to be chosen and established.

units.la: A nomine: Lex dicitur & judicium. Ergo in jure fundata est, & ad observantiam obligat; non usurpatio, quæ iniquitas audit, & legis est violatio, nec hoc nominis meretur.
units.tr: From the name: the law is called both a law and a judgment. Therefore it is grounded in right and obliges to observance. It is not usurpation, which is called iniquity and is a violation of law, and does not deserve this name.

units.la: A Causa hujus legis.
units.tr: From the cause of this law.

units.la: Προκαταρκτικὴ [?] quæ fuit populi petitio. Ipse verò non petiit tyrannum & usurpatorem, sed Regem qui ipsum judicet & educat in prælium, instar omnium gentium. Ergo tale est jus Regum, quale hic describitur.
units.tr: The preliminary point [Προκαταρκτικὴ] was the people's petition. But he himself did not ask for a tyrant and usurper, but for a king who would judge them and lead them out to battle, like all the nations. Therefore the right of kings is of the kind described here.

units.la: Primaria Deo: qui hoc populi votum approbavit, & tali potestati Regiæ ipsum subjecit, neutiquam suo suffragio iniquam potestatem approbaturus. Locus communis, de Legum Dei sanctitate inviolabili, licet duræ videantur. Illustretur comparatione, cum aliis legibus humanis. Prolepf. Deus aliam dederat legem Regiam. Deut. 17. Resp. Populo volente in hanc posteriorem consenserat. Lex v. posterior derogat priori. Deus aliis dat leges,non sibi eripit mutandi potestatem: &c.
units.tr: Primarily from God, who approved this wish of the people and subjected them to such royal power, never intending by his own vote to approve an unjust power. A common topic: on the inviolable holiness of God's laws, even if they seem harsh. Let it be illustrated by comparison with other human laws. Prolepsis. God had given another royal law, Deut. 17. Reply: when the people willed it, he had agreed to this later one. A later law repeals an earlier one. God gives laws to others; he does not snatch from himself the power to change them, etc.

units.la: A natura omnis Regni: quæ in eo est, ut sit aliqua potestas suprema, cui nemo queat resistere. 1. Illustretur à contrario sensu confusio, rebellio; si populus arbiter esset statutorum regiorum. Probetur inductione regnorum & testimonio Aristot: 3. Politic: ubi ultimam speciem regni μεταβασιλείαν dicit. Locus communis addatur. Laus monarchiæ absolutæ.
units.tr: From the nature of every kingdom, which consists in there being some supreme power that no one can resist. 1. Let confusion and rebellion be illustrated from the contrary sense: if the people were the judge of royal statutes. Let it be proved by induction from kingdoms and by the testimony of Aristotle in Politics book 3, where he calls the last species of kingship "metabasileia" [μεταβασιλεία]. Add a common topic. Praise of absolute monarchy.

units.la: Ab irrito conatu contradicentium. Videlicet clamabitis, sed non exaudiam vos. Ratio: quia non audit Deus clamantes contra legitimam potestatem, anditurus contra tyrannum.
units.tr: From the fruitless attempt of those who contradict. Namely: "You will cry out, but I will not hear you." Reason: God does not hear those who cry out against lawful power, but he will hear those who cry out against a tyrant.

units.la: d. A praxi c. A praxi regum. Saul egit pro lubitu impiè sæpe, tamen occidere ipsum noluit David. David, Tibi soli peccavi, dixit. Ergo non tenebatur reddere rationem populo. Salomon intolerabili jugo oppresserat populum, equis uxoribusque omnia impleverat, nec propterea reprehensus. Prolepsis. Defecit populus a Rhehabeam. Resp. Rebellio fuit populi, pœna Dei. Non exemplis sed legibus judicandum.
units.tr: d. From practice. c. From the practice of kings. Saul often acted impiously at his pleasure, yet David would not kill him, and David said, Against thee only have I sinned. Therefore he was not bound to render an account to the people. Solomon had oppressed the people with an intolerable yoke and had filled everything with horses and wives, yet he was not rebuked for it. Prolepsis. The people revolted from Rehoboam. Reply: the rebellion was the people's, and it was God's punishment. Judgment must be made not by examples but by laws.

units.la: f. A Testimonio plurimorum ita accipientium.
units.tr: f. From the testimony of many who so understand it.

units.la: D. Conclusio hanc legis sententiam inculcans, omnesque subditos ad regum ac magistratuum obedientiam cohortans.
units.tr: D. Conclusion, inculcating this sense of the law and exhorting all subjects to obedience to kings and magistrates.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Num bene dictum: LATENTER ESSE VIVENDUM. Ex Plutarcho.
units.tr: Whether it was well said: ONE SHOULD LIVE HIDDEN. From Plutarch.

units.la: I. Affirmative.
units.tr: I. Affirmative.

units.la: A. Exord. a loco generis: Nihil salubrius est, quàm in promtu habere semper sententias sapientum practicas. Illustretur a fine & effectu; sunt enim norma vivendi, hoc fine prolatæ. Applicetur ad hanc sententiam, commendetur autor, dictumque paraphrasi illustretur.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the topic of the genus: Nothing is more wholesome than always to have at hand the practical maxims of the wise. Let it be illustrated from its end and effect: for these maxims, uttered for this end, are the rule of living. Let it be applied to this saying, let the author be commended, and the saying be illustrated by a paraphrase.

units.la: B. Propositio. & sic statuatur propositio, Rectè & sapienter esse dictum.
