units.tr: B. Proposition. And so let the proposition be laid down: that the saying was rightly and wisely uttered.

units.la: C. Confirmatio.
units.tr: C. Confirmation.

units.la: I. A causa vitæ hujusmodi tacitæ: quæ est modestia, virtutum præstantissima: quod probatur. a. Descriptione. b. Illustratur inductione reliquarum aliquot virtutum, quæ facile vitium admixtum habent, ut fortitudo, liberalitas, parsimonia, humanitas. c. Concluditur inferendo thema,
units.tr: I. From the cause of such a hidden life, which is modesty, the most excellent of the virtues; this is proved: (a) by description; (b) it is illustrated by the induction of several other virtues which easily admit a mixture of vice, such as courage, generosity, thrift, and humanity; (c) it is concluded by inferring the theme.

units.la: II. Ab effectis & adjunctis vitæ latentis: quæ sunt quies, item vacuitas ab affectibus noxiis, invidia, ira, odio; contemplatio, studium. Exaggerentur hæc ab oppositis.
units.tr: II. From the effects and accompaniments of the hidden life: these are quiet, and likewise freedom from harmful affections, envy, anger, hatred; contemplation and study. Let these be magnified by their opposites.

units.la: III. A contraria vita publica & negotiosa: quæ matrem habet ambitionem & avaritiam, sobolem verò laborem, ægritudinem animi, cunctosque noxios affectus, avocat a studio & contemplatione & in vulgaribus, sordidis, odiosis hominem occupat. Illustretur inductione quarundam occupationum publicarum.
units.tr: III. From the contrary, the public and busy life: which has ambition and avarice as its mother, and as its offspring labour, sickness of mind, and all harmful affections; it calls a man away from study and contemplation and occupies him with common, sordid, and hateful things. Let it be illustrated by the induction of certain public occupations.

units.la: IV. A simili, videlicet vita beatorum & ipsius Dei; quæ in hac quiete tranquilla gaudeat. Item ab eo qui supra lunam, aut in vertice montis supra nubes & tempestates consistit.
units.tr: IV. From a likeness, namely the life of the blessed and of God himself, which rejoices in this calm tranquillity; likewise from one who stands above the moon, or on the summit of a mountain above the clouds and storms.

units.la: V. ExemV. Ab Exemplo quod præbent plerique veteres Philosophi, in specie Diogenes, Cleas, alii. Contra proponas tibi Alcibiadem, Themistoclem, Philippum, Alexandrum, Pompejum. Cæsarem, omnesque Magnates. Hypotyposis vitæ magnatum.
units.tr: V. From the example which most of the ancient philosophers offer, especially Diogenes, Cleanthes, and others. On the other side, set before yourself Alcibiades, Themistocles, Philip, Alexander, Pompey, Caesar, and all the great men. A sketch of the life of the great.

units.la: VI. A Testimonio, inter quod & hoc ipsum.
units.tr: VI. From a testimony, between which and this itself.

units.la: D. Conclusio laudans hanc sententiam, & approbans vitam latentem.
units.tr: D. Conclusion, praising this saying and approving the hidden life.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: LATENTER ESSE VIVENDUM.
units.tr: THAT ONE MUST LIVE IN OBSCURITY.

units.la: 2. Negatè.
units.tr: 2. Negatively.

units.la: A. Exord. Ab hypocrisi sapientum: qui sæpè consilia dant facto proprio contraria. Tale illud λαθε βιωσας. Cur in publicum locutus est, si latere voluit? &c.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the hypocrisy of the wise, who often give advice contrary to their own practice. Like that saying, "live hidden" [λαθε βιωσας]. Why did he speak in public, if he wished to remain hidden? etc.

units.la: B. Propositio. Pessimè dictum esse.
units.tr: B. Proposition. That it has been said very badly.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. A causa, quæ 1. negatè non modestia: 2. affirmatè, sed ignaviæ, & quandoque superbia, vitiorum turpissima. Probetur exemplis talium philosophorum. Illustretur oppositò studio societatis humanæ cunctis innato.
units.tr: I. From the cause, which is: (1) negatively, not modesty; (2) affirmatively, but sloth, and sometimes pride, the most shameful of vices. Let it be proved by examples of such philosophers. Let it be illustrated by the opposite zeal for human society, which is innate in all.

units.la: II. Ab effectis, per distributionem.
units.tr: II. From the effects, by distribution.

units.la: a. Imperiti & mali latendo pejores evadunt. Exemplo ægroti latentis.
units.tr: a. The unskilled and the wicked become worse by hiding. Let it be shown by the example of a sick man who keeps himself hidden.

units.la: b. Docti & boni dona defodiunt: unde neglectus omnis cultus, & tandem vita belluina. Probetur exemplo illorum qui a cultu abfuerunt, & similli, ab agris non consitis.
units.tr: b. The learned and the good bury their gifts; whence comes the neglect of all culture, and finally a brutish life. Let it be proved by the example of those who have kept away from cultivation, and by a similar example of fields left unsown.

units.la: c. Quieti ut ociosi in pessimos affectus abripiuntur. Simile ab aqua stagnante.
units.tr: c. Those who withdraw into quiet, being idle, are carried off into the worst passions. Let there be a similar comparison with stagnant water.

units.la: III. A contrario: hominum in societate viventium, ut Solonis, Lycurgi, Pythagoræ, Platonis, Aristotelis, Epaminondæ, Thrasibuli, ad salutem humani generis natorum. Illustretur proleptsi gemina. 1. vitæ negotiosæ se miscet ambitio. 2. illa parit molestias. Quod non ex ambitione, sed studio juvandi genus humanum proficiscitur. Non ægritudinem generat; sed voluptatem honestam.
units.tr: III. From the contrary: the lives of men who lived in society, such as Solon, Lycurgus, Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle, Epaminondas, Thrasybulus, who were born for the good of the human race. Let there be a twofold anticipation: (1) an ambitious mind mixes itself into an active life; (2) that ambition brings forth troubles. But that this springs not from ambition but from a desire to help the human race. It does not produce sadness, but an honourable pleasure.

units.la: IV. A simili, Sole, luce, astris, quæ dum conspicua sunt, prosunt sunt. Illustretur à contrariis tenebris. Et applicetur ad propo-situm.
units.tr: IV. From a likeness: the sun, light, and the stars, which, while they are visible, are of benefit. Let it be illustrated from the contrary, darkness. And let it be applied to the proposition.

units.la: V. Ab Exemplo: quod sunt Heroes, qui in luce viventes, publicè profuerunt.
units.tr: V. From an example: there are heroes who, living in the light, have served the public good.

units.la: VI. A Testimoniis vitam publicam probantibus.
units.tr: VI. From testimonies that approve a public life.

units.la: d. Conclusio. Prodeundum in lucem, dicta veterum cum discretio-ne & judicio æstimanda.
units.tr: d. Conclusion. One must come forth into the light, and the sayings of the ancients are to be weighed with discretion and judgment.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: NARRATIO SEU HYPOTYPOSIS CÆDIS POMPEJI JUSSU PTOLOMÆI.
units.tr: NARRATIVE, OR HYPOTYPOSIS, OF THE SLAUGHTER OF POMPEY BY THE ORDER OF PTOLEMY.

units.la: Vid. Flor. lib. 4. c. 2. Dion Cass. lib. 42. Appianus, Paterculus, Plutarchus.
units.tr: See Florus, book 4, chapter 2; Dio Cassius, book 42; Appian, Paterculus, Plutarch.

units.la: A. Exordium. à mutabilitate fortunæ, etiam magnatum.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the changeability of fortune, even that of the great.

units.la: B. Propositio. Applicetur ad hypothesin in exemplo mortis Pompeji
units.tr: B. Propositio. Let it be applied to the hypothesis, in the example of Pompey's death.

units.la: C. Tractatio. I. A descriptione Personæ, bonis corporis, animi, fortunæ, & rebus gestis hactenus præ cæteris felicis. Unde & Magni cog-nomen. Vid. Orat. pro L. Manil.
units.tr: C. Tractatio. I. From a description of the person: his goods of body, mind and fortune, and his deeds, which until now were happier than those of others. Whence also the surname Magnus. See the oration for Lucius Manilius.

units.la: II. Ab Antecedentibus, uti sunt.
units.tr: II. From the antecedents, which are as follows.

units.la: a. Æmulatio contra Cæsarem.
units.tr: a. Rivalry against Caesar.

units.la: b. Clades in acie Pharsalica.
units.tr: b. Defeat in the battle of Pharsalus.

units.la: c. Fuga in Ægyptum, ubi rex Ptolomæus junior, & imploratio re-ceptûs. Explicentur causæ, 1. hujus fugæ, videlicet perplexitas secuta nimiam ejus fiduciam de victoria, 2. consilii hujus, quia Patrem Ptolomæi in Regnum restituerat. Addatur τυφλὸς a sal-laci spe in viribus propriis & auxilio humano.
units.tr: c. Flight into Egypt, to King Ptolemy the Younger, and a plea to be received. Let the causes be explained: 1. of this flight, namely the perplexity that followed his excessive confidence in victory; 2. of this plan, because he had restored Ptolemy's father to the kingdom. Add the blindness [τυφλὸς] of a deceptive hope placed in his own strength and in human help.

units.la: III. Causæ cædis.
units.tr: III. The causes of the slaughter.

units.la: a. Malum consilium datum regi à Theodoto & Photino, ut consideret potiùs malum secuturum ex adventu Cæsaris victo-ris, quam beneficium præteritum.
units.tr: a. The bad advice given to the king by Theodotus and Photinus, that he should consider the harm that would follow from the arrival of the victorious Caesar rather than the benefit already received.

units.la: b. Imperitia Regis adolescentis 13. annorum.
units.tr: b. The inexperience of the young king, aged thirteen.

units.la: c. Mandatum factum Achillæ Regio præfecto, & L. Septimo, mi-liti quondam Pompeji, ut in littore occidant. Addatur τυφλὸς a labili memoria benefactorum apud Magnates.
units.tr: c. The command given to Achillas, the royal prefect, and to L. Septimius, once a soldier of Pompey, that they should kill him on the shore. Add the blindness [τυφλὸς] arising from a fickle memory of benefits among the great.

units.la: IV. Facinus ipsum.
units.tr: IV. The deed itself.

units.la: a. Rogatur ut exscendat in lembum, quia mare vadosum majo-rem navem non admittat. Paret Pompejus contra consi-lium lium suorum, ipse hæsitans hæc addit verba: Tyranni si quis intret domum. Fit servus, liber etsi venerit.
units.tr: a. He is asked to step into a boat, since the shallow sea does not admit a larger ship. Pompey obeys, against the advice of his own people; hesitating himself, he adds these words: against the advice of his friends, and hesitating, he adds these words: If anyone enters a tyrant's house, he becomes a slave, even if he came in free.

units.la: b. Exscensurus in litore trucidatur, nihil locutus, sed toga capite obvelato cædi se præbuit; pridie natalis, eodem die, quo ante de Mithridate & Piratis triumphasset. Πάθος a rei indignitate & instabilitate rerum humanarum, amplificetur per comparationem pristinæ fortunæ.
units.tr: b. As he is about to disembark on the shore, he is cut down. He says nothing, but offers himself to the slaughter with his toga drawn over his head, on the day after his birthday, on the same day on which he had earlier celebrated his triumph over Mithridates and the pirates. Pathos [πάθος] from the unworthiness of the event and the instability of human affairs; amplify it by comparison with his former fortune.

units.la: V. Conseq. a Corpus in litore jacuit, & rogo crematum.
units.tr: V. Consequences. a. His body lay on the shore and was burned on a pyre.

units.la: b. Amici partim capti, partim cum uxore & filio fugerunt.
units.tr: b. His friends were partly captured, and partly fled with his wife and son.

units.la: c. Caput & annulus a Theodoto Cæsari missa.
units.tr: c. His head and signet ring were sent to Caesar by Theodotus.

units.la: D. Conclusio: Pathetice, miseriam illorum repræsentans, qui sua sapientia, potentia, & Magnatum fiducia nituntur.
units.tr: D. Conclusion: Pathetically, representing the misery of those who rely on their own wisdom, power and the confidence placed in the great.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: II. HYPOTYPOSIS PARRICIDII CÆSARIS.
units.tr: II. Hypotyposis of Caesar's Murder.

units.la: Dion. Cass. lib. 43. Flor. lib. 4. c. 2.
units.tr: Dion. Cass. lib. 43. Flor. lib. 4. c. 2.

units.la: A. Exordium. A periculo & ærumnis, quibus subjecta vita magnatum: comparetur cum ipsorum felicitate apparente, & vita privata.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the dangers and hardships to which the life of great men is subject, compared with their apparent happiness and with private life.

units.la: B. Propositio. Exemplum habemus illustre in C. Jul. Cæsare.
units.tr: B. Propositio. We have a famous example in Gaius Julius Caesar.

units.la: C. Expositio.
units.tr: C. Expositio.

units.la: I. A descriptione personæ, ejusque genere ac indole ad summa enitentis.
units.tr: I. From the description of the person, his family and character, and his striving for the highest things.

units.la: II. Antecedentibus, uti erant victoriæ crebræ & triumphi, 2. Dignitates omnes usque ad dictaturam & diadema.
units.tr: II. From the antecedents: his frequent victories and triumphs; 2. all his offices, up to the dictatorship and the diadem.

units.la: III. A Causis. 1. decretum ab adulante senatu, ut per decennium consulatus ipsi continuaretur, potestati ejus magistratus, milites, pecuniæ publicæ committerentur, statua erigeretur juxta statuam Regum & Bruti, qui Tarquinium fugaverat. 2. Infractio veterum Legum & consuetudinum. 3. Fastus, quod non assurrexit senatui referenti de novis honoribus ipsi decretis. 4. Dictatura perpetua. 5. Tacita approbatio tituli Regii. 6. Invidia hinc nata in auribus magnatum, præcipuè M. Bruti & C. Cassii. Addatur Pathos, à periculo nimiæ felicitatis, quæ semper suspecta esse debet. Amplificetur ab ominibus Cæsarem dehortantibus.
units.tr: III. From the causes: (1) a decree of the fawning senate that his consulship should be continued for ten years, that the magistracies, the soldiers and the public money should be committed to his power, and that a statue should be erected beside the statues of the kings and of Brutus, who had driven out Tarquin; (2) the breaking of ancient laws and customs; (3) arrogance, in that he did not rise for the senate when it reported the new honours decreed for him; (4) the perpetual dictatorship; (5) tacit approval of the royal title; (6) the resentment arising from this in the ears of the great men, especially Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius. Add pathos from the danger of excessive good fortune, which should always be suspected. Amplify this with the omens that warned Caesar off.

units.la: IV. Factum ipsum cum suis circumstantiis, personarum, loci, tempotemporis, modique referatur. Addatur pathos a comparatione persone & mortis indignæ.
units.tr: IV. The deed itself is to be related with its circumstances: the persons, the place, the time and the manner. Add pathos from the comparison of the man's rank and his unworthy death.

units.la: V. A consequentib9: Luctu per urbem, parricidæ in Capitolium supplicaturi procedunt. Lepido milite forum occupat, concione sub aurora habet contra percussores. Antonius in æde telluris senatum cogit. Senatus consultum de amnestia suadente Cicerone. Antonius posito ante rostra cruento corpore, oratione cives ad quærendos percussores commovit. Cadaver in foro combustum, ara in loco ubi rogus fuerat exstructa, & sacrificia instituta. A Senatu percussores in provincias ablegati. Antonius, Octavius & Lepidus triumviratum invexerunt.
units.tr: V. From the consequences: with mourning throughout the city, the parricides go up to the Capitol as suppliants. Lepidus, with soldiers, occupies the forum; at dawn he addresses an assembly against the assassins. Antony convenes the senate in the temple of Earth. A decree of the senate on amnesty is passed at Cicero's urging. Antony, placing the bloody corpse before the rostra, stirs the citizens by his speech to seek out the assassins. The body is burned in the forum, an altar is built on the spot where the pyre was raised, and sacrifices are instituted. The senate sends the assassins away into the provinces. Antony, Octavius and Lepidus establish the triumvirate.

units.la: D. Conclusio. Παθητικῶς miserias magnatum exaggerans & vitam privatam præferens cum Seneca. Stet quisquis optet. &c.
units.tr: D. Conclusio. Pathetically [Παθητικῶς] exaggerating the miseries of great men and preferring private life, with Seneca. Let whoever wishes, stand. etc.

units.la: XX. HYPOTYPOSIS CÆDIS MAURITII IMPER.
units.tr: XX. A Hypotyposis of the Murder of the Emperor Maurice

units.la: V. Niceph. lib. 18. c. 40. Pezel. Chron. Phil. lib. 3.
units.tr: V. Niceph. lib. 18. c. 40. Pezel. Chron. Phil. lib. 3.

units.la: A. Exordium. a dicto Syracidis, Potentes potenter puniuntur. Applicetur ad hypothesin.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the saying of the son of Sirach: Mighty men shall be mightily punished. Let it be applied to the hypothesis.

units.la: B. Propositio. Hoc vobis A. proponam.
units.tr: B. Propositio. A., I will set this before you.

units.la: C. Expositio.
units.tr: C. Expositio.

units.la: I. A descriptione personæ.
units.tr: I. From the description of the person.

units.la: a. A patria & officio, conditione Cappadox, scriba Justini Imperatoris, post Comes prætorianorum.
units.tr: a. From his country and office: of Cappadocian origin, secretary to the Emperor Justin, and afterwards Count of the praetorian guards.

units.la: b. A dotibus animi, vir pius, gravis & humanus.
units.tr: b. From the qualities of his mind: a pious, serious and humane man.

units.la: c. A Rebus gestis, rem in toga & sago bene gessit, præcipue contra Persas.
units.tr: c. From his deeds: he acquitted himself well in civil and military affairs, especially against the Persians.

units.la: d. A Dignitate. Tiberius II. Cæsar dedit ipsi filiam, designavit imperatorem: electus post a populo coronatur à Johanne Patriarcha Constantinopolitano gessitque res maximas contra Persas. Addatur ἐπίκλησις: quod dignus maximè qui imperet, fuerit.
units.tr: d. From his dignity: Tiberius II Caesar gave him his daughter in marriage and designated him emperor. Chosen afterwards by the people, he was crowned by John, Patriarch of Constantinople, and carried out very great achievements against the Persians. Add the epithet [ἐπίκλησις]: that he was most worthy to rule.

units.la: II. A Causis procatarcticis cædis: uti sunt.
units.tr: II. From the preceding causes of the murder, which are these:

units.la: a. Mutatio morum per imperium, illustretur sententia: subiit in locum virtutum iracundia, suspicio, avaritia. Exaggeretur vitiorum horum turpitudo maximè in Monarcha.
units.tr: a. The change of his character brought about by power. Illustrate the saying: anger, suspicion and avarice took the place of the virtues. The baseness of these vices should be enlarged upon, especially in a monarch.

units.la: b. Mandatum quod dedit duci suo Philippico, ut legiones hosti proderet.
units.tr: b. The order he gave to his general Philippicus, that he should betray the legions to the enemy.

units.la: c. Neglectus 12000. captivorum, quorum singulos aureo nummo poterat redimere, quos proinde Caganus Rex Hungarorum trucidavit: arguatur vilipendium militum.
units.tr: c. The neglect of 12,000 captives, each of whom he could have ransomed for a single gold coin, and whom Caganus, king of the Hungarians, therefore slaughtered. Let the contempt for the soldiers be argued.

units.la: d. Defensio ducis ab ipso suscepta contra instantes per Legatum Phocam milites. Inculpetur nimia obstinatio contra supplices milites, & praepostérus affectus erga suum ducem.
units.tr: d. The defence of his general, undertaken by himself against the soldiers who pressed him through the envoy Phocas. Let the excessive obstinacy against the suppliant soldiers, and the perverse affection for his general, be blamed.

units.la: III. Ab antecedentibus, uti sunt.
units.tr: III. From the events that went before, which are these:

units.la: a. Conspiratio militum adversus imperatorem, & delatio imperii in Phocam in clypeos sublatum.
units.tr: a. The conspiracy of the soldiers against the emperor, and the transfer of the empire to Phocas, who was raised up on shields.

units.la: b. Accessus exercitus ad urbem, in quam intromissus Phocas & coronatus est.
units.tr: b. The army's approach to the city, into which Phocas was admitted and crowned.

units.la: c. Prodigia, ut 1. cometa conspectus instar gladii. 2. somnium, quo sisti se Dei judicio visus est, & tradi Phocae, unde peti pro se Ecclesiam voluit, ut hic poenas luat. Attentio ex affectu prodigiorum haud frustraneo.
units.tr: c. Portents: first, a comet seen in the shape of a sword; second, a dream in which he seemed to be brought before the judgement of God and handed over to Phocas, whereupon he wished the Church to pray on his behalf, so that he might pay the penalty here. Attention is drawn by the emotion aroused by the portents, which is not without purpose.

units.la: d. Fuga Mauritii cum uxore & liberis Chalcedonem versus & retractio ex fuga. Fiat hinc augurium certum mortis Mauritii, postquam homo vilissimus & turpissimus centurio Phocas eo usque audaciae semel processerat.
units.tr: d. Mauritius' flight with his wife and children towards Chalcedon, and his being dragged back from the flight. From this let a sure omen of Mauritius' death be drawn, since the most worthless and vile centurion Phocas had once advanced so far in audacity.

units.la: IV. Ipsa caedis descriptio seu facti species.
units.tr: IV. The description of the slaying itself, or the appearance of the deed.

units.la: a. Deducitur cum familia ad littus, committitur carnifici.
units.tr: a. He is led down with his household to the shore and handed over to the executioner.

units.la: b. Mactantur liberi, minimus ab uberibus nutricis abripitur.
units.tr: b. The children are slaughtered; the youngest is snatched from the breast of his nurse.

units.la: c. Trucidatur uxor; intuente omnia patre, & proloquente: Justum es Domine & justa sunt judicia tua, Pathos a πάθη parentum, & mente male conscia.
units.tr: c. The wife is slain while the father looks on at everything and says: Just art thou, O Lord, and just are thy judgements. The pathos comes from the passions of the parents and a conscience ill at ease.

units.la: d. Jugulatur ipse Imperator 63. annorum. Exaggeretur jam a circumstantiis omnibus.
units.tr: d. The emperor himself, aged 63, is cut down. Let it now be amplified by all the circumstances.

units.la: V. A Consequentibus.
units.tr: V. From the consequences.

units.la: a. Cadavera in littore relicta usquedum foeterent.
units.tr: a. The corpses are left on the shore until they stink.

units.la: b. Caesi deinceps reliqui omnes ex ipsius familia, mares, foeminae &c.
units.tr: b. Then all the rest of his household, males, females and so on, are slain.

units.la: C. Conclusio. Hortans ad modestiam Magnates, & admirans Dei judicia, qui evehit & e solio deturbat Reges.
units.tr: C. Conclusio. Exhorting the magnates to moderation, and marvelling at the judgements of God, who raises up kings and casts them down from the throne.

units.la: XXI. THEMA LIBERUM IN GENERE DIDASCALICO
units.tr: XXI. THEMA LIBERUM IN GENERE DIDASCALICO

units.la: Utrum scientia praeferenda sit prudentiae, seu Philosophia contemplativa, practica.
units.tr: Whether knowledge is to be preferred to prudence, that is, contemplative philosophy to practical.

units.la: I. Pro scientia seu Philos. Contempl.
units.tr: I. For knowledge, or contemplative philosophy.

units.la: A. Exordium. A vi mentis humanae, quae in judicando rebus momentum vel addit vel adimit pro lubitu. Hoc I. Proponatur. II. Exaggeretur ab ambigua rerum plurimarum natura, ubi dubium quid eligendum. III. Applicetur ad institutum: addita commendatione quaestionis a pondere in eligendo, & dissensu doctorum, antiquorum, recentium.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the power of the human mind, which at its pleasure adds weight to things in judging them or takes it away. Here (I) the point is put forward; (II) it is amplified by the uncertain nature of very many things, where it is doubtful what should be chosen; (III) it is applied to the present undertaking, adding a recommendation of the question from the weight of the choice and from the disagreement of teachers, both ancient and recent.

units.la: B. Propositio. Praeferendam scientiam & Phil. speculativam, salvo aliorum judicio.
units.tr: B. Propositio. Knowledge and speculative philosophy are to be preferred, saving the judgment of others.

units.la: C. Confirmatio.
units.tr: C. Confirmatio.

units.la: I. A praestantia subjecti, seu facultatis animae cui competit, quae est intellectus speculativus, cujus praestantia explicetur comparatione reliquarum animae facultatum, & in specie intellectus practici & appetitus sensitivi, quos philosophia practica informat.
units.tr: I. From the excellence of the subject, or of the faculty of the soul to which it belongs, which is the speculative intellect. Its excellence is to be explained by comparison with the other faculties of the soul, and especially with the practical intellect and the sensitive appetite, which practical philosophy shapes.

units.la: II. A dignitate & amplitudine objecti: quae sunt res omnes; imprimisque aeternae & certissimae, uti est Deus, intelligentiae, essentiae ac veritates rerum perpetuae. Ostendatur per inductionem facultatum speculativarum, Matheseos, Physicae, Metaphysicae, ipsiusque adeo Theologiae.
units.tr: II. From the dignity and breadth of the object, which is all things, and above all things eternal and most certain, such as God, the intelligences, the essences and the perpetual truths of things. This is to be shown by enumerating the speculative faculties: mathematics, physics, metaphysics, and theology itself.

units.la: III. A certitudine, quae i, probetur ex certitudine objecti.
units.tr: III. From certainty, which is proved from the certainty of the object.

units.la: a. Commendetur a jucunditate. Exaggeretur a comparatione cum incertitudine philosophiae practicae: quae patet inductione exempli ex Ethica, Oeconomica, Politica.
units.tr: a. It is commended from its pleasantness. It is enlarged by comparison with the uncertainty of practical philosophy, which becomes plain by the example of ethics, economics and politics.

units.la: IV. Ex comparatione a. cum Philosophia practica. 1. Ratione dependentiae. Practica dependet a theoretica. 2. Ratione causae: Practica ex indigentia & malis moribus nata: Theoretica ex objecti pulchritudine & sua sufficientia. 3. Ratione adjunctorum seu organorum quibus indiget, Practica multis, Vide Aristot. 10. Moral. Theoretica nullis. Item practica in coetu tantum, Theoretica etiam in solitudi-ne operatur. Practica cum molestia conjuncta & confliʇu; theoretica cum jucunditate.
units.tr: IV. From a comparison (a) with practical philosophy. (1) By reason of dependence: the practical depends on the theoretical. (2) By reason of cause: the practical arises from need and bad morals, the theoretical from the beauty of its object and its self-sufficiency. (3) By reason of its accompaniments or instruments, which the practical needs in great number (see Aristotle, Ethics 10), while the theoretical needs none. Likewise the practical works only in company, whereas the theoretical works even in solitude. The practical is joined with trouble and conflict, the theoretical with pleasure.

units.la: b. Cum artibus mechanicis: ubi præstantior Architectus, quam faber? &c.
units.tr: b. With the mechanical arts: where is the architect not superior to the carpenter? And so on.

units.la: V. Ex effectis utriusque, practica turbulentum, theoretica quietum hominem efficit: illa hominum, hæc Dei & angelorum consortio nos jungit, & supra sortem humanam evehit.
units.tr: V. From the effects of each: the practical makes a man restless, the theoretical makes him quiet. The former joins us to the company of men, the latter to the fellowship of God and the angels, and lifts us above the human lot.

units.la: VI. Ex Testimonio Arist: qui hoc innuit. 1. Metaph. Laërt. lib.1. aliorumque.
units.tr: VI. From the testimony of Aristotle, who hints at this (Metaphysics 1), and of Diogenes Laertius, book 1, and others.

units.la: D. Refutatio illorum, qui utilitatem Philosophiæ practicæ crepant. Resp. Res non ex æstimatione hominum, sed ex sua præstantia judicandas. Secus aurum virtuti præferendum.
units.tr: D. Refutation of those who decry the usefulness of practical philosophy. Reply: things are to be judged not by men's estimation but by their own excellence. Otherwise gold would have to be preferred to virtue.

units.la: E. Conclusio. Argumenta præcipua recolligit, & thema inculcat.
units.tr: E. Conclusio. He gathers up the chief arguments and drives the theme home.

units.la: XXII. PRO PRUDENTIA ET PHILOSOPHIA PRACTICA.
units.tr: XXII. FOR PRUDENCE AND PRACTICAL PHILOSOPHY.

units.la: Per inversionem assertionis Antecessoris.
units.tr: By inversion of the assertion of the previous author.

units.la: A. Exordium de vi mentis humanæ, videlicet hinc fieri sæpe, ut suis speculationibus dedita, suum ipsius & humanæ societatis commoda negligat. Applicetur ad hypothesin in repetitione thematis tractati ab antecessore.
units.tr: A. Exordium on the power of the human mind, namely that from this it often happens that one devoted to his own speculations neglects his own advantage and that of human society. It is to be applied to the hypothesis in the repetition of the thesis treated by the predecessor.

units.la: Propos. Contrarium te docturum: videlicet prudentiam & Philosophiam practicam esse præferendam.
units.tr: Proposition. I shall teach the contrary: namely, that prudence and practical philosophy are to be preferred.

units.la: C. Confirmatio.
units.tr: C. Confirmation.

units.la: I. A fine Philosophiæ practicæ, qui idem est cum fine hominis, videlicet non ociose contemplari, sed agere honesta. Hoc 1. probetur comparatione finis reliquarum creaturarum.
units.tr: I. From the end of practical philosophy, which is the same as the end of man, namely not to contemplate idly but to do honourable things. This is proved first by comparison with the end of the remaining creatures.

units.la: 2. Illustretur comparatione finis philosophiæ theoreticæ,
units.tr: 2. It is illustrated by comparison with the end of theoretical philosophy.

units.la: II. A Materia, quæ est doctrina de virtutibus. Hic 1. instituatur comparatio inter virtutes & nudam scientiam. 2. Illustretur a contrario utriusque, videlicet vitiis & errore, illa pejora ostendens.
units.tr: II. From the matter, which is the doctrine of the virtues. Here (1) a comparison is set up between the virtues and bare knowledge; (2) it is illustrated from the contrary of each, namely vices and error, showing those to be the worse.

units.la: III. Ab effectis seu utili. Illud præstantius, quod homini ac humanæ societati fructuosius. At philosophia practica & prudentia sunt homini & societati humani fructuosiores. Prob. hoc inductione utilitatum, quas Philosophia practica fert homini, domui civitati. 2. Illustretur à comparatione philosophiæ theoreticæ & contemplativæ.
units.tr: III. From the effects or usefulness. That is the more excellent which is more fruitful for man and human society. But practical philosophy and prudence are more fruitful for man and human society. This is proved by induction over the advantages which practical philosophy brings to the man, the household and the state. Second, it is illustrated by comparison with theoretical and contemplative philosophy.

units.la: IV. Ab imperio civilis prudentiæ in reliquas omnes scientias: vide Arist. cap. 2. lib. 1. moral. Nicom.
units.tr: IV. From the rule of civil prudence over all the remaining sciences: see Aristotle, book 1, chapter 2 of the Nicomachean Ethics.

units.la: V. A conspirante testimonio Socratis, Platonis Aristotelis, Senecæ Epist. 20. & 89. Ipsiusque adeo Dei.
units.tr: V. From the agreeing testimony of Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Seneca (Epist. 20 and 89), and indeed of God himself.

units.la: D. Refutatio argumenti à præstantia & certitudine philosophiæ theoreticæ. Resp. 1. Ex usu æstimandam præstantiam, non ex imaginatione. 2. Sat certum esse, unde certa vitæ emendatio & utilitas.
units.tr: D. Refutation of the argument from the excellence and certainty of theoretical philosophy. Reply: (1) excellence is to be judged by use, not by imagination; (2) it is certain enough whence comes sure amendment of life and usefulness.

units.la: E. Conclusio. Argumenta præcipua recolligit, & thema inculcat.
units.tr: E. Conclusion. He sums up the chief arguments and drives home the thesis.

units.la: XXIII. VOLUPTATEM NON ESSE SUMMUM BONUM.
units.tr: XXIII. That pleasure is not the chief good.

units.la: A. Exordium ex re ipsa, videlicet à desiderio summi boni in cunctis.
units.tr: A. The introduction (exordium) drawn from the matter itself, namely from the desire for the chief good in all people.

units.la: I. Proponatur. Omnia desiderant bonum aliquod.
units.tr: I. Let it be laid down: all things desire some good.

units.la: II. Probetur inductione brevi à summo ad imum.
units.tr: II. Let it be proved by a brief induction from the highest to the lowest.

units.la: III. Illustretur oppositο errore plerorumque circa summum bonum, maxime illorum, qui voluptatem, divitias, honores bona sua æstimant.
units.tr: III. Let it be illustrated by the opposite error of most people concerning the chief good, especially of those who count pleasure, riches and honours as their goods.

units.la: IV. Concludatur: Horum proinde error refutandus.
units.tr: IV. Let the conclusion be drawn: therefore the error of these people must be refuted.

units.la: B. Propositio. in præsentiarum ostendam voluptatem non esse summum bonum.
units.tr: B. The proposition: at present I will show that pleasure is not the chief good.

units.la: C. Confirmatio.
units.tr: C. The confirmation.

units.la: I. A fœditate voluptatis & præstantia ac amabilitate summi boni, Amplificetur descriptione.
units.tr: I. From the foulness of pleasure and from the excellence and loveliness of the chief good; the argument is to be enlarged by description.

units.la: II. A subjecto voluptatis, videlicet pecudum propria est. Exaggeretur antithesi pecudis & hominis.
units.tr: II. From the subject of pleasure: it belongs properly to beasts. The contrast between beast and man is to be heightened.

units.la: III. A noxiis effectis voluptatum in corpore & anima; qualia consistere non possunt cum summo bono: utpote cujus effecta contraria sunt.
units.tr: III. From the harmful effects of pleasures on body and soul, which cannot coexist with the chief good, since its effects are contrary to theirs.

units.la: IV. Ab instabilitate voluptatum & stabilitate summi boni. Probetur inductione variorum impedimentorum voluptatis.
units.tr: IV. From the instability of pleasures and the stability of the chief good. Let it be proved by an induction of the various hindrances to pleasure.

units.la: D. Increpatio Epicuri, Eudoxi, Aristippi similiumque, qui voluptatem commendarunt; cum conclusione thematis, addito insuper argumento, quòd nemo inde bonus denominari mereatur.
units.tr: D. A rebuke of Epicurus, Eudoxus, Aristippus and those like them, who commended pleasure; with the conclusion of the thesis, and with the further argument that no one deserves to be called good on account of it.

units.la: XXIV. EXPLICATIO SENTENTIÆ.
units.tr: XXIV. AN EXPLANATION OF THE SENTENCE.

units.la: Cic: Voluptas pecudis bonum est, non hominis.
units.tr: Cic: Pleasure is good for a beast, not for a man.

units.la: A. Hic loco Exordii commendetur breviter Autor cum relatione dicti.
units.tr: A. Here, at the place of the introduction, the author briefly commends the saying together with a report of it.

units.la: B. Expositio: mens ejus praevia commendatione dicti, paraphrasi exponatur; quæ veluti propositio est.
units.tr: B. Exposition: its meaning, after a preliminary commendation of the saying, is set out in a paraphrase, which serves as the proposition.

units.la: C. Expositio & illustratio.
units.tr: C. Exposition and illustration.

units.la: I. A causa, videlicet natura voluptatis, & fine pecudum ac hominis. Hic ostendatur voluptatem fini pecudum convenientem, hominis vero adversam esse.
units.tr: I. From the cause, namely the nature of pleasure, and the end of beasts and of man. Here it is shown that pleasure suits the end of beasts, but is opposed to the end of man.

units.la: II. Ab antithesi scil. homine voluptati dedito.
units.tr: II. From the antithesis, namely the man given over to pleasure.

units.la: a. Proponatur talis per hypotyposin.
units.tr: a. Let him be set forth thus, by way of vivid description.

units.la: b. Ostendatur ejus vitam & actiones non homini sed bruto convenire. Adeoque talem potius brutum & porcum esse, quam hominem.
units.tr: b. It is shown that his life and actions befit not a man but a brute; and so such a man is rather a brute and a pig than a man.

units.la: III. A simili: videlicet simia ornata regiis vestibus, quæ ex vita & actionibus simia arguitur; ita porcus licet aureum gestet monile: addatur apodosis.
units.tr: III. From a likeness: namely an ape dressed in royal robes, who is judged to be an ape from its life and actions; so too a pig, though it wears a golden necklace. The apodosis is to be added.

units.la: IV. Ab exemplo, Sardanapali, Heliogabali, & principis omnium Epicuri.
units.tr: IV. From examples: Sardanapalus, Heliogabalus, and the chief of them all, Epicurus.

units.la: V. A Testimoniis.
units.tr: V. From testimonies.

units.la: D. Conclusio approbet dictum & voluptatem ex allatis rationis detestetur.
units.tr: D. The conclusion approves the saying and, from the reasons adduced, condemns pleasure.

units.la: XXV. THEMA LIBERUM.
units.tr: XXV. A FREE THEME.

units.la: De Fatalibus limitibus ambitionis ac potestatis humanæ.
units.tr: On the fated limits of human ambition and power.

units.la: Exord. I. Merito mirandum esse dicat, quod hoc tempore in tanta & Christianæ veritatis & scientiarum omnium claritate, inveniantur, qui Empedoclis, aliorumque veterum gentilium Philosophorum deliria recoquunt; & ex singulis astris novam terram, adeoque infinitos mundos somniant: non contenti unica hac terra, uno mundo, quem sapiores omnes, quem sacra Scriptura statuit.
units.tr: Exordium. I. One may rightly marvel that in this age, so rich in both Christian truth and every kind of learning, there are still people who rehash the follies of Empedocles and other ancient pagan philosophers, and who dream of a new earth from each star, and so of infinite worlds, not content with this one earth and one world, which all the wiser men and holy Scripture have affirmed.

units.la: II. Causam hujus rei alleget vanitatem mentis humanæ,quæ sæpe novaturiens intra terminos continere se nequit.
units.tr: II. Let him assign the cause of this to the vanity of the human mind, which, always craving novelty, cannot keep itself within its bounds.

units.la: III. Opponat rationes: videlicet. At verò nihil infinitum voluisse esse Deum; qui solus infinitus, omnia reliqua numero pondere ac mensura crearit. Probetur hoc inductione, videlicet mare tam vastum littoribus, flumina rapidissima ripis; terram tam amplam ambiente aëre, aërem fluidissimum coelo finiri; cœlum ipsum in suo contineri spacio,non patere extra se. Porrò solem & reliqua astra suum habere orbem,quem non egrediuntur. Ipsos spiritus agilissimos ac subtilissimos modum ac sphæram habere suæ activitatis.
units.tr: III. Let him set out the arguments, namely: God, who alone is infinite, willed nothing infinite, but created all other things by number, weight and measure. Let this be proved by induction: the sea is so vast yet bounded by its shores, the swiftest rivers by their banks; the earth so wide is enclosed by the surrounding air, and the most fluid air is bounded by the heavens; the heavens themselves are contained within their own space and do not extend beyond themselves. Furthermore, the sun and the other stars have their own orbit, which they do not leave. Even the most nimble and subtle spirits have a measure and sphere of their activity.

units.la: IV. Concludat comparatione mentis humanæ, quæ sola terminum nescit, omnia scrutans, omnia expetens ambitu infinito, at frustraneo: quia Deus uti omnibus & scientiæ, ita & potentiæ humanæ certos posuit limites, quos frustra excedere satagat mortalis.
units.tr: IV. Let him conclude by comparing the human mind, which alone knows no limit, searching everything and desiring everything in an infinite but fruitless sweep. For God has set certain limits to human knowledge and power alike, and it is in vain that mortals strive to exceed them.

units.la: Propos: Hoc in præsentiarum oratione licet longè impari rei magnitudini evincendum; quo solam infinitam Dei majestatem venerari & modestiam ac sanctam ἀντάχνεια discant mortales.
units.tr: Proposition: This can be demonstrated in the present speech, though far below the greatness of the matter, so that mortals may learn to venerate the infinite majesty of God alone, and holy modesty and antacheia [ἀντάχνεια] (a yielding without contention).

units.la: Tractatio ostendat.
units.tr: Treatment should show:

units.la: I. In vita privata.
units.tr: I. In private life.

units.la: 1, immoderatum ambitum ac cupiditatem hominum. Hîc In genere verum esse dicatur illud Horat. Optat ephippia bos piger, optat arare caballus, addita brevi paraphrasi, qua sensus dicti explicetur.
units.tr: 1. The immoderate ambition and greed of men. Here let it be said that, in general, the saying of Horace is true: "The sluggish ox wishes for the harness, the horse wishes to plough," with a short paraphrase added to explain the sense of the saying.

units.la: β. Probetur inductione diversorum vitæ generum & exemplorum: v. g. Quis contentus opibus ac possessionibus paternis? probetur exemplis ex Græca & Rom. Rep. Quis contentus conditione avita? quin semper ulteriora petat. Quis contentus conditione sua? quin alterius ambiat: Agricolam laudet juris legumq; peritus &c: Et figulis figulo invidet & Cantor cantori &c.
units.tr: β. Let it be proved by induction from various ways of life and examples. For instance: who is content with his paternal wealth and possessions? Let it be proved by examples from Greek and Roman history. Who is content with the rank of his forebears? Rather, he always seeks more. Who is content with his own station? Rather, he covets another's: "Let the lawyer praise the farmer's life, and so on," and "the potter envies the potter, and the singer the singer," etc.

units.la: 2. Frustrationem ambitus in plerisque; qui multum machinando parum efficiunt. Vide exempla & adde rationem a Dei providentia, quæ uti unicuique certam staturam, ita & vitæ,& ordinis,opum ac conditionis mensuram posuit; contra quam frustra ringitur mortalis; licet crepet cum rana Æsopica, quæ inflando se bovem æquare voluit. Fiat digressiuncula invectiva in modernum ambitum privatum, quo quisque altero superior esse nititur.
units.tr: 2. The frustration of ambition in most people, who, by scheming much, achieve little. See the examples, and add the reason from God's providence, which, as it has set for each person a fixed stature, so also a measure of life, of rank, of wealth and of condition; against this measure mortals strive in vain, though, like Aesop's frog who wished to swell itself to the size of an ox, they burst with their puffing. Let a short invective digression be made against the present private ambition, by which each person strives to be above another.

units.la: 3. Ruinam aliorum, si qui forte voti compotes facti, supra sortem avitam, supra semet ipsos eluctati sint. Illustretur a causa: quia superbis adversus Deus, qui sæpe vota implet ad pœnam; effert ut præcipitet &c, Ut multis melius fuisset, nunquam egressos se esse sortem pristinam.
units.tr: 3. The ruin of others, if any by chance, having gained their wish, have struggled above their ancestral lot and beyond themselves. Let this be illustrated by its cause: God, who often fulfils men's wishes as a punishment, lifts up in order to cast down, and so on; so that for many it would have been better never to have left their former lot.

units.la: II. In vita publica, Hic explicet.
units.tr: II. In public life. Here let him explain:

units.la: I. Ambitum, quo
units.tr: I. The ambition by which:

units.la: a. Inferior dignitate non contentus suo statu, ambit superiorem. Amplificetur inductione dignitatum ac statuum: V. g. plebeus vult esse patricius. Civis affectat dignitatem nobilis, hic Baronis, hic Comitis, hic Principis, Regis, Imperatoris. Illustretur exemplis v. g. plebis Romanæ Vide Florum lib. 1. Pseudophilippi, Marii, Cæsaris: vide & Historiam Græcam: exemplum Alexandri, Alcibiadis &c. Quid non turbarum hinc in Republ. Extendatur hoc ad vanum ambitum titulorum, licet re potiri nequeant: quo præcipue laboret præsens seculum, ceu aqua intercute: quo in speciem majus quidem, at longe deterius ac languidius effectum sit præsens seculum. Frustra Caffanæum contexuisse catalogum gloriæ mundi, quo a summo ad imum omnes dignitatum ordines recensuerit; jam alio longe majori opus esse, cùm unusquisque tantus haberi velit, non quantus est, sed quantum semetipsum æstimat. Utinam in politicis substiterit hic ambitus, imò & ordinem Ecclesiasticum invasisse: hinc tot præsules, Abbates, Episcopos, Archiepiscopos, Primates, Patriarchas, Cardinales, Papas enatos.
units.tr: a. One of lower dignity, not content with his station, aspires to a higher one. Let it be amplified by induction of ranks and states. For example: a plebeian wants to be a patrician; a citizen aspires to the dignity of a noble, one to that of a baron, another of a count, another of a prince, king or emperor. Let it be illustrated by examples, for instance from the Roman plebs; see Florus, book 1, on the Pseudo-Philip, Marius and Caesar; see also Greek history, the examples of Alexander, Alcibiades and others. How many disturbances have arisen in commonwealths from this! Let this be extended to the vain ambition for titles, even when they cannot obtain the reality; this is the chief disease of the present age, like dropsy, which has produced a greater-seeming but far worse and more languid age. In vain has Caffarelli woven his catalogue of worldly glory, in which he has listed all the orders of dignities from highest to lowest; now another, far larger work is needed, since each person wishes to be held as great not as he is, but as great as he esteems himself. Would that this ambition had stopped in political life, and had not even invaded the ecclesiastical order: hence so many prelates, abbots, bishops, archbishops, primates, patriarchs, cardinals and popes have sprung up.

units.la: b. Minor|& imbecillior non contentus sua ditione, principatu, regno, plura ambit: exemplo Assyriorum, Persarum, Alexandri, Romanorum, Turcæ, qui provincias provinciis adjicientes, regna regnis, vasta ista Monarchiarum corpora conflavere. Scilicet quod privati in cumulandis opibus, hoc principes in augendis & amplificandis provinciis agitare. Excusetur aliquatenus hoc amplificandi studium, cum & in ipsa natura fundatum hoc videamus : illustretur si-milibus v. g. 1. Leonis, aquilæ generosæ, qui arceant reli-qua animalia & veluti territorium sibi vindicent. 2. arboris robustæ quæ latè propaget radices & augescat,efferatque ca-cumen supra vicinas: Interim tamen certum unicuique ar-bori mensuræ ac vitæ spacium præfixum &c: Ita etiam obti-nere in rebus humanis. Hinc explicet.
units.tr: b. One who is lesser and weaker, not content with his own domain, principality or kingdom, aspires to more. Take the example of the Assyrians, Persians, Alexander, the Romans and the Turks, who, adding province to province and kingdom to kingdom, have built up those vast bodies of monarchies. Clearly, what private men do in piling up wealth, princes do in enlarging and expanding provinces. This eagerness to expand may be excused to some extent, since we see it founded in nature itself. Let it be illustrated by similes: 1. the lion and the noble eagle, which keep off other animals and claim a territory for themselves; 2. a sturdy tree, which spreads its roots widely, grows, and raises its crown above its neighbours. Yet for each tree a fixed space of size and life is assigned, and so on. It is the same in human affairs. Let him explain from this.

units.la: 2. Frustrationem ambitus : Videlicet uti loca habitationis circum-scripta divinitus, ita & potentiæ terminos fixos esse. Hoc pro-betur.
units.tr: 2. The frustration of ambition: namely, just as the places of habitation have been divinely circumscribed, so also the limits of power are fixed. Let this be proved:

units.la: a. Exemplis quatuor Monarchiarū,quæ licet maxima tunc tem-poris imperia fuerint, tamen universale regnū erigere non po-tuêre,Ita secunda monarchiaHellespontum nunquam sine cla-de transgredi tentavit: probetur exemplis Darii & Xerxis Græciam invadentium. vide Justin. Eadem monarchia Per-sarum ultra Massagetas & Scythas ascendere non potuit. Hinc Cyrus a Thomyri Regina occisus est, Darius Hystaspes frustra Scythas oppugnavit. Porrò ambitus & frustratio Alexandri Magni hic perstringatur. Frustra Campanellam monarchiæ Hispanicæ fundamenta molitum esse. Licet enim sol nunquam occidat in ditionibus Hispani, tamen & in fini-timis suis provinciis detrimentum ipsam pati quotidie.
units.tr: a. By the examples of four monarchies, which, although they were the greatest empires of their time, nevertheless could not raise a universal kingdom. Thus the second monarchy, that of the Persians, never attempted to cross the Hellespont without disaster; let this be proved by the examples of Darius and Xerxes invading Greece; see Justin. The same Persian monarchy could not advance beyond the Massagetae and the Scythians. Hence Cyrus was killed by Queen Tomyris, and Darius Hystaspes attacked the Scythians in vain. Furthermore, the ambition and frustration of Alexander the Great should be touched on here. In vain did Campanella labour to lay the foundations of the Spanish monarchy. For although the sun never sets on the Spaniard's dominions, nevertheless even in their neighbouring provinces they suffer loss every day.

units.la: b. A causa prima Deo, qui solus mundi Monarcha, unicuique regno ac principatui fatales posuerit limites,aut opposita po-testate coërcuerit. Atque hoc esse, quod præcipue jam por-rò evincendum sit. Hinc fiat inductio Regnorum ac Re-rump:
units.tr: b. From the first cause, God, who alone is the Monarch of the world, has set fated limits to each kingdom and principality, or restrained them with opposing power. This is what must now be proved above all. Hence let there be induction of kingdoms and realms:

units.la: a. Antiquorum : quorum præter quatuor Monarchias, qua-rum supra facta est mentio, quædam, ut regnum Ægypti, Sicyonium, Judæorum,Philistæorum, Edomitarum, Amor-rhæorum,Siculorum. Respubl. Athen. Spartana, Romana olim, & Carthaginensis &c. Enarranda, & varia eorun-dem molitio, ejusdemque frustratio explicanda, videl. quod semper intra pristinos ac præstitutos divinitus ter-minos cohibita sint. Ita Romana potentia olim Euphra-tem ab Oriente terminum habuit : quem Crassus, Traja-nus, Valerianus, Julianus,non sine clade transire sategere; à septentrione habuit Caucasum montem, imò ultra Mithridatis regnum in Pontum penetrare non potuere. Claudatur epiphonemate; frustra vatales ac divinitus positos limites, egredi nititur humanus faustus. Illustretur simili ab oceano & fluviis inflatis, quæ frustra repagula a natura posita perrumpere tentant & licet egrediantur, tamen intra terminos redire. Hic se ponent inflati fluctus tui. &c.
units.tr: a. Of the ancients. Among these, besides the four monarchies mentioned above, there were some, such as the kingdom of Egypt, the Sicyonian, Jewish, Philistine, Edomite, Amorite and Sicilian kingdoms, and the Athenian, Spartan, once Roman, Carthaginian and other commonwealths. These are to be recounted, and their various endeavours and the frustration of each explained, namely that they were always confined within their original and prescribed divine limits. Thus the Roman power once had the Euphrates as its boundary to the east, which Crassus, Trajan, Valerian and Julian attempted to cross, not without disaster; to the north it had the mountain Caucasus, and indeed it could not penetrate beyond the kingdom of Mithridates into Pontus. Let it be closed with an epiphonema: human presumption tries in vain to go beyond the fated and divinely appointed limits. Let it be illustrated by a simile from the ocean and swollen rivers, which try in vain to break through the barriers set by nature, and even when they overflow, return within their bounds: "Here shall your swelling waves be stayed," etc.

units.la: <bl>β.</bl> Modernorum, quorum quædam
units.tr: <bl>β.</bl> Of the moderns, some of which:

units.la: α. Natura limitavit: uti v. gr. Angliam, Siciliam, Sardiniam, Japoniam, Candiam, cæterasque insulas, & peninsulas quas mari conclusit, Italiam mari supero & infero, Asiam minorem, Peloponnesum mari &c. Alia montibus altissimis limitavit, ut Hispaniam & Galliam Pyrenæis jugis; Italiam a Gallia & Germania Alpibus, Bohemiam montibus vallavit. Quæ naturæ claustra licet peruperit humana audacia, tamen raro stabilem extra illa sedem posuit. Sic Annibal olim perrupit quidem Pyrenæos & Alpes, at propagare imperii limites non potuit. Romanum imperium subjugaverat Galliam, Hispaniam, Germaniam, at regna ista rursus separata sunt, natura semper recurrente ad pristinos limites. Alia denique Regna rapidis fluminibus distinxit, ut Galliam & Germaniam olim Rheno, Germaniam & Romanas ditiones olim Danubio, Germaniam & Poloniam Vistula, Persiam & Indias Indo flumine, &c.
units.tr: α. Nature has limited: for example England, Sicily, Sardinia, Japan, Crete and the other islands and peninsulas which the sea encloses; Italy by the upper and lower seas; Asia Minor; the Peloponnese by the sea, and so on. Others nature has limited with very high mountains, as Spain and Gaul by the Pyrenean ridges; Italy from Gaul and Germany by the Alps; Bohemia it has walled round with mountains. Although human daring has broken through these barriers of nature, it has rarely established a secure seat beyond them. Thus Hannibal once indeed broke through the Pyrenees and the Alps, but he could not extend the limits of his empire. The Roman empire had subjugated Gaul, Spain and Germany, but these kingdoms were soon separated again, nature always returning to its original limits. Finally, nature has divided other kingdoms by rapid rivers: Gaul and Germany once by the Rhine, Germany and the Roman domains once by the Danube, Germany and Poland by the Vistula, Persia and India by the Indus river, and so on.

units.la: b. Quædam oppositio regno æmulo intra limites continentur, ut orbis ejusque Dominium contineatur in æquilibrio. Hoc ibidem ostendatur inductione. Videl Regno Chinensi robusto Magnus Cham Tartarorum oppositus est ab Septentrione, ab occasu Indorum viribus coërcetur. Tartaris objectus est Moscus & Polonus. Persæ Regnum oppositum est ab Oriente Turcæ, & eidem Magnus Mogor, objectus est. Ejusdem Turcæ, tanquam immanis Leonis potentiæ in Africa Prester S. Johannis & Seriffus Mauritaniæ ac Hispanus oppositi sunt. Ab occidente in Europa Turcæ potentiam coërcent Veneti & Austriaci atque Transilvani; quorum collustationes referendæ breviter. Ita scil. ceu oceanus validis rapibus, ita Turcæ excedens potentia a diversis principibus compecompescitur. Ita Hispaniæ exuberanti potentiæ objectus Gallus, provinciis quidem minor, at quia junctas habet copias ac consilio manuque expeditior par æstimandus. Ita Dania Suëciæ, utrisque Polonus & Moscus & Imperium oppositum est. Vide Trutinam statuum Europæ. Ita Principes ac Resp. imperii, uti & principes Italiæ mutuo metu intra terminos continentur. Sabaudo Helvetia viribus suppar objecta. Pollenti-mari Reip. Belgicæ Anglicana nuper opposita. Quin imò exiguæ Resp. Ragusa & Geneva, illa contra Turcam, hæc contra Sabaudum protectione aliorum se tuentur; alii minores principes & Resp. fœdere conservantur. Papa ficta sanctitate ac vicariatus Christi titulo se tuetur; tanto magis Christianis principibus metuendus, quo ille peculiare veluti Regnum & Remp. in reliquis Regnis ac Rebuspubl. molitur: unde & merito à multis ipsius fictus dominatus rejectus est.
units.tr: b. Certain rival powers are kept within limits by one another, so that the world and its dominion stay in balance. This may be shown by induction. Namely, the strong Chinese kingdom is opposed on the north by the Great Khan of the Tartars, and on the west it is restrained by the forces of the Indians. Opposed to the Tartars are the Muscovite and the Pole. The kingdom of Persia is opposed on the east by the Turk, and the Great Mogul is set against it too. Against the power of the same Turk, like that of a huge lion, are set in Africa the Prester John, the Sherif of Morocco and the Spaniard. On the west, in Europe, the Venetians, the Austrians and the Transylvanians restrain the power of the Turk; their campaigns should be recounted briefly. Thus, as the ocean is checked by strong currents, so the overgrown power of the Turk is checked by various princes. So the Frenchman is set against the overflowing power of Spain; he is smaller in provinces, but since he has united forces and is more ready in counsel and in hand, he is to be reckoned an equal. So Denmark is opposed to Sweden, and to both of them the Pole, the Muscovite and the Empire are opposed. See the balance of the states of Europe. So the princes and free cities of the Empire, as well as the princes of Italy, are kept within their bounds by mutual fear. Switzerland, of no less strength, is set against the Savoyard. The English were lately set against the Dutch Republic, a power at sea. Indeed, the small republics of Ragusa and Geneva defend themselves by the protection of others, the one against the Turk, the other against the Savoyard; other lesser princes and republics are preserved by alliance. The Pope protects himself by feigned holiness and the title of Christ's vicar; he is all the more to be feared by Christian princes, inasmuch as he builds up, as it were, a peculiar kingdom and commonwealth within the other kingdoms and commonwealths; whence his pretended lordship has rightly been rejected by many.

units.la: c. Unum Turcæ imperium in medio orbis veluti situm, expers videtur limitum; dum invicta potentia, versus omnes mundi plagas erumpit. &c. Verum & hanc Turcæ potentiam validissimis viribus a diversis cohiberi; ab Oriente a Persis, a Meridie ab Africæ Regulis & Hispano, a Septentrione à Polonis, Russis, Tattaris, ab occasu a Principibus Italiæ, Rep. Veneta tot victoriis contra ipsum clara, itemque ab Hisp. ab Equitibus Melitensibus, & præcipuè ab Imperio Romano: quod veluti repagulum est, quo ab Ecclesiæ terris communis Christiani nominis terror arcetur. Hinc fiat digressio in querelam de discordia ac bellis inter Reges & principes Christianorum quibus se hactenus invicem attrivere.
units.tr: c. The empire of the Turk alone, placed as it were in the middle of the world, seems to lack limits, since its unconquered power bursts out toward every quarter of the world, etc. But in truth this power of the Turk too is restrained by very strong forces of various kinds: on the east by the Persians, on the south by the kings of Africa and by the Spaniard, on the north by the Poles, the Russians and the Tartars, on the west by the princes of Italy, by the Venetian Republic, famous for so many victories against him, and likewise by the Spanish, by the Knights of Malta, and above all by the Roman Empire, which is as it were a bar by which the common terror of the Christian name is kept off from the lands of the Church. Hence let a digression be made into a lament over the discord and wars among the kings and princes of the Christians, by which they have hitherto worn one another down.

units.la: Conclusio. Votum habeat pacis ac concordiæ, & ἀνταρκείας, quo quisque sive Princeps sive privatus, conditione ac ditione sua contentus, eandem justitiâ regat, & vires animosque contra communem hostem conferat; quo ita Regnum Christi amplificetur. Terminetur precibus ad Deum, ut ipse exundantes populorum motus compescat, & aure am reddat pacem ac tranquillitatem.
units.tr: Conclusio. Let it express a wish for peace and concord, and for self-sufficiency [ἀνταρκεία], so that each person, whether prince or private man, content with his own condition and domain, may rule it justly and direct his strength and spirit against the common enemy; so the kingdom of Christ may be enlarged. Let it end with prayer to God that he would restrain the overflowing movements of the peoples and give back peace and tranquillity.

units.la: XXVI. DE
units.tr: XXVI. ON

units.la: XXVI. THEMA DE LINGUÆ ROMANÆ MAJESTATE.
units.tr: XXVI. A THESIS ON THE MAJESTY OF THE ROMAN TONGUE.

units.la: Exord. à Majestate Imperii Romani. videlicet.
units.tr: Exordium on the Majesty of the Roman Empire, namely:

units.la: I. Ambitiosam inter veteres præsertim juris interpretes agitari quæstionem, utrum Imperatores Romani sint Domini orbis universi; adeò ut si non facto habuerint, de jure tamen ipsis debeatur orbis imperium.
units.tr: I. A keen question is debated, especially among the older jurists, whether the Roman emperors are lords of the whole world; so that, even if they have not held it in fact, the rule of the world is nonetheless due to them by right.

units.la: II. Affirmativam tueri JurisConsultos Italos præsertim & Germanos præcipue veteres ex quarundam Legum & Constitutionum assertione; quas acriter urget vetus juris auriga Bartolus, hæreticum appellans, qui dissentit; & peccare mortaliter ait Hostiensis, & quotquot hosce sequuntur, quos recenset Arturus Duckius de auth. juris Rom.
units.tr: II. The affirmative is defended chiefly by the older Italian jurists and above all by the Germans, on the strength of the assertion of certain laws and constitutions. The old charioteer of law, Bartolus, presses these hard, calling anyone who dissents a heretic; Hostiensis says they sin mortally, and so do all who follow them, whom Arturus Duckius lists in his work on the authentic law of Rome.

units.la: At refellere hanc assertionem merito reliquorum regnorum, Galliæ, Hispaniæ, Angliæ, Daniæ, Suecia Jurisconsultos & recentiores fere omnes; quippe quæ nec in facto nec in jure divino nec humano, aut gentium placito fundata.
units.tr: But the jurists of the other kingdoms, of France, Spain, England, Denmark and Sweden, and almost all the more recent writers, rightly refute this assertion, since it is founded neither on fact, nor on divine law, nor on human law, nor on the consent of nations.

units.la: III. Latissimè quidem olim in omnibus orbis partibus regnasse Romanos, imposuisse jugum & leges devictis gentibus; at sæpe injusta bella gessisse; unde & excussum multis jugum Romanum majori jure quam impositum fuerat. Deinde quàm multa in Oriente & Africa regna & provinciæ fuere Romanis armis incognita? Ut merito hæc sententia sua sponte concidat. Nec ipsos Imperatores, quanta etiam majestate & gloria in Oriente & Occidente fulserint, hoc jus unquam sibi arrogasse; nec capacem esse naturam humanam tantæ molis; quæ ex reservatis est divinæ majestatis, quæ Christo servatori hanc gloriam concessit: hujus celsissimos ministros in regnis & provinciis sibi creditis esse Imperatores, Reges, principes, non orbis Dominos.
units.tr: III. It is true that the Romans once ruled very widely in all parts of the world, and imposed their yoke and laws on conquered peoples; but they often waged unjust wars, and so many peoples shook off the Roman yoke with greater right than it had been imposed. Furthermore, how many kingdoms and provinces in the East and Africa were unknown to Roman arms? Thus this opinion rightly collapses of its own accord. Nor did the emperors themselves, however much majesty and glory they shone with in East and West, ever claim this right for themselves; nor is human nature capable of so great a burden, which is reserved to the divine majesty, who granted this glory to Christ the Saviour. The emperors, kings and princes are the most exalted ministers of His in the kingdoms and provinces entrusted to them, not lords of the world.

units.la: IV. Hæc licet ita sint, tamen non esse negandum, Romano Imperio eximias prærogativas præ reliquis non modo regibus, verum & priorum trium Monarchiarum Dominis fuisse concessas. Et quidem non modo, quod robustissimas totius orbes gentes sibi habuit subjectas; verum etiam, quod supremus mundi Monarcha Jesus Christus subditus Augusti primi Romani ni Monarchæ nasci voluit. Cui & hoc accedit, quod æquissimis instructum sit imperium legibus, unde & Lingua ipsa Rom, suam in hodiernum adhuc majestatem imperatoriam veluti tuetur.
units.tr: IV. Although these things are so, it must not be denied that the Roman Empire was granted distinguished prerogatives above not only other kings, but even the lords of the three earlier monarchies. And indeed this is so not only because it held all the most powerful nations of the whole world subject to itself, but also because the supreme Monarch of the world, Jesus Christ, willed to be born a subject of Augustus, the first Roman monarch. To this is added the fact that the empire was furnished with the most equitable laws, whence the Roman tongue itself still, even today, as it were preserves its imperial majesty.

units.la: Propositio. De hac majestate Linguæ Latinæ dicendum. Sperare te haud indignum aut ingratum fore nobilissimo auditorio argumentum, cui omnes in juventute dediti fuere, & cujus subsidio, Ecclesia, tribunalia, curia & aula in arduis maximè negociis & orbis pace concilianda, conservanda etiam salubiter, utatur. Dicam de re ampla strictè & tenuiter; vestra, A. humana æquitas aliis etiam exhibita sublevabit detectum ruditatemque dicentis.
units.tr: Proposition. Concerning this majesty of the Latin tongue something must be said. I hope that the subject will not be unworthy or unwelcome to this most noble audience, all of whom were devoted to it in their youth, and with whose aid the Church, the courts, the chancery and the court make use of it in the most arduous affairs, especially in establishing and beneficially preserving the peace of the world. I shall speak on a broad matter, briefly and slightly; your human fairness, A., which is shown also to others, will relieve the exposed roughness of the speaker.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Tractatio.

units.la: I. Exponat Linguæ Latinæ amplitudinem
units.tr: I. Showing the breadth of the Latin language

units.la: 1. Per comparationem cum Græca; quæ hactenus post victorias Alexandri Magni longè lateque in Orientem propogata fuerat; uti hactenus in occidente exculta & custos fida artium & disciplinarum: Ita necesse fuit, ut Euangelium per illam propagaretur. Ipsis Romanis in precio fuit, dominans tempore tertiæ Monarchiæ: uti Chaldæa olim sub 1. & 2. Monarchia: cum fœdus Dei cum solis Judæis in Lingua Hebraea continebatur: quod hic in gentium lingua expressum fuit, cum gentes in fœdus assumptæ fuere: Ita linguas olim turbatas in Babel, Deum rursus sanctificasse & organum fecisse suæ gratiæ ac veritatis cœlestis.
units.tr: 1. By comparison with Greek, which after the victories of Alexander the Great had been spread far and wide into the East, just as it had been cultivated in the West and was a faithful guardian of the arts and sciences. So it was necessary that the Gospel should be spread through it. It was held in high esteem by the Romans themselves, who ruled in the time of the third monarchy, just as Chaldea once did under the first and second monarchies. The covenant of God had been contained in the Hebrew language only, for the Jews; here it was expressed in the language of the nations, when the nations were taken into the covenant. Thus God, who once confused the languages at Babel, sanctified them again and made them an instrument of his grace and of heavenly truth.

units.la: 2. Persecutam Linguæ Latinæ dilatationem per Romanos,
units.tr: 2. The later spread of the Latin language through the Romans,

units.la: a. Post victos Carthaginenses hoc egisse Romanos, ut cum imperio linguam suam propagarent, & communi liugua gentes devincirent. Hinc victis gentibus Romanos leges suas imperasse, judicia peragi voluisse in lingua Rom: decreta omnia & rescripta & Senatusconsulta facta in lingua Latina. Hinc Augustinus lib. 19. de Civ. Dei, jussum hunc Linguæ Rom. imperiosum dixit, in omnibus provinciis exacte observatum: Contractus, Testamenta, pacta omnia & documenta, publica, privata, celebrata in hac lingua, ut in judiciis produci possent &c. Prudens institutum hoc ad propagandum imperium; quasi omnia sua bona & jura habehaberent beneficio istius linguæ &c. Sic Codex Gregoria-nus, Hermogenianus & Theodosianus in Latino sermone editus; ut ita in sacris & profanis Romanos Dominos agno-scerent, qui præsentes, absentes in sua lingua ipsis impera-bant. Ipsos Imperatores, licet græcè doctos, non nisi latinè loquutos, adeò ut Tiberius excusaret, cùm voce Monopolii usus esset &c.
units.tr: a. After the defeat of the Carthaginians, the Romans set out to spread their language along with their empire and to bind the nations together by a common tongue. Hence, once nations were conquered, the Romans imposed their laws on them and wanted judgments carried out in the Roman language; all decrees, rescripts and senatorial resolutions were made in Latin. Hence Augustine, in book 19 of The City of God, called this command of the Roman language imperious, strictly observed in all provinces: contracts, wills, all agreements and documents, public and private, were drawn up in this language so that they could be produced in courts, and so on. It was a prudent institution for extending the empire, as if all their goods and rights depended on the benefit of this language. So the Codes of Gregorianus, Hermogenianus and Theodosianus were published in Latin, so that in sacred and secular matters the Romans might be acknowledged as masters who, whether present or absent, commanded them in their own language. Even the emperors, though learned in Greek, spoke only in Latin, so much so that Tiberius apologised when he had used the word monopolium, and so on.

units.la: Equidem trantlata sede imperii Constantinopolin, Græcam Linguam invalescere rursus coepisse, cùm responsa & rescri-ta principis in Græca Lingua publicarentur, uti docent No-vellæ constitutiones Græcæ. Ita corrumpi coepisse in Orien-te linguam Latinam, & ad Ravennam, sedem Exarcharum relegatam & per incursionem barbararum gentium valde corruptam, & in varias dialectos, Italicam Hispanicam, Galli-cam, Anglicam commutatam fuisse; & judicia, contractus omnia græcè gesta in Oriente. Ita juxta Horat. Græcia cap-ta ferum cepit victorem.
units.tr: Indeed, after the seat of empire was transferred to Constantinople, the Greek language began to gain strength again, when the emperor's replies and rescripts were published in Greek, as the Greek Novels (new constitutions) show. Thus the Latin language began to be corrupted in the East, and was relegated to Ravenna, the seat of the exarchs, and was greatly corrupted by the invasion of barbarian peoples, and was changed into various dialects: Italian, Spanish, French, English; and all judgments and contracts were conducted in Greek in the East. So, according to Horace, Greece, having been captured, took its fierce conqueror captive.

units.la: Interim Justinianum Imperatorem in condendo jure operâ Triboniani reliquorumque JCtorum, reduxisse in usum Lin-guam Latinam; cùm exinde causæ disceptandæ essent, & interpretes leges explicarent. Hinc eximium thesaurum es-se linguæ Romanæ tersioris, ex veteribus JCtis depromtum, unde instaurari etiam corrupta lingua potuit paulatim.
units.tr: Meanwhile the Emperor Justinian, in compiling the law with the work of Tribonian and the other jurists, brought the Latin language back into use, since cases were then to be argued and interpreters were to explain the laws. Hence the remarkable treasury of the purer Roman language, drawn from the ancient jurists, from which the corrupted language could gradually be restored.

units.la: II. Explicet Majestatis Linguæ Latinæ instaurationem translato imperio Occidentis ad Carolum Magnum ubi penitus revixis-se Romanam linguam asserat.
units.tr: II. He shows the restoration of the majesty of the Latin language, after the empire of the West was transferred to Charlemagne, and asserts that the Roman language was thoroughly revived.

units.la: 1. Cum jura in hac per totum occidentem infummis passim cu-riis sponte reddita in regnis omnibus Europæ: Unde sermo-nem Romanum commune vinculum omnium mortalium di-cit Choppinus in sacra politica, & Lipsius sermonis latini com-mercio Europæos conjunctos dicit: de Lingua Latina In aula Caroli M. capitula scripta latinè sunt.
units.tr: 1. Since laws were drawn up in this language throughout the West, in the courts everywhere and voluntarily, in all the kingdoms of Europe. Hence Choppin, in his Sacra politica, calls the Roman language the common bond of all mortals, and Lipsius says that the Europeans are joined together by the commerce of the Latin language. Concerning the Latin language: in the court of Charlemagne the capitularies were written in Latin.

units.la: 2. Dum scientiæ omnes, artes ac facultates, Theologia, Juris-prudentia & Medicina in hac lingua publice privatimque tractantur in Ecclesia, Academiis & tribunalibus. Idque non in Germania solùm, sed & in reliquis regnis & rebusp. Idquod nulli adhuc linguæ evenit. Scilicet servare hoc sibi Linguam Rom. ex prisca sua majestate, ut docendo imperet, etiam cum imperatoria ejus majestas in exteris regnis cessat. Tentasse quidem Cardin. Richelium invehere Academiam Gallicam, sed rem in ortu periisse, manssisse linguae Romanae antiquam majestatem.
units.tr: 2. Since all the sciences, arts and faculties, theology, jurisprudence and medicine, are publicly and privately treated in this language in the Church, in the academies and in the courts; and this is so not only in Germany but also in the other kingdoms and republics. This has not happened to any other language. Clearly the Roman language keeps this for itself from its ancient majesty, so that it rules by teaching, even when its imperial majesty ceases in foreign kingdoms. Cardinal Richelieu indeed attempted to introduce a French Academy, but the matter perished at its birth, and the ancient majesty of the Roman language remained.

units.la: Dum publici contractus a Notariis celebrati, collationes beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum in hac lingua celebrantur. Aliique scriptores plerique publica & victura latina lingua utuntur, ut sic ubique locorum legi queant. Reliquas linguas raro extra patriam suam legi: Latina longe lateque &c.
units.tr: Since public contracts are drawn up by notaries in this language, and collations of ecclesiastical benefices are made in it. Most other writers also use the public and enduring Latin language, so that they can be read in every place. Other languages are seldom read outside their own country; Latin is read far and wide, and so on.

units.la: Dum Tractatus omnes inter peregrinos populos ac Monarchias in hac lingua celebrantur; in Legationibus hac tanquam communi interprete Legati utuntur. Quis nisi hac probe instructus publicum munus obire audet?
units.tr: Since all treaties between foreign peoples and monarchies are concluded in this language, ambassadors use it in embassies as a common interpreter. Who, unless thoroughly trained in it, dares to undertake a public office?

units.la: Quo minus mirandum tantopere hanc linguam a veteribus & modernis excultam esse excoliq; a melioribus ingeniis, cui ideo impendendum est studium, quod non sine rubore in ejus puritatem vir doctus impingere queat. In lingua vernacula, quis veretur impingere, at quis non erubescit vel solœcismum in hac lingua imperatrice? Characterem hunc esse dicat priscae & fere congenitae huic linguae majestatis, ut nisi in consueta purpura in publicum prodire vereatur.
units.tr: It is therefore less surprising that this language has been cultivated so much by the ancients and moderns, and is still cultivated by the better minds, and that a learned man ought to devote study to it, since he could not stumble over its purity without a blush. A man may fear to stumble in his vernacular, but who does not blush at even a solecism in this imperial language? Let him say this is the mark of the ancient and almost innate majesty of this language: that it is ashamed to appear in public except in its accustomed purple.

units.la: Hinc comparet Recessus imperii terfissimo sermone Germanico conscriptos. At legem fundamentalem Imperii, Aueam Bullam, licet pro conditione istorum temporum minus terse, terfissimè vero Pacem Augustam, & pacificationem Monasteriensem, vera imperii Palladia, tanquam in aeternis monumentis esse reconditas in lingua hac imperatrice.
units.tr: Hence the recesses of the Empire appear written in a most polished German style. But the fundamental law of the Empire, the Golden Bull, though less polished for the conditions of those times, and most polished the Peace of Augsburg and the Peace of Münster, the true Palladia of the Empire, are preserved as in eternal monuments in this imperial language.

units.la: Colligat inde tacitam praescriptionem contra regna & provincias avulsas ab imperio, quod nimirum tacite majestatem imperii, autoritatem Legum Romanarum adhuc comiter venerari videantur; quippe cujus lingua utuntur; quam olim victis populis Roma imposuit, qua jam, tum sponte, tum necessitate quadam omnes utuntur, eamque venerantur.
units.tr: Let him infer from this a tacit prescription against kingdoms and provinces torn away from the Empire, since they evidently still tacitly venerate, with courtesy, the majesty of the Empire and the authority of Roman law; for they use the language of that law, which Rome once imposed on conquered peoples, and which all now use, both willingly and from some necessity, and which they revere.

units.la: Hanc praescriptionem declinaturos reges & vicinos in suis quemque regnis leges sibi condidisse, quae tamen ex legibus Romanis originem traxerunt, uti ipsae ex sana ratione.
units.tr: The kings and neighbours who wish to avoid this prescription have each made laws for themselves in their own kingdoms; yet these have drawn their origin from Roman laws, as they themselves do from sound reason.

units.la: Hinc
units.tr: Hence

units.la: IV. Hinc speciatim exponat studium Regum Galliæ in Legibus & Lingua Latina declinanda: dum
units.tr: IV. Hence he shows in particular the zeal of the kings of France in reforming the laws and the Latin language, while

units.la: 1. Ludovicus XII. & Franciscus I. in lingua Gallica leges suas publicarunt, & in illa, controversias judicari voluerunt: quod reliqui reges secuti sunt in Gallia.
units.tr: 1. Louis XII and Francis I published their laws in the French language and wished disputes to be decided in it; the other kings in France followed this.

units.la: 2. Ludovicus XIII. & XIV. imprimis linguæ Gallicæ cultum promoverunt, ut in prosa & lingua cum cultissimis linguis, Græcâ atque Romanâ contendere queat.
