units.tr: 2. Louis XIII and XIV above all promoted the cultivation of the French language, so that in prose and in language it might compete with the most cultivated languages, Greek and Roman.

units.la: 3. Hinc frequentari Galliam hodie ab exteris: unde in Germania & Belgio præsertim, in militia, in mercatura, in aulis Gallicam linguam frequentari: & uti Belgicam; ita Germanicam linguam interpolatione vocum & terminorum Gallicorum delectari. Imò cum lingua & habitus virorum, mulierum, & cum vestibus mores Gallicos propagari; hisque omnibus adjungi matrimonia magnatum, ut paulatim magnates Gallicis moribus imbuantur; deinceps facile secuturos videri imperium, cujus lingua, habitu, moribus adeo delectantur.
units.tr: 3. Hence France today is frequented by foreigners; so that in Germany and Belgium especially, French is commonly used in the army, in trade and at courts, and, just as Dutch is used, so the German language delights in an admixture of French words and terms. Indeed, along with language, dress and manners, the French fashions of men and women are spread, and marriages of the great are added to these, so that gradually the great become imbued with French manners; and it seems that the Empire will easily follow, since it so delights in their language, dress and manners.

units.la: Conclusio: Hæc cum ita se habeant, dandam omnino Germaniæ operam, ut non tantum suam vernaculam, sed & Latinam Linguam in debito splendore conservet, & cum illa devolutam ad se imperii majestatem: optandumque ut relegato lepore Gallico, priscum decus linguæ Romanæ etiam in aulas Principum postliminio reducatur, ut in Legibus Salicis aliisque Capitularibus Caroli Magni & successorum usitatum fuisse videmus. Uti moneta publica monela est de majestate imperantis, ita & multo magis lingua, cujus usus quotidianus: ut semper imperantis memores maneant subditi.
units.tr: Conclusion: Since these things stand thus, effort must certainly be given in Germany to preserve not only its vernacular but also the Latin language in due splendour, and with it the majesty of the Empire, which has passed to it; and it is to be wished that, with French charm banished, the ancient glory of the Roman language may be restored by right of return even to the courts of princes, as we see it was customary in the Salic Laws and other capitularies of Charlemagne and his successors. Just as public coinage is a reminder of the majesty of the ruler, so much more is language, whose daily use keeps subjects always mindful of their ruler.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: DE FATIS JUDÆORUM.
units.tr: ON THE FATES OF THE JEWS.

units.la: Exord. A differentia inter homines: videl. uti incomparabilis præferentia hominis præ brutis, ita stupenda differentiam inter homines esse, tam eximio axiomate proditos. Hæc jam 1. per inductionem ostendatur virtuosorum, sceleratorum. 2. Extendatur ad integras gentes & nationes illarumque differentia etiam ostendatur, præsertim quod sapientes aliæ, aliæ barbaræ, aliæ ad imperandum, aliæ ad serviendum natæ: ad imperandum, Assyrii, Persæ, Græci, Romani. ad serviendum Thraces, Indi, Scythæ &c. Causam inquirat, Dei beneplacitum, & hominum socordiam vel industriam, &c. 3. In specie admiretur Judæos præ cunctis gentibus olim ab antiquo in Dei populum electos: quorum juxta Paul. Rom. 2. Sunt adoptio & gloria & federa & legis constitutio, cultus jacer & promissiones; quorum sunt Patres, ex quibus & Christus secundum carnem, &c. Quo magis miranda hodierna ipsorum abjectio.
units.tr: Exordium. On the difference between men. Just as man's incomparable preeminence over the brutes is clear, so the astonishing difference among men is attested by an axiom of such distinction. This is to be shown first by induction, from the virtuous and the wicked. Second, it is to be extended to whole peoples and nations, and their differences are to be shown as well: some nations are born wise, others barbarous; some for ruling, others for serving. For ruling: the Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, Romans. For serving: the Thracians, Indians, Scythians, etc. Let the cause be inquired into: God's good pleasure, and men's sloth or industry, etc. Third, let him marvel in particular at the Jews, who above all nations were long ago chosen as God's people. Of them, according to Paul (Rom. 2), "are the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises; of whom are the fathers, and of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came," etc. All the more remarkable, then, is their present abjection.

units.la: Propositio. Hæc causa quare ipsorum statum & fata paucis consideraturi simus, ut divinam bonitatem juxta & severitatem contemplantes, ipsorum sorte cauti evadamus.
units.tr: Propositio. The reason for this subject is that we shall briefly consider their state and fates, so that, contemplating the divine goodness as well as its severity, we may learn caution from their lot.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Expendat gloriam Judæorum pristinam:
units.tr: Tractatio. I. Let him weigh the former glory of the Jews:

units.la: 1. In Nomine a confessione & laude dicto, & à Juda ad Regium sceptrum evehendo.
units.tr: 1. From the name itself, which is derived from confession and praise, and from Judah, who was raised to the royal sceptre.

units.la: 2. Chaldæis, Babyloniis, Assyriis, Persis, Ægyptiis, Indis &c. quorum a. prædicet potentiam, b. deploret ignorantiam Numinis & veræ virtutis, &c. c. Extollat privilegium Judæorum, quod adoptati à Deo, ad hæreditatem cœli.
units.tr: 2. Compared with the Chaldeans, Babylonians, Assyrians, Persians, Egyptians, Indians, etc., of whom he should a. proclaim the power, b. lament the ignorance of the Deity and of true virtue, etc.; c. extol the privilege of the Jews, that, adopted by God, they are heirs of heaven.

units.la: 3. In gloria, hoc est gloriosa Dei inter illos præsentia, per præsentē allocutionem, per Prophetas, per Ignem, per Urim & Thummim, per altare, templum. Cùm contra reliquerat reliquas gentes ire in viis suis.
units.tr: 3. In the glory, that is, God's glorious presence among them: through direct address, through the prophets, through fire, through the Urim and Thummim, through the altar and the temple; whereas he had left the other nations to walk in their own ways.

units.la: 4. In federibus cum Abrahamo initis, & sæpius repetitis, & solennibus sigillis confirmatis. Quid mirandum magis, quam Deum supremum coire in fedus cum mortali? &c.
units.tr: 4. In the covenants made with Abraham, often repeated and confirmed with solemn seals. What is more wonderful than that the supreme God should enter into covenant with a mortal? etc.

units.la: 5. In Legis datione, ut norint quomodo in sacris & profanis gerere se debeant. Quid sanctius hac lege, sive ejusdem publicationem in Sinai, sive præcepta ejus intueamur? &c. Quid simile in cunctis gentibus? Finxere Legumlatores Dei alloquia &c. At Moses cœlitus revera expertus est.
units.tr: 5. In the giving of the Law, so that they might know how to conduct themselves in sacred and in common matters. What is holier than this law, whether we look at its publication on Sinai or at its precepts? etc. What is similar among all nations? The lawgivers invented God's speeches to them, etc. But Moses truly experienced this from heaven.

units.la: 6. In cultu sacro. Hoc quid sanctius, ubi major reverentia Numinis, in assiduitate, in castitate cultus, in sacrificiis, in ritibus? &c. Cum contra abominabilis cultus & idololatria gentilium, in immolatione hominum, in ludis obscœnis, &c.
units.tr: 6. In the holy worship. What is holier than this, where there is greater reverence for the Deity, in the constancy and purity of the worship, in the sacrifices and in the rites? etc. Whereas the abominable worship and idolatry of the Gentiles, with human sacrifice and obscene games, etc.

units.la: 7. In promissionibus, non temporalibus tantùm, de terra Canan delicatissima &c, sed æternis, & spiritualibus, de gratia, justitia, vita æterna, de Messia ex illorum gente oriturō; cujus majestas extollatur præ cunctis regibus, qui regnum erecturus erat æternum & universale &c. Claudatur epiphonemate : Hanc esse gloriam Judæorum præ cunctis gentibus &c. Hoc jam amplif. potest, comparatione dissimilium illorum, quæ eximia fuere in gentibus reliquis. v.g. 1. Decus Monarchiæ in Assyr: Pers:Græc: Romanis. Illustre illud esse, at quanto illustrior gloria, Dei regi legibus, Christum habere Regem? 2. Leges Draconis, Lycurgi, Solonis, Romanæ: At quanto sanctior Lex Mosis? 3. Oracula gentilium: at quanto divinius Dei oraculum ex propitiatorio, Ephod, per Urim & Thummim, per tot Prophetas &c. 4. Templum Dianæ Ephesinæ: Apollinis, Jovis, at quanto celebrius Templum Hierosolymitanum. &c.
units.tr: 7. In the promises: not only temporal ones, concerning the most delightful land of Canaan, etc., but eternal and spiritual ones, concerning grace, righteousness, eternal life, and the Messiah who was to arise from their nation, whose majesty is to be exalted above all kings, since he was to establish an eternal and universal kingdom, etc. Let it be closed with an epiphonema: this is the glory of the Jews above all nations, etc. This can be further amplified by comparison with the dissimilar things which were outstanding among other nations. For example: 1. The splendour of monarchy among the Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, and Romans. That was illustrious, but how much more illustrious is the glory of being governed by God's laws and having Christ as King? 2. The laws of Draco, Lycurgus, Solon, and the Romans; but how much holier is the Law of Moses? 3. The oracles of the Gentiles; but how much more divine is God's oracle from the mercy seat, from the ephod, through the Urim and Thummim, through so many prophets, etc. 4. The temple of Diana at Ephesus, or of Apollo and Jupiter; but how much more celebrated the temple at Jerusalem, etc.

units.la: II. Exponat contra miseriam Judæorum comparatè cum præcedenti gloria:
units.tr: II. Let him set out, in comparison with the preceding glory, the misery of the Jews:

units.la: 1. Ab antiquo: videl. adoptatos illos quidem esse a Deo in populum, in Abrahamo, Isaco, Jacobo, tanquam singulariter Deo dilectis : at a. tentatos varie (quod ostendat ex histor.) b. peregrinos & captivos in Ægypto ibidemque afflictos dura servitute. Quid hic reliquum ex pristina gloria? &c. c. Eductos quidem, at duris conditionibus; dum duplicabatur labor; transeundum erat mare; peregrinandum; moriendum fuit in deserto; armis occupanda Canaan. Per varios hostes affligendi erant sub Judicibus, Saule &c. Regno quidem inclaruere; at & internis motibus & armis hostium varie concutiendi captivitate Babylonica castigandi; & tandem armis Romanorum, exscindendi. O Populum selicem quidem, at & graviter contra afflictum! &c. Quid simile in cunctis gentibus? Conferat hic reliqua regna; quæ sausto omine ob heroibus condita, floruere, donec eversa, aut ad alium Dominum, sæpe mitiorem, translata sunt. &c. vid. Histor.
units.tr: 1. From of old: namely, that they were indeed adopted by God as a people, in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, as those singularly beloved by God; but a. they were variously tested (which he should show from history); b. they were strangers and captives in Egypt, and there afflicted by harsh servitude. What is left here of their former glory? etc. c. Indeed they were led out, but on harsh terms: their labour was doubled, they had to cross the sea, to wander, to die in the desert, and to seize Canaan by arms. Under the Judges and under Saul they were to be afflicted by various enemies, etc. They shone indeed under their kings, but were also shaken by internal disorders and by the arms of enemies, chastised by the Babylonian captivity, and at last destroyed by the arms of the Romans. O people, indeed happy, but grievously afflicted in turn! etc. What is similar among all nations? Let him here compare the other kingdoms, which, founded under a favourable omen by heroes, flourished until they were overthrown or transferred to another lord, often a milder one, etc. See the histories.

units.la: 2. Tempore moderno: ubi propter spretum & rejectum Servatorem, (crimen longe gravissimum)
units.tr: 2. In modern times, where, on account of the rejected and despised Saviour (by far the gravest crime),

units.la: a. Rejecti sunt à Deo, sine cultu, sine sacris, veluti viva cadavera, postquam vitæ veræ authorem Christum rejecerunt.
units.tr: a. They have been rejected by God, without worship and without sacred rites, like living corpses, since they rejected Christ, the author of true life.

units.la: Quid durius? qui antea populus Dei, jam non populus; antea in gratia, jam in aversione: antea venerabiles omnibus, jam abominabiles &c.
units.tr: What could be harsher? They who were formerly the people of God are now no people; formerly in grace, now in aversion; formerly venerable to all, now abominable, etc.

units.la: Sunt sine regno, sine rege aut rep. opprobrium sunt gentibus omnibus separati, dissipati & dispersi per orbem universum, sine certa sede. Quid tristius? &c, vid Cunæum 1. 3. cap. 4.
units.tr: They are without kingdom, without king or commonwealth, a reproach to all nations, separated, scattered and dispersed throughout the whole world, without any fixed seat. What is sadder? etc. See Cunaeus, bk. 3, ch. 4.

units.la: Sunt sine spe emendationis, quia ipsis fatentibus tempus adventui Messiæ determinatum, diu præteriit: unde & maledicunt illi, qui tempora computat. At verò 1. 70. hebdomadæ Danielis præterlapsæ jam pridem. 2. Sceptrum ablatum & legislator à Juda. 3. Urbs & templum secundum eversa, & desolatio durabit ad finem usque. 4. Gentes conversæ sunt ad Deum. 5. Omnia de Messia prædicta in Christo impleta sunt. 6. Gentes assumptæ sunt in populum Dei, ipsi rejecti.
units.tr: They are without hope of amendment, because, as they themselves admit, the time appointed for the coming of the Messiah has long passed; hence they also curse those who compute the times. But in fact: 1. The seventy weeks of Daniel have long since run out. 2. The sceptre has been taken away, and the lawgiver from Judah. 3. The city and temple were afterwards destroyed, and the desolation will last to the end. 4. The nations have been converted to God. 5. All the things foretold of the Messiah have been fulfilled in Christ. 6. The Gentiles have been taken into the people of God, while they themselves have been rejected.

units.la: Tempore futuro: ubi
units.tr: In future time, where

units.la: Acceptio per prolepsin: vid. Hæc licèt in præsens Judæorum conditio sit, miserabilis & desperata, & indigna illo populo, quem Deus olim elegerat præ cunctis gentibus.
units.tr: Taken by prolepsis: see. Although this is the present condition of the Jews, miserable and desperate, and unworthy of that people whom God once chose above all nations.

units.la: Spem reliquam tamen esse melioris sortis sub ultimis diebus. Hoc
units.tr: Nevertheless, there remains hope of a better lot in the last days. This

units.la: Probetur missis prophetiis variis, V.T. ex Rom. 11. v. 25. & seqq. ubi juxta mentem plerorumque interpretum spes conversionis facta est judæis, vid. Pareum & alios, & argumenta quæ istic suggeruntur in textu.
units.tr: Is to be proved by various prophecies of the Old Testament, and from Rom. 11:25 and following, where, according to the mind of most interpreters, hope of conversion is held out to the Jews; see Pareus and others, and the arguments that are suggested there in the text.

units.la: Vindicetur: Licet n. temporibus Apostolorum, multi ex judæis ad Christum conversi sint, tamen non ita ut ex omnibus gentibus recollecti fuerint; Neque tunc adhuc plenitudinem gentium ingressam fuisse in Ecclesiam.
units.tr: Is to be defended: although in the time of the Apostles many Jews were converted to Christ, yet not in such a way that they were gathered from all nations; nor had the fullness of the Gentiles then entered into the Church.

units.la: Explicetur: quando & qualiter ista judæorum conversio futura sit, non prædictum esse; sed patefactum iri, cum vaticinium illud implebitur.
units.tr: Is to be explained: when and how this conversion of the Jews is to take place has not been foretold, but it will be made plain when that prophecy is fulfilled.

units.la: Peroratio: Hæc esse fata Judæorum, illustria præ cunctis gentibus, pariterque miseranda; at meditanda omnibus, quia in illo populo exemplum beneficiorum & judiciorum divinorum Deus extare publicè voluit, ut in illis & bonitatem & severitatem Dei spe-
units.tr: Peroration: These are the fates of the Jews, illustrious above all nations and equally pitiable, yet to be pondered by all, because in that people God willed to set publicly before us an example of his benefits and judgments, so that in them the goodness and the severity of God may be seen.

units.la: XXVIII. DE FATIS GENTIUM ET POPULORUM RELIQUORUM.
units.tr: XXVIII. ON THE FATES OF THE GENTILES AND OF THE REMAINING PEOPLES.

units.la: Exord. A fatorum vi ineluctabili: videl. passim fata fatorumq; vim ineluctabilem fateri Authores; qui, quæ alii sorti fortunæ, illi rectius fatis adscripsere. Quæ vera sententia est, si fatum recte accipiant, non Stoicum, sed à Deo determinatum. Tale fatum esse tum in rebus physicis; tum in humanis, atque in integris regnis & civitatibus; ita fatum magnarum urbium, fatum insularum notat Florus passim. De fatis Judæorum dictum in præcedenti Oratione.
units.tr: Exordium. On the inescapable power of the fates: namely, authors everywhere acknowledge fates and an inescapable power of the fates, and those who ascribed to fate what others ascribed to chance spoke more rightly. This is the true opinion, if fate is understood rightly: not the Stoic fate, but one determined by God. Such fate exists both in physical things and in human affairs, and in whole kingdoms and states; thus Florus everywhere notes the fate of great cities and the fate of islands. The fates of the Jews were discussed in the preceding oration.

units.la: Propos. Jam de fatis reliquarum gentium & populorum dicendum esse; ut appareat etiam inter gentes remotissimas viguisse Dei providentiam.
units.tr: Proposition. It remains to speak of the fates of the other nations and peoples, so that it may appear that the providence of God flourished even among the most remote nations.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. Præmittat generalem fatorum in gentibus divisionem, quod sint quadruplicia, videl. 1. circa ortum. 2. circa incrementum. 3. circa decrementum, & 4. circa interitum. Hanc enim rerum sublunarium esse conditionem: &c. Solum Deum exemptum, cujus est esse perpetuum & immutabile, ipsum omnium fata dispensare &c. quibus frustra obluctetur mortalis. &c.
units.tr: I. Let him first set out the general division of the fates among the nations, namely that they are fourfold: (1) concerning origin; (2) concerning growth; (3) concerning decline; and (4) concerning destruction. For this is the condition of things under the moon, etc. God alone, who is exempt, whose being is perpetual and unchangeable, dispenses the fates of all things, etc., against which mortal men struggle in vain, etc.

units.la: II. Exponat partes singulas.
units.tr: II. Let him explain the individual parts.

units.la: 1. Circa ortum populorum notet:
units.tr: 1. Concerning the origin of peoples, let him note:

units.la: a. Illum, ut omnium rerum, esse humilem ut plurimum: Deü veluti ex semine exiguo arboré; ita ex imbecilici infantia deducere gentem per secundam generationem, stabilitam initio rerum. Et hunc naturalem esse: ita Patriarchas ipsorumque liberos excrevisse paulatim.
units.tr: a. That this origin, as with all things, is usually lowly: as God brings a tree from a small seed, so He brings a nation from the feeble infancy of a second generation, established at the beginning of things. And this origin is natural: thus the patriarchs and their children grew gradually.

units.la: b. Alium esse civilem, cum mortales se junxerunt & novas sedes vacuas sibi quæsiverunt terra patente & sufficiente omnibus: exemplo Caini reliquorumque, in confusione linguarum; uti &Abrahami, Lothi, &c vide Lazium de migrat. populorum, item Ionum reliquorumq; Græcorum; Turcarum. c. Aliam denique militarem & violentam, cum Heroes aliique violenti alios subegerunt, ut Nimrodus &c. Cyrus, Alexander; Romani etiam spontanea deditione. Vide exempla. Scilicet ex talibus initiis gentes, regna, resp. conflata fuisse olim: jam rarius, quia occupata omnia & stabilita potentia sunt.
units.tr: b. Another origin is civil, when mortals joined together and sought new settlements for themselves in a land lying open and sufficient for all: an example is Cain and the others, at the confusion of tongues; likewise Abraham, Lot, etc.; see Lazius on the migrations of peoples; likewise the Ionians and the other Greeks, and the Turks. c. Finally, there is a third origin, military and violent, when heroes and other violent men subdued others, as Nimrod, etc., Cyrus, Alexander; the Romans too by voluntary surrender. See the examples. Clearly, from such beginnings, nations and kingdoms and commonwealths were formed in former times; now more rarely, because all things are occupied and power is established.

units.la: Circa incrementum notet.
units.tr: Concerning growth, let him note:

units.la: Quosdam populos exiguo durasse tempore, alios longo. Terminios fatales quidem regnorum, rerumpubl. determinasse politicos 200. 500. vel mille annos, sed nihil certi statui posse, Deo determinante haec pro arbitrio. Vide exempla ex Graeca Historia.
units.tr: That some peoples endured for a short time, others for a long time. Political writers have indeed set fated limits to kingdoms and commonwealths, 200, 500, or a thousand years, but nothing certain can be laid down, since God determines these things at His pleasure. See examples from Greek history.

units.la: Quosdam late imperasse, alios exiguo spacio coarctatos. V:Act.17. & exempla.
units.tr: That some ruled widely, others were confined to a small space. See Acts 17, and examples.

units.la: Quosdam virtutibus floruisse; alios vitiis se mancipasse. Et hanc esse causam praecipuam floris & contra interitus populorum. vide exempla in Dario Medo & Alexandro Magno, in Romanis, in Gallis praesertim, Hispanis, Anglis, Suecis, Danis, Venetis, Helvetiis, Belgis &c. Praedicet hic per quae gens quaeque emerserit &c.
units.tr: That some flourished in virtues, others gave themselves over to vices. And this is the chief cause of the flourishing and, on the contrary, of the destruction of peoples. See examples in Darius the Mede and Alexander the Great, in the Romans, especially in the Gauls, Spaniards, English, Swedes, Danes, Venetians, Swiss, Belgians, etc. Let him here proclaim through what means each nation has risen.

units.la: Circa decrementa. Hic:
units.tr: Concerning decline. Here:

units.la: Ostendat fatalem circulum; summis scilicet negatum esse stare diu. Ostendatur in rebus naturalibus & humanis.
units.tr: Let him show the fated cycle: namely, that it has been denied to the highest things to stand for long. Let this be shown in natural and human things.

units.la: Ostendat exemplis Romanorum praesertim, ex summo fortunae culmine, paulatim deficientium; item imperii Orientalis, penitus subjugati a Turcis.
units.tr: Let him show, by examples chiefly of the Romans, who gradually failed from the highest peak of fortune, and likewise of the Eastern empire, utterly subjugated by the Turks.

units.la: Causam arguat praesertim luxum & securitatem, nascentem ex nimia felicitate. vide Sallust. Conjur: Catilin: initio.
units.tr: Let him argue for the cause, chiefly luxury and security, arising from excessive prosperity. See Sallust, at the beginning of the Conspiracy of Catiline.

units.la: Circa interitum. Hic:
units.tr: Concerning destruction. Here:

units.la: Casum & finem praecipuorum aliquot regnorum & populorum explicet. vide Bisselii Illustres Ruinas.
units.tr: Let him explain the fall and end of some of the principal kingdoms and peoples. See Bissel's Illustrious Ruins.

units.la: Causam inquirat ordinationem Dei, qui nihil voluit esse aeternum in mundo.
units.tr: Let him inquire into the ordering of God, who willed that nothing in the world should be eternal.

units.la: Peroratio. 1. Summam breviter repetat. 2. Usum doceat, ut revereri discant omnes, summi, infimi, supremum Numen, tanquam stratorem regnorum, & judicem populorum etiam remotissimorum ac barbarissimorum; utq; ad Regnum illud ἀμετάβατον aspiremus.
units.tr: Peroration. (1) Let him briefly repeat the sum. (2) Let him teach the use, so that all, high and low, may learn to revere the supreme Deity as the overthrower of kingdoms and the judge of peoples, even the most remote and most barbarous; and so that we may aspire to that kingdom which is unchangeable [ἀμετάβατον].

units.la: XXIX. THEMA LIBERUM.
units.tr: XXIX. FREE THEME.

units.la: Japhetus pellectus in tentoria Semi, seu irruptiones Barbararum Gentium in Imperium.
units.tr: Japheth enticed into the tents of Shem, or the invasions of the barbarous nations into the Empire.

units.la: Exord. à perpetuo æstu & inquietudine populorum. Videlicet magnos tempestatum mariumque motus esse; at longe majores populorum ac regnorum. Horat. Non sic Lybicis &c. Causam esse mentium humanarum inquietudinem ac ambitionem immensam &c. Hinc semper bella, turbæ, cædes, exilia. Moderatricem interea in omnib9 divinam esse providentiam; quæ per ipsas gentium turbas sua exsequitur consilia & exorbitantias reducit ad harmoniam decentem.
units.tr: Exordium. From the perpetual agitation and restlessness of peoples. Clearly there are great movements of storms and seas; but far greater ones of peoples and kingdoms. Horace: Not so the Libyan sea... The cause is the restlessness and immense ambition of human minds, etc. Hence always wars, disturbances, slaughters, exiles. Meanwhile, that divine providence governs all things, which through the very tumults of the nations carries out its counsels and brings its irregularities back into a fitting harmony.

units.la: Propositio. In præsentiarum de fatalibus gentium septentrionalium irruptionibus in Imperium Romanum paucis dicendum esse; & in ipsis confusionibus spectandum Moderatorem Deum, qui ex tenebris lucem splendescere facit.
units.tr: Proposition. At present, something must be said briefly about the fated invasions of the northern nations into the Roman Empire; and amid these confusions we must regard God as the Governor, who causes light to shine out of darkness.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Proponat vaticinium Noachi, quo divino illustratus Spiritu Orbis novi fata prædixit. Ita fortuito affectu humano dicta sæpe videri, quæ à prænuncio futurorum Dei Spiritu profecta. Ita Gen.9. Noah. loquitur Maledictus Chanaan, servus servorum erit fratribus. Benedictus Jehova Deus Semi, eritque Canaan servus illius. Dilatabit seu alliciet Deus Japhetum, ut habitet in tentoriis Semi, eritque Canaan servus illorum. En paucis verbis amplissimum vaticinium, statumorbis universi aperiens.
units.tr: Treatment. I. Let him set forth the prophecy of Noah, in which, illumined by the divine Spirit, he foretold the fates of the new world. Thus words spoken from a chance human feeling often seem to be from the Spirit of God who foretells the future. So Noah speaks in Gen. 9: Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers. Blessed be Jehovah, the God of Shem, and Canaan shall be his servant. God shall enlarge, or entice, Japheth, that he may dwell in the tents of Shem, and Canaan shall be their servant. Behold, in a few words, a most ample prophecy, setting out the state of the whole world.

units.la: Hoc jam ordine explicer.
units.tr: I shall now explain this in order.

units.la: I. Initium.
units.tr: I. Beginning.

units.la: 1. En! Chamo ejusque posteris servitus prædicitur, in publica hac orbis distributione. Chamo loca meridionalia, Africa præsertim assignata. Verum ad servitutem nata erat gens, uti Æthiopes, &c. Affectabat mature nepos Chami Nimrodus imperium; at expulsi ipsius posteri à dominio Orientis, quod Semo debebatur. Hinc ostendat quis status Africæ fuerit succedentibus temporibus: scil. barbari & ad servitutem nati fuere. Cananei floruere ad tempus, donec exitio maturescerent, & Semi posteris daretur terra illorum, Vide Hist. Genef. Ægyptus Nebucadnezari & Cambysi subacta fuit tandem. Semo contigit benediction: inde enim florentes imperio gentes & natio Hebræorum, decus orbis universi suo tempore. &c.
units.tr: 1. Behold! Servitude is foretold for Ham and his posterity in this public distribution of the world. Ham was assigned the southern regions, Africa especially. But the nation was born for servitude, like the Ethiopians, etc. Nimrod, the grandson of Ham, early aspired to empire; but his descendants were expelled from the dominion of the East, which was owed to Shem. Hence let him show what the state of Africa was in the succeeding times: namely, that they were barbarous and born for servitude. The Canaanites flourished for a time, until they ripened for destruction and their land was given to the posterity of Shem. See the History of Genesis. Egypt was at last subdued by Nebuchadnezzar and Cambyses. Shem received the blessing: for from him came the nations flourishing in empire and the Hebrew nation, the glory of the whole world in its time, etc.

units.la: Japhetus alliciendus dicitur in tentoria Semi, ultimis scilicet temporibus. Primo cum posteri ejus in Græciam, Italiam, Hispaniam, Galliam, Germaniam extremumque Septentrionem Scythiâ depulsi fuere, densis tenebris gentilissimi obruti, barbarie sepulti. Donec tandem illuxit tempus restitutionis. Alexander Macedo Japhetæus, pellici cœpit per Jaddum ad aliquam notitiam; & ipse Linguam Græcam, tanquam futurum organum conversionis gentium ad tentoria Semi, ad Christum filium Davidis, profeminavit in Orientem; sic perductî ad tentoria Semi.
units.tr: Japheth is said to be enticed into the tents of Shem, namely in the final times. First, when his posterity were driven into Greece, Italy, Spain, Gaul, Germany and the farthest North, Scythia, overwhelmed by the thick darkness of the most heathen, buried in barbarism. Until at last the time of restoration dawned. Alexander the Macedonian, a son of Japheth, began to be enticed through Jaddus to some knowledge; and he himself, sowing the Greek language abroad in the East as the future instrument of the conversion of the nations to the tents of Shem, to Christ the son of David; thus were they brought to the tents of Shem.

units.la: III. Successum uberiorem:
units.tr: III. A more abundant success:

units.la: In irruptione Barbarorum in imperium Romanum occidentale: ab anno 300. & seqq.
units.tr: In the invasion of the barbarians into the western Roman Empire: from the year 300 onward.

units.la: Germanicarum nationum, ut Gothorum, Vandalorum, Anglo-Saxonum, Francorum, Gepidarum, Herulorum, Longobardorum, Burgundionum, Nortmannorum, vide Histor. & in specie Jornandem & Hornii orbem politicum. p. 144. & seqq.
units.tr: Of the German nations, such as the Goths, Vandals, Anglo-Saxons, Franks, Gepids, Heruli, Lombards, Burgundians, Normans; see the histories, and in particular Jornandes and Horn's Orbis politicus, p. 144 and following.

units.la: Hunnorum, ut sunt Avares, Alani, Ungari, Turci, Tattari.
units.tr: Of the Huns, such as the Avars, Alans, Hungarians, Turks, Tatars.

units.la: Sarmatarum, ut sunt Slavi, Russi, Obotritæ, Sorabi, Zechi, Venedi, Croatæ, Moravi, Bosnii, Rossii, Servi, Bulgari.
units.tr: Of the Sarmatians, such as the Slavs, Russians, Obotrites, Sorbs, Czechs, Wends, Croats, Moravians, Bosnians, Rossi, Serbs, Bulgarians.

units.la: Ex hisce regna occidentis fundata ipsumque imperium occidentis. Vid. Horn. orb. polit pag. 144. & seqq.
units.tr: From these the kingdoms of the west were founded, and the western empire itself. See Horn, Orbis politicus, p. 144 and following.

units.la: In invasione Sarmatarum, & post Turcorum in imperium orientis ab Anno 600.
units.tr: In the invasion of the Sarmatians, and afterwards of the Turks, into the eastern Empire from the year 600.

units.la: Eventum. Licet magna inde clades imperio utrique, tamen sic factum fuisse, ut gentes Japheticæ densis gentilissimi & barbariei tenebris involutæ, ex parte ad Ecclesiam reductæ, et sic in tentoria Japheti pellectæ fuerint.
units.tr: The outcome. Although great disaster came from this to both empires, nevertheless it came about that the Japhetic nations, wrapped in the thick darkness of heathenism and barbarism, were in part brought back to the Church, and thus enticed into the tents of Japheth.

units.la: Imo, ut Semi posteritas orbis imperium obtinuit tempore primæ & secundæ Monarchiæ; ita tempore tertiæ & quartæ Monarchiæ Japheti progenies rerum potitur, & imperat, servit interim fœdissimis dominis Turcis allisque Mahumedanis & Barbaris, Chami maledicti soboles; servietque donec ad benedinedictam Semi posteritatem ad Christum & Ecclesiam postli- minio revertetur.
units.tr: Indeed, just as the posterity of Shem obtained dominion of the world in the time of the first and second monarchies, so in the time of the third and fourth monarchies the progeny of Japheth holds and exercises power, while meanwhile the cursed son of Ham, the offspring of the most foul masters the Turks and other Mahometans and barbarians, serves; and he will serve until, by a return of right, he is restored to the blessed posterity of Shem, to Christ and the Church.

units.la: Conclus. Hanc esse brevem delineationem fatorum orbis, quam prae- nuncio Dei spiritu Noachus, orbis instaurati haeres & possessor uni- cus suis posteris praedixit. Impleta ita videre nos pleraque, & implenda esse reliqua, antequam ad magnam illam panegyrim gen- tes universae congregabuntur, & ad aeternum decus, aut dedecus dispescentur. &c.
units.tr: Conclusion. This is a brief outline of the fates of the world, which Noah, heir and sole possessor of the restored world, foretold to his posterity by the prophetic Spirit of God. Thus we see that most of it has been fulfilled, and the rest is yet to be fulfilled, before all the nations are gathered to that great assembly, and are divided to eternal glory or shame. etc.

units.la: XXX. DE LEGUM ORIGINE, MONUMENTIS AC NECESSITATE SALUTARI.
units.tr: XXX. On the Origin, Monuments and Salutary Necessity of Laws.

units.la: Exord. A sententia Platonis aliorumque de aureo seculo sub Satur- no: quod nihil confusum, nihil ferum, nullae leges, nulla seditio nullum bellum fuerit; nec, Deo regente, civitatum constitutiones ullae exstiterint: cui concinit Ovid. 1. Met. Aurea prima sata est aetas, quae vindice nullo, Sponte sua sine lege fidem rectum- que colebat. Scil. splendide jactari haec, sed nusquam inveniri. Nisi quod forte de statu Paradisi ante lapsum inaudiverint gentes. Verum hunc statum exigui fuisse temporis. Dehinc legum reti- naculis cohibendam semper fuisse hominum malitiam; nec nisi efferatos quorundam mores leges respuisse. Imo nec illos sine omni juris legumque freno vivere posse existimandum esse; cum nec latrones sine illis una degere queant. &c.
units.tr: Exordium. The opinion of Plato and others about the golden age under Saturn: that there was no confusion, no savagery, no laws, no sedition, no war; and that under God's rule no constitutions of states existed. Ovid agrees in Met. 1: "The first age was the golden one, which, with no avenger, of its own accord without law kept faith and right." That is to say, these things are boasted of splendidly but nowhere found. Except that perhaps the nations have heard something of the state of Paradise before the Fall. But that state lasted only a short time. Afterwards, the malice of men has always had to be restrained by the nets of laws; and only the savage morals of certain people have rejected laws. Indeed, it must be thought that such people cannot live without some bridle of right and law, since not even robbers can live together without them. Etc.

units.la: Propof. In praesentiarum itaque de Legum Origine ac salutari ne- cessitate differendum.
units.tr: Proposition. Accordingly, at present we are to discuss the origin of laws and their salutary necessity.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. Inquirat legum Originem:
units.tr: I. Let us inquire into the origin of laws:

units.la: 1. Deus est, uti autor naturae, ita fons omnis ordinis ac recti. Hoc enim justum esse, non quod opinioni hominum, sed quod menti ac voluntati divinae conforme est. Illam enim legem aeternam esse, ex qua omnes bonae leges. vid. Cic. 1. de Legg. initio.
units.tr: 1. God is, as the author of nature, so also the fountain of all order and of what is right. For that is just which conforms not to the opinion of men but to the divine mind and will. For that is the eternal law from which all good laws derive. See Cicero, De Legibus, 1, at the beginning.

units.la: Hinc ostendat porro:
units.tr: Hence he should further show:

units.la: a. Leges primas a Deo latas in populo Dei, v.g. de non com- edendo ex arbore: scil. ut sic de supremo Dei dominio edoedocerentur: de laborando horto, obediendo marito: de plectendo homicida: sic vitæ, bonorum, libertatis dominum ac arbitrum se ostendit. Subducens se hisce legibus Cainus, suas leges vi armata suis obtrusit, exstructa urbe, invectis armis: Succeßit lex judæorum à Deo lata, cujus irrefragabilis authoritas explicetur; quippe quæ in conspectu totius populi lata cœlitus.
units.tr: a. That the first laws were given by God to the people of God: for example, about not eating from the tree; about working the garden and obeying the husband; about punishing the murderer. Thus he showed himself lord and arbiter of life, goods and liberty, in respect of his supreme dominion. Cain, withdrawing from these laws, imposed his own laws on his people by armed force, after building a city and bringing in weapons. The law of the Jews, given by God, succeeded it; its irrefragable authority is to be explained, since it was given from heaven in the sight of the whole people.

units.la: Legumlatores Dei autoritatem mentitos fuisse ad autoritatem legum, ut Minos Cretensis Jovem, Solon Palladem, Lycurgus Apollinem, Numa Deam Ægeriam seu Junonem, Mahomet ipsum Deum: vid. Machiav. lib. 1. de rep. c. 11.
units.tr: That lawgivers falsely claimed the authority of God for the authority of their laws: as Minos of Crete claimed Jupiter, Solon Pallas, Lycurgus Apollo, Numa the goddess Egeria or Juno, and Mahomet God himself. See Machiavelli, Discourses on Livy, book 1, chapter 11.

units.la: Concludat, Deum esse unicum Legislatorem, qui solus suo jure, & quidé justa imperat, cujus voluntas norma omnis recti & fonsfincerus est. Reliquas leges tantum valere, quantum in thesi cum hac consentiunt.
units.tr: He should conclude that God is the sole Lawgiver, who alone commands by his own right, and indeed justly, and whose will is the norm of all right and the pure fountain. The other laws have only as much validity as they agree in principle with this.

units.la: Recta ratio, utpote Dei imago quædam, cui ipse radios suæ rectitudinis impressit. Hinc
units.tr: Right reason, as a certain image of God, upon which he has impressed the rays of his own uprightness. Hence:

units.la: Prædicet rationis præstantiam.
units.tr: He should extol the excellence of reason.

units.la: Deploret ejus per peccatum obfuscationem.
units.tr: He should lament its clouding through sin.

units.la: Gratuletur de reliquiis luminis & rectitudinis in naturalibus & civilibus: ex quibus salutares tot leges etiam inter gentes fluxere. vid. Cic. 1. 1. de Legib. & Hug. Grot.
units.tr: He should rejoice at the remnants of light and rectitude in natural and civil matters, from which so many salutary laws have also flowed among the nations. See Cicero, De Legibus, book 1, and Hugo Grotius.

units.la: Viri sapientes, & in Philosophia practica præsertim ac historia Rerum p. versati; qui ex naturæ fontibus leges deduxerunt; quales fuere illi qui jura condiderunt & cum authoritate explicarunt; quorum præcipuos aliquot adducat. vid. Cic. lib. 3. de LL.
units.tr: Wise men, especially those well versed in practical philosophy and the history of things, who drew laws from the springs of nature; such were those who framed and expounded the laws with authority. He should adduce some of the most outstanding of them. See Cicero, De Legibus, book 3.

units.la: Deducat hinc porisma: videl.
units.tr: Hence he should draw this corollary, namely:

units.la: Immotos esse fontes, & certa principia ex quibus jus ac leges derivatæ sunt, rectam ratione in scil. quatenus illa intuetur regulam æternam in mente divina.
units.tr: That the fountains are unmoved, and that the certain principles from which right and laws are derived are fixed, insofar as right reason beholds the eternal rule in the divine mind.

units.la: Tanto sinceriores esse leges, quanto minus à fonte recedunt, uti in rivis hoc videmus & fluminibus.
units.tr: That laws are the purer the less they recede from the source, as we see in streams and rivers.

units.la: Variare leges pro varietate ingeniorum, prout illa limpidiora, aut turbida magis sunt affectibus; itemque pro varievarietate circumstantiarum, & applicatione ad singularia, &c.
units.tr: That laws vary according to the variety of minds, as those are clearer or more turbid by the passions; and likewise according to the variety of circumstances and their application to particulars, etc.

units.la: Discutiat hinc quæstionem, utrum jus natura an opinione constet; distinguendo inter fontes & applicationem ad singularia. vid. Juris Consultos.
units.tr: Hence he should discuss the question whether right is grounded in nature or in opinion, distinguishing between the sources and their application to particulars. See the jurists.

units.la: II. Monumenta celebriora recensentur uti sunt.
units.tr: II. The more famous monuments are enumerated as they are.

units.la: 1. Lex Israelitarum per Mosen lata. Hanc fuere ex fonte limpidissimo, Deo in monte Sinai illam publicante. vid. Exod. 20. Hujus autem allationem paucis referat. b. Sanctitate pro conditione istius reip. commendet, c. Et finem cum sine reip. judaicæ consentientem.
units.tr: 1. The law of the Israelites given through Moses. This came from the purest source, God proclaiming it on Mount Sinai. See Exodus 20. He should relate briefly its promulgation; commend its holiness in view of the condition of that commonwealth; and note that its end agreed with the purpose of the Jewish state.

units.la: 2. Leges Græciæ, Draconis, Solonis & Lycurgi, in Rep. Athen. & Lacedæm. uti & Minois & Rhadamanti in Creta. Hasce multa severitate conscriptas, respublicas istas & Græciam tenuisse in obsequio & statu suo, donec paulatim neglectæ, primo discordias, deinde ruinam celeberrimarum civitatum induxerint. vid: Xenophont. de rep. Athen. & Laced. Plut. A. Gell. Cic. de Legib. &c.
units.tr: 2. The laws of Greece: of Draco, Solon and Lycurgus, in the commonwealths of Athens and Sparta; and of Minos and Rhadamanthus in Crete. These, written with great severity, held those commonwealths and Greece in obedience and in their condition, until, being gradually neglected, they first brought about discords and then the ruin of the most famous cities. See Xenophon, On the Republic of the Athenians and Lacedaemonians; Plutarch; Aulus Gellius; Cicero, De Legibus; etc.

units.la: 3. Leges Romanæ: a. descriptæ ex Legibus Solonis per decemviros in XII. tabulis. b. Variis interpretationibus emendatæ auctæ & reip. Rom. accommodatæ per Prætores præsertim, c. Per Salvianum in Edictum perpetuum translatæ. d. JCtorum & Sapientum commentationibus illustratæ. e. Auspicio Justiniani per Tribonianum, Dorotheum &c. contractæ, in ordinem collectæ, & in luculentam hanc consonantiam redactæ. f, Postmodum per Lotharium Imperatorem instauratæ & in Academias & tribunalia introductæ, a Germanis aliisque populis cultioribus receptæ tanquam plenissimæ, æquissimæ. vid. t. Cod. de Orig. juris. Forsneri Histor. juris Rom. Scultzium aliosque ad instituta, &c.
units.tr: 3. The Roman laws: a. drawn up from the laws of Solon by the decemvirs in the Twelve Tables. b. emended, enlarged by various interpretations and adapted to the Roman commonwealth, chiefly by the praetors. c. transferred into the Perpetual Edict by Salvius Julianus. d. illustrated by the commentaries of jurists and wise men. e. under the auspices of Justinian, gathered together by Tribonian, Dorotheus and others, arranged in order, and brought into this clear harmony. f. afterwards restored by the Emperor Lothar and introduced into the academies and courts, and received by the Germans and other more cultivated peoples as most complete and most equitable. See the title On the Origin of Law in the Code; Forsner's History of Roman Law; Schultingius and others on the Institutes, etc.

units.la: III. Agat de Legum necessitate salutari, vidisse nos breviter Legum originem ac monumenta præcipua; jam paucis salutarem earundem necessitatem considerandam esse. Patere illam.
units.tr: III. He should treat of the salutary necessity of laws. Having briefly seen the origin and the principal monuments of laws, now in a few words the salutary necessity of the same is to be considered. It is evident as follows.

units.la: 1. Quia nullum regnum, nulla resp. nullus pagus, nulla domus sine legibus saltem tacitis esse queat. Hinc scil. ipsis Rebus per leges coire cœpisse homines. Unde de enim societas, nisi quod in certa pacta conspirarunt? Adeo ut nec fures aut latrones sine Legibus esse queant.
units.tr: 1. Because no kingdom, no commonwealth, no village, no household can exist without laws, at least unwritten ones. Hence, indeed, men began to come together by means of laws in the things themselves. For what is society but that men have agreed upon certain covenants? So much so that not even thieves or robbers can exist without laws.

units.la: Quia invicta malitia hominum plurimorum est; quæ sine legum repagulis contineri in officio nequit. Hinc horuisse regna, Resp. quamdiu legum authoritas valuit; pessum ivisse, cum leges collapsæ aut neglectæ fuere.
units.tr: Because the invincible malice of very many men is such that it cannot be kept in duty without the barriers of laws. Hence kingdoms and commonwealths have flourished as long as the authority of the laws prevailed; and have perished when the laws collapsed or were neglected.

units.la: Quia lex anima est civitatis, juxta Synesium; quod simile exponatur in protasi & apodosi: itemque quod Lex norma est rerum agendarum & judiciorum. Quanta jam necessitas, quanta utilitas regulæ & normæ, tantam etiam Legis esse. Hinc tot apud authores Legum encomia, quorum notabiliora aliquot afferat.
units.tr: Because law is the soul of the state, according to Synesius; this can be explained by a protasis and apodosis. Likewise, law is the norm of things to be done and of judgments. As great as the necessity and usefulness of a rule and norm is, so great also is that of law. Hence the many encomiums of law among the authors, of which he should set forth some of the more notable.

units.la: Quia hinc nulla Resp. sine legibus, primò quidem non scriptis, cum arbitria principum pro legibus essent; postmodum vero scriptis: ut in Rep. Hebræorum, Græcorum, Rom. & dehinc omnium politarum gentium, &c.
units.tr: Because hence no commonwealth exists without laws: at first indeed unwritten, since the wills of princes were in place of laws; afterwards written, as in the commonwealths of the Hebrews, the Greeks, the Romans, and thereafter of all civilized nations, etc.

units.la: Paucis summa capita repetat, & ad legum observantiam cultumque excitet. Legibus enim obedire veram libertatem esse; uti contra refragari legibus, summum scelus, summa miseria ac servitus.
units.tr: He should briefly recall the chief heads and rouse men to the observance and cultivation of the laws. For to obey the laws is true liberty; whereas to resist the laws is the greatest crime, and the greatest misery and servitude.

units.la: XXXI. DE FATIS TEMPORUM.
units.tr: XXXI. Concerning the Fates of the Times.

units.la: A dicto Senecæ Tragœdi: Fatis regimur mortale genus.
units.tr: A saying of the tragic poet Seneca: "We mortals are ruled by the fates."

units.la: Proponatur cum elogio Autoris tanquam rerum ac styli majestate longe gravissimi, & salutaribus vitæ monitis saluberrimi.
units.tr: It is to be put forward with the praise of the author, as by far the most serious in the dignity of his matter and style, and most wholesome in his salutary admonitions for life.

units.la: Illustretur dictum paraphrasi: vid. indicare ipsum voluisse, non forte fortuna jactari res humanas ut Epicuræi & Sceptici putabantur, sed certa lege divinitus posita gubernari omnia, & præcipue res mortalium.
units.tr: The saying is to be illustrated by a paraphrase: namely, to show that he meant not that human affairs are tossed about by chance, as the Epicureans and Sceptics supposed, but that all things, and especially the affairs of mortals, are governed by a certain law divinely established.

units.la: Addatur ratio: quia præcipuè curæ sunt Deo homines, propter quos condita sunt omnia. Uti igitur divina providentia se extendit ad omnia minima, maxima; ita illam præcipue vigilare in rebus mortalium. vid. Psalm. 139. aliaque testimonia de divina providentia. Illustretur simili à patrefamilias, qui uti totam domum, ita præcipuè liberos suos curat & diligit: ita Deus societatem humanam. Concludatur merito igitur dixisse Senecam. Fatis regimur, &c.
units.tr: A reason is to be added: because men are the special concern of God, for whose sake all things were made. Just as the divine providence extends to all things, the least and the greatest, so it watches especially over the affairs of mortals. See Psalm 139 and other testimonies concerning divine providence. Let it be illustrated by a simile from the head of a household, who cares for and loves his children especially, as he does the whole house; so God cares for human society. Let it be concluded, therefore, that Seneca rightly said: "We are ruled by the fates," etc.

units.la: IV. Hoc ulterius explicetur: videl. At non semper eodem modo regires mortalium, sed habere suas vices ac mutationes perpetuas, unde constans rerum vicissitudo, superans captū mortalium. Propof. De constanti hac rerum varietate, seu fatis temporum dicendum, si solita patientia ac benevolentia juvare conantem velint.
units.tr: IV. This is to be explained further: namely, that the government of mortals is not always the same, but has its turns and constant changes, whence comes the constant vicissitude of things, which surpasses the grasp of mortals. Proposition. Concerning this constant variety of things, or the fates of the times, something is to be said, if they wish to help one attempting it with their accustomed patience and goodwill.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Exponat vocem, videl. 1. De fatis temporum acturum, Non intelligere te fatum Stoicum, quod dicitur immutabilis connexio rerum fatali necessitate ita fluentium, ut nec ipse Jupiter mutare illum queat; vid. Sen. passim & Lipf. de philos. Stoica. Hoc enim esset constituere nume Deo oppositum & in rebus ipsis necessitatem, & Deum excludere a gubernatione mundi: quod impium est. &c. 2. Sed per fatū notari illud quod Deus fatus est & ordinavit, adeoque illum ordinem, quem Deus stabilivit, decreto sapientissimo & immutabili. Uti enim ipse creavit omnia, ita & gubernat Deus eadem juxta suum beneplacitum sapientissimum, sanctissimum &c.
units.tr: Treatment. I. Let him explain the word, namely: 1. That he will speak of the fates of the times. Let it not be understood as the Stoic fate, which is called an unchangeable connection of things flowing by fatal necessity, so that not even Jupiter himself could alter it; see Seneca passim and Lipsius, on Stoic philosophy. For this would be to set up a power opposed to God, and a necessity in things themselves, and to exclude God from the governance of the world, which is impious, etc. 2. But by "fate" is meant that which God has decreed and ordained, and thus that order which God has established by a most wise and unchangeable decree. For just as he himself created all things, so God also governs the same according to his most wise, most holy good pleasure, etc.

units.la: II. Inquirat causam horum fatorū temporis, Deum: Hunc supremū esse moderatorem temporum, a quo laeta & infesta tempora immittuntur. Hoc ostendatur. 1. a dispensatione dierum & noctiū, aestatis & hyemis, sanitatis & morborum, pacis & belli. Quis neget haec beneficia vel judiciaDei esse, immissa mortalibus? &c. 2. Testimoniis sacris & profanis: Esaias: Ego sum dominus faciens bonum & malū, poenae scil: creans lucem & tenebras &c. videatur locus Cōm: de providentia. 3. A testimonio omnium gentiū, ad Deum recurrentium in publicis privatisque malis, & ipsi gratias & sacrificia offerentium in magnis benefactis. Probetur exemplis Davidis Psalm. 18. item Graecorum, Romanorum publica festa ac triumphos celebrantium. Norant enim Deum esse, unde fata temporum dependent.
units.tr: II. Let him inquire into the cause of these fates of the times, namely God: that he is the supreme governor of the times, by whom joyful and hostile times are sent. This is shown: 1. From the arrangement of days and nights, of summer and winter, of health and sickness, of peace and war. Who would deny that these benefits, or judgments, are of God, sent upon mortals? etc. 2. From sacred and profane testimonies. Isaiah: "I am the Lord who makes good and evil," that is, who creates light and darkness, etc. See the common place on providence. 3. From the testimony of all nations, who turn to God in public and private evils, and offer him thanks and sacrifices in great benefits. Let it be proved by the examples of David, Psalm 18; likewise of the Greeks and Romans, who celebrated public festivals and triumphs. For they knew that there is a God on whom the fates of the times depend.

units.la: III. Exponat causam physicam fatorum, quae instrumentum est causae supremae. Uti sunt astra in signa temporum ordinata divinitus. Hinc igitur 1. praedicet illorum multitudinem & virtutem stupendam, qua semper agunt in haec inferiora benignis vel infestis influentiis: unde fertilitates, sterilitates, siccitates, eluviones, venti, serenitates, cometae, salubritates & lues quas astra vel efficiunt vel prædagiunt, non semper tanquam causæ, sed tanquam signa & præsagia, &c. Vid.Lips. polit.
units.tr: III. Let him set out the physical cause of the fates, which is the instrument of the supreme cause: as the stars are divinely ordained as signs of the times. Hence let him first declare their multitude and their astonishing power, by which they always act upon these lower things with kindly or hostile influences: whence fertility, barrenness, droughts, floods, winds, clear skies, comets, healthfulness and plagues, which the stars either bring about or foretell, not always as causes, but as signs and omens, etc. See Lipsius, Politics.

units.la: IV. Est causa moralis: uti sunt.
units.tr: IV. There is a moral cause, such as the following.

units.la: 1. Principes & imperantes sive boni, sive mali. Utrique enim dantur àDeo ad salutem vel poenam subditorum. Vide exem- pla in libro Judicum & regum Israëlis: Quis non videt uti Josua, Otniel, Gideon, David, Salomon, Hiskias, Josias in salutem; ita, Jaroboanmum, Achabum, Ezechiam in justam poenam datos. Ita & in regnis gentium. vid. Gruter. discurs. in Tac. 2.& 6. & Orphei carm.
units.tr: 1. Princes and rulers, whether good or bad. For both are given by God for the salvation or punishment of subjects. See examples in the Book of Judges and the Kings of Israel: who does not see that Joshua, Othniel, Gideon, David, Solomon, Hezekiah, Josiah were given for salvation, and thus Jeroboam, Ahab, Ezekiel (?) were given for just punishment. So also in the kingdoms of the nations. See Gruter, discourses on Tacitus, 2 and 6, and the Orphic songs.

units.la: 2. Ipsi cives & subditi, pietati vel impietati, justitiæ & injustitiæ, temperantiæ aut luxui dediti. Hasce enim esse veras & proximas causas conservantes aut corrumpentes civitatum regnorum & rerump. Hoc probetur 1. Ratione qua, uti virtutes istæ conciliant Dei favorem; ita vitia irritant Dei iram. Unde divina benedictio, vel maledictio super regna & nationes. 2. Testimoniis ex florilegiis colligendis. 3. Exemplis vid.Grut. dicto loco & historiam Sleidani ac Promptuariu Exemplorum 4.Illustretut prolepsi: videl. sæpe florere malos, &c. At tandem venire poenam; exemplo Judæorum, Nebucadnezaris, Dionysiorum.
units.tr: 2. The citizens and subjects themselves, given to piety or impiety, justice or injustice, temperance or luxury. For these are the true and proximate causes preserving or corrupting cities, kingdoms and commonwealths. This is proved: 1. By reason: as these virtues win the favour of God, so vices provoke the anger of God. Whence come the divine blessing or curse upon kingdoms and nations. 2. By testimonies to be gathered from anthologies. 3. By examples: see Gruter, in the passage cited, and the history of Sleidan and the Promptuarium Exemplorum. 4. Let it be illustrated by prolepsis: namely, that evil men often flourish, etc., but at last punishment comes, as in the example of the Jews, Nebuchadnezzar, the Dionysii.

units.la: Concluf. Agnoscamus igitur & nos fata temporum, ubi judicia Dei incumbunt passim, ut bella, fames, pestis, tempestates, diluvia; ut pacem redintegremus cum Deo, atque ita non metuamus à signis cœli atque agnoscamus Dei benignitatem, cum bonos largitur principes & magistratus, illorumque virtutes imitemur, &c.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let us therefore also acknowledge the fates of the times, where the judgments of God fall everywhere, as wars, famine, pestilence, storms, floods; so that we may restore peace with God, and thus not fear the signs of heaven, but acknowledge the goodness of God when he bestows good princes and magistrates, and imitate their virtues, etc.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: I. EXEMPLUM THEMATIS LIBERI SIMPLICIS
units.tr: I. EXAMPLE OF A SIMPLE FREE THEME

units.la: Mundus.
units.tr: The World.

units.la: A. Exord. A thematis præstantia, illustrata comparatione minorum, illorum scilicet quæ in mundo continentur; videlicet cum nihil sit ab imo terræ centro usque ad supremum cœli ambitum, quod considerationem non mereatur; imprimis totum hoc universum, contemplatione dignum esse. Addatur causa, quia maximum magni Dei opus, & virtutis divinæ illustre speculum. Amplii: ab opposito; interim raro illud considerari à mortalibus, qui instar talparum in terra degunt.
units.tr: A. Exordium. The excellence of the theme is shown by comparison with lesser things, namely those contained in the world; for there is nothing from the lowest centre of the earth up to the highest circuit of heaven that does not deserve consideration, and above all this whole universe is worthy of contemplation. The reason is added: it is the greatest work of the great God and an illustrious mirror of divine power. Further, by contrast: that it is rarely considered by mortals, who live like moles in the earth.

units.la: B. Propositio. Ideo brevem ejus contemplationem te instituturum, addatur stipulatio attentionis.
units.tr: B. Proposition. Therefore I will undertake a brief contemplation of it; let an assurance of attention be added.

units.la: C. Tractatio habeat
units.tr: C. The treatment should have:

units.la: I. Παρασκευὴν seu praeparationem qua
units.tr: I. A preparation (παρασκευή), or preparation, by which

units.la: a. Liberetur vox ab ambiguitate, videlicet te non loqui jam de mundo, quatenus in sacris corruptionem ac vanitatem connotet 1.Joh.5. neque qua homines Joh.3. aut etiam improbos notat Joh. 17, sed pro splendidissimo hoc theatro coelo undique terminato.
units.tr: a. The word is freed from ambiguity: namely, that you are not now speaking of the world as far as in the sacred writings it denotes corruption and vanity (1 John 5); nor as it denotes the people (John 3), or even the wicked (John 17), but as this most splendid theatre, bounded on all sides by heaven.

units.la: b. Consideretur nomen, itemque synonyma, quod & in Latina & Graeca lingua ab ornatu habeat. Addatur ratio: quia eo nihil pulchrius, uti jam porro explicandum.
units.tr: b. The name is considered, and likewise its synonyms, which in both Latin and Greek derive from ornament. Add the reason: because nothing is more beautiful than it, as will now be explained further.

units.la: II, Expositionem
units.tr: II. The exposition

units.la: a. à descriptione aliqua luculenta.
units.tr: a. from some illuminating description.

units.la: b. à Causa efficiente: καθ' ἀρχὴν; videlicet non fortuito ut philosophi veteres somniarunt; κατὰ θεόν; sed à Deo optimo maximo conditum. Probetur non tantum testimonio Mosis; verum etiam ratione; videlicet quia finitus, ordinatus. Ergo habet finitorem, ordinatorem &c.
units.tr: b. from the efficient cause: κατ' ἀρχήν (in the beginning); that is, not by chance, as the ancient philosophers dreamed; κατὰ θεόν (according to God); but founded by God, the best and greatest. Let it be proved not only by the testimony of Moses but also by reason: namely, because it is finite and ordered. Therefore it has a finisher, an orderer, etc.

units.la: β. à Causa materiali: quae non fuit materia aliqua praexistens. Unde enim illa? Nec enim res talis informis & iners esse potuit, nec debuit, nulli usui inserviens.
units.tr: β. from the material cause: which was not some pre-existing matter. For whence would that come? Such a thing could not be, nor ought it to be, formless and inert, serving no use.

units.la: c. A partibus seu materia compositionis: uti sunt.
units.tr: c. From the parts, or the matter of its composition, such as:

units.la: α. Corpora superiora, coelorum orbes, stellae fixae erraticae; Horum motus perpetuus ac usus brevibus explicetur & natura vix satis perspecta dicatur mortalibus.
units.tr: α. The upper bodies: the spheres of the heavens, the fixed stars and the wandering stars. Their perpetual motion and use are to be explained briefly, and their nature is to be said to be scarcely known well enough by mortals.

units.la: β. Corpora media, ut aër & meteora varia: horum natura mirabilis & perpetua varietas indigitetur.
units.tr: β. The middle bodies, such as air and the various meteors: their wonderful nature and perpetual variety are to be pointed out.

units.la: γ. Infima, uti terra in continentem & insulas vastissimas distincta & maria ac flumina, fontes usibus humanis destinata; itemque mineralia varia in ipsis terrae visceribus.
units.tr: γ. The lowest, such as the earth divided into continents and vast islands, and the seas and rivers, springs destined for human uses; likewise the various minerals in the very bowels of the earth.

units.la: d. à forma quae est aptissima omnium dispositio & contrariantium temperamentum, ad perpetuam vegetationem, motum generationem & consistentiam universi. e. Ab adjunctis, magnitudine, pulchritudine, durabilitate & perpetua veluti juventa.
units.tr: d. From the form, which is the most fitting arrangement of all things and the tempering of opposites, for the perpetual growth, motion, generation and consistency of the universe. e. From its accompanying qualities: greatness, beauty, durability and, as it were, perpetual youth.

units.la: f. à simili, homine scilicet: ubi brevis instituatur comparatio ratione partium corporis. β. ratione animæ, quæ actuat ac regit corpus: ubi rejectis somniis Epicureorum, Stoicorum, Peripateticorum ostendatur Deum regere hoc palatium per similia ab imperio ac aula regis ordinatissima, quæ non nisi a duce aliquo supremo in ordinem redigitur: à navi seu triremi, quæ non nisi à navarcha regitur.
units.tr: f. From a likeness, namely to man: where a brief comparison is made with regard to the parts of the body; β. with regard to the soul, which actuates and governs the body: where, the dreams of the Epicureans, Stoics and Peripatetics being rejected, it is shown that God governs this palace by likenesses drawn from the most orderly command and court of a king, which is brought into order only by some supreme leader; and from a ship or trireme, which is steered only by a navarch.

units.la: D. Conclusio transeat in admirationem tam egregii operis, indeque ad Creatoris ac Rectoris laudes evehatur:
units.tr: D. The conclusion should pass into admiration of so excellent a work, and thence be raised to the praises of the Creator and Ruler.

units.la: XXIII. ALIUD EXEMPLUM THEMATIS LIBERI SIMPLICIS De Republica.
units.tr: XXIII. ANOTHER EXAMPLE OF A SIMPLE FREE THEME: On the Commonwealth.

units.la: A. Exord. Ab occasione Orationis præcedentis de mundo; cujus systema longe cultissimum & spectatissimum non immerito ab antecessore depictum sit: addatur ratio: turpissimum scilicet esse mundi incolas ignorare proprium domicilium. At vero si totum mundum perlustremus, nihil esse in illo præstantius juxta Cic: in homine, quam coetus humanos jure & æquitate sociatos. Addatur ratio a præstantia hominis præ cæteris creaturis; & a præstantia hujusmodi societatum seu rerumpublicarum præ cunctis institutis humanis.
units.tr: A. Exordium. Taken from the occasion of the preceding oration on the world, whose system has been depicted by its predecessor, most elegantly and deservedly so. Add the reason: it is most shameful, of course, for the inhabitants of the world not to know their own dwelling. But indeed, if we survey the whole world, there is nothing more excellent in it than man, according to Cicero, than human assemblies joined together by law and equity. Add the reason from the excellence of man above other creatures, and from the excellence of such societies or commonwealths above all human institutions.

units.la: B. Propof. Harum naturam proinde cum bona venia Auditorum te explicaturum, sperare itaque benevolam auscultationem.
units.tr: B. Propositio. Therefore, with your kind permission, Hearers, I shall explain their nature, and so hope for a kindly hearing.

units.la: C. Tractatio, (præmissa nominis explicatione per sepositionem ambiguitatis vocis, itemque per synonyma, ut sunt civitas, civilis & politica societas, regimen, imperium.) habeat.
units.tr: C. Tractatio. (With the explanation of the name premised, by setting aside the ambiguity of the word, and likewise through synonyms, such as state, civil and political society, government, empire.) Let it have the following.

units.la: I. Descriptionem; quod cum rempubl. dicimus, societatem intelligamus imperantium & parentium ad se conservandum sufficientem, sub una aliqua suprema potestate. Hæc definitio paucis explicetur juxta omnes partes, videlicet societas, quia plures esse debent, & quidem sufficientes ad se conservandum, tum intrinsece quoad victum & propagationem, tum extrinsecus contra vim: imperantium & parentium: quia scilicet ordo esse debet in Republ. secus confusio futura, & quidem sub aliqua summa summa potestate, secus enim quies esse nequit; sive illa penes unum sive penes plures sit.
units.tr: I. Description. When we say commonwealth, let us understand a society of rulers and subjects, sufficient to preserve itself, under some one supreme power. This definition is to be explained briefly in all its parts: namely, society, since there must be several, and indeed sufficient to preserve themselves, both internally as to sustenance and propagation, and externally against force; of rulers and subjects, since there ought to be order in the commonwealth, otherwise there would be confusion; and under some supreme power, otherwise there cannot be peace, whether that power rests with one or with several.

units.la: II. Causam 1. efficientem quae primaria est Deus, autor omnis ordinis & suo exemplo magnum mundi reimp: moderans: secundaria est mens hominis cui ordo implantatus; hincque viri prudentes, Nimrodus, Solon, Lycurgus, Romani &c.
units.tr: II. The efficient cause: the primary one is God, the author of all order, who by his own example governs the great restoration of the world; the secondary one is the mind of man, into which order was implanted; and hence the wise men, Nimrod, Solon, Lycurgus, the Romans, etc.

units.la: 2. Materialem, quae suntincolae in varias societates & collegia distributi.
units.tr: 2. The material cause: the inhabitants, distributed into various societies and collegia.

units.la: 3. Formalem, quae est ordo inter superiores & inferiores: qui ut eo sanctior sit, legibus continetur: quae veluti anima sunt Reipublicae & vinculum, quo continetur.
units.tr: 3. The formal cause: the order between superiors and inferiors, which, that it may be more sacred, is contained by laws; these are as it were the soul of the commonwealth and the bond by which it is held together.

units.la: 4. Finalem; quae est publica salus & honestas.
units.tr: 4. The final cause: which is public safety and honesty.

units.la: III. Accidens uti est 1. antiquitas quae ostendatur inde ab origine mundi. 2. Amplitudo, quod nulla gens sit in qua non sit forma reipublicae. 3. Utilitas, tum in conservanda honestate publica, tum in curanda rerum abundantia. Illustretur a contrario.
units.tr: III. Accidents, such as: 1. antiquity, which is shown from the origin of the world onward; 2. breadth, in that there is no nation in which the form of a commonwealth is absent; 3. utility, both in preserving public honesty and in providing for abundance of goods. Let it be illustrated from the contrary.

units.la: IV. Similia; alleget rempublicam apum, item imperium rationis in affectus Dei in orbem universum. Tractentur protasi & apodoli.
units.tr: IV. Similarities: let him cite the commonwealth of bees, and likewise the rule of reason over the affections, and God's dominion over the whole world. Let these be treated by protasis and apodosis.

units.la: V. Species, videlicet Resp: vel ab uno, vel a pluribus regi; esse vel Monarchicas vel Aristocraticas vel Democraticas.
units.tr: V. Species: namely, that a commonwealth is ruled either by one or by several; and that it is either monarchical, or aristocratic, or democratic.

units.la: VI. Opposita, uti sunt ἀναρχία, tyrannis, Oligarchia, Ochlocratia, aliaeque confusiones; itemque deliria Anabaptistarum respublicas & ordinem Magistratuum abominantium.
units.tr: VI. Opposites, such as ἀναρχία [anarchy], tyranny, oligarchy, ochlocracy, and other confusions; likewise the ravings of the Anabaptists, who abominate commonwealths and the order of magistrates.

units.la: D. Concluf. Dictorum summa capita recolligat & ex iis intelligi dicat, quid de rebuspublicis sentiendum; videlicet nullum illustrius esse Dei donum inter mortales, cujus proinde conservationi unusquisque studere debeat, etiam cum jactura saepe proprii commodi. Addatur πολιτικά: rempubl; enim singulorum utilitates complecti.
units.tr: D. Conclusion. Let him gather up the principal heads of what has been said and say that from them one should understand what is to be thought about commonwealths: namely, that there is no more illustrious gift of God among mortals, and that therefore each one ought to strive for its preservation, even often at the cost of his own private advantage. Add the politics: for a commonwealth embraces the advantages of individuals.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: 1. Exemplum thematis liberi conjuncti: Utrum armorum, an literarum studia antiquiora? PRO ARMIS.
units.tr: 1. Example of a free conjoined theme: Which are older, the studies of arms or of letters? FOR ARMS.

units.la: A. Exord. Hic 1. alleget causam dicendi; quae est frequens inter literatos at Martis alumnos de praerogativa contentio; utrisque priprimas sibi vendicantibus. 2. Concedatur utrisque sua laus, additatione; quia pacis tempore literati, belli vero milites maxime necessarii. Seponat istam quæstionem in aliud tempus: in præsentiarum vero simplicis veritatis amore de antiquitate utriusque studii inquiturum, & quidem arma literarum studia vincere tibi videri; id quod breviter evincendum.
units.tr: A. Exordium. Here (1) he states the subject of his speech, which is a frequent contest between the literate and the nurslings of Mars over precedence, each side claiming the first place for itself. (2) Let each side be granted its praise, with the addition that letters are most needed in time of peace, while soldiers are most necessary in war. Let him set that question aside for another occasion. For the present, out of love of simple truth, he will inquire into the antiquity of each study, and indeed it seems to you that arms surpass letters, which must be shown briefly.

units.la: B. Propositio. Qua de re cum breviter dicturus sis, petere te benevolam attentionem; præsertim ab illis, qui vel armis delectantur, vel veritatis studiosi sunt.
units.tr: B. Proposition. Since you are about to speak briefly on this matter, you ask for the kind attention of your hearers, especially of those who either delight in arms or are devoted to the truth.

units.la: C. Confirmatio.
units.tr: C. Confirmation.

units.la: I. A causa procatarctica armorum; quæ sunt injustitia quorundam & hominum dissidia; unde factum esse dicatur ut unusquisque de defensione sui fuerit sollicitus. Jam ostendatur dissidia ab initio fuisse, probetur exemplo Abelis & Caini, Lamechi qui vulnera & mortem minitatus. Sic in prima fundatione Romæ dissidia nata inter fratres. Idque eo magis, postquam jam urbes & imperia moliri coeperunt mortales: hinc factum esse, ut Cainus & ipsius posteri arma & æramenta invexerint: Nimrodus vi homines subegerit. Frustra hæc sine armorum usu fieri.
units.tr: I. From the procatarctic cause of arms, which are the injustice of certain men and the quarrels between people; whence it is said that each man became anxious to defend himself. Now let it be shown that quarrels existed from the beginning, proved by the example of Abel and Cain, and of Lamech, who threatened wounds and death. So at the first founding of Rome, quarrels arose between brothers. And this all the more after mortals began to undertake cities and empires. Hence it came about that Cain and his posterity introduced arms and metal tools, and Nimrod subdued men by force. It is in vain to suppose that these things happened without the use of arms.

units.la: II. A fine armorum: qui est a. defensio sui, contra feras & homines omni fera ferociores: Amplif. digrediendo breviter in locum de insito unicuique amore & defensione sui. Unde ipsa natura cornibus, dentibus, unguibus, jugulis armaverit animantia; homini rationem dederit, ut istis destitutus, ipse sibi arma fabricet. b. Recuperatio ablatorum. Quæ cum legibus obtinuerit, obtinuisse etiam arma.
units.tr: II. From the end of arms, which is (a) the defence of oneself against wild beasts and against men fiercer than any beast. (Amplification: digressing briefly to the place on the love of self and self-defence, which is implanted in everyone.) Whence nature itself armed animals with horns, teeth, claws and throats; to man it gave reason, so that, lacking those natural weapons, he might fashion arms for himself. (b) The recovery of what has been taken away. And since this is secured by laws, arms also were secured.

units.la: III. Ab effectis armorum uti sunt. a. Securitas, quam quisque exoptat, nec sine armis obtinere potest, ad arma recurrendum fuit. b. Gloria & fama. Cujus studium cum ab initio homini insitum, eaque per arma facillime obtineatur, quis dubitet inde ab initio armorum quoque viguisse studium. Hic ostendatur, quotquot antiquitus viri illustres fuerunt, illos non sine armis tales exstitisse, nisi fortassis Diogenem aliquê Cynicū, magno Alexandro comparare velimus. Illustrentur à contrario neglectu armorum, ubi nec gloria, nec tuta sui possessio, aut ulla securitas.
units.tr: III. From the effects of arms, which are these: (a) Security, which everyone desires and cannot obtain without arms; recourse had to be made to arms. (b) Glory and fame. Since the pursuit of these was implanted in man from the beginning, and they are most easily obtained through arms, who would doubt that the zeal for arms also flourished from the very beginning? Here let it be shown that however many illustrious men there were in antiquity, they did not become such without arms, unless perhaps we wish to set Diogenes the Cynic beside great Alexander. Let it be illustrated by the contrary case: the neglect of arms, where there is neither glory, nor safe possession of oneself, nor any security.

units.la: IV. Ab exemplis omnium gentium, quibus armorum usus semper usitatus fuit; plurimæ contra quibus nec literæ unquam innotuere; & quibus innotuere, illis tum demum excoli cœperunt, cùm armis pacem ac securitatem sibi acquisiverunt.
units.tr: IV. From the examples of all peoples, among whom the use of arms has always been practised; very many, on the contrary, among whom letters were never known; and among those to whom letters became known, they began to be cultivated only when they had won peace and security for themselves by arms.

units.la: Conclus. Ex repetitis breviter argumentis præcipuis propositionem inferat, & vulgatum illud; Cedant arma togæ, explodat; addito pondere ab ipsius Dei titulo, qui Dominum exercituum antiquissima dignitate se dictitet.
units.tr: Conclusion. From the principal arguments, briefly repeated, he infers the proposition, and explodes that commonplace, "Let arms give way to the gown"; adding weight from the very title of God, who calls himself the Lord of hosts, a dignity of most ancient standing.

units.la: XXXV. Exemplum thematis Conjuncti.
units.tr: XXXV. Example of a conjoined theme.

units.la: PRO ANTIQUITATE LITERARUM.
units.tr: FOR THE ANTIQUITY OF LETTERS.

units.la: A. Exord. Occasione sumat ab oratione Antecessoris qui armorum antiquitatem astruere sategerit; hic per prolepsin concedi quidem posse dicas, usum armorum satis probh, dolor antiquum; cum semper fuerint, qui æquo jure haud contenti ad vim prosiluëre: at minimè interim ferendum, studia armorum cum literarum studiis antiquitate contendere.
units.tr: A. Exordium. Let him take his occasion from the speech of the predecessor, who strove to establish the antiquity of arms. Here you may say by prolepsis that it is granted that the use of arms is sufficiently proved, though it is unfortunately ancient, since there have always been those who, not content with equal right, leapt to violence. But at the same time it must by no means be borne that the study of arms should contend in antiquity with the study of letters.

units.la: B. Propos. Te itaque literarum patrocinium suscepturum cum bona pace antecessoris & venia Auditorum, non quod armis suam gloriam invideas, sed quod veritati litandum existimes.
units.tr: B. Proposition. Accordingly, you will take up the defence of letters, with the good peace of the predecessor and the indulgence of the hearers: not because you begrudge arms their glory, but because you think truth must be served.

units.la: C. Examen & refutatio argumentorum antecessoris; ad quam struatur accessus, videlicet ne forte præjudicium pariant dicta ab antecessore &c. Hinc repetitio summatim.
units.tr: C. Examination and refutation of the predecessor's arguments. An approach is to be built for this, namely, lest the things said by the predecessor perhaps cause prejudice, etc. Hence a summary repetition.

units.la: I. Argumento respondeatur a. per concessionem antiquitatis dissidiorum; at pacem fuisse antiquiorem, neque etiam omnem vim & oppressionem v. g.
