Caini Lamechi, militaris mereri peritiæ nomen. b. per inversionem, imò enatis dissidiis per literas & sapientiam armorum disciplinam invectam fuisse.
units.tr: I. The argument is answered: a. by conceding the antiquity of quarrels; but peace was older, and not every force and oppression, for example that of Cain and Lamech, deserves the name of military skill. b. by inversion: indeed, once quarrels arose, the discipline of arms was introduced through letters and wisdom.

units.la: II. Argumento Resp. a. Per instantiam: defensionem bellicam tum demum habere locum, cum rationes ac leges obtinere nequeant. b. per inversionem, belluas cornibus; hominem ratione arnatum.
units.tr: II. To the argument: a. by instance: defence by war has its place only when reasons and laws cannot prevail. b. by inversion: beasts are armed with horns, man with reason.

units.la: III. Argumento Resp. 1. Securitatis præsidium primò esse prudentiam. 2. Veram gloriam mentis dotibus acquiri, sive illæ belli sive pacis tempore se exserant. In gloria non spectari vanam pompompam & judicia imperitorum, plus galeatum militem, quam virum cordatum admirantium.
units.tr: III. To the argument: 1. The safeguard of security is first of all prudence. 2. True glory is acquired by the gifts of the mind, whether these show themselves in time of war or of peace. In glory one should not look to vain pomp and the judgments of the unskilled, who admire the helmeted soldier more than the wise man.

units.la: IV. Argumento Resp. 1. Exempla barbarorum non curanda. 2. Cordatiores gentium literis inclaruisse: uti jam porro probandum. Hinc transeatur ad
units.tr: IV. To the argument: 1. The examples of barbarians are not to be heeded. 2. The wiser nations became famous through letters, as will now be further proved. Hence we pass to

units.la: D. Confirmationem.
units.tr: D. Confirmation.

units.la: I. Ab Exemplis plerarumq; gentium, per inductionem, Chaldaeorum Aegyptiorum, Persarum, Graecorum, qui prius ingenii dotibus, quam armis inclaruerunt. Imo ipsam Adamum antiquissimum ipsiusque filios institutioni incubuisse. Ostendatur quomodo Adam filios instituerit, in sacris, in oeconomicis. Ab hac disciplina cum defecisset Cain, in beluinam crudelitatem incidisse. Sethum autore Josepho 1 Antiqq. coelestium rerum disciplinam excoluisse, & duabus columnis incidisse. Imo ipsum Nimrodum, non sine literis & singulari prudentia Imperium molitum esse. Addatur de necessitate literarum in erigendo imperio, Exemplo Caesaris, Augusti &c. Concludatur hinc literarum antiquitas mundo omnibusque imperiis coeva.
units.tr: I. From the examples of most nations, by induction: Chaldeans, Egyptians, Persians, Greeks, who became famous for gifts of mind before arms. Indeed, Adam himself, the most ancient man, and his sons devoted themselves to instruction. Let it be shown how Adam instructed his sons, in sacred matters and in household management. When Cain had departed from this discipline, he fell into brutish cruelty. Seth, according to Josephus, Antiquities book 1, cultivated the knowledge of heavenly things and engraved it on two pillars. Indeed Nimrod himself undertook his rule not without letters and singular prudence. Add something on the necessity of letters in establishing an empire, from the example of Caesar, Augustus, etc. Conclude hence that the antiquity of letters is coeval with the world and with all empires.

units.la: II. A causa effic. primaria, quae est Deus, qui uti fons omnis sapientiae, ita primus fuit, qui Adamum instituit; Mosen & prophetas ad scribendum excitavit & suo spiritu afflavit. Abrahamus ac reliqui Patriarchae liberos instituerunt. Ipse Adamus nomina rebus imposuit, omnis literaturae fundamenta. Fiat hic digressiuncula de vera literatura, quae non sit in nugis Grammaticorum Sophisticis aut Criticis sed in noscenda rerum natura ac veritate. Huc conspirare omnes artes ac scientias, Quae cum a Deo ipso profectae sint, jure merito antiquissimas habendas esse.
units.tr: II. From the primary efficient cause, which is God, who, as the fount of all wisdom, was also the first to instruct Adam; he stirred up Moses and the prophets to write and breathed his Spirit into them. Abraham and the other patriarchs instructed their children. Adam himself gave names to things, the foundations of all literature. Here let there be a short digression on true literature, which lies not in the sophistical trifles of the grammarians or critics, but in knowing the nature and truth of things. To this all arts and sciences converge; since they have proceeded from God himself, they are rightly to be considered most ancient.

units.la: III. Ab effectis literarum uti sunt 1. cognitio Dei, probetur: quia licet semina religionis menti insita, tamen institutione fovenda sunt. 2. Ordinatio vitae privatae & civilis & erectio rerump. Quae uti antiquissima, ita literarum, quibus haec traduntur, antiquitatem evincunt. In legibus enim salus rerump. quae non natae in republ Gigantum aut Cyclopum, sed in collegiis sapientum.
units.tr: III. From the effects of letters, such as 1. the knowledge of God: let it be proved, because although the seeds of religion are implanted in the mind, they must nevertheless be cherished by instruction. 2. The ordering of private and civil life and the establishment of commonwealths. These, being most ancient, likewise prove the antiquity of the letters by which they are handed down. For the safety of commonwealths lies in laws, and these were born not in the commonwealths of Giants or Cyclopes, but in the assemblies of the wise.

units.la: IV. A contrario; si concipiat quis literas indeque natam sapientiam vel ad momentum e vita sublatam, qualis status futurus?
units.tr: IV. From the contrary: if one imagines that letters, and the wisdom born from them, were removed from life even for a moment, what would the state be?

units.la: D. Conclusio ex collectis in cumulum argumentis antiquitatem literarum
units.tr: D. Conclusion, drawn from the arguments gathered into a heap for the antiquity of letters.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Exemplum tractationis Chriæ.
units.tr: An example of the treatment of a chreia.

units.la: Alphonsus Rex Arragoniæ Consiliarios mortuos dixit esse optimos.
units.tr: Alphonso, King of Aragon, said that dead counsellors are the best.

units.la: A. Loco Exordii breviter commendetur Autor tum a dignitate Regia, tum a singulari eruditione & prudentia; qua regnum administraverit, & eximie auctum posteris tradiderit insignemque hanc sententiam aliis regentibus documento reliquerit.
units.tr: A. In the introduction, the author should be briefly commended, both for his royal dignity and for his singular learning and prudence, by which he governed his kingdom, handed it on to posterity greatly enlarged, and left this noteworthy saying as a lesson for other rulers.

units.la: B. Loco proposit. ponatur sententia eum paraphrasi, videlicet longa experientia ipsum edoctum comperisse, nullos consiliarios meliores esse iis, qui defuncti in doctissimis suis Scriptis consulentibus loquuntur.
units.tr: B. In the proposition, the saying is set down with a paraphrase: that, taught by long experience, he found that no counsellors are better than those who, dead, speak to those who consult them in their most learned writings.

units.la: C. Tractatio astruat hoc dictum.
units.tr: C. The treatment confirms this saying.

units.la: I. A causa aliqua, & quidem
units.tr: I. From some cause, and indeed:

units.la: a. A primariis requisitis consiliarii; uti sunt. 1.Prudentia. 2.integritas sine studio sui, sine odio partium. Hæc verò in nemine melius, quam in eruditorum scriptis inveniri: quippe qui amoris ac invidiæ causas procul habeant; & non privatim uni, sed publicè universis scripserunt.
units.tr: a. From the chief requisites of a counsellor, which are: (1) prudence; (2) integrity, without self-interest and without partisan hatred. Now these qualities are found in no one better than in the writings of learned men, since they keep far away the causes of favour and envy, and have written not privately to one person but publicly to everyone.

units.la: b. A defunctorum incorruptibilitate per munera aut spes lautiores: Probetur, quia posteris scripserunt: & plerorumque scripta etiam non nisi post mortem in lucem prodierunt, in quibus proinde nulla metuenda corruptio.
units.tr: b. From the incorruptibility of the dead, who are not swayed by gifts or by more lavish hopes. This may be proved because they wrote for posterity, and most of their writings were published only after death, so that in them there is no corruption to be feared.

units.la: II. à contrario, videlicet a consiliariorū vivorum quandoque ignorantia; utpote, qui vel excæcantur; vel saltem perversis aliquot affectibus ducuntur. Unde consilia sæpe corrumpuntur. Nil tale in mortuis.
units.tr: II. From the contrary: namely, from the ignorance of living counsellors, which sometimes occurs, since they are either blinded or at least led by various perverse passions. Hence their advice is often corrupted. Nothing of this kind is found in the dead.

units.la: III. a simili, Legum optimarum scilicet, quæ uti meliores sunt judice, qui non semper justitiæ consulit, sed sæpe favori, unde Arist. dicit melius esse ab optima Lege quàm ab optimo Rege regi; ita & consiliarii mortui, seu monumenta virorum prudentum uno tenore loquuntur. Illustretur ratione: uti enim privati legibus; ita principes consilio regi, &c. IV. Ab exemplis, ipsius scilicet Alphonsi, Jul. Cæsaris, Augusti præsertim qui ex autoribus colligebat monita, quæ præfectis suis transmittebat. Imperatoris Porphyrogenatæ, qui universam Historiam in locos politicos digeri jussit, ut inde rerum agendarum consilia caperentur. Hi optimè præfuerunt. Illustretur exemplis contrariis: videlicet Tiberii, qui Sejani consiliis deceptus, & Rehabeami, qui a junioribus male consultus, regnum fere amisit.
units.tr: III. From a likeness: of the best laws, namely, which are better than a judge who does not always consult justice but often favour; whence Aristotle says it is better to be ruled by the best law than by the best king. So too dead counsellors, or the records of prudent men, speak with one consistent voice. Let this be illustrated by reason: just as private persons are ruled by laws, so princes are ruled by counsel, etc. IV. From examples: of Alphonso himself; of Julius Caesar, and especially of Augustus, who gathered admonitions from the authors and sent them to his prefects; of the Porphyrogenite emperor, who ordered the whole of history to be arranged under political headings, so that counsels for managing affairs might be drawn from it. These men governed very well. Let this be illustrated by contrary examples: those of Tiberius, who was deceived by the counsels of Sejanus, and of Rehoboam, who, badly advised by the younger men, nearly lost his kingdom.

units.la: V. A Dictis in hanc sententiam ex autoribus vel Floril. collectis.
units.tr: V. From sayings to this effect taken from authors or gathered from anthologies (Florilegia).

units.la: D. Conclusionis loco laudetur hæc sententia Alphonsi, & regentibus commendetur.
units.tr: D. As the conclusion, this saying of Alphonso should be praised and commended to rulers.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Exemplum tractationis sententiæ. SUMMISQUE NEGATUM STARE DIU.
units.tr: An example of the treatment of a sentence. "To the highest it is denied to stand long."

units.la: A. Exord. Ex loco generis; videl. à rerum omnium mutabilitate. Hæc
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the topic of the genus, namely from the mutability of all things. The following:

units.la: 1. Ostendatur brevi ac nervosa inductione rerum physicarum & moralium. Et illustretur simili a globo volutato, qui nunquam eodem est situ. 2. In specie exemplo illorum summatim allegato, qui in magna fortuna constituti; de quibus verissimè dictum sit, summisque negatum stare diu.
units.tr: 1. Let it be shown by a brief and forceful induction from physical and moral things. And let it be illustrated by the simile of a rolling globe, which is never in the same position. 2. Specifically, by an example briefly cited of those who have been placed in great fortune, of whom it is most truly said: "to the highest it is denied to stand long."

units.la: B. Propositio. Habeat paulò uberiorem paraphrasin hujus sententiæ, porrò jam consideranda, cum stipulatione auscultationis.
units.tr: B. Proposition. Let it have a somewhat fuller paraphrase of this sentence, to be considered further, with the condition that it is heard out.

units.la: C. Tractatio. Confirmet sententiam eodem modo uti in tractatione Chriæ.
units.tr: C. Treatment. Let it confirm the sentence in the same way as in the treatment of a chria.

units.la: I. A Causa, 1. negatè, vid. non cæca fortuna. Hic breviter illa exsententia gentilium referatur: deinde refellatur sententia hæc, quippe figmentum esse fortunam, nihil contingere fortuito, sed regi cuncta providentiâ Numinis. 2. affirmatè; vid. Deum ita disposuisse, ut illis, qui ad summum evecti sunt, nihil nisi casus restet. Probetur testimoniis sacris & profanis. Ratio quia Deus resistit superbis.
units.tr: I. From the cause. 1. Negatively, namely, not blind fortune. Here that saying of the Gentiles should be briefly reported; then this saying should be refuted, namely that fortune is a fiction, that nothing happens by chance, but that all things are governed by the providence of God. 2. Affirmatively, namely, that God has so arranged things that for those who have been raised to the highest point nothing remains but chance. Let it be proved by sacred and profane testimonies. The reason: because God resists the proud.

units.la: II. A Contraria humilitate & statu mediocri, qui tutus est. Additur ratio. 1. quia Deus favet humilibus. 2. Quia non habet æmulos & invidos.
units.tr: II. From the contrary: a humble and middling state, which is safe. The reason is added: 1. because God favours the humble; 2. because they have no rivals and no envious critics.

units.la: III. A similli 1. Montium, turrium, arborum celsarum; quæ subjecta Ṇta ventis,fulminibus. 2. Nubium,quæ subito in imbres &c.resol-vuntur. 3. Ipsius solis, qui altissimus, vergit ad occasum. Solus Deus hic exsors. Illustretur similibus contrariis v. g. tectorum, plantarum humilium, quæ tuta.
units.tr: III. From a simile: 1. of mountains, towers, and tall trees, which, exposed to winds and lightning, are struck; 2. of clouds, which are suddenly dissolved into rain, etc.; 3. of the sun itself, which, though highest, sinks toward its setting. Only God is exempt here. Let it be illustrated by contrary similes, e.g. of low roofs and of low plants, which are safe.

units.la: IV. Ab Exemplis v. g. Nabuchodonosoris, Croesi, Alexandri, Pompeji, Cæsaris. &c.
units.tr: IV. From examples, e.g. of Nebuchadnezzar, Croesus, Alexander, Pompey, Caesar, etc.

units.la: V. Dicto uno atque altero, sacro profano ex florileg. deligendo in hanc sententiam.
units.tr: V. One or two sayings, sacred or profane, to be chosen from the anthologies in support of this sentiment.

units.la: D. Conclusio Inculcet hanc sententiam, & ad humilitatem breviter hortetur.
units.tr: D. Conclusion: let it impress this sentiment and briefly exhort to humility.

units.la: XXXVIII. Exemplum tractandæ legis.
units.tr: XXXVIII. An example of how a law is to be handled.

units.la: Lex Platonis statuit communionem uxorum.
units.tr: Plato's law established the communal possession of wives.

units.la: Epictetus apud Stobæum dicit: verba non mentem Viri capere, qui cum vulgo hanc intelligunt,
units.tr: Epictetus, as reported by Stobaeus, says that the words do not grasp the mind of the man, who understand this in the common way,

units.la: A. Exord. I. Dicat aliquid in laudem Platonis, præsertim de ipsius sapientia, qua veteres omnes superet. 2. scriptis, quibus Socratis Philosophiam ab interitu vindicarit, multa vitæ humanæ salubria tradiderit.
units.tr: A. Exordium: (1) he should say something in praise of Plato, especially of his wisdom, by which he surpasses all the ancients; (2) by his writings, in which he defended the philosophy of Socrates from destruction, he handed down many things wholesome for human life.

units.la: II. Opponat legem satis absurdam, qua communionem non bonorum tantum, sed & uxorum introduci in suam remp. voluerit.
units.tr: II. He should set out the rather absurd law, by which he wanted the communal holding not only of goods but also of wives introduced into his commonwealth.

units.la: III. Addat suum judicium; videl. non videri hanc fuisse mentem viri Sapientis, quæ vulgo ipsi tribuitur.
units.tr: III. He should add his own judgment, namely that this was not the mind of the wise man that is commonly attributed to him.

units.la: B. Propositio. Quod breviter ostendendum cum bona pace Audit.
units.tr: B. Proposition. This is to be shown briefly, with the good leave of the hearers.

units.la: C. Tractatio. habeat.
units.tr: C. Development. He should have:

units.la: I. Destructionem sententiæ vulgatæ, quæ urget τὸ ῥητὸν.
units.tr: I. The refutation of the common opinion, which presses the letter [τὸ ῥητὸν].

units.la: a. Ab inhonesto: quod ostendatur a contrarietate Legis divinæ, naturæ, Gentium, omniumque civilium, quæ matrimonii reverentiam inculcant. Jam vero quis credat virum juris peritum tam absonum quippiam statuisse?
units.tr: a. From dishonour: this is shown from its contrariness to divine law, to nature, to the nations, and to all civil laws, which inculcate reverence for marriage. Now who would believe that a man skilled in law laid down anything so absurd?

units.la: b. Ab absurdo: videl. hinc mariti, uxoris, matrimonii, liberorum nomen & naturam penitus exolere & perverti. Si enim communes uxores, quis maritus, quomodo uxor, cujus liberi erunt, quomodo matrimonium? &c. Quis credat hanc sententiam cadere in virum sanum, nedum sapientem.
units.tr: b. From absurdity: namely that by it the name and nature of husband, wife, marriage and children are utterly destroyed and perverted. For if wives are common, who is the husband, how is she a wife, whose children will they be, how is there marriage? and so on. Who would believe that this opinion could fall upon a sane man, let alone a wise one?

units.la: c. A contradictione tacita; vid. quomodo communis esse potest, test, quae uxor, id est uni viro nupta: quomodo uxor dici potest, si communis, quis ita oblitum sui credat Platonem?
units.tr: c. From tacit contradiction: see how she can be common, which wife it is, that is, one married to one husband? How can she be called a wife if she is common? Who would believe that Plato had forgotten himself to this degree?

units.la: II. Abadstructione sententiae verae.
units.tr: II. Confirmation of the true opinion.

units.la: a. Ex praecedentibus inferatur itaque merito quaerenda sententiam eamque exponat: videlicet Platonem cum communionem bonorum & uxorum sancivit, nihil aliud voluisse, quam curam pro bonis uxoribus & liberis in Rep. debere esse communem & publicam; manente unicuique sua proprietate.
units.tr: a. From what has gone before, it follows that the meaning rightly sought should be stated and set out: namely that Plato, when he sanctioned the communal holding of goods and wives, meant nothing other than that the care of good wives and children should be common and public in the commonwealth, each person's own property remaining intact.

units.la: b. Probet hanc interpretationem.
units.tr: b. Let him prove this interpretation.

units.la: 1. A scopo Platonis in sua politica: qui est devincire cives mutuo amore, tum inter se, tum erga Remp. Atque hoc obtinere non potuisset tali lege. Unde potius Zelotypiae, digladiationes & dissidia; sed optime per legem, quae omnes communi cura sollicite sunt de conservatione Reipubl. & singulorum. Huc tendere omnes leges.
units.tr: 1. From Plato's aim in his Politics, which is to bind the citizens together by mutual love, both among themselves and towards the commonwealth. This could not have been obtained by such a law. It would rather produce jealousies, quarrels and dissensions; but it is achieved very well by a law which makes all anxiously concerned with the common preservation of the commonwealth and of individuals. All laws tend to this.

units.la: 2. a verborum generalitate, quae cum hoc scopo, & natura omnium rerumpubl. conveniat. Jam vero verba generalia nunquam contra scopum autoris & naturam rei explicanda sunt. Hic ostendi possunt per digressiunculam incommoda, si quis in legibus semper ὁ φιλὸν urgere vellet.
units.tr: 2. From the generality of the words, which agrees with this aim and with the nature of all commonwealths. Now general words must never be explained against the author's aim and the nature of the matter. Here the inconveniences can be shown by a short digression, if anyone wished always to press the sense of φιλόν [τὸ φιλόν] in the laws.

units.la: 3. a testimonio Epicteti apud Stobaeum qui dicit, verba non mentem viri capere, qui cum vulgo haec intelligunt.
units.tr: 3. From the testimony of Epictetus in Stobaeus, who says that the words do not grasp the mind of the man, who understand this in the common way.

units.la: D. Conclusio. vulgatam interpretationem ex repetitis breviter dictis rationibus repudiet, & Platonis autoritatem defendat.
units.tr: D. Conclusion. He should reject the common interpretation by briefly repeating the reasons given, and defend the authority of Plato.

units.la: XXXIX. DE RERUM HUMANARUM INTERITU ET INSTABILITATE.
units.tr: XXXIX. On the Perishing and Instability of Human Things.

units.la: Exord. Ab effato Apost. 1 Cor. 7, v. 31.
units.tr: Exordium. From the saying of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 7, v. 31.

units.la: I. Proponatur, scilicet magna completi Apostolum paucis verbis cum ait: praeterit scena mundi hujus.
units.tr: I. Let it be set forth, namely, that the Apostle comprehends a great matter in few words when he says: the stage of this world passeth away.

units.la: II. Explicetur, quod mundum comparet cum scena versatili, ubi modo palatium aliquod regium, modo hortus amoenus repraesentatur, & in iis personae & actiones diversae (quarum enarrentur aliquot) verum momento citius, non personae modo, verum & theatrum ipsum ex oculis subducitur: ita ut videntes & vigilantes somniasse sibi in ipso meridie videantur.
units.tr: II. Let it be explained that the world is compared to a revolving stage, where now a royal palace, now a pleasant garden, is presented, and in these various persons and actions (some of which are to be recounted). In an instant, and more quickly than that, not only the persons but the theatre itself is withdrawn from sight, so that those who watched and saw it seem to have dreamed it at high noon.

units.la: III. Applicetur ad propositum: videlicet egregiam imaginem ac emblema nobis sic proponi mundi omniumque actionum humanarum, quae speciem habent magnificam, revera nil nisi vanitas sunt; ut Ecclesiastes ait.
units.tr: III. Let it be applied to the proposition: namely, that an excellent image and emblem of the world and of all human actions is thus set before us, which have a splendid appearance but in truth are nothing but vanity, as Ecclesiastes says.

units.la: IV. Illustretur adversativa: Interim mortales hic fixam habere spem suam, & tanta moliri in re evanida ac ludicris somniis! dum alter opes, alter dignitates, alter possessiones amplas hic ambit, etiam cum jactura saepe coelestium & verorum bonorum. Unde hoc? nisi quod rerum vanitatem vel ignorant, vel non cogitant, cum Ixione nubem pro Junone amplexantes, existimantes veritatem esse; quae umbra est,
units.tr: IV. Let the contrast be illustrated: meanwhile mortals fix their hope here, and strive for such great things in what is fleeting and in playful dreams! One seeks wealth, another dignities, another ample possessions here, often even at the cost of heavenly and true goods. Whence is this? Only because they either do not know the vanity of things or do not consider it, embracing a cloud like Ixion instead of Juno, supposing that to be truth which is a shadow.

units.la: Propos. Hanc causam sibi visam esse idoneam, cur de rerum humanarum vanitate pro ingenii modulo dicere constituerit. Petere &c.
units.tr: Proposition. This cause seemed to me suitable, why I have resolved to speak, according to the measure of my ability, on the vanity of human things. I ask, etc.

units.la: Tractatio incipiat per ἀπορίαν, nescire se unde incipiendum, ubi terminandum, tantam enim rerum speciosissimarum se oculis exhibere multitudinem. Hinc
units.tr: The treatment should begin through aporia: to be unsure whence to begin and where to end, for such a multitude of most splendid things presents itself to the eyes. Hence:

units.la: I. Praedicet extrinsecam rerum sensibilium speciem magnificam, quae mundus & mundana omnia se commendant oculis. Neque enim errare sensus, sed revera esse aliquod speciosum in mundo; quod oculis, auribus, manibus, gustu, odoratu deprehendimus: lecus atque novi lincei & cogitabundi sensuum mastiges nonnulli existimant. Hinc porro per inductionem ostendat rerum extrinsecam speciem juxta sensum
units.tr: I. Let him set forth the outward magnificent appearance of sensible things, by which the world and all worldly things commend themselves to the eyes. For the senses do not deceive, but there truly is something attractive in the world, which we perceive by the eyes, ears, hands, taste and smell, though some sharp-eyed and thoughtful chewers of the senses think otherwise. Then let him show, by induction, the outward appearance of things according to each sense:

units.la: 1. Oculorum: hos enim in frontispicio constituisse naturam sagacem tanquam speculatores, ut obvia quaeque menti suggerant: uti sunt.
units.tr: 1. Of the eyes: for nature, being wise, has placed these in the forefront like watchmen, so that they may suggest to the mind whatever presents itself, namely:

units.la: a. Rerum formae extrinsecae earumque varietas amabilis, ubi praecipue pulchritudo corporum. Quantam vim habet illa? &c.
units.tr: a. The outward forms of things and their pleasing variety, especially the beauty of bodies. How great a power does that have! etc.

units.la: b. Rerum Magnitudo & multitudo. Non esse ens otiosum, quantitatem, sed mammonis esse pedissequam. Huc faciunt magni multique agri, domus, &c.
units.tr: b. The size and number of things. Quantity is not an idle being, but the attendant of Mammon. Large and many fields, houses, etc., serve this purpose.

units.la: c. Rerum color: quo flores, vestes immo gemmae & fulgidum, aurum se commendant. Quam multi hoc idolo seducuntur? &c.
units.tr: c. The colour of things: by which flowers, garments, and even gems and gleaming gold commend themselves. How many are seduced by this idol? etc.

units.la: 2. Aurium: quae capiuntur. a. fabulis & vaniloquio ac sermonibus, nibus ociosis, imo obscœnis. Quam speciosum hoc carni!
units.tr: 2. Of the ears: which are captivated a. by fables, idle talk and conversations, indeed obscene ones. How attractive this is to the flesh!

units.la: b. Musica: quàm dulcis hæc, quàm splendida in Comœdiis, in epulis magnatum, in saltationibus: Capite Johannis redimenda fuit.
units.tr: b. Music: how sweet it is, how splendid in comedies, at the feasts of great men, in dances. John's head had to be bought with it.

units.la: 3. Manuum totiusque corporis per tactum: Unde voluptas corporis, quam preciosa illa visa fuit primo mundo, Sodomitis, Sybaritis hodieque plurimis.
units.tr: 3. Of the hands and of the whole body through touch: whence the pleasure of the body, which seemed so precious to the first world, to the Sodomites, to the Sybarites, and to very many today.

units.la: 4. Odoratus: quanta hic odorum suavitas, quanta varietas unguentorum.
units.tr: 4. Of smell: how great the sweetness of odours here, how great the variety of perfumes.

units.la: 5. Gustus: hic adeundæ mensæ magnatum, quantus hic apparatus, quantus luxus, quam suavis convictus!
units.tr: 5. Of taste: here the tables of the great are to be approached, what a display here, what luxury, how pleasant the feasting!

units.la: II. Admiretur magnificentiam rerum, quæ mente æstimantur: uti sunt.
units.tr: II. Let him admire the magnificence of things which are valued by the mind, namely:

units.la: 1. Dignitates & honores; in imperiis, regnis, principatibus, præfecturis ac magistratibus variis. Quid sublimius erectioribus mentibus videri queat? Vitet quis sensuum blandimenta aut contemnat; quis nisi abjectus splendidos honorum gradus & mundi gloriam despexerit? Hic magni & parvi pariter; huc politici & Ecclesiastici pari studio properant. &c. Imo Ecclesiastici majori vecordia &c.
units.tr: 1. Dignities and honours: in empires, kingdoms, principalities, prefectures and various magistracies. What can seem more lofty to minds raised up? Who would avoid the allurements of the senses or despise them, unless he were abject, or had despised the splendid steps of honour and the glory of the world? Here great and small alike, here politicians and churchmen hasten with equal zeal, etc. Indeed churchmen with even greater madness, etc.

units.la: 2. Vana scientia. &c.
units.tr: 2. Empty learning. etc.

units.la: III. Evincat superiorum omnium vanitatem: idque
units.tr: III. Let him prove the vanity of all the above, and this:

units.la: 1. Per inductionem quandam.
units.tr: 1. By a certain induction.

units.la: a. Rerum sensualium: utpote quæ & brutis communes sunt, animam corrumpunt & corpori mancipant.
units.tr: a. Of sensible things: which, as they are common even to the beasts, corrupt the soul and enslave it to the body.

units.la: b. Rerum sensu inperceptibilium: quæ animi turbant quietem, & maximis vitiis ambitione, avaritia, æmulatione, invidia, replent &c.
units.tr: b. Of things imperceptible to the senses: which disturb the peace of the mind and fill it with the greatest vices: ambition, avarice, emulation, envy, etc.

units.la: 2. Per rationes generales.
units.tr: 2. By general reasons.

units.la: a. Quia omnia ista caduca sunt & transitoria. Quid enim constans sub sole. Ubi fastus primi mundi, ubi luxuria Sodomæ, ubi gloria Nabuchodonosuris, Alexandri? &c. Ubi potentia Carthaginis, Corinthi, Romæ? &c.
units.tr: a. Because all these things are frail and transitory. For what is constant under the sun? Where is the pride of the first world, where the luxury of Sodom, where the glory of Nebuchadnezzar and Alexander? etc. Where is the power of Carthage, of Corinth, of Rome? etc.

units.la: b. Quia hominis vita ipsa brevis & ærumnosa est, quæ instar umbræ transit &c.
units.tr: b. Because human life itself is brief and full of trouble, passing like a shadow, etc.

units.la: c. Quia sic falli sunt sapientes omnes: vide dicta aliquot.
units.tr: c. Because all the wise have been deceived in this way: see some examples cited.

units.la: d. Quia Deus ipse mundana omnia damnat vanitatis, uti ex Jobi historia, Davidis psalmis, ut psal. 90. & 103. patet, & ex Ecclesiaste.
units.tr: d. Because God himself condemns all worldly things as vanity, as is clear from the history of Job, from the Psalms of David, such as Ps. 90 and 103, and from Ecclesiastes.

units.la: 1. Propositionem inferat: orbis bona universa vanitati & aerumnis esse obnoxia. 2. Solam veritatem, & mentem, quae hanc percipit, aeternam esse ac stabilem. 3. Moneat de quaerendis bonis stabilibus, quae non in naufragio tantum, sed & in morte, imo in mundi hujus interitu perseverent.
units.tr: 1. Let him draw the proposition: that all the good things of the world are subject to vanity and troubles. 2. That only truth, and the mind which perceives it, is eternal and stable. 3. Let him admonish concerning the seeking of stable goods, which persist not only in shipwreck but also in death, and indeed in the ruin of this world.

units.la: XL. DE SECULO FERREO, SEU VITIIS TEMPORUM. Exord. ex Tacit. de mor. Germ. c.18. videlicet. I. Memorabile esse & dignum Germana virtute encomium incomparabilis Taciti, cum inquit de veteribus Germanis: Nemo illic vitia ridet: nec corrumpere & corrumpi seculum vocatur; II. Addat causam: 1. Vidisse ipsum scilicet in gente Germana non vitia ista, quae Romae & in Romanis provinciis grassabantur, injustitiam, luxum, avaritiam; sed non modo vitam naturae congruam, verum etiam severam censuram, si quis forte exorbitasset, nec excusasse se reos consuetudine temporum; & ut vitiis obex positus, ita & poenam secutam comitem delicti. 2. Viguisse istos mores incorruptos in gente, nondum exteris permixta, sed vivente in sua nativa simplicitate juxta naturae ductum. Quae licet originali labe infecta, tamen exemplis aliorum, & conniventia Majorum se ipsa quotidie pejor evadit. Non secus ac fluvius seces plures contrahit, quo magis a fonte dilabitur: ita & homines &c. Et ut poetae quatuor Secula finxere, quorum posterius deterius praecedente: ita revera orbem quotidie abire in pejus; adeo ut postremis temporibus saeva & infesta omnia praedixerint ipsi Apostoli. III. Applicet ad tempora praesentia: Haec si unquam certe hisce temporibus metuenda esse: ubi a virtute majorum longissime recessum & verissimum illud Horatii. Aetas parentum pejor avis, tulit Nos nequiores, mox daturos Progeniem vitiosiorem. Propos. De hac labe temporum, & seculo vere ferreo paucis pro ingenii & experientiae mediocritate te dicturum, non ad exagitanda vitia, quod grandioris aetatis, sed ad notanda signa temporum,
units.tr: XL. ON THE IRON AGE, OR THE VICES OF THE TIMES. Exordium from Tacitus, Germania c. 18, namely: I. The incomparable Tacitus's praise of the Germans, worthy of their native virtue, is memorable, when he says of the ancient Germans: No one there laughs at vices, nor is it called corrupting or being corrupted to live in that way. II. He should add the reason: 1. Tacitus had evidently seen among the German people not those vices that raged at Rome and in the Roman provinces, injustice, luxury and greed; but a way of life not only suited to nature, but also strict discipline, so that if anyone had by chance gone astray, he did not excuse the offender by the custom of the times; and just as a barrier was placed against vices, so punishment followed as the companion of the offence. 2. Those uncorrupted morals flourished among a people not yet mixed with foreigners, but living in their native simplicity according to the guidance of nature. Although that people is tainted by original sin, nevertheless, through the examples of others and the tolerance of their elders, it grows worse every day. Just as a river gathers more streams the further it flows from its source, so also do men, and so on. And just as the poets imagined four ages, each later one worse than the one before, so in truth the world declines daily for the worse; so much so that the Apostles themselves foretold that in the last times all things would be savage and hostile. III. He should apply this to the present times: if these things were ever to be feared, they are surely to be feared in these times, when there has been the greatest departure from the virtue of our ancestors, and that most true saying of Horace: The age of our parents, worse than that of our grandparents, produced us, who are more worthless, and who will soon bring forth a more vicious progeny. Proposition. About this plague of the times, and the truly iron age, I will speak briefly, according to the modest measure of my talent and experience, not to lash out at vices, which belongs to a riper age, but to note the signs of the times,

units.la: porum, & ad numerandum dies nostros; quod David monet.
units.tr: of the times, and to number our days, as David counsels.

units.la: Tractatio I. Fœcunda vitiis tempora esse patere ex ipsis quæ in terris grassantur plagis ac armis desperatissimis, illa testari de nostris vitiis Deum enim justum esse, nec plectere innocentes, sed nec dimittere nocentes. Adstruat hanc Dei justitiam ex natura Dei, & sacris testimoniis &c. Ac quando tandem plura orbi mala incubuisse quam hisce temporibus roget. Illustretur comparatione illorum temporum: videlicet semper quidem clades, bella, pestes viguisse: asser exempla quædam ex veteri historia, vide Orosium; At hæc tempora superare præcedentia, tum frequentia, tum cæcitate, quod ipsi sibi accersant mala sua. Olim barbaræ gentes vastabant regna & imperium; jam ipsi manus inferimus, & in propria sæ-vimus viscera. Gentes olim sollicitæ erant de causa malorum, ipsis etiam causas cladium imputantibus Christianis: jam ipsi Christiani authores & securi sunt. Æternam stabilitam pacem videri potuisse post bellum 30. annorum. At quam subito rupta? Quæ causa, quàm quod nostra recrudescunt vitia, ut vulnus male curatum, aut desperatum.
units.tr: Treatment I. That the times are fruitful in vices is evident from the most desperate plagues and arms that rage on earth, which bear witness to our vices: for God is just, and does not punish the innocent, but neither does He let the guilty go unpunished. He should establish this justice of God from the nature of God and from the sacred testimonies, etc. And he should ask when the world has ever suffered more evils than in these times. Let it be illustrated by comparison with those times: indeed, there have always been slaughter, wars and pestilences; assert some examples from ancient history, see Orosius. But these times surpass the preceding ones, both in frequency and in blindness, since men bring their own evils upon themselves. Once barbarian peoples laid waste kingdoms and empires; now we ourselves lay hands on them and rage against our own vitals. Peoples once were anxious about the cause of evils, even Christians imputing the causes of disasters to them; now the Christians themselves are the authors and are secure. It could have seemed that a peace eternal and established had come after the Thirty Years' War. But how suddenly was it broken! What is the cause, other than that our vices break out again, like a wound badly healed, or incurable.

units.la: II. Inquirat causas specialiùs, publice grassantibus vitiis per inductionem: uti est.
units.tr: II. He should inquire into the causes more particularly, by induction, as the vices spread publicly, as follows.

units.la: 1. Impietas, malum fœdissimum, deserens illum, unde omnis prosperitas & salus &c. At quanta illa hodie? Nonne religio materia odii, contentionum, bellorum? Annon in jactantia potius, quam in vita? Non jam est in corrigendis vitiis, sed in censurandis formulis verborum, & disputationibus contentiosis &c. O tempora vere ferrea, verà plumbea; ubi pacis magistra vertitur in materiam litium; ubi nostra nos crimina premunt &c. Conferantur tempora prisca, ubi sub martyriis quotidianis fervebat charitas & Zelus pietatis; ubi confessio Christiana brevis erat, juxta Symbolum Apostolicum; at tota vita erat Christiana &c.
units.tr: 1. Impiety, the most foul evil, which forsakes Him from whom comes all prosperity and salvation, etc. But how great is it today! Is not religion now a matter of hatred, contention and war? Is it not in boasting rather than in life? It is no longer in correcting vices, but in censuring the formulas of words and in contentious disputations, etc. O times truly iron, truly leaden, where the teacher of peace is turned into a matter of quarrels; where our own crimes weigh us down, etc. Let us compare the earlier times, when charity and zeal for piety glowed under daily martyrdoms; when the Christian confession was brief, according to the Apostles' Creed; but the whole life was Christian, etc.

units.la: 2. Injustitia; vitium pessimum, vastans humanam societatem vide Locos Communes. Leges habemus, sed non juxta illas vivimus; sed ut fraudes & iniquitatem specie legum tegamus &c. Quæ causa tam iniqua, quæ patronum non invenit. Corruptioris ævi indicium est, multitudo legum, & in illa litium copia. Aliter in aureo seculo, ubi quisque sibi lex erat &c. vide Ovid. Jam ferrea secula, ubi pugnis & ferro sibi quisque jus dicit. Ibi jus ubi maxima merces. Post cædes, post bella cruenta, de jure quæritur, quando ferro violata & pulsa justitia Sed hoc seculum dicitur. Inter gentes ac Turcas sic agi nil mirum; at probrum Christianis, æquissima charitatis lege à Christo formatis &c.
units.tr: 2. Injustice; the worst vice, laying waste human society; see the Common Places. We have laws, but we do not live according to them; rather we cover up frauds and iniquity under the appearance of laws, etc. What cause is so unjust that it cannot find a patron? The multitude of laws, and the abundance of lawsuits in them, is a sign of a more corrupt age. It was otherwise in the golden age, when each was a law to himself, etc., see Ovid. Now comes the iron age, when each man declares right for himself with fists and steel. There is right where the reward is greatest. After slaughters, after bloody wars, right is sought, when justice has been violated and driven out by steel. But this is called the age. That it goes this way among the nations and the Turks is no wonder; but it is a reproach to Christians, who have been formed by Christ under the most equitable law of charity, etc.

units.la: 3. Intemperantia & luxus; fiat transitio: sed deseramus campum Martis, desistamus à foro & judiciis; intremus domus privatas, agite quænam hic scelera grassantur? Quid dicam a. De luxu in cibo, potu, supellectili superflua. Frugalitas veteribus in precio erat, nobis fastidio. Toto jam accersitur ab orbe quo gens quæque perit. Vide Satyricos, Juvenalem, Pers. Horat. passim. Annon æquamus, imò superamus veteres? Sed hoc seculum vocatur. &c.
units.tr: 3. Intemperance and luxury; let there be a transition: but let us leave the field of Mars, let us desist from the forum and the courts; let us enter private homes. Look, what crimes rage here! What shall I say? a. Of luxury in food, drink and superfluous furnishings. Frugality was prized by the ancients; to us it is loathsome. Now from the whole world are fetched things by which each nation perishes. See the satirists, Juvenal, Persius, Horace throughout. Do we not equal, indeed surpass, the ancients? But this is called the age, etc.

units.la: b. Quid dicam de avaritia, vitio fidei ac professioni Christianæ contrario, Quis jam contentus suo, quis non fraude, vi alienis inhiat? Quis omnia fraudum genera enumerare valeat &c. Quis virtutem credit esse αὐτάρκειαν, Apostolo tantopere commendatam? Inertium est suo contentos vivere: affectare, rapere omnia, hodie seculum vocatur. Sed ô seculum vere ferreum, verè plumbeum, &c.
units.tr: b. What shall I say of avarice, a vice contrary to faith and to the Christian profession? Who is now content with his own, who does not covet what belongs to others by fraud or force? Who could enumerate all kinds of fraud, etc.? Who believes that self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκειαν], so highly commended by the Apostle, is a virtue? It is for the idle to live content with what is theirs; to aspire to and seize everything is today called the age. But O truly iron age, truly leaden age, etc.

units.la: c. De superbia quid dicam? Aureum videtur hoc vitium, sed verè plumbeum, & ultimo seculo proprium est; animam gravans & fœdam reddens in conspectu Dei: cui modestia & humilitas placet. Vide Locum Comm. Sed hoc seculum vocatur, hic modus est.
units.tr: c. What shall I say of pride? This vice seems golden, but it is truly leaden, and peculiar to the last age; it weighs down the soul and makes it foul in the sight of God, who is pleased by modesty and humility. See the Common Place. But this is called the age; this is the fashion.

units.la: III. Damnet omnia vanitatis ac profanitatis, degenerantis à fide ac vita Christiana, in qua sola salus est, quæ non de hoc seculo, sed janua ad futurum seculum est.
units.tr: III. He should condemn all the things of vanity and profanity, which degenerate from the Christian faith and life, in which alone salvation lies, which is not of this age, but is the gate to the age to come.

units.la: Conclus. Hæc esse, quæ de vitiis præcipuis temporum & more seculi corrupti, pro tenuibus viribus, tyrocinii loco dicere voluerit, petere, ut æquis animis accipiantur: & optare ut tandem deposito ferro, priscum redeant tempora in aurum &c.
units.tr: Conclusion. These are the things which, according to my slender powers, I have wished to say, by way of an apprenticeship, about the chief vices of the times and the manner of a corrupt age; I ask that they be received with fair minds, and I pray that, the iron being at last laid down, the times may return to the former golden age, etc.

units.la: XLI. DE USU VESTIUM.
units.tr: XLI. On the Use of Clothing

units.la: Exord. A dicto Plin. lib. 9. c. 35. Parum scil. fuerat, in gulas condimaria, ria, nisi manibus, auribus, capite totoque corpore a fœminis juxta virisque gestarentur: scil. de margaritis tractaturus, in sui seculi luxum invehitur, non in vestibus minus cultuque corporis, quam in gula effusi ac prodigiosi: cum, uti Sen. lib. 8. nat. quæst. Muliebres munditias, colores meretricios, matronis quidem non induendos, viri jumpserunt. Unde, ut Seneca Pater controv. 9. Torpebant ingenia desidiosæ juventutis: cantandi saltandique obscœna studia effœminatos tenebant: & capillum frangere, & ad muliebres blanditias vocem extenuare; mollitie corporis certare cum fœminis, & immundissimis se excolere munditiis adolescentium specimen erat. Addatur causa: postquam scil. Asiæ Africæque divitiæ Romam translatæ essent: illæ opes affixere seculi mores mersamque suis vitiis, quasi sentina, Remp. pessum dedere ait Flor. lib. 3. c. 12. Oppositæ fuere leges sumptuariæ, Fannia, & Oppia præsertim, at frustra, &c. Idem non injuria de nostris temporibus dicendum; quæ tanto pejora, quanto difficiliora, non auro opibusque ut Roma olim, sed pauperie onusta, tota tamen in luxum, epulis vestibusque exæstuant. &c.
units.tr: Exordium. From the saying of Pliny, book 9, chapter 35: It was not enough, of course, to have seasonings for the throat, unless women and men also wore them on their hands, ears, head and whole body. Intending to treat of pearls, he inveighs against the luxury of his own age, and not less against the extravagance and prodigality in clothing and bodily adornment than against gluttony. As Seneca says in book 8 of the Natural Questions: Men have taken up the feminine elegance and the colours of harlots, which matrons themselves should not put on. Hence, as Seneca the Elder says in Controversia 9: The minds of idle youth grew sluggish; obscene pursuits of singing and dancing held them effeminate; to curl the hair, to soften the voice to women's coaxing tones, to vie with women in softness of body, and to groom themselves with the dirtiest refinements, was the mark of a young man. Add the cause: after the riches of Asia and Africa had been carried to Rome, those resources fastened the morals of the age upon it, and drowned in its own vices, like a sewer, the commonwealth was brought to ruin, says Florus in book 3, chapter 12. Sumptuary laws were passed against it, especially the Fannian and Oppian, but in vain, etc. The same may rightly be said of our own times, which are the worse for being the more difficult: burdened with poverty, not, as Rome once was, with gold and wealth, yet wholly seething with luxury in feasts and clothing, etc.

units.la: Propos. Hæc causa, quare in præsentiarum præsertim de vestium usu legitimo dicendum mihi sumpserim, &c.
units.tr: Proposition. This is the reason why I have resolved to speak, especially at present, about the lawful use of clothing, etc.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Doleat conditionem hominis præ cunctis animantibus, quæ diversis tegumentis munivit natura: solus post lapsum homo nudus indigusque nascitur, aliis opibus fovendus. Illustretur collatione status integritatis, ubi nudus quidem fuit, at innocentia ac sanctitate tectus, vestibus non indiguit; qualis & futurus est in statu gloriæ: at in peccatum prolapsus, & justitia & omni ope destituitur, & nobilissima creatura exuviis vilibus brutorum operiendus est: Utinam illis non superbiat.
units.tr: Treatment. I. Let him lament the condition of man, who alone of all living creatures was furnished by nature with various coverings: since the fall, man alone is born naked and destitute, needing to be cherished by other resources. Let him illustrate this by comparison with the state of integrity, where man was indeed naked, yet clothed in innocence and holiness, and had no need of garments, as he will also be in the state of glory. But having fallen into sin, he is deprived both of righteousness and of every resource, and this most noble creature must be covered with the cast-off skins of beasts. Would that he did not take pride in them.

units.la: II. Vestium usum doceat: videl. ut Cic. 2. de Orat. ait. Vestis depellendi frigoris causa primo reperta fuit, post ea ad ornatum & corporis dignitatem habere cœpta. Hinc
units.tr: II. Let him teach the use of clothing, namely as Cicero says in book 2 of On the Orator: Clothing was first discovered to ward off the cold, and afterwards began to be had for ornament and for the dignity of the body. Hence

units.la: I. Ostendat initium vestium, ut homo a. primo a Deo inclamatus foliis arborum se texerit ob verecundiam, conscius nuditatis, non corporis modo, sed & animæ, quæ nudata erat imagine Dei. Hanc veram nuditatem esse, &c. b. Pellibus opertus fuerit a Deo: qui sic consuluit & nuditati & frigori. Hæc scil. prima vestimenta fuisse, & diu postmodum gestata priscis mortalibus, vid. Heb. 11. Polydorum Virgil. de rerum inven.
units.tr: I. Let him show the origin of clothing: that man, when first called to account by God, covered himself with leaves of trees out of shame, conscious of nakedness, not only of the body but also of the soul, which had been stripped of the image of God. This is the true nakedness, etc. b. He was clothed by God with skins, who thus provided both for his nakedness and for the cold. These, namely, were the first garments, and were worn for a long time afterwards by the early mortals; see Hebrews 11, and Polydore Vergil, On the Discovery of Things.

units.la: a. Hebr. 11. inventor. & Alex. ab Alexandro. Accesisse deinceps plumas avium magnarum, quibus Æthiopes Indi etiamnum utuntur. Postea verò artem textoriam & lanificii & linificii usum,&c. Scilicet primitus vestium usus fuit in tegenda nuditate & arcendo frigore. Ratio: quis enim superbiat illo, quod perpetuum commissi sceleris memoriale est? aesi fur laqueo superbire velit. &c.
units.tr: a. Hebrews 11, the discoverers, and Alexander ab Alexandro. Afterwards the feathers of large birds were added, which the Indian Ethiopians still use. Later, however, the art of weaving and the use of wool and flax, etc. Clearly, at first clothing was used to cover nakedness and to keep off the cold. The reasoning is this: who would take pride in that which is a perpetual memorial of the crime committed? Even a thief would not wish to boast of the noose. Etc.

units.la: 2. Doceat progressum vestium & usum ulteriorem.
units.tr: 2. Let him teach the progress of clothing and its further use.

units.la: a. Quod invectae ad dignitatem. Talis enim quis praesumitur qualem habitus demonstrat. Bartolus: & Quintil. lib. 8. Cultus addit hominibus dignitatem. Ratio: quia primo incurrit in oculos: cùm animi dotes occultae, &c:
units.tr: a. That clothing was introduced for dignity. For a person is presumed to be such as his dress shows him to be. Bartolus; and Quintilian, book 8: Dress adds dignity to men. The reason is that it strikes the eye first, whereas the endowments of the mind are hidden, etc.

units.la: b. Vestes invectae ad distinctionem.
units.tr: b. Clothing introduced for distinction.

units.la: a. Sexus, etiam apud Barbaros, ipsa natura duce, ut cuique sexui suus constet honos, vitentur vagae & promiscuae libidines. Spartani non satis cauti hic, non satis tegentes foeminas. Hinc prohibita mutatio vestium sexui propriarum in Lege Mosis. Inde alius habitus virginis, viduae, matronae, meretricis, vid. Cassan. part. 2. confid. 32. Salmuth epigr. 8. lib. 1. num. 17. 18. 20.
units.tr: a. Sex: even among the barbarians, nature herself being the guide, so that each sex keeps its own honour, and wandering and promiscuous lusts are avoided. The Spartans were not careful enough in this respect, and did not cover their women sufficiently. Hence in the Law of Moses a change of garments proper to one's sex is forbidden. Hence there is a different dress for the virgin, the widow, the matron and the harlot; see Cassan, part 2, consilium 32; Salmuth, epigram 8, book 1, numbers 17, 18, 20.

units.la: β. Dignitatis: quae & hac notâ commendatur publicè. Unde alius habitus.
units.tr: β. Dignity: which is also publicly marked by this badge. Hence a different dress.

units.la: α. Sacerdotalis; etiam ab ipso Deo ordinatus: vid. Exod. 27. & lib. Levit. & notentur vestes sacerdotales apud Gentiles. Causa: ut decori compareant coram Deo & venerandi coram hominibus. Huc pertinent ordines Monachorum: similes monachi, similes cappæ &c.
units.tr: α. Priestly: ordained even by God himself; see Exodus 27 and the book of Leviticus. The priestly vestments among the Gentiles should also be noted. The purpose is that they may appear becoming before God and venerable before men. To this belong the orders of monks: similar monks, similar cowls, etc.

units.la: b. Regalis, ut purpura, diadema, trabea, aurum, gemmæ; vestes angustiores, ampliores, invectæ à Romulo, item Numa, Pompilio, & præcipuè Tarquinio Prisco, vide Dionys. Halicarn. Liv. Flor. Talibus enim ornamentis indigere majestatem. vid. Salmuth. d. l. n. 3.
units.tr: b. Royal, such as purple, diadem, the trabea, gold, gems; narrower and fuller garments, introduced by Romulus, likewise by Numa Pompilius, and especially by Tarquinius Priscus; see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Livy, Florus. For majesty needs such ornaments; see Salmuth, loc. cit., number 3.

units.la: c. Civicus, variorum ordinum & graduum: Unde & alius herilis, alius servilis: uti membra diversa diversam habent figuram, diversum loci & situm. Item aliae quotidianae vestes, aliae festivae, nuptiales, convivales. Notatur in in Evangelio, qui sine vestle nuptiali comparuit.
units.tr: c. Civic, of various orders and ranks. Hence also one dress for masters and another for servants, just as different limbs have different shapes and different places and positions. Likewise some garments are everyday, others festive, nuptial, or for feasts. It is noted in the Gospel that the man who came without a wedding garment was rejected.

units.la: 3. Functionum & status, ubi in pace toga, in bello sagum, &c. Salmuth. d. 1. num. 4. Vestis philosophica. Salmuth. n. 5. 6. Seneca epist. 5. Alia hilaritatis, alia luctus: ut sic omni & functioni ac statui habitus respondeat. &c. Alex. ab Alexandr. c. 18. lib. 5.
units.tr: 3. Of functions and status: where in peace the toga, in war the sagum, etc.; Salmuth, loc. cit., number 4. The philosophical garment; Salmuth, numbers 5, 6; Seneca, letter 5. Some garments are for cheerfulness, others for mourning, so that dress corresponds to every function and station. Etc. Alexander ab Alexandro, chapter 18, book 5.

units.la: Conclus. Hunc vestium usum esse & sacris & profanis historiis probatum. Optandum, ut quisque ordini & conditioni suae conformem se gerat; semperque meminerit, vestem tegumentum esse nuditatis, adjumentum indigentiae & monumentum esse tristissimi lapsus Adami.
units.tr: Conclusion. That this use of clothing is approved both by sacred and by profane histories. It is to be wished that each person conduct himself in conformity with his order and condition, and always remember that clothing is a covering of nakedness, a help to need, and a monument of Adam's most sorrowful fall.

units.la: XLII. DE ABUSU VESTIUM.
units.tr: XLII. On the Abuse of Clothing

units.la: Exord. Ab Exemplo C. Oppii tribuni plebis: videl. verendum sibi, ne taxaturo luxum in vestibus contingat, quod C. Oppio quondam: cui contra praevalentem in Rom. Rep. luxum dicenti mulieres litem ac molestiam movebant, vid. Liv. l. 34. Dicturum se tamen quae sentiat: neque enim minorem debere esse licentiam in taxandis, quam patrandis vitiis: cum in libera Rep. liberae debeant esse voces. Dixisse antecessorem nuper de usu vestium; cum negari nec abusus hic queat, nec silendum de excessu: quod nemini ingratum esse queat, nisi suam culpam saltem tacite confiteatur. Merito statim initio exclamandum esse; ubi es prisca frugalitas, prisca severitas & disciplina majorum? Semetipsum vix agnoscere mundum ac civitatem, nedum avi proavique queant suos nepotes, suos posteros, exotica pompa vestitos, &c.
units.tr: Exordium. From the example of C. Oppius, tribune of the plebs: he had to fear that in censuring luxury in clothing he might meet what happened to C. Oppius once, when women brought suit and harassment against him as he spoke against the luxury then prevailing in the Roman Republic (see Livy, book 34). Yet he will say what he thinks, since the freedom to censure vices ought not to be less than the freedom to commit them, and in a free commonwealth voices ought to be free. His predecessor recently spoke about the use of clothing. This abuse cannot be denied, nor can the excess be passed over in silence, and no one can be displeased by it unless he at least tacitly confesses his own fault. Rightly, at the very beginning, one should cry out: where is your ancient frugality, your ancient severity and discipline of our forebears? Scarcely can one recognize the world and the state as one's own, much less can grandfathers and great-grandfathers recognize their grandchildren and descendants, clothed in foreign pomp, etc.

units.la: Propos. Abusum igitur sine acerbitate sibi taxandum esse; maximè cum illa quae ab antecessore dicta, rapere in suam rem queant ambitiosi.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore the abuse is to be censured by him without harshness, especially since the things said by the predecessor can be seized upon by the ambitious for their own purposes.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Approbet illa quae dicta ab antecessore. Quis enim neget necessariam sexus, dignitatis &c. discriminatricem esse vestem? At uti olim, ita & jam majorem abusum esse in vestibus; adeò enim diversos invehi modos ac figuras, ut histrioniam agere mundus videatur. Olim Comoedos mutasse habitum; jam seculum hoc esse: morem tanto magis deplorandum, quo magis in proproprio opprobrio gloriam quærere videtur. Olim legibus vestiariis coercitum, jam vagari luxum indomitum, aut legibus robustiorem.
units.tr: Treatment. I. Let him approve what was said by the predecessor. For who would deny that clothing is necessary to distinguish sex, rank and so on? But as in former times, so now there is a greater abuse in clothing; for such diverse modes and shapes are introduced that the world seems to be acting a stage play. Formerly comic actors changed their dress; now this is the age, and a custom all the more to be deplored because it seems to seek glory in its own disgrace. Formerly restrained by sumptuary laws, luxury now roams unbridled, or grows stronger than the laws.

units.la: II. Concedat mulieribus præsertim mundum muliebrem & ornatum permitti sed moderatum vid. Cassaneum d. loco. Attamen intra limites modestiæ ac statuscujusque. Ornatum modestum in Julia placuisse Augusto, at non meretricium, &c.
units.tr: II. Let him concede that women in particular should be allowed a womanly elegance and adornment, but a moderate one (see Cassaneus in the place cited), yet within the limits of modesty and of each one's station. A modest adornment pleased Augustus in Julia, but not a harlot's, etc.

units.la: III. Recenseat taxetque abusus varios:
units.tr: III. Let him enumerate and censure the various abuses:

units.la: 1. In confusione & licentia promiscua; ubi non ad necessitatem aut ornatu, sed ad pompam, æmulatione ac luxu destinantur; ubi opulentiores, aut etiam qui videritales volunt, neglecto ordine ac statusratione, licere sibi putant omnia: imitantes divitem epulonem apud Lucam. Tales pavonibus similes esse, cujus pennæ splendidæ, caro insuavis. At everti sic ordinem ac harmoniam ex Rep. quæ ex diversi generis membris composita; ut corpus humanum, Illustret exemplo veterum Rom. contrario & majorum nostrorum. Viguit tunc ordo, modestia, viguit frugalitas & concordia, &c.
units.tr: 1. In confusion and promiscuous license, where garments are intended not for need or ornament but for display, rivalry and luxury; where the wealthier, or even those who want to seem such, disregard order and the reckoning of station and think everything is permitted to them, imitating the rich man feasting in Luke. Such people are like peacocks, whose feathers are splendid but whose flesh is unpleasant. Yet thus order and harmony are overturned in the commonwealth, which is composed of members of different kinds, as the human body is. Let him illustrate this with the contrary example of the ancient Romans and our forefathers. Then order flourished, modesty flourished, frugality and concord flourished, etc.

units.la: 2. In neglectu decori, quid quemque deceat. Ut enim sagatum gladiatum incedere non licebat Romæ tempore pacis, ut infula sacerdotalis, non quadrat militi; nec gladius habitusque militaris Philosopho &c. ita nec promiscuos habitus diversis generis civibus. Uti diversis ordinibus constat civitas, ita & diversi diversos decent habitus, &c. Ordinem esse in angelis, in mundo universo, in exercitu; cur non etiam in civitate? &c.
units.tr: 2. In neglect of propriety, of what befits each person. For just as it was not permitted at Rome in time of peace for a gladiator to walk about in a sagum, and a priestly fillet does not suit a soldier, nor a sword and military dress a philosopher, etc., so neither should mixed dress be worn by citizens of different classes. As the state consists of different orders, so different people suit different dress, etc. Order exists among the angels, in the whole universe, in an army; why not also in the state? etc.

units.la: 3. In luxu, quo modus excedRitur ab omnibus ordinibus. Ostendatur hoc a. exemplo veterum Romanorum: & varia ac luxuriosa vestium genera invecta, & querelas desuper Satyricorum & historicorum, legesque sumptuarias oppositas & varia inde nata certamina referr & secutam Reip. cladem ac eversionem. Sævior armis Luxuria invaluit, victumque ulciscitur orbem. b. Exemplo modernorum, qui exsuperant luxum veterum, licet non æquent censum. Hinc variantes vestium materias formasque, quas novis rebus dedita Gallia invenit, exagitet: (recenseat hic paucis genera vestium novarum vid. Jun. Orat. & Progymn. Pontani &c.) Et dolendum doceat, sic expelli pristcam frugalitatem severitatemq; Germanorum; & me-tuentuendum doceat, ne cum vestibus Gallia paulatim & mores imperiumque propaget ; uti Romani olim cum Imperio mores & linguam. vid. Lanfium in Consultat, de Gall. & Germ. &c.
units.tr: 3. In luxury, by which the measure is exceeded by all ranks. Let this be shown by the example of the ancient Romans: how various and luxurious kinds of clothing were introduced, the complaints about them of satirists and historians, the sumptuary laws set against them, the various contentions arising from them, and the ruin and overthrow of the commonwealth that followed. "Luxury has grown stronger than arms, and avenges the conquered world." b. By the example of the moderns, who surpass the luxury of the ancients, though they do not match their wealth. Here let him criticize the varying materials and shapes of clothing that Gaul, given over to novelties, has invented (let him briefly list here the kinds of new garments; see Junius, Orat., and the Progymnasmata of Pontanus, etc.). And let him teach with lament that the ancient frugality and severity of the Germans is thus driven out; and let him teach with fear that Gaul, through its clothing, gradually spreads its customs and rule, as the Romans once spread their customs and language along with their empire (see Lanfius, in Consultation on Gaul and Germany, etc.).

units.la: IV. Deploret effectus hujus luxus : uti est jactura
units.tr: IV. Let him deplore the effects of this luxury, such as the loss

units.la: 1. Opum & enervatio familiarum ac negociationum:
units.tr: 1. Of wealth, and the enfeebling of families and businesses:

units.la: 2. Debilitatio Reip. cum primò sic opes efferuntur ad exteros & crepundia rursus importantur : deinde mores molles invehuntur, & ab honestis occupationibus ad ocium, ad comoedias, ac choreas, ad vanitatem ac superbiam juventus seducitur, &c.
units.tr: 2. The weakening of the commonwealth: when wealth is first carried off to foreigners and trinkets are imported in return; then soft manners are introduced, and youth is seduced from honest occupations to idleness, to comedies and dances, to vanity and pride, etc.

units.la: 3. Concitari iram Dei, qui minatur luxui tali exitium, &c. Esaiae. cap. 4.
units.tr: 3. The wrath of God is aroused, who threatens such luxury with destruction, etc. Isaiah, chap. 4.

units.la: Concluf. Laudet mores antiquos, optet uti liberi ac nepotes avis atavisque potius, quam Comoedis & Sybaritis similes esse malint. Moribus antiquis res stat Romana caditque.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him praise the ancient manners and wish that children and grandchildren may resemble their grandfathers and great-grandfathers rather than prefer to resemble comic actors and Sybarites. On ancient morals the Roman state stands or falls.

units.la: XLIII. DE MERCATURA ET COMMERCIIS.
units.tr: XLIII. Of Trade and Commerce.

units.la: Exordium. A Prolepsi, videl. miretur fortasse quis, cur inter doctos de mercatura, argumento inter doctos minus usitato, tractet. Resp. Propterea tanto magis tractandum, ne res regnis ac Rebus p. saluberrima, spreta ac neglecta videatur; uti sane minime neglecta est politicis. Ratio, quia uti corpus constat ex plurimis membris, ita corpus civitatis ex diversis partibus, earumque harmonia componitur, ex quibus haud postrema Mercatura, illa praesertim, quae non sordida; sed lautior illa, (quam auctores & JCti semper distinguunt, alios mercatores, alios negotiatores vocantes) quae vinculum est civitatis, qua aliunde necessaria importantur, superflua exportantur, saluberrimum semper fulcrum existimatum regnorum & Rerum publicarum.
units.tr: Introduction. Someone may perhaps wonder, by way of anticipating an objection, why a scholar should treat trade, a subject not much used among scholars. Answer: for that very reason it must be treated all the more, so that a matter most wholesome for kingdoms and commonwealths does not seem despised and neglected. It is certainly not neglected by the political writers. The reason is that, as the body consists of many members, so the body of the state is made up of diverse parts and their harmony. Among these, trade is by no means the least, especially that trade which is not sordid but more refined, which the authors and jurists always distinguish, calling some merchants and others businessmen. This trade is the bond of the state, by which necessary goods are imported from elsewhere and surplus goods exported, and it has always been regarded as the most wholesome support of kingdoms and commonwealths.

units.la: Propositio. De hac impraesentiarum dicendum, ea moderatione, ut non quaesitis laudibus efferatur, sed ne debita laus ipsi detracta esse videatur, quod omnino cavendum, ne despecto ac deserto commercio nervis suis Respubl. destituatur.
units.tr: Proposition. This is what must be said about it at present, with such moderation that it is not puffed up with unsought praise, yet also that due praise is not seen to be withheld from it. This must be guarded against above all, lest by despising and abandoning commerce the commonwealth be deprived of its sinews.

units.la: Tractatio. Proponat Mercaturae.
units.tr: Treatment. He sets out the following points about trade.

units.la: I. Dignitatem, idque
units.tr: I. Its dignity, and that

units.la: 1. A prima causâ Deo, qui humanam societatem ac fœdera populorum instituit, hominem creans animal Politicum, quæ societas sine commerciis mutuis consistere nequit.
units.tr: 1. From its first cause, God, who instituted human society and the covenants of peoples, creating man a political animal, a society that cannot exist without mutual commerce.

units.la: 2. Ab exemplis a. Patriarcharum, quorum studia agricultura & pecuaria, eisque connexa necessariò commercia. b. Magnatum & regum antiquissimorum, Solomonis, cujus naves Indiam profectæ, vid. 1. Reg. c. Modernorum magnatum, in Italia præsertim, ut ducis magni Florentiæ, Nobilium Venetorum, etiam Germanorum. vid. Politicos: utrum nobilem deceat Mercatorem esse.
units.tr: 2. From examples: (a) of the patriarchs, whose pursuits were agriculture and herding, and commerce necessarily joined to them; (b) of the most ancient magnates and kings, such as Solomon, whose ships sailed to India (see 1 Reg. c.); of modern magnates, especially in Italy, such as the great duke of Florence and the noblemen of Venice, and also among the Germans (see the political writers on whether it becomes a nobleman to be a merchant).

units.la: 3. A consensu Politicorum ipsiusque Aristotelis; qui æstimat optimates in Republ. etiam ex opibus vid. lib. 3. Polit. Hinc etiam Romæ ex censu civium differentia & præferentia suffragiorum instituta à Servio Tullio; quod per brevem digressionem referatur ex Historia. vid. Liv. & præsertim Dionys. Halicarnassæum, adde & Cic. in off: At inter præcipua media parandarum opum esse commercia. Inferatur hinc mercaturæ dignitas, & cum antiquissimis dignissimisque occupationibus illam contendat: fiatque translitio ad
units.tr: 3. From the agreement of the political writers and of Aristotle himself, who holds that the best men in the commonwealth are chosen also by their wealth (see Pol. bk. 3). Hence also at Rome the distinction and precedence of votes according to the census of citizens was instituted by Servius Tullius, which may be mentioned by way of a brief digression from history (see Livy, and especially Dionysius of Halicarnassus; add also Cicero, On Duties). But among the chief means of acquiring wealth are commerce. From this the dignity of trade is inferred, and it is set alongside the most ancient and most worthy occupations. A transition is then made to

units.la: II. Utilitatem insignem, & quidem per præteritionis figuram.
units.tr: II. Its notable usefulness, indeed by the figure of preterition.

units.la: 1. Privatam, videl. divitias, quæ non facilè aliunde parantur, si prudenter exerceatur. Ingrediatur sic in laudem modestam divitiarum, tanquam benedictionis divinæ, quæ neutiquam cum Diogene & Stoicis spernendæ: quippe: a. benedictio divina promissa industriis & Deum timentibus, b. Patriarchis & regibus piis non negletæ; c. organa necessaria in toga & saga, in sacris & profanis. d. omnibus in quocunque vitæ genere expetitæ, tanquam media sustentandi vitam mortalé.
units.tr: 1. Private usefulness, namely riches, which are not easily obtained elsewhere if trade is practised prudently. Here he enters into a modest praise of riches, as a gift of divine blessing, which by no means is to be despised with Diogenes and the Stoics. Indeed: (a) the divine blessing is promised to the industrious and to those who fear God; (b) it was not neglected by the pious patriarchs and kings; (c) riches are necessary instruments in both the toga and the cloak, in sacred and secular life; (d) they are desired in every kind of life as the means of sustaining mortal life.

units.la: 2. Publicam: vid. a. ad victum tenuioribus, quorum in Republ. maxima copia, quibus non nisi vigente mercatura prospici potest. Illustretur ex contrario exemplo interclusæ aut obsessæ urbis. b. ad reditus publicos in teloniis, vectigalibus & portoribus. vid Orat. pro lege Manil. Illustretur remediis extraordinariis, capitatione, decimatione, contributione, unde seditio & paupertas. At mercatura locupletat ærarium, & nutrit tenuiores, ornat, beat, locupletat omnes. c. ad propagationem religionis, quæ beneficio Mercaturæ ad alterum orbem propagatur, d. ad incrementa & florem urbium bium & regiminum. Ostendatur inductione exemplorum, & in specie Venetiarum & Belgii, quarum florem luculentius ostendat, efferatque præ cunctis regnis & regionibus. Addanturque exempla urbium veterum, Tyri & Sidonis, Carthaginis, Corinthi & illustretur comparatione Romæ, quæ sola bellis crevit, Excudant alii &c. Tu regere imperio populos Romane memento.
units.tr: 2. Public usefulness: (a) for providing food to the poorer classes, who make up the greatest part of the commonwealth and can be supplied only while trade flourishes. This is illustrated by the contrary example of a city that is shut in or besieged. (b) For public revenues from tolls, taxes and harbour dues (see the oration for the Manilian law). This is illustrated by extraordinary remedies, the poll tax, the tithe, and forced contributions, whence come sedition and poverty. But trade enriches the treasury, nourishes and adorns the poorer classes, makes all happy and wealthy. (c) For the propagation of religion, which by the benefit of trade is spread to the other hemisphere. (d) For the growth and prosperity of cities and governments. This is shown by induction from examples, and in particular from Venice and the Netherlands, whose flourishing he displays more brilliantly and raises above all kingdoms and regions. Examples of ancient cities are added, Tyre and Sidon, Carthage, Corinth, and the comparison with Rome, which alone grew by wars: "Others will fashion bronze more softly... but you, Roman, remember to rule the peoples with your empire."

units.la: III. Difficultatem, quæ probetur.
units.tr: III. Its difficulty, which is proved.

units.la: 1. Ex eo, quod multi quidem eam profiteantur, at pauci emergant, plurimi foro etiam cedant, hoc existentes inter mercatores, (si sua culpa aut fraude fiat) quod suci inter apes, male docti inter doctos.
units.tr: 1. From the fact that many indeed profess it, but few rise to the top, and most even give way in the forum; these become, among merchants (if it happens through their own fault or fraud), like the dregs among bees, poorly taught among the learned.

units.la: 2. Ex requisitis mercatoris, uti est, I. peritia locorum exterorum, quid quisque ferat, quibus indigeat. II. Notitia hominum & ingeniorum ne decipiatur. III. Peritia linguarum exoticarum, arithmeticæ, nauticæ, aliarum artium nonnullarum, uti & legum nauticarum & mercatoriarum.
units.tr: 2. From the requirements of a merchant, such as: I. skill in foreign places, what each produces and what each needs; II. knowledge of men and their characters, so as not to be deceived; III. skill in foreign languages, arithmetic, navigation, and some other arts, as well as the laws of navigation and of trade.

units.la: IV. Solertia & dexteritas singularis, dignoscendi occasiones, negligendi quandoque lucrum; evitandi fraudes æruscatorum &c. hinc rejiciatur error illorum, qui sapientiam eruditis tantum arrogant, cum contra experientia & usus rerum mundi hujus, veram gignat prudentiam. &c.
units.tr: IV. Singular shrewdness and dexterity: discerning opportunities, sometimes letting go of gain, avoiding the frauds of usurers, etc. Hence is rejected the error of those who ascribe wisdom only to the learned, whereas on the contrary experience and practice of the affairs of this world produce true prudence, etc.

units.la: IV. Necessitatem, quæ evincatur.
units.tr: IV. Its necessity, which is shown.

units.la: 1. Ex indigentia locorum, quia scil: non uni regioni Deus dedit omnia, sed diversa loca diversis beavit dotibus. Vid. Lansii consultationes & Geographos, hic defectus non nisi per commercia suppleri potest. Quod ostendatur inductione, per commercia auro Peruviano, ebore Indico & Africano, aromatibus Arabicis, balsamo Palæstino, marmore Italico, serico Chinensi, vino Cretico &c. in remotissimis oris septentrionis populi utuntur, fruuntur.
units.tr: 1. From the need of places, because God did not give all things to one region, but endowed different places with different gifts. See Lansius' Consultations and the geographers. This deficiency can be supplied only through commerce. This is shown by induction: through commerce, peoples in the most remote regions of the north use and enjoy Peruvian gold, Indian and African ivory, Arabian spices, Palestinian balsam, Italian marble, Chinese silk, Cretan wine, etc.

units.la: 2. Ex necessaria communicatione cum peregrinis, quæ sine commerciis vix constare potest.
units.tr: 2. From the necessary communication with foreigners, which can scarcely exist without commerce.

units.la: 3. Ex natura vitæ humanæ, ubi alii abundant certis rebus, alii indigentia earum laborant, quarum sine commercio mutuo permutatio fieri nequit. Unde & ipsi Reges, Principes & Resp: illam exercere necesse habent, Epilogus. Recolleͤtis ſummatim argumentis, commerciorum uſum & conſervationem commendet, addito hoc argumento, quod ipſa jura gentium eorundem libertatem terra marique tueantur, quia norunt, illam animam vitalem eſſe, & nervum civitatum, tantumque creviſſe aut decreviſſe, quantum commercia creve-runt, & decreverunt.
units.tr: 3. From the nature of human life, where some abound in certain things and others suffer want of them, and without mutual commerce exchange cannot take place. Hence kings, princes, and commonwealths themselves are obliged to practise it. Epilogue. Having briefly recalled the arguments, he commends the use and preservation of commerce, adding this argument: that the laws of nations themselves protect its freedom by land and sea, because they know it to be the vital soul and sinew of states, and that states have grown or declined exactly as commerce has grown or declined.

units.la: XLIV. DE MARI.
units.tr: XLIV. ON THE SEA.

units.la: Exord. a prolepſi: videlicet forte mirum videri dicere de Mari, argumento inſueto & vulgari. Reſp. Quia inſuetum, ideo tracandum, ne dicta aliis tanquam crambe bis cocta reponantur. Vulgaria vero ſæpe ea continere, quæ nec eruditiſſimis displicent. Imo omnia magnæ naturæ opera contemplanda homini divinitus eſſe propoſita ad Dei Creatoris gloriam & humanum uſum. Errare, qui in arcanis & reconditis Philoſophorum ſpeculationibus ſapientiam omnem repoſitam arbitrantur, & aſtra contemplantes, infe-riora negligunt: &c.
units.tr: Exordium from anticipation: it may perhaps seem strange to speak about the sea, a subject that is unusual yet commonplace. Answer: because it is unusual, it must be treated, lest what is said be served up to others like cabbage reheated twice. Commonplace matters, however, often contain things that do not displease even the most learned. Indeed, all the works of great nature have been set before man by God to be contemplated, for the glory of God the Creator and for human use. They err who think that all wisdom is laid up in the hidden and recondite speculations of the philosophers, and who, while gazing at the stars, neglect the lower things: etc.

units.la: Addatur præparatio ad propoſitionem: videlicet non dicturum de jure maris, quod magnis ingeniis tractatum argumentum tuum captum ſuperans, & uti olim ita & hodie magnis animis ac appa-ratibus inter principes ac respublicas diſputatum:
units.tr: Add a preparation for the proposition: namely, that he will not speak of the law of the sea, a subject which exceeds your argument's grasp, which great minds have treated, and which, as in the past so today, has been disputed among princes and commonwealths with great spirit and elaborate effort.
