units.la: Propoſitio Sed de admiranda natura, & insigni utilitate maris te verba facturum. Fiat petitio attentionis.
units.tr: Proposition But you will speak of the admirable nature and the remarkable usefulness of the sea. Let attention be requested.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: A. Admirandam maris naturam prædicet: ubi
units.tr: A. Let him proclaim the admirable nature of the sea, where:

units.la: I. Magnitudo, quæ aliquoties terram tam ſpecioſam exſuperat, uti elementa ſuperiora inferius, quippe quod centro universi proximum. Tantam vero ejus eſſe magnitudinem, ut terram universam ambiat, veluti inſulas, omnesque ejus cavitates ac ſinus expleat, omnes fluvios effundat, recipiatque sine decremento aut incremento. Maximi Creatoris magnum argumentum; ut merito Plin. proëm. lib 32. immensum potentiæ occultæ documentum vocet.
units.tr: I. Its magnitude, which at times surpasses the land, however fair, as the higher elements surpass the lower, being nearer the centre of the universe. Its magnitude is such that it encircles the whole earth, fills the islands and all its hollows and bays, pours out all the rivers, and receives them without decrease or increase. It is a great proof of the mighty Creator, so that Pliny rightly calls it, in the preface to book 32, an immense proof of hidden power.

units.la: II. Motus & agitatio perpetua tum per ventos diversos ad usum in diversa loca navigantium; tum per æstum internum; quo intumescit & in semetipsum resident: de cujus causis disquiraturVid: Physicos & Plinium & Geographos: & miretur exaſtas semper horarum vices, quibus fluat, refluatque.
units.tr: II. Its motion and perpetual agitation, both through the various winds, which serve navigators travelling to different places, and through its internal tide, by which it swells and subsides again. Concerning its causes let him inquire: see the natural philosophers, Pliny and the geographers; and let him marvel at the exact and ever-regular alternation of the hours at which it flows and ebbs.

units.la: III. Coitio in globum, ita ut una cum terra unum globum constituat, quod contra naturam corporis liquidi videtur. Multò mirabilius in tam vasto corpore, & tanta aquarum copia, quæ sua ponderositate ad unam partem vergere posse videtur. Probetur interim rotunditas ex situ universi, ex navigatione & natura partium in guttis pluviarum, in liquore in foliis herbarū colle-cto. Vid. Plin. lib.9. c.2.3 & Physicos.
units.tr: III. Its gathering into a globe, so that together with the earth it forms one globe, which seems contrary to the nature of a liquid body. This is far more wonderful in so vast a body and so great a mass of waters, which might seem bound to lean to one side by its own weight. Meanwhile let the roundness be proved from the position of the universe, from navigation, and from the nature of the parts in drops of rain and in liquid gathered on the leaves of herbs. See Pliny, book 9, chapters 2 and 3, and the natural philosophers.

units.la: IV. Repagula exigua quibus continetur, videlicet littora & exi-guas sæpe arenarum moles, illa interiora multū alto mari, cum alias satis potens esset ad operiendam terram universam, uti factum in diluvio universali, aliisque eluvionibus particularibus, uti sunt Deucalionis, Ogygis, similibusque in diversis partibus orbis. Admiretur hinc divinam potentiam, quæ hosce posuit terminos, vide Job. & Psal. 147.
units.tr: IV. The slight barriers by which it is contained, namely the shores and often a small heap of sand, while the sea within is much higher than these; although it would be quite powerful enough to cover the whole earth, as happened in the universal Flood and in other particular inundations, such as those of Deucalion and Ogyges and similar ones in different parts of the world. Let him thence admire the divine power which set these boundaries: see Job and Psalm 147.

units.la: B. Facta transitione accedat ad partem alteram, extollatque insignem ejus utilitatem.
units.tr: B. Having made the transition, let him proceed to the other part and extol its remarkable usefulness.

units.la: I. In piscatione: ubi exponat.
units.tr: I. In fishing, where he should set out:

units.la: 1. Copiam piscium inexhaustam tot gentibus accolis, & mi-ram varietatem in monstris marinis, ipsas terrestrium ani-malium species non modo æquantē, sed & superantē, vid. Plin. d. lib.9. c.3. Jonstonum, aliosque. Argumentum singularis providentiæ divinæ, cum terra non sufficiat alendis tot gen-tibus, mare supplere defectum inexhausta piscium copia.
units.tr: 1. The inexhaustible abundance of fish for so many peoples living on its shores, and the wonderful variety of sea monsters, which not only equal but even surpass the species of land animals: see Pliny, the book cited, chapter 3, Jonston and others. It is an argument of singular divine providence that, since the land does not suffice to feed so many peoples, the sea supplies the deficiency by its inexhaustible store of fish.

units.la: 2. Fructum exinde in pastu non modo accolarum, sed & remo-tiorum populorum, per haleces, asellos, passeres, salmones arefactos; ditibus pariter pauperibusque pascendis aptos. Quid jam de aliis commodis balenarum ad usum lychnorum tot populis, ad axungiam? Quid de sale longe communissimo ac maximè necessario. Imo quid de rebus preciosissimis, unio-nibus gemmisque Magnatum ornamentis. Quid de succino ex extremo septentrione per mare Balthicum appulso litto-ribus Borussiæ? Claudatur admiratione divinæ bonitatis in elemento tam tremendo ac barbaro.
units.tr: 2. The produce from this for the food not only of the neighbouring peoples but also of more distant nations, through herring, sprats, sparrows (?), and dried salmon, suitable for feeding rich and poor alike. What shall we say of the other benefits of whales, for lamps for so many peoples, and for their fat? What of salt, by far the most common and most necessary? Indeed, what of the most precious things, pearls and gems, the ornaments of magnates? What of the amber cast up from the far north by the Baltic Sea onto the shores of Prussia? Let him end in admiration of divine goodness in an element so terrible and savage.

units.la: II. In Commerciis maritimis, ad ultimos & inaccessos alios mun-di terminos. Hinc
units.tr: II. In maritime commerce, reaching the furthest and otherwise inaccessible ends of the world. Here:

units.la: 1. Exponat navigationes præcipuas antiquorum, ut Solomonis, Tyri, Sidonis; & recentium Portugallorum, Hispanorum, Anglorum & Belgarum præcipue. Quid non detectum? quantum emolumentum Europæ per hasce navigationes. Percurre breviter merces varias ac preciosas ex Africa & India utraque advectas.
units.tr: 1. Let him set out the principal voyages of the ancients, such as those of Solomon, Tyre and Sidon, and of the more recent ones, especially those of the Portuguese, Spaniards, English and Dutch. What has not been discovered? How great the advantage to Europe through these voyages! Run briefly through the various and precious goods brought from both Africa and India.

units.la: 2. Comparet commercia terrestria, utpote 1. minora, 2. majori sumptu, minori celeritate peragenda, quam maritima; ubi omnia contraria.
units.tr: 2. Let him compare land trade, which is 1. smaller, 2. carried on at greater expense and with less speed than maritime trade, where everything is the reverse.

units.la: 3. Emolumenta hinc ostendat in illustribus maxime emporiis ex maritimis commerciis aucta.
units.tr: 3. Let him show the advantages thence derived, in the most famous trading centres, from increased maritime commerce.

units.la: C. Deploret abusum maris.
units.tr: C. Let him lament the abuse of the sea.

units.la: I. In navigationibus hybernis; unde crebra naufragia: aliter ac veteres faciebant, qui hyeme clausum mare arbitrabantur. Cupiditas lucri incusetur tanquam causa hujus mali.
units.tr: I. In winter voyages, whence come frequent shipwrecks, unlike the ancients, who thought the sea closed in winter. Let the lust for gain be blamed as the cause of this evil.

units.la: II. In bellis ac praeliis maritimis, qualia olim inter Carthaginenses & Romanos, inter Persas ac Athenienses; hodieque inter Turcam & Venetos, & inter Anglos ac Belgas. Doleatur saeva dominandi libido, cui nec terra satis, nisi & oceanus classibus sternatur, ut non una morte homines pereant.
units.tr: II. In naval wars and sea battles, such as those formerly between the Carthaginians and the Romans, between the Persians and the Athenians, and today between the Turks and the Venetians, and between the English and the Dutch. Let him lament the savage lust for dominion, for which not even the land is enough unless the ocean too is strewn with fleets, so that men perish not by a single death.

units.la: Peroratio Desinat in admirationem divinae sapientiae ac bonitatis, in cujus laudes & ipsa maria ac monstra marina incitantur Pf. 147. & homines in mari agentes commercia animantur Pf. 107. &c.
units.tr: Peroration Let him end in admiration of divine wisdom and goodness, to whose praise the seas themselves and the sea monsters are stirred up, Psalm 147, and men who work at sea are encouraged to trade, Psalm 107, etc.

units.la: XLV. DE ORIGINE ET NATURA POPULORUM.
units.tr: XLV. ON THE ORIGIN AND NATURE OF PEOPLES.

units.la: Exord. à stupenda populorum varietate; quae tanta est ut vix verisimile rationi videatur esse tatum Pauli Act. 17.26. Deus fecit ex uno sanguine totum genus hominum.
units.tr: Exordium: from the amazing variety of peoples, which is so great that it seems hardly credible to reason that all were made from one blood, as Paul says in Acts 17:26: "God made of one blood all the nations of men."

units.la: 1. Illustretur comparatione reliquorum animantium, quae in suo quaeque genere sibi similia: at in hominibus quanta differentia tum ratione corporum, tum maxime animorum! Ostendatur quadam inductione,
units.tr: 1. Let it be illustrated by comparison with the other living creatures, each of which is like its own kind; but among men what a difference there is, both in the constitution of their bodies and, above all, in their minds! Let this be shown by a certain induction.

units.la: II. Asseratur interim veritas dicti Apostolici in genere ex historia creationis
units.tr: II. Meanwhile let the truth of the apostolic saying be affirmed in general from the history of creation.

units.la: III. Evincatur dignitas hujus considerationis ex Cicer. de Orat. ubi duo dicit esse capita Reip. videlicet nosse remp. & civium cognicognitos habere mores: utriusque afferatur ratio: quia non omni statui reip. & non omnibus populis eadem conveniunt; qua in re fi erretur, sequi ut plurimum concussionem aut everlio- nem rerumpublicarum.
units.tr: III. Let the dignity of this consideration be established from Cicero, De Oratore, where he says there are two chief heads of the commonwealth, namely, to know the state and to have knowledge of the citizens' morals. Let the reason for each be given: because the same things do not suit every condition of the state, nor the same things all peoples; and if one errs in this matter, it usually follows that the commonwealths are shaken or overthrown.

units.la: Propositio. In præsentiarum considerandam paucis originem & naturam populorum; ut sic eò magis ad cognitionem nostri ipsorum & prædicandam gloriam Creatoris, qui unicuique certos habitandi terminos aflignavit, & ex omnibus populum sibi formavit, excitemur:
units.tr: Proposition. Let us now briefly consider the origin and nature of peoples, so that we may be stirred all the more to know ourselves and to proclaim the glory of the Creator, who assigned to each its fixed bounds of habitation and from all formed a people for himself.

units.la: Tractatio. A. de origine. Hanc
units.tr: Treatment. A. On origin.

units.la: I. Arcessat à Deo conditore & inftauratore naturæ universæ: quod ostendat 1. ex sacris. 2. ex silentio historiæ antiquioris: quod argumento est, in origine mundi à Mose assignato subsistendum esse. Hinc paucis ostendat antiquissimos gentium historicos & quod ultra Ninum non ascendant. Hinc refellat.
units.tr: I. Let him begin from God, the creator and restorer of all nature; this he should show (1) from the sacred writings, (2) from the silence of more ancient history, which is evidence that one must hold to the origin of the world assigned by Moses. Here let him briefly show that the most ancient historians of the nations do not go back beyond Ninus. Then let him refute:

units.la: a. Ægyptios in suorum regum Dynastiis ultra mundi originem ascendentes. Vid. Diod. Sicul. & Chronol. Helvicum &c.
units.tr: a. the Egyptians, who, in the dynasties of their kings, go back beyond the origin of the world. See Diodorus Siculus, and Helvicus's Chronology, etc.

units.la: b. Philosophos mundi æternitatem afferentes, videlicet Physicos.
units.tr: b. the philosophers who assert the eternity of the world, namely the natural philosophers.

units.la: II. Referat generaliter propagationem populorum, uti ante diluvium ab Adamo, ita post diluvium ex Noacho ipsiusque liberis. vid. Gen. 10. cap. & Arcam Noæ Hornii &c.
units.tr: II. Let him relate in general the propagation of peoples: as before the flood from Adam, so after the flood from Noah and his sons. See Genesis chapter 10, and Hornius, Arca Noae, etc.

units.la: III. Inquirat causam hujus deductionis omnium populorum ab uno principio: 1. Ut sic manuducamur ad unitatem Creatoris, qui omnia ex uno deduxit principio, ut ex terra animalia, ex mari omnia flumina & fontes; ex sole lumen & calorem; ita & ex uno sanguine genus hominum. 2. ut homines sic eo magis tendant ad unionem & concordiam, per unionem in regno ac republica, & per fœdera ac commercia.
units.tr: III. Let him inquire into the cause of this derivation of all peoples from one source: (1) so that we may be led to the unity of the Creator, who derived all things from one source, as from earth the animals, from the sea all rivers and springs, from the sun light and heat; so also the human race from one blood. (2) So that men may thereby tend all the more to union and concord, through union in kingdom and commonwealth, and through covenants and commerce.

units.la: IV. Refellat hinc 1. illos, qui ex terra, uti cætera animantia, ita & homines prognatos volunt:
units.tr: IV. Let him refute hence: (1) those who want men to have been born from the earth, just like the other animals;

units.la: 2. Authorem Præadamitarum, qui alios diu ante Adamù natos invehere voluit ex vetustis fabulis & malè detorta Scriptura, refutatus passim.
units.tr: (2) the author of the Preadamites, who wished to introduce others born long before Adam, drawing on old fables and a badly twisted Scripture; refuted in many places.

units.la: Concludat hanc partem admiratione sapientiæ divinæ, quæ uti vultuum, ita & ingeniorum ac morum tantam varietatem ex uno stipite pite deduxit, & tam varios rursum sub unnm regimen & ad unum caput Christum reduxit.
units.tr: Let him conclude this part with wonder at the divine wisdom, which derived such great variety of faces, and likewise of minds and morals, from one stock, and again brought such varied peoples under one rule and to one head, Christ.

units.la: B. De natura.
units.tr: B. On nature.

units.la: I. Originaria. 1. generatim
units.tr: I. Original. 1. In general.

units.la: a. Quòd ad societatem inclinat: & quidem α. œconomicam unde conjugiorum & familiarum jura β. politicam, quâ in vicos, pagos, civitates, principatus, regna, imperia coëunt & in commune consulunt. qua re nihil ad culturam virtutum & vitæ commoditatem salubrius. γ. Ecclesiasticam, qua conscientiæ instinctu communi tendunt ad reverentiam & cultum Dei, & ad vitam civili hac vita sublimiorem; adeò ut nulla gens tam barbara sit, quam non imbuat metus Numinis. 1. Illustretur dissimili reliquorum animantium. 2. Adstruatur a causa, videlicet Deum indidisse animis hominum hanc inclinationem, tum ad solatium indigentiæ humanæ, tum ad exercitium virtutum, tum denique ad necessariam sui conservationem & defensionem. Unde commerciorum, fœderum, & bellorum jura enata apud omnes gentes. Vide Hugonem Grotium de jure belli & pacis.
units.tr: a. That it inclines to society: and indeed (α) the domestic, whence the laws of marriages and families; (β) the political, by which they come together into villages, districts, cities, principalities, kingdoms, and empires, and take counsel for the common good; nothing is more wholesome for the cultivation of virtues and the convenience of life. (γ) The ecclesiastical, by which, through the common impulse of conscience, they tend to reverence and worship of God, and to a life higher than this civil life; so that no nation is so barbarous that it is not imbued with fear of the Deity. (1) Let it be illustrated by the unlikeness to the other living creatures. (2) Let it be affirmed that the cause is that God implanted in the minds of men this inclination, partly for the solace of human need, partly for the exercise of virtues, and finally for their necessary self-preservation and defence. Whence the laws of commerce, covenants, and wars arose among all nations. See Hugo Grotius, On the Law of War and Peace.

units.la: 2. Speciatim quod interim diversa diversorum natura uti indicatum ab initio: & quidem
units.tr: 2. Specifically, that meanwhile the diverse natures of the diverse peoples, as indicated from the beginning, are also these:

units.la: a. Ratione diversæ educationis, cujus vis explicetur etiam in ipsis animantibus; & major adhuc in hominibus. Hinc alios populos bellicosos, alios molles ac luxuriosos: vide exempla in Europæis præcipuis & Asiaticis. Alios mansuetos, alios efferatos. Alios frugales, alios deliciosos: illustretur exemplis &c.
units.tr: a. By reason of diverse education, whose force is explained even in the animals themselves, and is still greater in men. Hence some peoples are warlike, others soft and luxurious; see examples among the chief European and Asiatic peoples. Some are gentle, others savage. Some frugal, others given to pleasures; let it be illustrated with examples, etc.

units.la: b. Ratione loci & habitationis; locorum indole paulatim insinuante se ipsis ingeniis. Hoc ostendatur jam inductione præcipuarum gentium, & indoles singularum explicetur. Vide Synopf. Polit. Besold. part. 2 c. 11. vide Flor. lib. 2. c. 3. 4. Cic. de fato c. 4. Plin. p. 8. c. 58.
units.tr: b. By reason of place and habitation; the character of places gradually insinuating itself into the minds themselves. This should now be shown by a survey of the chief nations, and the character of each explained. See Besold, Synopsis Politica, part 2, ch. 11; see Florus, book 2, ch. 3-4; Cicero, On Fate, ch. 4; Pliny, book 8, ch. 58.

units.la: c. Ratione variæ commixtionis ex migrationibus populorum ortæ; unde vel meliores, vel etiam pejores sæpe evadunt populi. Ita barbaras nationes ingerentes se in diversas imperii provincias, meliores factas: ita Romanos per colonias passim emendasse mores &c. Vide Lazium de migrat. gentium, & Jornandem de rebus Geticis, Longobard. &c.
units.tr: c. By reason of the various mixture arising from migrations of peoples; whence peoples often become either better or even worse. Thus barbarous nations, pressing into the various provinces of the empire, became better; thus the Romans, through colonies everywhere, amended their morals, etc. See Lazius, On the Migration of Peoples, and Jordanes, On the Affairs of the Getae, Lombards, etc.

units.la: d. Ratione decursus seculorum, quo ruditas paulatim mitigatur, aut etiam luxus certaque vitia in certis nationibus invalescunt. Vide exempla in Germanis, contra in Asiaticis & Græcis, Romanis, Judæis &c.
units.tr: d. By reason of the course of the centuries, through which rudeness is gradually softened, or luxury and certain vices take hold among certain nations. See examples among the Germans, and on the contrary among the Asiatics and Greeks, Romans, Jews, etc.

units.la: II. Adscititia, quæ fit per disciplinas & informationem & literas: quibus incultissimi cultissimi evasere. Vid. exempla, quomodo Græcis Romanisq; literis orbis paulatim excultus fuerit; quibus accedit Christiana Religio, qua ad unum ovile Christi tandem etiam barbarissimi reducuntur: ut sic ad unum Deum à quo conditi revocentur.
units.tr: II. Acquired, which comes about through learning, instruction, and letters; by which the most uncultivated have become most cultivated. See examples of how the world was gradually cultivated by Greek and Roman letters; to which is added the Christian religion, by which at last even the most barbarous are brought back to the one fold of Christ, so that they may thus be recalled to the one God by whom they were created.

units.la: Perorat. Repetitâ summâ dictorum
units.tr: Peroration. Having repeated the sum of what was said:

units.la: I. Indicet prudentiam necessariam in tractandis diversis populis, notetque imperitiam illorum, qui omnes eodem modo tractare volunt: quo factum ut maximi Monarchæ lautissimas provincias perdiderint.
units.tr: I. Let him point out the prudence necessary in dealing with diverse peoples, and note the inexperience of those who wish to treat all in the same way; whence it has happened that the greatest monarchs lost the richest provinces.

units.la: II. Addat præconium divinæ sapientiæ ac bonitatis, qua ex tam diversis ingeniis harmonicum hujusmodi ordinem universi stabilivit & conservat &c.
units.tr: II. Let him add a eulogy of the divine wisdom and goodness, by which from such diverse natures he established and preserves this harmonious order of the universe, etc.

units.la: XLVII. DE INCREMENTIS ET POTENTIA REGNORUM AC RERUMPUBLICARUM.
units.tr: XLVII. ON THE GROWTH AND POWER OF KINGDOMS AND COMMONWEALTHS.

units.la: Exordium. Ab admiratione poetæ Ovid. de exiguo initio & stupendo incremento urbis Romæ: Hic, inquit, ubi nunc Roma est, quondam fuit ardua sylva: Tantaque res paucis pascua bobus erat. Merito mirari ipsum. Licet enim postmodum sat amplo spacio sita fuerit Roma, tamen initio exiguis terminis conclusam fuisse. vid. Florum &c. At postmodum in splendidam illam orbis metropolin excevisse; ut regum Patria Pyrrhi legato videretur.
units.tr: Introduction. From the poet Ovid's wonder at the small beginning and remarkable growth of the city of Rome: Here, he says, where Rome now stands, there was once a high wood, and so great a thing was once a pasture for a few oxen. He rightly marvels at it. For although Rome was afterwards situated in a fairly wide space, at first it was enclosed within narrow bounds. See Florus, etc. But afterwards it rose to that splendid metropolis of the world, so that it seemed to Pyrrhus's envoy to be the homeland of kings.

units.la: Extendatur hoc ad omnia regna ac resp: illas ab exiguo initio ad tantam potentiam excrevisse. vid. Justin. initio, & ostendatur inductione ftione 4. Monachiarum, aliarumque Rerump. aliquot, ut Carthaginensis, Tyri, Venetæ, Belgicæ &c.
units.tr: Let this be extended to all kingdoms and commonwealths, which rose from a small beginning to such great power. See Justin at the beginning, and let it be shown by induction, in the fourth section, from several monarchies and other commonwealths, such as Carthage, Tyre, Venice, the Belgic provinces, etc.

units.la: Propos. Quæ causæ tanti incrementi & potentiæ paucis dispiciendum; fi Excellentissimi & humanißimi Auditores benevolas aures tenui conatui accommodare dignari velint.
units.tr: Proposition. What causes lie behind such great growth and power must be examined briefly, if the most excellent and most humane hearers will deign to lend benevolent ears to this slight effort.

units.la: Tractatio. Recenseat causas aliquot, & quidem
units.tr: Treatment. Let him list some causes, and indeed:

units.la: I. Prima ac princeps dicatur Deus, qui uti Regnorũ Rerp. conditor, ita & auctor & fotor; qui vocat illa quæ non sunt ut sint. Excitat ex pulvere tenuem, qui designavit loca habitattionis. Hic enim Rex regum &c. Illustretur testimoniis aliquot. Hinc pietas basis regnorum dicitur; secus ac Machiavellus arbitratur. Frustra sunt vires humanæ, nisi ipse evexerit populum, &c.
units.tr: I. First and foremost, let God be named, who, as the founder of kingdoms and commonwealths, is also their author and preserver; who calls into being the things that are not. He raises the lowly out of the dust, he who has appointed the places of habitation. For he is King of kings, etc. Let this be illustrated by several testimonies. Hence piety is called the foundation of kingdoms, contrary to what Machiavelli supposes. Human strength is in vain unless he himself has raised up the people, etc.

units.la: II. Dehinc & humana succedunt consilia ac opera, quibus Deus utitur tanquam instrumentis: ad conciliandum Reip. majestatem & decus. Hic 1. Non aspernandam potentiam & incrementum doceat, sed omni ratione parandum, viis legitimis: idque
units.tr: II. Next come human counsels and works, which God uses as instruments to secure the majesty and dignity of the commonwealth. Here he should teach: (1) that power and growth are not to be despised, but are to be pursued by every means, by lawful ways; and this

units.la: a. Quia donum Dei est, quo ipsi assimilantur.
units.tr: a. Because it is a gift of God, by which men are made like him.

units.la: b. Quia necessaria est ad ferenda onera Reip. ad instaurandas clades, ad reprimendos rebelles, ad repellendos hostes. Illustretur simili ab hominibus, animalibus, quæ ad defensionem fui instructa sunt à natura.
units.tr: b. Because it is necessary for bearing the burdens of the commonwealth, for repairing disasters, for restraining rebels, and for repelling enemies. Let this be illustrated by a comparison with humans and animals, which nature has equipped for their own defence.

units.la: 2. Modos augendæ potentiæ recenseat: uti sunt
units.tr: 2. Let him recount the ways of increasing power, which are:

units.la: a. In munienda metropoli & limitibus. Metropolis et enim veluti cor est, quod uti natura costis veluti repagulo circumdedit, ita munienda quàm accuratissimè, arcibus, ropugnaculis, aggeribus, fossis. Uti sanè hodie ars illa ad summum pervenit. Licet enim in viribus civium optimum munimentum; tamen & illa juvant, maxime postquam tormenta inventa, &c.
units.tr: a. In fortifying the metropolis and the borders. For the metropolis is like the heart, which nature has surrounded with ribs as with a barrier; so it should be fortified as carefully as possible, with citadels, bulwarks, ramparts, and ditches. Indeed that art has today reached its height. For although the best fortification lies in the strength of the citizens, yet these also help, especially since cannon were invented, etc.

units.la: Nec minus limitanea loca, ubi primum periculum: Ut pedes, manus, caput tegimus contra cœli injurias. Huc facere & colonias eo missas, uti olim Romani &c. vid. L.C. d munim & illustretur ex historia.
units.tr: Nor are the frontier places less important, where danger first appears, just as we cover feet, hands, and head against the injuries of the sky. Here also belong colonies sent out there, as the Romans once did, etc. See L.C. on fortification, and let it be illustrated from history.

units.la: Ad defensionem verò requiruntur, Armamentaria, omni machinarum, armorum, reliquorumque necessari orum copiâ referta, hinc Venetia, Helvetica, Belgica, Argentoratum, Noriberga reliquæque Civitates Germaniæ, hosti formidabiles; & tot fereprovinciæ expugnandæ, quot civitates imperiales. Facilem hinc nuper expugnationem Poloniæ, locis munitis destitutæ. Cur Gallia loca tantum limitanea munierit? Quia metuit oppressæ religionis vindicias, &c.
units.tr: For defence, arsenals are required, stocked with an abundance of all machines, arms, and other necessary supplies. Hence Venice, Switzerland, Belgium, Strasbourg, Nuremberg, and the other cities of Germany are formidable to the enemy; and nearly as many provinces are to be conquered as there are imperial cities. Hence the recent easy conquest of Poland, which was left destitute of fortified places. Why has France fortified only its border places? Because it fears for the defence of the oppressed religion, etc.

units.la: Pertinent ad munimenta etiam milites duces. Hi vel stipendio conducuntur & aluntur ad præsidium locorum; ubi consultum ut pacis tempore artem calleant; Ducum gradus numerusque minuantur, ut sine gravi onere ali queant. Vel subsidiarius miles formatur ex civibus, per exercitia militaria, quo spectant præmia honoris. Ita Helvetia suis militibus militat.
units.tr: Soldiers and commanders also belong to the fortifications. These are either hired for pay and maintained to garrison the places, where it is prudent that they should learn their craft in time of peace; the ranks and numbers of commanders should be reduced, so that they can be supported without heavy burden. Or a reserve soldiery is formed from the citizens through military exercises, to which rewards of honour attach. Thus Switzerland wages war with its own soldiers.

units.la: b. Opes & pecunia: quæ acquiruntur
units.tr: b. Resources and money, which are acquired:

units.la: α. Ex cultura & melioratione soli: in exsiccandis paludibus, excolendis agris sterilibus, ducendis follis, &c. exemplo Atheniensium, Constantinopolitanorum, Germanorum, Belgarum præsertim. Neque enim in latitudine territorii, sed in cultu opulentia est, &c.
units.tr: α. From cultivation and improvement of the soil: by draining marshes, tilling barren fields, leading out ditches, etc. Following the example of the Athenians, the Constantinopolitans, the Germans, and especially the Belgians. For wealth lies not in the extent of territory but in cultivation, etc.

units.la: β. Ex opificiis, unde publicus & privatus quæstus est. Exemplo Noribergenf. Parisienf. Londinenfium, Gandavenfium, Genevenfium, &c.
units.tr: β. From trades, whence public and private gain arises. Following the example of Nuremberg, Paris, London, Ghent, Geneva, etc.

units.la: γ. Ex commerciis, quæ anima vitalis civitatum & regnorum. Hinc crevisse Resp. opibus publicis & privatis & incolis omnis generis. Huc facere flumina, marium, portuum commoditates. Horum beneficio jungi veluti loca remotissima. Illustretur exemplis Tyri olim & Carthaginis; Corinthi, Venetiarum: hodieque Lisbonæ, Londini, Amstelodami totiusque Belgii. Uti enim sufficiens, ita liber est oceanus, nullius hactenus potentia domitus.
units.tr: γ. From commerce, which is the vital breath of cities and kingdoms. Hence commonwealths have grown in public and private resources and in inhabitants of every kind. Here belong rivers, seas, and the advantages of harbours; by their benefit even the most remote places are joined together. Let this be illustrated by examples of Tyre and Carthage of old, Corinth and Venice, and today Lisbon, London, Amsterdam, and all of Belgium. For the ocean, as it is sufficient, so it is free, and hitherto has been subdued by no one's power.

units.la: c. Federa cum propinquis & remotis, illis præsertim qui eosdem habent amicos & hostes. Ubi cavendum, ne debiliores potentioribus in clientelam se tradant; unde periculum libertatis. Æsopus hoc notavit fabulâ equi hominis opem implorantis. Silhonius tutius hoc putat debiliori-bus, bus, si in potentioris clientelam concedant: sed fallitur &c. Rectius sentiunt principes & respubl: Italicæ &c. Huc pertinet superiori seculo Liga Cathol. Unio Protestantium, hodie Liga triplex. Item fœdus Hanseaticum ad commerciorum securitatem, Helvetiorum contra Austriacos, Belgarum contra Hispanos, Hispanorum contra Gallos antipathiâ stabilitum. Augmentum seu copia civium & incolarum. Huic inserviunt.
units.tr: c. Alliances with neighbours, near and distant, especially with those who share the same friends and enemies. Here one must take care lest the weaker surrender themselves into the clientage of the stronger, whence comes danger to liberty. Aesop noted this in the fable of the horse that implored the help of man. Silhon thinks this safer for the weaker, if they submit to the clientage of the stronger, but he is mistaken, etc. The princes and commonwealths of Italy judge more rightly, etc. To this belongs, in the last century, the Catholic League, and the Union of the Protestants; today, the triple league. Likewise the Hanseatic League, established for the security of commerce; the Swiss alliance against the Austrians; the Belgians against the Spanish; the Spanish against the French, established by mutual antipathy. Increase, or abundance of citizens and inhabitants, is served by these.

units.la: Propagatio sobolis legitima per conjugium, huic fini divinitus institutum. Hinc præmia soboli copiosæ, poenæ cœlibatus inter Græcos & Romanos.
units.tr: Lawful propagation of offspring through marriage, which God instituted for this end. Hence the rewards for abundant offspring, and the penalties for celibacy, among the Greeks and Romans.

units.la: Evocationes peregrinorum per Asyla, ut Romulus olim fecit, haud licita hodie; artificum per immunitates & præmia; iuniorum per illustres Scholas & Academias: nobilium per Aulæ celebritatem.
units.tr: Calling in foreigners through asylums, as Romulus once did (not lawful today); craftsmen through immunities and rewards; young men through famous schools and academies; nobles through the splendour of the court.

units.la: Æqua justitia & bonum regimen ac publica libertas. Hinc crevit Venetia, subsistit Geneva: contra desolata Hispania, Turcia, &c.
units.tr: Equal justice, good government, and public liberty. Hence Venice grew and Geneva subsists; by contrast, Spain, Turkey, etc. are laid waste.

units.la: Conclus. Hos esse fontes præcipuos potentiæ ac floris Regnorû ac Rerump. detestandum verò morem augendæ potentiæ esse bella injusta, sollicitationes aliorum subditorum ad defectionem, Asyla facinorosis aperta, oppressiones tenuiorum, &c. Orandum igitur Deum, ut Reges, principes, civitatum Rectores gubernet, ut deposito armorum desiderio istas augendæ potentiæ vias sequantur, quas Deus, natura & sana Politica præscribit: sic licet minus terrarum, plus certæ veræque potentiæ futurum esse,
units.tr: Conclusion. These are the chief sources of the power and flourishing of kingdoms and commonwealths. The detestable ways of increasing power are unjust wars, incitements of other men's subjects to revolt, asylums opened to criminals, and oppression of the lowly, etc. We must therefore pray God to govern kings, princes, and the rulers of cities, so that, laying aside the desire for arms, they may follow those ways of increasing power which God, nature, and sound politics prescribe; thus, though they may have less of the earth, there will be more of sure and true power.

units.la: XLVIII. DE ÆSTU ET MOTIBUS POPULORUM.
units.tr: XLVIII. CONCERNING THE TIDES AND MOVEMENTS OF PEOPLES.

units.la: Exord. A motu maris: cujus
units.tr: Exordium. From the motion of the sea, of which:

units.la: I. Exponatur natura mirabilis, qua certis in diversis locis horis intumescit & in semetipsum residet
units.tr: I. Let the wonderful nature be set forth, by which at certain hours in different places it swells and settles back again into itself.

units.la: II. Inquirantur causæ, externæ, sidera & luna præsertim. Interna, spiritus inclusi & erumpentes statis temporibus Suprema, Deus qui ita ordinavit, ob varias rationes acusus.
units.tr: II. Let the causes be inquired into: external ones, chiefly the stars and the moon; internal ones, enclosed winds breaking out at fixed times; and the supreme cause, God, who so ordained it, for various reasons.

units.la: III. Applicetur ad motus populorum, qui simili ratione veluti per vices, exæstuant residuntque.
units.tr: III. Let it be applied to the movements of peoples, which in a similar manner, as if by turns, surge and subside.

units.la: Propof. De hisce motibus ac æstu populorum dicendum; maximè ob dicta de natura, & gloria populorum ab antecessoribus.
units.tr: Propositio. These movements and the tides of peoples are to be discussed, chiefly because of what was said above about the nature and glory of peoples by our predecessors.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. Adstruat veritatem ex historia. Hic itaque ex historiæ sinopsi præcipuos motus populorum juxta ordinem temporis exponat interpositis congruis affectibus admirationis, ut suavitatem habeat relatio. vid. Orosium.
units.tr: I. Let him establish the truth from history. Here, then, from a synopsis of history, let him set forth the principal movements of peoples in the order of time, with fitting expressions of admiration inserted, so that the narrative may have charm. See Orosius.

units.la: II. Inquirat causas horum motuum, & quidem
units.tr: II. Let him inquire into the causes of these movements, and indeed:

units.la: 1. Supremam, Deum: qui sic
units.tr: 1. The supreme cause, God, who thus

units.la: a. Exercet judicia sua, ad castiganda peccata enormia. Ita Nebucadnezari dederat populos omnes, & ipso utebatur Assyrio tanquam virga iræ & baculo furoris sui; vid. lib. Judic. Samuelis, Regum, & Esaiam.
units.tr: a. Exercises his judgments to punish heinous sins. So Nebuchadnezzar was given all the peoples, and he used the Assyrian as the rod of his anger and the staff of his fury; see the books of Judges, Samuel, Kings, and Isaiah.

units.la: b. Præstat beneficia interim, non secus ac quando Deus fulmine terret orbis incolas, & simul dat pluvias fœcundas. Sic enim sæpe per subactiones bellicas.
units.tr: b. Bestows benefits meanwhile, just as when God terrifies the inhabitants of the world with lightning and at the same time gives fruitful rains. For so often through military conquests.

units.la: c. Propagatur cultus civilis, bonæ literæ, & ipsa religio. Ita per motus Israelitarum exeuntium ex Ægypto, & abductorum in captivitatem Assyriacam, dispersorumque per gentes plurimi facti sunt Proselyti, &c. Per Romanorum motus & arma victricia, passim jura ac politia ipsorum propagata fuit. Illustrentur comparatione æstus marini, qui aliorum terras inundat, aliorum vegetat, quosdam compellit in portum, quosdam repellit.
units.tr: c. Civil culture, good letters, and religion itself are propagated. So through the movements of the Israelites going out of Egypt, and those led away into Assyrian captivity and scattered among the nations, many became proselytes, etc. Through the movements and victorious arms of the Romans, their laws and polity were propagated everywhere. Let them be illustrated by the comparison of the tide of the sea, which floods the lands of some, nourishes those of others, drives some into harbour, and drives others back.

units.la: β. Liberantur oppressi & captivi, uti Israëlitæ liberati sunt per victoriam Cyri &c.
units.tr: β. The oppressed and captives are set free, as the Israelites were freed through the victory of Cyrus, etc.

units.la: 2. Internam; uti sunt motus vehementes animorum
units.tr: 2. The internal cause; such as the violent movements of minds:

units.la: a. boni, ut est Zelus heroum.
units.tr: a. Good ones, such as the zeal of heroes.

units.la: α. pro gloria Dei: tales fuere plerique judices Israëlis divinitus excitati. vid. lib. judic. Talis fuit Constantinus Magnus Ecclesiæ oppressæ vindex, item Theodosii, Carolus Magnus, & Principes Protestantes armis Evangelicam veritatem vindicantes.
units.tr: α. For the glory of God: such were most of the judges of Israel, raised up by divine appointment; see the book of Judges. Such was Constantine the Great, the avenger of the oppressed Church; likewise Theodosius, Charlemagne, and the Protestant princes who defended evangelical truth by arms.

units.la: β. pro liberatione oppressorum. Talis fuit motus Godofredi Bulionæi cæterorumque, qui terram sanctam & regnum Hierosolymitanum recuperarunt, vid. Gesta Dei per Franc. Tales & nostris temporibus in Germania vidimus &c.
units.tr: β. For the deliverance of the oppressed. Such was the movement of Godfrey of Bouillon and the others who recovered the Holy Land and the kingdom of Jerusalem; see the Gesta Dei per Francos. Such movements we have seen in our own times also in Germany, etc.

units.la: Pro plantatione egenorum, cum natio aliqua exundans aut crescens nimium, alias sedes quaerit, aut emittit colonias. Ita antiquitus per viros heroicos coloniæ in diversas orbis partes ductæ fuere. Interim & Lusitani, Galli, Hispani, Belgæ sic novû orbê & insulas incultas excoluere.
units.tr: For the planting of the needy: when some nation overflows or grows too great, it seeks other seats or sends out colonies. So in ancient times colonies were led into various parts of the world by heroic men. Meanwhile the Portuguese, French, Spanish, and Belgians likewise cultivated the new world and uncultivated islands.

units.la: Mali motus animorum, uti est cupiditas honorum, seu vasta ambitio magnatum. Exemplum in Nimrodo, Nebucadnezare, Alexandro Magno, atque utinam hic non esset fons plerorumque bellorum: ipsi Romani ab hoc affectu non fuere vacui. vid. Cic. in offic. 1.
units.tr: Bad movements of minds, such as the desire for honours, or the boundless ambition of magnates. An example is in Nimrod, Nebuchadnezzar, Alexander the Great; and would that this were not the source of most wars. The Romans themselves were not free from this passion. See Cicero, De Officiis, book 1.

units.la: Opum & amplarum possessionum. Pessima consultrix honesti. Quantum hic malorum inter privatos non modo, sed & inter Principes & magnates. Ipsis Romanis Campaniæ accessio sufficiens belli causa fuit. vid. Flor. 1. Facile conveniret inter principes, nisi spes amplioris dominationis & lautiorum reddituum animos acueret; accedente praesertim cupiditate illorum, quibus bellum lucrum praestat.
units.tr: Of wealth and extensive possessions. The worst counsellor of what is honourable. How many evils arise from this, not only among private persons but also among princes and magnates. For the Romans themselves the annexation of Campania was a sufficient cause of war. See Florus, book 1. Princes would easily agree, were it not that the hope of wider dominion and richer revenues sharpened their minds, especially with the greed of those for whom war brings profit.

units.la: Calamitatum publicarum, seu crudelitas: Haec impellit omnes Tyrannos, ut motus concitent. Talis Sylla & Marius olim in Rep. Rom. Talis Alcibiades in Graecia, Talis Turca insatiabili cupiditate sitiens sanguinem Christianorum.
units.tr: Of public calamities, or cruelty: this drives all tyrants to stir up movements. Such were Sulla and Marius of old in the Roman Republic; such was Alcibiades in Greece; such is the Turk, thirsting for the blood of Christians with insatiable greed.

units.la: 3. Externam causam, uti est Angustia loci, paupertas nationis, vel etiam infestatio hostilis. Primi exemplum est in Gallis Senonibus apud Florum; secundi, irruptio Hunnorum, Vandalorum, Gothorum, Longobardorum, Pannoniam, Italiam, Galliam, Hispaniam &c. invadentium. vid. Jornandem. Tertii exemplum est in omnibus bellis defensivis.
units.tr: 3. An external cause, such as the narrowness of a place, the poverty of a nation, or even hostile attack. An example of the first is the Senones of Gaul in Florus; of the second, the irruption of the Huns, Vandals, Goths, and Lombards invading Pannonia, Italy, Gaul, Spain, etc.; see Jordanes. An example of the third is in all defensive wars.

units.la: Peroratio repetita summâ, revocet sibi in memoriam motus vehementes, quos & passim elapsis annis expertus sit orbis, optetque ut Deus qui maris aestus componit refrænatque, pacis studio revinciat Magnatum animos, ut optata orbi redeat tranquillitas.
units.tr: Peroratio. Having repeated the sum, let him recall to memory the violent movements which the world has experienced here and there in the years past, and let him pray that God, who calms and restrains the tides of the sea, may by a zeal for peace bind the minds of the magnates, so that the desired tranquillity may return to the world.

units.la: XLIX. DE DECREMENTO ET INTERITU POPULORUM.
units.tr: XLIX. ON THE DECLINE AND DESTRUCTION OF PEOPLES.

units.la: Vid. Tolof. de rep. lib.21.22. & Hornium in Arca Noë.
units.tr: See Tolosanus, On the Commonwealth, books 21 and 22, and Hornius, in the Ark of Noah.

units.la: Exord. ex loco generis. ortu scilicet & interitu omnium rerum. Hoc I. Proponatur ex Salust. Ego sic existimo, orta omnia intereunt.
units.tr: Exordium from the topic of genus: the origin and destruction of all things. First, let it be put forward from Sallust: "I am of the opinion that all things which have arisen also perish."

units.la: II. Adstruatur 1. a natura rerum fluxa & caduca. 2. Inductione quadam, etiam illarum rerum, quæ firmæ videntur, & ipsius hominis. 3. testimonio Juvenci poët: Immortale nihil mundi compage tenetur. Non orbis, non regna hominum, non aurea Roma; Non mare non tellus, non ignea sidera mundi.
units.tr: II. Let it be confirmed: (1) from the frail and perishable nature of things; (2) by an induction, also from those things which seem firm, and from man himself; (3) by the testimony of the poet Juvencus: "Nothing immortal is held together by the frame of the world. Neither the globe, nor the kingdoms of men, nor golden Rome; neither sea nor earth, nor the fiery stars of the world."

units.la: III. Applicetur ad propositum: videlicet; cum hactenus de ortu & natura; de incremento & gloria, de motibus & æstu populorum ab antecessoribus dictum; dicendum jam etiam videri de decremento ac interitu eorundem.
units.tr: III. Let it be applied to the proposition: since hitherto the earlier writers have spoken of origin and nature, of growth and glory, of the movements and surges of peoples, it now seems right to speak also of their decline and destruction.

units.la: Proposit. Roget hinc Audit. ut eadem, qua antecessores attentione & patientia, & ipsum audire ne graventur; in argumento haud ingrato, aut intricato.
units.tr: Proposition. Let the hearer be asked to give the same attention and patience that the earlier speakers received, and not to be reluctant to listen to this theme, which is neither unpleasant nor intricate.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Adstruat τὸ ἔτη, seu decrementum & interitum populorum ex historia: videlicet totum primum mundum aquis diluvii absorptum. Antiquam Assyriorum gloriam abolitam, Gentes Canaan ab Israëlitis pulsas; hos vicissim a Babyloniis transportatos è suis sedibus &c. Vide Hist. juxta secula antiqua & recentiora. imprimisque quomodo Græci, Romani, Hispani, Galli per barbarorum in imperium incursum exstirpati, & Alani, Hunni, Longobardi, Gothi in ipsorum sedes successerint. Vid. Histor. & Tolof. de rep. lib.21.22. Comparentur populi cum aquis fluviorum, ubi semper in locum defluentium, novæ succedunt: ita & populos perpetuis belli & migrationibus se invicem trudere. Ita ut nihil stabile sit inter mortales. Unde deploret vanitatem illorum, qui in suis familiis perpetuitatem quærunt. Ubi jam illustres familiæ heroum Græcorum, Romanorum? Ubi illorum, qui hic & alibi gloria claruernnt. Vid.Hamelmannum de familiis emortuis,& Lindenspur de satis famil.
units.tr: Treatment. I. Let him confirm the "that" [τὸ ὅτι], that is, the decline and destruction of peoples, from history: namely, the whole first world swallowed up by the waters of the flood; the ancient glory of the Assyrians abolished; the nations of Canaan driven out by the Israelites, and these in turn carried off from their seats by the Babylonians, and so on. See history, both ancient and more recent, and especially how the Greeks, Romans, Spaniards and Gauls were wiped out by the incursion of barbarians into the empire, and how the Alani, Huns, Lombards and Goths succeeded them in their seats. See the histories, and Tolosanus, On the Commonwealth, books 21 and 22. Let peoples be compared with the waters of rivers, where new waters always succeed into the place of those that flow away; so peoples too push one another out by constant war and migration, so that nothing is stable among mortals. Hence he may lament the vanity of those who seek perpetuity for their families. Where now are the famous families of the Greek and Roman heroes? Where are those who shone here and elsewhere in glory? See Hamelmann, on extinct families, and Lindenspur, on sufficient families.

units.la: II. Inquirat τὸ διότι, seu causas harum vicissitudinum.
units.tr: II. Let him inquire into the "why" [τὸ διότι], that is, the causes of these changes.

units.la: I. Externas, uti sunt: Contagiones, & diluvia particularia, quale Deucalionis & Ogygis. vid. alia exempla apud Plin. & Historicos diversis seculis.
units.tr: I. External causes, such as contagions and particular floods, like that of Deucalion and of Ogyges. See other examples in Pliny and in historians of various ages.

units.la: Incursiones & oppressiones hostiles ac tyrannicæ. Ita Troja olim per Græcos, Seleucidæ per Parthos, Bactrianos; Parthi per Persas, Persæ per Sarracenos, hi per Turcas pulsi fuere. Indi Potanenses & Sinenses per Tattaros dissipati in insulis Indicis refugium quæsivere. &c. Asiam Minorem, & Græciam olim florentissimas terras vastatas fuisse per tyrannidé Turcicam. Ita Romanos per novos colonos paulatim exegisse sedibus veteres incolas, & gentem ac linguam suam propagasse.
units.tr: Hostile and tyrannical incursions and oppressions. Thus Troy was once destroyed by the Greeks, the Seleucids by the Parthians and Bactrians, the Parthians by the Persians, the Persians by the Saracens, and these by the Turks. The Indians of Potanensis and the Chinese, scattered by the Tartars, sought refuge on the Indian islands, and so on. Asia Minor and Greece, lands once most flourishing, were laid waste by Turkish tyranny. Thus the Romans gradually drove the old inhabitants from their seats by new colonists, and spread their own people and language.

units.la: Per legitima bella: ita Sabinos coaluisse cum Romanis, Samnites aliosque excisos penitus. vide Florum. Verum hoîce duos modos hodie non ita usitatos esse, tum quia auctiores jam sunt populi; tum quia oppressi facile inveniunt alienum auxilium; tum quia immanitas illa in victos, & servitus veterum abolita est; maximè inter Christianos. Fiat digressiuncula in laudem saluberrimæ doctrinæ Euangelii, quod barbariem passim orbe expulit.
units.tr: By lawful wars: thus the Sabines merged with the Romans, and the Samnites and others were utterly destroyed. See Florus. But these two modes are not so commonly used today: first, because peoples are now more numerous; second, because the oppressed easily find foreign help; third, because that savagery towards the conquered and the slavery of old have been abolished, especially among Christians. Let a short digression be made in praise of the most wholesome doctrine of the Gospel, which has everywhere driven barbarism out of the world.

units.la: 2. Internæ morales, uti
units.tr: 2. Internal moral causes, such as:

units.la: Peccata enormia, quæ divinam vindictam provocant, ut bella, pestem, fera animalia immittat. Vide comminationes divinas Deut.27. & apud Prophetas passim; itemque exempla in populo Judaico, & terris Turcicæ tyrannidi subjectis.
units.tr: Enormous sins, which provoke the divine vengeance, so that God sends wars, plague and wild beasts. See the divine threats in Deuteronomy 27 and throughout the Prophets; likewise the examples in the Jewish people, and in lands subject to Turkish tyranny.

units.la: Segnities & vecordia, ipsaque adeo barbaries. Per hasce provocari alios, ut excindantur, ac domentur servitute. Hanc occasionem fuisse Hispanis, excindendi Americanos & Indos. Utrum juste, quaeritur? & præpollet negativa: 1. quia populi illi ab antiquo terras illas occuparunt & possederunt; indeque & alios arcere jure potuerunt. 2. quia ad dominium acquirendum aut tenendum non requiritur virtus moralis aut certa religio. Unde & male Plato 2. de rep. c.3. Græcis jus belli asserit contra barbaros. vid. Hugo. Grot. lib. 2. de jure belli & pacis c.22. At alia ratio est in feris hominibus, & societati humanæ inteinfestis; quos expellere sedibus licet & exstirpare ob quietem humani generis. vid. Grot. ibid. c. 20. Discutiatur hic quæstio, utrum ob diversam religionem pellere aut exstirpare populum liceat? uti asserit author Classici sacri, & praxis habet Pontificum? Negatur: quia jura populorum & politiarum fluunt ex jure gentium, non Evangelii. 2. Quia conscientiæ armis non possunt convinci. 3. quia judæi tolerantur merito.
units.tr: Sloth and folly, and barbarism itself. Through these other peoples are provoked to be destroyed and subdued by slavery. The Spaniards had this occasion to exterminate the Americans and Indians. Was this done justly? The answer is negative, for three reasons: (1) because those peoples had occupied and possessed those lands from of old, and so could justly keep others away; (2) because acquiring or holding dominion does not require moral virtue or a particular religion; hence Plato, in the second book of the Republic, chapter 3, wrongly asserts that the Greeks have a right of war against barbarians; see Hugo Grotius, On the Law of War and Peace, book 2, chapter 22. But the case is different with wild men who are hostile to human society; these may lawfully be driven from their seats and exterminated for the peace of the human race; see Grotius, ibid., chapter 20. Let the question be discussed here: whether it is lawful to expel or exterminate a people on account of a different religion, as the author of the Sacred Classics asserts, and as the practice of the Pontiffs holds? It is denied, for three reasons: (1) because the rights of peoples and states flow from the law of nations, not from the Gospel; (2) because consciences cannot be convinced by arms; (3) because Jews are rightly tolerated.

units.la: Rebellio & seditiones. Per hasce enim evertuntur politiæ, & jus nascitur superiori in rebelles. Sic excisos olim Samnites, Vejentes, Carthaginenses, &c.
units.tr: Rebellion and sedition. For by these commonwealths are overthrown, and a right arises for the superior against the rebels. Thus the Samnites, Veientes and Carthaginians were once destroyed, and so on.

units.la: III. Assurgat ad causam primam, quæ uti mundum universum, terram, astra, mare movet ac gubernat, ita & excitat, componitque hos populorum motus, ad justa judicia sua exercenda, exstirpat unam, plantat aliam gentem, rursusque auctam & radicatam exscindit ob prævalentia peccata: exemplum evidens adducatur populus judaicus: ut ita nomen ipsius sit formidabile in tota terra &c.
units.tr: III. Let him rise to the first cause, which, just as it moves and governs the whole world, the earth, the stars and the sea, so also stirs up and calms these movements of peoples: to carry out its just judgments, it uproots one nation and plants another, and again destroys a people that has grown and taken root because of prevailing sins. Let the Jewish people be adduced as clear example, so that its name might be feared through the whole earth, and so on.

units.la: Perorat. Desinat in admirationem, quòd inter tot gentium mutationes & excidia, natio Germanica jam inde à nepotibus Noachi pristinas sedes tuita fuerit, imò & Imperii ac ultimæ Monarchiæ gloriâ auxerit, diversas regiones ac regna suis coloniis occupaverit; oretque Deum, ut eam imposterum, imprimisque & patriam hanc in pristina sede, quiete, gloriaque conservet & tueatur, avertatque illa peccata, propter quæ regna de gente in in gentem transferantur &c.
units.tr: Peroration. Let him end with wonder that, amid so many changes and overthrows of nations, the German nation has, from the grandsons of Noah onward, kept its ancient seats, and indeed has increased the glory of the Empire and of the last monarchy, and has occupied diverse regions and kingdoms with its colonies; and let him pray God that He would preserve and defend it hereafter, and especially this fatherland, in its ancient seat, in peace and glory, and turn away those sins on account of which kingdoms are transferred from nation to nation, and so on.

units.la: L. QUIBUS GRADIBUS SE EXTULERIT ROMANA GLORIA.
units.tr: L. BY WHAT STEPS THE ROMAN GLORY RAISED ITSELF.

units.la: Exord. ab excellentia Reip. Rom. Videlicet nullum regnum aut rempubl. unquam exstitisse illustriorem, sive gentem ipsam, ex Trojanis oriundam, sive reip. amplitudinem & robur sive denique durationem spectes. Evincatur hoc & illustretur 1. comparatione cum reliquis tribus Monarchiis. 2. Elogiis aliquot de virtute & gloria Romanorum vid. Sallust.
units.tr: Exordium: from the excellence of the Roman Commonwealth. That is, no kingdom or commonwealth has ever been more illustrious, whether you look at the people itself, descended from the Trojans, or at the greatness and strength of the commonwealth, or finally at its endurance. This is proved and illustrated, 1. by comparison with the other three monarchies; 2. by several eulogies on the virtue and glory of the Romans, see Sallust.

units.la: Propos. Operæ precium itaque videri, si paucis ex historia contemplemur plemur, quibus præsertim gradibus Romanæ reip. gloria se extulerit; ut appareat, non forte fortuna, sed prudentia, consilio, virtute ac industria, Deum supremum regnorum arbitrum evehere gentem.
units.tr: Proposition: It seems worth our effort, therefore, if we briefly consider from history by what steps especially the glory of the Roman commonwealth raised itself, so that it may appear that God, the supreme arbiter of kingdoms, exalted this people not by chance, but by prudence, counsel, virtue and industry.

units.la: Tractatio exponat causas tam stupendi incrementi: & quidem
units.tr: Treatment: let him set out the causes of so astonishing a growth; and indeed:

units.la: I. Fuisse virtutem bellicam, & assiduum armorum exercitium & disciplinam; quæ præ cæteris exculta in hac gente: ubi quot fuere capita, tot fuisse magnos imperatores. Hoc
units.tr: I. That there was martial virtue, and constant practice and discipline in arms, cultivated among this people above all others, so that as many heads as there were, so many great commanders there were. This

units.la: 1. Ostendat exemplis ex historia Rom. inde à Romulo tempore regni: deinde tempore consulum; ubi illustriores aliquot heroes proponat laudetque ex Floro & Livio:
units.tr: 1. Let him show by examples from Roman history, from the time of Romulus's reign, then from the time of the consuls; where he should set forth and praise several of the more illustrious heroes, from Florus and Livy.

units.la: 2. Illustretur ex thesi: videlicet. Haud facile esse emergere gentem ad celsam regni ac durabilem gloriam, sine virtute bellica. Hoc astruatur a. exemplis celebriorum aliquot populorum per præteritionem; quid dicam Assyrios, Persas? &c. Quid Græcos, quid Macedonas evexit? &c. b. Testimoniis. c. Rationibus & quidem tum ab inquietudine subditorum, qui non nisi armis contineri queunt: tum ab oppositione hostium, quam primum gens aliqua incipit inclarescere, illico se alii opponunt, vicinam potentiam sibi periculosam existimantes. &c.
units.tr: 2. Let it be illustrated from the thesis: namely, that it is by no means easy for a people to rise to a lofty and lasting glory without martial virtue. This is established: a. by examples of several more famous peoples, passed over in silence; what shall I say of the Assyrians, the Persians? etc. What raised the Greeks, what the Macedonians? etc. b. by testimonies; c. by reasons, and indeed both from the restlessness of subjects, who can be held in check only by arms, and from the opposition of enemies, since as soon as any nation begins to grow famous, others at once set themselves against it, judging its growing power dangerous to themselves. etc.

units.la: II. Esse virtutem togatam; præcipue prudentiam, justitiam ac moderationem. Qualis quantusque hic populus Romanus, si splendidum hoc virtutis theatrum ingrediamur? si contemplemur viros omni virtutum laude cumulatissimos? &c. Quàm hic elucet
units.tr: II. That there is civil virtue, chiefly prudence, justice and moderation. What kind and how great is this Roman people, if we enter this splendid theatre of virtue? if we contemplate men heaped with every praise of virtue? etc. How clearly here shines

units.la: 1. Prudentia Romanorum?
units.tr: 1. The prudence of the Romans?

units.la: a. In ordinanda & constituenda rep. 1. sub regibus: ubi omnia quidem manu regia; attamen consilio Seniorum, seu senatus gerebantur. Scilicet consilium erat à patribus, & vis agendi apud principem. Quid salubrius? quid ad res magnas gerendas accommodatius? Tolle alterutrum, & magnum deprehendes rei bene gerendæ impedimentum. &c. 2. sub consulibus ubi prudenter ad conservandam pacem tres reip. formæ mixtæ fuere: Regius splendor in Consulibus, Aristocratia in Senatu, Democratia in provocatione ad populum & Tribunitia potestate; itemque in comcommunione conjugiorum & honorum' vid. Flor. Adstruatur forma mixta reip. contra Bodinum, & præferatur formis reliquis: Unde & in ipso imperio Rom. etiamnum quodammodo obtinet, Monarchiam repræsentante Imperatore; Aristocratiam Senatu Principum, Democratiam vero Collegio Civitatum.
units.tr: a. In ordering and establishing the commonwealth: 1. under the kings, where indeed everything was done by royal hand, yet by the counsel of the elders, or senate. Clearly counsel came from the fathers, and the power of acting lay with the prince. What is more wholesome? What is better suited to accomplishing great things? Remove either one, and you will find a great hindrance to well-conducted affairs. etc. 2. Under the consuls, where prudently, for preserving peace, there were three mixed forms of commonwealth: regal splendour in the consuls, aristocracy in the senate, democracy in appeal to the people and in the tribunician power; likewise in the common sharing of marriages and honours; see Florus. Let the mixed form of commonwealth be affirmed against Bodin and preferred to the other forms. Hence it still obtains in some measure even in the Roman empire itself, the emperor representing the monarchy, the senate of princes the aristocracy, and the college of cities the democracy.

units.la: Prudentia in administranda rep. dum Senatus decreta ratificanda fuere a tribunis; unde rata fuere penes populum tanquam a proprio suo Magistratu approbata. Simile fere obtinet hodieque in Gallia, dum regia edicta non obtinent valorem, nisi a parlamento Parisiensi verificata. Frustra vi armata & rigore omnia efficere sata gis; peragit tranquilla potestas, quod violenta nequit &c.
units.tr: Prudence in administering the commonwealth: while the decrees of the senate were to be ratified by the tribunes; whence they were held to be approved by the people as by its own magistrate. Something similar still obtains today in France, where royal edicts have no force unless they have been verified by the Parisian parliament. In vain you try to achieve everything by armed force and rigour; quiet authority accomplishes what violence cannot, etc.

units.la: Judicia capitalia per populi suffragium peracta fuere in Comitiis. Quàm sapiens hæc agendi ratio? quàm salubris, licet invidiosa sic declinabant patricii, peragebat ipse populus, in quem omnis redundabat invidia. Quantum tibi nocuit Cicero, quod neglecta hac lege, solo senatus jussu Lentulum, Cetegum, Catilinæ socios in carcere necari fecisti &c.
units.tr: Capital trials were conducted by the vote of the people in the assemblies. How wise is this manner of acting! How wholesome, even if unpopular, since in this way the patricians avoided it, and the people itself conducted it, on whom all the odium fell. How much Cicero harmed you, because, ignoring this law, by the sole order of the senate you had Lentulus, Cethegus and Catiline's associates put to death in prison, etc.

units.la: Censura peracta fuit per viros graves & bene meritos, quanto cum reip. emolumento! Scilicet sic ad curam ac sollicitudinem, ad laborem & industriam excitabantur cives, magni æque ac parvi; sic ociosi pellebantur tanquam fuci, toti reip. graves. &c. Extollantur hinc commoda ex censura redundantia. &c. vid. Flor. Liv. Gell.
units.tr: The censorship was carried out by men of weight and good desert, to what advantage for the commonwealth! Clearly citizens, great and small alike, were thus stirred to care and concern, to labour and industry; the idle were driven out like drones, burdensome to the whole commonwealth. etc. Let the advantages flowing from the censorship be extolled here, etc. See Florus, Livy, Gellius.

units.la: In Coloniis plantatis in locis subjugatis: ne scilicet gravi præsidio onerarentur populi recens subacti, sed sic paulatim cum civibus Rom. in eosdem mores ac linguæ communionem consuescerent &c.
units.tr: In colonies planted in conquered places: so that the peoples newly subdued should not be burdened by a heavy garrison, but should thus gradually grow accustomed to the same manners and the common language with the Roman citizens, etc.

units.la: Quàm illustris hic justitia Romanorum, & quidem in descriptione juris æquabili per Legem XII. tabul. & interpretationem sapientum; qui leges ex æquitate interpretabantur & ad remp. Rom. accommodabant; itemque per Edicta Prætorum; qui quotidie in foro versantes, jus scriptum per Edicta annua corrigebant, & æquitate temperabant &c. vid. Flor. Liv.
units.tr: How illustrious here is the justice of the Romans, and indeed in the even-handed description of law through the Law of the Twelve Tables and the interpretation of the wise men; who interpreted the laws according to equity and adapted them to the Roman commonwealth; likewise through the edicts of the praetors, who, daily active in the forum, corrected the written law by annual edicts and tempered it with equity, etc. See Florus, Livy.

units.la: In coërcitione fœneratorum & oppressorum, ut sic plebs à violentia & oppressione potentum liberaretur. Lentam fœnus esse tabem, qua consumuntur pauperes. Turbas hinc sæpius concitatas in rep: at prudenti moderatione malo isti obvium itum fuisse ostendatur.
units.tr: In the restraint of usurers and oppressors, so that the plebs might be freed from the violence and oppression of the powerful. Usury is a slow plague by which the poor are consumed. Hence tumults were often stirred up in the commonwealth; let it be shown that these evils were met with prudent moderation.

units.la: In cohibitione iniquitatis Prætorum, Præsidum omniumque magistratuum per legem repetundarum, qua à privatis repetere licebat data aut extorta tempore gesti magistratus. Quàm salubre hoc fuit moderamen & frænum mite potestatis! &c.
units.tr: In the curbing of the injustice of praetors, governors and all magistrates, through the law on extortion, by which it was lawful to recover from private persons what had been given or extorted during the time of a magistracy. How wholesome this moderation was, and how gentle a bridle on power! etc.

units.la: In temperantia,
units.tr: In temperance:

units.la: In moderato regimine provinciarum, quando optimi eò mittebantur, ita ut melius esset exteris regnis ac provinciis vinci à Romanis, quàm proprio frui imperio aut libertate. Sic imperium in animos non in corpora modò acquisitum fuit, & raræ aut nullæ fuere seditiones in provinciis dissitis.
units.tr: In the moderate governing of the provinces, when the best men were sent there, so that it was better for foreign kingdoms and provinces to be conquered by the Romans than to enjoy their own rule or liberty. Thus empire was won over minds, not merely bodies, and seditions in distant provinces were rare or none.

units.la: In cohibenda ambitione. 1. per legem annariam, qua certi anni magistratibus singulis erant præfixi, ut juniorum ambitus præposterus reprimeretur: Nomen & à senio mite senatus habet. vid. Manutium de Sen. Rom. & Romam illustratā.
units.tr: In restraining ambition: 1. by the annual law, by which fixed years were set for individual magistracies, so that the preposterous ambition of the younger men might be checked. The name "senate" also derives gently from old age; see Manutius, On the Roman Senate, and Rome Illustrated.

units.la: Per annuam magistratus mutationem. Utrum consultum hoc ubique, dubium quidem esse; at Romæ tum propter amplitudinem potestatis, tum propter copiam virorum illustrium, necessarium fuisse. Unda & continuatio turbas movit, triumviratum invexit, remp: evertit &c. Quæ jam tum eo potentiæ creverat, ut non nisi propriis viribus, uti Græciæ olim contigerat, everti posset.
units.tr: By the annual change of magistrates. Whether this measure was of universal value is indeed doubtful; but at Rome, both because of the greatness of the power and because of the abundance of illustrious men, it was necessary. Hence also continuance stirred up tumults, introduced the triumvirate, overthrew the commonwealth, etc. which by then had grown to such a height of power that it could be overthrown only by its own strength, as had once happened to Greece.

units.la: Conclus. Haud igitur mirandum Romanam Rempublicam ad tam sublime culmen honoris ac potentiæ ascendisse, ut in reliquum orbem imperium indeptum fuerit. Scilicet virtutem, justitiam &c. conservatricem esse regnorum ac rerump.
units.tr: Conclusion: It is therefore no wonder that the Roman commonwealth ascended to so lofty a summit of honour and power that it obtained dominion over the rest of the world. Clearly virtue, justice, etc. are the preservers of kingdoms and commonwealths.

units.la: LI. DE CONSILIO AUGUSTI DE COERCENDO INTRA TERMINOS IMPERIO.
units.tr: LI. Augustus's Plan for Keeping the Empire Within Its Limits.

units.la: Ex Tacit. Annal. 1. c. 11.
units.tr: From Tacitus, Annals, book 1, chapter 11.

units.la: Exord. A voto Romæ apud Claudian. videl. Memorabilem esse Romæ mæ florentis, prolatis longè latéque finibus,querelam apudClau-dian. cum ita quiritantem nimiam felicitatem suam introducitPa-triam: Heu prospera fata! Quid mihi septenos montes, turbamque dedistis. Quæ parvo non posset ali? Felicior essem Augustis opibus. Scil. ipsa mole ac imperii amplitudine tandem laborare se sensit Respubl. cum omnes orbis partes complexa, non tam invidia apud exteros,quam propriis vitiis, majori indies ambitione, luxu, dissidiis conflictari coepit. Causam fuisse: quod vitia hæc veluti sentina Reip. navem paulatim merserint. Illustretur simili à corpore nimis obeso, quod variis morbis præbet materiam: ita & Romam cum hostibus exteris superior esset, veluti gangrænam intra se generasse. Ostendatur inductione quadam malorum inde natorum ex Flori lib. 3. c. 12. Hæc prævidisse Augustum principem sagacissimum, & experimento didicisse superiorum temporum; ideoque salubri consilio in rationario suo seu libello sua manu exarato inter alia monita & consilium dedisse, coercendi intra terminos imperii, uti incomparabilis Tacitus, Suetonius & Dion Cassius referunt.
units.tr: Introduction. A memorable prayer by Claudian: when the city of Rome was flourishing and its borders had been extended far and wide, Claudian introduces the Fatherland itself complaining of its excessive good fortune, lamenting: "Alas, cruel fate! Why did you give me seven hills and a crowd that a small land could not feed? I would have been happier with Augustus's resources." That is, the Commonwealth at last felt itself burdened by the very bulk and extent of its empire, once it had embraced all parts of the world. It began to be torn apart not so much by envy from abroad as by its own vices: ever greater ambition, luxury and dissension. The cause was that these vices, like a bilge in a ship, gradually sank the Commonwealth. This may be illustrated by a comparison with an overweight body, which offers material for various diseases; so Rome, though superior to its foreign enemies, had as it were bred a gangrene within itself. This may be shown by an inductive survey of the evils that arose from it, drawn from Florus, book 3, chapter 12. The wise prince Augustus had foreseen these things and had learned them from the experience of earlier times. Therefore, by a wholesome plan, he gave in his account book, or little book written in his own hand, among other warnings and counsels, the advice to keep the empire within its borders, as the incomparable Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio Cassius report.

units.la: Propos. Sive metu sive invidia hoc factum, uti in dubio hoc relinquit Tacitus, sane saluberrimum hoc monitum videri: id quod paucis uberius aliquanto expendendum, si humanissimi & spectatissimi Domini Auditores benevolas ad exiguum temporis aures rudiler breviterque de amplo ac momentoso argumento dicenti accommodare ne graventur: id quod pro insigni erga exteros ac vicinos benevolentiæ documento habiturus ac quacunque occasione prædicaturus sit.
units.tr: Proposition. Whether this was done out of fear or envy, which Tacitus leaves in doubt, this advice certainly seems most salutary. This is something that should be weighed somewhat more fully in a few words, if the most kind and most distinguished gentlemen, my listeners, will not hesitate to lend their gracious ears for a short time to one who speaks, roughly and briefly, on a large and weighty subject. They will regard this as a notable proof of my goodwill towards foreigners and neighbours, and will proclaim it on any occasion.

units.la: Tractatio. Approbans consilium Augusti. Hinc
units.tr: Treatment. Approving Augustus's plan, hence:

units.la: I. Exponat Statum Imperii sub Augusto: videl.
units.tr: I. Let him set out the state of the empire under Augustus, namely:

units.la: 1. Amplitudinem ejus in Asia ad Euphratem usque, ultra quem nunquam auspicatus progressus fuerat, ut docet exemplum C. Crassi: vide Florum in Africa ad Lybios & Æthiopes, gentes barbaras & Sole adustam regionem. Ab occasu ad Oceanum ultimum: ipsa etiam Anglia subjecta Romanis. A Septentrione ad Danubium & Germanos: gentem nulli hactenus domitam.
units.tr: 1. Its extent in Asia as far as the Euphrates, beyond which Augustus never ventured to advance, as the example of Crassus shows (see Florus); in Africa, among the Libyans and Ethiopians, barbarous peoples in a region scorched by the sun; from the west to the furthest Ocean, Britain itself being subject to the Romans; from the north to the Danube and the Germans, a people hitherto never subdued.

units.la: 2. Limites robustos; maria, montes, flumina maxima, Tac. I. 9. Mari oceano & amnibus longinquis septum Imperium ait. EuphraEuphrates scil. mons Taurus, Carpates, Pontus Euxinus, Danubius, Rhenus; qui amnes validis praesidiis Rom. custodiebantur. Et licet copiae Rom. essent in Germania, tamen, ut Strabo ait lib. 7. Albim nunquam transire voluit Augustus, nec quietas illic gentes turbare, ne turbatae vicinas nationes traherent ad res novas. Nec proferre limites potuit, quin Germanos, Parthos, aut Dacas Scythas & Sarmatas, aut Aethiopes & Lybios populos ferocissimos lacessferet.
units.tr: 2. Strong boundaries: seas, mountains, very great rivers. Tacitus, book 1, chapter 9, says the empire was enclosed by the ocean and distant rivers: the Euphrates, namely, the Taurus mountains, the Carpathians, the Black Sea, the Danube and the Rhine, which rivers were guarded by strong Roman garrisons. And although the Roman forces were in Germany, nevertheless, as Strabo says in book 7, Augustus never wished to cross the Elbe, nor to disturb the peoples quietly living there, lest, if disturbed, they should draw the neighbouring nations into revolution. Nor could he extend the borders without provoking the Germans, the Parthians, or the Dacians, Scythians and Sarmatians, or the Ethiopians and the most fierce Libyan peoples.

units.la: Nuperam cladem in Germania, ubi tres robustae legiones sub Varo, cum ipso Duce caesae: unde turbatus adeo Augustus, ut saepe exclamarit: Quintili Vare, redde legiones.
units.tr: Consider the recent disaster in Germany, where three strong legions were cut to pieces with their commander Varus. Augustus was so disturbed by it that he often cried out: "Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!"

units.la: Nondum adultum principatum suum, qui facile labefactari potuisseт, si in remotis provinciis bella mota fuissent, aut irritatae gentes claustra imperii perrupissent. Unde Tiberius postea subnatis bellis, Romae semper substitit, nec deserere voluit caput rerum, ne turbae concitarentur Romae &c. Consiliis & astu res moliri, arma procul habere statuit Tiberius lib. 6.
units.tr: His principate was not yet fully grown, and it could easily have been shaken if wars had been stirred up in remote provinces, or if the provoked peoples had broken through the barriers of the empire. Hence Tiberius later, when wars arose, always remained at Rome and did not wish to leave the head of affairs, lest tumults should be stirred up at Rome, and so on. Tiberius decided, in book 6, to manage affairs by counsel and craft and to keep arms far away.

units.la: Concludat hinc, prudenter monuisse Augustum de coercendo intra terminos imperio: & ipsum, juxta Dionem c. 56. servasse hoc constanter, non verbis modo, sed re ipsa. Cum enim multa barbarorum posset in suam ditionem redigere, nunquam tamen voluisse. Novisse enim Augustum, id quod dicit Valerius Max. lib. 4. c. 1. eam demum potentiam tutam esse, quae viribus suis modum imponit. Atque hoc esse, quod jam porro, juxta disciplinam magni Taciti, paulo uberius consideran-dum
units.tr: Let him conclude from this that Augustus wisely advised keeping the empire within its borders, and that he himself, according to Dio, chapter 56, kept this constantly, not only in words but in deed. For although he could have reduced many barbarians to his dominion, he never wished to do so. For Augustus knew what Valerius Maximus says in book 4, chapter 1: that only that power is safe which sets a limit to its own strength. And this is what we must now consider somewhat more fully, following the method of the great Tacitus.

units.la: II. Rationes afferat porro contra nimiam Regni aut Imperii amplitudinem.
units.tr: II. Let him next set out reasons against an excessive extent of kingdom or empire.

units.la: Quia Deus, uti unicuique homini, ita & Regno ac Reip. suos posuit limites. Uti enim mari littora & scopulos objecit; ita & exundanti potentiae populorum, & ambitioni Principum: qui licet potentes sint, tamen humanam conditionem egredi nequeunt, quia singulis monarchis potentes vicinos oppositus. Vanum itaque Alexandri effatum, quando ut mundus uno sole, ita & orbem terrarum ab uno Rege gubernandum rescripsit Dario.
units.tr: Because God, as he has set limits for each man, has set them also for kingdoms and commonwealths. For as he set shores and rocks against the sea, so he set them against the overflowing power of peoples and the ambition of princes, who, though powerful, cannot escape the human condition, since powerful neighbours stand opposed to every monarch. Vain, therefore, was the saying of Alexander, who, when he wrote to Darius that as the world has one sun, so the whole earth ought to be governed by one king.

units.la: Quia amplo nimis imperio unus non sufficit. Probetur
units.tr: Because one man is not sufficient for an overly vast empire. Let this be proved:

units.la: Quoniam remotas provincias ipse obire nequit: Unde sequitur aut desertio aut oppressio subditorum per praefectos proprios, ac rebelliones. Uti contigit Alex. Max. in Indias progressio: Hinc in Persidé, in Græcia defectiones & tyrannicæ oppressiones enatæ fuere passim. vid. Curtium lib. §. 9.
units.tr: Because he cannot himself visit remote provinces. It follows that either they are abandoned or the subjects are oppressed by their own governors, and rebellions arise.
