This happened to Alexander the Great in his advance into India; hence revolts and tyrannical oppressions arose everywhere, in Persia and in Greece. See Curtius, book 9.

units.la: Quoniam nuncii tarde ad regem pertingunt, si vel seditio oriatur, vel hostis limites invadat. Et licet nuncietur per ignes succensos, ut Arist. refert de regno Persiæ, tamen copiæ mature submitti nequeunt. Expertum hoc & experiri adhuc regem Hispaniæ in Indiis. Vid. Forstner. ad Tacit.
units.tr: Because messages reach the king slowly, if a sedition arises or an enemy invades the borders. And although news may be passed on by fires lit in succession, as Aristotle reports of the kingdom of Persia, nevertheless troops cannot be sent in time. The king of Spain has learned this by experience, and still experiences it in the Indies. See Forstner on Tacitus.

units.la: Quia diversarum ac remotarum gentium diversi sunt mores; vid. Forstn. qui tamen noti esse debent Principi bene imperaturo. Errasse hîc consilium Philippi II. Hisp. cum contra monitum Parentis Caroli V. Belgas durius imperio regio more Hispanico coercere vellet, missō præsertim Granvellano ad consilia sanguinaria, & post Albano tyranno: unde avulsa penitus & in libertatem vindicata Belgia fuit.
units.tr: Because the customs of different and distant peoples differ. See Forstner; these must nevertheless be known to a prince who intends to govern well. Philip II of Spain erred here, when, against the advice of his father Charles V, he wished to govern the Belgians more harshly, in the royal manner of Spain, sending especially Granvelle to devise bloody counsels, and afterwards the tyrant Alba. Hence Belgium was utterly torn away and vindicated to liberty.

units.la: Quia magnis periculis subjectum magnum imperium.
units.tr: Because a great empire is exposed to great dangers.

units.la: Ob nascentem ex nimia fortuna magnam superbiam; vitium pessimum maximè in Principe, ut cum Nebucadnezare se efferat, & pœnam incurrat. vid. Forstn. & Rupert. Orat. 5.
units.tr: Because an excessive fortune gives rise to great pride, the worst vice, especially in a prince, who, like Nebuchadnezzar, exalts himself and incurs punishment. See Forstner and Rupert, oration 5.

units.la: Ob invidiam & hostes quos provocat nimia imperii amplitudo. Experti hoc Carthaginenses quærentes dominium maris, tenentes Siciliam. Item Veneti affectantes Dominium Italiæ: vid. Zevecot. ad Flor. p. 357. 388. Item Carolus V. Item Rex Hispaniæ: vide Amiratum discursu 6. Hinc auctus Indiis minor factus dicitur Bocalino in Relat. ex Parnasso & Rohanæo in trutina statuum Europæ. Ratio addatur 1. quia sic distrahuntur regni vires, per varia præsidia in locis longinquis disponendæ, vid. Zevecot. loco dict. 2. Ampla retineri nequeunt. Periculosum enim est prægrave imperium: vid. Orat. Darii apud Curt. lib. 4. c. 11. & legatorum Scythicorum apud
units.tr: Because of the envy and enemies that an excessive extent of empire provokes. The Carthaginians experienced this when they sought dominion of the sea while holding Sicily; likewise the Venetians, aspiring to dominion over Italy. See Zevecot on Florus, pp. 357, 388. Likewise Charles V, and likewise the king of Spain; see Amiratus, discourse 6. Hence he is said to have become smaller by growing in the Indies, in Bocalinus's Report from Parnassus and in Rohan's Balance of the States of Europe. Add the reason: first, because the strength of a kingdom is thus dispersed, since it must be distributed among various garrisons in distant places (see Zevecot, loc. cit.); second, because vast empires cannot be retained, for a very heavy empire is dangerous (see the speech of Darius in Curtius, book 4, chapter 11, and of the Scythian envoys in Curtius, book 7, chapter 3).

units.la: Curt. lib. 7. c. §. 3. Quia summa non sunt diuturna. Summisque negatum stare diu. Singulæ enim res suam habent mensuram modumque. vid. Forstn. ad c. 11. Tacit.
units.tr: Because the greatest things are not lasting, and what is at the summit cannot stand long. Each thing has its own measure and limit (see Forstner on Tacitus, chapter 11).

units.la: 4. Quia bella temeraria raro felicia sunt. Ostendatur exemplo Alexandri Magni; qui licet felicissimus, quanta tamen pericula in Silicia, in Sogdianis, in Indis expertus est? & quid tandem obtinuit? quid Julius Cæsar, qui tot millium nece triennale imperium & mortem cruentam meruit? Scilicet arduum ac ferale esse decretum belli, ubi de tot millium, nocentum pariter ac innocentum vita sententia fertur: ad quod lente & non nisi gravissimis de causis accedere debet princeps. Si judex circumspecte agit in causa capitis, quid ni princeps in decernendo bello, ubi tot hominum vita versatur: uti statuit Silhonius part. 2. Ministri Stat. Laudentur hinc Belgæ, qui non pro dilatandis, sed defendendis limitibus bella gesserunt, promti ad pacem, licet & plurium acquirendorum spes esset; & in bellis Dano-Suecico, Anglicano, nil nisi pacem quæsivere: & jam vias pacis tentant; satisfactionem offerentes etiam ubi necdum bellum indictum est.
units.tr: 4. Because rash wars are rarely fortunate. Let this be shown by the example of Alexander the Great, who, though most fortunate, what dangers did he undergo in Cilicia, among the Sogdians, in India? And what did he finally gain? What of Julius Caesar, who, through the slaughter of so many thousands, earned a three-year dictatorship and a bloody death? Clearly the decision to wage war is grave and deadly, when the lives of so many thousands, guilty and innocent alike, are judged; a prince ought to approach it slowly and only for the gravest causes. If a judge acts with caution in a capital case, why should not a prince in deciding on war, where the lives of so many men are at stake? So Silhonius decided in part 2 of Ministre d'État. Here the Belgians should be praised, who waged war not to extend but to defend their borders, ready for peace even when there was hope of acquiring more; and in the Danish-Swedish and English wars they sought nothing but peace, and now they try the ways of peace, offering satisfaction even where war has not yet been declared.

units.la: Conclusio. Optet ut principes & Resp. suo jure contenti, laudabiliter potius, quam late imperare satagant; ut pax parta vigeat & pereneet.
units.tr: Conclusion. May princes and commonwealths, content with their own right, strive to rule laudably rather than widely, so that the peace won may flourish and last.

units.la: LII. DE FATALI ROMÆ AC IMPERII VETERIS DECREMENTO.
units.tr: LII. ON THE FATAL DECLINE OF ROME AND OF THE OLD EMPIRE.

units.la: Exord. à fatali, uti rerum omnium, ita & regnorum ac imperiorum mutatione. Hoc
units.tr: Exordium: from the fatal change of all things, and so also of kingdoms and empires. This is the

units.la: I. Proponatur. Videlicet verissime & veluti ex tripode dictum esse illud Poëtæ: In se magna ruunt, latis hunc Numina rebus crescendi posuere modum. Observasse quippe authorem perpetuas mutationes, quas non modo in mundo universo, verum etiam in rebus humanis, ipsisque etiam regnis maximis ac summis orbis Monarchiis perpetuo cernimus: quæ quando ad culmen summum ac apicem pervenerunt, propria etiam mole sua, nullo impellente ad casum vergunt, aut notabili mutatione concutiuntur. Scilicet nihil stabile præter semetipsum in rebus humanis manis voluisse esse supremum Numen, arcanâ suâ providentiâ ita temperans rerum vices; ut modum mensuramque ne egrediantur.
units.tr: I. Proposition. That is, the line of the poet is most truly said, as if from the tripod: "Great things collapse under their own weight; the gods have set a limit to growth for broad realms." For the author has observed the perpetual changes which we see not only in the whole world but also in human affairs, and even in the greatest kingdoms and the highest monarchies of the globe. When these reach their summit and peak, they tend to fall, by their own mass and with no one pushing them, or they are shaken by some notable change. Clearly nothing in human affairs is stable except God himself, the supreme Power, who by his hidden providence so regulates the changes of things that they do not overstep measure and limit.

units.la: II. Ostendatur hoc uberius per inductionem: videlicet, nonne quotidie cernimus Solem, cum punctum attigit verticale, & plenum fecit nobis meridiē, eodem veluti momento relicto cœli vertice declinare paulatim ad occasum? Quid solis pedisequa Luna? Crescit illa donec pleno orbe luceat; at quam primum illud perfectionis attigit, illico rursus incipit decrescere, usque dum penitus obmutescat, mater fecunda mutationum & speculum instabilitatis. Quid dicemus de herbis & arboribus? habent & illæ suam periodum. Crescit annosa quercus per aliquot secula, at cum terminum suum attigit, sua se mole eruit & exarescit. Sunt suæ animantibus, sunt suæ hominibus statæ ætates, quibus expletis, sibimetipsis oneri sunt & sua sponte evanescunt. Ipsa montium rupiumq; durata ævo cacumina temporı fatisque succumbunt. Familias si intueamur, cernimus illas perpetua novorum veluti stolonum successione perpetuari, verum tandem & antiquissimas degenerare & deficere cernimus, & novas exoriri. Et quid hasce dicimus? ipsas resp. & regna validissima, quæ æterna dici solent, interire cernimus. Ubi jam Troja, Carthago, Corinthus, jam campus est ubi Troja fuit, & domitrix orbis Roma minaces regibus fasces imbelli seni submisit. Verè de omnibus nitidius Paterculus, scriptor judiciosus, Apparet, ait, quemadmodum urbium imperiorumque, ita gentium nunc florere fortunam, nunc senescere, nunc interire. Sed utinam & ipsum Romanum imperium, quartæ Monarchiæ gloria conspicuum, eadem fata non expertū sit & etiamnum experiretur: cui ruinam etiam alii præsagire, alii minari videntur, nisi etiam altiori præsagio viri istius desiderorum Danielis, uti debilitatio & multiplex clades; ita vice versa duratura stabilitas, & ferri robur in luteis pedibus perseverans prædicta essent. Hanc imperii fortunæ varietatem, jam maturè notari posse, manente licet semper robore Monarchico, licet illa varie subinde concussa & labefactata fuerit.
units.tr: II. This is to be shown more fully by induction. Do we not see every day the sun, once it has reached the vertical point and made midday for us, begin at once to decline gradually from the zenith of the sky toward the west? What of the moon, the sun's attendant? She waxes until she shines with a full disc; but as soon as she has reached that perfection, she begins at once to wane again until she is wholly silent, the fruitful mother of changes and the mirror of instability. What shall we say of herbs and trees? They too have their period. The aged oak grows for several centuries, but when it has reached its limit it collapses under its own weight and withers. Animals and men have their appointed ages, and when these are complete they become a burden to themselves and vanish of their own accord. Even the peaks of mountains and the crags that have lasted for ages yield to time and fate. If we look at families, we see them kept alive by a constant succession of new shoots, yet at last we see even the most ancient degenerate and fail, and new ones arise. And why speak of these? We see commonwealths and the most powerful kingdoms, which are commonly called eternal, perish. Where now are Troy, Carthage, Corinth? Now there is only a plain where Troy stood, and Rome, the conqueror of the world, has submitted her threatening fasces to an old man without strength. Paterculus, a judicious writer, has spoken more brilliantly than all others about this: "It is clear," he says, "that just as cities and empires, so also the fortunes of peoples now flourish, now grow old, now perish." But would that the Roman empire itself, conspicuous for the glory of the fourth monarchy, had not experienced and were not still experiencing the same fates! Some seem to foretell its ruin, others to threaten it; yet, if we had the higher foresight of that man of desires, Daniel, we would be told that, just as weakening and manifold disaster, so conversely a lasting stability and an iron strength persisting in feet of clay were also foretold. This variety of the empire's fortune can be noted early, even though its monarchic strength always remains, though it has been variously shaken and weakened from time to time.

units.la: Propos: In præsentiarum de maturo veteris imperii decremento dicendum esse, & invicta interim ejusdem constantia ac stabilitate ferrea: ut ex veteribus præsentia æstimare liceat. Imparem sé quidem argumento, sed fiduciam habere in benivolentia Auditorum qui sua bonitate non exteros minus, quam indigenas fovere consueverint.
units.tr: Proposition: At present it is to be said that the early decline of the old empire, and meanwhile the unconquered constancy and iron stability of the same, so that from the past we may judge the present. I am unequal to the subject, but I have confidence in the goodwill of my hearers, who are accustomed to cherish foreigners no less than natives by their kindness.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Paucis prædicet robur ac potentiam Imperii, postquam longè latéque regna & provincias propinquas longinquas virtute Martia subegisset, justitia ac æquitate retineret in tribus orbis partibus, ubi quicquid dignum erat vinci fascibus Rom. subjecerat. Et quidem non modo gentes barbaras & bellorum rudes; sed & bellicosissimas, Græcos, Asiaticos, Afros, Gallos, Hispanos, Britannos, ipsosque etiam hactenus invictos populos Alpestres, & qui omnibus terrorem incutiebant Germanos, quibus nemo in bellis ante erat &c. Sic gloriam nominis Romani longe lateque celebratam, veterum etiam Monarcharum non æquasse modò sed & superasse: cùm non modo præsenti potentia ac virtute, sed & veterum Heroum gloria Roma triumpharet. Quis enim orbis noti angulus, Fabios, Metellos, Scipiones, quis Coruncanos, Syllas, Marios; quis Pompejos, quis Cæsares & Augustos nominis claritate non noscēret? &c.
units.tr: Treatment. I. Let him briefly declare the strength and power of the empire: after it had subdued far and wide the kingdoms and provinces, near and distant, by Martial valour, it held them by justice and equity in three parts of the world, where it had subjected to the Roman fasces whatever was worth conquering. And indeed it subdued not only barbarous nations unskilled in war, but also the most warlike: Greeks, Asians, Africans, Gauls, Spaniards, Britons, and even the Alpine peoples, hitherto unconquered, and the Germans, who struck terror into all, and against whom no one had yet been successful in war, etc. Thus the glory of the Roman name, celebrated far and wide, not only equalled but surpassed that of the ancient monarchs, since Rome triumphed not only by present power and valour but also by the glory of the heroes of old. For what corner of the known world does not know by the fame of their names the Fabii, Metelli, Scipios, the Coruncanii, Sullas, Marii, Pompeys, Caesars and Augustus? etc.

units.la: II. Verum enim verò ferreæ licet, imò adamantinæ nascentis Imperii columnæ fuerint, non tamen ingruentes subinde clades & fatalia decrementa evitare potuere: ita ut semper lutum ferro permixtum videretur. Hic jam recenseat causas quasdam decrementi imperii:
units.tr: II. But although the columns of the rising empire were iron, indeed adamantine, they could not avoid the disasters that kept coming and the fatal declines, so that it always seemed that clay was mixed with iron. Here he should now enumerate certain causes of the decline of the empire:

units.la: A. Antiquiores: uti est
units.tr: A. Earlier causes, such as:

units.la: 1. Eversio ac ruina veteris nobilitatis per bella civilia. Maturè cœpisse illa ostendat ex Floro sub Mario & Sylla, quorum cruentis concertationibus generosa juventus attrita fuit. Quorum parentes ac majores orbem latè domuerant, qui adoleverant inter arma ac triumphos &c. Illi civilibus lanienis magno numero absorpti fuere. Vid: Flor. lib.III. c.21, Eutropl. 5. Oros.l. 5. &c.
units.tr: 1. The overthrow and ruin of the old nobility through civil wars. Let him show from Florus that this began early under Marius and Sulla, by whose bloody contests the noble youth was worn down. Their parents and ancestors had widely subdued the world, and they had grown up amid arms and triumphs, etc. A great number of them were swallowed up in civil butchery. See Florus, book 3, chapter 21; Eutropius, book 5; Orosius, book 5, etc.

units.la: 2. Enervatio civium per luxum.
units.tr: 2. The enervation of citizens through luxury.

units.la: Quid commemorem hic, quantâ cladem passa resp. per luxū Catilinæ, sic enervata virtus masculā in illis quos bellum reliquos fecerat. Vid. Salust. in Conjurat. Catilin. Item Juvenal. & Martialem passim &c. Scilicet sævior armis luxuria incaincubuit & victum ulciscitur orbem &c. Amplificetur comparatione priscæ frugalitatis Romanæ.
units.tr: Why should I recall here how greatly the commonwealth suffered through the luxury of Catiline, and how manly virtue was thus enfeebled in those whom war had left behind? See Sallust, in the Conspiracy of Catiline. Likewise Juvenal and Martial throughout, etc. Indeed luxury, fiercer than arms, has sunk down and avenges the conquered world, etc. Let this be amplified by comparison with the old Roman frugality.

units.la: 3. Quantum denique generosi sanguinis fusum pro afferenda & vindicanda libertate tempore Cæsaris & Pompeji? ubi quilibet partem eligebat, & urbs in partes discedebat Cæsaris aut Pompeji. Heu quantùm hic fusum sanguinis! &c. Dion Cassius hinc dixit; ut quisque generosissimus erat, ita eum maxime bellis istis civilibus cecidisse. Ipsa domus Cæsaris exstincta hic. Hinc supplendus subinde numerus patriciorum fuit ab imperatoribus diversis.
units.tr: 3. Finally, how much noble blood was shed in asserting and defending liberty in the time of Caesar and Pompey? Where each man chose a side, and the city was divided into the parties of Caesar or of Pompey. Alas, how much blood was shed here! etc. Dio Cassius therefore said that the more noble a man was, the more he fell in those civil wars. The very house of Caesar was extinguished here. Hence the number of patricians had to be made up from time to time by different emperors.

units.la: 4. Quantam jacturam passa nobilitas sub Tiberio, Caligula, Nerone, Claudio per delationes, quibus tollebatur, aut relegabatur quicquid tyrannidem ferre non poterat. Vid. Taciti Tiber. Caligulam &c. Alii vero inertiæ se dabant, ut honoribus extollerentur; gnatones principum, ocii sectatores. Ita elanguit Martia virtus & in gulam, structuras, inania, incumbebat.
units.tr: 4. How great a loss the nobility suffered under Tiberius, Caligula, Nero and Claudius through the denunciations by which whatever could not bear tyranny was removed or banished. See Tacitus on Tiberius, Caligula, etc. Others indeed gave themselves to idleness, so that they might be raised to honours: flatterers of princes, seekers of leisure. Thus Martial virtue grew faint, and men devoted themselves to the belly, buildings, and empty things.

units.la: 5. Secuta hinc paupertas, quæ reliquos evertit, exemplum præbet Hortensia familia & Gracchiana, aliæque plurmæ, vide Florum. Ita dejecti sunt animi generosiorum, & fœdæ adulationi se manciparunt. Qui dare solebat Imperium, fasces, tantum nunc anxius optat Panem & Circenses. Juven. Ita jam Aud. ab antiquo inclinari coepit res Romana & male mixta ex luto & ferro compages: quam deinceps cum jam suis cruribus innixa stabat, gravior adhuc tempestas impulit.
units.tr: 5. Poverty followed, which overthrew the rest; the families of Hortensius and the Gracchi, and many others, provide examples; see Florus. Thus the spirits of the more noble were cast down, and they surrendered themselves to foul flattery. "He who once bestowed empire, fasces, now anxiously desires only bread and circuses." Juvenal. Thus, already from of old, the Roman affair began to lean, and the structure badly mixed of clay and iron, which then, while it stood on its own legs, was struck by a still heavier storm.

units.la: II. Posteriores decrementi causas exponat: uti sunt.
units.tr: II. Let him set out the later causes of decline, such as:

units.la: 1. Sævitia imperatorum gentilium contra Christianos & 10. istæ famosæ persecutiones. Hic a extollat florem imperii sub Augusto, ubi pace ac prosperitate reflorescere coepit imperium longè lateque diffusum, vide Tacit. initio: b. Deploret secutas sub Nerone reliquisque Imperatoribus persecutiones Christianorum, quibus trucidati, fugati plurimi, & innoxio Martyrum sanguine maculatum passim per provincias æque ac Romæ imperium. Cum jam ante lautissima provincia Judæa excisa, atque vastata esset. Ita scilicet quod de Græcis Justin? ait, externis bellis fessum imperium in propria viscera arma convertit, &c.
units.tr: 1. The savagery of the pagan emperors against the Christians, and the ten famous persecutions. Here let him praise the flourishing of the empire under Augustus, when, through peace and prosperity, the empire, widely spread far and wide, began to bloom again; see Tacitus at the beginning. Let him deplore the persecutions of the Christians that followed under Nero and the other emperors, by which very many were slaughtered and put to flight, and the empire, in its provinces as well as at Rome, was everywhere stained with the innocent blood of martyrs; since the most flourishing province, Judea, had already been destroyed and laid waste. So indeed, as Justin says of the Greeks, the empire, weary of foreign wars, turned its arms against its own vitals, etc.

units.la: 2. Translatio sedis imperatoriæ ex Occidente in Orientem. Hic
units.tr: 2. The transfer of the imperial seat from the West to the East. Here

units.la: 3. Agn-
units.tr: 3. Inva-

units.la: a. Agnoscat gloriam renascentem imperii sub Constantino Magno, qui domitis Tyrannis pacem reddidit Christianis ac imperio &c.
units.tr: a. Let him acknowledge the renewed glory of the empire under Constantine the Great, who, having subdued the tyrants, restored peace to the Christians and to the empire, etc.

units.la: b. Repraesentet clades imperii ex translatione sedis imperatoriae, quia sic gloria urbis istius aeternae, ut credebatur, obscurata fuit, & coepit evilescere, & vicinae provinciae negligi; & hinc porro invaluit divisio & distractio, dum alius in Oriente, alius in Occidente praerat; ut Honorius & Arcadius &c.
units.tr: b. Let him set forth the disaster to the empire arising from the transfer of the imperial seat, because thus the glory of that eternal city, as it was believed, was obscured and began to grow feeble, and the neighbouring provinces were neglected; and from this division and distraction grew stronger, since one ruled in the East and another in the West, as Honorius and Arcadius, etc.

units.la: 3. Incursio barbararum nationum in imperium.
units.tr: 3. The incursion of the barbarian nations into the empire.

units.la: a. Occidentis, ut Gothorum, Hunnorum, Vandalorum, Longobardorum, qui per Pannoniam trajecto Danubio in Imperii viscera se effuderunt, & expugnata dirutaque; Roma regnum Gothicum sub duce Alarico, Totila, Attila; regnum Veronense sub Theodorico postmodum; & regnum Longobardicum Duce Alboino condidere, imo Gothi progressi in Hispania sedem collocarunt. Gallia a Francis Germaniae populis, duce Pharamundo avulsa fuit, Anglia itidem praesidio idoneo destituta, Romanas reliquias expulit. Licet Exarchae Ravennates ab Imperatoribus constituti fuerint, licet Justinianus Imperator ducibus Belisario & Narseta vindicaverit imperii provincias: tamen praevaluit vis barbarorum, & occidentale imperium exstinctum fuit; & provincia Pannonia, Noricum, Maesia, Thracia per Hunnos avulsa. Ita labefactatum Imperium universum, & occidens misere laceratus & oppressus fuit.
units.tr: a. Of the West: the Goths, Huns, Vandals and Lombards, who, crossing the Danube through Pannonia, poured themselves into the vitals of the empire. Having taken and laid waste Rome, they founded the Gothic kingdom under the leaders Alaric, Totila and Attila; afterwards the kingdom of Verona under Theodoric; and the Lombard kingdom under the leader Alboin. Nay, the Goths advanced into Spain and settled there. Gaul was torn away by the Franks, a German people, under their leader Pharamond. Britain, likewise deprived of an adequate garrison, expelled the Roman remnants. Although the Exarchs of Ravenna were appointed by the emperors, and although the Emperor Justinian, through his generals Belisarius and Narses, recovered the provinces of the empire, nevertheless the force of the barbarians prevailed, the Western empire was extinguished, and the provinces of Pannonia, Noricum, Moesia and Thrace were torn away by the Huns. Thus the whole empire was shaken, and the West was miserably torn apart and crushed.

units.la: b. In Imperio Orientis, quod per Persas subinde, vehementissime vero per Saracenos direptum, Cyprus, Rhodus, Creta, Cilicia, Galatia lautissimae Imperii provinciae debellatae occupatae a Mahumedanis. Haec exaggerentur suis locis, & concludantur deploratione miserabilis lacerationis lautissimi Imperii; quod pessum sane iviset, nisi ferrum luto mixtum sustinuisset imperii corpus. &c.
units.tr: b. In the Eastern empire, which was from time to time plundered by the Persians and most violently by the Saracens, Cyprus, Rhodes, Crete, Cilicia and Galatia, the most splendid provinces of the empire, were conquered and occupied by the Mohammedans. These things are to be enlarged upon in their proper places, and the discussion concluded with a lament over the wretched dismemberment of that most splendid empire, which would certainly have perished utterly, had not the body of the empire held together, like iron mixed with clay. &c.

units.la: 4. Corruptio morum per mixturam barbararum nationum; quae veteres leges & jura Romana everterunt, suis moribus statuta accommodarunt; artium & scientiarum fundamenta perverterunt, lingua Romana & monumenta sapientiae veteris corruperunt. perunt. Sic convulsis fundamentis, quis miretur imperium labefactatum? &c.
units.tr: 4. The corruption of morals through the mixing in of the barbarian nations, which overturned the ancient laws and Roman rights and fitted the statutes to their own customs; they subverted the foundations of the arts and sciences, and corrupted the Roman language and the monuments of ancient wisdom. With the foundations thus shaken, who would wonder that the empire was weakened? &c.

units.la: LIII. DE ECCLESIÆ WALDENSIUM ORTU, OBSTACULIS, ET PROGRESSU.
units.tr: LIII. On the Origin, Obstacles and Progress of the Church of the Waldenses.

units.la: Exord. A mirabili natura lucis: quæ divinitus
units.tr: Exord. From the wonderful nature of light, which divinely

units.la: I. Proponatur 1.In ortu ejusdem; videlicet jussa splendescere extebris. 2. In natura sua: quod pateat omnibus, lateat omnes; nec corpus fuit, nec spiritus; nec substantia, nec qualitas nuda: adeo ut oculissimi hic etiam cæcutiant in re clarissima. 3. In effectis: quod detegat semetipsam & omnia alia: quod occultari nequeat, sed presla erumpat fortius; quod exhilaret & foveat omnia: adeo ut & sidera exigui temporis ecclipsin passa, mala præsagiant & operentur: adeo nihil memorabilius, nihil efficacius ac salubrius luce. vid. Physicos Scalig. de Subtil: des Cartes, &c.
units.tr: I. Let the following be proposed: 1. Its origin: namely that it was commanded to shine out of darkness. 2. Its nature: it lies open to all yet is hidden from all; it is neither body nor spirit, neither substance nor bare quality, so that even the sharpest-sighted here go blind in a most clear matter. 3. Its effects: it reveals itself and all other things; it cannot be concealed but breaks out all the more strongly; it cheers and warms all things; so that even the stars, after a brief eclipse, presage and bring about evils. Thus nothing is more remarkable, nothing more effective and wholesome than light. See the natural philosophers, Scaliger on Descartes' Subtilitas, etc.

units.la: II. Applicetur ad veritatem cœlestem in omnibus partibus: vid. 1. a Deo est revelata: 2. patet publicè, latet mundum, qui cum Pilato quærit: quid est veritas? 3. At fulget sua luce & omnia arguit <bl>πᾶν ἐλεγχόμενον φῶς ἐστι</bl>: presla emergit fortius; lætificat cor hominis vid. psal. 9. & fovet ac conservat Ecclesiam, nunquam occultata sine ejusdem damno & tristi augurio. Hoc probetur exemplo Papatus ubi oppressa diu maximo cum damno, at occultari penitus non potuit, quin semper sparserit radios, non secus ac lucerna sub lacero modio aut cilicio occultata. Hinc nunquam defuere contradictores abusuum & lumina in generatione ista perversa. Vid. Historiam & Catalogum testium veritatis Illirici: & ultimo adducantur Waldenses, qui in spississimis tenebris papatus de cœlesti luce testati fuere.
units.tr: II. Let it be applied to heavenly truth in all its parts. See: 1. It has been revealed by God. 2. It lies open publicly yet is hidden from the world, which asks with Pilate: what is truth? 3. But it shines with its own light and convicts all things: "everything that is made manifest is light" [πᾶν ἐλεγχόμενον φῶς ἐστι]. It rises up the more strongly, gladdens the human heart (see Psalm 9), and warms and preserves the Church, never hidden without loss to the Church and a sorrowful omen. Let this be proved by the example of the Papacy, where truth, long oppressed to the great loss of the Church, yet could not be entirely hidden, but always sent out its rays, like a lamp hidden under a torn bushel or sackcloth. Hence there were never lacking opponents of the abuses, and lights in this perverse generation. See the History and Catalogue of the Witnesses of Truth by Illyricus. And finally let the Waldenses be adduced, who in the thickest darkness of the Papacy bore witness to the heavenly light.

units.la: Propositi. De horum ortu, progressu, obstaculis & victoria paucis agendum: quæ dissertatio tanto minus ingrata esse queat Auditoribus quod ipsa tenebris quibusdam involuta & passim dispersa in historia, & mendaciis hostium obfuscata; dignissima tamen, quæ eruatur; quoniam & iidem illi primi fuere, qui veluti albescens aurora renascenti Euangelio præluxere; & plenum diem mox oriturum prædixerunt, & in diversis regnis multo cum martyrio de coelesti veritate testati sunt necdum etiamnum exstincti. Tractatio explicet Waldensium
units.tr: Propositi. The origin, progress, obstacles and victory of these people are to be treated briefly. This discourse may be the less unwelcome to the audience, since it is involved in some darkness and scattered here and there in history, and obscured by the lies of enemies; yet it is most worth extracting, since these were the very first who, like a whitening dawn, shone forth to the reborn Gospel, foretold that the full day would soon rise, and in various kingdoms bore witness to the heavenly truth at great cost of martyrdom, and are not yet extinct. The treatment shall explain the Waldenses'

units.la: I. Ortum: ubi
units.tr: I. The origin: where

units.la: 1. Exponat occasionem, videlicet statū Ecclesiae istis temporibus corruptissimum in plena exuberantia Papatus circa annum Christi 1159. sedente Alex. III. qui Fridericū Barbarossam Imperatorē pedibus suis subjecit: quo eodem anno magis nomen Waldensiū innotuit. Vide & exaggera tenebras papatus praecedentes ex historia universali Sleidani &c. Et compara cum tenebris Aegypti antegressis, antequam Deus educeret populū suum. Illustretur ex Loco Communi de invicta virtute verbi divini, quod splenduit etiam tempore desperatissimo.
units.tr: 1. Let him set out the occasion, namely the state of the Church at that time, most corrupt in the full exuberance of the Papacy, around the year of Christ 1159, with Alexander III sitting, who put Frederick Barbarossa the Emperor under his feet; in the same year the name of the Waldenses became better known. See and magnify the darkness of the preceding Papacy from Sleidan's Universal History, etc., and compare it with the darkness of Egypt before God led out his people. Let it be illustrated from the Common Place on the invincible power of the divine Word, which shone even in the most desperate time.

units.la: 2. Defectionem; ubi
units.tr: 2. The defection: where

units.la: a. Nomen: videlicet dicti Waldenses a Wâldone cive opulento Lugdunensi, benefico in pauperes, in cujus aedibus convenire consueverat, qui vitia cleri Romani taxare & aliis dehortari consueverat. Unde & pauperes Lugdunenses dicti. Et Leonitae, mox Albii & Albigenses dicti ab Albinate civitate in Tolosatibus: ab aliis Humiles & humiliati dicti: Piccardi post ab illa provincia. Fratres Bohemi, quia qui in Bohemiam migraverant, fratrum instar vicitabant. Hinc
units.tr: a. The name: the Waldenses were so called from Waldo, a wealthy citizen of Lyons, a benefactor of the poor, in whose house they were accustomed to gather, and who used to censure the vices of the Roman clergy and dissuade others from them. Whence they were also called the Poor of Lyons. They were also called Leonists, and soon Albigenses, from the city of Albi in the territory of Toulouse; by others, the Humble and Humiliati; later Picards, from that province; Bohemian Brethren, because those who had migrated to Bohemia lived like brothers. Hence

units.la: b. In vicinas Tolosanam & Narbonnensem provincias digressi ibique tolerati caetus egere, Unde porro
units.tr: b. Having departed into the neighbouring provinces of Toulouse and Narbonne, and there tolerated, they formed gatherings. Whence further

units.la: c. Colligat ortum illorū, videlicet obscurū initio & exiguum; natum ex micante veritate inter spissas istas tenebras papatus; vitiis & turpibus moribus Ecclesiasticorum ansam praebentibus examinandi etiam doctrinam. Hinc Reinerus quidam libro contra Waldenses: Haeresis Waldensium, ait, magna habet speciem pietatis, eo quod coram hominibus juste vivant, & bene omnia de Deo credant, & omnes articulos, qui in symbolo continentur; solummodo Romanam Ecclesiam blasphemant & clerum &c. Illustrentur haec ex thesi: videlicet Deum semper servare sibi Ecclesiam, & ipsis vitiis uti ad patefaciendum veritatem. Exemplo seditionis Corae ad stabiliendam autoritatem Mosis & Aaronis: persecutionis Christianorum ad propagatio- nem Euangelii &c. Hinc accedatur ad membrum.
units.tr: c. Let him gather their origin: obscure and small at the beginning, born from the gleaming truth amid the thick darkness of the Papacy, the vices and base morals of ecclesiastics providing occasion for examining even the doctrine. Hence a certain Reiner, in a book against the Waldenses: the heresy of the Waldenses, he says, has a great appearance of piety, because they live justly before men and believe all things rightly about God, and all the articles contained in the creed; only they blaspheme the Roman Church and the clergy, etc. Let these be illustrated from the thesis: namely that God always preserves his Church for himself and uses even vices to reveal the truth. Compare the sedition of Korah, which established the authority of Moses and Aaron, and the persecution of Christians, which spread the Gospel, etc. Hence let us proceed to the next part.

units.la: II. Obstacula nempe varia: uti fuere
units.tr: II. The obstacles, which were various, namely:

units.la: 1. Excommunicatio in Concilio. I. Laterano ab Alex. III, Lu- cio III, aliisque, ubi tanquam hæretici proscripti: cum haẞte- nus pacatè vixerant studiis pietatis & vitæ inculpatæ dediti: Unde & Cathari seu Puritani dicti fuere. Illustretur ex thesi, odio scilicet sceleratorū adversus pios jam inde a Caino &c.
units.tr: 1. Excommunication at the First Lateran Council by Alexander III, Lucius III and others, where they were proscribed as heretics, though until then they had lived peaceably, devoted to the pursuits of piety and blameless living. Whence they were also called Cathari or Puritans. Let it be illustrated from the thesis: namely the hatred of the wicked against the godly from Cain onward, etc.

units.la: 2. Oppositio duorum ordinum a Papa Lucio III. Franciscano- rum & Dominicanorum, authoritate & potentia pollentium. Fiat digressiuncula ad taxandos ordines illos ex cacozelia or- tos in stabilimentum papatus.
units.tr: 2. Opposition from two orders under Pope Lucius III: the Franciscans and Dominicans, mighty in authority and power. Let a short digression be made to censure those orders, which arose from misguided zeal as a prop for the Papacy.

units.la: 3. Oppugnatio hostilis & armata; tum per Ludovicum regem Galliæ, tum per Papam Gregor. IX. & Innocent. III. qui exercitum cruciatorum contra illos produxerunt annis 1209. & 1218. diffamantes illos tanquam facinorosos; promiscui concubitus, adulterii, perjurii, majestatis & Manichæismi reos; principibus Tolosatibus, & Narbonnensibus frustra illos protegentibus. Hinc excisi isti principes, & Albigenses dispersi. Illustretur allusione ad Locum Communem prætextu religionis cum petuntur regiones; vide dictum Pauli Æ- milii in hist. Galliæ apud Boxh. pag. 710. Et de more hostium Ecclesiæ à verbis ad verbera progredientium.
units.tr: 3. Hostile and armed assault, both by Louis, king of France, and by Popes Gregory IX and Innocent III, who led an army of crusaders against them in the years 1209 and 1218, defaming them as criminals: guilty of promiscuous intercourse, adultery, perjury, treason and Manichaeism; the princes of Toulouse and Narbonne protected them in vain. Hence those princes were cut down and the Albigenses scattered. Let it be illustrated by allusion to the Common Place that regions are attacked under the pretext of religion; see the saying of Paul Aemilius in his History of France, in Boxhorn p. 710, and the custom of the enemies of the Church, who progress from words to blows.

units.la: 4. Dissipatio in diversas oras & provincias: videl. in Picardiam, Allobroges, vicinumque Dephinatum & Narbonnensem tractum & Pedemontium &c. Angliam, Bohemiam; tandem & Calabriam & Germaniá passim. Boxh. p. 714. Illustretur ex Loco Communi de frustra tentata exstirpatione Ecclesiæ per gladium: cum sanguis Martyrum semen Ecclesiæ; exemplo primitivæ Ecclesiæ, quæ persecutionibus facta fuit robustior &c. Ita nec per inauditam lanienam in Delphinatu ubi sine discrimine sexus & ætatis trucidati anno 1545. excisa.
units.tr: 4. Dispersal into various shores and provinces: namely into Picardy, the Allobroges, the neighbouring Dauphiné, the Narbonne region, Piedmont, etc., England, Bohemia; finally Calabria and Germany as well, everywhere. Boxhorn p. 714. Let it be illustrated from the Common Place on the vainly attempted extirpation of the Church by the sword, since the blood of martyrs is the seed of the Church; by the example of the primitive Church, which grew stronger through persecution, etc. So too by the unheard-of slaughter in Dauphiné, where in 1545, without distinction of sex or age, they were butchered and cut off.

units.la: 5. Injusta criminatio pontificiorum, acsi pessimarum ac horrendissimarum hæresium participes essent; unde passim exosi & pressi fuere: maximè in Gallia & Germania: Exaggeretur, quod lingua ita trucidaverint, quos gladio non potuissent. Illustretur exemplo Christi & primitivæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 5. Unjust accusation by the Papists, as though they were partakers of the worst and most horrible heresies; whence they were everywhere hated and oppressed, especially in France and Germany. Let it be magnified that they slaughtered with the tongue those whom they could not with the sword. Let it be illustrated by the example of Christ and the primitive Church.

units.la: III. Narret victoriam inter mille mortes ac persecutiones: accessus fiat per allusionem ad Locum Communem nimirum, tectam ac pressam fortius emicare lucem veritatis. Hinc expona-tur 1. Constantia ipsorum in fide, cujus rationem reddidere & probavere Regi Galliæ Ludovico XII. adversus ipsos a Cardinalibus aliisque incitato: hic summatim capita doctrinæ ipsorum referantur ex Thuano lib 6. vide Boxh. p. 716. 717. 718. & hinc retundantur calumniæ papalium.
units.tr: III. Let him narrate the victory amid a thousand deaths and persecutions. The approach is made by allusion to the Common Place, namely that the light of truth, covered and pressed down, shines all the more brightly. Hence let there be set out: 1. The constancy of their faith, the account of which they gave and proved to Louis XII, king of France, who had been stirred up against them by the cardinals and others. Here the heads of their doctrine are summarily reported from Thuanus, book 6; see Boxhorn pp. 716-718; and thus the calumnies of the Papalists are refuted.

units.la: 2. Protectio suscepta a comitibus Tolosanis aliisque
units.tr: 2. The protection taken up by the counts of Toulouse and others.

units.la: 3. Constantia in supplicis vid. Boxh.719.
units.tr: 3. Constancy in supplications; see Boxhorn p. 719.

units.la: 4. Perseverantia usque ad hodierna tempora, licet crudelissimis etiam nuper lanienis in Sabaudia, & Pedemontio antiqua sede ipsorum mactati fuerint, frustra ringente Satana adversus veritatem, quæ premi quidem, opprimi minimè potest; non magis quàm lux solis exstingui poterit.
units.tr: 4. Perseverance until the present times, although they were recently slaughtered with the cruelest butcheries in Savoy and Piedmont, their ancient seat, while Satan struggled in vain against the truth, which can indeed be pressed but cannot be crushed at all, no more than the light of the sun can be extinguished.

units.la: Peroratio summatim capita dictorum repetat & Auditorio gratias agat ac valedicat, cum voto prosperitatis ad civitatem & Gymnasium.
units.tr: Peroratio Let him briefly repeat the heads of the foregoing, thank the audience and bid them farewell, with a wish for the prosperity of the city and the Gymnasium.

units.la: LIV.
units.tr: LIV.

units.la: Cic. 1. Offic.
units.tr: Cic. 1. Offic.

units.la: PARVA SUNT FORIS ARMA, NISI EST CONSILIUM DOMI.
units.tr: ARMS ARE SMALL ABROAD, UNLESS THERE IS COUNSEL AT HOME.

units.la: Exord. A conditione temporum præsentium; ubi omnia strepunt armis. Hoc
units.tr: Exord. From the condition of the present times, when everything rings with arms. This:

units.la: I. Proponatur: videl. in ea nos, proh dolor incidisse tempora, ubi nil nisi arma, tubarum clangor, tormentorum fulmina. excidia urbium, strages populorum audiuntur.
units.tr: I. Let it be set forth: that we have fallen, alas, upon such times, in which nothing is heard but arms, the blare of trumpets, the thunder of artillery, the destruction of cities and the slaughter of peoples.

units.la: II. Explicetur uberius per brevem inductionem bellorum in omnibus orbis partibus, apud ipsos etiam antipodes, &c.
units.tr: II. Let it be explained more fully by a brief survey of wars in every part of the world, even among the antipodes themselves, etc.

units.la: III. Illustretur a consequenti: videri hinc fas omne abruptum armis & ferro gerenda omnia; & juxta monitum Servatoris, vendendam vestem, & emendum gladium: jam reges, consilium, sacra, profana cedere victori.
units.tr: III. Let it be illustrated from the consequence: that from this it seems all right is broken off by arms, and everything must be done by the sword and iron; and in accordance with the Saviour's warning, one must sell one's garment and buy a sword. Now kings, counsel, sacred and profane things yield to the victor.

units.la: IV. Sternatur accessus ad propositionem sententiâ disertissimi cordatissimique Consulis Romani, cum inquit: Cedant arma toga, & parva esse foris arma, nisi est consilium domi, scil. consilio prudenprudentiaque frangendum hostium impetum, ne latius serpat vastitas.
units.tr: IV. Let the approach to the proposition be prepared by the most eloquent and wise sentence of the Roman consul, when he says: Let arms yield to the toga, and let arms be small abroad, unless there is counsel at home, namely that the enemy's assault is to be broken by prudent counsel and wisdom, lest devastation creep more widely.

units.la: Propos. De hac Consilii Sapientum necessitate ac eminentia in praesentiarum in Consessu hoc tot Sapientum & eruditorum dicendum : quod tanto minus displicebit; quoniam laudatissima haec Resp. hactenus per Dei gratiam armorum truculentiam, non tam viribus armorum, quam prudentia consilii avertit. Gloriae sibi ducere, in urbe justitiae, Sacrorum ac Literarum laude famigeratissima, in consessu tot virorum omni laude celebratissimorum, licet impari facundia, publice dicere licitum.
units.tr: Proposition. Concerning this necessity and eminence of the counsel of the wise, it must be said at present in this assembly of so many wise and learned men; and it will displease all the less, since this most praiseworthy commonwealth has hitherto, by the grace of God, turned away the savagery of arms not so much by the strength of arms as by the prudence of counsel. It is permitted me to glory, in the city of justice, most famous for the praise of sacred and literary things, to speak publicly before an assembly of so many men celebrated with every praise, though with unequal eloquence.

units.la: Tractatio. Et quidem ut hinc exordiatur, videndum.
units.tr: Treatment. And indeed, to begin from here, let us consider:

units.la: I. Unde coetus hominum, civitates, Regna ac Resp. ortum sumpserint? Hic
units.tr: I. Whence assemblies of men, cities, kingdoms and commonwealths took their origin. Here

units.la: 1. Ab armis putare plurimos, a metu statuere Hobbesium Anglum, qui arma parat. Uti sane primus dominator Nimrodus fortis venator dicitur coram domino ferro ut videtur homines, uti feras venator, subigens.
units.tr: 1. Most men think it arose from arms and from fear; Hobbes the Englishman, who prepares arms, lays it down. Indeed the first ruler, Nimrod, is said to have been a mighty hunter before the Lord, subduing men with iron as a hunter subdues wild beasts.

units.la: 2. At rectius a consilio Sapientum civitatum ortus derivari. Hoc ostendat jam inductione quadam praecipuarum aliquot Rerump. Ipsum Nimrodum non sine consilio callido incrementa sumpsisse: plures sine dubio prudentiae ac legu laqueis, quam ferri violentia subegisse homines & ad unam Metropolin redegisse. Assyrii sapientiam praedicari, cujus beneficio se extulit. Esa. 10. v. 11, &c. Quid de Lacedaemoniorum, Atheniensium Rebusp. dicendum, quarum illa legibus Lycurgi, haec Solonis sapientissimis constituta floruit? vid. Cic. 1. offic. Quid de celeberrima Romana Monarchia? Armis quidem Romuli coepisse, at consilio Senatus convaluisse. Hujus constitutione expone ex Floro, Livio, & quomodo praecipue sub consulum Regimine creverit, &c. Eandem esse omnium hodieque Rerump. conditionem. Ferro quidem invadi regionem, erigi potentiam posse, at consilio conservari. Armis invaluisse Annibalem & postea Parthos, at prudentia Romana repressos fuisse. &c. Solius hoc Turcici imperii esse, ut armorum potentia nitatur. Sed fatalem illam vim esse, ad castigandam securitatem Christianorum. Interim a mi-nonoribus viribus subinde etiam fusos fuisse Turcas; nec dubium esse vinci posse, fi fana junctaque consilia Christiani Principes opponerent. Jam quia ipsi fe laniant, crescit Turca, &c. Digreffiuncula fiat, deploratione discordiæ Christianorum principum. Utinam meliori consilio prudentum tandem corrigatur.
units.tr: 2. But more rightly the origin of states is derived from the counsel of the wise. Let him show this now by a certain survey of some of the chief commonwealths: that Nimrod himself did not grow great without crafty counsel; and that without doubt more men were subdued by the snares of prudence and laws than by the violence of iron, and brought back into one metropolis. The wisdom of the Assyrians is praised, by whose benefit he exalted himself (Isa. 10.11, etc.). What is to be said of the commonwealths of the Lacedaemonians and Athenians, of which the former flourished under the laws of Lycurgus, the latter under the most wise laws of Solon? See Cic. 1. Offic. What of the famous Roman monarchy? Indeed it began by the arms of Romulus, but grew strong by the counsel of the Senate. Set out its constitution from Florus and Livy, and how it grew especially under the rule of the consuls, etc. The condition of all commonwealths even today is the same: a region may indeed be invaded with iron and its power raised up, but it can be preserved only by counsel. Hannibal grew strong by arms, and afterwards the Parthians, but both were repressed by Roman prudence, etc. This power of the Turkish empire alone, it is said, rests on the strength of arms; but this is a fated force, to chastise the security of Christians. Meanwhile the Turks have at times been routed even by smaller forces, and there is no doubt they can be conquered if Christian princes oppose them with united and sound counsels. Now, because they tear themselves apart, the Turk grows, etc. Let there be a small digression, a lament over the discord of the Christian princes. Would that they might at last be corrected by the better counsel of the prudent.

units.la: Quàm necessarium Consilium ac Senatus prudentum ad Rerump. conservationem?
units.tr: How necessary is counsel, and a senate of the prudent, for the preservation of the commonwealth?

units.la: 1. Adversus internam corruptionem
units.tr: 1. Against internal corruption

units.la: a. Per profanitatem, dissolutionem ac luxum: Hic 1. Exponat, quàm facilè illa vitia invadant civitatem, propter naturalem populi ad vitia hæc inclinationem. Probetur exemplis Reip. Judaicæ & Romanæ præsertim. 2. Ostendat, non nisi consilio prudentum, per leges salutares illa corrigi posse; & correcta fuisse. Prædicet hinc Leges, tanquam ex recta ratione, adeoque ex mente divina velut fonte primo, per consilium prudentum, inventas & latas fuisse. Probetur exemplo Romanorum præsertim: ubi notentur præcipuæ aliquot leges sumptuariæ, & contra alia vitia. Frustra armis egeris hic; imò legibus, judiciis opus esse. &c.
units.tr: a. Through profanity, dissolution and luxury. Here: 1. Let him set out how easily those vices invade a state, on account of the natural inclination of the people toward them. Let it be proved by examples, especially from the Jewish and Roman commonwealths. 2. Let him show that these vices can be corrected only by the counsel of the prudent, through salutary laws; and that they have been corrected. Let him proclaim that laws were devised and enacted by the counsel of the prudent, as from right reason, and so from the divine mind as from a first fountain. Let it be proved especially by the example of the Romans, where some chief sumptuary laws and laws against other vices are noted. In vain would you act here with arms; indeed laws and courts are needed, etc.

units.la: b. Per æmulationem & ambitum ac turbas magnatum & populi: uti factum Romæ sub Gracchis, sub Mario & Sulla, sub Cæsare & Pompejo, &c. At quomodo sopienda? nisi prudentia & consilio sapientum? &c.
units.tr: b. Through rivalry, ambition and the tumults of nobles and people: as happened at Rome under the Gracchi, under Marius and Sulla, under Caesar and Pompey, etc. But how are these to be quieted, unless by the prudence and counsel of the wise? etc.

units.la: 2. Adversus bella externa. Hic
units.tr: 2. Against external wars. Here

units.la: a. Nullam ostendat esse Remp. aut Regnum sine bello necessario. Rationes addat; videl. 1. ob violentiam ac ambitionem hostium alienis inhiantium. 2. Ob invidiam & infidelitatem vicinorum. 3. Ob vindicationem læsæ famæ, violatorum Legatorum, &c. vide politicos & singula illustrentur exemplo uno atque altero. 4. Imò & ipsam religionem, magistram concordiæ ac pacis, apud Christianos proh dolor materiam sæpe bello præbere; ex quo terrenis opibus & principatibus gaudere cœpit Ecclesia. Hinc bellum contra Waldenses, Hussiticum in Bohemia, Germanicum superiori & hoc sæculo. Locustas istas Apocalypticas ex lucis & claustris
units.tr: a. Let him show that there is no commonwealth or kingdom without necessary war. Let him add reasons: 1. because of the violence and ambition of enemies who covet what belongs to others; 2. because of the envy and faithlessness of neighbours; 3. for the vindication of injured reputation, violated ambassadors, etc. See the political writers, and let each point be illustrated by one or two examples. 4. Indeed religion itself, the teacher of concord and peace, has alas often furnished the matter of war among Christians, from which the Church began to rejoice in earthly wealth and principalities. Hence the war against the Waldenses, the Hussite war in Bohemia, the German war in the last century and this one. Those Apocalyptic locusts, coming forth from their smoky pits

units.la: seis suis egressas ad reges & principes terrae, armatis ad bellum equis similes, incentores saepe bellorum esse.
units.tr: to the kings and princes of the earth, like horses armed for battle, are often the instigators of wars.

units.la: b. Armis dicat non semper parem esse partem offensam seu laesam; aut non semper tutum ac opportunum esse confligere. Ergo ad foedera aut ad tractatus veniendum. At quomodo, nisi consilium sit domi? Ita Philippus Macedo cum omnibus par esse non poterat, quaedam bella pactis componebat: plura consilio, quam armis gessit, &c. & Romani sedendo fortiores fuere, hoc est consilio.
units.tr: b. Let him say that by arms the party offended or injured is not always equal, nor is it always safe or fitting to join battle; therefore one must come to covenants or to negotiations. But how, unless there is counsel at home? Thus Philip of Macedon, since he could not be a match for everyone, settled some wars by treaties; he waged more by counsel than by arms, etc. And the Romans, by sitting still, were the stronger; that is, by counsel.

units.la: c. Bellum ipsum doceat raro armis terminari; maxime si validae sint partes confligentes. At quomodo fiet, nisi consilium domi sit. 2. Quae conditionibus sanari possunt, non sunt ferro dijudicanda. Novit hoc Tiberius Imper. qui dicit plura se pactis quam armis terminasse cum Germanis: qui tutius internis dissidiis & tempori reliti sint. Bellum Germanicum sub Carolo V. & recentius sub Ferdin. II. pactis terminatum fuisse. &c. vide alia exempla.
units.tr: c. Let war itself teach that it is rarely ended by arms, especially if the parties fighting are strong. But how will this be done, unless there is counsel at home? 2. Those things which can be healed by conditions are not to be decided by the sword. Tiberius the Emperor knew this, who says he ended more matters with the Germans by treaties than by arms, and that they are safer left to internal dissensions and to time. The German war under Charles V, and more recently under Ferdinand II, was ended by treaties, etc. See other examples.

units.la: d. Bellum geri consilio. Raro nasci Conquestores, qui armorum impetu omnia sibi subjiciant, ut Alex. Magnus, Julius Caesar. Gallus modernus, contra pleraque bella consilio gerit feliciter, ut olim duces Romani consilio Senatus, Hoc seculo vero Ludovicus XIII. ex consilio Richelii omnia prospere gessit. Unde inscriptio Parisiis, Ludovicus fecit, Armandus invenit. Porro Philippus II. Hisp. plura consilio quam armis gessit &c. Et hoc seculo invasa quoque regna & regiones vidimus veluti diluvio armorum, & rursus deperdita. E contrario quid factum numerosis exercitibus Xerxis, & Darii? Eversi sunt ac dissipati magis consilio, quam armis.
units.tr: d. War is to be waged by counsel. Conquerors who subject everything to themselves by the onrush of arms rarely arise, such as Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar. The modern Frenchman, against most wars, wages them successfully by counsel, as the Roman generals formerly did by the counsel of the Senate. In this century Louis XIII, by the counsel of Richelieu, conducted everything prosperously; hence the inscription at Paris: "Louis made it, Armand invented it." Further, Philip II of Spain waged more by counsel than by arms, etc. And in this century we have seen kingdoms and regions invaded as if by a flood of arms, and again lost. On the contrary, what happened to the numerous armies of Xerxes and Darius? They were overthrown and scattered more by counsel than by arms.

units.la: 3. Ad negocia necessaria Reip. necessarium consilium; uti sunt a. Legationes. Quantum litum sit in idoneis legatis doceat. vide Politicos quanta prudentia esse debeant, &c.
units.tr: 3. Counsel is necessary for the necessary affairs of the commonwealth, such as a. embassies. How much depends on suitable ambassadors, let him show. See the political writers on how much prudence these should have, etc.

units.la: b. Ad foedera. Quanta prudentia hic opus, cum quibus, & quibus conditionibus facienda. vide Politicos Cardinalis Mazarinus ad Pignorolum pacem fecit sub ipso conflictu &c. 4. Ad pacem faciendam & conservandam: quo tandem omnia referenda: ipsa arma sumuntur, ut in pace vivatur. Quid hic sine consilio? Praeterea stabilienda est religio, constituenda justitia, consulendum commerciis & victui, prospiciendum securitati.
units.tr: b. For covenants: how much prudence is needed here, with whom and on what conditions they are to be made. See the political writers: Cardinal Mazarin made peace with Pignerol even in the midst of the conflict, etc. 4. For making and preserving peace, to which all things must in the end be referred: arms themselves are taken up so that one may live in peace. What is done here without counsel? Besides, religion must be established, justice constituted, provision made for commerce and sustenance, and care taken for security.

units.la: Hic optet illud tempus, quo cessante furore Martis, almae Pacis consilia tractentur inter Monarchas Principesque Europae, ut consilio sapientum arma cedant & refloreat pax optima rerum, &c.
units.tr: Here let him wish for that time when, the fury of Mars ceasing, the counsels of kindly Peace are taken up among the monarchs and princes of Europe, so that by the counsel of the wise arms yield and the best peace of affairs flourishes again, etc.

units.la: Perorat 1. Excuset quòd de magno argumento tenuiter dixerit, prout in peregrinia à parum exercitato & peregrinante fieri potuit: Volupe sibi fuisse in Civitate Religionis Orthodoxae, justitiae & Literarum tutrice prima dicendi tyroconia deponere, &c.
units.tr: In the peroration: 1. Let him excuse himself for having spoken slightly on a great subject, as could be expected of one little practised and a foreigner abroad; and let him say it was pleasing to him to lay aside, in the city of the Orthodox Religion, the guardian of justice and letters, his first apprenticeship in speaking, etc.

units.la: 2. Gratias agat Auditoribus, & promittat memoriam hospitalitatis humanitatisque perpetuam.
units.tr: 2. Let him thank the hearers and promise a perpetual memory of their hospitality and humanity.

units.la: 3. Voveat ut consilio amplissimi Senatus salubri, semper vigeat religio, floeratjustitia, perennent Literae, & pax omnisque prosperitas beet universam Civitatem,
units.tr: 3. Let him pray that by the wholesome counsel of the most august Senate, religion may always flourish, justice may flourish, letters endure forever, and peace and every prosperity bless the whole city.

units.la: LV. DE CONSCIENTIA.
units.tr: LV. ON CONSCIENCE.

units.la: Exord. a figmento poëtico de furiis quae homines sceleratos affligere dicebantur. Hoc I. Proponatur II. Explicetur ex Cic: in Pilon: ubi inquit nolite putare P. C. ut in scena videtis homines conscelerados impulsu Deorum terreri furiarum taedis ardentibus: sua quemque fraus, suum facinus, suum scelus, sua audacia de sanitate ac mente deturbat: hae sunt impiorum furiae, hae flammae, hae faces, itemque paradoxo 2. in Anton. te conscientiae stimulant &c. III. Illustretur a causa, Deo scilicet qui secretum hoc tribunal erexit in mentibus nostris: quo judice nemo nocens absolvitur. b. a diversis aliis judicibus, quos vel gratia vel ira abripit, vel fraus eludit; At hic secus.
units.tr: Exordium from the poetic fiction of the Furies, which were said to torment wicked men. Here, (I) state it; (II) explain it from Cicero, In Pisonem, where he says: "Do not think, Conscript Fathers, that wicked men, as you see them on the stage, are terrified by the torches of the Furies, driven on by the gods. Each man's own fraud, his own crime, his own wickedness, his own audacity drives him out of his sanity and mind. These are the Furies of the impious, these their flames, these their torches." Likewise in the second Philippic against Antony: "conscience goads you," etc. (III) Illustrate it from the cause, namely God, who has set up this secret tribunal in our minds, and before whose judgment no guilty person is acquitted; unlike other judges, whom favour or anger carries away, or whom fraud eludes.

units.la: Vel Exord. sumatur ab occultis judiciis a Carolo Magno in Germ. institutis, ubi sine examine ex conscientia istorum judicum damnabantur rei. Hoc ita I. proponatur. II. arguatur tanquam iniquum, uti etiam eventus docuit. III. opponatur judicium occultum, quod Deus in omnium cordibus erexit.
units.tr: Or the exordium may be taken from the secret courts established by Charlemagne in Germany, where, without trial, the accused were condemned on the conscience of those judges. This is to be: (I) proposed thus; (II) argued against as unjust, as the outcome also showed; (III) set against the hidden judgment which God has set up in the hearts of all.

units.la: Propos. De hoc igitur conscientiæ judicio & secreto Dei tribunali agendum.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore we are to treat of this judgment of conscience and God's secret tribunal.

units.la: Tractatio. I. An fit. Hîc
units.tr: Treatment. I. Whether it exists. Here:

units.la: 1. Concedat multos esse, qui judicium hoc aboleverunt, qui vel nullam, vel cauteriatam habent conscientiam; videlicet homines profanos & suis cupiditatibus deditos. Hosce describe & exempla aliquot hujusmodi atheorum propone, ut Epicuri præsertim.
units.tr: (1) Let him concede that there are many who have abolished this judgment, who have either no conscience or a cauterised one: namely profane men given over to their own desires. Let him describe these and set forth some examples of such atheists, especially Epicurus.

units.la: 2. Causam inquirat hujus ἀναισθησίας videlicet esse insaniam ac furorem potius, quam fanum judicium. vide Cic. in Pifon. ex professa malitia & desperatione profectum.
units.tr: (2) Let him inquire into the cause of this insensibility [ἀναισθησία], which is really madness and frenzy rather than sound judgment; see Cicero, In Pisonem: it arises from deliberate malice and despair.

units.la: 3. Tacitum remorsum & recursum notet, & illustret exemplis Saulis, Achitophelis, Judæ; adde ex profana historia videlicet Appium decemvirum similesque, qui tandem infestas sibi manus intulerunt. Claudatur Epiphonemate videlicet: Frustra Dei judicium expellere satagit mortalis. &c.
units.tr: (3) Let him note the silent remorse and its recurrence, and illustrate it with the examples of Saul, Ahithophel, and Judas. Add from profane history Appius the decemvir and others like him, who at last laid violent hands on themselves. Let it be closed with an epiphonema, namely: "In vain does mortal man strive to drive out the judgment of God," etc.

units.la: 4. Exponat contrà peccare quosdam in excessu, qui scrupulosam sibi formant conscientiam, aut dubiam vel errantem habent; & unde illud? videlicet quia jus Dei ignorant, aut non attendunt, &c.
units.tr: (4) On the contrary, let him set out that some sin in excess: they form for themselves a scrupulous conscience, or have one that is doubtful or erring. And whence is this? Namely, because they do not know God's law, or do not heed it, etc.

units.la: II. Quid fit: hîc
units.tr: II. What it is. Here:

units.la: 1. Definiat conscientiam judicium hominis de semetipso & factis suis fubordinatum judicio Dei.
units.tr: (1) Let him define conscience as man's judgment of himself and his deeds, subordinate to the judgment of God.

units.la: 2. Evolvat definitionem,
units.tr: (2) Let him unfold the definition:

units.la: a. A partibus & requisitis hujus judicii, uti sunt συντήρησις, συνείδησις & κρίσις. Hinc explicet officium singularum partium. Συντήρησις suggerit jus Dei scriptum vel in cordibus, vel præscriptum in Lege. vid. Rom. 1. 2. συνείδησις suggerit proprium factum legi vel consonum vel adversum; nam nemo novit quæ in corde hominis, nisi mens hominis. Κρίσις denique fert sententiam de facto juxta legem per fynterefin suggestam, nisi scilicet avertatur per nova phantasmata aut exsurdetur.
units.tr: (a) From the parts and requisites of this judgment, namely synteresis [συντήρησις], syneidesis [συνείδησις] and krisis [κρίσις]. Hence let him explain the office of each part. Synteresis suggests God's law, either written in the hearts or prescribed in the Law; see Romans 1 and 2. Syneidesis suggests one's own deed as either agreeing with or opposing the law; for no one knows what is in a man's heart except the man's own mind. Krisis, finally, pronounces sentence on the deed according to the law suggested by synteresis, unless indeed it is turned aside by new fancies or made deaf to it.

units.la: b. Ab objecto: quod est ipse homo & factum suum, jam perpetratum, aut perpetrandum. Adeoque quæstio practica.
units.tr: (b) From the object: which is the man himself and his deed, either already committed or yet to be committed. Hence it is a practical question.

units.la: c. A causa 1. negate: non ipse homo, quippe, qui sibi philautos, benignus & facilis; non metus solus magistratus; cum etiam de occultis accuset & judicet conscientia. 2. affirmaté: sed solus Deus, Dominus conscientiæ & animæ nostræ, qui hoc tribunal erexit sibi soli, & vivum sui vultum ibidem exserit; quem expellere non potest mortalis, Psal. 50. arguam te in faciem &c. Accedit & diabolus, exaggerans peccatum & legis comminationes, & justitiam Dei. Exemplum in Juda, similibusque, qui occulti & a nemine accusati semetipsos prodiderunt, interemerunt.
units.tr: (c) From the cause: (1) negatively: not the man himself, who is self-loving [philautos], lenient and easy-going; nor the fear of the magistrate alone, since conscience accuses and judges even of hidden things. (2) Affirmatively: but God alone, the Lord of our conscience and soul, who has set up this tribunal for himself alone, and there displays his living face; which a mortal cannot drive out. Psalm 50: "I will reprove you to your face," etc. The devil also joins in, magnifying sin, the threats of the law, and the justice of God. Example: Judas and those like him, who, hidden and accused by no one, betrayed themselves and killed themselves.

units.la: a fine & effecto: videlicet 1. ut refrænetur hominis malitia, 2. ut adigatur ad pœnitentiam, 3. ut lætentur in bono justi, & torqueantur in nequitia impii.
units.tr: (d) From the end and effect, namely: (1) that man's wickedness may be restrained; (2) that he may be driven to repentance; (3) that the righteous may rejoice in goodness, and the wicked be tormented in their wickedness.

units.la: III. Tractationem hanc applicet.
units.tr: III. Let him apply this treatment:

units.la: 1. ad terrorem profanorum, qui vel Deum non esse, vel non curare mortalia arbitrantur.
units.tr: (1) to the terror of the profane, who think either that God does not exist or that he does not care about mortal affairs;

units.la: securorum, qui cumulant peccata, dum silet conscientia; quæ tandem evigilabit.
units.tr: of the secure, who heap up sins while conscience is silent, but which will at last awake;

units.la: 2. ad monelam, ut hunc testem internum ne negligamus: qui veluti perpetuus Dei residens, de jure Domini & Dei nostri protestatur.
units.tr: (2) to the admonition that we should not neglect this inner witness, who, as though continually present as God's deputy, bears witness to the right of our Lord and God;

units.la: 3. ad laudem illorum ac solatium, qui sollicite & veluti in Dei conspectu ambulant.
units.tr: (3) to the praise and comfort of those who walk carefully and, as it were, in the sight of God.

units.la: Conclusio habeat brevem repetitionem & gratiarum actionem ad Auditores.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let it have a brief recapitulation and a thanksgiving to the hearers.

units.la: LVI. DE ANTIQUISSIMA POSSESSIONE PACIS ET PRÆSCRIPTIONE CONTRA ARMORUM JURA.
units.tr: LVI. Of the Most Ancient Possession of Peace, and the Prescription against the Rights of Arms.

units.la: Exord. a laude pacis & concordiæ & dicto Poëta: Pax optima rerum, quas homini novisse datum, Pax una triumphis innumeris potior. Hoc. 1. proponatur cum elogio. 2. Astruatur & illustretur paucis instar Chriæ. 3. Concludatur approbatione dicti, videl. Loco Communi. &c.
units.tr: Exordium: from the praise of peace and concord, and from the saying of the poet: "Peace, the best of all things that man has been allowed to know, one peace worth more than countless triumphs" (Horace, Odes 1). First, the saying is to be put forward with its commendation. Second, it is to be confirmed and illustrated briefly, in the manner of a chreia. Third, the argument is to be concluded by approving the saying, namely by a commonplace, etc.

units.la: Propos. In præsentiarum de antiqua possessione pacis &c. dicendum. Sperare te haud ingratum fore Auditorib. argumentum, quod omnes etiam inter arma amare debent & meditari: cum ut recte solidissimus Grotius lib.3. c.25. ait. In tota belli administratione non potest securus & Deo fidens animus retineri, nisi semper in pacem prospectet.
units.tr: Proposition: At present it is to be said concerning the ancient possession of peace, etc. You may hope that the subject will not be unwelcome to the hearers, since everyone, even among arms, ought to love and meditate upon it; as the very solid Grotius says correctly in book 3, chapter 25: "Throughout the whole conduct of war, a mind that is secure and trusting in God cannot be maintained unless it always looks toward peace."

units.la: Tractatio: I. Merito antiquissimam dici pacis possessionem, quoniam ante omne bellum fuit: Hoc ostendatur 1. ex pace & concordia, in qua creata & constituta omnia à Deo pacis, trinuno fonte omnis concordiæ. Hic exponat harmonicam mundi totius, superioris, inferioris constructionem; ubi in tanta rerum motuumque varietate nihil discordet dissideatve. Hoc evincat enumeratione quadam partium præcipuarum. 2. Ex statu prioris mundi. Talem etiam harmoniam ante lapsum Adami fuisse inter animalia & inter homines, post lapsum etiam primitus bella fuisse non legimus, sed veluti in aureo Saturni seculo vixisse primos mortales. Viros illustres ac robustos ac gigantes fuisse dicit Moses; sed autoritate potius, quam vi ac armis pollentes aut usos. Ita pacem tenuisse omnia sub suo imperio: beatissimè, nisi ex profunda pace aliud malum enatum fuisset, promiscua scilicet libido & luxuries, primi orbis fatale malum. Ita scilicet quos sævitia & arma vastare non poterant, luxuria corrupit, pestis dirissima regnorum ac rerumpubl. 3. ex antiquissimo statu gentium post diluvium: ubi suam sibi quisque pro ratione familiæ portionem occupavit sine lite, sine armis, arcuitque tanquam primus possessor alios; suis quisque contentus: vide Justinum initio; Juris hoc naturalis antiquissimi esse doceat, in ipsis animantibus conspicui; quæ suo antro, suo victu contenta degunt, sinunt secum eadem sylva degere alia, omnino probè in suo genere. Vid. Cic. 1. offic. Non vero sœviunt in suum genus.
units.tr: Treatment. I. It is rightly called the most ancient possession of peace, since it existed before any war. This is shown: (1) from peace and concord, in which all things were created and established by God of peace, the threefold-one fountain of all concord. Here one should set out the harmonious construction of the whole world, higher and lower, where in so great a variety of things and motions nothing disagrees or dissents. This should be proved by a certain enumeration of the principal parts. (2) From the state of the earlier world. We do not read that such harmony existed also among the animals and among men before the fall of Adam, and that after the fall wars were not at first; rather the first mortals lived as in the golden age of Saturn. Moses says that they were illustrious and robust men, even giants, yet they were powerful and used authority rather than force and arms. Thus all things under their rule kept peace, most blessedly, unless some other evil had arisen out of deep peace, namely promiscuous lust and luxury, the fatal evil of the first world. Thus those whom cruelty and arms could not lay waste, luxury corrupted, the most deadly plague of kingdoms and commonwealths. (3) From the most ancient state of the nations after the flood, where each one, according to the reckoning of his family, occupied his own portion without dispute and without arms, and as first possessor kept others away; each being content with his own. See Justin at the beginning. Let him teach that this is of the most ancient natural right, seen plainly in the animals themselves, which live content with their own cave and their own food, and allow others to live in the same forest, each perfectly well in its own kind. See Cicero, De Officiis, book 1. Indeed they do not rage against their own kind.

units.la: II. Serius invecta arma & bella doceat, & quidem 1. per Nimrodum vid. Gen. 10. 2. Hinc postea commotum Ninum reliquosque mortales, ut vi ac armis rem gererent, magis de augenda, quam bene regenda provincia solliciti. Sic fas omne abruptum armis fuisse, cum quisque sibi raperet. Quanta bella hinc. Enumeret hic præcipua aliquot ab initio. Vide Justin. & Orosium. &c.
units.tr: II. Let him teach that arms and wars were introduced later, and indeed (1) through Nimrod, see Genesis 10. (2) Hence afterwards Ninus and the rest of mortals were stirred up to conduct affairs by force and arms, more anxious to enlarge a province than to govern it well. Thus all right was broken off by arms, since each seized for himself. How great were the wars from this source! Here he should list some of the chief ones from the beginning. See Justin and Orosius, etc.

units.la: III. Juris primævi hoc esse & perpetui probet porrò 1. a natura hominis: utpote quem non cornibus, rictu, unguibus instruxit natura, ut reliqua animalia, quæ ad vim armavit natura ipsa v. g. leonem unguibus, aprum dentibus, taurum cornibus &c. Sed placidum conversabilemque condidit Deus, & ratione instruxit & sermone ad obeundos cœtus, ad inquirenda, tradenda jura; quibus pax conservetur & concordia, arma & vis sopiapiatur. Vid. Cic. in offic. &c. 2. à praxi perpetua populorum civiliorum, (de barbaris non dicendum quibus jus in armis; semper bella ex bellis serentes) quippe etiam bello collisi semper de pace cogitandum existimarunt; & etiam post damna perpessa rursus in pacem coivere. Vide exempla aliquot ex historia veteri illustriorum pacificationum, ex Græca antiqua. vide Justin.l.7.&c. Itemque ex historia recentiori, præsertim bello Protestantiū, unde enata pax religionis; & bello Germanico nupero; unde exstitit pax Europæ. Digrediatur hic in deploratiónem ruptura nimis properæ ex ambitione & cupiditate imperandi. Unde dirum rursus metuendum incendium: dum sua repetunt læsi & subditos tuentur. &c. Sed & hic spem concipiat ex jure pacis, quæ ablata suis dominis restituet, & præscribet limites regnis, provinciisque, ut concordia & pax redeat oppressis. 3. à præsentibus tractatibus optima intentione ab imperatore, regibus, magnatibusque institutis, ut exundans populorum æstus, veluti intra alveum & nota littora redigatur ut prisca sua majestate pax aurea postlimio rursus gaudere queat. &c. 4. à violento & ambiguo belli jure. Quod quidem ob hominum malitiam & sua jura habet, adeo ut & a Christi mansueta disciplina imbutis geri legitime possit &c. attamen 1. violentum est, quale leonis in sylva. 2. magnoq; proinde labore, sumptu exercendum. 3. anceps & periculosum est, non semper justiori savens. 4. à suavitate ac fructu pacis. Amplificetur ex Loco Communi de pace.
units.tr: III. Let him further prove that this is of the first and perpetual right: (1) from the nature of man, who was not furnished by nature with horns, jaws, or claws as the other animals are, for which nature itself armed them for force: for example the lion with claws, the boar with tusks, the bull with horns, etc. But God made man gentle and sociable, and endowed him with reason and speech to attend assemblies and to inquire into and hand down laws, by which peace and concord might be preserved, and arms and violence put to rest. See Cicero, De Officiis, etc. (2) From the perpetual practice of civilized peoples (nothing is to be said of barbarians, for whom right lies in arms, always sowing wars from wars). Indeed, even when struck by war, civilized peoples have always thought of peace, and even after suffering losses they have again come together into peace. See some examples from ancient history of more famous pacifications from Greek antiquity; see Justin book 7, etc. Likewise from more recent history, especially the war of the Protestants, whence the peace of religion arose; and the recent German war, whence the peace of Europe came forth. Here let him digress into a lament over the breaking of the peace too hastily, through ambition and the desire to rule, whence a dreadful fire is to be feared again, while the injured seek back their own and defend their subjects, etc. But here too let him conceive hope from the right of peace, which will restore what was taken from its lords, and will prescribe limits to kingdoms and provinces, so that concord and peace may return to the oppressed. (3) From the present treaties, instituted with the best intention by the emperor, kings, and magnates, so that the overflowing tide of peoples may be led back, as within a channel and known shores, so that peace may rejoice again after the return of the golden age in its former majesty, etc. (4) From the violent and ambiguous law of war. Indeed, on account of human malice, it has its own rights, so that it may lawfully be waged even by those imbued with the gentle discipline of Christ, etc. Yet (1) it is violent, like that of the lion in the forest; (2) it must therefore be carried on with great labour and expense; (3) it is uncertain and dangerous, not always favouring the more just; (4) it is contrary to the sweetness and fruit of peace. Let this be amplified from the commonplace on peace.

units.la: Conclus. Votum habeat, ut brevi veniant illa tempora, quæ repressam vim Martis, restitutam auream pacem, ejusque pristina contra Martem jura, serant. Quod quia non hominis, sed Dei opus est, orandum Deum pacis authorem, ut ipse corda uniat, pacemque optatam postliminio reducat.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him express the wish that those times may soon come which will bind the repressed force of Mars, restore the golden peace, and its former rights against Mars. Since this is the work not of man but of God, let God, the author of peace, be prayed to, that He Himself may unite hearts and bring back the desired peace by postliminy.

units.la: LVII. DE CELSÆ FORTUNÆ PERICULIS.
units.tr: LVII. Of the Dangers of a Lofty Fortune.

units.la: Exord. a dicto Thyestis apud Senecam act.3. Verissimum dictum esse, cum inquit: Humi jacentem scelera non intrant casam, tutusq; capitur mensa angusta cibus, venenum in auro bibitur. 1. Sensus aperiatur paraphrasi illustriori. 2.
