Addatur ratio: a. quia humilem ac mediocrem sortem ordinarié comitatur modestia, quæ optima custos securitatis &c. b. quia fors mediocris caret hostibus ac insidiis. c. quia fortem modicam sequitur favor ac studia bonorum, in quibus maximum tutissimumque praesidium: quale non est in praesidio armato; quod saepe arma contra dominum vertit. 3. Illustretur a contraria celsa fortuna, quae uti splendida, ita & pluribus exposita periculis est. 4. Accommodetur ad propositum; Quod cum ab omni aevo usque in praesens experientia docuit doceatque quotidie, haud ineptum videri paucis de hoc argumento dispicere, ut quisque sua forte contentus & circumspectus degat, & divinam majestatem, quae sola celsa, sola secura, humili submissione reveratur.
units.tr: Exordium: from the words of Thyestes in Seneca, act 3: "Most true is that saying: 'Those who lie low are not visited by crimes; the humble table takes its food safely; poison is drunk from gold.'" (1) The sense is to be laid open in a fuller paraphrase. (2) Add the reason: (a) because modesty, the best guardian of security, ordinarily accompanies a humble and moderate lot; (b) because a moderate lot lacks enemies and snares; (c) because a modest fortune is followed by the goodwill and zeal of good men, which is the greatest and safest protection, a thing not found in an armed guard, which often turns its arms against its master. (3) Illustrate by the contrary, a lofty fortune, which is as dazzling as it is exposed to many dangers. (4) Apply it to the purpose: since experience has taught from every age down to the present, and teaches daily, it seems not unfitting to examine this subject briefly, so that each may live content with his own lot and watchful, and reverence with humble submission the divine majesty, which alone is lofty and alone secure.

units.la: Propos. dicendum itaque hac vice de celsae fortunae periculis, argumento amplo ac illustri, tenui facundia; cui nihil fiduciae nisi in materiae dignitate & benevolentia Auditorum. &c.
units.tr: Proposition: therefore I shall speak on this occasion of the dangers of a lofty fortune, a broad and illustrious theme, with a slender eloquence, in which my only confidence lies in the dignity of the subject and the goodwill of my hearers, etc.

units.la: Tractatio I. In genere consideret fortem Magnatum per comparationem gloriae & casuum quibus subjecti. Hinc
units.tr: Treatment I. In general, consider the lofty fortune of the great by comparing their glory with the chances to which they are subject. Hence:

units.la: 1. Extollat eximiam celsitudinem & gloriam mundi, qua velut Dii eminent summa illa orbis capita, gloria & honore prae caeteris decorata. Huc facere supremas illas dignitates Imperatorum, Regum, Principum & Magnatum (vide Castaneum de gloria mundi) non re minus salubres, quam tituli splendore decoras, ita ut merito Deorum vocabulo illos exornet ipse Deus: Rationem addat ab officio & veneratione Magistratus supremi inter omnes gentes ac Christianos, ubi majestas supereminet, & semper invicta ac sacro sancta habita.
units.tr: 1. Extol the outstanding eminence and glory of the world, by which those highest heads of the earth stand out like gods, adorned with glory and honour above others. To this belong the supreme dignities of emperors, kings, princes and magnates (see Castanaeus on the glory of the world), no less wholesome than they are adorned with the splendour of titles, so that God himself rightly graces them with the name of gods. Add the reason drawn from the office of, and reverence for, the supreme magistrate among all nations and Christians, where majesty stands pre-eminent and is always regarded as unconquered and sacrosanct.

units.la: 2. Opponat pericula in genere, quae omnibus altis imminent, ut arboribus, turribus, montibus celsioribus, quae plurimum ventis, turbinibus, fulminibus obnoxia. Vide Horat. Saepius ventis &c. Illustretur a causa: 1. quia Deus non vult illos oblivisci humanae fortis. Probetur exemplo Nebucadnezaris & Belzazaris apud Danielem &c. 2. Quia vult Deus ut agnoscant ab ipso se habere celsitudinem suam &c. 3. Quia officium Magnatum provocat invidiam & hostes: ut cum a. custodire & protegere tenentur subditos contra hostium violentiam. Hinc concitari aemulos, vicinos b. cum firmare limites, repellere hostes teneatur; indeque indicere tributa, collectas, vectigalia aliaque onera. Hinc odia concipere cives, movere turbas ac seditioditiones. vide exempla. c. cum administranda justitia, plesten- di sontes: qui proinde eversum vellent Magistratum, d. Quia Magistratus adversus est machinationibus diaboli, qui hostis perpetuus boni ordinis & rerump. tanquam spiritus confusio- nis ac vertiginis, & infestus illis, qui ordinem ac tranquillita- tem publicam tuentur &c. Illustretur hoc digressiuncula de Christo ipso Rege regum omnium: quem inde à teneris Draco ille rufus. Apoc. 12. persecutus est usque ad extremum vitæ halitum. Eandem & sortem esse aliorum Ecclesiæ vindicum & Reip. protectorum. &c.
units.tr: 2. Set forth the dangers that in general hang over all high things, as over trees, towers and higher mountains, which are very much exposed to winds, whirlwinds and lightning. See Horace: "More often by the winds," etc. Illustrate by the cause: (1) because God does not want them to forget human frailty; prove it by the example of Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar in Daniel, etc. (2) Because God wills that they acknowledge that they have their loftiness from him, etc. (3) Because the office of the great provokes envy and enemies: (a) since they are bound to guard and protect their subjects against the violence of enemies, whence rivals and neighbours are stirred up; (b) since they must fortify the borders and repel enemies, and therefore impose tributes, levies, taxes and other burdens, whence citizens conceive hatred and stir up tumults and seditions; see examples; (c) since in administering justice they must punish the guilty, who would therefore wish the magistrate overthrown; (d) because the magistrate is opposed to the machinations of the devil, the perpetual enemy of good order and of the commonwealth, a spirit of confusion and vertigo, hostile to those who maintain public order and tranquillity, etc. Illustrate this by a short digression on Christ himself, King of kings, whom that red dragon has persecuted from his tender years to his last breath (Rev. 12). The same is the lot of other defenders of the Church and protectors of the commonwealth, etc.

units.la: II. Specialius pericula & casus tragicos magnatum exponat per exempla præsertim. Sternatur accessus per transitionem, moneatque non omnia sigillatim persequenda, sed quædam illustria afferenda esse; ut constet quàm grave pondus sit gloria, & quam lubricus summis locus. Hinc jam colligat exempla illustriora.
units.tr: II. Set out more particularly the dangers and tragic falls of the great, chiefly by examples. Prepare the approach by a transition, and advise that not everything is to be pursued point by point, but that some outstanding instances are to be brought forward, so that it may be clear how heavy a burden glory is and how slippery the heights are. Then from these let him gather the more illustrious examples.

units.la: 1. Ex veteri historia in singulis Monarchiis regnisque.
units.tr: 1. From ancient history, in each of the monarchies and kingdoms.

units.la: 2. Ex historia recentiori, & moderna: vide historiam universalem Justini, Cluverii, Matthiæ, & Orbé Politicû Hornii &c. indeque maximè illustria exempla quædam colligat, tractetq; stylo nervoso & Oratorio, ad hunc scopum, ut appareat omnibus seculis verum esse: excelsam fortunam Magnatum maximis semper periculis fuisse subjectam; inseratque subinde noëmata ac sententias ex auctoribus, rem hanc confirmantia.
units.tr: 2. From more recent and modern history: see the universal history of Justin, Cluverius, Matthias, and Hornius's Politicus Orbis, etc.; and from these let him gather certain most illustrious examples, and treat them in a vigorous and oratorical style, to this end, that it may appear in every age that it is true that the lofty fortune of the great has always been subject to the greatest dangers; and let him insert from time to time maxims and sentences from authors confirming this matter.

units.la: III. Atrocitatem criminis majestatis seu machinationum adversus Principes exaggeret.
units.tr: III. Let him magnify the atrocity of the crime of treason, or of plots against princes.

units.la: 1. Quia sacra est persona imperantium apud omnes gentes quippe qui Deum repræsentant in terris veluti Dii visibiles: quorum proinde personæ inviolabiles &c.
units.tr: 1. Because the person of rulers is sacred among all nations, since they represent God on earth as visible gods; their persons are therefore inviolable, etc.

units.la: 2. Quia hinc legibus Majestatis munita persona Principis. Et gravissima pœna in authore ipsiusque tota posteritate plectitur: cum in aliis delictis pœna tantum urgeat authores &c.
units.tr: 2. Because hence the person of the prince is protected by laws of majesty, and the most grievous penalty is inflicted on the author and his whole posterity, whereas in other crimes the penalty falls only on the authors, etc.

units.la: 3. Quia si evadant judicia humana, tamen rarissime divinâ vindictam evadunt. vide exempla in sacra & profana historia, & apud Val. Max. ac Plutarchum de sera Num. vind.
units.tr: 3. Because if they escape human judgments, yet very rarely do they escape divine vengeance; see examples in sacred and profane history, and in Valerius Maximus and Plutarch, On the Delay of Divine Vengeance.

units.la: Conclus. Quæ cum ita sint, 1. merito vota esse concipienda pro incolumitate Principum, juxta monitum Apostoli, ut & ipsi tuti sint, & subditi tranquillam vitam sub ipsis degere queant. 2. Haud invidendam esse fortem magnatibus, nec affectandam coronam tot spinis periculisque implexam, &c.
units.tr: Conclusion. These things being so: (1) prayers ought rightly to be offered for the safety of princes, according to the admonition of the Apostle, that they themselves may be safe and their subjects may be able to lead a quiet life under them; (2) the lot of the great is not to be envied, nor is the crown, entangled with so many thorns and dangers, to be coveted, etc.

units.la: LVIII.
units.tr: LVIII.

units.la: UTRUM FOEMINÆ ADMITTENDÆ AD IMPERIUM.
units.tr: WHETHER WOMEN ARE TO BE ADMITTED TO RULE.

units.la: I. Negatè.
units.tr: I. In the negative.

units.la: Exord. ab encomio ordinis ac harmoniæ in omnibus mundi partibus.
units.tr: Exordium: in praise of order and harmony in all parts of the world.

units.la: I. Proponantur. videl. Mundum constare ordine ac harmonia.
units.tr: I. Let it be proposed, namely, that the world consists of order and harmony.

units.la: II. Probetur inductione quadam in corporibus superis, inferis, in homine item & rebuspubl. Tamdiu omnia incolumia esse, quamdiu superiora inferioribus, præstantiora vilioribus, potentiora infirmioribus veluti imperant.
units.tr: II. Let it be proved by a certain induction from the heavenly bodies, from the lower bodies, likewise from man and from commonwealths: that all things remain sound so long as the higher rule the lower, the more excellent command the baser, and the more powerful the weaker.

units.la: III. Illustretur a contraria ordinis ac harmoniæ hujus perturbatione ejusque incommodis.
units.tr: III. Let it be illustrated from the contrary disturbance of this order and harmony, and from its inconveniences.

units.la: IV. Accessus fiat ad hypothesin: videl, inter hasce perturbationes etiam referendum, cum illi qui nati ad obediendum, imperium accipiunt.
units.tr: IV. Let us approach the hypothesis: namely, that among these disturbances must also be counted the case where those who were born to obey receive rule.

units.la: Propos. Non immerito itaque quæri a politicis, utrum fœminæ admittendæ ad imperium: quæ quæstio valde controversa breviter tractanda: & tibi quidem arcendas fœminas esse a regimine melioribus subnixum videri rationibus, &c.
units.tr: Proposition: It is not undeservedly, therefore, that politicians ask whether women are to be admitted to rule. This question is very controversial and is to be treated briefly; and indeed it seems to you that women are to be kept from government, on grounds that rest on sounder reasons, etc.

units.la: Confirmatio, I. Præmittat præparationem seu excusationem.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. Let him premise a preparation or excuse.

units.la: 1. Ad sexum fœmineum, quod illi suum honorem minimè detractum velit; utpote quem norit suis præditum dotibus corporis & animi, & sæpe supra viros nonnullis excellentibus. Hîc prædicentur prærogativæ ac dotes sexus fœminei. vid. Contzen. Polit. lib. 1 c. 26. §. 1. 3.
units.tr: 1. To the female sex: let him not wish their honour to be detracted from in any way, since he knows they are endowed with gifts of body and mind, and some of them often excel men. Here let the prerogatives and gifts of the female sex be proclaimed. See Contzen, Politics, book 1, ch. 26, §§ 1–3.

units.la: 2. Ad illa regna, ubi gynæcocratia usu obtinet, quod nolit in dubium vocare jus fœminis ibi acquisitum, aut cupiat mutatas pristinas regnorum leges: utpote qui norit nihil periculosum esse quam mutationes in regnis ac Rebuspubl. adeò ut non immerito laqueo innodari collum voluerint Locrenses illius, quia novam legem propositurus esset, strangulandum si lex displiceat, &c. Sed de jure hic tandem disquirendum, quod fœminis minus videtur contrarium, etiam juxta Leges Justineaneas, quæ alias propensæ videntur in hunc sexum.
units.tr: 2. To those kingdoms where gynaecocracy prevails by custom: let him not wish to call into doubt the right women have acquired there, nor desire the ancient laws of those kingdoms to be changed; for he knows that nothing is more dangerous in kingdoms and commonwealths than change. Thus the Locrians rightly wished that the neck of a man who proposed a new law should be bound with a noose, to be strangled if the law displeased them, etc. But the right must be examined here at last, which seems less contrary to women, even according to the laws of Justinian, which otherwise seem inclined towards this sex.

units.la: II. Confirmet sententiam hanc contra fœminas ab inhonesto quod probetur.
units.tr: II. Let him confirm this opinion against women from what is shown to be dishonourable.

units.la: 1. Ab autoritate Legis divinæ, quæ fœminam sociam, non dominam fecit viro; & subesse, non præesse voluerit; quæque duces, judices, reges præesse populo suo, non fœminas voluerit. Non igitur a Deo, sed a perversa consuetudine invectum esse muliebre imperium. Et adeò quidem, ut & inter pœnas Deus connumeret, cum pueri ac fœminæ imperant, Esa. 3. vide Bodin. lib. 6. de rep. c. 5.
units.tr: 1. From the authority of the divine law, which made woman a companion to man, not his lord; which willed her to be subject, not to preside; and which willed leaders, judges and kings to preside over their people, not women. Therefore the rule of women was introduced not by God but by a perverse custom. And indeed God counts it among the punishments when boys and women rule: Isa. 3. See Bodin, On the Republic, book 6, ch. 5.

units.la: 2. A natura ipsa; quæ 1. marem in omnibus animantibus fœminæ præstulit. Virum aptiorem generavit ad imperandum, instructum animi & corporis dotibus præ fœmina. Pudorem ac verecundiam fœminis commendavit, & domus curam, non dominii. vid. Bodin. lib. 6. c. 5. Arnisæum de rep. c. 2. sect. 12 n. 71. seqq.
units.tr: 2. From nature itself, which first preferred the male to the female in all living creatures. It produced man more apt for ruling, furnished with gifts of mind and body beyond woman. It commended modesty and shamefastness to women, and the care of the household, not of dominion. See Bodin, book 6, ch. 5; Arnisaeus, On the Republic, ch. 2, sect. 12, nn. 71ff.

units.la: 3. Ex jure civili Romano, quo jam plerique Europæ populi utuntur, fœmina ab omnibus officiis publicis exclusa est: ostendatur inductione ex jure: imò ipsa sub perpetua viri curatela est. Quanto minus itaque aptæ imperio? vid. Contzen. Polit. lib. 1. c. 26. §. 2. Arnisæum de rep. c. 2. sect. 12. n. 69. seqq.
units.tr: 3. From the Roman civil law, which most peoples of Europe now use, woman is excluded from all public offices; let this be shown by induction from the law. Indeed she herself is under the perpetual guardianship of a man. How much less, then, is she fit for rule? See Contzen, Politics, book 1, ch. 26, § 2; Arnisaeus, On the Republic, ch. 2, sect. 12, nn. 69ff.

units.la: 4. Ab exemplis cordatiorum populorum, antiquorum modernorum. Fiat inductio. Judæorum, Assyriorum, Ægyptiorum, Persarum, Græcorum, Romanorum: Gallorum, Italorum, Polonorum, Turcarum, Germanorum, vid. Bod. dict. lib. 6. c. 5.
units.tr: 4. From the examples of the more judicious peoples, both ancient and modern. Let an induction be made: of the Jews, Assyrians, Egyptians, Persians, Greeks, Romans; Gauls, Italians, Poles, Turks, Germans. See Bodin, loc. cit., book 6, ch. 5.

units.la: III. Ab inutili seu damnoso.
units.tr: III. From what is useless or harmful.

units.la: 1. Quia fœmina non est capax onerum imperii. Hic jam 1. exponat molem imperii in toga ac pace; & porro quæ requirantur ad imperium, videl. prudentia eximia, constantia, fortitudo bellica & togata: vide politicos & Lipsi in polit. 2. Ostendat hæc non ita reperiri in fœminis, sed potius infirmitates imperio contrarias: videl. non dicam de cognata mulieribus mutabilitate, loquacitate, studio placendi viris; sed de debilitate mentis & corporis, è contra fastu ac superbia, quam ostende vitium fœmineū esse, vid. Buchan. l. 12. rer. Scot. Arnisæum c. 2. sect. 12. n. 82. seq. Illustretur prolepsi, 1. & in viris ris reperiri. ꝯ. Hosce etiam non magis quam fœminas aptos esse imperio. Inveniri heroinas. ꝯ. Rariores & utplurimum paribus vitiis pollutas. vide exempla Semiramidis, Jesabelis, Liviæ &c.
units.tr: 1. Because woman is not capable of the burdens of rule. Here let him first set out the weight of rule in peace and in war; and then what is required for rule, namely outstanding prudence, constancy, and military and civil fortitude. See the politicians and Lipsius, Politics. 2. Let him show that these qualities are not found in women, but rather weaknesses contrary to rule: I will not speak of the mutability innate to women, their talkativeness, or their desire to please men, but of the weakness of mind and body and, on the other hand, of pride and arrogance, which shows itself to be a feminine vice. See Buchanan, book 12 of the Rerum Scoticarum; Arnisaeus, ch. 2, sect. 12, nn. 82f. Let it be illustrated by anticipation: (1) that these qualities are found in men; (2) that men too are no more fit for rule than women; (3) that heroines are found, but they are rarer and mostly tainted by equal vices. See the examples of Semiramis, Jezebel, Livia, etc.

units.la: 2. Quia fœmineum imperium plurima semper mala invexit: factiones, luxum, libidinem, regnorum ac provinciarum alienationem, majestatis contemtum, regni exitium, confusionem œconomiarum, quæ regni ad exemplum componuntur. vide exempla. vide Jun. in quæst. polit. lib.1. quæst.13. p. 29. & Arnisæum de rep. c.2. sect.4. n.137. seq. & sect.12. n.131.147.150.171.
units.tr: 2. Because female rule has always brought very many evils: factions, luxury, lust, the alienation of kingdoms and provinces, contempt of majesty, the ruin of the realm, and the confusion of the household economies, which are ordered on the model of the kingdom. See examples. See Junius, Quaestiones politicae, book 1, question 13, p. 29; Arnisaeus, On the Republic, ch. 2, sect. 4, n. 137f., and sect. 12, nn. 131, 147, 150, 171.

units.la: Conclus. Ex repetitis summatim argumentis, propositionem repetat, laudetque illas gentes, quæ naturam ac publicam honestatem, & virilem dignitatem masculè tuentur: uti imprimis Germanos, quæ nec puerum, nedum fœminam, sed virum volunt, priscum gentis Martiæ decus tuentes.
units.tr: Conclusion. From the arguments repeated in summary, let him repeat the proposition, and praise those nations which manfully maintain nature, public honour and male dignity: above all the Germans, who want a man to rule, not a boy, much less a woman, preserving the ancient glory of the Martial race.

units.la: LIX. FOEMINAS ESSE AD MITTENDAS AD IMPERIUM.
units.tr: LIX. That women are to be admitted to government.

units.la: II. Affirmatè.
units.tr: II. Affirmatively.

units.la: Exord. Non mirum esse, in illum sexum multa dici, qui à nullo defenditur, rectè dictum esse à magno Politico: Vitium seculi esse, ut quisque suam causam agat, seposita publica. Illustretur exemplo fortitudinis togatæ & militaris. Eruditos suum, milites suum defendere ordinem; at pro diversitate temporum alterum altero utiliorem, utrumque Reip. necessarium esse. Idem de præferentia sexus judicium esse. Neutro carere posse Remp. Unde & ipsa veritate victus suas laudes sexui sequiori concedere coactus fuerit antecessor; in eo reprehendendus, quod fœminas ab imperio arcere penitus voluerit. II. Limitet ac restringat sententiam: videl. licet ob adductas ab antecessore rationes præcipuè quidem maribus deferendum imperium, idque semper in aristocratia & democratia & electitiis regnis, non tamen in illis regnis, ubi jus quæsitum habent fœminæ, illas a solio regali arcendas esse.
units.tr: Exordium. It is no wonder that many things are said about that sex which nobody defends. The great political writer rightly said that it is the vice of the age that each man pursues his own cause, neglecting the public good. Let this be illustrated by the example of civil and military courage: scholars defend their own order, soldiers theirs; and, according to the diversity of the times, one is more useful than the other, but both are necessary to the commonwealth. The same judgment holds concerning the preference of sex: the commonwealth cannot do without either. Hence the opponent, too, overcome by truth itself, was compelled to grant praise to the weaker sex; he is to be blamed in this, that he wished women to be utterly shut out from government. II. Let him limit and restrict his view: namely, that although, for the reasons adduced by the opponent, government is to be committed chiefly to men, and this always in aristocracies, democracies and elective kingdoms, yet in those kingdoms where women have an acquired right, they are not to be kept away from the royal throne.

units.la: Propos. Hanc sententiam contra dissentientes plurimos & maximè contra Joh.Bodinum, qui ex sua Gallia reliqua metiri consuevit regna, paucis asserendum esse: petat, ut eadem, qua antecessorem patientia audiant.
units.tr: Proposition. This view, against the many who dissent, and especially against Jean Bodin, who is accustomed to measure the remaining kingdoms by his own France, is to be asserted in a few words: let them ask that they hear it with the same patience with which they heard the opponent.

units.la: Confutatio. I. Acceptet hoc, quod antecessor & dotes egregias imò virtutes heroicas, & consuetudinem successionis fœminarum conconcedere coactus fuerit Ita scil. veritatem sua radiare luce. Adda-tque commendationem foeminarum quarundam heroicarum: de quibus saepe dicendum : Vos etenim juvenes animum geritis muliebrem, illa viragov iri.
units.tr: Refutation. I. Let him accept this: that the opponent was compelled to concede both outstanding gifts and even heroic virtues, and the custom of female succession; thus truth shines by its own light. Let him add the commendation of certain heroic women, about whom much must be said: "For you, young men, have a womanish spirit; those women will become virago-like."

units.la: II. Refutet hinc
units.tr: II. Let him refute from this:

units.la: 1. Quae dixit, de imbecillitatibus sexus foeminei : videl. illas non semper comitari omnes, illas praesertim quae ad spem regni educantur. Item aequales aut etiam majores saepe esse in moribus. vide exempla Sardanapali, Heliogabali, &c.
units.tr: 1. What he said about the weaknesses of the female sex: namely, that not all of them are such, especially those who are brought up with hope of the kingdom. Likewise they are often equal, or even superior, in morals. See the examples of Sardanapalus, Heliogabalus, etc.

units.la: 2. Quae dixit de incommodis & periculis ex gynaecocratia: videl. non minora ex imperio virorum metuenda, ut certamina, vagae libidines, luxum, bella continua, &c. Haec mala esse contingentia.
units.tr: 2. What he said about the inconveniences and dangers of female rule: namely, that the dangers of male rule are no less to be feared, such as quarrels, roaming lusts, luxury, continual wars, etc. These evils are accidental.

units.la: 2. Contra laudabiliter saepe a foeminis imperatum. Vide exempla.
units.tr: 2. On the contrary, women have often ruled commendably. See the examples.

units.la: 3. Quae ex jure divino adduxit antecessor, 1. distinguendo inter subjectionem oeconomicam & Politicam. Ita filium saepe dominum & magistratum fieri patris. 2. Esa. 8. de moribus, non de sexu sermonem esse. Molles ac luxuriosos, insipientes ac pueros etiam inter viros esse.
units.tr: 3. What the opponent drew from divine law: first, by distinguishing between economic and political subjection; thus a son often becomes the master and magistrate of his father. Second, Isaiah 8 speaks of morals, not of sex. Effeminate and luxurious, foolish and childish men are also found among men.

units.la: 4. Quae de jure civili protulit, dicat in favorem sexus statuta esse ab Imperatore illo, quia pronior erat in suam Theodoram, cujus consilio saepe usus in corrigendis legibus. Atque hinc foeminas maribus in successionibus exaequatas esse.
units.tr: 4. What he advanced from civil law, let him say that those statutes were established in favour of the sex by that Emperor, who was rather inclined toward his own Theodora, whose counsel he often used in correcting the laws; and hence women were made equal to men in successions.

units.la: 5. Exemplis contraria exempla opponat. Hinc transeat ad Confirmationem.
units.tr: 5. Let him oppose contrary examples to examples. From here let him pass to the Confirmation.

units.la: Confirmationem.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. Satis ex dictis constare dicat, quantum tribuendum rationibus antecessoris, qui cum nihil probarit, foeminas debito honore non esse privandas:
units.tr: I. Let him say that it is sufficiently clear from what has been said how much weight is to be given to the opponent's arguments, which, since he proved nothing, show that women are not to be deprived of due honour;

units.la: II. Maxime quia habent jus quaesitum in plurimis regnis vide Arnisaeum de rep. lib. 2. c. 2. sect. 12. num. 2. seqq. Melch. Jun. in quaest. polit. lib. 1. quaest. 13. ipsum adversarium sensisse, ideoque praecavere voluisse.
units.tr: II. Especially because women have an acquired right in very many kingdoms: see Arnisaeus, On Government, book 2, chapter 2, section 12, number 2 onward; Melchior Junius, Political Questions, book 1, question 13; and that the adversary himself held this view and therefore wished to guard against it.

units.la: III. Quia aequalibus dotibus ad regimen requisitis instructae sunt foeminae nonnullae. Hic 1. per prolepsin respondeat Aristoteli 1. Polit. quod foeminae imbecilliores, videl. verum esse juxta cursum ordinarium: at saepissime fallere in illustrioribus. Hinc 2. exponere praecipuas aliquot heroinas. vide autores laudatos &
units.tr: III. Because some women have been endowed with qualities equal to those required for rule. Here, 1. by prolepsis, let him answer Aristotle, Politics book 1, who says that women are weaker: this is true according to the ordinary course, but it very often fails in the more illustrious cases. Hence, 2. let him set forth several outstanding heroines. See the authors cited and

units.la: P Plut. de claris mulieribus. 3. Et reges saepe in regnis maximè successivis ineptissimos esse ad imperandum. 4. Per consiliarios ac regni Senatum suppleri posse defectum, si quis sit.
units.tr: Plutarch, On Famous Women. 3. And kings in the most hereditary kingdoms are very often most unfit to rule. 4. The defect, if there is one, can be supplied through counsellors and the senate of the kingdom.

units.la: IV. Quia laudabiliter saepissime imperarunt foeminae & regnum bearunt. Probetur inductione: vide Jun. quaest.13. ab initio & Arnisaeum, & Contzen Polit. lib. 1. cap. ult. §. penult. & ult.
units.tr: IV. Because women have very often ruled commendably and made the kingdom prosper. Let this be proved by induction: see Junius, question 13 from the beginning, and Arnisaeus, and Contzen, Politics book 1, last chapter, penultimate and last sections.

units.la: V. Quia a maritis, summis imperatoribus salubriter saepe adhibitae ad consilium regni, tutelis regum proficiuntur in ipso regno Galliae, quod urgendum contra Bodinum. Probentur haec rursus inductione exemplorum illustriorum. vide Jun. & Arnisaeum. loc. alleg.
units.tr: V. Because women, often employed profitably in counsel by their husbands, who were supreme commanders, have served as guardians of kings in the kingdom of France itself, which must be pressed against Bodin. Let these things be proved again by induction from more illustrious examples. See Junius and Arnisaeus, the places cited.

units.la: Conclusio. Licet igitur quaedam virorum praerogativae sint, tamen illas non esse tantas, ut ubi usu hoc receptum est, foeminae ab imperio sint excludendae; Majora saepe ex tentata mutatione, quam sperata emendatione esse incommoda. Boni civis esse, laudare statum optimum, sed contentum esse praesenti.
units.tr: Conclusion. Although, therefore, certain prerogatives belong to men, yet they are not so great that, where custom has received female rule, women are to be excluded from government; greater evils often arise from an attempted change than the improvement hoped for. It is the mark of a good citizen to praise the best state, but to be content with the present one.

units.la: LX. DE CAROLO MAGNO.
units.tr: LX. Concerning Charlemagne.

units.la: Exord. A dicto Liv. lib. 1. Hoc illud praecipue in cognitione rerum salubre ac frugiferum, omnis te exempli documenta, &c.
units.tr: Exordium. From the saying of Livy, book 1: "This above all is wholesome and fruitful in the knowledge of things, that you may see the lessons of every example, etc."

units.la: Illustretur paraphrasi: hoc velle ipsum, nihil salubrius esse, quam intueri exempla varia in historia nobis proposita, indeque capere documenta vitae nostrae. Speculum enim esse historiam lucidum omnibus in vita privata, publica. Statuas & imagines proponebant Romani ad imitandum, vide Rosinum At quanto illustrior est historia a summis ingeniis conscripta, &c.
units.tr: Let it be illustrated by a paraphrase: the speaker wishes to say that nothing is more wholesome than to look at the various examples set before us in history and to draw from them the lessons for our life. For history is a mirror, bright for everyone in private and public life. The Romans set up statues and images for imitation; see Rosinus. But how much more illustrious is history when written by the greatest minds, etc.

units.la: Propos. Hac vice Carolum Magnum celsissimum Germanicae gentis Imperatorem & Imperii occidentalis Instauratorem contemplandum esse. Non posse pigere Auditores, tanti Principis spectare imaginem brevissima tabula repraesentatam.
units.tr: Proposition. On this occasion we are to contemplate Charles the Great, most exalted Emperor of the German nation and restorer of the western Empire. Let not the hearers be reluctant to gaze upon the image of so great a prince, presented in a very brief tablet.

units.la: Tractatio. I. De genteunde ortus est, controversiam esse, vindicare illum sibi Gallos, qui tertiam familiam Regum suorum numerant hinc Carolingorum, uti sane Rex Galliae fuit. Sed ortus ex Francis Germanis fuit, natus sive in Moguntino, sive in Turingiae agro; Germanorum etiam rex fuit, linguam locutus Germanicam. vide Sleidanum &c. Masculae gentis, mascula & genuina soboles boles, &c. Talis esse debebat, qui Germaniæ imperaturus, & imperium collapsum atq; tot tantisque tempestatibus concutiendum restituturus erat, &c. Addat de majoribus; qui non ex fabulosa antiquitate, sed ex recentiori historia petendi virtute clarissimi, Pharamundo, Clodio Merovingo &c. Francorum Heroibus &c. vide Hist.
units.tr: Treatment. I. Concerning the people from which he sprang: there is a dispute, since the French claim him for themselves, reckoning him the third family of their kings, that of the Carolingians, as he indeed was king of France. But he sprang from the Franks, who were Germans, born either in the territory of Mainz or in the land of Thuringia; he was also king of the Germans and spoke the German language; see Sleidanus, etc. He came of a male stock, a male and genuine offspring, etc. He had to be such a one as was destined to rule Germany and to restore the empire that had collapsed and was to be shaken by so many and such great storms, etc. Let him add concerning his ancestors, who are to be sought not from fabulous antiquity but from more recent history, men most famous for their valour: Pharamond, Clodio, Merovingus, etc., heroes of the Franks; see the history.

units.la: II. De educatione & studiis ipsius, scil. doctrina virtutem fovet insitam, excolenda à parentibus ingenita virtutum semina, &c. Ita fecisse Carolum in linguis, in humanioribus exercuisse se, adeo ut & Grammaticam, Carmina, Calendaria elaboraverit. Non quòd hisce Principes macerandi, sed laudandi, si quis humanitatem didicerit ex humanioribus literis. Sed ultra progressum Carolum, dum, quod principis est, Patronus atque promotor fuit studiorum, Academiarum inspector, vide historias. Hoc principis esse docet opus eximium, & præ cæteris curandum, &c.
units.tr: II. Concerning his education and studies: learning nourishes the virtue implanted in us, and the seeds of virtue born in us must be cultivated by parents, etc. That Charles did so in languages, and that he exercised himself in the humanities, so that he also composed a grammar, poems, and calendars: not that princes should be worn out by these studies, but that one should be praised if he has learned humanity from the humane letters. But Charles progressed further, since, as is the duty of a prince, he was patron and promoter of the studies, and an overseer of the academies; see the histories. This, he teaches, is the particular work of a prince, and to be cared for above all others, etc.

units.la: III. De ipsius pietate insigni. Quis nescit hanc basin esse Regni. Dis te minorem quod geris imperas, Hor. &c. Hanc curæ maximæ fuisse Carolo doceat ex Historia Sleidani &c. dum tot Ecclesias fundavit, Saxones ad fidem adduxit, &c. vide Hist. Quanto zelo sacrum cultum promovit? Noverat sine illo frustra esse omnia, &c.
units.tr: III. Concerning his remarkable piety. Who does not know that this is the foundation of a kingdom? "You rule because you are less than the gods," Horace, etc. Let him teach from the History of Sleidanus, etc., that this was the greatest concern of Charles, since he founded so many churches and brought the Saxons to the faith, etc.; see the history. With what zeal did he promote the sacred worship? He knew that without it all things are in vain, etc.

units.la: VI. De ipsius Virtutibus: uti sunt 1. frugalitas & modestia, quæ non minima virtus in summis istis capitibus; unde exempla in omnes, & certissimæ divitiæ Reip. cultusque cæterarum virtutum. Quàm insignis illa in Carolo? Fercula quaterna quotidiana, præter ferinas carnes, quibus delectabatur. Ter bibit tantum in epulis. Quantum distant alii veteres, moderni! Quantum mensæ, repotiorum luxus? &c.
units.tr: VI. Concerning his virtues, such as: 1. frugality and moderation, which is no small virtue in such high positions; whence examples for all, and the surest riches of the commonwealth and the cultivation of the other virtues. How remarkable was this in Charles? Four daily courses, besides the wild meats in which he delighted. He drank only three times at banquets. How far removed are other men, ancient and modern! How far removed is the luxury of tables and feasts, etc.?

units.la: 2. Clementia. Quàm necessaria, quia salutaris principibus. &c. quanta illa in Carolo? Bis ignovit filio ex pellice Pipino, & cœnobio inclusit. Non ignovit tantùm, sed & benignè tractavit Cancellarium Eginhartum, generum faciens ex sectatore filiæ. Referatur uberius ex Ruperto 1071.
units.tr: 2. Clemency. How necessary it is, since it is wholesome for princes, etc. How great was this in Charles? He twice pardoned his son by the concubine Pippin, and shut him up in a monastery. He not only pardoned but also treated kindly the chancellor Eginhart, making him his son-in-law after he had been a suitor of his daughter. More fully to be related from Rupert, 1071.

units.la: 3. Fortitudo & fortuna. Subacti Aquitani, domiti Longebardi, subjugati Hispani debellati Saxones, Westphali, Britones, &c. Sueci, Suevi, Bohemi. &c. populi inaumiti. vide Histor. Merito sic Augustus Magnus dictus fuit.
units.tr: 3. Courage and fortune. The Aquitanians were subdued, the Lombards tamed, the Spaniards subjugated, the Saxons, Westphalians, Britons, etc. conquered; the Swedes, Suevians, Bohemians, etc., and unconquered peoples. See the history. Rightly was he thus called Augustus the Great.

units.la: 4. Quid mirum si cessit tibi Oriens, & occidentale tibi Imperium concessit, digno cui utrumque subderetur. Sed moderatio tua vicit potentiam &c.
units.tr: 4. What wonder if the East yielded to you, and the western Empire was granted to you, worthy to whom both might be subjected? But your moderation conquered power, etc.

units.la: V. De ipsius exitu post tanta opera, reddita orbi pace 5. Feb. anni 1814. gloriose expiravit, maximis principibus major.
units.tr: V. Concerning his end after such great works, when peace had been restored to the world, on 5 February of the year 814 he gloriously expired, greater than the greatest princes.

units.la: Conclusio. Vivat felix semper Caroli memoria, verus imperii Occidentalis instaurator, quod inde ad gentem tuam, ad Germanos pervenit, & virtute ac Lege perpetua in illa gente perennaturum est. O perennet floreatque perpetuò.
units.tr: Conclusion. May the memory of Charles live happily forever, the true restorer of the western Empire, which from him has passed to your nation, to the Germans, and will endure forever in that nation through virtue and perpetual law. O may it endure and flourish for ever.

units.la: LXI. DE HISTORIÆ PRÆSTANTIA AC UTILITATE IN VITA POLITICA.
units.tr: LXI. ON THE EXCELLENCE AND USEFULNESS OF HISTORY IN POLITICAL LIFE.

units.la: Exord. a dicto Ciceronis, ex Platonis Timæo: Nescire quid antequam natus sis, accideriit, est semper esse puerum.
units.tr: Opening. From Cicero's saying, taken from Plato's Timaeus: not to know what happened before you were born is always to be a child.

units.la: I. Proponatur dictum cum commendatione prævia Autorum Ciceronis, Platonis, qui illud ex Sacerdote Ægyptio refert, quod Soloni cæterisque Græcis objecerit, illos semper esse pueros, ob ignorantiam antiquitatis,
units.tr: I. The saying is to be put forward, with a prior recommendation of its authors: Cicero, and Plato, who reports it from an Egyptian priest, who said it to Solon and the other Greeks, that they were always children because of their ignorance of antiquity.

units.la: II. Examinetur.
units.tr: II. Let it be examined.

units.la: a. Expositione terminorum, quid sit, nescire ante gesta; quid, esse puerum? videl. ignarum ac rudem esse Historiarum & antiquitatis, est esse imperitum rerum, expertem judicii & consilii; obnoxium passionibus immoderatis: tales enim sunt pueri &c.
units.tr: a. By explaining the terms: what is it not to know what happened before, and what is it to be a child? Namely, to be ignorant and untrained in histories and antiquity is to be inexperienced in affairs, without judgment or counsel, and subject to immoderate passions, for such are children, and so on.

units.la: b. Disquisitione, quomodo hoc esse queat, per prolepsin; cum tot viri docti sint, fuerintque olim in Græcia, (cui hoc objectum,) qui tamen historiarum notitia caruerunt carentque. Exaggeretur hæc objectio a sede veluti Musarum, quæ in Græcia fuerit. Sed
units.tr: b. By inquiring how this can be, by way of prolepsis, since there have been, and still are, so many learned men in Greece (to which this was objected) who nevertheless lacked, and lack, knowledge of histories. This objection is sharpened by the seat, as it were, of the Muses, which Greece was. But

units.la: III. Concludatur dicti hujus veritas, vel ob solam autoritatem Ciceronis, aliorumque doctorum, qui authenticum veluti suo suffragio e tatum hoc fecerunt. Addantur Rationes. a. Quia saltem magnam eruditionis partem ignorat, qui Eruditorum, Prudentum, omninoque illustrium Virorum res gestas ignorat. b.
units.tr: III. The truth of this saying is to be concluded, if only from the authority of Cicero and other learned men, who by their vote made it, as it were, authoritative. Reasons should be added. a. Because whoever does not know the deeds of learned, prudent, and altogether illustrious men is at least ignorant of a large part of learning. b.

units.la: Quia licet præcepta & regulas norit aliquis, tantú tamen abest ut hinc sapiens prudensque evadat, ut potius in illis disputandis nimium ἀκριβολογῶν in suis speculationibus evanescat, quod philosophis gentilium objicit Apostolus Rom. 1. & cum Astronomo isto, astrorum observans vias, iple a vitæ via deflectat & in baratrum incidat.
units.tr: Because, although a person may know the precepts and rules, it is so far from making him wise and prudent that, rather, while disputing them too overly exact [ἀκριβολογῶν] in his speculations, he vanishes away. This is what the Apostle objects to the philosophers of the Gentiles (Rom. 1.), and with that astronomer who observes the paths of the stars, he himself turns aside from the way of life and falls into the pit.

units.la: Quia verissimè pueris similes sunt Ἀνίσοφες qui licet ex matribus, & nutricibus multa addidicerint, tamen prudentia & consilio omninò destituuntur.
units.tr: Because those who are unwise [ἀνίσοφες] are truly similar to children, who, although they have learned much from mothers and nurses, are nevertheless wholly lacking in prudence and counsel.

units.la: Proposit. Hæc cum ita se habeant, Auditores, Historiæ præstantiam ac utilitatem insignem altius paulò inquirendam, & rudiori licet penicillo vobis repræsentandam existimavi; vestra fretus humanitate, quæ &c.
units.tr: Proposition. Since these things stand thus, hearers, I have thought that the notable excellence and usefulness of History should be inquired into a little more deeply, and presented to you with a rather rough brush, relying on your kindness, which, etc.

units.la: Expositio.
units.tr: Exposition.

units.la: Partis primæ de Hist. Præstantia, quæ patescit.
units.tr: Part first on the excellence of History, which is set out.

units.la: I. Ex antiquitate; quæ semper veneranda est, uti vel ex ipsis vetustis monumentis, numismatibus, cimeliis manifestum est. Cæterum antiquitatem ostendat.
units.tr: I. From its antiquity, which is always to be venerated, as is plain even from the ancient monuments, coins, and relics themselves. Moreover, let him show its antiquity.

units.la: α. A causa efficiente Deo: qui revelavit se
units.tr: a. From the efficient cause, God, who revealed himself

units.la: α. Adamo, dum fundavit jus suum in Creatione, quam proinde ipsi exposuit, cum creaturas ad ipsum adduxit, & mandata dedit de non comedendo ex arbore vetita. Hinc
units.tr: a. to Adam, when he founded his right in Creation, which he then set out for him, when he brought the creatures to him and gave commands about not eating from the forbidden tree. Hence

units.la: 1. Adam narrando propagavit ad liberos & nepotes, unde & sacrificiorum ritus ad omnes dimanavit.
units.tr: 1. Adam, by narrating, passed it on to his children and grandchildren, whence the rite of sacrifices also spread to all.

units.la: 2. Sethus duabus columnis insculpsisse dicitur rerum seriem. Joseph. lib. 1. antiquit. c. 3.
units.tr: 2. Seth is said to have engraved the sequence of events on two columns. Josephus, Antiquities, bk. 1, ch. 3.

units.la: β. Abrahamo, dum 1. illi repetiit promissionem de mediatore, quæ jam magis magisque obliterata erat. Gen. 15. c. 17.
units.tr: β. to Abraham, when 1. he repeated to him the promise about the mediator, which was now more and more obscured (Gen. 15, 17).

units.la: 2. Commendavit tacite, ut liberis & nepotibus narret Dei gesta. Gen. 18. v. 19. Hactenus oralis Historia.
units.tr: 2. He commended it tacitly, that he should narrate God's deeds to his children and grandchildren (Gen. 18, v. 19). Thus far oral history.

units.la: γ. Mosi, cui jam dictavit per inspirationem Historiam universam ab orbe condito. Hoc magnum jam illud lumen est, quod Deus orbi accendit.
units.tr: γ. to Moses, to whom he then dictated by inspiration the whole history from the creation of the world. This is now that great light which God kindled for the world.

units.la: Illustretur
units.tr: Let it be illustrated

units.la: 1. Comparatione cum sole, aut lucerna ἐν ἀὐχμηρῷ τόπῳ.
units.tr: 1. By comparison with the sun, or with a lamp in a dark place [ἐν αὐχμηρῷ τόπῳ].

units.la: 2. Comparatione cum reliquis historiis, quæ universæ recentioris sunt originis; ut patet ex historia Ægyptiorum, GræGræcorum, Romanorum. Et si quæ altius ascendunt, ut Ægyptii πρoσηλήνιοι, illæ fabulis & absurditatibus sunt respersæ: adeo ut et primus Historicorum Herodotus tabulosus esse in multis arguatur.
units.tr: 2. By comparison with the other histories, which are all of more recent origin, as is clear from the histories of the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans. And if some ascend higher, like the Egyptians who claimed to be before the moon [προσέληνοι], those are sprinkled with fables and absurdities, so much so that Herodotus, the first of the historians, is charged with being full of fables in many things.

units.la: b. A causa efficace secundaria: quæ fuerunt Autores Historiæ profanæ, Herodotus, qui pater historiæ dicitur, Thucydides, Xenophon, Polybius; qui continuant seriem rerum gestarum, temporumque, ubi sacra deficit Historia: Prophetis sanctis detectum Historiæ sacræ supplentibus, dum vaticiniis faciem temporum sequentium designarunt, veluti repræsentantibus in speculo, cujus profani historici exhibuerunt corpus: Unde sacræ & profanæ Historiæ factum est connubium, & præludium veluti conjunctionis gentium & judæorum.
units.tr: b. From the secondary efficient cause, which were the authors of profane history: Herodotus, who is called the father of history, Thucydides, Xenophon, Polybius, who continue the series of events and times where sacred history fails. The holy prophets had disclosed the outline of sacred history, and profane historians supplement it, since by their prophecies the prophets had designated the face of the following times, as if representing them in a mirror, whose body the profane historians displayed. Whence a marriage of sacred and profane history came about, and a prelude, as it were, to the union of the nations and the Jews.

units.la: Illustretur hoc comparatione cum scientiis & facultatibus reliquis, quæ omnes natæ ex observationibus aut exemplis ab Historicis annotatis. Ostendatur inductione unius atque alterius v. gr. Jurisprudentiæ & Medicinæ, Politicæ. Hinc dies diem docere dicitur, videlicet propter auctam observationem Historicam.
units.tr: Let this be illustrated by comparison with the other sciences and faculties, all of which arise from observations or examples recorded by historians. Let it be shown by induction, for instance, in jurisprudence, medicine, and politics. Hence it is said that "day teaches day," namely on account of the increased historical observation.

units.la: II. A Materia, quæ est τὸ ὑπο. Explicetur
units.tr: II. From its matter, which is the subject [τὸ ὑποκείμενον]. Let it be explained

units.la: a. In genere per comparationem cum Philosophia & reliquis scientiis, quarum quælibet tantum partem sibi vendicat: Historia totum, quod tamen restringitur ad maximè illustria & memorabilia.
units.tr: a. In general, by comparison with philosophy and the other sciences, each of which claims only a part for itself, whereas History claims the whole, though this is restricted to the most illustrious and memorable things.

units.la: β. In specie per inductionem
units.tr: β. In particular, by induction

units.la: a. In rebus sacris, percurrantur præcipua capita historiæ sacræ, juxta seriem temporis.
units.tr: a. In sacred matters, the principal heads of sacred history are to be run through in the order of time.

units.la: b. In rebus naturalibus; & hic afferenda capita quædam notabilia v. g, ex Historia naturali Plinii, Geographorum, Strabonis, Munsteri.
units.tr: b. In natural matters, and here certain notable heads are to be brought forward, for example from the Natural History of Pliny, from the geographers Strabo and Münster.

units.la: c. In rebus moralibus; antiquis, modernis: Fiat hic inductio.
units.tr: c. In moral matters, ancient and modern. Let induction be made here.

units.la: 1. Juxta seriem temporis præcipuorum capitum Historiæ profanæ, ut ortus, interitus, mutationum, conflictationum Regnorum, rerump. consiliorum, actionum, dictorum &c. 2. Juxta scientias & artes præcipuas, quarum in Historia fundamenta. v. g. Moralis & imprimis politica &c.
units.tr: 1. According to the order of time, the principal heads of profane history, such as the origin, decline, and changes of kingdoms, the conflicts of states, and their counsels, actions, sayings, and so on. 2. According to the principal sciences and arts, of which history holds the foundations, for example moral philosophy, and especially politics, and so on.

units.la: III. Ab adjunêta immutabilitate, & impossibili restitutione si se-mel deperdita sit. Explicetur & illustretur comparatione reli-quarum scientiarum quæ varié mutantur, & perditæ restitui possunt.
units.tr: III. From its attached immutability, and its impossible restoration if once lost. Let it be explained and illustrated by comparison with the other sciences, which change in various ways and can be restored if lost.

units.la: IV. Ab encomiis & elogiis eximiis, quibus passim ab authoribus ornatur Historia.
units.tr: IV. From the eulogies and outstanding praises with which History is everywhere adorned by authors.

units.la: V. Ab æstimio maximorum regum, principum, omnium sapien-tum. ex gr. Alexandri, Scipionis Africani. Alphonsi, Caroli V. i-pisius Selimi Turcæ, Demosthenis qui Thucydidem vel oɗies sua manu descripsit &c.
units.tr: V. From the esteem of the greatest kings, princes, and all wise men: for example Alexander, Scipio Africanus, Alphonso, Charles V, Selim the Turk, and Demosthenes, who copied out Thucydides with his own hand, and so on.

units.la: Pars secunda de ejusdem Utilitate.
units.tr: Part Two: On the Same Subject's Usefulness.

units.la: Accéssus per transitionem. Non sine causa tanto in precio habita fuit, quippe quæ veluti fons perennis est omnis sapientiæ. Utilitas hæc ostendatur.
units.tr: Transition by way of approach. It is not without reason that history has been held in such high esteem, since it is, as it were, a perennial fountain of all wisdom. Let this usefulness be shown.

units.la: I. Per inductionem
units.tr: I. By induction.

units.la: a. Præteritoriam (hoc est quæ fit per figuram prærit eritionis.)
units.tr: a. By way of passing over (that is, what is done by the figure of preterition).

units.la: α. In Theologia, ubi ipsa religionis fundamenta aperit, Deum ex luce inaccelsibili præsentem veluti sistit. Quod Theologis uberius explicandum relinquatur.
units.tr: α. In theology, where it lays open the very foundations of religion and sets God, present out of inaccessible light, before us, as it were. This is to be left to the theologians to explain more fully.

units.la: β. In Jure, ubi veterum Leges, Statuta Senatus-Consulta, plebiscita, principum constitutiones refert; Quod Juris Consultis relinquendum.
units.tr: β. In law, where it relates the laws of the ancients, decrees of the senate, plebiscites and the edicts of princes; this is to be left to the jurists.

units.la: γ. In vita privata ad formandos mores, compescendos animi motus exemplis aliorum, quod privatæ cujusque curæ committendum,
units.tr: γ. In private life, for forming morals and restraining the movements of the mind by the examples of others; this is to be committed to each person's private care.

units.la: b. Specificatoriam in vita Politica;
units.tr: b. By specification, in political life.

units.la: α. Theoretica, ubi politiarum constitutionem quis contemplatur, insignis hic usus est Historiæ.
units.tr: α. In theory, where one contemplates the constitution of states; here history has its notable use.

units.la: β. ad formanda aut intelligenda præcepta & theoremata politica; quippe quæ ex observatione singularium formata sunt. Hoc
units.tr: β. For forming or understanding political precepts and theorems, since these have been formed from the observation of particular cases. This is shown

units.la: 1. Probatur 1. exemplo Arist. toto lib.2. Polit. ubi nihil aliud agit, quàm ut varias respublicas veteres, ab historicis & politicis descriptas, earumque leges ac statustatuta cursumque examinet; & recentes, tanquam historiam præsentem contempletur, ut inde suam Rempublicam efformet.
units.tr: 1. First, by the example of Aristotle throughout the second book of the Politics, where he does nothing else than examine the various ancient commonwealths, as described by historians and political writers, together with their laws, statutes and course of events; and he contemplates recent ones as present history, so that from them he might shape his own commonwealth.

units.la: 2. Ratione: quia politica tradit resp. non ex idea Platonis; sed ex vivis exemplis.
units.tr: 2. By reason: because politics teaches about commonwealths not from the idea of Plato, but from living examples.

units.la: 2. Illustretur exemplo Physices, quæ ex observationibus singularibus conflata rerum naturalium. Sic Logica, Rhetorica, nihil aliud sunt, quam generales regulæ, ex observatione bene ratiocinantium & dicentium concinnatæ.
units.tr: 2. Let it be illustrated by the example of physics, which is put together from the particular observations of natural things. So too logic and rhetoric are nothing other than general rules drawn up from the observation of those who reason and speak well.

units.la: b. Ad probanda & illustranda præcepta, quod vicissim fit ex historia. Probatur
units.tr: b. For proving and illustrating precepts, which in turn is done from history. This is proved

units.la: 1. Exemplo reliquarum disciplinarum. Sic Theologus ex scriptura sua format axiomata; eademque ex scriptura demonstrat.
units.tr: 1. By the example of the other disciplines. Thus the theologian forms his axioms from Scripture and demonstrates the same from Scripture.

units.la: 2. Exemplo Imperatoris Porphyrogenatæ; qui universum Historiæ corpus ad loca politica redigi fecit; ut inde in quavis materia exempla imitanda caperentur.
units.tr: 2. By the example of the Emperor Porphyrogenitus, who had the whole body of history reduced to political topics, so that examples to be imitated might be drawn from it on any subject.

units.la: 3. Exemplis omnium institutionum Politicarum, quæ per exempla & observationes Historicas procedunt.
units.tr: 3. By the examples of all political institutions, which proceed through examples and historical observations.

units.la: β. In vita Politico-Practica: ubi quis ad clavum sedet Reipublicæ, tum pacis, tum belli tempore. Et quidem
units.tr: β. In political-practical life, where one sits at the helm of the commonwealth, both in time of peace and in time of war. And indeed

units.la: a. Ad præcavenda pericula imminentia
units.tr: a. For guarding against impending dangers:

units.la: 1. Ab impietate invalescente: quæ semper evertit Regna & Resp. Probetur exemplo uno atque altero & testimoniis.
units.tr: 1. From growing impiety, which always overturns kingdoms and commonwealths. Let this be proved by one or two examples and by testimonies.

units.la: 2. à Superbia, luxu, ac libidine dominante. Tractetur eodem modo, ut membrum præcedens.
units.tr: 2. From pride, luxury and dominant lust. Let it be treated in the same way as the preceding member.

units.la: 3. Ab injustitia grassante. Tractetur eodem modo. Concludatur hoc membrum Epiphonemate: O quam felices hic sunt, qui aliorum intuentes exempla, imminentia pericula matura emendatione avertunt! &c.
units.tr: 3. From rampant injustice. Let it be treated in the same way. Let this member be concluded with an epiphonema: O how happy are those who, looking upon the examples of others, avert impending dangers by timely amendment! etc.

units.la: 4. Ab hostibus. Tractetur ut superiora.
units.tr: 4. From enemies. Let it be treated as the points above.

units.la: b. Ad invenienda consilia. Transitio: Non tantum monstrat pericula, sed & suggerit remedia.
units.tr: b. For discovering counsels. Transition: history not only shows dangers, but also suggests remedies.

units.la: 1. Ad reformationem politiæ. Ostendatur
units.tr: 1. For the reform of the polity. Let it be shown

units.la: 1. Necessitas : quia semper declinant respublicæ
units.tr: 1. The necessity: because commonwealths always decline.

units.la: 2. Remedium in Historia: ubi semper exemplum si- milis mali & salubris adhibiti remedii invenitur. Sic Romani Leges a Græcis transscripserunt. Pec- cata enormia, exemplo Ninivitarum emendanda. Si Angli remedium ad emendandos forte defectus ex Historia petiissent, non facile in inaudito exem- plo remedium noxium famosum ƒ calamitosum quæsivissent &c.
units.tr: 2. The remedy is found in history, where an example of a similar evil and of the wholesome remedy applied is always to be found. Thus the Romans copied their laws from the Greeks. Enormous sins were corrected by the example of the Ninevites. If the English had sought a remedy from history for correcting perhaps their defects, they would not easily have sought in an unheard-of example a harmful, infamous and calamitous remedy, etc.

units.la: 2. Ad componendam seditionem Civilem. Militarem. Exem- pla.
units.tr: 2. For settling civil and military sedition. Examples.

units.la: 3. Ad restituendam pacem, exemplum Thrasybuli, in stabilienda ἀμνηστία sæpissime salubre fuit,
units.tr: 3. For restoring peace: the example of Thrasybulus, since in establishing an amnesty it has very often been salutary.

units.la: 4. Ad obsidendas, turbandas, defendendas urbes, vide exempla varia, & stratagemata, literas occultas apud antiquos, Æneam præsertim.
units.tr: 4. For besieging, disturbing and defending cities, see various examples and stratagems, the secret letters among the ancients, especially Aeneas.

units.la: s. Ad ordinandas acies, captandum tempus, locum ad conflictum. Exempla.
units.tr: 5. For ordering battle lines, seizing the moment, and choosing the place for conflict. Examples.

units.la: Claudatur locus hic generaliter, nullum esse periculum aut casum, cui non possit inveniri remedium ex Historia. Illustretur comparatione experientiæ propriæ & Historicæ: illa exigua, hæc amplissima est, longéque certior. Hinc Alexander Severus semper exemplo veteris Historiæ fundari voluit consilia. &c.
units.tr: Let this place be closed in general terms: there is no danger or accident for which a remedy cannot be found in history. Let it be illustrated by a comparison of one's own experience with history: the former is small, the latter very ample and far more certain. Hence Alexander Severus always wished his counsels to be founded on the example of ancient history, etc.

units.la: ɕ. Ad excitandum animum ad ardua; quod non nisi æmulatione maximorum virorum, quos refert Historia, fieri potest: Videantur exempla Alexandri, Scipionis, Themistoclis, Luculli. Pompeji. &c.
units.tr: 6. For stirring the mind to difficult undertakings, which can be done only by emulating the greatest men whom history relates: let the examples of Alexander, Scipio, Themistocles, Lucullus and Pompey be considered, etc.

units.la: ȹ. Ad muniendum pectus adversus aspera. Hic nihil fortius exemplis veterum; videatur unum atque alterum. Illustretur a contrario, illorum exemplis, qui nullam habent neque experientiam, neque notitiam rerum mundanarum, illi ad quamvis tempestatem contremiscunt & despondent animum: Comparatio a nauta inexperto.
units.tr: 7. For fortifying the breast against hardships. Here nothing is stronger than the examples of the ancients; let one or two be considered. Let it be illustrated by the contrary, from those who have neither experience nor knowledge of worldly affairs: these tremble at every storm and lose heart. Comparison with an inexperienced sailor.

units.la: Concludatur locus & superiores omnes a comparatione Historiæ cum editissima rupe, unde latè universæ vitæ contemplatio, unde antegressa, praesentia, futura in omnem casum prospiciuntur.
units.tr: Let this place and all the foregoing be concluded with a comparison of history to a very high rock, from which the whole of life may be surveyed widely, and from which past, present and future are seen in every case.

units.la: II. Per testimonia illustriora Veterum, Modernorum.
units.tr: II. By the more distinguished testimonies of the ancients and moderns.

units.la: Conclusio. 1. Summam dictorum breviter & nervose repetens. 2. Usum addens, ut praeterita, quorum memoria Dei singulari providentia nobis in utraque Historia conservata est, ita recolamus, ut inde divinam providentiam annotemus, & vitam, consilia & actiones omnes prudenter regere discamus.
units.tr: Conclusion. 1. Briefly and forcefully repeating the sum of what has been said. 2. Adding the use: that we should so recall past things, whose memory has been preserved for us in both histories by the singular providence of God, that from them we may take note of the divine providence, and learn to govern our life, counsels and all actions prudently.

units.la: LXI. DE MILITIA CHRISTIANA.
units.tr: LXI. CONCERNING THE CHRISTIAN WARFARE.

units.la: Exord. a dicto Job. c.7. v.1. nonne militiae dies mortali in terra; unde militandi necessitas, patet. Tractetur instar Chriae.
units.tr: Exordium from the saying of Job, ch. 7 v. 1: "Is not the life of man upon earth a warfare?" From this the necessity of fighting is evident. The topic is to be treated in the manner of a chreia.

units.la: 1. Brevi paraphrasi, quae militiae hujus necessitatem aperiat.
units.tr: 1. With a brief paraphrase that sets out the necessity of this warfare.

units.la: 2. Causa: Quia Deus voluit, ut ante coronam repositam in coelis, certemus hic in terris; ideoque hic hostibus nos objecit variis; ut in omnibus duci nostro Christo conformemur.
units.tr: 2. Reason: because God willed that we should contend here on earth before the crown laid up in heaven; and therefore here he has set us against various enemies, so that in all things we might be conformed to Christ our leader.

units.la: 3. Simili a militia humana, ubi nemo triumphat, nisi qui vicit.
units.tr: 3. By a comparison with human warfare, where no one triumphs unless he has conquered.

units.la: 4. Exemplis sanctorum V. & N. Test. & ipsius Christi.
units.tr: 4. By the examples of the saints of the Old and New Testaments and of Christ himself.

units.la: Hinc rursus inferatur necessitas hujus militiae; indeque porro Propositio. De hac itaque militia hic dicendum, & ita quidem ut perlustremus. I. Ducem. II. Hostes. III. Conflictum & victoriam.
units.tr: From this the necessity of this warfare is again inferred; and from it follows the Proposition. Concerning this warfare, therefore, we must speak here, and in such a way that we go through it thoroughly: I. the leader; II. the enemies; III. the conflict and the victory.

units.la: Expositio partis I.
units.tr: Explanation of Part I.

units.la: Dux militiae est Christus; 1. vide Elogia, Leo de tribu Judae, Rex regum, Dominus dominorum, Deus fortis, Deus exercituum, fidelis ille, qui animam posuit pro suis, qui sanguine vindicavit populum; qui tentatus in omnibus, novit succurrere. 2. Probetur *. a fine missionis in mundum, qui fuit, ut Satanae opera ac potestatem destrueret, mundum vinceret, & suos gloriose educeret. Illustretur exemplo Liberationis ex Aegypto. β. a statu nostro ac imbecillitate, qui sine tali duce ne subsistere quidem potuissemus. Explicetur per inductionem partium. Illustretur comparatione cum militia mundana, ubi sine duce frustra pugnatur; multo magis hic. γ. ab hostium astutia potentia, qui non sunt caro & sanguis, sed tota orci rabies. Illustretur a comparatione cum militia seculari.
units.tr: The leader of the warfare is Christ. 1. See the titles given him: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, King of kings, Lord of lords, the mighty God, the God of hosts, that faithful one who laid down his life for his own, who redeemed the people with his blood, who, having been tempted in all things, knows how to succour. 2. Let it be proved *. a. from the purpose of his being sent into the world, which was to destroy the works and power of Satan, to overcome the world, and to lead his own forth in triumph. Let it be illustrated by the example of the deliverance from Egypt. β. from our condition and weakness, since without such a leader we could not even stand. Let it be explained by an enumeration of the parts. Let it be illustrated by a comparison with worldly warfare, where without a leader men fight in vain; much more so here. γ. from the cunning and power of the enemies, who are not flesh and blood but the entire rage of the pit. Let it be illustrated by a comparison with secular warfare.

units.la: Expositio partis II.
units.tr: Explanation of Part II.

units.la: Hostes sunt Diabolus, mundus, caro nostra, mors.
units.tr: The enemies are the devil, the world, our own flesh, and death.

units.la: 1. Diabolus hic dux est totius exercitus malignantium. α. qualis ille? vide! 1. Pet. f. β. quam causam ac jus habeat bellandi? Peccatum, propter quod a Deo desertus, ipsius traditus erat homo potestati. Hic redemtos & liberatos per Christum retrahere satagit in pristinam servitutem. Illustretur exemplo Pharaonis & Israelitarum. γ. quas copias? Legiones habet malorum spirituum, quorum potentiam & malitiam describit Apostolus Eph. 2. & 6. capp. Videantur exempla potentiae ac saevitiae illorum in Historia Jobi, Sennacheribi, Christi. δ. Quaenam arma illorum? 1. Imperiu ac tyrannis. 2. Miseriae hujus vitae, uti sunt, bellum, fames, morbi. 3. Felicitates vitae imaginariae, ut voluptates, opes, honores mundi. ε. Quo modo nos oppugnat? 1. Palam per afflictiones varias exemplo Jobi, &c. 2. Clam per securitatem & amorem mundi, sic Davidem, Christum, Math. 4. &c. Exaggeretur periculum ubi fumus, ab imparium comparatione, Romanorum cum Hannibal ante portas effet.
units.tr: 1. The devil is here the leader of the whole army of evil beings. α. What is he like? See 1 Pet. (the chapter cited). β. What cause and right has he to make war? Sin, on account of which man was deserted by God and delivered into his power. He strives to drag back into their former slavery those who have been redeemed and set free through Christ. Let it be illustrated by the example of Pharaoh and the Israelites. γ. What forces does he have? He has legions of evil spirits, whose power and malice the Apostle describes in Eph. chs. 2 and 6. Let examples of their power and savagery be seen in the histories of Job, Sennacherib, and Christ. δ. What are his weapons? 1. Dominion and tyranny. 2. The miseries of this life, such as war, famine, and disease. 3. The imaginary happinesses of life, such as the pleasures, riches, and honours of the world. ε. In what way does he attack us? 1. Openly, through various afflictions, as in the example of Job, etc. 2. Secretly, through complacency and love of the world, as with David, and with Christ in Matt. 4, etc. The danger should be magnified where there is smoke, by comparing the forces, as when the Romans had Hannibal before their gates.

units.la: 2. Alter hostis est mundus 1. Exaggeretur in genere ab adjunctis & a comparatione cum aliis Regum Principumque hostibus, qui exiguam tantum mundi partem faciunt. 2. Explicetur per partes. α. Objicit nobis exempla luxuriae ac voluptatis, quibus juventam praecipue oppugnat. Exaggeretur potentia hujus hostis per inductionem objectorum vel comparationem propriae carnis proditoris instar: exemplis, ut Jofephi; Sic filii Dei corrupti in mundo priori Sodomitico. b. Objicit divitias & opes; explicetur per inductionem; exempla, dicta, ut Jacobi. Exaggeretur comparatione cum priori offendiculo voluptatis; praesertim ratione durationis, augetur scilicet 1. ipsa fruitione, & augmento aetatis: 2. subjectis; est cupiditas haec opum in senibus & magnatibus. 3. effectis; quae sunt omnia scelera. Vide exempla, ut divitis Epulonis, alterius, cujus horrea plena. c. Objicit gloriam mundi. Exaggeretur a potentia hujus tentationis; quippe quae superet & ipsam avaritiam; a periculo, quia ad pessima quaeque hominem animat: probetur hoc exemplis ipsius Satanae, primorum parentum, prioris mundi; ratione, quia ipsam animam ejusque partem nobiliorem de fede movet.
units.tr: 2. The second enemy is the world. 1. It should be magnified in general, from its attendant circumstances and by comparison with the other enemies of kings and princes, which make up only a small part of the world. 2. It should be explained part by part. α. It sets before us examples of luxury and pleasure, by which it chiefly assails youth. The power of this enemy should be magnified by an enumeration of the objects, or by comparison with one's own treacherous flesh, as with the examples of Joseph; so too the sons of God were corrupted in the former, Sodomitic world. b. It sets before us riches and wealth; this should be explained by enumeration, with examples and sayings, such as that of James. It should be magnified by comparison with the earlier allurement of pleasure, especially with regard to its duration, which of course increases: 1. the enjoyment itself, and the growth of age; 2. the subjects, since this lust for wealth is found in old men and great men; 3. the effects, which are all kinds of wickedness. See examples, such as that of the rich Epulo, and the other man whose barns were full. c. It sets before us the glory of the world. This should be magnified by the power of this temptation, since it surpasses even avarice; by its danger, since it spurs a man on to every kind of evil; this should be proved by the examples of Satan himself, of the first parents, and of the former world; and by reason, since it moves the very soul and its nobler part away from faith.

units.la: 3. Hostis est propria cato. 1. Probetur a corruptione nativa, a lucta quam quilibet experitur: unde gentiles philosophi affectus rationis, scriptura, carnis & spiritus certamen allegat. 2. Explicetur per inductionem tentationum; modo ad socordiam, modo tristitiam, modo exultationem, elationem & insolentiam, modo ad pusillanimitatem, & desperationem, modo ad iram caeterosque affectus: probentur haec omnia exemplis. 3. Exaggeretur a periculo, licet reliquos caveamus. Illustretur simili ab hoste intra moenia degente. 4. Ab effectis & machinationibus quibus perpetuo hominem infestat teste Apostolo. Rom.7.
units.tr: 3. The third enemy is our own nature. 1. It should be proved from our native corruption, from the struggle which everyone experiences; hence the heathen philosophers allege the conflict of reason, the Scripture, the flesh, and the spirit. 2. It should be explained by an enumeration of temptations: now to sloth, now to sadness, now to exultation, pride and insolence, now to faintheartedness and despair, now to anger and the other passions; all of these should be proved by examples. 3. It should be magnified from its danger, even though we guard against the others. Let it be illustrated by the simile of an enemy dwelling within the walls. 4. It should be magnified from its effects and the stratagems by which it constantly harasses man, as the Apostle testifies, Rom. 7.

units.la: 4. Ultimus hostis mors est. Qui, cum omnes copiae hostiles superatae, ultimum tentat assultum de omnibus & rei summa dimicans. Exaggeretur 1. a contrario amore vitae omnibus insito. 2. a triumpho Satanae veluti.
units.tr: 4. The last enemy is death. When all the hostile forces have been overcome, it makes the final assault of all, fighting for the sum of the matter. It should be magnified 1. by the contrary love of life implanted in all men; 2. by the triumph, as it were, of Satan.

units.la: Pars III.
units.tr: Part III.

units.la: Expositio Conflictus & Victoria.
units.tr: Exposition of the Conflict and Victory.

units.la: 1. Conflictus, qui est. a. Externus, cum seditiones, persecutiones & bella concitat diabolus adversus fideles: uti Cainum contra Abelem, Esavum contra Jacobum, Judaeos contra Christianos, Gentium tyrannos contra eosdem & sanctos Martyres praecipue. Probetur a praedictione Christi, qui bellum minatus est.
units.tr: 1. The conflict, which is: a. External, when the devil stirs up sedition, persecutions and wars against the faithful: as he did Cain against Abel, Esau against Jacob, the Jews against the Christians, and the tyrants of the Gentiles against the same, and especially against the holy martyrs. Proved from the prediction of Christ, who foretold war.

units.la: b. Internus longe gravior, quod ostendatur comparatione. Explicetur per inductionem: cum diabolus conscientiam terreat mole peccati, justitiae divinae rigore, virium nostrarum imbecillitate; ut fecit Caino, Sauli, Achitopheli, Judae.
units.tr: b. Internal, far more grievous, which is shown by comparison. Explained by induction: when the devil terrifies the conscience with the weight of sin, the rigour of divine justice, and the weakness of our own powers; as he did to Cain, Saul, Ahithophel and Judas.

units.la: 2. Cum mundus pravis aliorum exemplis, felici improborum flore, urgente necessitate, caro ebullientibus affectibus hominem impugnat; Mors denique ejusque metus angit. Opponitur hisce omnibus Christus, qui vitam ponit pro suis, Joh.10. qui diabolum, mundum, peccatum & mortem devicit. Qui suppetias ac praesidium nobis mittit suum Spiritum, qui novas cohortes adducit, sanctos Angelos Probetur pf.91. & exemplo Sennacherib & Elisaei: qui denique totam illam armaturam nobis induit. Eph.6. Sic hoc duce vincimus per inductionem, hostes externos per patientiam, exemplo martyrum: diaboli impetus per fidem, exemplo Jobi, Pauli: mundum per temperantiam & modestiam ac humilitatem: carnem per jejunia, contusionem exemplo Pauli: Mortem per vitam Christi ducis. Job.19. qui supremus super pulverem &c.
units.tr: 2. When the world attacks a man with the evil examples of others and the happy prosperity of the wicked; when necessity presses, when the flesh attacks with boiling passions; and finally, death and the fear of it torment him. Christ is set against all these, who lays down his life for his own (John 10), who has conquered the devil, the world, sin and death. He sends us help and protection, his Spirit, who brings up fresh cohorts, the holy angels. Proved from Psalm 91, and by the example of Sennacherib and Elisha; who at last clothes us with that whole armour (Eph. 6). Thus under this leader we conquer: by induction, external enemies through patience, by the example of the martyrs; the assaults of the devil through faith, by the example of Job and Paul; the world through temperance, modesty and humility; the flesh through fasting and mortification, by the example of Paul; death through the life of Christ our leader (Job 19), who is supreme over the dust, etc.

units.la: Conclusio. Hortatoria ad viilantiam & robur. &c.
units.tr: Conclusion. Exhortatory, to vigilance and strength, etc.

units.la: DISPOSITIONUM ORATORIARUM. In GENERE DEMONSTRATIVO. PARS I.
units.tr: DISPOSITIONES ORATORIAE. In GENERE DEMONSTRATIVO. PARS I.

units.la: Continens laudes & vituperia personarum. I.
units.tr: Containing the praises and censures of persons. I.

units.la: LAUS PERSONÆ CONSTANTINI MAGNI.
units.tr: PRAISE OF THE PERSON OF CONSTANTINE THE GREAT.

units.la: Xord. A simili ab architecto, qui magnum ædificium moliens egregium jacit fundamentum. Ita Deus magna moliens excitat viros magnos. Illustretur exemplis, & novissimè Constantini Magni.
units.tr: Exordium. From a similar case: an architect, who undertakes a great building, lays an excellent foundation. So God, undertaking great things, raises up great men. Let this be illustrated by examples, and most recently by Constantine the Great.

units.la: Propos. Hujus herois vitam & facta prædicanda.
units.tr: Proposition. The life and deeds of this hero are to be proclaimed.

units.la: Tractatio. Prædicet I. Genus & majores. Pater Constantini Chlorus, imperio clarus, avus Eutropius, Romanorum nobilissimus: Mater Helena, pietate insignis. Illustretur ex loco communi: Fortes creantur fortibus & bonis. II. Præmisso loco communi de matura manifestatione virtutis, prædicet Ætate primam & indolem generosam exactâ sub Galerio, adolescens Sarmatas stravit, capto duce. Ex invidia cum Leone certare jussus a Galerio vicit, & fugit ad patrem in Gallias. Illustretur loco communi de invidia comite virtutis. III. Res gestas juxta genera virtutis: ubi 1. Amor & benevolentia erga subditos & milites. Exaggerentur comparatione Diocletiani, Maximiniani, Galerii, Maximini, Maxentii tyrannorum eo tempore. Illustretur ex loco communi de amore subditorum.
units.tr: Treatment. Let him proclaim: I. His birth and ancestors. Father Constantius Chlorus, famous for his rule; grandfather Eutropius, the most noble of the Romans; mother Helena, remarkable for piety. Let this be illustrated from a commonplace: brave men are born of brave and good men. II. Having premised a commonplace about the early manifestation of virtue, let him proclaim that in his youth he had an excellent disposition, trained under Galerius; as a young man he overthrew the Sarmatians and took their leader captive. Ordered by Galerius to contend with Leo out of envy, he conquered him, and fled to his father in Gaul. Let this be illustrated by the commonplace that envy is the companion of virtue. III. His deeds, arranged according to the kinds of virtue: where 1. Love and goodwill towards his subjects and soldiers. Let these be magnified by comparison with the tyrants of that time: Diocletian, Maximian, Galerius, Maximinus, and Maxentius. Let this be illustrated from the commonplace about the love of subjects.

units.la: 2. Fortitudo : quæ laudetur a. ex rebus gestis dum subegit Maxentium, Licinium,Sarmatas,Gothos,exstruxit Constantinopolin contra excursiones barbarorum movit in Persas b. Cognomine Magni. c. a causa Deo ipsum armante contra tyrannos.
units.tr: 2. Courage, which is praised a. from his deeds, when he subdued Maxentius, Licinius, the Sarmatians and the Goths, built Constantinople against the incursions of the barbarians, and moved against the Persians; b. from his surname, "the Great"; c. from the cause, since God himself armed him against the tyrants.
