units.la: 3. Pietas a. protectio Christianor contra persecutiones b. abolitio superstitionis gentilis & propagatio Christiani illustretur comparatione præcedentium persecutionum, & ex Loco Communi de officio Principum erga Regnum Christi.
units.tr: 3. Piety: a. his protection of the Christians against persecutions; b. the abolition of pagan superstition and the spread of the Christian faith. Let this be illustrated by comparison with the earlier persecutions, and from the commonplace about the duty of princes towards the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: VI. Mors naturalis ætatis 66. illustretur comparatione magnatu, qui raro sine sanguine ceciderunt.
units.tr: VI. His natural death at the age of sixty-six. Let this be illustrated by comparison with great men, who rarely fell without bloodshed.

units.la: Conclus. Omnibus antecedentibus imperatoribus ipsum præferat, dum primus nomen Christo dedit.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him set him above all the emperors who went before, since he was the first to give his name to Christ.

units.la: II. VITUPERATIO HELIOGABALI.
units.tr: II. The Invective Against Heliogabalus.

units.la: Exord. à justitiæ distributivæ officio; quæ uti præmia bonis,ita pœnas malis rependit. Inter hasce non minimum esse,justum vituperium & infamiam;uti laus & gloria optimum præmium. Amplificetur a fine: ut ad bonorum imitationem, malorum vero fugam posteri excitentur;ne vitia pro virtutibus subeant.
units.tr: Exordium, from the office of distributive justice, which, as it repays good men with rewards and bad men with punishments, so among these punishments there is no small one: just reproach and infamy, just as praise and glory are the best reward. It is amplified from the end: that posterity may be stirred to imitate the good and to flee the wicked, lest they take vices for virtues.

units.la: Propos. Eum in finem Heliogabalum imperatorum pessimū breviter in theatrum deducendum.
units.tr: Proposition: to that end, Heliogabalus, the worst of emperors, is to be briefly brought onto the stage.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Ab ortu & vita anteacta: videl.quòd homo peregrinus, origine obscura , sacerdos quondam Syriæ, tandem miles temerarius. Hæc illustrentur exthesi; quid de illis talibus tandem desperandum, si ad summa emergant?
units.tr: Treatment. I. From his birth and former life: namely, that he was a foreigner of obscure origin, once a priest in Syria, and at last a reckless soldier. These points are to be illustrated by a thesis: what must finally be despaired of in such men, if they rise to the highest positions?

units.la: II. A moribus : quòd homo nefandæ libidinis & vitæ flagitiosissimæ:qui divina humanaq; omnia pessundedit, vestalem duxit uxorem spretis religionibus, Illustrentur invectiva in libidinem & profanitatem, maximè in principe : unde crimina diffunduntur latius.Deducat hinc lamentationem, quòd tales summa ad fastigia rerum evehantur , unde nil nisi scandala & clades publica. Hinc transeat
units.tr: II. From his morals: namely, that he was a man of unspeakable lust and most disgraceful life, who overturned all things divine and human, took a Vestal as his wife, and scorned religion. Here the invective against lust and profanity is to be illustrated, especially in a prince, since crimes spread more widely from him. From this he may move on to lament that such men are raised to the summit of affairs, whence nothing comes but scandals and public ruin. Hence he may pass on

units.la: III. Ad acta & res gestas. Hic 1. Nihil exspectari posse à talibus, ostendat exemplis Sardanapali similiumque ocio & luxui deditorium 2. Exponat acta ipsius quædam : videl.
units.tr: III. To his deeds and actions. Here, 1. he should show, by examples of Sardanapalus and others like him given over to idleness and luxury, that nothing can be expected from such men. 2. He should set out certain of his acts, namely:

units.la: Ridicula, dum Senatum mulierum instituit in monte Quirinali: Unde ridicula Senatus consulta: vide allegata ante, videlicet de habitu & luxu muliebri &c. Illustrentur ex thesi.
units.tr: Ridiculous acts, such as when he established a Senate of women on the Quirinal hill; hence the ridiculous decrees of that Senate, see those cited before, namely concerning women's dress and luxury, etc. These are to be illustrated from the thesis.

units.la: Vecordia, dum turri aureas laminas substravit ut imminente periculo praecipitem se daturus preciose moreretur. Haec similiaque tanquam tali homine digna exagitentur.
units.tr: Madness, as when he laid gold plates beneath a tower so that, when danger threatened, he might throw himself headlong and die a precious death. These and similar things are to be censured as worthy of such a man.

units.la: Addat de morte digna tali vita, dum a Praetorianis in latrina latitans percussus & cadaver in Tiberim tractum: egregio exemplo, quod ne principalis quidem purpura tegat aut excusel crimina a justa nemesi divina.
units.tr: He should add the death that was fitting for such a life, when, hiding in a latrine, he was struck down by the Praetorians and his corpse dragged into the Tiber: an excellent example that not even the imperial purple covers or excuses crimes from the just vengeance of divine retribution.

units.la: III. EXCOMIUM DAVIDIS.
units.tr: III. THE PRAISE OF DAVID.

units.la: Ex I. Sam. 16. seqq.
units.tr: From 1 Sam. 16 onward.

units.la: Ab utilitate memoriae virorum illustrium. Videlicet hinc excitamur ad imitationem virtutis, fugam vitiorum.
units.tr: From the usefulness of remembering illustrious men. Namely, from this we are stirred up to imitate virtue and to flee vices.

units.la: I. Proponatur in genere: addita causa, quia exempla magis movent.
units.tr: I. It is proposed in general, with the reason added, because examples move us more.

units.la: II. Restringatur in specie ad sacra exempla, addita ratione ab incorrupto judicio, quod ferunt autores sacri.
units.tr: II. It is narrowed down to a particular sacred example, with the reason added from the unerring judgment which the sacred authors report.

units.la: Davidem, virum Dei ipsius judicio probatum vobis proponam.
units.tr: I will set before you David, a man approved by God's own judgment.

units.la: I. A Natione: per figuram praeteritionis exponatur verbo laus Gentis Judaicae, comparata cum reliquis.
units.tr: I. From his nation: by the figure of preterition, the praise of the Jewish people is set out in words, compared with the rest.

units.la: II. A parentibus, tenuibus quidem, at ex tribu, cui sceptrum etiam per praeteritum destinatum. Quid referre esse: Amplificetur ex loco generis: saepe emori familias, ut reflorescant illustrius. Illustretur simili ab arboribus.
units.tr: II. From his parents, humble indeed, yet of that tribe to which the sceptre was also destined by prior prophecy. What this means: it is amplified from the place of his family: families often die out, only to flourish again more illustriously. It is illustrated by a comparison with trees.

units.la: III. A genere vitae pastoritiae, abjectae quidem, at innoxiae, & talis, quae custodiam & cura docere queat: Unde gloriosior ascensus, quam si degenerum de turba quis thronum conscendisset.
units.tr: III. From his way of life as a shepherd, lowly indeed but blameless, and such as can teach watchfulness and care. Hence his ascent was more glorious than if someone had climbed to the throne from a crowd of degenerate men.

units.la: IV. A bonis Corporis vigore ac pulchritudine, quae indicia bonorum animi, uti sunt patientia, dexteritas, humilitas, fortitudo, pietas. Exaggerentur breviter a comparatione cum vitiis ordinariis magnatum. a bonis fortunae: videl. ungitur in Regem, evocatur in aulam, ducit filiam Regis. Exaggerentur haec 1. comcomparatione fortunæ pristinæ 2. a causa, consilio Dei, qui ducem populi ipsum designaverat.
units.tr: IV. From the gifts of body, its vigour and beauty, which are signs of the gifts of mind, such as patience, dexterity, humility, courage, and piety. These are briefly magnified by comparison with the ordinary vices of the great. From the gifts of fortune: namely, he is anointed king, summoned to the court, and marries the king's daughter. These are magnified (1) by comparison with his former fortune, (2) from the cause, the counsel of God, who had himself designated him leader of the people.

units.la: V. A rebus gestis, ordine temporis recensendis.
units.tr: V. From his deeds, to be recounted in order of time.

units.la: Percussit Goliathum, & sæpe Philiftæos. Exaggeretur 1. a comparatione utriusque 2. A conditione certa. 3. Ab antecedenti pavore populi. 4. Ab effectu, salute populi, invidia apud Regem & persecutionibus variis; ubi exaggeranda ipsius constantia & moderatio & studium pro judæis. 1. Sam. 19. usque ad 27.
units.tr: He struck down Goliath, and often the Philistines. It is magnified (1) by comparison of the two, (2) from the certain condition, (3) from the preceding fear of the people, (4) from the effect: the safety of the people, the envy at the king's court and various persecutions; where his constancy, moderation and zeal for the Jews is to be magnified. 1 Sam. 19 to 27.

units.la: Regnum adit primò Judæ, post totius Israelis. Notetur hic ipsius moderatio & patientia in expectando.
units.tr: He first enters the kingdom of Judah, afterward of all Israel. Here his moderation and patience in waiting is to be noted.

units.la: Philiftæos bis fundit, Tzionem occupat. Exaggeretur a circumstantia temporis & loci. Et hostes compescit circumquaq; Illustretur comparatione cum administratione Saulis.
units.tr: He twice routs the Philistines and occupies Zion. It is magnified from the circumstances of time and place. And he restrains enemies on every side. It is illustrated by comparison with the administration of Saul.

units.la: Aream Dei adducit in Tzionem, molitur templum. Amplificetur ex loco generis; scil. officio regentum, & comparatione Saulis.
units.tr: He brings the ark of God into Zion and plans the temple. It is amplified from the place of kind: namely, the office of rulers, and by comparison with Saul.

units.la: Prolepsis: commisit enormia peccata, 1. Et pœnam sustinuit in cladibus domesticis, magna cum patientia. 2. Idoneam egit pœnitentiam.
units.tr: Prolepsis: he committed grievous sins, (1) and bore the punishment in domestic calamities with great patience; (2) he performed a fitting repentance.

units.la: Rebelliones varias compescuit, ut Absolonis, Sebæ, Adoniæ. Exaggerentur hæc 1. a circumstantia personarum, temporis. 2. Ab effectu felici.
units.tr: He suppressed various rebellions, such as those of Absalom, Sheba, and Adonijah. These are magnified (1) from the circumstances of the persons and time, (2) from the happy effect.

units.la: VI. A morte tempestiva, pia, placida.
units.tr: VI. From his timely, pious and peaceful death.

units.la: D. Per epiphonema repetantur summa capita, & commendetur exemplum cunctis regentibus.
units.tr: D. By an epiphonema the chief heads are repeated, and the example is commended to all rulers.

units.la: IV. VITUPERATIO SAULIS.
units.tr: IV. THE CENSURE OF SAUL.

units.la: Ex 1. Sam. 9. & seqq.
units.tr: From 1 Sam. 9 and following.

units.la: A. Exord. A fallaci judicio, quod a specie & prærogativis externis vulgò sumitur. Applicetur ad hypothesin, at comparetur cum exemplo Davidis:
units.tr: A. Exord. From a deceptive judgment, the kind commonly formed from outward appearance and external advantages. Let it be applied to the hypothesis, and compared with the example of David.

units.la: B. Propos. Viri a Deo rejecti, Saulis regis nævos vobis detegam, ad fugam hypocriseos.
units.tr: B. Propos. I will lay bare to you the blemishes of King Saul, a man rejected by God, so that you may flee hypocrisy.

units.la: C. Expositio. ubi est.
units.tr: C. Expositio. Where it is.

units.la: 1. Genus: ex tribu Benjamin pater, vir, dives quidem, at ex tribu minima. Ipse in ira clamatus rex fuit: unde parum boni sperandū. Locus communis: Tales saepe Deus evehit in poenā. Haec breviter
units.tr: 1. Kind: he was the son of a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a man of means, but of the smallest tribe. He himself was made king in anger, whence little good was to be hoped for. Commonplace: God often raises such men for punishment. These things briefly.

units.la: II. Bona corporis, juventus, pulchritudo, statura. Bona haec quidē at 1. communia, 2. ad regimen parum facientia. Bona animi. Spiritu Dei quidem fuit indutus, at ille per ipsum exstinctus vecordiā, hypocrysi, praecipitantia, ambitione, invidia, crudelitate: quae vitia turpia cunctis, maximè regi: breviter.
units.tr: II. Goods of the body: youth, beauty, stature. These goods are indeed (1) common, and (2) of little use for government. Goods of the mind: he was indeed clothed with the Spirit of God, but by his own fault he quenched that Spirit through madness, hypocrisy, rashness, ambition, envy and cruelty. These vices are shameful to all, and especially to a king. Briefly.

units.la: III. Res gestae.
units.tr: III. Deeds done.

units.la: a. In genere: parum memorabiles, at parum felices.
units.tr: a. In general: little memorable, and little fortunate.

units.la: b. In specie
units.tr: b. In particular:

units.la: 1. Contra Philist. c. 13. 14. ut ubi lapsus diffidentia de Deo, πλυ-παγμοσύνη & praepostero zelo. Exaggeretur breviter.
units.tr: 1. Against the Philistines, chap. 13 and 14: where he fell through distrust of God, through rashness, and through a misguided zeal. Let this be enlarged on briefly.

units.la: 2. Contra Amalekitas: ubi inobedientia & ambitio ac hypocrisis. De malo in pejus semper ivit. Recessit Dei spiritus. Amplificetur breviter ex loco generis de natura hypocriseos & ambitione. quae non diu latent.
units.tr: 2. Against the Amalekites: where there was disobedience, ambition and hypocrisy. He always went from bad to worse. God's Spirit withdrew. Let this be amplified briefly from the general topic on the nature of hypocrisy and ambition, which do not stay hidden for long.

units.la: 3. Contra Philistaeos & Goliathum. Pusilanitas, invidia, Exaggerentur comparatione cum reliquis.
units.tr: 3. Against the Philistines and Goliath: cowardice and envy. Let these be enlarged by comparison with the others.

units.la: 4. Persequutio contra David. Exaggeranda hic facti turpitudo, odii obstinatio; erga benefactorem, servatorem regni, divinitus destinatum successorem.
units.tr: 4. The persecution of David. The baseness of this deed is to be enlarged upon here, and his obstinate hatred toward his benefactor, the preserver of the kingdom, the successor divinely appointed.

units.la: 5. Trudidatio sacerdotum. cap. 21. ubi exaggeretur profanitas. Scopus totius vitae, qui fuit emolumentum proprium non gloria Dei. Comparetur cum David.
units.tr: 5. The slaughter of the priests, chap. 21: where the profanity is to be enlarged upon. The aim of his whole life was his own advantage, not the glory of God. Let it be compared with David.

units.la: IV. Mors tali rege digna, videl. post cladem populi. Ostendenda facti foeditas.
units.tr: IV. A death worthy of such a king, namely after the defeat of the people. The foulness of the deed is to be shown.

units.la: D. Conclus. detestans vitam ac finem impiorum.
units.tr: D. Conclusion: detesting the life and end of the wicked.

units.la: V. CAROLI MAGNI LAUS.
units.tr: V. The Praise of Charlemagne

units.la: A Exord. A comparatione Heroum Antiquorū cum recentioribus.
units.tr: A. Exordium: on comparing the heroes of antiquity with more recent ones.

units.la: 1. Errare illos, qui nil nisi antiquos Ethnicos admirantur.
units.tr: 1. Those who admire only the ancient pagans are wrong.

units.la: 2. Majori jure nos recentiores Christianos proferre.
units.tr: 2. We Christians of more recent times may be set above them with greater right.

units.la: B. Proof. Laudandus itaque erit Carolus Magnus.
units.tr: B. Proof: Charlemagne therefore deserves to be praised.

units.la: C. Exegesis seu ipsum encomium.
units.tr: C. Exegesis, or the encomium itself.

units.la: I. A genere & Natione: Patre natus Pipino Rege Francorum illustri Ingelhemi in Franconia scil. magni patris major filius, nationis bellicosæ decus. Frustra tibi illum vendicas Gallia.
units.tr: I. From his family and nation: born of Pepin, the illustrious King of the Franks, at Ingelheim in Franconia, namely the elder son of a great father, and the glory of a warlike nation. Gaul claims him for herself in vain.

units.la: II. Institutionem sub Petro Pisano & Alcuino Anglo in omni genere literarum, philosophiæ,ac in Theologia.
units.tr: II. His education under Peter of Pisa and Alcuin the Englishman, in every branch of literature, in philosophy, and in theology.

units.la: III. Dotibus corporis & animi. Illud natura præparaverat dignum talis animæ hospitium. Hic pietate & omni virtutum genere instructissimus fuit. Amplificetur a causa efficiente, institutione scil.finali,quia ad magna destinatus a Deo:& ab effectis:uti & revera magna geslit.
units.tr: III. From the gifts of body and mind. Nature had prepared a dwelling worthy of such a soul. He was furnished with piety and every kind of virtue. Let it be amplified from its efficient cause, namely his education; from its final cause, namely that he was destined by God for great things; and from its effects, since he in fact accomplished great things.

units.la: IV. A rebus gestis, per figuram ἀπὸ εἰκός, unde incipiam? &c.
units.tr: IV. From his deeds, by the figure apo eikos [ἀπὸ εἰκός]: where shall I begin? etc.

units.la: a. Proponantur in genere, quod eluceant in bello, in Politia,in Ecclesia.
units.tr: a. Let them be set out in general: that they shone forth in war, in government, and in the Church.

units.la: b. Explicentur ordine
units.tr: b. Let them be explained in order.

units.la: 1. In bello
units.tr: 1. In war.

units.la: α. Italico,quo Regnum Longobardorū vetustum fortiter exstinxit. Exaggeretur a potentia hostium, & ignavia Imperatorum Orientalium, & effectis, dignitate imperatoria Romæ ipsi oblata.
units.tr: α. Italian, in which he strongly overthrew the ancient kingdom of the Lombards. Let it be amplified from the power of the enemy and the sloth of the Eastern emperors, and from its effects: the imperial dignity offered to him at Rome.

units.la: β. Saxonico,ubi Saxones gentem haĉtenus invictam & magnum Witekindum variis præliis subegit, & Leges dedit.
units.tr: β. Saxon, where he subdued the Saxons, a people hitherto unconquered, and the great Widukind, through various battles, and gave them laws.

units.la: γ. Hispanico, ubi tandem Sarracenos pessum dedit. Exaggeretur a duobus præliis, ubi victus Carolus, prostratus Rolandus.
units.tr: γ. Spanish, where at last he destroyed the Saracens. Let it be amplified from the two battles, in which Charles was defeated and Roland was struck down.

units.la: δ. Bohemico, Bavarico,Pannonico per præteritionem.Illustrentur effecto hæc omnia, videl.sic regnumGermaniæ Galliæ & Italiæ juntum.
units.tr: δ. Bohemian, Bavarian and Pannonian, passed over by praeteritio. Let all these be illustrated by the effect, namely that the kingdoms of Germany, Gaul and Italy were thus joined together.

units.la: 2. In Politia. Hic fiat
units.tr: 2. In government. Here let it be done thus:

units.la: α. Accessus per comparationem virtutis bellicæ &togatæ, scil. utraque necessaria.
units.tr: α. Approach through a comparison of military and civil virtue, since both are necessary.

units.la: β. Enarratio quid gesserit. Æquis legibus tum Italiam tum Germaniam,Hispaniam omniaque constituit.Cum Irene de imperio occidentis transegit. Quod proinde jure armorum,Electionis & transactionis ipsi debetur.
units.tr: β. Narration of what he accomplished. He established Italy, Germany, Spain and all the rest under just laws. He came to an agreement with Irene concerning the western empire, which is therefore owed to him by right of arms, of election, and of agreement.

units.la: γ. Effectus quod exteris regibus passim admirationi fuerit. 3. In Ecclesia: 1. Gentes per Germaniam ad fidem adduxit 2. Episcopatus passim erexit. 3. Luxum sacerdotum compescuit. Exaggerentur hæc ex loco generis de officio regentum, & comparatione cum aliis.
units.tr: γ. The effect: that he was everywhere an object of admiration to foreign kings. 3. In the Church: 1. He brought the peoples of Germany to the faith. 2. He set up bishoprics in many places. 3. He curbed the luxury of the priests. Let these be amplified from the topic of kind, from the duty of rulers, and by comparison with others.

units.la: V. A morte, partito ante filiis regno, exercita misericordia in pauperes, morte naturali obiit anno 72. ætatis morte tali vita digna.
units.tr: V. From his death: after dividing the kingdom among his sons beforehand, and exercising mercy towards the poor, he died a natural death in the seventy-second year of his age, a death worthy of such a life.

units.la: C. Conclusio. Quare merito semper ejus vivit memoria.
units.tr: C. Conclusion. Wherefore his memory deservedly lives on for ever.

units.la: VI. LAUS PERSONÆ ABRAHAMI. ex Gen. 10. & seqq.
units.tr: VI. THE PRAISE OF THE PERSON OF ABRAHAM. From Gen. 10 and following.

units.la: A. Exord. Ab antiqua consuetudine laudandi viros magnos. Ratio; ut sic ad imitationem excitarentur posteri.
units.tr: A. Exord. From the ancient custom of praising great men. The reason: so that posterity might be stirred up to imitate them.

units.la: Amplif. A comparatione minorum: si Ethnicorum alii, nos multò magis sanctorum memoriam recolimus: ratio, quia plus inde utilitatis.
units.tr: Amplification. From comparison with lesser things: if others have commemorated the pagans, we recall the memory of the saints much more; the reason is that there is far more profit in it.

units.la: B. Propositio. Ergo missis aliis, in præsentiarum Abrahami, patris omnium credentium laudes sine vanitate celebrabimus.
units.tr: B. Propositio. Therefore, setting other matters aside, at present we will celebrate without vanity the praises of Abraham, the father of all believers.

units.la: C, Tractatio laudet
units.tr: C, Tractatio: the praise is to proceed as follows.

units.la: I, Familiam, ubi referendus ipsius parens Thara: majores, & gens descendens ex Semo per Eberum, unde posteri Adami Hebræi dicti Genes. 11. Commendetur hæc prosapia comparatione reliquorum Noachi posterorum ex Chamo & Japheto, qui relicto Deo patrum suorum, idololatriam secuti sunt.
units.tr: I. The family, in which his parent Terah is to be mentioned: his ancestors, and the stock descending from Shem through Eber, from whom the posterity of Adam were called Hebrews (Gen. 11). This lineage is to be commended by comparison with the rest of Noah's descendants through Ham and Japheth, who, having abandoned the God of their fathers, followed idolatry.

units.la: II. Patria Chaldæa fuit, regio sapientiæ cultu insignis præ cæteris.
units.tr: II. His homeland was Chaldea, a region distinguished above others for its cultivation of wisdom.

units.la: III. Educatio, & institutio, in religione patrum licet non sine mixtura idololatriæ.
units.tr: III. His upbringing and instruction were in the religion of his fathers, though not without some mixture of idolatry.

units.la: IV. Vitæ genus pastoritium fuit; cujus commendetur antiquitas & innocentia, aliis mundi gloriam cum Nimrodo & Assure sequentibus. Hi contra modicis contenti, rus & pastoritiam coluere. De institutione liberorum in pietate, & applicatione ad certum vitæ genus. Addas hinc ipsum auctum opibus, benedicente Deo.
units.tr: IV. His way of life was that of a herdsman. Its antiquity and innocence are to be commended, while others followed Nimrod and Asshur in pursuit of worldly glory. These, by contrast, were content with modest means and cultivated the countryside and pastoral life. Here one may speak of the upbringing of children in piety and of their being fitted to a particular way of life. You may add here that he himself was increased in wealth, God blessing him.

units.la: V. Bona animi; fides inconcussa & pietas ipsi Deo probata.
units.tr: V. Goods of the soul: an unshaken faith and a piety approved by God himself.

units.la: VI. Quæ elucescunt, & quidem 1. ex eo quòd vocantem Deum secutus est in peregriniam. 2. Credidit promissioni de futuro semine & benedictione in futurum, post quadringentos annos. 3. paruit inaudito de immolando filio edicto. Exaggerentur hæc ab oppositis hæsitationibus, & tentationibus, quas superavit fretus Deo. Locus Communis de fidei sinceritate ac firmitate qua futura cernit præsentia, vincit mundum & omnia carnis ac rationis obstacula. Sic ipsum tandem etiam vicisse Abrahamum.
units.tr: VI. These qualities shine forth, and indeed: (1) from the fact that he followed God, who called him into a foreign land; (2) he believed the promise concerning a future seed and a future blessing, given after four hundred years; (3) he obeyed the unheard-of command to sacrifice his son. These things are to be heightened by the opposing hesitations and temptations which he overcame, relying on God. Here is the common place concerning the sincerity and firmness of faith, which discerns future things as present, conquers the world, and overcomes every obstacle of flesh and reason. Thus Abraham too, in the end, conquered himself.

units.la: VII. In fide mortuus, Heb. 11. fidei exemplum reliquit omnibus: pater credentium dictus Apostolo, elogio celeberrimo ac prosapiâ longè fœcundissima, qua hæres mundi factus est.
units.tr: VII. Having died in faith (Heb. 11), he left an example of faith to all. The Apostle calls him the father of believers, by a most famous commendation and by a lineage far the most fruitful, through which he was made heir of the world.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: VITUPERATIO PHARAONIS; ubi præcipuus respectus ad impietatem, infidelitatem & tyrannidem.
units.tr: DENUNCIATION OF PHARAOH; where the main focus is on his impiety, unbelief and tyranny.

units.la: Exord. A sententia: Magnorum scelerum magnæ sunt pœnæ. Explicetur a causa; justitia Dei, quæ licet ad tempus conniveat, tamen certo tandem puniat. Amplificetur a contrario: retributione operum bonorum.
units.tr: Exordium. From the saying: great crimes bring great punishments. It is explained from its cause: the justice of God, which, although it may wink for a time, nevertheless at last surely punishes. It is amplified from the contrary: by the reward of good works.

units.la: Propositio. Cujus proinde vita & actiones ad abominationem & fugam promendæ.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore his life and actions are to be set forth for abhorrence and avoidance.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. Familia, regum Ægypti fuit, regni antiquissimi, ditissimi, cujus initium juxta computum Manethonis ultra mundi initium excurrit; Sive hic jam Cenchres, sive Acherres fuerit, Pharao enim cognomen regum Ægypti, ut Cæsarum, Sophorum nomina. Concedantur ipsi omnis generis prærogativæ, at hæc vanitatis arguantur, si virtus desit.
units.tr: I. He belonged to the family of the kings of Egypt, a most ancient and most wealthy kingdom, whose beginning, according to the reckoning of Manetho, goes back beyond the beginning of the world. Whether this man was Cencheres or Acherres, Pharaoh was the title of the kings of Egypt, as Caesar was of the emperors, and Sophus of the sages. Let him be granted every kind of prerogative of birth, but these are shown to be vanities if virtue is lacking.

units.la: II. Educatione; quòd ignota sit, sine dubio verò talis, qualis principum ut plurimum esse solita est: videlicet in luxu, fastu ac adulatione aulica. Amplificetur à contrario, qualis esse deberet illorum, ad quorum exemplum totus componitur Orbis educatio.
units.tr: II. As to his upbringing: it is unknown, but without doubt it was such as is usually the case with princes for the most part, namely in luxury, pride and courtly flattery. It is amplified from the contrary: what the upbringing of those should be, after whose example the whole world is shaped.

units.la: III. Unde mores secuti sunt educationem, ut solet. Illustretur prolepsi, quod licet ingenium ipsi sat acre fuerit, uti apparet ex pessimo, quod de exstirpandis Israelitis fabricatus est consilio, tamen, ad malum ut fit, illud applicaverit: videlicet ad amplificationé potentiæ cum oppressione incolarû. Redarguantur hîc perversi mores magnatum, qui cum oppressione subditorum suæ autoritati ac potentiæ velificantur; obliti benefactorum.
units.tr: III. From this his manners followed his upbringing, as usually happens. It is illustrated by prolepsis: although his mind was quite keen, as appears from the wicked plan he devised for destroying the Israelites, nevertheless he applied it to evil, as happens, namely to the increase of his power by the oppression of the inhabitants. Here the perverse manners of the great are rebuked, who, by oppressing their subjects, sail on the winds of their own authority and power, forgetful of benefits received.

units.la: IV. Res gestæ, parum memorabiles, nisi quòd egit.
units.tr: IV. His deeds, scarcely memorable, except that he did them.

units.la: 1. Astutè ac tyrannicè, in impedienda multiplicatione Israelitarum.
units.tr: 1. Craftily and tyrannically, in hindering the multiplication of the Israelites.

units.la: 2. Impiè in prohibendo cultu publico, quem sanctiorem novisse poterat suo. Locus invehendi in torturam conscientiarum & inquisitionem, quæ illegitima est; nec eò usque jura sacrorum, quæ inter regalia sunt, se extendunt.
units.tr: 2. Impiously, in forbidding the public worship which he could have known to be holier than his own. Here is an occasion for inveighing against torture of consciences and inquisition, which is illegitimate; nor do the rights of sacred things, which are among the royal prerogatives, extend so far.

units.la: 3. Profanè ac contumaciter, dum toties monitus & castigatus per signa ac prodigia, fidem derogavit Mosi, obedientiam Deo. Hinc factum, ut callum obduxerit sibi atque in reprobum sensum datus sit divinitus.
units.tr: 3. Profanely and obstinately, since, although so often warned and chastised by signs and wonders, he disbelieved Moses and disobeyed God. Hence it came about that he hardened his heart and was given over by God to a reprobate mind.

units.la: V. Interitus in mari cum exercitu. Amplificetur ab antecedenti apparatu, insectatione, suffocatione.
units.tr: V. His death in the sea with his army. It is amplified from the preceding preparation, the pursuit, and the suffocation.

units.la: D. Conclusio Detestetur ejus tyrannidem, infidelitatem, impietatem, & magnates, ac promiscuè omnes ad contrarias virtutes cohortetur.
units.tr: D. Conclusion. Let him denounce his tyranny, unbelief and impiety, and exhort the magnates, and all people without distinction, to the contrary virtues.

units.la: VIII. LAUS COMPARATIVA ROMULI CONDITORIS REIP: ET BRUTI PRIORIS LIBERATORIS
units.tr: VIII. COMPARATIVE PRAISE OF ROMULUS, FOUNDER OF THE COMMONWEALTH, AND BRUTUS, ITS FIRST LIBERATOR

units.la: Reip. Roman. B. Vide Liv. Florum.
units.tr: Of the Roman commonwealth, B. See Livy, Florus.

units.la: Exord. Ex loco generis per comparationem: laude scilicet. 1. Proponatur, quòd illa debetur rerumpubl. conditoribus & conservatoribus; 2. Probet utrumque, quia illi homines a barbarie vindicarunt; hi præservant ab interitu & hostibus. 3. Illustretur a simili patris & præceptoris. 4. Applicetur ad hypothesin ad Romulum & Brutum: dubium cui laus major debeatur.
units.tr: Exordium. From the topic of kind, by comparison, namely praise. (1) Propose that such praise is owed to the founders and preservers of commonwealths. (2) Prove this of both: the former delivered men from barbarism, the latter preserve them from destruction and enemies. (3) Illustrate it by the analogy of a father and a teacher. (4) Apply it to the case of Romulus and Brutus, and raise the question to whom the greater praise is due.

units.la: Propositio. Vitam & acta utriusque conferenda esse.
units.tr: Proposition. The life and deeds of each are to be compared.

units.la: Tractatio. inclinans in præferentiam Bruti, conferat.
units.tr: Treatment. Let him compare them, inclining toward the preference for Brutus.

units.la: I. Ortum utriusque & educationem. Hic 1. præmittat in genere laudé honestæ familiæ & educationé. 2. Conferat utrumque: Romulum ex Marte quidem genitum jactari; sed commentum esse ad tegendum matris opprobrium, at Brutum ex nobilissima familia. Illum inter agrestes, hunc inter regias familias ad omnem virtutem educatum. 3. Per apostrophen ad utrumque, hunc illi præferat.
units.tr: I. Their origin and upbringing. Here (1) first set out, in general terms, the praise of an honourable family and education. (2) Compare the two: Romulus is indeed said to have been born of Mars, but this is a fiction devised to cover his mother's disgrace; Brutus came from a most noble family. The one was brought up among rustics, the other among royal households, trained in every virtue. (3) By an apostrophe to each, let him prefer the latter to the former.

units.la: II. Bona animi: Romulum animosum & in consiliis expeditum fuisse: probetur ex effectis: Brutum prudentia ac moderatione insignem, nec minus animosum: probetur itidem ex effectis. Amplif. ex thesi: collatione virtutum militarium & togatarum, ita ut hæ præferantur quoad fructum & solidam gloriam.
units.tr: II. Goods of the mind. Romulus was shown to be spirited and resourceful in counsel, as is proved from his effects. Brutus was distinguished by prudence and moderation, and no less spirited; this too is proved from his effects. Amplification from the thesis: a comparison of military and civil virtues, in which the latter are preferred as to their fruit and solid glory.

units.la: III. Res gestas. Hic 1. Extollatur fundatio novi & validissimi regni per Romulum. 2. Opponatur vindicatio imperii contra potentissimos tyrannos Tarquinios, & reductio libertatis inæstimabilis. Amplif. a. ex Loco Communi de præstantia aristocratiæ præ Monarchia b. ex concomitante difficultate utriusque dissimili c. ex consequente fructu utriusque: Reges exiguam portionem Italiæ, Consules orbem sibi subjecerunt.
units.tr: III. Deeds. Here (1) extol Romulus's founding of a new and very strong kingdom. (2) Set against it the vindication of empire against the most powerful tyrants, the Tarquins, and the restoration of inestimable liberty. Amplification: (a) from the commonplace on the superiority of aristocracy over monarchy; (b) from the difficulty that accompanies each, which differs in kind; (c) from the consequent fruit of each: the kings subjected a small portion of Italy, the consuls subjected the world to themselves.

units.la: Conclusio 1. Congestis in cumulum argumentis magnam quidem Romulo, majorem Bruto laudem deberi asserat. 2. a genere: prædicet Rerumpubl. conditores, & instauratoris præcipue:
units.tr: Conclusion. (1) Having heaped up the arguments, let him assert that great praise is indeed due to Romulus, but greater to Brutus. (2) From the general kind: let him proclaim the founders of commonwealths, and especially their restorers, worthy of praise.

units.la: IX. LAUS ADAMI tanquam primi generis humani propagatoris.
units.tr: IX. The praise of Adam as the first propagator of the human race.

units.la: A. Exord. Ab exemplo aliorum, quorum heroes quisque suos, imprimisque gentis conditores laudibus extulerunt. Hoc 1. propositum approbet. Amplif. inductione quadam. II. Applicetur ad institutione per comparationem minorum. videl: multo magis nos Adamum. Addatur ratio: quia ille omnium primus, cui totius generis humani fortuna concredita erat, ut cum ipso staret aut caderet. Amplif. comparatione cum illis, qui ambitiose familiæ suæ authores prædicant. &c.
units.tr: A. Exordium. Take the example of others, whose writers have each extolled their heroes with praises, above all the founders of their nations. Let this proposition be approved in the first place, by a certain induction. Second, let it be applied to the present subject by comparison with lesser men, namely: much more should we praise Adam. Add the reason: he was the first of all, to whom the fortune of the whole human race was entrusted, so that it would stand or fall with him. Amplify by comparison with those who boast of their ambitious family founders, and so on.

units.la: B. Narratio: breviter & nervose exponat Adami creationem.
units.tr: B. Narration: briefly and vigorously set out the creation of Adam.

units.la: C. Propositio: Hujus dotes ac felicitatem merito prædicandam, ut inde edocti, quantum perdidimus in Adamo primo, ad secundum Adamum generis nostri instauratorem confugiamus.
units.tr: C. Proposition: his gifts and happiness are rightly to be proclaimed, so that, taught by this, we may see how much we lost in the first Adam, and flee for refuge to the second Adam, the restorer of our race.

units.la: D. Tractatio.
units.tr: D. Treatment.

units.la: I. Alleget illa, quæ in laudem familiæ, nativitatis re: adduci a Rhetoribus solent; multum scilicet esse situm in hisce ad virtutem. Hæc tamen humilia vilia & esse in comparatione Adami: qui 1. ab ipso Deo conditus, Illustretur comparatione minorum ne reliquorum hominum.
units.tr: I. Let him bring forward those things which are usually adduced by the rhetoricians in praise of a family or of one's birth; namely, that much in these things contributes to virtue. Yet these are low and worthless in comparison with Adam, who (1) was created by God himself. Let him be illustrated by comparison with lesser men, not with the rest of mankind.

units.la: II. Laudet dotes
units.tr: II. Let him praise his gifts:

units.la: 1. Corporis, comparative cum reliquis animantibus juxta illud Ovidii Pronáque cum spectent. &c.
units.tr: 1. Of the body, compared with the other living creatures, according to that line of Ovid, Pronaque cum spectent, etc.

units.la: 2. Animæ, quæ ornata imagine Dei. Ubi est sapientia in mente: justitia universalis in voluntate, rectitudo in omnibus affectib'. Illustretur contrario, in homine corrupto &amplificetur simili a luna & heliotropio, quæ solem respiciunt, ita Adamus.
units.tr: 2. Of the soul, which was adorned with the image of God. Here is wisdom in the mind, universal justice in the will, and rectitude in all the affections. Let it be illustrated by the contrary, in corrupted man, and amplified by the simile of the moon and the heliotrope, which turn toward the sun; so Adam.

units.la: 3. Totius hominis: in quo refulsit majestas imperatoria; utpote cui destinatum imperium orbis. Hinc sedes regia ipsius in Paradiso, orbis veluti meditullio, cujus addatur encomium. Epiphonemate claudatur, quo præferatur regibus, comparetur cum angelis & Deo.
units.tr: 3. Of the whole man, in whom imperial majesty shone forth, since dominion over the world was destined for him. Hence his royal seat in Paradise, as it were at the centre of the world; let a eulogy of this be added. Let it be closed with an epiphonema, by which he is set above kings and compared with the angels and God.

units.la: III. Prædicet vitæ genus, videlicet contemplativum, quo in creatura & seipso contemplabatur creatorem, ejusque laudibus totus vacabat. Hoc competisse ipsi dicatur. 1. quia creatura maxime eximia fuit, cui sponte ministrabat orbis. 2. Quia hoc vitæ genus præstantissimum. Fiat digressiuncula in laudem vitæ contemplativæ.
units.tr: III. Let him proclaim his way of life, namely the contemplative, by which he beheld the Creator in creatures and in himself, and was wholly occupied with his praises. Let it be said that this suited him: (1) because he was the most excellent of creatures, to whom the world ministered willingly; (2) because this way of life is the most outstanding. Let a little digression be made in praise of the contemplative life.

units.la: IV. Laudet studia & res gestas. Hic
units.tr: IV. Let him praise his studies and deeds. Here:

units.la: 1. Proleptice conqueratur, quod non diu tanta felicitate gavisus sit; unde & parum de ea S. S. referat. Scilicet magnæ felicitatis vix capacem esse mortalem.
units.tr: 1. By anticipation, let him lament that he did not rejoice in so great happiness for long; whence also Holy Scripture says little about it. Namely, that mortal man is scarcely capable of great happiness.

units.la: 2. Referat gesta, videlicet. I. Instar regis lustravit regnum, & nomina imponens cunctis, veluti homagio illa sibi obstrinxit. Illustretur comparatione dissimilium cum Cyro, qui militum suorum nomina scivit: hic orbis universi. II. conjugem assumpsit, sollicitus de posteritate, & ampliori Dei gloria. Breviter dicatur in laudem matrimonii sui, & increpentur conjugii vituperatores Monachi. III. Regni hujus terreni & creaturarum contemplatione excitabat se ad laudem Creatoris & meditationem regni cœlestis. Ita utriusque Regni civis, terram corpore, animo ac spe cœlum tenebat. Digressio de scopo vitæ, scilicet ut ex creatura ad creatorem, ex terræ gloria ad politeuma illud in cœlum assurgamus.
units.tr: 2. Let him relate his deeds, namely: (I) Like a king he surveyed his kingdom, and by giving names to all things he bound them to himself, as it were by homage. Let it be illustrated by comparison with unlike figures, such as Cyrus, who knew the names of his soldiers; here, of the whole universe. (II) He took a wife, anxious about posterity and for the greater glory of God. Let it be said briefly in praise of his marriage, and the monks who disparage marriage are to be rebuked. (III) By contemplating this earthly kingdom and the creatures, he was roused to praise the Creator and to meditate on the heavenly kingdom. Thus, a citizen of both kingdoms, he held the earth with his body and heaven with his mind and hope. A digression on the purpose of life: namely, that from the creature we should rise to the Creator, and from the glory of the earth to that commonwealth in heaven.

units.la: E. Refutatio profani & inficeti Authoris, qui nuper hanc Adamo generi humano gloriam eripere voluit, dum prædamitas tanquam Cadmæos fratres diu ante Adamum ex terra, & ad terrena natos introducere satagit. Scilicet contra S. S- contra totius Ecclesiæ consensum, contra historiarum fidem, contra dignitatem & scopum proprium hominis, suis fidit somniis, dignus qui cum scarabeo ex stercore ortum ducat, indignus Adami nepos &c. Deus primus generis nostri plastes est; qui ex uno sanguine, Adamo produxit totum genus &c.
units.tr: E. Refutation of the profane and ignorant author who recently wished to snatch this glory from Adam and the human race, while he strives to introduce the pre-Adamites, like the brothers of Cadmus, born long before Adam from the earth and for earthly things. Clearly, against Holy Scripture, against the consensus of the whole Church, against the faith of history, and against the dignity and proper purpose of man, he trusts his own dreams; he is worthy to derive his origin from dung along with the beetle, unworthy to be a grandson of Adam, etc. God is the first maker of our race, who "of one blood" produced the whole human race from Adam, etc.

units.la: Peroratio usum inculcet, videlicet, I. Gratitudinem adversus Deum, ex consideratione excellentiæ in qua homo conditus. II. ad studium, ut quod in Adamo perdidimus, illud per Christum secundum Adamum, restitutum, grate amplectamur.
units.tr: Peroration. Let him inculcate the use of the subject, namely: (I) gratitude toward God, from the consideration of the excellence in which man was created; (II) zeal, so that what we lost in Adam, we may gratefully embrace as restored through Christ, the second Adam.

units.la: X. VITUPERATIO EJUSDEM ADAMI.
units.tr: X. Vituperation of the Same Adam.

units.la: A. Exord. a comparatione dissimilium: videl. quemadmodum parentes merito laudandi, qui nobilitatem, opes & honores reliquunt liberis; ita vituperandos maximè, qui dedecus, egestatem & infamiam transferunt. Addatur ratio: quia non modo in semetipsos, sed in totam innoxiam peccant prosapiam, &c. Applicetur ad institutum.
units.tr: A. Exordium from a comparison of unlike things: just as parents are rightly praised when they leave nobility, wealth and honours to their children, so those are most deserving of blame who pass on shame, poverty and infamy. Add the reason: because they sin not only against themselves but against their whole innocent posterity, etc. Apply this to the subject.

units.la: B. Hinc vituperandum maxime Adamum, unde tanta toti generi humano labes & malorum ilias: quod pace antecessoris fiat.
units.tr: B. Hence Adam is to be blamed most of all, from whom came such a great stain and a whole pile of evils upon the entire human race; this may be said with due respect to his predecessor.

units.la: C. Confirmatio habeat 1. καὶ ἀρχήν:
units.tr: C. The confirmation should have 1. the beginning [καὶ ἀρχήν]:

units.la: I. Præmollitionem; non animo cavillandi hoc thema suscipi. Ratio: quia sciat, quis honor parentibus & majoribus debeatur, quorum vitia etiam tegenda sint. Καλὰ ζῆλον: sed 1. justo dolore. 2. amore veritatis. 3. Exemplo Scripturæ, quæ exuere veterem Adamum jubeat, & a secundo Adamo Christo totam familiam salvandorum numeret. Id quodetiam antecessor innuerit.
units.tr: I. A preliminary softening: that this theme is taken up not with a mind to mock, for the reason that one should know what honour is owed to parents and ancestors, even when their faults must be covered. It is good to be zealous [Καλὰ ζῆλον]: but (1) with just grief, (2) with love of the truth, (3) following the example of Scripture, which bids us put off the old Adam and counts the whole family of those to be saved from the second Adam, Christ. His predecessor has also hinted at this.

units.la: II. Concessionem omnium prærogativarum, quas antecessor ipsi tribuit; quæ repetendæ per brevem enumerationem figuratam schematis communicationis. Quis enim eximium neget? &c.
units.tr: II. A concession of all the privileges which his predecessor has given him; these are to be repeated by a brief enumeration, in the figure of communication. For who would deny that he was outstanding? etc.

units.la: III. Oppositam vituperationem.
units.tr: III. The opposing vituperation.

units.la: 1. In genere, quod tam eximiis donis male usus sit, in ruinam totius generis. Amplificetur 1. ab ipsius persona, in qua repræsentasentatum totum genus humanum quod cum ipso staret aut caderet; unde solicitus esse debuerit. 2. A comparatione & simili patris, vasalli: quod exaggeretur dissimili, ab illo qui pro se tantum peccat.
units.tr: 1. In general: that he misused such remarkable gifts, to the ruin of the whole race. This is to be amplified (1) from his own person, in which the whole human race was represented, and which would stand or fall with him; hence he ought to have been anxious. (2) From the comparison and likeness with a father and his vassal, which is to be heightened by the unlike case of one who sins only for himself.

units.la: 2. In specie vituperentur.
units.tr: 2. In particular, let him be blamed.

units.la: I. Vitia unde lapsus hic manarit: uti sunt.
units.tr: I. The vices from which this fall arose, namely:

units.la: a. Securitas, qua Dei timorem exuerat.
units.tr: a. Carelessness, by which he cast off the fear of God.

units.la: b. Diffidentia de divina bonitate ac veritate.
units.tr: b. Distrust of the divine goodness and truth.

units.la: c. Facilitas in credendo spiritui seductori, qui Dei fidem ipsi suspectam reddebat:
units.tr: c. Readiness to believe the seducing spirit, which made the faith of God suspect to him.

units.la: d. Φιλαυτία & ambitio qua Deo similis esse gestiebat.
units.tr: d. Self-love [Φιλαυτία] and ambition, by which he longed to be like God.

units.la: e. Concupiscentia fructus. Exaggerentur hæc omnia comparatione dotium quibus instructus erat; & virtutum, quæ ipsi commendatæ.
units.tr: e. Desire for the fruit. All these are to be heightened by comparison with the gifts with which he was endowed, and with the virtues that had been committed to him.

units.la: II. Factum ipsum; utpote quod fuerit
units.tr: II. The deed itself, as being

units.la: a. Inobedientia adversus divinum mandatum; quid atrocius?
units.tr: a. Disobedience to the divine command: what could be more atrocious?

units.la: b. Desertio Dei, summi boni & benefactoris; quid tristius?
units.tr: b. Desertion of God, the highest good and benefactor: what could be more sorrowful?

units.la: c. Defectio ad Diabolum; quid fœdius? Exaggerentur oppositione officii.
units.tr: c. Defection to the Devil: what could be more foul? These are to be heightened by setting them against the duty owed.

units.la: III. Consequentia, videl. condemnatio, ejectio ex paradiso, ablatio dominii, mancipatio ad labores ac ærumnas, mors temporalis ac æterna tum in Adamo, tum in posteris. Exaggerentur singula.
units.tr: III. The consequences, namely condemnation, expulsion from paradise, loss of dominion, subjection to toil and hardship, and temporal and eternal death, both in Adam and in his posterity. Each of these is to be amplified.

units.la: D. Conclusio. I. Deploret conditionem illorum, qui in carne & illustri origine gloriantur; cum ipsa humana generis radix vitiata sit.
units.tr: D. Conclusion. I. Let him lament the condition of those who boast of their flesh and of an illustrious origin, since the very root of the human race has been corrupted.

units.la: II. Hortetur ad quærendum Adamum secundum, Christum per quem Adami labes purgata sit.
units.tr: II. Let him exhort them to seek the second Adam, Christ, through whom the stain of Adam has been cleansed.

units.la: XI. LAUS ABELIS.
units.tr: XI. The Praise of Abel

units.la: A. Exord. Ab utilitate memoriæ virorum illustrium.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the usefulness of remembering illustrious men.

units.la: Amplif. Comparatione paganorum & patriarcharum; ex quibus hi præferantur.
units.tr: Amplification. By comparison of the pagans and the patriarchs; from which the latter are preferred.

units.la: Propositio. Abeli s patriarchæ te igitur encomium decantaturum.
units.tr: Proposition. That you are therefore about to sing the encomium of the patriarch Abel.

units.la: Tractatio. Laudet Abelem. I. A familia antiquissima ipsius Adami & Evæ, quorum prærogativæ prædicentur, præsertim, quòd a Deo ipso conditi ad imaginem, & præferantur omnibus reliquis mortalibus.
units.tr: Treatment. Let him praise Abel. I. From the most ancient family of Adam and Eve themselves, whose prerogatives are to be proclaimed, especially that they were created by God himself in his image, and are preferred to all other mortals.

units.la: II. Patria, plaga Orientis, haud procul sine dubio Mesopotamia ubi Eden hortus fuerat.
units.tr: II. Country: the region of the East, not far, without doubt, from Mesopotamia, where the garden of Eden had been.

units.la: III. Educatione, pia sine dubio, qua de Deo, hominum conditione, atque accepta promissione instructi fuerunt.
units.tr: III. Education: surely pious, by which they were instructed about God, the human condition, and the promise received.

units.la: IV. Genere vitæ pastorali: hic 1. utile ostendatur, ut quis certo vitæ generi se applicet. 2. in specie laudetur antiquitas & innocentia vitæ pecuariæ, cui omnes patriarchæ dediti fuerunt.
units.tr: IV. Pastoral way of life: here (1) it should be shown that it is useful for a person to devote himself to a definite way of life; (2) the antiquity and innocence of the pastoral life, to which all the patriarchs were devoted, should be praised in particular.

units.la: V. Bonis corporis, animæ, fortunæ; illa sine dubio eximia dicas ista longe præstantiora, ex quibus est pietas uti apparet ex sacrificiis; hæc modica.
units.tr: V. Goods of body, soul and fortune: you may call the first outstanding, but these far more excellent, from which piety arises, as appears from the sacrifices; the last modest.

units.la: VI. Rebus gestis, parum notæ in ista simplicitate primæva, nisi quòd Deum coluit. Amplif. Comparatione pietatis cum omni gloria aliorum.
units.tr: VI. Deeds done: little known in that primeval simplicity, except that he worshipped God. Amplification: by comparison of piety with all the glory of others.

units.la: VII. Morte cruenta, at pia. Parum referre dicas, quo genere mortis quis obeat, dummodo pie.
units.tr: VII. Death bloody, yet pious. You may say that it matters little by what kind of death a man dies, provided he dies piously.

units.la: Conclusio. Merito igitur sacra ejus nobis est memoria, ut exemplum pietatis imitemur sæviente licet mundo.
units.tr: Conclusion. Rightly, therefore, his sacred memory is dear to us, so that we may imitate his example of piety, even though the world rages.

units.la: XII. VITUPERATIO CAINI.
units.tr: XII. THE CENSURE OF CAIN.

units.la: A. Exord. A fallaci judicio quod fundatur in externa specie felicitatis. Probetur exemplo Saulis, Epulonis & Caini, qui licet primogenitus Adami, primus Urbium ac imperii fundator, pessimus tamen fuisse ostendatur. Amplificetur: quòd utile proinde sit, examinare talium personarum vitam & actiones, ne vitia sub externa specie decipiant.
units.tr: A. Exordium. Against the deceptive judgment that is founded on the outward appearance of happiness. Let this be proved by the examples of Saul, Epulo and Cain, who, although he was Adam's firstborn and the first founder of a city and an empire, is to be shown to have been the worst of men. Let it be amplified: that it is therefore useful to examine the life and actions of such persons, lest vices deceive us under an outward show.

units.la: B. Propositio. Eum in finem, te breviter Caini primi parricidæ vitam examinaturum.
units.tr: B. Proposition. To that end, I shall briefly examine the life of Cain, the first parricide.

units.la: C. Tractatio.
units.tr: C. Treatment.

units.la: I. Concedat ipsi magnam prærogativam familiæ, nativitatis ac educationis; at dicat has & pessimis sæpe contingere, uti Chamo, Esavo, Absolomo, Judæ, ita & Caino; in quo proinde eo magis vituperandum, quod degeneraverit, contra spem matris; uti laudandum in aliis, quod malorum parentum fuerunt boni liberi. II. Exponat genus vitæ, rusticum scilicet, quod primò commen-detur, ut maxime antiquum, laboriosum ac innocens. Deinde ostendatur statum vitæ neminem commendare Deo, sed pietatem ac probitatem in quocunque vitæ genere. Digressiuncula fiat in primas mortalium occupationes.
units.tr: I. Let him concede to Cain the great advantage of family, birth and upbringing; but let him say that these are often granted even to the worst men, as to Ham, Esau, Absalom, Judah, and so also to Cain. In him, therefore, the more is he to be censured, in that he degenerated, contrary to his mother's hope; just as others are to be praised, in that they were good children of wicked parents. II. Let him set out his manner of life, namely rustic, which is commended first, as being very ancient, laborious and innocent. Then let it be shown that no station of life commends anyone to God, but piety and uprightness in whatever kind of life. Let a short digression be made on the first occupations of mortals.

units.la: III. Enumeret bona corporis, fortunæ. In omnibus excelluisse ipsum credibile. Verum hæc dicantur bona esse, prout iis bene quis utatur. Bona animi ipsi concedantur, quoad ingenium ac animositatem; at vera illa bona ipsi defuisse, pietatem scilicet erga Deum, parentes & fratrem. Amplificetur hoc comparatione cum aliis bonis, quibus longissimè præferatur; imò hæc sola vera dicantur bona esse. Hic per digressiunculam ostendatur præstantia pietatis & virtutum reliquarum.
units.tr: III. Let him enumerate the goods of body and fortune. It is credible that he excelled in all of them. But let it be said that these are goods only according as a man uses them well. Let the goods of mind be granted to him, as to talent and spirit; but let it be said that those true goods were lacking in him, namely piety towards God, his parents and his brother. Let this be amplified by comparison with other goods, to which it is far preferred; indeed let these alone be called true goods. Here, by a short digression, let the excellence of piety and of the remaining virtues be shown.

units.la: IV. Referat res gestas scil.
units.tr: IV. Let him relate the deeds, namely:

units.la: 1. Oblationem sacrificii unà cum fratre. Hic breviter dicatur de origine & natura sacrificiorum, videl. quòd à Deo injuncta, 2. ad Christum duxerint, & abnegationem sui.
units.tr: 1. The offering of a sacrifice together with his brother. Here let it briefly be said concerning the origin and nature of sacrifices, namely that they were enjoined by God, and 2. that they lead to Christ, and to self-denial.

units.la: 2. Admixtam hypocrisin ac invidiam: unde rejectum fuerit ipsum sacrificium.
units.tr: 2. The mixed hypocrisy and envy, on account of which the sacrifice itself was rejected.

units.la: 3. Conceptam iram adversum fratrem, indeque ortum parricidium, sine causa, in fratrem unicum, innocentem, sacris intentum.
units.tr: 3. The anger conceived against his brother, and the parricide that arose from it, without cause, against an only brother, innocent and intent on sacred things.

units.la: 4. Condemnationem & desperationem.
units.tr: 4. Condemnation and despair.

units.la: 5. Conversionem ad res mundanas, unde oppidum molitus est, & imperium, omnis profanitatis autor.
units.tr: 5. His turning to worldly affairs, whence he built a town and an empire, the author of all profanity.

units.la: V. Mors scripturæ non dicta, certè vitæ consona.
units.tr: V. His death is not told in Scripture, but certainly agrees with his life.

units.la: D. Concluf. Detestans ipsius vitam, & dehortans ab exemplo.
units.tr: D. Conclusion. Detesting his life, and dissuading from his example.

units.la: XIV. LAUS SOLOMONIS COMPARATIVA CUM TARQUINIO PRISCO.
units.tr: XIV. A COMPARATIVE PRAISE OF SOLOMON WITH TARQUIN THE ELDER.

units.la: A. Exordium. A comparatione Historicorum, cùm omnes laudandi, tum præcipuè illi, qui vitas virorum Illustrium conscripserunt. Ratio: quia in illis tanquam limpidissimo speculo imagines virtutum & vitiorum conspiciuntur. Amplificetur à comparatis, illis nempe, qui imagines & statuas principum efformarunt, qui tantùm corrporum, cùm historici animorum imagines nobis relinquant: Applicetur ad institutum scil. Solomonis historiam.
units.tr: A. Exordium. Taken from the comparison with historians, all of whom deserve praise, but especially those who have written the lives of illustrious men. Reason: because in those lives, as in the clearest of mirrors, the images of virtues and vices are seen. Let it be amplified from the things compared, namely those who fashioned images and statues of princes, since those craftsmen give only the likenesses of bodies, whereas historians leave us the images of minds. Let it be applied to the present subject, namely the history of Solomon.

units.la: B. Propositio. Et quidem ita ut cum Tarquinio Prisco eum conferas. Addatur thematis commendatio : videl. ad quem omnes nationes venerunt ut cognoscant sapientiam ipsius, illum vobis coram sistam.
units.tr: B. Proposition. And indeed, let it be done so that you compare him with Tarquin the Elder. Add the commendation of the theme: namely, that all nations came to know his wisdom, and I shall set him before you.

units.la: C. Tractatio. Exponat laudetque
units.tr: C. Treatment. Let him set forth and praise the following:

units.la: 1. Per præteritionem gentē virtutis cultricē utrāq; Judæos scil. & Romanos, præferatq; ratione familiæ Solomonē, qui ex Davide rege omniū optimo ortus. Filius uti in senecta natus, ita singulari cura tum patris tum Nathanis Prophetæ educatus ad spē regni. Locus Communis de educatione principum magna curā instituenda.
units.tr: 1. By preterition, a nation devoted to virtue, both Jews and Romans alike. He prefers Solomon in terms of family, since he was born of King David, the best of all kings. He was a son born, as it were, in old age, and was educated with singular care both by his father and by Nathan the prophet, with hope of the kingdom. Common topic: the education of princes is to be carried out with great care.

units.la: II. Accessum ad regnū. Tarquinius petens ultro obtinuit principatum : Solomon a Patre rege populo propositus, sponte receptus a populo, frustra contranitente Adonia. Illustretur comparatione cum aliis, ipsoque Adonia, qui per vim & fraudes ad regna grassantur, aut solo successionis jure nixi inhabiles sæpe invitis subditis obtruduntur. Ille contra verè imperat, qui & sanguinis jure & populi voto solium occupat &c. Illustretur exemplis.
units.tr: II. Access to the kingdom. Tarquin, seeking it, obtained the principate of his own accord. Solomon was proposed to the people by his father the king and was willingly received by the people, though Adonijah resisted in vain. Let it be illustrated by comparison with others, and with Adonijah himself, who rush to kingdoms by force and fraud, or, relying on the right of succession alone, are often foisted upon unwilling subjects as unfit. He, on the other hand, truly rules who takes the throne both by the right of blood and by the wish of the people, and so on. Let it be illustrated by examples.

units.la: III. Ipsum regimen conspicuum præclaris virtutibus. Hic sepositis illis per præteritionem, quæ de ipsius modestia, industria, liberalitate, justitia & clementia dici possent, non inferiorem in hisce ipsum fuisse regum optimis; sed alia esse singulariter in ipso prædicanda: commendetur.
units.tr: III. The rule itself, conspicuous for outstanding virtues. Here, setting aside those things passed over, which could be said of his modesty, industry, liberality, justice and clemency, let it be commended that he was not inferior to the best of kings in these qualities, but that other things are to be proclaimed singularly in him.

units.la: 1. Ipsius sapientia, quæ 1. laudetur in genere tanquam virtus maximè necessaria principi, qui caput, oculus, custos, & pastor populi. 2. Ostendatur in Solomone. a. A causa, voto, quo oblatam divinitus illam expetiit spretis opibus & potentia, & impetravit cumulatim. Exaggerentur hæc comparatione Tarquinii & aliorum. b. Ex effectis videl. sapienti judicio inter meretrices; constitutione regni & aulæ, discursibus de omni scibili, fama sparsa hinc per universum Orientem ; vide 1. Reg. 3. 4. & 10. Conserantur & exornentur singula. Tarquinus tanquam longe inferior adducatur.
units.tr: 1. His wisdom, which (1) is first praised in general as a virtue most necessary for a prince, who is the head, eye, guardian and shepherd of the people; and (2) is then shown in Solomon: (a) from its cause, namely the prayer by which he sought the wisdom offered by God, scorning wealth and power, and obtained it in abundance. Let these things be magnified by comparison with Tarquin and others. (b) From its effects, namely his wise judgment between the harlots; the establishment of his kingdom and court; his discourses on every knowable subject; and the fame spread from this throughout the whole East. See 1 Kings 3, 4 and 10. Let each point be compared and adorned, and Tarquin brought in as far inferior.

units.la: 2. Magnificentia: quæ ut modestia privatorum, ita propria & necessaria regibus virtus probetur exemplo ipsius Dei majestate conspicui. Locus Comm. de splendore Majestatis. Ostendatur in magnificentia aulæ regiæ & urbis, quam ex lateritia auream effecit. Conferatur Tarquinius.
units.tr: 2. Magnificence, which, as modesty is for private persons, is a virtue proper and necessary for kings. It is to be proved by the example of God himself, conspicuous in his majesty. Common topic: the splendour of majesty. Let it be shown in the magnificence of the royal court and city, which he made golden out of what was brick. Compare Tarquin.

units.la: 3. Pietate. Hæc r. commendetur in genere; tanquam fundamentum regni. Horat. Dis te minorem quod geris imperas. 2. Laudetur in Solomone præcipue ex effectis, splendido templo, ejusque inauguratione. Hæc exaggerentur contentione cum Tarquinii & aliorum magnatum studiis, compotationibus, venationibus. 3. Extenuentur humani errores Solomonis, tanquam minime pares istis virtutibus.
units.tr: 3. Piety. This is first commended in general as the foundation of a kingdom. Horace: "You rule because you bear yourself as less than the gods." (2) Let it be praised in Solomon above all from its effects: the splendid temple and its dedication. These are to be magnified by contrast with the pursuits of Tarquin and other magnates: their drinking parties and hunting. (3) Let the human failings of Solomon be minimised, as being by no means equal to those virtues.

units.la: D. Conclus. 1. Commendet ipsum tanquam exemplum regibus & principibus omnibus. 2. Prædicet regna & resp. quibus sapientes ac pii contingunt reges ac moderatores.
units.tr: D. Conclusion. (1) Let him commend Solomon as an example to all kings and princes. (2) Let him proclaim the kingdoms and commonwealths on which wise and pious kings or rulers fall.

units.la: XV. VITUPERATIO EJUSDEM COMPARATIVA CUM TARQUINIO SUPERBO.
units.tr: XV. A COMPARATIVE CENSURE OF THE SAME MAN, WITH TARQUIN THE PROUD

units.la: A. Exord. Ab approbatione effati antecessoris: videl. vitam magnatum speculum esse virtutum aut vitiorum. Hinc inferat. Ergo sedulo cavendū ne vitia pro virtutibus admiremur, uti fieri soleat in speculis parū limpidis ut objecta confundamus. Amplificetur a periculo, si vitia subeant animos magnis autoribus. 2. Applicet hoc ad Solomonem, in quo dubium utrum virtutes, an vitia exsuperent.
units.tr: A. Exordium. Taking as his starting point the approval of the predecessor's statement, namely that the life of great men is a mirror of virtues or vices, he infers from this: we must take care not to admire vices in place of virtues, as is usual with mirrors that are not very clear, which distort the objects reflected. The danger is magnified if vices creep into the minds of great authors. 2. He applies this to Solomon, in whom it is doubtful whether his virtues or his vices outweigh the other.

units.la: B. Propof. Videri sibi pace antecessoris Solomonem potius vituperio quam laude dignum, & Tarquinio Superbo potius, quam Prisco comparandum, idquod paucis evincendum. Ne sapientiæ ipsius admiratione etiam vitia ipsius probemus.
units.tr: B. Proposition. With due respect to the predecessor, it seems to him that Solomon deserves censure rather than praise, and is to be compared with Tarquin the Proud rather than with Priscus. This must be shown in a few words, so that we do not, by admiring Solomon's wisdom, also approve of his vices.

units.la: C. Tractatio.
units.tr: C. Treatment.

units.la: I. Concedat ipsi omnes prærogativas ab antecessore allegatas ipsam etiam initio pietatem. Opponat vero in genere enormia vitia & inconstantiam, unde similis flori pulchro, sed fœtido; homini formoso, docto, sed pravo, ipsique Tarquinio superbo, cui nec hæc defuerint, id quod porro evincendum.
units.tr: I. He grants him all the advantages cited by the predecessor, including his piety at the beginning. But he sets against them, in general terms, his enormous vices and inconstancy, by which he is like a beautiful but foul-smelling flower, or a handsome, learned man who is nonetheless wicked; and like Tarquin the Proud himself, in whom these qualities were not lacking either. This is what he goes on to prove.

units.la: II. Vituperet.
units.tr: II. He censures.

units.la: 1. Labem matris, quæ adulterio cognita prius Davidi: scil. culpam talem parentum sæpe puniri in liberis, dum exempla imitantur. Hujus instinctu inductum senem, ut exclusis natu majoribus, minor in regno succederet. Hujus novercalibus odiis instigatum ipsum, ut Adoniæ vitam eriperet. Contra superbum: scil. callida mater ad præcipitia consilia impellit sæpe juniores liberos. Ita Maria Medices in Gallia. Væ tibi regio, cujus rex puer est.
units.tr: 1. The stain of his mother, who had previously been known to David through adultery. That is, the guilt of parents is often punished in their children when the children imitate their examples. Under her influence the old king was induced, by setting aside the elder sons, to let the younger succeed to the kingdom. Stirred by his stepmother's hatred, Solomon himself was moved to take away the life of Adonijah. By contrast, the proud Tarquin: a crafty mother often drives her younger children into rash plans. So Maria de' Medici in France. Woe to you, land, whose king is a child.

units.la: 2. Solomonis prodigalitatem: Hic 1. laudet magnificentiam in construenda aula & templo. 2. vituperet: quod multiplicavit equos, currus, famulos gynæceü prodigioso numero, plantationes hortorum, & ædificia, delubra Deorum, Alienavit urbes: detestudis sumptibus excessit: vituperet vitium hoc expresse adeo regibus Israëlis vetium, regno perniciosum, exemplo noxium.
units.tr: 2. Solomon's prodigality. Here he 1. praises the magnificence in building the palace and the temple; 2. censures the fact that he multiplied horses, chariots and servants for the harem in prodigious numbers, as well as the planting of gardens and buildings and temples of the gods. He alienated cities and exceeded all bounds with ruinous expenditure. He censures this vice expressly, the more so because it was a vice hateful to the kings of Israel, ruinous to the kingdom and harmful as an example.

units.la: 3. Luxuriam & libidinem; quæ patet ex cumulatione portentosa uxorum & pellicum indigenarum, extranearum Exaggeretur hoc vitium ex effectis, præsertim in rege; exemplo Davidis cui maximum hinc malum & Tarquinio.
units.tr: 3. Luxury and lust, which are evident from the monstrous accumulation of wives and concubines, both native and foreign. This vice is to be magnified by its effects, especially in a king; take the example of David, to whom great evil came from it, and of Tarquin.

units.la: 4. Superbiam ac vanitatem, qua elatus in omnibus excellere voluit. vide Eccles. 2. Vituperetur vitium hoc in genere, & in specie taxetur in Solomone, quid regi cum philosophicationibus, quid cum hortorum cultura, cui regni cura commissa? Confer Superbum.
units.tr: 4. Pride and vanity, by which, being puffed up, he wished to excel in everything. See Ecclesiastes 2. This vice is to be censured in general, and in particular it is to be rebuked in Solomon: what has a king to do with philosophizing, what with the cultivation of gardens, when the care of the kingdom has been entrusted to him? Compare the proud Tarquin.

units.la: 5. Impietatem & idololatriam; qua non tantum idola indulsit feminis, sed & ab iisdem seduci se passus est ad idolorum cultum. Exaggeretur hoc oppositione sapientiæ ac pietatis pristinæ. Amplif. simili, ex optimo unguento pessimum venenum; & comparatione cum pessimis regibus Israëlis v. g. Jaroboamo, Achabo: scilicet horum cæcitati condonari aliquid posse; Solomoni non item. Item ipse gentilibus pejor esse arguatur.
units.tr: 5. Impiety and idolatry, by which he not only indulged idols for the sake of his women, but also allowed himself to be seduced by them into the worship of idols. This is magnified by setting it against his former wisdom and piety. Amplification by analogy: from the best ointment comes the worst poison. And by comparison with the worst kings of Israel, such as Jeroboam and Ahab: it is argued that something can be pardoned to their blindness, but not to Solomon's. Likewise, he is to be shown to be worse even than the Gentiles.

units.la: Conclusio: 1. Detestetur fœda hæc vitia Solomonis, propter quæ & ipsius in dubio pœnitentia & salus. 2. Per apostrophum moneat principes, ne excelsa sua fortuna seduci se patiantur.
units.tr: Conclusion: 1. He execrates these foul vices of Solomon, on account of which his repentance and salvation are also in doubt. 2. By an apostrophe he warns princes not to allow themselves to be seduced by their lofty fortune.

units.la: XV. LAUS HANNIBALIS POENI.
units.tr: XV. The Praise of Hannibal the Carthaginian

units.la: Ex Liv. 21. & Plut. in Parall. Flor. lib. 2. c. 6.
units.tr: From Livy 21 and Plutarch in the Parallels; Florus, book 2, ch. 6.

units.la: A laude virtutis bellicæ. Illustretur comparatione virtutis togatæ, quarum utraque Reip. pro ratione diversi licet temporis æque necessaria dicatur : quod ostendatur breviter. A vicissitudine belli & pacis. Ideoque bellicam suam merereri laudem.
units.tr: From the praise of military virtue. Let it be illustrated by comparison with civil virtue, each of which, though the times differ, may be said to be equally necessary to the commonwealth; this should be shown briefly. From the alternation of war and peace. And therefore military virtue deserves its praise.

units.la: Hoc cum ita sit, illustre bellicæ virtutis exemplum in Hannibale proponendum.
units.tr: Since this is so, the illustrious example of military virtue is to be set forth in Hannibal.

units.la: I. A genere & familia : quod ex Pœnorum gente bellicosissima natus ex Hamilcare, Carthaginensiū duce fortissimo. Amplif. ex loco generis: quòd parentum virtus reluceat in liberis. Illustretur exemplo uno atque altero, & sententia,
units.tr: I. From birth and family: he was born of the most warlike Carthaginian stock, the son of Hamilcar, the bravest of the Carthaginian generals. Amplify from the place of his lineage: the virtue of parents shines forth in their children. Let it be illustrated by one or two examples, and by a saying.

units.la: II. Ab educatione: inter arma fuit; adeò ut puer novem annorum cum Patre ad exercitū profectus sit, ibidemque sacramento ad vindictam contra Romanos confirmatus. Amplificetur ab indole præstantiori, quæ maturè elucet, & ad studium aliquod se applicat: exemplis Alexandri Magni, Cæsaris, Pompeji.
units.tr: II. From his upbringing: he was reared among arms, so much so that as a boy of nine he went with his father to the army and was there bound by oath to take vengeance on the Romans. Let it be amplified from his outstanding disposition, which showed itself early and applied itself to some pursuit; the examples of Alexander the Great, Caesar and Pompey.

units.la: III. A dotibus corporis animique. Videl. corpus ipli fuit vegetum ad labores, æstus frigorisque ac inediæ patiens, vultus acer ac vivax: Ingenium sagax ac prudens: animus audax, intrepidus, industrius; qualis necessarius militi; &c.
units.tr: III. From the endowments of body and mind. Namely: his body was vigorous for labour and enduring of heat, cold and hunger; his face was keen and lively. His intellect was shrewd and prudent; his spirit bold, fearless and diligent, such as a soldier needs; etc.

units.la: IV. A Rebus gestis.
units.tr: IV. From his deeds.

units.la: 1. Tyrocinia depositio apud Asdrubalem in bello Hispanico. Breviter ostendatur quantum momentū sit, uti in rebus omnibus, ita præsertim in militia, bonum habere exemplum quod imitemur.
units.tr: 1. His apprenticeship under Hasdrubal in the Spanish war. Briefly show how great a weight it carries, in all things but especially in soldiering, to have a good example to imitate.

units.la: 2. Dux surrogatus Asdrubali, Saguntum pressit, evertit. Unde fama ipsi ab initio, in quo magnum momentum ad res gerendas.
units.tr: 2. Made commander in place of Hasdrubal, he pressed hard upon Saguntum and overthrew it. Hence he had renown from the very start, and in the conduct of affairs a great deal depends on this beginning.

units.la: 3. Bellum infert Romanis ubi elucet ipsius prudentia in firmando prius regno, in tractandis ingeniis Gallorum & militum, committendis justo loco ac tempore præliis, & facienda pace; fortitudo in superandis Pyrenæis, Alpibus, & fluviis, & barbaris Alpinis, superandis heroibus Romanorum. V. A mortis genere, scilicet venenum hausit apud regem Bythiniæ Prusiam, ne traderetur consuli Flaminio. Magnanimitatis hoc esse dicatur apud gentes, exemplo Catonis.
units.tr: 3. He wages war on the Romans, where his prudence shines in first strengthening his kingdom, in handling the minds of the Gauls and his soldiers, in committing battles at the right place and time, and in making peace; and his fortitude in crossing the Pyrenees, the Alps and the rivers, in overcoming the Alpine barbarians and in overcoming the heroes of Rome. V. From the manner of his death: namely, that he drank poison at the court of King Prusias of Bithynia, lest he be handed over to the consul Flaminius. Let it be said that this is a mark of magnanimity among the nations, by the example of Cato.

units.la: D. Conclusio efferat Hannibalem & virtutem Bellicam.
units.tr: D. Conclusion: let it exalt Hannibal and military virtue.

units.la: XVI. VITUPERIUM HANNIBALIS.
units.tr: XVI. THE VITUPERATION OF HANNIBAL.

units.la: A. Exord. a simili, videlicet illustri flamma, quæ non sine fumo surgit. Applicetur ad ingenia hominum, in quibus vitiæ virtutibus vicina in specie ad Annibalem applicet, quem antecessor laudaverit.
units.tr: A. Exordium from a simile, namely of a brilliant flame, which rises not without smoke. It is applied to human talents, in which vices lie close to virtues in appearance; he applies it to Hannibal, whom his predecessor had praised.

units.la: B. Propos. Non frustra a Livio dictum: ingentes istas virtutes, pariter vitia facile æquasse. Hac propter illum potius vituperio quam laude dignum videri; quod pace antecessoris evicturus sit.
units.tr: B. Proposition: It was not without reason that Livy said that these immense virtues were easily matched by equally great vices. For this reason he seems to deserve blame rather than praise, because he was going to conquer by the peace of his predecessor.

units.la: C. Tractatio examinet.
units.tr: C. The treatment should examine.

units.la: I. Genus & familiam: videlicet harum gloria ipsi concedatur: at dicat potius hæc stimulú esse ad nequitiam & facinora multis turbulentis ingeniis. Illustretur exemplo Absolomi, Adoniæ, Alexandri; quibus parentum gloria calcar fuerit ad scelera.
units.tr: I. His birth and family: let their glory be conceded to him; but let him say rather that these things are a spur to wickedness and crimes for many turbulent minds. Let it be illustrated by the examples of Absalom, Adonijah, and Alexander, for whom the glory of their parents was a goad to crimes.

units.la: II. Educationem: illam ipsi contigisse militarem ad cædes & rapinas, inter milites, non ad justitiam ac pietatem. Hinc detestandum esse dicat, quod puer sacramento ad odium & vindictam contra Romanos fuerit obstrictus, devotus hostis, antequam quis hostis aut amicus, novisse per ætatem poterat.
units.tr: II. His upbringing: that it fell to him to be wholly military, for slaughter and plunder among soldiers, not for justice and piety. Hence let him say that it is to be detested that, as a boy, he was bound by an oath to hatred and vengeance against the Romans, and was devoted as an enemy before, by his age, he could know who was an enemy or a friend.

units.la: III. Dotes corporis ac animi. Et hæ ipsi concedantur; at paria aut majora vitia fuisse; videl. crudelitatem, perfidiam plus quam punicam, profanitatem ab omni observantia Numinis ac veritatis, quibus nihil sceleratius, quæq; omnes umbratiles virtutes obfuscant, ut spissa nubes solis lucem.
units.tr: III. The gifts of body and mind. Let these be conceded to him; but let it be said that his vices were equal or greater, namely cruelty, perfidy more than Punic, profanity void of all reverence for the Deity and for truth, than which nothing is more wicked, and which obscure all the shadowy virtues, as a thick cloud obscures the light of the sun.

units.la: IV. Res gestas fuisse quidem magnas; verum plerasque gestas.
