units.tr: IV. His exploits were indeed great, but for the most part they were ill-performed.

units.la: 1. Temerario impetu, ut quod bellum suscepit in regione & gente sibi ignota: Montes, flumina incognita, aggressus sit. Ex rerum exitu non posse judicari de consilio.
units.tr: 1. By a reckless rush, such that he undertook a war in a region and among a people unknown to him, and attacked mountains and rivers he did not know. From the outcome of affairs, his plan cannot be judged.

units.la: 2. Insolenter ac obstinatè potius, quam fortiter.
units.tr: 2. Insolently and obstinately rather than bravely.

units.la: 3. Ofcitanter in Campania præsertim, ubi luxu corrupit semetipsum, exercitum, & omnes victorias. Stulto similis, qui argutè quandoque dicta stoliditate corrumpit. V, Mortem maximum argumentum pusillanimitatis, scilicet ἀυξ​​νχεῖαν, argumento timiditatis, quæ detestanda.
units.tr: 3. Lazily, especially in Campania, where by luxury he corrupted himself, his army, and all his victories; like a fool who sometimes spoils cleverly spoken words by stupidity. V. His death is the greatest proof of pusillanimity, namely avxeneia [αὐξνχεῖαν], a proof of timidity, which is to be detested.

units.la: D. Refutentur hic breviter & in genere illa, quæ in laudem ipsius dicta fuere: videlicet quod vitia fuerint sub specie virtutis apparentia, aut saltem majoribus vitiis obfuscata.
units.tr: D. Let those things be refuted briefly and in general which were said in his praise: namely, that his vices appeared under the appearance of virtue, or at least were obscured by greater vices.

units.la: E. Conclusio. Hannibalem similesve belli furias detestans, & ad veram fortitudinem, quæ pugnat pro justitia, cohortans.
units.tr: E. Conclusion: denouncing Hannibal and similar furies of war, and exhorting to true courage, which fights for justice.

units.la: XVII. DAVID SEU PRINCEPS.
units.tr: XVII. DAVID, OR THE PRINCE.

units.la: Exord. Conciliet attentionem & benevolentiam.
units.tr: Exordium. Let him win attention and goodwill.

units.la: I. Commendatione thematis in genere, videlicet principatus: cujus ostendatur.
units.tr: I. Commendation of the theme in general, namely of principality, and let him show what kind of principality it is.

units.la: 1. Difficultas dicto Tiberii apud Tac. 1. An. c. 11. Se experiendo didicisse, quam arduum, quam subjectum fortunæ regendi cuncta omnes: Ratio addatur: quia nihil difficile magis quam tot capita ab uno coercere, omniaque ista obire, quæ ad regimen requiruntur. Vide præfationem Lipsii ad Polit. Illustretur in genere ab exemplis illorum, qui in hoc mari naufragium fecerunt.
units.tr: 1. The difficulty, from Tiberius' saying in Tacitus, Ann. 1, c. 11: "I have learned by experience how difficult it is, how subject to fortune, for anyone to rule everything." Add the reason: nothing is harder than to hold so many heads in check by one man and to carry out all the tasks that government requires. See Lipsius' preface to the Politics. Illustrate this in general by the examples of those who have been shipwrecked on this sea.

units.la: 2. Norma ad quam dirigendus sit: quæ est recta ratio & præcepta prudentum. Illustretur prolepsi: Licet enim principes legibus soluti, tamen Dei, naturæ ac regni legibus illos teneri. Hinc sapientes in legibus regni ac reip. conscribendis ab antiquo fuisse occupatos: Probetur exemplis Platonis, Aristotelis, Xenophontis & recentiorum plurimorum. Primum Machiavellum & sequaces ab hac regula deflexisse, & utilitate principis omnia metientes, Idolum politicum, Rationem Status, infausto fidere procudisse. Hinc tantam malorum segetem orbi natam, &c. Rectius sentire doctissimum Italorum Malvezzum, & Sgualdium aliosque, qui ex sacris corrigenda præcepta politica in Republica Christiana exstimarunt, & ad exempla sanctorum virorum formandum principem. Qui ad solvenda physica problemata recurrit ad Deum, est parum philosophus; qui in politicis ad Deum non recurrit, est parum Christianus, inquit Malvezzo. Hinc & te tentaturum, num principem divinitus formatum repræsentare queas.
units.tr: 2. The norm by which he is to be guided: namely right reason and the precepts of the wise. Illustrate it by prolepsis: although princes are loosed from human laws, they are nonetheless bound by the laws of God, of nature and of the kingdom. Hence the wise from antiquity were busy drafting laws for kingdom and commonwealth. Prove this by the examples of Plato, Aristotle, Xenophon and very many more recent writers. First, show that Machiavelli and his followers departed from this rule, measuring everything by the prince's advantage, and forged the political idol, Reason of State, a thing to trust to our misfortune. Hence so great a harvest of evils was sown in the world, and so on. More rightly thought the most learned Italians Malvezzi and Sgualdi and others, who drew from Sacred Scripture the precepts that should correct politics in the Christian commonwealth, and who held that the prince should be formed by the examples of holy men. "He who has recourse to God to solve problems of physics is little of a philosopher; he who in politics does not have recourse to God is little of a Christian," says Malvezzi. Hence you too will try whether you can present a prince formed by God.

units.la: II. Excusatione propriarum virium &c. Scilicet non ut alios doceas, ceas, sed te ipsum exerceas, contemplando virum illum divinitus commendatum, & eo magis venerari discant omnes Deo proximam in terris majestatem,
units.tr: II. An excuse for your own powers, etc. Namely, not so that you may teach others, but so that you may train yourself, by contemplating that man commended by God; and so that all may learn the more to venerate the majesty closest to God on earth.

units.la: Propositio. Huic fini te Davidem regum optimum, Virum juxta cor Dei, delineaturum, ut ex illo boni principis idea elucescat.
units.tr: Proposition. To this end you will sketch David, the best of kings, a man after God's own heart, so that from him the idea of a good prince may shine forth.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. Vocem exponat πατρονομικὸς. Videlicet principem 1. late dici primum in quolibet ordine, ut principem Senatus. 2. Rectius pro eo, qui principatu investitus est. 3. Rectissimè pro illo qui neminem recognoscit superiorem in terris, penes quem est τὸ κύριον in Monarchia ut Arist. loquitur talem & hic intelligi. Vide politicos; floridius tamen tractandum est.
units.tr: I. Let him explain the word [πατρονομικὸς]. That is, a prince is called (1) broadly, the first in any order, as the prince of the Senate; (2) more properly, one invested with principality; (3) most properly, one who acknowledges no superior on earth, in whom lies to kyrion [τὸ κύριον] in a monarchy, as Aristotle puts it; it is in this sense that the term is understood here. See the political writers, but this must be treated more floridly.

units.la: II. Rem ipsam persequatur, ita ut virtutes & requisita Principis in genere proponat & in Davide ostendat, aliisque exemplis illustret. Itaque.
units.tr: II. Let him pursue the matter itself, setting out the virtues and requisites of a prince in general, showing them in David, and illustrating them with other examples. Thus:

units.la: 1. In genere enumeret virtutes principi necessarias: Plato de legibus requirit Religionem, justitiam & scientiam militarem praecipue: sed et plenius dici posse quinque requiri videl. Pietatem, Justitiam, Prudentiam politicam, fortitudinem & amorem subditorum. Vide pro Cic. L. Manil. Haec omnes clarissime in Davide elucere dicat: &c.
units.tr: 1. In general, let him list the virtues necessary in a prince. Plato in the Laws requires religion, justice, and especially military skill; but it can be said more fully that five are required: piety, justice, political prudence, fortitude, and love of subjects. See Cicero's Pro Lege Manilia. Let him say that all of these shine most clearly in David, etc.

units.la: 2. In specie singulas persequatur: & quidem
units.tr: 2. Let him pursue each one individually, and indeed:

units.la: a. Pietatem: hujus a. doceat necessitatem in principe praesertim; videl. quia 1. basis omnis reip. juxta Platone. 2. quia regna à Deo sunt &c. Vide testimonia. β. In Davide illa ostendat. Videl. 1. Regnum sceleri rapere noluit, sed à Dei manu expectavit. 1. Sam. 24. & 26. punito etiam regicida. 2. Sam. 1. Aliter Caesar: si violandum jus, regnandi gratia. &c. 2. Adiit regnum autore Deo. 2. Sam. 2. & c. 5. 3. Prima cura constitutio cultus fuit. 2. Sam. 6. 7. 4. Obediens erga Prophetam Natanem. 2. Sam. 12. γ. A precibus coepit, gratiarum actione finiit praelia: passim. & 2. Sam. 22. 6. Breviter Majestatem & sceptrum Deo subjecit. Singula membra illustrentur rationibus; exemplis, similibus & contrariis. Claudatur Epiphonemate generali: scilicet: Dis te minorem quod geris imperas.
units.tr: a. Piety. Of this point a. let him teach the necessity, especially in a prince, namely because (1) it is the basis of every commonwealth, according to Plato; (2) kingdoms are from God, etc. See the testimonies. β. Let him show these things in David, namely: (1) he was unwilling to seize the kingdom by crime, but awaited it from the hand of God, 1 Sam. 24 and 26; he also punished the regicide, 2 Sam. 1. Caesar thought otherwise: if law must be violated, let it be for the sake of ruling, etc. (2) He approached the kingdom with God as its author, 2 Sam. 2 and 5. (3) His first concern was the establishment of worship, 2 Sam. 6 and 7. (4) He was obedient to the prophet Nathan, 2 Sam. 12. γ. He began with prayers and ended his battles with thanksgiving, passim, and 2 Sam. 22. (6) Briefly, he subjected majesty and sceptre to God. Each element is to be illustrated with reasons, examples, similar and contrary cases. Let it close with a general epiphonema: "You rule as one lesser than the gods, in that you rule."

units.la: δ. Justitiam. Hujus a. praemittas generalem commendationem nem; quod videlicet propter justitiam reges creati; sine illa regna latrocinia futura sunt. &c. β. Ostendas illam in Davide, tum testimonio 2.Sam.8. v.15. tum factis Davidis v. g. contra homicidam Saulis. 1.Sam. ult. Isbosethi. 2. Sam.4. Joabum homicidam toleravit, at commisit successori. 1.Reg.2. Remisit privatam vindictam Simei, at non absolvit reum, ibidem. Amplif. ex loco generis: homicidii nulla remissio. Ita & remuneravit benefacta, gratus in domum Jonathae, & Barsillai benefactorem. 2. Sam.9. 1. Reg. 2. Claudatur generali approbatione, videl. per justitiam pax Regno, & regi amor conciliatur: justitia vinculum civitatis.
units.tr: δ. Justice. For this, let him first put forward a general commendation: that kings were created on account of justice, and that without it kingdoms would be nothing but robbery, etc. β. Let him show it in David: both by the testimony of 2 Sam. 8:15, and by David's deeds, for example against the murderer of Saul, 1 Sam. last chapter, and against Ish-bosheth, 2 Sam. 4. He tolerated the murderer Joab, but committed him to his successor, 1 Kings 2. He remitted the private vengeance of Shimei, but did not acquit the guilty man, ibid. Amplify from the topic of the kind: there is no remission for homicide. So too he rewarded good deeds, showing gratitude to the house of Jonathan and to Barzillai his benefactor, 2 Sam. 9; 1 Kings 2. Close with a general approval: justice brings peace to the kingdom and wins love for the king; justice is the bond of the state.

units.la: Prudentiam. Accedatur per transitionem: Primo necessitas ejus in principe doceatur; Non haec tantum sed & alia requiri; & prudentia politicam: Testimonio Solomonis. 2.Reg.3. v. 9. Ratio addatur a difficultate regnandi & variis regni negotiis, & encomiis prudentiae politicae: videl hanc cynosuram in mari politico. Ostendatur illa in Davide 1. Quod regnum non sine solemni inauguratione adiit: hinc scilicet pendere obsequium subditorum & benevolentiam. 2. Glisscentes initio regni factiones avertit. 3. Aulam prudenter constituit, ex personis togatis & militaribus, politicis & Ecclesiasticis selectis. vide Psalm. 2.Sam.8.v.16.17.18. 2.Sam. 23. Locus communis de aula & Consiliis principum. 4. Concordiam quaesivit cum vicinis. 2.Sam.10. unde tranquillitas & commercia. 5. Hostibus initio regni se opposuit, & ipsam Metropolin Zionem invasit. 2.Sam.5. 6. Regno de sapienti successore prospexit. 1.Reg.1. Claudatur admiratione: & felices praedicet subditos cum regina Aethiopiae. Illustrentur singula ex loco generis & comparatione dissimili Tiberii, qui sagax fuit, ad propriam amplitudinem & regni detrimentum.
units.tr: Prudence. Let him approach it by transition: first, teach its necessity in a prince; that not only this but other qualities are required, and political prudence, by the testimony of Solomon, 1 Kings 3:9. Add a reason drawn from the difficulty of ruling and the many affairs of the kingdom, and the praises of political prudence, namely that it is the guiding star in the political sea. Show it in David: (1) he did not take up the kingdom without a solemn inauguration, since obedience and the goodwill of subjects depend on this; (2) he turned aside the factions that were stirring at the beginning of his reign; (3) he prudently constituted his court, choosing men both of the gown and of the sword, political and ecclesiastical men; see Psalm, 2 Sam. 8:16–18, and 2 Sam. 23. A commonplace on the court and the councils of princes. (4) He sought concord with his neighbours, 2 Sam. 10, whence came tranquillity and commerce. (5) He opposed his enemies at the beginning of his reign and himself invaded the metropolis Zion, 2 Sam. 5. (6) He provided for the kingdom a wise successor, 1 Kings 1. Close with admiration, and call the subjects happy, as the queen of Ethiopia did. Illustrate each point from the topic of the kind, and by dissimilar comparison with Tiberius, who was shrewd for his own aggrandisement and to the detriment of the kingdom.

units.la: Fortitudine. α. Evincatur ejus necessitas in rege ob assidua regnorum pericula, internas seditiones & externa bella; itemque ob molem imperii. β. Praedicetur in Davide. 1. quod mortuo Saule intrepide oblatum regnum spretis aemulis acceptaverit; fretus Deo, licet grave novisset coronae onus. Nil desperandum Deo duce. 2. Quod irritatos hostes fortiter ter aggressus sit. vide 1.Sam.5. & 8. & jam ante strenuè gestis publice notus; Locus Communis de virtutis bellicæ necessitate in principe. Ipse Deus Dominum exercituum se dicit, Frustra sceptrum affectat, qui gladium metuit. &c. 3. Rebellionem masculè compescuit, etiam in ipsis liberis. 2.Sam. 20. & c.5. &c. 4. Grandævus cordato consilio motibus Adoniæ se opposuit. 1.Reg.1, animosi leonis iftar, qui & recubans terribilis est. Claudatur allegatione causæ primæ; scilicet Deum esse qui gladio accingit reges & discingit.
units.tr: Fortitude. α. Prove its necessity in a king from the constant dangers to kingdoms, from internal sedition and external wars, and likewise from the vastness of the empire. β. Proclaim it in David: (1) that after Saul's death he accepted the kingdom when it was offered, fearlessly scorning his rivals, trusting in God, although he knew the weight of the crown was heavy; nothing is to be despaired of with God as leader. (2) That he bravely attacked the enemies who had been provoked, three times; see 1 Sam. 5 and 8, and he was already publicly known for his valiant deeds. A commonplace on the necessity of martial virtue in a prince: God Himself calls Himself the Lord of hosts; he aspires to the sceptre in vain who fears the sword, etc. (3) He manfully suppressed rebellion, even among his own sons, 2 Sam. 20 and 5, etc. (4) Though aged, he opposed the movements of Adonijah with sound counsel, 1 Kings 1, like a spirited lion, which is terrible even when lying down. Close with an appeal to the First Cause: God is the one who girds kings with the sword and ungirds them.

units.la: ε. Amorē erga subditos & clementiā. α. In genere hujus astruatur momentum: quia scilicet hoc vinculum est regnorum ac rerumpublicarum. Illustretur exemplo patris erga liberos. Hinc patres patriæ, hinc pastores, nutricios dici reges, hinc Deos, β. Prædicetur in Davide. I. Erga ipsam domum Saulis 2.Sam.9. aliosque rebelles. 2.Sam.19. II. Erga regnum, dum furere maluit coram Absolomo, quam periculo exponere subditos. 2. Reg. 5. 15. III. Maluit perire filium Absolomum, quam regnum sub invasore. 2.Sam.18. IV. Sollicitus fuit in caritate annonæ. 2.Sam 21. Maluit puniri & perire pro populo 2. Sam. ult. Claudatur exclamatione pathetica, & repetitis breviter virtutibus regiis Davidem ipsiusque sectatores extolle; merito Patres ac Deos dici pios reges.
units.tr: epsilon. Love towards subjects and clemency. alpha. In general, establish the importance of this, because it is the bond of kingdoms and commonwealths. Illustrate it by the example of a father towards his children. Hence kings are called fathers of the fatherland, shepherds, nurturers, and hence even gods. beta. Proclaim it in David. I. Towards the very house of Saul, 2 Sam. 9, and other rebels, 2 Sam. 19. II. Towards the kingdom, when he chose to flee before Absalom rather than expose his subjects to danger, 2 Sam. 15. III. He preferred that his son Absalom perish rather than the kingdom fall under an invader, 2 Sam. 18. IV. He was anxious about the scarcity of grain, 2 Sam. 21. He preferred to be punished and to die for the people, 2 Sam. last chapter. Close with a pathetic exclamation, briefly repeating the royal virtues, and extol David and his followers; rightly are pious kings called fathers and gods.

units.la: III. Invehatur.
units.tr: III. Invehatur.

units.la: 1. In Tyrannos & degeneres, qui Tiberios, Heliogabalos, Nerones, simulatores, guloncs, crudeles potius, quam hosce tales Davides, Solomones, Hiskias, Josias, Constantinos, Theodosios, Carolos Magnos, sospitatores & delicias humani generis imitari volunt.
units.tr: 1. Against tyrants and degenerate rulers, who prefer to imitate Tiberius, Heliogabalus, Nero, the dissemblers, the gluttons and the cruel, rather than these good men, the Davids, Solomons, Hezekiahs, Josiahs, Constantines, Theodosiuses and Charlemagnes, the saviours and darlings of the human race.

units.la: 2. In Machiavellum, & sequaces, qui principem formare non erubuit, divini & humani juris negligentem, non populi salutem, sed suam tantum magnitudinem curantem. Quasi regnum & resp. sine scelere administrari non possit, cum per virtutes geri debeat.
units.tr: 2. Against Machiavelli and his followers, who did not blush to shape a prince who neglects divine and human law and cares not for the safety of the people but only for his own greatness, as if a kingdom or commonwealth could not be administered without crime, when it ought to be governed by virtues.

units.la: 3. In illos, qui malos principes intuentes, ipsum regnum, ipsam majestatem oderunt & blasphemant, quæ tamen a Deo, & Dei imago ac radius ad salutem humani generis.
units.tr: 3. Against those who, looking at wicked princes, hate and blaspheme the kingdom itself and majesty itself, which nevertheless comes from God, and is the image and ray of God for the salvation of the human race.

units.la: Conclus. Desinat in laudem omnis legitimæ potestatis. 2. In votum, ut princeps & magistratus sacros potius heroes, quam pessimos Tiberios & Neroncs intueantur atque imitentur.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let it end in praise of every lawful authority. 2. A prayer that the prince and the magistrate may look upon and imitate holy heroes rather than the most wicked Tiberiuses and NEROS.

units.la: XVIII. LAUS AUGUSTI.
units.tr: XVIII. The Praise of Augustus.

units.la: Exord. Ex Loco Communi: Deum, cum magna molitur excitare viros magnos. Probetur 1. ratione: quia non immediate, sed per media Deus mundum regit: videl. uti naturam inferioris per astrorum influxum; ita regna & respubl. per Heroes & Magnates. 2. Exemplis sacris, profanis, & in specie ipsius Augusti, quem excitarit, cum ultimam Monarchiam fundare vellet, virum tantæ rei maximè idoneum.
units.tr: Exord. From a common topic: God, when he is about to raise up great men, brings about great things. Let this be proved: (1) by reason, because God governs the world not immediately but through means, namely, as he governs the nature of lower things through the influence of the stars, so he governs kingdoms and commonwealths through heroes and great men; (2) by examples, sacred and profane, and in particular that of Augustus himself, whom he raised up when he wished to found the last monarchy, a man most fitted for so great a task.

units.la: Propos. Cujus proinde laudes licet non pro dignitate dicere decreveris.
units.tr: Propos. Therefore, although you have decided that his praises cannot be spoken in full measure, you will nevertheless speak them.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: 1. Veluti per transitionem dicat de splendore natalium, & omine per Theogenem Astrologum. Scilicet talia magnum momentum habere ad imperium; maximè si alta indoles ac nativa virtus, accesserit: quæ breviter ostende in Augusto, & ex loco generis illustra.
units.tr: 1. Let him speak, as it were in passing, of the splendour of his birth and of the omen given by the astrologer Theogenes. That is to say, such things carry great weight for empire, especially if a lofty disposition and innate virtue have been added; show this briefly in Augustus, and draw it from the illustrious character of his family.

units.la: II. Laudet educationem & studia privata; in civitate Apollonia, & per totam vitam in omnibus artibus & eloquentia. Exaggeretur 1. a raritate in magnatibus. 2. a necessitate in viro principe; cui salus reipublicæ commissa. Addat de morum suavitate, temperantia & modestia ex Plutarcho & commendet ex Loco Communi: amplificetque a contrariis, noxiis præcipue regentibus. Adde pathos admirationis à sublimi fortuna principum.
units.tr: II. Let him praise his upbringing and private studies: at Apollonia, and throughout his whole life, in all the arts and in eloquence. Let it be magnified (1) by the rarity of such things among the great, and (2) by the necessity of such things in a prince, to whom the safety of the commonwealth is entrusted. Let him add something on the gentleness of his manners, his temperance and modesty, drawing on Plutarch, and recommend it from a common topic; and let him amplify it by the contraries, chiefly the harm done by rulers. Add a pathos of admiration arising from the lofty fortune of princes.

units.la: III. Prædicet virtutes politicas ac actiones heroicas bellicas:
units.tr: III. Let him proclaim his political virtues and his heroic deeds in war:

units.la: 1. Magnanimitatem ac fortitudinem, dum a. parricidas & reliquias Pompejanas persecutus est. b. Imperium tam vastum ac fluctuans post Jul. Cæs. post maturam deliberationem aggressus est. c. Provincias Angliam, Galliam, Hispaniam fortiter pacavit. Item Siciliam, Græciam, Asiam, Armeniā, Germaniam. Exaggeretur a statu imperii tunc temporis. A contrariis: frustra augustis niti natalibus, quibus angusta mens est; instar Phaetontis territi cum vastum cœli ambitum contemplatus esset.
units.tr: 1. Magnanimity and courage, in that (a) he pursued the parricides and the remnants of the Pompeian party; (b) he undertook an empire so vast and unsettled after Julius Caesar, after mature deliberation; (c) he bravely pacified the provinces of Britain, Gaul and Spain; likewise Sicily, Greece, Asia, Armenia and Germany. Let it be magnified by the state of the empire at that time. By the contraries: it is in vain that a mind of narrow compass strives for august birth, like Phaethon, terrified when he had surveyed the vast circuit of the heavens.

units.la: 2. Moderationem animi, dum a. consultavit de deponendo principatu, recusavit dictaturam. Exaggerentur à contrario: ambitu animi humani. b. Inimicis remisit offensam & clementia temperavit victoriam. Exaggerentur à raritate hujus virtutis in summa fortuna.
units.tr: 2. Moderation of spirit, in that (a) he consulted about laying down the principate, and refused the dictatorship. Let it be magnified by the contrary: the ambition of the human mind. (b) He remitted the offence to his enemies and tempered his victory with clemency. Let it be magnified by the rarity of this virtue in the highest fortune.

units.la: Hinc transeat ad virtutes togatas, illasque in genere præferat bellicis: in specie vero prædicet.
units.tr: Hence let him pass to the civil virtues, and in general prefer them to the military; but in particular let him proclaim:

units.la: Prudentiam, dum a. nomina ambitiosa detrectavit, principis contentus. Locus Communis contra ambitiosos titulos.
units.tr: Prudence, in that (a) he rejected ambitious titles, being content with the name of prince. A common topic against ambitious titles.

units.la: b. Veterem reliquit Senatus ordinem. Locus Communis contra novitates in Rep.
units.tr: (b) He left the ancient order of the Senate intact. A common topic against innovations in the commonwealth.

units.la: c. Pacem post bellum diuturum reddidit. Clauso Jani scilicet templo pax est.
units.tr: (c) He restored peace after a long war. Namely, peace comes when the temple of Janus is closed.

units.la: d. Rem publicam & privatam per leges varias restituit. Loc. de legum necessitate & utilitate.
units.tr: (d) He restored the public and private affairs of the state through various laws. A common topic on the necessity and usefulness of laws.

units.la: e. Calumnias sprevit. Scilicet regum est benefaciendo male audire.
units.tr: (e) He despised calumnies. Namely, it is the lot of kings to be ill spoken of for doing good.

units.la: f. Omnibus benefecit. Vide Tacitum ab initio. Locus de bonitate & Clementia principum.
units.tr: (f) He did good to all. See Tacitus from the beginning. A topic on the goodness and clemency of princes.

units.la: Conclus. Mors sera & placida referatur: extollat ipsius laudes: ad virtutum imitationem Principes exhortetur.
units.tr: Conclus. Let his death be recounted as late and peaceful; let him extol his praises and exhort princes to imitate his virtues.

units.la: XIX. LAUS MOSIS.
units.tr: XIX. The Praise of Moses.

units.la: Exord. Ab exemplo veterum: non sine causa memoriam heroum sacram habuere veteres. Ratio: quia reip. profuerunt, & quia in iis tanquam in speculo virtutum documenta elucent. Applicatio: Nos igitur merito viros sanctos, & inter illos Mosen, optimum & Virum & Legislatorem admiramur & prædicamus. Ratio: quia non uni Reip. sed orbi universo sanctissimis legibus profuit.
units.tr: Exordium. From the example of the ancients: the ancients were not without reason accustomed to keep the memory of heroes sacred. The reason: because they benefited the commonwealth, and because in them the lessons of virtue shine forth as in a mirror. Application: we therefore rightly admire and proclaim holy men, and among them Moses, the best both of men and of lawgivers. The reason: because he benefited not a single commonwealth but the whole world by his most holy laws.

units.la: Propositio. Hunc igitur tanquam perfectum omnis virtutis exemplar & sanctissimum Legislatorem proponam. Fiat stipulatio attentionis.
units.tr: Proposition. I will therefore set forth this man as a perfect pattern of every virtue and as the most holy lawgiver. Let the attention be secured.

units.la: Tractatio exponat
units.tr: Treatment, to set out:

units.la: I. Nativitatem & educationem. Exod. 2. Ubi notandum 1. quod natus ex electa tribu Levi. 2. sub gravissima afflictione Israelitarum. 3. occultatus & expositus jam morti. 4. Servatus mirabiliter & educatus in aula regis. Illustrentur haec translatione ad thesin, de fatis virorum illustrium: qui mirabiliter a Deo conservantur & evehantur. Ita Noah ex diluvio, Loth ex incendio. Adde exempla Cyri, Romuli; tandemque Davidis & ipsius Christi.
units.tr: I. His birth and upbringing (Exod. 2). Here note: (1) that he was born of the chosen tribe of Levi; (2) under the most severe affliction of the Israelites; (3) that he was hidden and exposed, already in peril of death; (4) that he was miraculously preserved and brought up in the royal court. Let these points be illustrated by a comparison with the thesis concerning the fates of illustrious men, who are miraculously preserved and raised up by God. So Noah from the flood, Lot from the burning. Add the examples of Cyrus and Romulus, and finally of David and of Christ himself.

units.la: II. Vitam ipsam
units.tr: II. His life itself.

units.la: 1. Privatam; ubi a. visitavit & vindicavit fratres Israelitas. Admireris motum heroicum, quo spreta aula, abjectos fratres non sprevit; exemplum humilitatis. b. In exilium abiit & opilionem egit, scilicet per aspera ad ardua. Illustretur exemplo Davidis, &c.
units.tr: 1. His private life, where (a) he visited and avenged his Israelite brothers. Admire the heroic impulse by which, having scorned the court, he did not scorn his lowly brothers: an example of humility. (b) He went into exile and tended sheep, that is, from rough ways to lofty heights. Let it be illustrated by the example of David, etc.

units.la: 2. Vitam publicam, ubi a. Vocatio miraculosa, ut ex pastore pecudum, ductor populi efficeretur; admireris modestiam, qua declinavit munus oblatum, quod alii cupide ambiunt. b. Acta cum Pharaone, quae breviter in genere refer per praeteritionem & extolle magnanimitatem. c. Ductus populi per mare rubrum ad montem Sinai. Extollas fidem & constantiam, qua Deum secutus nihil timuit. d. Formatio Reip. omnium sanctissimae per Lationem legis loquente ad ipsum coelitus Deo. Scilicet hinc bonarum legum originem esse; frustra allegante Lycurgo, Numa, Deum autorem legum suarum. Digressio hic fiat in laudem Reip. Judaicae & Legis Mosaicae, qua sacra, publica, privata sanctissime ordinata sunt. Illustrentur comparatione cum Rep. Spartana & Legibus Lycurgi, itemq; Solonis & nata inde lege xii. tab. in quibus naevi plurimi. e. Administratio Reipubl. per 40. annos in deserto magna cum molestia; ubi praedices ipsius patientiam & longanimitatem.
units.tr: 2. His public life, where (a) there was his miraculous calling, so that from a shepherd of flocks he became the leader of the people. Admire the modesty by which he declined the office offered him, which others eagerly seek. (b) His dealings with Pharaoh, which you should relate briefly in general terms by passing over them, and extol his magnanimity. (c) The leading of the people through the Red Sea to Mount Sinai. Extol the faith and constancy by which, following God, he feared nothing. (d) The formation of the most holy of commonwealths through the giving of the law, God speaking to him from heaven. From this, clearly, comes the origin of good laws, though Lycurgus and Numa falsely claimed God as the author of their laws. A digression may be made here in praise of the Jewish commonwealth and the Mosaic law, by which sacred, public and private matters were most holily ordered. Let them be illustrated by comparison with the Spartan commonwealth and the laws of Lycurgus, likewise those of Solon and the Twelve Tables derived from them, in which there are very many blemishes. (e) The government of the commonwealth for forty years in the wilderness, amid great hardship; here you should point out his patience and long-suffering.

units.la: III. Vitae exitum, ubi 1. antecedens solennis legis repetitio & populi in Lege adjuratio. vide Deut. 27. 28. Laudes hic ipsius zelu & fidelitatem, qua pro gloria Dei & salute populi, non pro sua domo fuit sollicitus. Illustres oppositione aliorum principum. 2. Mortem ipsam & sepulturam a Deo ipsi procuratam. Hic finem habuit ipsius molestia; at Dictator manet etiamnum cunctis gentibus in lege sua praecipiens.
units.tr: III. The end of his life, where (1) there was the solemn repetition of the law beforehand and the people's oath to the law (see Deut. 27, 28). Here praise his zeal and fidelity, by which he was concerned for the glory of God and the salvation of the people, not for his own house. Let them be made illustrious by contrast with other princes. (2) His death itself and his burial, arranged by God for him. Here his toil came to an end; yet as lawgiver he remains even now, instructing all nations through his law.

units.la: XX. COMMENDATIO ALEXANDRI MAGNI JUXTA GENERA VIRTUTUM.
units.tr: XX. A COMMENDATION OF ALEXANDER THE GREAT ACCORDING TO THE KINDS OF VIRTUE.

units.la: vid. Curt. præcip. lib. 10. c. 5. & Just. 11. 12. & Plut.
units.tr: See Curtius, the Praecepta, book 10, chapter 5, and Justin 11.12, and Plutarch.

units.la: Exord. Attentionem conciliet à materiæ dignitate per simile: videl. quod sol inter sidera, aurum inter metalla, gemmæ inter lapides; hoc heroes esse inter homines. Amplif. ulteriori similitudinis expositione, videl. uti illa miramur & magnificamus; ita & horum memoriam. Accommodetur ad hypothesin, videl. inter veteres heroes vix ullum majorem Alexandro ex rebus gestis Magno cognominato, cujus licet vita tota eximia, te tamen summa capita tantum longe impari stylo persecuturum.
units.tr: Exordium. Win attention by the dignity of the subject, through a comparison: namely, that as the sun is among the stars, gold among metals, and gems among stones, so heroes are among men. Amplify by a fuller exposition of the comparison: that just as we admire and magnify those things, so we should also admire and magnify the memory of these men. Apply this to the hypothesis: that among the heroes of old there is hardly any greater than Alexander, surnamed the Great, from his deeds; whose whole life, though outstanding, you will nevertheless pursue only in its chief points, and in a style far unequal to it.

units.la: Propos. Missis reliquis commendaturum te ipsius virtutes Imperatorias Prudentiam, justitiam, fortitudinem & temperantiam; ut in ipso perfecti principis imago elucescat. Addatur petitio attentionis.
units.tr: Proposition. Setting the rest aside, you will commend his imperial virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance, so that in him the image of a perfect prince may shine forth. Add a request for attention.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. In genere de causis tantarum virtutum dicat: videl. quòd ex magnis parentibus ortus, sub Magno Aristotele educatus, & à Deo fundator tertiæ Monarchiæ destinatus sit. Hæc esse dicat unde viri magni existere solent; uti magnæ arbores ex bono semine per culturam & cœlestem influentiam excrescunt.
units.tr: I. Under the general heading, speak of the causes of such great virtues: namely, that he was born of great parents, was educated under the great Aristotle, and was destined by God to be the founder of the third monarchy. Say that these are the things from which great men usually arise, just as great trees grow from good seed through cultivation and heavenly influence.

units.la: II. In specie virtutes singulas persequere, & quidem 1. fontem omnium prædicet pietatem, qua nihil ortus est sine præviis sacris.
units.tr: II. Pursue the individual virtues in particular, and first proclaim piety as the source of them all, since nothing arises without prior sacred things.

units.la: 1. Prudentiam: hanc a. Laudes tanquam necessariam principi, utpote qui velut oculus & nauclerus regni totius, qui instar solis omnia obire tenetur. b. In Alexandro illam ostende & prædica ex rebus gestis, cum Bucephalo, legatis Persicis, in præsidio & bello, audiendo consilio prudentum: in genere ex eo, quod tantum imperium in obedientia tenuit.
units.tr: 1. Prudence. Here (a) praise it as necessary for a prince, since he is, as it were, the eye and pilot of the whole kingdom, and is bound to go round everything like the sun. (b) Show and proclaim it in Alexander from his deeds: with Bucephalus, in the Persian embassies, in garrison and in war, in hearing the counsel of the wise; in general, from the fact that he kept so great an empire in obedience.

units.la: 2. Justitiam, quam præmissa transitione a. ostendat in Alexander ex eo quod ultus est percussorem patris, matrem in honore habuit, praeceptoribus dignam referri gratiam non posse dixit, unde Aristotelē & Leonidem magno praemio affecit; munificus in milites, in jure reddendo æquus fuit, alteram aurem servans reo, in hostes minime sævus; imprimis hic praedicetur humanitas erga familiam Darii. b.Per apostrophum ad ipsum regem de necessitate hujus virtutis in tanto rege disserat; videl. optime novisti rex inclyte, regnum viribus quidem acquiri posse, sed non nisi justitia retineri. vide Locos Communes.
units.tr: 2. Justice. After a suitable transition, (a) show it in Alexander: from the fact that he avenged the murderer of his father, held his mother in honour, said that a favour received from his teachers could not be repaid, and therefore rewarded Aristotle and Leonidas with great gifts; generous to the soldiers, fair in administering justice, keeping one ear free for the accused, and by no means cruel to enemies; above all, his humanity towards the family of Darius is to be praised here. (b) By an apostrophe to the king himself, discourse on the necessity of this virtue in so great a king: namely, "You best know, renowned king, that a kingdom can indeed be acquired by strength, but cannot be kept except by justice." See the Common Places.

units.la: Conclus. loco, dicat reliquum esse, ut & fortitudinem & moderationem ipsius in tanta fortuna praedicet; sed nimio virtutum ejus fulgore oculos obstringi, ideo successori praeconium reliquarum virtutum relinquendum; Merito nos beatum praedicare regnum, cui rex tam sapiens, tam justus praefuit.
units.tr: Conclusion. In place, say that it remains for him to praise both his fortitude and his moderation in so great a fortune; but that the eyes are dazzled by the excessive brilliance of his virtues, and therefore the proclamation of the remaining virtues must be left to his successor. Deservedly do we proclaim that kingdom happy, which was ruled by a king so wise and so just.

units.la: XXI. DE ALEXANDRI FORTITUDINE ET MODERATIONE.
units.tr: XXI. ALEXANDER'S FORTITUDE AND MODERATION.

units.la: Exord. Ex Loco Communi de difficultate servandi mediocritatem in magna fortuna. Probetur exemplo Nabuchodonosoris & Xerxis. Unde tanto magis praedicandi Principes moderati, qualis Augustus aliique & ipse Alexander Magnus, cujus antecessor prudentiam & justitiam laudarit;
units.tr: Introduction. On the common topic of the difficulty of keeping to moderation in great fortune. Let it be proved by the examples of Nebuchadnezzar and Xerxes. Hence all the more reason to praise moderate princes, such as Augustus and others, and Alexander the Great himself, whose predecessor had praised his prudence and justice.

units.la: Propositio. Ejus te magnanimitatem & moderationem exornaturum, ut pateat quantus vir fuerit, quiin tanta fortuna, fortuna se superiorem ostendit: fiat petitio attentionis.
units.tr: Proposition. I will set forth his magnanimity and moderation, so that it may be seen what a man he was, who, in such great fortune, showed himself superior to fortune. Let attention be requested.

units.la: Tractatio agat de ipsius
units.tr: Treatment. Let the discussion concern his

units.la: I. Fortitudine Hic 1. de ejusdē necessitate in principe dicatur in genere. 2. Ostendatur illa in Alexandro, & quidem primo toga-ta, qua sprevit assentatores & calumniatores, soli studuit famæ, non indulsit affectibus, in regno dignissimum succedere voluit. Deinde militaris, quæ emicuit in ipsa pueritia, dum doluit de patris victoriis, non nisi cum regibus voluit certare: exseruit se in adolescentia & juventute, in tot bellis & præliis quorum quædam alleganda. Claudatur admiratione pathetica.
units.tr: I. Fortitude. Here (1) it is to be said in general that this virtue is necessary in a prince. (2) It is to be shown in Alexander, and first his civil fortitude: he spurned flatterers and slanderers, pursued only fame, did not give way to the passions, and wished to succeed to the kingdom in a manner worthy of it. Then his military fortitude, which shone forth already in boyhood, when he grieved over his father's victories and would contend only with kings; it showed itself in his adolescence and youth, in so many wars and battles, some of which must be cited. Let it be concluded with a passionate exclamation of admiration.

units.la: II. De moderatione, fiat transitio: videl. per reliquas virtutes alios, per hanc semetipsū superasse Alex. qui regibus omnibus illustris, exemplo propositus. Praedicetur haec virtus ex historia. videl.1. Adolescentiam sobrie & caste egit.2. Darii uxorem & filios caste & humanissime habuit. Exaggerentur hæc comparatione cum moribus aulicis, ubi ebrietas & luxuria. 3. Moderate usus est victoriis. 4. Sprevit opes, & lautitias: quibus plus æquo addictum mortale genus. Addatur Epiphonema: hisce tantis virtutibus principem gentilem multos Christianos vincere.
units.tr: II. On moderation, let there be a transition: namely, that Alexander surpassed others in the other virtues, but in this one he surpassed himself; he is famous above all kings and is set forth as an example. This virtue is to be praised from his history, namely: (1) he spent his youth soberly and chastely; (2) he treated the wife and children of Darius chastely and most humanely, and this is to be heightened by comparison with the manners of courts, where there is drunkenness and luxury; (3) he used his victories with moderation; (4) he spurned riches and luxuries, to which the mortal race is too much given over. Let an epiphonema be added: that a pagan prince, by such great virtues, surpasses many Christians.

units.la: Perorat. 1. Per admirationem sumnatim repetat præconium virtutum ipsius. 2. Usum addat; videl. talia exempla calcar esse debere ad virtutem summis & infimis; & cogitandum illud Servatoris. Regina austri surget & condemnabit generationum hanc in novissimo die.
units.tr: Peroration. (1) Through admiration, let him briefly repeat the praise of his virtues. (2) Let him add a use: namely, that such examples ought to be a spur to virtue for high and low alike; and let the words of the Saviour be considered: "The queen of the south shall rise up and condemn this generation in the last day."

units.la: XXII. ALEXANDRI VITUPERATIO.
units.tr: XXII. An Invective against Alexander.

units.la: Exord. A virtutum gentilium imperfectione. Proponatur per simile a flamma, quæ non sine fumo surgit; ita nec virtutes gentilium sine vitiis. Probetur inductione quadam. Amplif. a causa, quæ fuit, tum cæcitas mentis, tum perversitas voluntatis ob philautiam gentilium. Applicetur ad Alexandrum, quem antecessores laudarint tanquam principem optimum.
units.tr: Exordium. From the imperfection of pagan virtues. It is set out by a comparison with a flame, which does not rise without smoke; so the virtues of the Gentiles are not without vices. It is proved by a kind of induction. It is amplified from the cause, which was both blindness of mind and perversity of will arising from the self-love of the Gentiles. It is applied to Alexander, whom his predecessors praised as an excellent prince.

units.la: Propos. Te vitia ejus enormia detecturum, ne sub umbra virtutis decipiant.
units.tr: Proposition. That you will expose his enormous vices, lest under the shadow of virtue they deceive.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Concedat illi omnia ista, quæ antecessores in ipso admirati sunt, & sic amoveat suspicionem invidiæ, calumniæ. Sed alia esse quæ in ipso vituperanda.
units.tr: Treatment. I. Let him grant Alexander all those qualities which his predecessors admired in him, and so remove the suspicion of envy and calumny. But there are other things in him that deserve censure.

units.la: II. Redarguat vitia, videl.
units.tr: II. Let him refute the vices, namely:

units.la: 1. Vanitatem & fastum in ipso puero, dum metuit ne pater omnem gloriæ materiam ipsi præriperet; in juvene; dum 1. unus mundus ipsi non sufficit; 2. dum Jovis filiù se dicit, adorari cupit; habitum & diadema Persicū capit spreto patrio. Exagitates hic fœdam superbiā regibus maxime noxiam & exosam cum exprobatione Alexandri, quòd Aristotelis præcepta oblivioni tradiderit.
units.tr: 1. Vanity and arrogance: in the boy himself, when he feared that his father would snatch from him every material for glory; in the young man, when (1) the one world was not enough for him, and (2) when he called himself the son of Jupiter and wished to be worshipped, and took the Persian dress and diadem, scorning his native custom. Here he should lash the foul pride, most harmful and hateful in kings, with a reproach to Alexander for having consigned Aristotle's precepts to oblivion.

units.la: 2. Crudelitatem: Hic 1. concedat ipsi moderationem in prima ætate. 2. detestetur degenerationem, rigorem in milites, & tyrannidem in Parmenionem, Philotam, Ajuntam, Attalum, Paufaniam, Clytum, Callisthenem, Lysimachum, vide Curtium. Exaggera haec oppositione officii regii, quod jure, non affectu agi debet.
units.tr: 2. Cruelty: here let him (1) concede to Alexander moderation in his early age; (2) let him detest the degeneration, the harshness toward soldiers, and the tyranny against Parmenion, Philotas, Hagnon, Attalus, Pausanias, Clitus, Callisthenes, and Lysimachus; see Curtius. Amplify these by contrast with the duty of a king, which ought to be exercised by right, not by passion.

units.la: 3. Luxum & intemperantiam in Venere & gula, praesertim postquam Asia potitus fuerat. Exaggeranda haec a felicitate horum vitiorum, maximè in rege, orbis domitore, si ipse à vitiis superetur.
units.tr: 3. Luxury and intemperance in love and gluttony, especially after he had gained possession of Asia. These are to be magnified by setting them against the good fortune of such vices, above all in a king, conqueror of the world, if he himself is overcome by vices.

units.la: III. Extenuet virtutes ab antecessoribus ipsi arrogatas, tanquam corruptas hisce vitiis.
units.tr: III. Let him diminish the virtues ascribed to Alexander by his predecessors, as if they were corrupted by these vices.

units.la: Conclus. 1. Moneat ne splendore majestatis occæcati, vitia magnatum pro virtutibus complectantur. 2. Laudet fortunam moderatam, ubi minus periculi: merito ipsum periisse apud Thessalum medicum ex potu.
units.tr: Conclusion. 1. Let him warn that men blinded by the splendour of majesty should not embrace the vices of the great in place of virtues. 2. Let him praise a moderate fortune, where there is less danger; and rightly, that Alexander perished from a drink given him by the Thessalian physician.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Dispositio orationis habitæ in obitum Serenissimi Principis Hassiæ WILHELMI. Anno 1663.
units.tr: Arrangement of an oration delivered at the death of the Most Serene Prince of Hesse, WILHELM, in the year 1663.

units.la: Exord. Affectum prodat tristitiæ ex collatione spei conceptæ, & secutæ frustrationis. Hoc
units.tr: Exordium. He should reveal his grief by setting the hope that was conceived against the disappointment that followed. This is done as follows:

units.la: I. Proponatur: Sed frustra fuit, ô mea Hassia, frustra fuit, quod de temporum tuorum felicitate tibi gratulabaris: frustra fuit, quod aurea sæcula tali sub Principe tibi pollicebaris!
units.tr: I. Let it be stated: "But in vain, O my Hesse, in vain did you congratulate yourself on the happiness of your times; in vain did you promise yourself golden ages under such a Prince!"

units.la: II. Exponatur felicitas: quod scil. ex diuturno & funesto bello toti Germaniæ fatali, veluti post nubila Phœbus, restituta pax aurea, restitutus Princeps optimus, restituta religio, justitia, fides. Unde publicum ubique gaudium & fautitas beata.
units.tr: II. Let the happiness be set out: namely, that after a long and deadly war, fatal to all Germany, peace was restored like the sun after clouds, a golden peace; that the excellent Prince was restored, and religion, justice and good faith were restored. Hence public joy everywhere and blessed prosperity.

units.la: III. Opponatur casus insperatus, mors Principis: qua ereptus dulcissimæ conjugi maritus, suavissimæ proli Parens, & patrespatriæ toti regioni. Hinc summatim virtutes ipsius prædicet: opponatque insperatam mortem: Sed eheu! occidit spes illa columenque ingens illustrissimæ domui & patriæ universæ!
units.tr: III. Let the unexpected misfortune, the death of the Prince, be set against this: by it the husband was snatched from his most beloved wife, the parent from his sweetest offspring, and the father of the fatherland from the whole region. Here he should briefly speak of the Prince's virtues and oppose to them his unexpected death: "But alas! that hope has perished, and a great pillar of the most illustrious house and of the whole fatherland!"

units.la: Propos. Impulisse dicat communem patriæ, omniumque bonorum luctum; ut loqueretur etiam ineptus; ut contestetur dolorem etiam peregrinis, quos tamen & communis causa moveat. Arte compositas orationes ambitio conscribat; Justus dolor sine arte, sine ornatu, sine fuco prodit, sine ordine erumpit. Unde excusandus sit, si de tanto Principe impar verba faciam.
units.tr: Propositio. He should say that the common grief of the fatherland and of all good people has moved him, so that even one who is unskilled might speak; that even foreigners bear witness to their sorrow, though they are moved by a common cause. Ambition may compose orations with art; just grief breaks forth without art, without ornament, without paint, without order. Hence he should ask to be excused if he speaks of so great a Prince unequal to the task.

units.la: 1. Genus & familiam. Hic a. accessum sibi sternat ex thesi: videl. cum in privatis, imò brutis virtus parentum in natis elucescat; multo magis in personis illustribus, ex puriori sanguine natis, & magnis exemplis domesticis ad magna semper excitatis. Unde raro diuturna magna dignitas in infimos lapsa. b. accedat ad hypothesin, videl. Principes Hassiae ex antiquissima prosapia ducum Brabantiae descendere, ex qua Ludovicus III. Dux Brab. primus Thuringiae & Hassiae Landgravius constitutus fuit à socero Lothario Imperatore. Dehinc Henricus Brabantinus Henrici Magnanimi filius de jure successionis in Thuringia & Hassia cum Henrico illustri Marchione Misniae bello contendit, & transactione, Thuringia Marchioni, Hassia Brabantino cessit Anno 1308. Hic conditor familiae illustris Landgraviorum Hassiae. Hinc Otto qui fratrem collegam admisit: Henricus II. ferreus. Ludovicus; Hermannus, Ludovicus Pacificus, primus comes in Zigenheim & Nidda, qui Caesar electus, recusavit magno animo; Ludovicus III. Wilhelmus, Philippus Academiae Marp: conditor, qui tumultum rusticorum suppressit, dux foederis Smalcaldici contra Carolum V. astu Albani detentus captivus Halae Saxonum, & liberatus per generum Mauritium: hujus itaque prae dicetur Zelus pro religione, qui huic haereditarius domui. Hujus filii Wilhelmus III. & Mauritius principatum diviserunt, illi Darmstadiensis huic Cassellana ditio obtigit. Mauritius princeps literatissimus & pietate ac justitia optimus. Wilhelmus libertatis & religionis assertor strenuissimus, bello Germaniae nupero notissimus heros ex hisce gentibus: Wilhelmus, cujus memoriam veneramur. Hisce per figuram praeteritionis addantur cognati materni & illustrissima affinitas per sorores cum plerisque principibus Germaniae: & claudatur quod quicquid clarum & illustre in majoribus, illud omne in hoc uno conspirasse. Hinc transeat.
units.tr: 1. Birth and family. Here a. he prepares his approach from a thesis: namely, that since in private persons, indeed even in brute animals, the virtue of parents shines forth in their offspring, so much more does it do so in illustrious persons born of purer blood and always roused to great deeds by great domestic examples. Hence great dignity rarely endures long once it has fallen to the lowest. b. He comes to the hypothesis: namely, that the Princes of Hesse descend from the most ancient stock of the dukes of Brabant, from which Louis III, Duke of Brabant, was first made Landgrave of Thuringia and Hesse by his father-in-law, the Emperor Lothair. Then Henry of Brabant, son of Henry the Magnanimous, contended in war with the illustrious Margrave Henry of Meissen over the right of succession in Thuringia and Hesse; by an agreement in 1308 Thuringia went to the Margrave and Hesse to the Brabantine. He was the founder of the illustrious family of the Landgraves of Hesse. Then Otto, who admitted his brother as co-ruler; Henry II, the Iron; Louis; Hermann; Louis the Peaceable, first count of Ziegenhain and Nidda, who, though elected Emperor, refused with great spirit; Louis III; Wilhelm; Philip, founder of the Academy of Marburg, who suppressed the peasants' uprising, leader of the Schmalkaldic League against Charles V, taken captive by the trickery of Alba and held at Halle in Saxony, and freed through his son-in-law Maurice. Of him, therefore, his zeal for religion is to be spoken of, which is hereditary in this house. His sons, Wilhelm III and Maurice, divided the principality: the former received the Darmstadt territory, the latter the Kassel domain. Maurice was a most learned prince, and excellent in piety and justice. Wilhelm, the most vigorous champion of liberty and religion, a hero most famous in the recent German war: from these stocks came Wilhelm, whose memory we revere. To these, by way of praeteritio, should be added his maternal kinsfolk and the most illustrious affinity through sisters with most of the princes of Germany; and it should be concluded that whatever was bright and illustrious in his ancestors, all of it has come together in this one man. Let us pass on from here.

units.la: 2. Ad dotes corporis animique & educationem accuratissimam per curam sapientissimam Matris Ameliae Elisabethae Comitis in Hanaw, Principis omni virtutum genere cumulatissimae, postquam Maritus maturius inter expeditiones bellicas in Fri-sia fia Orientali diem obiit. Hæc vidua non modo gravissimum bellum & fœdus cum potentissimis coronis Gallica & Suecica generose continuavit; verum etiam unicum, qui post præmaturam mortem fratris restabat, filium hunc ex consilio cordatissimi Senatus Aulici, educari curavit, & instrui iis virtutibus & artibus quibus belli pacisque tempora continentur. Illustretur Loco Communi de momento in educatione principis; quippe unde salus regionis. Adde de peregrinatione Gallica, ubi ipsius dotes aulæ regiæ cunctisque magnatibus tanquam dignissimi cum tanto rege confederati innotuere & prædicatæ sunt. Obiter tangatur quæstio, de peregrinatione principum, & affirmativam tueatur; tum ne inter gnatones aulicos domi corrumpatur ætas tenera, tum ut ipsorum dotes innotescant; tum ut mores ac consuetudines aularum exterarum videant: neque enim soli Germaniæ concessa esse omnia. Quantum profuit Philippo Macedoni patri Alex. Magni, quod Thebis per triennium domi Epaminondæ egit. vide Just. lib. 7.
units.tr: 2. His bodily and mental endowments and his most careful education, through the most wise care of his mother Amalia Elisabeth, Countess of Hanau, a princess most richly endowed with every kind of virtue, after her husband died prematurely during military campaigns in East Friesland. This widow not only nobly continued the most grievous war and the alliance with the most powerful crowns of France and Sweden, but also, on the advice of the most prudent Aulic Council, saw to it that this son, the only one left after the untimely death of his brother, was educated and instructed in those virtues and arts by which the times of war and peace are governed. Here let the common topic on the importance of a prince's education be illustrated, since the safety of the region depends on it. Add his journey to France, where his gifts became known to the royal court and to all the nobles, who joined with so great a king as most worthy men, and were praised. In passing, the question of princes' travels may be touched upon, and the affirmative defended: both so that tender youth is not corrupted at home among courtiers who flatter, and so that their gifts may become known, and so that they may see the manners and customs of foreign courts; for not everything is granted to Germany alone. How much it profited Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great, that he spent three years at Thebes in the house of Epaminondas. See Justin, book 7.

units.la: 3. Regimen auspicatissimum. Hic prædicet
units.tr: 3. His most auspicious government. Here he should praise

units.la: a. Quod redux tradente matre, regimen ipse suscepit, applaudente tota regione, & ex tali principe, nil nisi fausta omnia sibi promittente. Illustretur a contrario: videl, uti regnante impio, juxta Solomonem, gemit populus, ita contra regnante justo florent omnia. vide Ps. 72. & huc per felix augurium transfer. Videbant enim revivisere hic magnanimitatem Henrici ferrei, pacificum imperium Ludovici I. Zelum pro religione & literis Philippi; Sapientiam Wilhelmi: pietatem, justitiam, eruditionem avi Mauritii, fortitudinem & prudentiam Patris Wilhelmi, & quicquid inter illustres proavos dispersum fuerat, in hoc veluti copiæ cornu conjunctum & cumulatum providebant.
units.tr: a. That, on his return, when his mother handed over the government, he himself took it up, with the whole region applauding, and promising himself nothing but prosperity from such a prince. Let it be illustrated by the contrary: just as, under an impious ruler, the people groan, according to Solomon, so under a just ruler all things flourish. See Ps. 72. And by a happy omen he should transfer this to the present: for they saw that here the magnanimity of Henry the Iron, the peaceful rule of Louis I, the zeal for religion and letters of Philip, the wisdom of Wilhelm, the piety, justice and learning of his grandfather Maurice, the courage and prudence of his father Wilhelm, and whatever had been scattered among the illustrious ancestors, was seen to be united and heaped up in him as in a horn of plenty.

units.la: b. Studium reducendæ pacis inter arma. Hic 1. Exponatur Status imperii initio regiminis turbatissimus, dum trigesimale illud bellum Germanicum ad catastrophen inclinabat, partibus utrinque & bellum & pacem pari studio urgentibus. 2. Quomodo ipse segesserit: videl. fortiter urgens gesta feliciter hactenus à Patre & Matre arma, edoctus sub umbone clypei optioptimam fieri pacem : strenuè incussibens promotioni pacis, quæ tunc in Westphalia magna Europæ parturitione agitabatur. Hic porrò explicetur dexteritas Legatorum Hassiacorum; qui & libertati principum & religionis reformatæ præsertim, simul & saluti imperii consulendum existimarunt in gravissimo illo Europæ theatro, ubi duraturæ securitatis in sacris & profanis fundamenta jacienda in futura seculà. Scilicet coeperat feliciter Proavus Philippus agere causam Evangelii, & libertatis Germaniæ, continuavit in pace avus Mauritius, asseruit eandem armis Pater, absolvit felicissime & armis & consilio Pronepos. Scil. erat hoc felicitatis temporum tuorum heros generosissime, ut tu operi isti speratissimo finem imponeres & reduceres pacem diu desideratam! &c. jam nihil supererat, quàm ut parta pace frueris, frueretur tota ditio tua, frueretur universa Germania, Hinc explicet nuptias auspicatissimas An. 1649. cum dignissima Principe Hedevviga Sophia, Serenifsimi Electoris Brandeb. filia, cujus dotes prædicet, & par virtus in utroque, par rebus pro religione & flore patriæostendatur. Erat hoc pietatis majorum, non nisi religione reformata & virtutibus parem sibi deligere. Quid non sperandum hinc Hassiæ? quid non Ecclesiæ Reformatæ universæ; cum talis Mater Hassiæ præficeretur. Videor mihi videre egressam sedibus Hassiam ad illam recipiendam, &c.
units.tr: b. His zeal for restoring peace amid arms. Here: 1. Let the state of the realm at the beginning of his rule be set out as most troubled, while that thirty years' German war was tending towards catastrophe, both sides pressing war and peace with equal eagerness. 2. How he himself acted: namely, vigorously pressing the arms which his father and mother had until then carried on successfully, having learned that under the shield's boss the best peace is made; and energetically spurring on the promotion of peace, which was then being brought to birth with great labour for Europe in Westphalia. Here the skill of the Hessian envoys should further be explained, who judged that both the liberty of the princes, especially of the reformed religion, and the welfare of the empire had to be looked after in that most grave theatre of Europe, where the foundations of a security to last in sacred and profane matters for ages to come were to be laid. To be sure, his ancestor Philip had happily begun to plead the cause of the Gospel and of German liberty; his grandfather Maurice continued it in peace; his father asserted the same by arms; and his great-grandson completed it most happily by both arms and counsel. Indeed, this was the happiness of your times, most noble hero, that you should put an end to that most hoped-for work and bring back the peace so long desired! And so nothing remained but that, with peace won, you should enjoy it, and your whole realm should enjoy it, and all Germany should enjoy it. Here he should explain your most auspicious marriage in the year 1649 to the most worthy princess Hedwig Sophia, daughter of the Most Serene Elector of Brandenburg, and set forth her gifts, and the equal virtue of both, equal in their devotion to religion and to the welfare of the fatherland. This was the piety of their ancestors, to choose for themselves none but a match equal in reformed religion and in virtues. What could not be hoped for Hesse from this? What could not be hoped for the whole Reformed Church, since such a mother was set over Hesse? I seem to see Hesse going forth from her seats to receive her, etc.

units.la: ε. Administratio iplà: dum
units.tr: ε. The administration itself, while:

units.la: α. Optimè constituta aula, tanquam exemplar virtutum omnium.
units.tr: α. The court was most excellently ordered, as a pattern of all virtues.

units.la: β. Restituta Ecclesia refloruit, pressa hactenus hostium impetitionibus, & de eventu armorum sollicita, dum non professi modo hostes, sed & ejusdem olim causæ assertores minari videbantur. At sub hoc Principe libera rursus Evangelii vox sonuit.
units.tr: β. The Church was restored and flourished, hitherto oppressed by the assaults of enemies and anxious about the outcome of arms, while not only open enemies but also former defenders of the same cause seemed to threaten. But under this Prince the free voice of the Gospel sounded again.

units.la: γ. Restituta Academia, quæ sæviente hactenus Marte langueràt; jam rursus caput extulit, rediere Musæ diu exules, & celebris illa quondam Marpurgensis rursus pristinum decus recuperavit.
units.tr: γ. The Academy was restored, which had languished while Mars raged until then; now it raised its head again, the Muses returned after long exile, and that once famous Marburg recovered its former glory.

units.la: δ. Restitutajustitia per universam ditionem, quæ inter arma fere conticuerat: abolita onera, quibus Mars terram afflixerat: reversi exules ad pristinos lares. In summa ex sepulchro veluti decus omne, omnisque prosperitas emicuit, &c.
units.tr: δ. Justice was restored throughout the whole realm, which had fallen nearly silent amid arms; the burdens with which Mars had afflicted the land were lifted, and exiles returned to their former homes. In sum, as if from a sepulchre, all honour and all prosperity shone forth, etc.

units.la: II. Deploret subito prostratam auream hanc felicitatem; dum ex insperato tantus princeps fatis concessit. Scil. ita gaudia nostra luctus occupat. Deploretur ista rerum humanarum incertitudo; quae neminem ex asse patitur diu esse felicem. Ascendatur ad causam, peccata populi; unde calamitates publicae, quod modo per bella, modo per pestem, modo per insolitas tempestates, terrae motus, fulgura, incendia, mortes principum affligantur regiones. Omina hinc concipiat sinistra majorum malorum, exemplo Ezechiae, Josiae, quibus ereptis appropinquabat Judaeis exitium. Deploret hinc mala imminentia a Turca, qui faciliorem viam inventurus sit, si talia fulcra (quod absit) Deus Germaniae subtraxerit. Avertat orationem ad Germaniam, quod decumana vitia post recuperatam pacem ipsam urgeant, unde praeludia haec majorum malorum.
units.tr: II. He should lament that this golden happiness has been suddenly laid low, since so great a prince has died unexpectedly by fate. Thus grief seizes our joys. Let him bewail this uncertainty of human affairs, which never allows anyone to be wholly happy for long. Let him go on to the cause, the sins of the people, from which public calamities afflict the regions: now by war, now by plague, now by unusual storms, earthquakes, lightning, fires, and the deaths of princes. From this let him draw ominous forecasts of greater evils, after the example of Hezekiah and Josiah, with whose removal ruin drew near to the Jews. Let him lament from this the evils threatening from the Turk, who would find an easier path if God were to withdraw (which God forbid) such supports from Germany. Let him turn his speech to Germany, because the chief vices press on her even after peace has been recovered, and these are the preludes of greater evils.

units.la: III. Spem rursus concipiat
units.tr: III. Let him again conceive hope:

units.la: 1. Ex superstite conjuge optima; quae capax sustinere molem Regiminis: illo praesertim obtinente Consilio, quod prudentissimus Princeps ex optimis & flore regionis sibi legit.
units.tr: 1. From the surviving consort, most excellent, who is capable of bearing the weight of government, especially with that Council which the most prudent Prince has chosen for himself from the best men and the flower of the land.

units.la: 2. Ex liberis relictis: cum praeter filias principes Carolottam & Louisam, triplici prole mascula, Wilhelmo, Carolo, Philippo, ceu dignissimis fulcris Serenissima domus innitatur: ex quibus primogenitus Wilhelmus jam duodecimum agens annum, paternarum uti virtutum, ita & regiminis haeres suo tempore Illustrissimum ac Optimum Dominum Parentem, uti nomine, ita & vita ac moribus repraesentabit.
units.tr: 2. From the children left behind: since, besides the princesses Charlotte and Louisa, the Most Serene House rests upon a threefold male offspring, Wilhelm, Charles and Philip, as most worthy supports. Of these, the firstborn Wilhelm, now in his twelfth year, will in due time inherit his father's virtues and his government, and will represent the most illustrious and excellent Lord Father in name, and in life and manners as well.

units.la: Conclus. Finiat in fausto hoc omine & serenissimae Matri solatium, illustrissimis liberis omnem prosperitatem pacemque ditioni veat.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him end with this auspicious omen, and as a consolation to the most serene Mother, pray that prosperity and peace may be granted to the illustrious children and to the realm.

units.la: XXIV. LAUS IMITATIONIS ET PRAESERTIM CICERONIS.
units.tr: XXIV. THE PRAISE OF IMITATION, AND ESPECIALLY OF CICERO.

units.la: Exord. 1. Mirandum merito cur pauci ad laudem eloquentiae perveniant. Hinc
units.tr: Exordium. 1. It is rightly a wonder why so few attain to the praise of eloquence. Here

units.la: 2. Causam exponat 1. quia rem facilem credunt. 2. Alii rem minus difficilem putant. 3. Alii perperam illam sectantur.
units.tr: 2. The cause may be set out: (1) because they believe the thing to be easy; (2) others think it less difficult; (3) others pursue it wrongly.

units.la: 3. Multa desiderari ad illam, praesertim imitationem.
units.tr: 3. Many things are lacking for it, especially imitation.

units.la: Propos. Hanc proinde & in specie Cic. imitationem commendandam.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore this imitation, and Cicero in particular, is to be commended.

units.la: Confirm. Bimembris.
units.tr: Confirmation. It has two parts.

units.la: I. 1. Quod utilis ac necessaria; imitatio, probetur 1. authoritate Plat. qui optimos in Reip. imitandos ait: Plutarchi, qui ad gloriam contendentes hederas imitari jubet, quae arboribus robustissimis se applicant 2. exemplis Pictorum, Statuariorum, &c. Item Demosthenis & Cic. 3. item testimoniis Socratis, Aristot: 4. Illustretur prolepsi: quam servilium hoc ingeniorum. Resp. imitationem aliam servilem, aliam liberam, qualis Virgilii, Horatii.
units.tr: I. 1. That imitation is useful and necessary is proved (1) by the authority of Plato, who says that the best men in the commonwealth are to be imitated; of Plutarch, who bids those who strive for glory to imitate ivy, which clings to the most robust trees; (2) by the examples of painters, sculptors, and so on, and likewise of Demosthenes and Cicero; (3) also by the testimonies of Socrates and Aristotle; (4) let it be illustrated by the prolepsis: that this is the mark of servile talents. Reply: there is one kind of imitation that is servile and another that is free, such as that of Virgil and Horace.

units.la: II. In specie imitandum Ciceronem 1. Quia perfectissimus, in quo eloquentia omnes vires exseruit juxta Quintil. conferatur cum Demosth. Isocrate, & praeferatur Cicero. 2. Quia in omnibus partibus, & omni Orationis genere, humili, mediocri, sublimi versatur, ostendatur inductione quadam scriptorum ipsius. Parens hinc eloquentiae. 3. Quia optimi ipsum imitati sunt & commendarunt, ut Quintilianus Muretus, Sturmius, Palearius. &c.
units.tr: II. Cicero is especially to be imitated: (1) because he is most perfect, in whom eloquence has displayed all its powers, according to Quintilian; let him be compared with Demosthenes and Isocrates, and Cicero preferred. (2) Because he excels in all parts and in every kind of oratory, plain, middle, and lofty; this is shown by a certain induction from his own writings. Hence he is the parent of eloquence. (3) Because the best men have imitated him and commended him, such as Quintilian, Muretus, Sturm, Palearius, and others.

units.la: Conclus. Hortetur ad ipsius lectionem & imitationem addito argumento a felici effectu secuturo.
units.tr: Conclusion. He exhorts the reader to read and imitate him, adding an argument from the happy effect that will follow.

units.la: XXV. VALERIUS CONSUL LAUDAT COLLEGAM DEFUNCTUM BRUTUM IN ACIE INTERFECTUM.
units.tr: XXV. VALERIUS THE CONSUL PRAISES HIS FELLOW CONSUL BRUTUS, WHO FELL IN BATTLE.

units.la: Exord. Ex Loco Communi de praemiis & poenis necessariis in republica sic justitia distributiva exerceatur ex aequitate, malefactis poena, laus benefactis retribuantur, & alii exemplo deterreantur a malo, excitentur ad virtutum imitationem. Hinc & ad exemplum Graecorum, Brutum fortissime pro patria defunctum meritis laudibus decorandum.
units.tr: Exordium. From the common topic of rewards and punishments, which are necessary in a commonwealth: justice distributive is exercised with equity, so that wrongdoers receive punishment, the good receive praise, and others are deterred from evil by the example and stirred to the imitation of virtues. Hence, and following the example of the Greeks, Brutus, who died most bravely for his country, is to be honoured with merited praise.

units.la: Propos. Hinc paucis de ortu, cursu & exitu vitae ipsius dicendum.
units.tr: Propositio. Hence something shall be said briefly about the origin, course and end of his life.

units.la: Tractat. I. consideret ortum, ibique laudet 1. genus patricium. 2. periculum a Tarquinio. 3. Prudenter declinatione machinationum inimici. Transferat ad thesin, & hanc fortem esse dicat celsarum mentium, ut invidia & insidiis petantur, sed elucentur gloriosius &c. II. Cur-
units.tr: Tractatio. I. Let him consider his origin, and there praise: 1. his patrician stock; 2. the danger from Tarquin; 3. his prudent avoidance of the enemy's schemes. Let him pass to the thesis, and say that it is the lot of lofty minds to be assailed by envy and plots, but that they shine forth more gloriously, etc. II. The course...

units.la: II. Cursum vitæ: ubi 1. virtus togata & bellica; sed occultatæ metu Tarquinii.
units.tr: II. The course of his life: where 1. his virtue in peace and war; but it was kept hidden through fear of Tarquin.

units.la: Amplif. Ex loco: bene qui latuit bene vixit. 2. Vindicatio reipublicæ a Tyrannis. Hoc factum præcipuè laudet a. tanquam honestum. Hinc exaggeret tyrannidem Regum, tanquam intolerabilem victori populo. b. tanquam difficile, ob potentiam regis, & præsentem expeditionem militarem; & vilitatem Bruti. c. tanquam salutare reip. ob acquisitam libertatem, qua nihil preciosius. 3. Mors heroica pro patria, & hinc acquisita victoria. Hinc comparet cum Codro aliisque heroibus pro patria mortuis.
units.tr: Amplificatio. From the commonplace: he who lay hidden lived well. 2. The vindication of the commonwealth from tyrants. He should praise this deed chiefly: a. as honourable; hence he should magnify the tyranny of the kings as intolerable to a free people; b. as difficult, on account of the power of the king and the military expedition at hand, and the lowliness of Brutus; c. as salutary for the commonwealth, on account of the liberty won, than which nothing is more precious. 3. A heroic death for the country, and hence the victory won. Hence he should compare him with Codrus and other heroes who died for their country.

units.la: Peroràt. Dignum itaque dicat cujus laus & memoria immortalis sit Reip. Romulum fundasse quidem Romam, at Brutum libertatem intulisse. Hunc vere tanquam patrem reip. monumentis perpetuis decorandum.
units.tr: Peroratio. Let him therefore say that he deserves that his praise and memory be immortal: Romulus indeed founded Rome, but Brutus brought liberty to the commonwealth. Let him be honoured with lasting monuments as the true father of the commonwealth.

units.la: XXVI. VITUPERATIO AQUILIORUM ET LIBERORUM BRUTI.
units.tr: XXVI. A Denunciation of the Aquilii and the Sons of Brutus.

units.la: Exord. Ex dicto Horat. Omne animi vitium tanto conspectius inse Crimen habet, quanto major qui peccat habetur. Dilatetur paucis instar Chriæ, & inferatur inde.
units.tr: Exordium. From the saying of Horace: every vice of the mind carries a guilt that is the more conspicuous the greater the person who commits it is considered to be. This is to be expanded briefly in the manner of a chreia, and an inference drawn from it.

units.la: Propositio. Merito itaque hosce licet nobilissimos juvenes detestandos, tanquam degeneres: ut alii à simili scelere deterreantur.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore these most noble young men deserve to be detested as degenerates, so that others may be deterred from a similar crime.

units.la: Confirmat. I. Concedat ipsis natalium splendorem: & bonam educationem: verum tanto fœdiorem & conspectiorem esse degenerationem. Non secus ac si macula sit fœda in facie. Exaggeretur comparatione cum malè natis & educatis, quibus venia danda.
units.tr: Confirmation. (1) Grant them the splendour of their birth and their good upbringing; yet their degeneracy is all the fouler and more conspicuous for it, just as a foul blemish is more visible on the face. Let this be heightened by comparison with those who were badly born and badly brought up, to whom pardon should be given.

units.la: II. Non improbet in ipsis vitam aulicam durante regno: quippe quæ concessa imò laudabilis nobilioribus, ad notitiam regiminis & servitia regis: qui instar solis est, a quo nobiles lumen suum habent.
units.tr: (2) Let him not condemn in them the court life they led while the kingdom stood. That life is granted and even praiseworthy in nobles, since it gives them knowledge of government and opportunity to serve the king, who is like the sun, from whom the nobles have their light.

units.la: III. At detestatur quod legitime ejecto regi adhæserint: idque 1. contra decretum Senatus, 2. ex amore luxus & insolentiæ, 3. ad proditionem & ruinam patriæ. Ubi invehatur in proditores tanquam pestes civilis societatis, maximè proditores patriæ: cujus amor optimo cuique semper charissimus 4. & quidem ad opoppressionem recens acquisitæ libertatis : quæ sola incomparabilis.
units.tr: (3) But he detests that they clung to the king after he had been legitimately expelled. This was (1) against the decree of the Senate; (2) out of love of luxury and arrogance; (3) for the betrayal and ruin of their country. Here he should inveigh against the traitors as the plague of civil society, and above all against traitors to the fatherland, whose love is always dearest to every good citizen; (4) and indeed for the overthrow of the liberty just won, which alone is beyond compare.

units.la: IV. Approbet dignum facto exitum : deploretque quòd illi qui in splendore vivere potuerint, cum dedecore manu carnificis tanquam piaculares victimæ mactati fuerint.
units.tr: (4) Let him approve an outcome fitting to the deed, and lament that those who could have lived in splendour were put to death with disgrace by the executioner's hand, like expiatory victims.

units.la: Conclusio. Merito omnibus bonis infamem esse ipsorum memoriam; ut vitare huiusmodi scelera discant, & amorem patriæ ac libertatis unice amplectantur.
units.tr: Conclusion. Their memory rightly deserves to be infamous among all good men, so that they may learn to avoid crimes of this kind and embrace love of country and of liberty alone.

units.la: XXVII. BENAJA NOMINE DAVIDIS SALOMONEM REGEM RENUNCIAT.
units.tr: XXVII. BENAIAH PROCLAIMS SOLOMON KING IN THE NAME OF DAVID.

units.la: Exord. I. Adstruat sibi authoritatem a re ipsa: videlicet sisti hic, quod saustum velit esse Deus, jussu regis Davidis legitimum regni hæredem Salomonem.
units.tr: Exord. I. Let him establish his authority from the fact itself: namely, that he appears here by the order of King David, with Solomon as the lawful heir to the kingdom, whom God wishes to be fortunate.

units.la: II. Rationem exponat. 1. a senio Davidis. 2. à turbis excitatis per Adoniam & Joabum, quibus obviam eundum præsentatione novi regis.
units.tr: II. Let him set out his reasons: (1) from the old age of David; (2) from the disturbances stirred up by Adonijah and Joab, which must be met by presenting the new king.

units.la: Propositio. Hunc recipiendum & audiendum imposterum.
units.tr: Propositio. That he is to be received and heeded from now on.

units.la: Confirmat. I. A voluntate Davidis: cujus 1. prædicet jus & laudabile regimen hactenus; doleatque decrepitamætatē, quæ regni curis non amplius sufficiat. 2. Alleget mandatum ad regios ministros, ut impositum mulæ regiæ ostendant populo, & publicè renunciert. Id quod solemnissimè hic fieri velint. 3. Gaudium, quod vivus regnare filium videat.
units.tr: Confirmat. I. From the will of David: (1) let him proclaim David's right and his praiseworthy rule until now, and lament his decrepit age, which is no longer equal to the cares of the kingdom; (2) let him cite the command given to the royal ministers to show the people the mule set under him, the royal mule, and to proclaim it publicly, which they wish to be done here most solemnly; (3) let him note the joy of seeing his son reign while he is still alive.

units.la: II. A voluntate Dei, qui hunc a teneris sceptro hæredem ostenstenderit per Nathanem Prophetam præsentem. Illustret a contrario ambitu; quod non se ingesserit &c.
units.tr: II. From the will of God, who, through Nathan the prophet, who is present, showed this heir to the sceptre from his tender years. Let him illustrate by contrast the ambition of others: that Solomon did not thrust himself forward, and so on.
