units.la: III. A dotibus Salomonis: ubi prædicet 1. ipsius educationem accuratam sub Zadoco sacerdote & Nathane propheta, inspectore ipso rege: cujus vivam & corporis ac animi imaginem in ipso videant. 2. ipsius virtutes regias, sapientiam excellentem, justitiam ac moderationem & studium legis divinæ. Vide Orat. pro lege Manilia.
units.tr: III. From the endowments of Solomon, where he should proclaim: (1) his careful upbringing under Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet, with the king himself overseeing it, in whom they see a living image of his body and mind; (2) his royal virtues: excellent wisdom, justice and moderation, and zeal for the divine law. See the oration for the Manilian law.

units.la: Conclus. 1. Dehortetur ne turbulentis aliorum machinationibus aurem præbeant, quas veluti nebulas præsentis regis regiminis aurora dissipatura sit. 2. Moneat ut hunc debite suscipiant, huic obediant. diant, hunc sequantur. 3. Addat votum felicis regiminis cum fausta acclamatione.
units.tr: Conclus. (1) Let him urge them not to lend their ears to the turbulent schemes of others, which the dawn of the present king's rule is about to scatter like clouds; (2) let him advise them to receive him duly, obey him and follow him; (3) let him add a wish for a happy reign, with a propitious acclamation.

units.la: XXVIII. DE MAJESTATE VIRTUTE ET FATIS REGIIS IN EXEMPLO DAVIDIS.
units.tr: XXVIII. Of the Majesty, Virtue and Fortunes of Kings, in the Example of David.

units.la: Exord. Ex Ps. 82. v. 6. 7. Hoc
units.tr: Exordium. From Ps. 82. vv. 6, 7. Here

units.la: I. Proponatur cum elogio: videlicet, Augustum esse summi monarchae de legibus cunctisque in eminentia constitutis, at severum simul elogium; cum inquit: Dixi dii estis &c.
units.tr: I. Let it be proposed with its eulogy: namely, that Augustus is the supreme monarch over the laws and over all who are set in eminence; but at the same time it is a stern eulogy, since he says: "I have said, Ye are gods," etc.

units.la: II. Exponatur brevi paraphrasi, videlicet tria indicari. 1. Regum principumque majestatem; Dii estis, a Deo scilicet constituti in terris vicarii, & radio divinitatis collustrati. 2. Dotes ac virtutes eorundem; & filii altissimi, singulari cura enutritii, ornati donis, & donati jure haereditario, ut repraesentetis Deum in terris, 3. fata ac casus regum: sed moriemini ut homines, & ut aliquis principum peribitis, videlicet licet officio dotibusque tam sublimes sitis, tamen humanam sortem non effugietis, quia adversae fortunae ac mortis spiculis aeque ac subditi aut saltem praefecti vestri estis expositi.
units.tr: II. Let it be explained in a brief paraphrase, namely that three things are indicated. 1. The majesty of kings and princes: "Ye are gods," that is, appointed by God as vicars on earth, and illumined by a ray of divinity. 2. The gifts and virtues of the same: "and sons of the Most High," nurtured with singular care, adorned with gifts, and endowed by hereditary right, so that you may represent God on earth. 3. The fates and falls of kings: "but you shall die like men, and you shall perish like one of the princes"; that is, although you are so exalted in office and gifts, you will nevertheless not escape the human lot, because you are exposed to the darts of adverse fortune and of death just as your subjects, or at least your prefects, are.

units.la: III. Probetur: A causa illustrata prolepsi. Licet enim pro diis habeantur inter homines, & veneratione sint conspicui ac gloria; tamen homines sunt ejusdem naturae iisdemque fatis expositi.
units.tr: III. Let it be proved: from a cause made clear by anticipation. For although among men they are regarded as gods, and are conspicuous in veneration and glory, yet they are men, of the same nature and subject to the same fates.

units.la: IV. Concludatur & sternatur via ad propositum: dignum esse, ut haec regum principumque conditio consideretur; tum ut subditi proximam Deo majestatem sine fuco, sine adulatione veneren- tur; tum ut reges humanae conditionis memores commissas sibi Dei vices imitatione virtutum divinarum decore gerere satagant. Dignissimam hanc materiam visam esse; quae oratione licet longe impari tractetur; & quidem ne in re ardua aberres, ex sacris heroibus cordatissimum regem Davidem te consideraturum, ita ut in ipso.
units.tr: IV. Let it be concluded, and the way cleared to the purpose: that it is fitting this condition of kings and princes be considered; so that subjects may venerate the majesty next to God without pretence or flattery; and so that kings, mindful of their human condition, may strive to bear with grace the office of God committed to them by imitating the divine virtues. This material is seen to be most worthy, though it is treated in a speech far unequal to it; and indeed, lest you go astray in a difficult matter, you will consider the most wise king David among the sacred heroes, in the following way, in him.

units.la: Propofit. 1. Regiam majestatem, 2. virtutes & 3. fata regia expendas. Addatur brevis materiae commendatio, & stipulatio attentionis.
units.tr: Proposition. 1. You shall weigh the royal majesty, 2. the virtues, and 3. the royal fates. Let a brief commendation of the matter be added, and a request for attention.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. De regia majestate. Hic exponatur.
units.tr: I. Concerning royal majesty. Let it be set out here.

units.la: 1. Per modum prolepseos, humilis ipsius ortus & omnia majestati contraria. vid. 1. Sam. 16. Addatur consideratio politica. Videlicet licet magnum quid in regibus splendor natalium & exempla avita; non tamen hinc pendet majestas illa, quam quaerimus. Nam & ex magnatibus saepe degeneres, & ex infimis Reges. Addatur exemplum unum atque alterum.
units.tr: 1. By way of anticipation: his humble origin and everything contrary to majesty. See 1 Sam. 16. Let a political consideration be added. That is, although the splendour of birth and ancestral examples are something great in kings, that majesty which we seek does not depend on this. For kings have often sprung from degenerate nobles, and kings from the lowest ranks. Let one or two examples be added.

units.la: 2. Unctio, qua regius ipsi character veluti imprimitur. Hinc de unctione agat, quod non nuda caerimonia, sed veluti sacramentum conferendorum donorum regiorum. Scilicet coelo datur majestas sacris regno capitibus. Hoc ostendatur uberius. Per me Reges regnant. Prov. 8. &c. Vide Salmas. in defensione regia, Irnerium de regno &c.
units.tr: 2. The anointing, by which the royal character is, as it were, impressed upon him. Here let him treat of the anointing, which is not a bare ceremony but as it were a sacrament of conferring royal gifts. That is, majesty is given from heaven to heads consecrated to the kingdom. Let this be shown more fully. "By me kings reign," Prov. 8, etc. See Salmasius in his Defensio regia, Irnerius on kingship, etc.

units.la: 3. Via ad regnum, 1. per evocationem ad aulae ministerium: vilius initio, post illustrius. 2. Per strenue gesta indeque natam gloriam. 3. Per regium matrimonium sine ambitu. 4. Per receptionem & applausum populi. vid. 1. Sam. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. & 2. Sam. 2. 3. 4. 5. capp. Singula ista considerentur in thesi ex politicis & exemplis pro re nata illustrentur; & ex hisce conspirantibus augustum cunctisque venerandum majestatis decus arcessatur. Hinc transeatur ad
units.tr: 3. The way to the kingdom: 1. by being called to the service of the court, humbler at first, afterwards more distinguished; 2. through deeds performed with vigour and the glory born from them; 3. through a royal marriage without ambition; 4. through the reception and applause of the people. See 1 Sam. 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, and 2 Sam. 2, 3, 4, 5. chapters. Each of these should be considered as a thesis and illustrated from political writers and examples as the matter requires; and from these converging points let the august and venerable adornment of majesty be drawn. Hence let us pass to

units.la: II. De regiis virtutibus; qualis fuit in Davide.
units.tr: II. On the royal virtues; what kind of man David was.

units.la: 1. Pietas, quam ostende ex rebus gestis videl. petitus a Saule, fugit ad Samuelem & collegium prophetarum. 1. Sam. 19. Parcit Sauli aliquoties c. 24. 25. 26. Rex factus arcam & cultum Dei promovet. 2. Sam. 6. Consilium capit de aedificando templo. c. 7. In omnibus ad Deum respicit. vid. c. 22. & 23. Hinc transeatur ad thesin & pietatem regibus prae caeteris necessariam ostendat, quippe qui dignitatem suam a Deo habeant Deique vicarii sint. vid. Lips. initio politicorum.
units.tr: 1. Piety, which is shown from his deeds: first, when he was sought by Saul, he fled to Samuel and the college of prophets (1 Sam. 19). He spares Saul several times (ch. 24, 25, 26). Once made king, he advances the ark and the worship of God (2 Sam. 6). He takes counsel about building the temple (ch. 7). In all things he looks to God (see ch. 22 and 23). From here pass to the thesis, and show that piety is more necessary for kings than for anyone else, since they hold their dignity from God and are God's vicars (see Lipsius, at the beginning of the Politics).

units.la: 2. Justitia: cujus necessitas primo ostendatur in genere in regibus, quippe quorum praecipuum munus est, administrare justitiam subditis. Hac propter primitus reges constituti sunt, sine qua regna latrocinia sunt, &c. Deinde exempla quaedam ostendat in Davide. Videlicet occidere privatus adhuc voluit regem hostem; imo nuncium caedis punivit. 2. Sam. 1. Joabi caedem improbavit: aulam ordinavit c. 9. Supplicio affecit superstites Saulis ad instantiam Gibeonitarum. c. 11. Claudatur epiphonemate. Clementia, quæ præcipuè elucet ex perdonatione Simei aliorum-que; Amplif. ex loco generis, quantum ornamentum regi ex clementia.
units.tr: 2. Justice: its necessity should first be shown in general in kings, since their chief duty is to administer justice to their subjects. For this reason kings were first appointed; without justice kingdoms are nothing but robber bands, etc. Then he should set out some examples from David. Namely, while still a private man he was unwilling to kill the king who was his enemy; indeed he punished the bearer of the news of the killing (2 Sam. 1). He disapproved of Joab's murder (2 Sam. 3). He set in order the royal household (ch. 9). At the request of the Gibeonites he put to death the survivors of Saul's house (ch. 21). Let it be closed with an epiphonema. Clemency, which shines especially in the pardoning of Shimei and others; amplify from the topic of kind, how great an ornament clemency is to a king.

units.la: 4. Fortitudo. Hæc 1. commendetur in rege in genere tanquam illa virtus sine qua subditi defendi nequeant. Gladius scilicet justitiæ & militiæ commissus divinitus regibus contra facino-rosos, rebelles, hostes, &c. 2. Ostendatur ex fortibus factis Davidis: vide passim.
units.tr: 4. Fortitude. This is to be commended, first, in a king in general, as the virtue without which subjects cannot be defended: the sword of justice and of war has been entrusted by God to kings against wicked men, rebels, enemies, etc. Second, it should be shown from David's brave deeds: see throughout.

units.la: 5. Prudentia, quæ ostendatur ex factis passim, & præcipuè in declinandis insidiis Saulis, retundendis insultibus rebellium liberorum, & præcipue elidendo conatu ultimo Adoniæ. Hinc digrediatur in Locū Commune de prudentiæ necessitate ac usu in regimine, exemplo Solomonis, hanc præ ceteris exoptantis, &c. Rex enim prospicere debet toti regno. Vide Isocrat. ad Nicocl. Atque ex omnibus superioribus formet sibi descriptionem regis veri, qui non majestate solum, sed & donis ac virtutibus Deum referat. Tales dii sunt, tales filii altissimi. Hunc talem admiretur & prædicet, &c. Fiat transitus ad partem tertiam: videlicet; sed meminerint tamen se homines esse, & perituros &c. Hinc agat.
units.tr: 5. Prudence, which is shown from his deeds throughout, and especially in avoiding the snares of Saul, in repelling the attacks of rebellious sons, and above all in crushing the last attempt of Adonijah. From here digress into a commonplace on the necessity and use of prudence in government, using the example of Solomon, who desired it above all else, etc. For a king ought to look out for the whole realm (see Isocrates to Nicocles). And from all the foregoing let him form for himself a description of the true king, who reflects God not only in majesty but also in gifts and virtues: "such are gods, such are sons of the Most High." Let him admire and proclaim such a king, etc. Make the transition to the third part, namely: yet let them remember that they are men, and will die, etc. From here proceed.

units.la: III. De fatis regiis, ubi occurrunt.
units.tr: III. Of the royal falls, where they occur.

units.la: 1. Errores & peccata; de quibus 1. in genere: quod illa facile comitentur tam excellàm fortunam, v. g. superbia, ut in Nobucodonosore Alex: Cæsare. Libido, ut in Sardanapalo &c. Luxus, ut in Tiberio, Heliogabalo; Crudelitas, ut in Pharaone, Antiocho Epiphane, &c. 2. In specie ostendatur in Davide, ne quis malos tantum hisce subjectos putet, peccavit libidine fœda cum Batsheba, crudelitate & proditione cum Uria, quam in animo etiam habuit cum Nabale; denique elatione in numerando populo, &c. Claudatur epiphonemate.
units.tr: 1. Errors and sins, which 1. in general: that they readily accompany so exalted a fortune, e.g. pride, as in Nebuchadnezzar and Alexander Caesar; lust, as in Sardanapalus, etc.; luxury, as in Tiberius and Heliogabalus; cruelty, as in Pharaoh, Antiochus Epiphanes, etc. 2. Let it be shown in particular in David, so that no one thinks only bad men are subject to these: he sinned with foul lust toward Bathsheba, with cruelty and treachery toward Uriah, whom he also intended to destroy in the case of Nabal; and finally with pride in numbering the people, etc. Let it be closed with an epiphonema.

units.la: 2. Hinc fluunt pœnæ seu mala publica, quibus exercitus a juventute fuit David. Fiat inductio præcipuorum ex lib. Samuel. Digressio hinc fiat ad generale, videlicet: Publicas calamitates, licet præcipue privatos feriant, tamen principum culpæ præcipue adscribi, illosque sæpissimè tangere, ut cum Davide fugere ex regno sæpe necesse habeant &c. Vide Xenophont. in Dionysio. 3. Mala domestica, ne se exsortes existiment vide clades domesticas Davidis, aliaque exempla confer, & digrediendo ad considerationem generalem locum hunc pathetice concludè.
units.tr: 2. From these flow the punishments or public evils with which David's reign was troubled. Let the principal instances from the books of Samuel be brought forward. Let a digression then be made to the general point, namely: public calamities, although they strike chiefly private persons, are nonetheless chiefly to be ascribed to the faults of princes, and they very often touch the princes themselves, so that they are often obliged to flee the kingdom with David, etc. See Xenophon in the Dionysius. 3. Domestic evils: lest they think themselves exempt, look at the domestic calamities of David and compare other examples, and, digressing to a general consideration, conclude this place movingly.

units.la: Epilogus 1. breviter refellat illos, qui aut nimii admiratores, aut spretores sunt regiæ majestatis; ex repetita breviter summa superiorum.
units.tr: Epilogue 1. Let him briefly refute those who are either excessive admirers or despisers of royal majesty, by briefly repeating the sum of what has gone before.

units.la: 2. Desinat in præconium majestatis: omnes ad humile obsequium; reges & modestiam hortetur.
units.tr: 2. Let him end in praise of majesty: he should exhort all to humble obedience, and kings to modesty.

units.la: XXIX. ORATIO GRATULATORIA, QUA SOLOMON PATERNO SOLIO IMPOSITUS EXCEPTUS. EST.
units.tr: XXIX. A CONGRATULATORY ORATION, IN WHICH SOLOMON, PLACED ON HIS FATHER'S THRONE, IS WELCOMED.

units.la: I. Præloquium generale ad Auditores;
units.tr: I. A general preamble to the hearers;

units.la: Exord. Consilii rationem exponat ex Proverb. c 8. Per me reges regnant & dominatores decernunt justitiam. Itaque hoc I. Proponatur cum encomio: videl. Auguste admodum ac tanto fastigio dignissimè ex supremæ majestatis solio profatur æterna illa Dei sapientia per os sapientiss. regis Solom. Per me &c.
units.tr: Exordium. He should explain the reason for his counsel from Proverbs ch. 8: By me kings reign, and rulers decree justice. Accordingly, first, this is to be set forth with praise: that the eternal wisdom of God, from the supreme throne of majesty, most worthily and in such a lofty manner, spoke through the mouth of the most wise king Solomon: By me, etc.

units.la: II. Illustretur luculenta paraphrasi.
units.tr: II. It is to be illustrated with a lucid paraphrase.

units.la: III. Addatur causa: quia jus majestatis nemini sine arbitrio supremi Monarchæ competere potest, a quo illud pro lubitu communicatur.
units.tr: III. A reason is to be added: because the right of majesty can belong to no one except by the decision of the supreme Monarch, from whom it is communicated at his pleasure.

units.la: IV. Amplificetur distributione imperantium: videl. non potentibus modo, sed & pusillis & infimis; imò non bonis modo, sed & pessimis illud sæpe attribui in ira Dei: Unde vel florens, vel afflictus regni ac reip. status imperantibus tanquam benignis vel infestis astris in totum corpus influentibus. Illustretur exemplo Saulis & Davidis ac Solomonis præsertim. Unde justas populo quiritandi vel exsultandi causas pro conditione imperantium.
units.tr: IV. It is to be amplified by distinguishing the rulers: namely, that it is attributed not only to the powerful but also to the weak and the lowliest; and indeed not only to the good but often also to the worst, in the anger of God. Hence the flourishing or afflicted state of a kingdom and commonwealth comes from its rulers, as from kindly or hostile stars flowing into the whole body. It is to be illustrated by the example of Saul and David, and especially of Solomon. Hence the people have just causes for complaint or rejoicing, according to the condition of their rulers.

units.la: V. Applicetur ad hypothefin: Hac propter in præsentiarum lætitiam & exultationem populi Israëlitici te repræsentaturum, qua Solomonem sulio paterno impositum exceperit: quod eò minus ingratum erit auditoribus, cum & hodie talia contingant, & passim læta pacis nuncia Europam afflictam refocillent,
units.tr: V. It is to be applied to the hypothesis: for this reason, at present, I shall represent the joy and exultation of the Israelite people when they welcomed Solomon placed on his father's throne. This will be the less unwelcome to the hearers, since such things happen today as well, and glad tidings of peace everywhere revive a Europe in affliction.

units.la: II. Ipsa Prosopopœia sub persona Senioris cujusdem ex populo Israelitarum.
units.tr: II. The prosopopoeia itself, under the persona of a certain elder of the Israelites.

units.la: Exord. Ex abrupto, gaudium & meritam gratulationem populi explicet, addita causa; quod languescente, at vivo adhuc Davide dignissimum ex semine ipsius successorem regio throno impositum videant: in quo impleantur illæ Dei promissiones Davidi factæ. Amplificetur ex minacibus regno motibus, dum Adonia sine parente, sine Numine, inauspicato thronum conscendereategerit: qui cordata Davidis prudentia uno veluti ictu sopiti sint.
units.tr: Exordium. Abruptly, he should explain the joy and deserved congratulation of the people, adding the cause: that, while David was failing but still alive, they saw a successor most worthy of his seed placed on the royal throne, in whom those promises of God made to David were fulfilled. It is to be amplified from the threatening disturbances to the kingdom, when Adonijah, without a father, without the divine will, and under evil omens, tried to mount the throne; and those disturbances were quieted, as it were with a single blow, by David's wise foresight.

units.la: Propos. Hanc causam esse, cur populus exsultet, & ipsius voce hanc suam lætitiam contestari, & regi novo, ac Patri Davidi congratulandum exstimaverit.
units.tr: Proposition. That this is the cause why the people rejoice, and thought they should bear witness to their gladness with their own voice, and offer congratulations to the new king and to his father David.

units.la: Confirmatio causas lætitiæ exponat splendidè.
units.tr: Confirmation. He should set out the causes of joy splendidly.

units.la: 1. A periculo imminente ab Adonia, qui in societatem vocatis præcipuis regni ministris, jam solium regium occupaverat. Quanta enim æstimanda illa tempestas! &c. Exaggeret a malis inde metuendis: videlicet regno militari, non justitia sed armis subnixa; prævalituris adulatoribus & sceleris ministris, qui in sacris & profanis primas habituri fuissent: discordia ac concertatione domus regiæ; unde pronus lapsus in bellum civile, & exitium omnium illorum qui tyrannidem probare non potuerint. Hæc omnia prudenti consilio Davidis averla esse: dum illum sceptris admovit, cui & divinitus promissa, & ob regias virtutes debita erant. Claudatur epiphonemate ad Solomonem. Te igitur quibus laudibus excipiam! &c.
units.tr: 1. From the danger threatening from Adonijah, who, having called together the chief ministers of the kingdom into a conspiracy, had already seized the royal throne. For how dreadful must that storm be considered! etc. He should enlarge on the evils to be feared from it: namely, a kingdom of soldiers, resting not on justice but on arms; flatterers and agents of crime prevailing, who would have held first place in sacred and profane affairs; discord and strife within the royal house; whence a headlong fall into civil war and the ruin of all who could not approve of tyranny. All this, he says, was averted by David's prudent counsel, when he raised to the scepter the one to whom both divine promises and the royal virtues were due. It is closed with an epiphonema addressed to Solomon: With what praises, then, shall I welcome you! etc.

units.la: II. A persona ac dotibus ipsius regis Solomonis: utpote
units.tr: II. From the person and gifts of King Solomon himself, namely:

units.la: 1. Qui natus ex Davide: cujus celebret 1. electionem factam ab ipso Deo, 2. regimen gloriosum: addita illustratione ex comparatione status miseri tempore Saulis. 3. Promissionem ipsi factam divinitus, quod regnum mansurum sit & prosperum futurum in ipsius semine: imo quod exinde oriturus sit Messias, cujus regnum propagabitur per universum orbem & non habiturum sit finem. Hujus regni jacta hodie esse fundamenta in Solomone. vide Orat. pro Marcell.
units.tr: 1. That he was born of David. He should celebrate: (a) his election, made by God himself; (b) his glorious reign, with the addition of an illustration drawn from the comparison with the wretched state in the time of Saul; (c) the promise made to him by God, that the kingdom will endure and be prosperous in his seed; indeed, that the Messiah will arise from it, whose kingdom will spread through the whole world and will have no end. The foundations of this kingdom are today laid in Solomon. See the oration for Marcellus.

units.la: 2. Oraculo regno destinatus, non scilicet in ira ipsum datum, ut olim Saulem, sed a benigno Numine: nec irruisse, ut alii, sed a patre impositum solio. 3. Singulari cura in spem regni educatus a rege & Nathane propheta. Neque enim rem exiguam esse regere regnum, & quidé populi Dei, qui non ex beneplacito hominū sed juxta Dei legem gubernari debeat. Comparet alios populos soedis vitiis inquinatos & perversis legibus reɛtos,& hanc legem sanctissimos judæorum opponat, cujus meditatio commendata sit regi. Non in luxu & sastu regio, non sub adulatoribus, sed ad sapientiam & pietatem rege sene, & sub propheta hunc educatum prædicet.
units.tr: 2. He was destined for the kingdom by an oracle, not given to him in anger, as once to Saul, but by a kindly Divinity; and he did not rush in, as others did, but was placed on the throne by his father. 3. He was brought up with singular care, for the hope of the kingdom, by the king and the prophet Nathan. For governing a kingdom is no small matter, and especially the kingdom of the people of God, which ought to be governed not by the pleasure of men but according to the law of God. He should compare other peoples, stained with foul vices and ruled by perverse laws, and set against them the most holy law of the Jews, the meditation on which was commended to the king. He should proclaim that Solomon was brought up not in royal luxury and pomp, nor under flatterers, but toward wisdom and piety, with an aged king and under a prophet.

units.la: 4. Divinis dotibus, pietate, sapientia, justitia, moderatione ac temperantia prædítus: quæ virtutes tanquam regibus necessariæ prædicentur in Solomone vide Orat. pro Leg. Manil. Quis igitur non exsultet? &c. Avertat hinc Orat. ad Davidem; quod ipse superstes hoc tantum bonum oculis suis videat, & promissiones Dei impleri cernat.
units.tr: 4. He was endowed with divine gifts: piety, wisdom, justice, moderation and temperance; these virtues, as necessary for kings, are to be proclaimed in Solomon. See the oration for Manilius's law. Who, then, would not rejoice? etc. From here he turns away to David: that he himself, still living, sees this great good with his own eyes, and beholds the promises of God being fulfilled.

units.la: III. A secutura regni prosperitate, quam auguretur futuram.
units.tr: III. The prosperity of the kingdom that is to follow, which he foretells as about to come.

units.la: 1. In pace, quam ipsum nomen spondeat, quæ florebit sub ipso.
units.tr: 1. In the peace which his very name promises, which will flourish under him.

units.la: 2. In æquissimo regimine ad Dei gloriam & subditorum salutem.
units.tr: 2. In a most equitable government, to the glory of God and the salvation of his subjects.

units.la: 3. In copia & opulentia regni ac regnicolarum.
units.tr: 3. In the abundance and opulence of the kingdom and of its inhabitants.

units.la: 4. In splendore ac sama apud exteros; adeò ut ipsi hostes se ipsi subjiciant & munera ac tributa ferant. vide Psal. 2. & 72. Psal. 110.
units.tr: 4. In splendour and fame among foreign nations, so that even the enemies themselves submit to him and bring gifts and tribute. See Psal. 2. and 72. Psal. 110.

units.la: 5. In religione ac pietate, quæ sub ipso florescet. Hunc esse illum, cui Deus ædificationem Templi reservaverit: unde futurum, ut Deus inter ipsos habitet in perpetuum, qui hactenus veluti hospes fuit: ut mons Zionis efferatur supra omnes montes, ut inde Lex prodeat in omnem terram & eo confluant omnes gentes: quò ita nomen Domini magnificetur usque ad extremitates terræ.
units.tr: 5. In religion and piety, which will flourish under him. That this is the one to whom God reserved the building of the Temple; whence it will come about that God dwells among them for ever, He who until now was, as it were, a guest. That the mountain of Zion will be lifted up above all mountains, that from there the Law will go forth into all the earth, and all nations will flow together to it; so that thus the name of the Lord may be magnified to the ends of the earth.

units.la: Peroratio: Merito igitur exsultare Israelem in hoc tanto bono suo dicat. 2. Gratias agat Davidi de hac sollicitudine pro populo. 3. Vota concipiat pro regis novi vita longæva, regimine prospero, & regni salute; ad gloriæ divinæ amplificationem per universam terram.
units.tr: Peroration: Israel may therefore rightly say that it rejoices in this great good of its own. 2. Let it give thanks to David for this care for the people. 3. Let it conceive prayers for the long life of the new king, for a prosperous government, and for the safety of the kingdom, to the enlargement of the divine glory throughout the whole earth.

units.la: XXX. LAUS SCIPIONIS AFRICANI.
units.tr: XXX. The Praise of Scipio Africanus.

units.la: Exord. I. Laudet consuetudinem veterum, qui virorum illustrium effigie figies exstare voluerunt ad memoriam & excitationem postero- rum.
units.tr: Exordium. I. Let him praise the custom of the ancients, who wished the likenesses of illustrious men to stand as images, for the memory and stimulus of posterity.

units.la: II. Præferat monumenta hæc historica: quibus non corporis & vultus, sed animorum effigies relictæ.
units.tr: II. Let him prefer these historical monuments, in which are left not the bodily form and features, but the images of minds.

units.la: III. Applicet ad hypothesin: inclytum illud esse in historia Scipionis Africani.
units.tr: III. Let him apply this to the hypothesis: that the renown of Scipio Africanus is famous in history.

units.la: Propos. Hujus igitur memoriam laudesque breviter repetendas esse, ut appareat quibus virtutibus creverit Resp. Rom.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore his memory and praises are to be recalled briefly, so that it may appear by what virtues the Roman commonwealth grew.

units.la: Tractatio. Prædicet
units.tr: Treatment. Let him proclaim:

units.la: I. parentes & natales. vide Corn. Nepotem: illustrentur ex thesi: videl. magnum esse incitamentum liberis, exempla & virtutes parentum. vide Plutarchum de educatione puerorum.
units.tr: I. his parents and birth. See Cornelius Nepos. These are to be illustrated from the thesis: namely, that the examples and virtues of parents are a great incitement to children. See Plutarch, On the Education of Children.

units.la: II. Educationem in literis sub Ennio & exercitiis bellicis sub Patre. Digrediatur in Locum Communem de educatione Romanorum, & Musarum ac Martis consortio. Vide Cic. pro Archia. Itemque de ratione inclarescendi non per otium, sed per specimina virtutis.
units.tr: II. His education in letters under Ennius, and in military exercises under his father. Let him digress into the common place on the education of the Romans, and on the association of the Muses and Mars. See Cicero, For Archias. Likewise on the way of gaining renown not through leisure, but through proofs of virtue.

units.la: III. Dotes corporis & facundiam.
units.tr: III. His bodily gifts and eloquence.

units.la: IV. Res gestas; quæ referantur ad capita virtutum cardinalium, uti sunt prudentia, justitia, fortitudo, temperantia, singulasq; ut necessarias duci laudet, & exemplis ex historia ipsius adstruat, ad exemplum Orationis pro Lege Manilia. Vide dictos autores Liv. & Nepot. Hæ breviter referantur & laudibus decorentur ex virtutibus in illo relucentibus, ut fuerunt præcipue, prudentia, fortitudo, castitas.
units.tr: IV. His deeds, which are to be referred to the heads of the cardinal virtues, such as prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance; and he should praise each as necessary and confirm it by examples from his history, following the model of the speech For the Manilian Law. See the aforementioned authors, Livy and Nepos. These are to be briefly related and adorned with praises drawn from the virtues shining forth in him, namely above all prudence, fortitude and chastity.

units.la: V. Vitæ exitum, videl. falso accusatus voluntarium elegit exilium. Illustrentur ex Loco Communi de fatis summorum virorum.
units.tr: V. The end of his life, namely that, falsely accused, he chose voluntary exile. Let these be illustrated from the common place on the fates of outstanding men.

units.la: Conclus. Desinat in ipsius laudes, optetque ut Christiani horum heroum exemplis ad pie fortiterque agendum pro patria excitentur.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him end with praises of the man himself, and pray that Christians may be stirred by the examples of these heroes to act piously and bravely for their country.

units.la: XXXI. PANEGYRICUS IN LAUDEM COMITIS SERINI.
units.tr: XXXI. PANEGYRIC IN PRAISE OF COUNT SERINI.

units.la: Exord. A præpostera admiratione temporis antiqui. Videl. I. Quod Horat de Senibus ait: Laudator temporis acti; idem de omnibus ferè hodie dici posse. II. Hinc laudari veteres duces, negligi præsensentes. III. Horum tamen haud inferiorem esse virtutem veteribus.
units.tr: Exord. Against a preposterous admiration of former times. Note: I. What Horace says of old men, "a praiser of times past," can be said of nearly everyone today. II. Hence old commanders are praised, while those of the present day are neglected. III. Yet their virtue is not inferior to that of the ancients.

units.la: Propos. Hoc breviter in illustri heroe Comite Serinio te ostensurum; qui tanquam fortissimum propugnaculum exundanti potentiae Ottomannicae hactenus se opposuit.
units.tr: Propos. I will show this briefly in the illustrious hero Count Serini, who, like a most brave bulwark, has so far opposed himself to the overflowing power of the Ottomans.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Per praeteritionem percurrat illa quae de familia & natalibus vulgo afferri solent. Habere & hunc in quo se jactet gens Hungarorum & hinc ipse Comes; sed non sanguine & factis majorum, sed propria virtute nitendum viris fortibus. Hinc breviter laudata prosapia ad virtutes & facta illustria properare dicat orationem.
units.tr: Tractatio. I. By way of preterition, let him run briefly through what is commonly brought forward about family and birth. The Hungarian people have this too, in which they take pride, and so does the Count himself; but brave men must rely not on the blood and deeds of their ancestors but on their own virtue. Having briefly praised his lineage, let him then hasten to his virtues and famous deeds.

units.la: II. Laudet in ipso, quod tempore pacis de futuro bello prospexerit, muniens oppidum natale. Causam addat ob infidam cum barbaris vicinis pacem. Illustretur ex Loco Communi de vitanda securitate & parando bello dum adhuc pax est.
units.tr: II. Let him praise in him that, in time of peace, he foresaw the coming war and fortified his native town. Let him add the reason: the peace with the neighbouring barbarians is untrustworthy. Let this be illustrated from the common topic of avoiding complacency and preparing for war while peace still lasts.

units.la: III. Praedicet ipsius animositatem & fortia facta, quod imparibus longe copiis impetum Turcarum subinde retardaverit, impressiones diversas fecerit, commeatum intercepepit, pontem ruperit, tueaturque arcem suam contra vim Ottomannicam &c. dum interim robusta munimenta cedere hostis violentiae. Illustretur ex thesi, videlicet ita Deum excitare semper heroes, qui exundanti se hostium potentiae opponant. Illustretur exemplis ex historia Judicum, Constantini, Theodosiorum & Carolorum.
units.tr: III. Let him commend his courage and brave deeds: that, with forces far inferior, he repeatedly checked the Turkish assault, made various sallies, intercepted supplies, broke the bridge, and held his citadel against Ottoman violence, while the strong defences yielded to the enemy's fury. Let this be illustrated from the thesis that God always raises up heroes to oppose the overflowing power of enemies, and by examples from the history of the Judges, Constantine, the Theodosiuses and the Charleses.

units.la: Conclus. Avertat Orationem ad ipsum Comitem & ipsius armis ulteriorem victoriam voveat.
units.tr: Conclus. Let him turn the oration to the Count himself and pray for further victory by his arms.

units.la: XXXII. NIMROD SEU DOMINATOR.
units.tr: XXXII. Nimrod, or the Lord (Dominator)

units.la: Exord. A facto Historicorum; qui non frustra illustres personas nobis discribunt,
units.tr: Exordium. From the deed of the historians, who do not describe illustrious persons for us in vain.

units.la: Addatur ratio: videlicet ut in illorum exemplo virtutes ac vitia sectari vel fugere discamus.
units.tr: Let the reason be added: namely, that by their example we may learn to pursue virtues and flee vices.

units.la: Amplif: comparatione cum praeceptis: quae segnius movent animos. Sternatur accessus ad hypothesin. videl. praecipue vero illos notabiles esse, qui rerum autores primi exstitere. Qualis hic Nimrodus, primus imperii ac Dominationis Autor.
units.tr: Amplification: by comparison with precepts, which move minds more sluggishly. Let the approach to the hypothesis be laid down, namely that those are especially notable who first arose as authors of things. Such is this Nimrod, the first author of empire and dominion.

units.la: Narratio. Breviter rem exponat ex Gen.10. v.8.9.10.
units.tr: Narration. Briefly set out the matter from Gen. 10. vers. 8, 9, 10.

units.la: Propositio. Licet a multis tanquam invasor ac tyrannus vituperetur, tibi tamen pace aliorum maxime laudandum videri.
units.tr: Proposition. Although he is censured by many as an invader and tyrant, nevertheless he seems to you, with the agreement of others, most worthy of praise.

units.la: Tractatio. celebret
units.tr: Treatment. Let him extol (the subject).

units.la: I. Genus & familiam, quòd Chami ex Chuso nepos. Licet Cham maledictus videatur a Noacho, tamen non tam Chamum ipsum, quam filium ipsius juniorem Canaanem maledictionem subiisse. Vide Gen.9. Saltem non omnes liberos Chami reos fuisse. Saepe etiam ex pessimis parentibus probos nasci liberos.
units.tr: I. His birth and family: that he was a grandson of Cush through Ham. Although Ham seems to have been cursed by Noah, the curse fell not so much on Ham himself as on his younger son Canaan. See Gen. 9. At least not all the children of Ham were guilty. Often also good children are born of the worst parents.

units.la: II. Educatione quae colligatur ex gestis postea, videl. quia servitus praedicta erat Canaani; patre sine dubio liberos reliquos ad magnanimitatem & imperium educasse. Amplif. ex loco generis. Videl. ita saepe corrigi homines per errores commissos, ut fortius resurgant, & desperationem in virtutem vertant.
units.tr: II. His upbringing, which is gathered from the deeds he did afterward, namely because servitude had been foretold for Canaan; without doubt the father brought up the remaining children to greatness of spirit and to rule. Amplification from the place of birth: namely, men are often so corrected by the errors they have committed that they rise up more strongly and turn despair into virtue.

units.la: III. Studia & genus vitae. Venator dicitur fortis coram Domino. Ergo primo venationi ferarum fuit deditus; quod exercitium commendetur, tanquam magnatibus frequentatum & utile ad belli usum, & applicetur ad Nimrodum.
units.tr: III. His studies and way of life. A hunter is called strong before the Lord. Therefore he was first devoted to the hunting of wild beasts; this exercise is commended as frequented by great men and useful for the business of war, and let it be applied to Nimrod.

units.la: IV. Res gestas: videlicet 1. à ferarum venatu ad hominum ferocium subactionem se convertit, superbos debellando, oppressos vindicando, quo nihil praeclarius. Hinc fortis venator coram Domino; Dei scilicet opera exercens, qui alta humiliat. &c.
units.tr: IV. His deeds: namely, (1) from hunting wild beasts he turned to subduing fierce men, crushing the proud and vindicating the oppressed, than which nothing is more distinguished. Hence "a strong hunter before the Lord," that is, one exercising God's work, who brings down the high, etc.

units.la: 2. Regnum exorius est, & fundamenta jecit primae monarchiae. Hic Locus Communis de regnorum initiis, vide Politicos de praestantia politiarum.
units.tr: (2) He became king and laid the foundations of the first monarchy. Here is the commonplace concerning the beginnings of kingdoms; see the political writers on the excellence of commonwealths.

units.la: V. Exitum De quo non constat, nisi quòd sine dubio in tali gloria vitam finivit, quia scilicet successores habuit perpetua serie usque ad Sardanapalum. Hinc refellatur sententia illorum, qui ipsum hominem violentum esse existimant. Imò cum violentum nihil diuturnum, contrarium praesumendum esse.
units.tr: V. His end: nothing certain is known about it, except that without doubt he ended his life in such glory, since he had successors in an unbroken line down to Sardanapalus. Hence the opinion of those who think the man himself was violent should be refuted. Indeed, since nothing violent is lasting, the contrary must be presumed.

units.la: Conclus. 1 Refellat illos, qui regna ac magistratus abominantur, eo quod tyrannicum a Nimrodo habuerint initium. 2. Nimrodi magnanimitatem & politiarum utilitatem depraedicet, & ad obsequium subditos omnes cohortetur.
units.tr: Conclusion. (1) Let him refute those who abhor kingdoms and magistracies because they had a tyrannical beginning in Nimrod. (2) Let him proclaim the magnanimity of Nimrod and the usefulness of civil organisation, and exhort all subjects to obedience.

units.la: DISPOSITIONUM GENERIS DEMONSTRATIVI.
units.tr: DISPOSITIONS OF THE DEMONSTRATIVE KIND.

units.la: PARS II. CONTINENS LAUDES RERUM NATURALIUM ET MORALIUM. I.
units.tr: PART II. CONTAINING PRAISES OF NATURAL AND MORAL THINGS. I.

units.la: DE PRÆSTANTIA IMPERII ROMANO-GERMANICI.
units.tr: ON THE EXCELLENCE OF THE ROMAN-GERMAN EMPIRE.

units.la: Xord. A præstantia Rerump. in genere ex Dan. 2. Hæc I. Proponatur per comparationem : videl. cum nihil illustre & eximium magis in mundo, quam cœtus jure sociati, quas civitates & respublicas vocamus, tú præ cæteris eminent 5. ista regna a Daniele in illustri emblemate adumbrata.
units.tr: Exordium. On the excellence of commonwealths in general, from Daniel 2. First, let it be set out by comparison: since nothing in the world is more illustrious and remarkable than bodies lawfully united, which we call cities and commonwealths, these kingdoms, foreshadowed by Daniel in a famous emblem, stand out above the rest.

units.la: II. Reddatur ratio: ab ipsorum amplitudine, durabilitate & commercio cum Ecclesia : unde & spiritus sanctus illa tam illustri imagine & elogio condecorare voluerit. Breviter proponatur visio Nabucodonosoris,
units.tr: II. Give the reason: from their greatness, their durability and their dealings with the Church, for which the Holy Spirit wished to adorn them with so illustrious an image and eulogy. Briefly set out the vision of Nebuchadnezzar.

units.la: III. Expoliatur prolepsi : qua refellatur sententia Bodini aliorumque, qui sententiam de 4. summis imperiis refellere satagunt : videl. summa dici & monarchias, non quod sola fuerint, sed quod præcipua, quod hospitio Ecclesiæ illustria, quod successive duratura ad finem mundi, reliquis regnis sua fata ordinaria sortientibus,
units.tr: III. Forestall an objection by refuting the view of Bodin and others who strive to refute the opinion about the four great empires. They say that these are called the great empires or monarchies not because they alone existed, but because they were the chief ones, renowned for sheltering the Church and destined to endure in succession until the end of the world, while the other kingdoms met their ordinary fates.

units.la: IV. Accommodetur ad propositionem : videl. tria illorum jam finem sortita, sub quarto nos vivere : cujus proinde gloriam ac splendorem merito admiremur, prædicemus.
units.tr: IV. Apply this to the proposition: three of those empires have already met their end, and we live under the fourth; therefore we rightly admire and proclaim its glory and splendour.

units.la: B. Proposit. Qui præsentis orationis scopus sit, Captetur attentio à mamateriæ dignitate ; & benevolentiaab extenuatione virium quòd in magnis voluisse satis sit.
units.tr: B. Proposition: What is the aim of the present speech? Let attention be won from the dignity of the subject, and goodwill from disclaiming one's own powers, since in great matters it is enough to have wished well.

units.la: C. Tractatio explicet.
units.tr: C. The treatment explains.

units.la: I. Imperii Romani dignitatem: quam astruat
units.tr: I. The dignity of the Roman Empire, which he establishes:

units.la: 1. Ab ejusdem antquitate & durabilitate. De antiquitate per præteritionem 1. attingat prima ejus initia ex Liv. & Halicarnassæo &c.& multiplicem virtutem,quæ jam priscis istis temporibus emicuerit, ut Livius dicat; nec majorem, nec sanctiorem, nec bonis exemplis ditiorem fuisse, nec in quam tam serò avaritia luxuriaque migrarint: nec ubi tantus ac tam diu paupertati ac parsimoniæ honos fuerit. Quid mirum igitur, ex tam egregio semine tam florentem surrexisse arborem.2.Florem ac vigorem statuat in Augusto, qui imperium a Julio vi inchoatum, faustioribus omnibus continuavit, & per Legem regiam, qua populus omnem in ipsum potestatem transtulit, domitis late provinciis & pace solidatis, vere Monarchicum reddidit, jam ante 17.Sæcula. Exaggerentur hæc comparatione cum aliis regnis, & testimoniis. Et ne quid deesset, Mundi Dominus & Servator hoc Imperii initio nasci voluit. Quid magnificentius? &c. De durabilitate 1. alleget continuam hactenus successionem tot imperatorum. Illustretur prolepsi, licet varias ecclipses passum sit, per inundationem barbarorum gentium antiquitus, licet oriens, licet alia regna quam plurima & membra ipsumque quondam caput, Roma, avulsu, & Aquila Romana deplumata, ipsum tamen pectus & cor, unde vitalis spiritus, jus & Leges pristinæ in salvo esse. vide Limnæum, Tales mutationes à Daniele per mixturam pedum ex ferro & luto prædictas. Deinde ibidem ominetur durationem usque ad finem mundi; idque ex vaticinio Danielis; & deinceps ex optimo ejusdem temperamento: id quod jam potro ex seqq. constare poterit.
units.tr: 1. From its antiquity and durability. On antiquity, by way of preterition, let him touch on its first beginnings from Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and others, and on the manifold virtue that had already shone forth in those early times, so that Livy says it was neither greater, nor holier, nor richer in good examples, nor did avarice and luxury creep into it so late, nor was there ever such great and long-lasting honour for poverty and frugality. What wonder, then, that from so noble a seed so flourishing a tree should have arisen? 2. Let him place the flower and vigour of the empire in Augustus, who continued with all the more fortunate omens the empire begun by Julius through force, and who, by the lex regia, by which the people transferred all its power to him, with the provinces subdued far and wide and peace consolidated, made it truly monarchical, more than seventeen centuries ago. Let these things be magnified by comparison with other kingdoms and by testimonies. And that nothing might be lacking, the Lord and Saviour of the world willed to be born at the beginning of this empire. What could be more magnificent? And so on. On durability, let him cite the unbroken succession of so many emperors until now. Let it be illustrated by prolepsis: although it has suffered various eclipses, through the inundation of barbarous peoples in ancient times, and although the East, many other kingdoms and members, and even the former head, Rome, have been torn away, and the Roman eagle plucked of its feathers, yet the breast and heart itself, whence the vital spirit flows, and the ancient rights and laws, remain safe. See Limnaeus. Such changes were foretold by Daniel through the mixture of iron and clay in the feet. Then let him there foresee its duration until the end of the world, and this from Daniel's prophecy, and thereafter from its excellent temperament, which can now be established from what follows.

units.la: 2. Ab optimo ejusdem temperamento: (addatur per transitionem) Hoc constare dicas tum
units.tr: 2. From its excellent temperament (to be added by transition). You may say this is established both

units.la: a. Ex capite & membris.
units.tr: a. From its head and members.

units.la: *. Caput est Imperator, de cujus tum nomine, tum axiomatimatibus seu dignitate dicendū ex juris publici autoribus. Vide supra laudatos autores. Et comparatio instituenda cum aliis regibus, ipsoque Turcarum Imperatore.
units.tr: *. The head is the Emperor, concerning whose name, as well as whose axioms or dignity, one must speak from the authors of public law. See the authors praised above. A comparison is to be made with other kings, and with the Turkish Emperor himself.

units.la: Membra sunt trium generum, videl. a. Electores hodie tres Ecclesiastici & seculares, antiquæ & immemorialis institutionis, salutari temperamento secularium & Ecclesiasticorum, ne quid religio aut resp. capiat detrimenti, &c. b. Principes, Comites & Barones magno numero; quorum tum splendor familiæ, tum potentia extollenda; ut & ipse Carolus V. regulos illos dixerit. c. Liberæ Civitates quam plurimæ, antiquitate ac viribus insignes. Scilicet ex tam robustis artubus vasta hæc moles constituitur.
units.tr: The members are of three kinds, namely: a. the electors, today three ecclesiastical and secular, of ancient and immemorial institution, through the salutary balance of secular and ecclesiastical electors, lest religion or the commonwealth suffer harm, and so on; b. the princes, counts and barons in great number, whose family splendour and power are to be extolled, as Charles V himself called them petty kings; c. the many free cities, notable for their antiquity and strength. Clearly, from such sturdy limbs this vast mass is made up.

units.la: Ex utrorumque colligatione arctissima per Legem fundamentalem Aureambullam, inter Carolum IV. & Imperii Status erectam, & dictam, & diversos Imperii recessus ac Capitulationes cum Imperatoribus initas. Hinc scil. nasci optimum illud politicis tantopere commendatum Monarchiæ temperamentum; ut capiti sua eminentia, corpori reliquo sua constet incolumitas. Digressio fiat in comparationem variarum formarum reip. & ex rationibus politicis allegatis præferatur Aristocratico-Monarchica: qualis dicatur esse forma Imperii Romani.
units.tr: From the very close bond between the two, established by the fundamental law, the Golden Bull, set up between Charles IV and the states of the Empire and so called, and by the various recesses of the Empire and the capitulations entered into with the emperors. Hence arises, namely, that best temperament of monarchy so much commended by the politicians: the head has its eminence, and the rest of the body its safety. Let a digression be made into a comparison of the various forms of commonwealth, and, on the political reasons alleged, let the aristocratic-monarchical form be preferred, which is said to be the form of the Roman Empire.

units.la: A legibus seu jure privato Justinianæo, quo membra & partes omnes reguntur. Hoc ipsum commendatur, & merito Romanum Imperium, Romanis legibus gubernari dicat: quippe quod tanta æquitate a tot seculorum interpretibus constitutum & expositum sit.
units.tr: From the laws, that is, the private law of Justinian, by which all the members and parts are governed. This itself is commended, and he rightly says the Roman Empire is governed by Roman laws, since they have been framed and expounded with such equity by interpreters of so many centuries.

units.la: Ex prætensionibus antiquis, quas habeat imperium, non modo ad diversos principatus & provincias, totamque Italiam avulsam recuperandam, verum etiam contra ipsum Turcam, qui tanquam prædo imperium invasit.
units.tr: From the ancient claims which the empire has, not only to recover the various principalities and provinces and all of Italy torn away, but also against the Turk himself, who invaded the empire like a robber.

units.la: II. Romani Imperii utilitatem
units.tr: II. The Usefulness of the Roman Empire

units.la: 1. Quia præcipuam sedem præbuit semper præbetque etiamnum Ecclesiæ. Hoc ostendatur inductione
units.tr: 1. Because it has always given, and still gives, a principal seat to the Church. This is shown by induction:

units.la: Temporum antiquorum quibus 1. prædicatus passim Servator in diversis orientis & occidentis provinciis, frustra animante manteipsos Imperatores contra Ecclesiam Satana. Imò ipsi Romani gentiles inserviere Ecclesiæ propagationi; dum persequendo Christianos latius sparserunt semen Ecclesiæ, destruendo templum & Rempubl. Judaicam, Christo viam straverunt. 2. Receptus Servator, ab ipsis imperatoribus, Constantino Magno, ipsiusque liberis, & à Theodosiis; Carolo Magno aliisque; qui magno zelo Evangelii veritatem propagarunt, &c.
units.tr: From ancient times, when the Saviour was preached everywhere in the various provinces of East and West, and the emperors, though they raged in vain against the Church, were themselves the instruments of Satan. Indeed, the Roman pagans themselves served the propagation of the Church: by persecuting Christians they scattered the seed of the Church more widely, and by destroying the temple and the Jewish commonwealth they prepared the way for Christ. 2. The Saviour was received by the emperors themselves: by Constantine the Great and his children, by the Theodosiuses, by Charlemagne and others, who with great zeal propagated the truth of the Gospel, etc.

units.la: Modernorum temporum; ubi tot Electoratus, tot principatus Ecclesiæ cesserunt. Tractetur per prolepsin breviter quæstio; utrum licitum ac consultum, ut Ecclesiastici politica potestate instructi sint, dicaturque utile hoc fuisse visum Carolo Magno, ad cohibitionem meliorem barbarorum, &c.
units.tr: Of modern times, when so many electorates and principalities have yielded to the Church. The question is briefly treated by way of anticipation: whether it is lawful and expedient for churchmen to be furnished with political power; and it is said that this seemed useful to Charlemagne for the better restraint of the barbarians, etc.

units.la: Quia præcipuum propugnaculum Christianorum est adversus vim Turcarum. Hoc ostendatur
units.tr: Because it is the principal bulwark of Christians against the force of the Turks. This is shown:

units.la: Exaggerando potentiam Turcarum & stupendos progressus in Oriente, & contra, oppositionem Romani Imperii, ne occidentem etiam invaserit.
units.tr: By magnifying the power of the Turks and their astonishing advances in the East, and, on the other hand, the opposition of the Roman Empire, lest they should also invade the West.

units.la: Exprimendo molitiones eorundem in occidente præcipue superiori seculo; & contrariam resistentiam Imperii. vide Historiam.
units.tr: By setting out their attempts in the West, especially in the last century, and the opposing resistance of the Empire; see history.

units.la: Deplorando præsentes jam ab aliquo tempore dissensiones, quibus factum, ut insuperabilem vim suam imperium in propria viscera converterit; qua totum Orientem vindicare potuisset.
units.tr: By lamenting the dissensions which have now been present for some time, by which the Empire, invincible in its strength, has turned its power against its own vitals, with which it could have vindicated the whole East.

units.la: Conclus. Voveat meliora tempora, & pacem ac florem pristinum optet tam eximio corpori, quo bene habente, vigebunt ac quiescent reliqua etiam regna, &c.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him pray for better times, and wish peace and its former flourishing to so distinguished a body, since, when it is in good health, the remaining kingdoms too will flourish and be at rest, etc.

units.la: II. DE MODESTIA.
units.tr: II. ON MODESTY.

units.la: Exord. A dicto Christi Matth. II. vers. pen. Discite à me, quoniam mansuetus sum & humilis corde- Hic
units.tr: Exordium. From the saying of Christ in Matthew 11, the penultimate verse: "Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart." Here

units.la: I. Mirandum merito dicat, cur ex cunctis virtutibus hanc præcipue suo exemplo commendaverit: cum tot aliæ eximiæ sint virtutes, justitia, &c. Modestia & humilitas apud philosophos vix proprio nomine notæ, post reliquas demum tradantur.
units.tr: I. He should say that it is rightly to be wondered at why Christ commended this virtue above all others by his own example, since there are so many other excellent virtues, justice and so on. Modesty and humility, scarcely known by their proper names among the philosophers, are handled only after the rest.

units.la: II. Causam reddat facti Servatoris; quia nihil magis congenitum homini, quam superbia, ambitio, jactantia. Hoc probetur i. inductione, Adami, Caini, primi mundi, in coelum aditum molientis. Nimbroti reliquorumque Magnatum, qui supra reliquos se extulerunt, ut Nabucodonosoris, Philippi, Alexandri, qui homines se obliti; Menecratis medici jovem se dicentis, Campanorum quorum superbia in proverbium abiit, & ne quid desit, ipsorum Christi discipulorum. 2. A causa prima, quae est tum eminentia hominis, tum impulsor diabolus; qui saftu praecipitatus, socios quaerit.
units.tr: II. He should give the reason for the Saviour's action: because nothing is more innate in man than pride, ambition and boasting. This is proved (1) by induction: from Adam, from Cain, from the first world that attempted to make its way into heaven; from Nimrod and the other magnates who raised themselves above the rest, such as Nebuchadnezzar, Philip, Alexander, who forgot that they were men; from Menecrates the physician, who called himself Jupiter; from the Campanians, whose arrogance became proverbial; and, lest anything be lacking, from Christ's own disciples. (2) From the first cause, which is both the eminence of man and the instigator, the devil, who, thrown down by pride, seeks companions.

units.la: III. Applicet ad propositum. Hinc merito Christum, regnum Satanae destructurum ipsam radicem tollere voluisse, & commendare modestiam: quae definiatur populariter ex Ethicis, & corrigatur ex Theologia quae etiam velit ut infra mediocritatem illam Aristotelicam Christianus se humiliet.
units.tr: III. He should apply this to his purpose. Hence it is rightly said that Christ, who was to destroy the kingdom of Satan, wished to remove its very root and to commend modesty. This is defined in a popular way from the Ethics and corrected from Theology, which also wishes the Christian to humble himself below that Aristotelian mean.

units.la: B. Propof. Cum nec hodie cessed hic Satanae spiritus, te divinam hanc virtutem, modestiam praedicaturum: Materiam uti ab ipso Christo suppeditatam, ita Christianis haud ingratam, qui nec humilem de modestia orationem aspernaturi sint.
units.tr: B. Propositio. Since this spirit of Satan has not ceased even today, I shall preach this divine virtue, modesty. The subject is supplied by Christ himself, and it is not unwelcome to Christians, who will not scorn a humble discourse on modesty.

units.la: C. Tractatio Praedicet Modestiam
units.tr: C. Tractatio. Let him commend modesty:

units.la: I. Ab ejusdem dignitate. Hinc
units.tr: I. From its dignity. Hence:

units.la: 1. Removeat speciem vilitatis apparentis in oculis mundi praesentis: cui nihil eximium, nisi quod cum pompa incurrit in oculos. Amplif. per inductionem illorum, quae admirantur homines; videl. opes, dignitates, aurum & vestes pretiosas, adeo ut mirandum adhuc, ipsas gentes saniores saltum inuni-di improbasse, & praeceptis atque legibus severis coercuisse. Ipsis contra Christi discipulis sordere modestiam: cujus
units.tr: 1. He should remove the appearance of baseness which it has in the eyes of the present world, to which nothing is excellent unless it runs into the eyes with pomp. Amplify by enumerating the things men admire: namely wealth, dignities, gold and costly garments; so that it is still a matter for wonder that even the wiser nations, on the other hand, condemned luxury and restrained it by strict precepts and laws. By contrast, modesty was despised by Christ's own disciples, whose

units.la: 2. Doceat dignitatem, & quidem
units.tr: 2. He should teach its dignity, and indeed

units.la: a. Quia ipse Christus, mundi Servator illam exercuit & commendavit. Hic breviter ostendatur exemplum Christi, qui cum in forma Dei esset, se humiliavit: &c. & saltum omnem redarguit. Quid hac virtute excellentius? &c.
units.tr: a. Because Christ himself, the Saviour of the world, practised and commended it. Here the example of Christ should be briefly shown, who, though he was in the form of God, humbled himself, etc.; and it refutes all pride. What is more excellent than this virtue? etc.

units.la: b. In ipso Deo refulget: qui in alto habitans, humilia respicit. Exaggeretur hoc ab effectis: quia sic mundum regit, hominum necessitatibus adest. Abest enim ut cum profanis & ipso Aristotele coelorum cura ipli tantum tribuamus.
units.tr: b. It shines forth in God himself, who dwells on high yet regards the lowly. This should be magnified by its effects: for thus he rules the world and attends to the needs of men. For it is far from the case, as with the profane writers and Aristotle himself, that we attribute the care of the heavens only to him.

units.la: Imo Imò mediis actionibus nostris ipse intervenit, &c. Illustretur à contrario.
units.tr: Indeed, he himself intervenes in our most ordinary actions, etc. Let it be illustrated by the contrary.

units.la: Imaginem humilitatis in sole & altissimis sideribus Deus nobis proposuit: quæ deorsum spargunt lumina. Amplif. 1. ab effectis salutaribus hinc in mundo hoc inferiori. 2. a contrario; videl. luto & paludibus; quæ sursum spargunt exhalationes, repellendas cum fulgure & tonitru. Tales scilicet esse ambitiosos. videl. societatis humanæ turbines.
units.tr: God has set before us an image of humility in the sun and the highest stars, which pour their light downwards. Amplify: (1) from their saving effects in this lower world; (2) by contrast, from mud and marshes, which send up exhalations that are to be driven off with lightning and thunder. Such, of course, are the ambitious: the whirlwinds of human society.

units.la: Summis Monarchis & principibus probatioribus singulari honori esse humilitatem & modestiam; qui officio sublimes, animo ad infimorum curam se demittunt; clementiæ ac mansuetudinis encomio volunt esse conspicui. Illustretur exemplo Jul. Cæsaris, qui teste Plutarcho oblatum nomé regis & diadema recusavit, aliorumque. Amplif. à contrario; inter homines statu inferiores & civilis conditionis ut plurimum regnare ambitionem & superbiam: Modestiam ac mansuetudinem magni ingenii virtutem esse. Illustretur exemplis & testimoniis, & claudatur epiphonemate & comparatione cum aliis virtutibus.
units.tr: Humility and modesty are a singular honour to the highest monarchs and to the more upright princes, who, though sublime in office, lower their minds to care for the lowliest, and wish to be conspicuous for the praise of clemency and gentleness. Let it be illustrated by the example of Julius Caesar, who, according to Plutarch, refused the title of king and the diadem offered to him, and by others. Amplify by the contrary: among men of lower rank and civil condition, ambition and pride mostly reign, whereas modesty and gentleness are the virtue of a great mind. Let it be illustrated with examples and testimonies, and closed with an epiphonema and a comparison with other virtues.

units.la: II. Ab ejusdem utilitate, quæ ostendatur:
units.tr: II. From its usefulness, which is shown:

units.la: 1. A comitante favore Dei. 1. Petr. 5. 6. Jac. 4. 6. Deus resistit superbis, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Luc. v. 15. extollit ex pulvere humiles. &c. Quod & Plato aliique agnoverunt. Exaggeretur ex effectis favoris Dei per exclamationem, & exemplo Davidis; oppositisque exemplis Pharaonis & Nabucodonosoris.
units.tr: 1. From the favour of God that accompanies it. 1 Peter 5:6; James 4:6: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." Luke 1:52: he exalts the humble from the dust, etc. Plato and others also recognised this. Amplify from the effects of God's favour by exclamation, and by the example of David; and set against them the examples of Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar.

units.la: 2. A comitante favore & honore hominum. Hoc probetur 1. à contraria invidia & contemtu, quo laborat superbus & ambitiosus. Hinc talis thraso graphicè describatur ad odium omnium. Amplificetur ex loco communi de superbia & ambitione, 2. opposita amabilitate modestiæ, qua tanto magis extollitur homo, quanto magis se humiliat exemplo Danielis, &c.
units.tr: 2. From the favour and honour of men that accompany it. Prove this (1) from its contrary, envy and contempt, which the proud and ambitious man suffers. Hence such a braggart should be vividly described, to the hatred of all. Amplify from the common topic of pride and ambition; (2) set against them the lovableness of modesty, by which a man is raised the more, the more he humbles himself; example of Daniel, etc.

units.la: 3. A securitate in qua agit modestus. Probetur hoc 1. ratione à favore Dei & hominum, quo gaudet. 2. simili ædium, arborum humilium; illustrari potest etiam exemplis. 3. Contrario periculo cui expositi superbi & elati. vide hic exempla Tragica magnatum, qui vix ad momentum securi. e.g. Phaëton, Pompejus, pejus, Cæsar, Sejanus, quorum exempla uberius paulo proponantur.
units.tr: 3. From the security in which the modest man acts. Prove this (1) by reason, from the favour of God and of men which he enjoys; (2) by the simile of buildings and of low trees, which may also be illustrated by examples; (3) from the contrary danger to which the proud and haughty are exposed. Here see the tragic examples of magnates, who are scarcely safe for a moment: e.g. Phaethon, Pompey, Caesar, Sejanus, whose examples should be set out a little more fully.

units.la: III. Ab æquitate & congruentia modestiæ cum nostra natura. Hinc explica naturæ nostræ vilitatem & fragilitatem, vitæ incertitudinem, rerum de quibus turget homo vanitatem, & in ipso sinu gestare hominem dicas argumenta modestiæ.
units.tr: III. From the fitness and congruity of modesty with our nature. Hence explain the baseness and frailty of our nature, the uncertainty of life, and the emptiness of the things over which man swells; and you may say that man carries about in his very bosom the arguments for modesty.

units.la: IV. A necessario, quod probetur dicto Servatoris Matth. 18. v. 3. 4. Amen dico vobis, nisi conversi facti fueritis tanquam pueri, non intrabitis in regnum cœlorum. Quisquis igitur humiliaverit semetipsum &c. adde Matth. 23. v. 12. Hic exaggera 1. dicti hujus veritatem, juramento firmatam. 2. ejusdem claritatem. 3. gravitatem, qua cœlum negatur contravenientibus. Hinc per apostrophen vehementiorem increpet superbos spretores, qui spiritui superbiæ ac ambitiosis potius, quam Dei Spiritui obediunt. &c.
units.tr: IV. From necessity, which is proved by the saying of the Saviour in Matthew 18:3-4: "Verily I say unto you, unless you are converted and become as little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever therefore humbles himself, etc." Add Matthew 23:12. Here amplify (1) the truth of this saying, confirmed with an oath; (2) its clarity; (3) its gravity, by which heaven is denied to those who oppose it. Hence, by a more vehement apostrophe, he should rebuke the proud despisers who obey the spirit of pride and of ambition rather than the Spirit of God, etc.

units.la: D. Peroratio repetita breviter argumentorum summa flectat in adhortationem ad modestiam & humilitatem, ut a Deo suo tempore extollamur.
units.tr: D. Peroration: briefly repeating the sum of the arguments, let him turn to an exhortation to modesty and humility, so that we may be exalted by God in his time.

units.la: III. TRIUMPHUS PACIS.
units.tr: III. The Triumph of Peace.

units.la: Exord. A dicto illo Poetæ: Pax optima rerum, quas homini novisse datum, Pax una triumphis innumeris potior. Verissime dictum. Illustretur a consuetudine Romanorum, qui triumphos, solennitates omnium augustissimas, instituerunt ob victoriam. Hæc consuetudo 1. approbetur ex rationibus. a. ob debellatos hostes. b. adsolemniorem gratiarum actionem diis reddendam. c. ad illustrius decus ducis victoris & militum. d. ad excitationem virtutis, optimus enim quisque maximè gloriâ ducitur. 2. corrigatur: videlicet quod potius ob conservatam aut restitutam pacem triumphandum fuisset; quàm ob domitos hostes, aut virtutem victoris. Verum homines potius hærere in splendore ac pompa externa, quàm in vero bono, ad quod externa ista manuducunt. Hoc vero revera nullum aliud esse, quàm pacem, qua nihil salubrius humanæ societati.
units.tr: Exordium. From that saying of the poet: "Peace is the best of all things that man has been granted to know; peace alone is worth more than countless triumphs." Most truly said. Let it be illustrated from the custom of the Romans, who instituted triumphs, the most solemn of all ceremonies, on account of victory. This custom is approved, first, by reasons: (a) because enemies were overcome; (b) so that a more solemn thanksgiving might be rendered to the gods; (c) for the more illustrious honour of the victorious general and the soldiers; (d) to stir up virtue, for each of the best men is especially led by glory. Second, it is to be corrected: namely, that a triumph ought rather to have been celebrated on account of peace preserved or restored, than on account of conquered enemies or the valour of the victor. For men cling rather to the splendour and external pomp than to the true good, to which those external things lead us by the hand. Yet the true good is in fact nothing other than peace, than which nothing is more wholesome for human society.

units.la: Propos. De cujus proinde triumpho præcunctis victoriis dicendum; hoc præsertim tempore; quo & illa nobis reddita, & conservata toti imperio : ut digné tantum beneficium cœleste æstimare discamus.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore of this triumph, above all victories, is to be spoken, especially at this time, when both peace has been restored to us and preserved for the whole empire, so that we may learn to esteem so great a heavenly benefit as it deserves.

units.la: Tractatio. Rationes afferat
units.tr: Treatment. Let him set out the reasons.

units.la: I. Quia in rei veritate triumphi omnes propter pacem vel obtentam vel sperătam instituti. Neque enim triumphus concessus nisi hostibus penitus subactis. Unde Cicero pro L. Manil. carpit Lucullum triumphantem de Mithridate nondum domito.
units.tr: I. Because in the truth of the matter all triumphs were instituted on account of peace, either obtained or hoped for. For a triumph was granted only when the enemies had been utterly subdued. Hence Cicero, in the speech for Lucius Manilius, censures Lucullus for triumphing over Mithridates while he was not yet subdued.

units.la: II. Quia bellum belluinum est: pax hominem decet.
units.tr: II. Because war is beastlike; peace becomes man.

units.la: III. Quia bellum viribus præsertim geritur & fortunæ maximè subjectum: quod exemplis ostendatur: Pax verò consilio & prudentia conservatur & reducitur. Comparentur actiones bellicæ & togatæ, & hæ præferantur. vide Orat. pro Marcell.
units.tr: III. Because war is waged chiefly by strength and is very much subject to fortune, as examples show; but peace is preserved and brought back by counsel and prudence. Let warlike and civil actions be compared, and let the latter be preferred. See the oration for Marcellus.

units.la: IV. Quia bellum omne cruentum utrinque, & cum clade ac vastitate urbium & agrorum conjunctum: Pax contrà incruenta, secura, salutifera, beans urbes, agros, politiam, Ecclesiam, Scholas.
units.tr: IV. Because every war is bloody on both sides and joined with the ruin and devastation of cities and fields; peace, on the contrary, is bloodless, secure, and salutary, and blesses cities, fields, the state, the Church, and the schools.

units.la: V. Quia bello subiguntur tantum corpora; at pace uniuntur animi; utpote quæ sola firmissimum vinculum populorum.
units.tr: V. Because by war only bodies are subdued, but by peace minds are united; peace alone being the firmest bond of peoples.

units.la: VI. Quia bella a quolibet turbulento ingenio, Mario, Sulla, Catilina similibusque concitari possunt: at Pax non nisi a magnis ingeniis conservari & restitui potest, quales Salomon, Numa, Augustus, &c. Adde exempla recentioris ævi, quales Rudolphus, Matthias, Ferdinandus I. & III. & recentissime Imperator Leopoldus, reliquique imperii proceres. Hinc ostendatur, quomodo minitantibus passim imperio bellis, pax restituta & conservata.
units.tr: VI. Because wars can be stirred up by any turbulent disposition, such as Marius, Sulla, Catiline, and the like; but peace can be preserved and restored only by great minds, such as Solomon, Numa, Augustus, and others. Add examples of more recent times, such as Rudolf, Matthias, Ferdinand I and III, and most recently the Emperor Leopold, and the other nobles of the empire. Hence let it be shown how, while wars threaten the empire on every side, peace has been restored and preserved.

units.la: VII. Quia pax omnium bonorum votis expetitur; bellum omnes detestantur, deprecantur.
units.tr: VII. Because peace is sought by the prayers of all good men; all men detest and deprecate war.

units.la: Conclus. Votum habeat, ut tandem compositis bellis, aurea pax ubique restituatur, ut homines, Christiani maximè, publicæ salutiac ædificationi, non mutuæ destructioni ac laniena incumbant.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him make the wish that, at last, wars being settled, a golden peace may be restored everywhere, so that men, Christians above all, may devote themselves to the public welfare and building up, and not to mutual destruction and slaughter.

units.la: IV. POTESTAS TENEBRARUM PRÆVALENS ADVERSUS LUCIS AUTOREM.
units.tr: IV. THE POWER OF DARKNESS PREVAILING AGAINST THE AUTHOR OF LIGHT.

units.la: Exord. Ex abrupto facti indignitatem exaggerans per exclamationem: nem: Erumpe', erumpe Deo moriente : debitis exsequiis Servatoris, parentalis dolor. O diem tristem quo iux tenebris, vita morti succubuit.
units.tr: Exordium. Beginning abruptly, he magnifies the indignity of the deed by exclamation: Burst forth, burst forth, while God is dying; let the grief of a parent pay the due funeral rites to the Saviour. O sad day, on which light yielded to darkness and life to death.

units.la: Amplificetur 1. comparatione aliorum tristium v. gr. diluvii, mactationis Isaci, tristitiæ Jacobi ob Josephum & Benjaminū, obsidionis sub Ezechia, & tandem eversionis Hierof. ac captivitatis Babylonicæ ex Threnis Jeremiæ.
units.tr: Let it be amplified, first, by comparison with other sad events, for example the flood, the sacrifice of Isaac, the grief of Jacob over Joseph and Benjamin, the siege under Hezekiah, and finally the overthrow of Jerusalem and the Babylonian captivity, from the Lamentations of Jeremiah.

units.la: 2. Dubitatione, unde exordium, ubi finis; num loquendum, an plorandum? involuta mente tenebris, præpedita lingua pavore; dum illum perplexum videt & paventem, qui fiduciæ nobis fons est, dum tenebris involutum, qui vera lux & lucis Autor.
units.tr: Second, by hesitation: where to begin, where to end; should he speak or weep? His mind is wrapped in darkness and his tongue hindered by fear, while he sees him perplexed and trembling who is the source of our confidence, wrapped in darkness, who is the true light and the Author of light.

units.la: 3. Revocationem sui auditorumque, ut concepta fiducia tristissimam hanc tragœdiam introspiciant, qua nulla intuitu luctuosior, exemplo & fructu salubrior.
units.tr: Third, by recalling himself and his hearers, so that, with confidence conceived, they may look into this most sorrowful tragedy, than which none is more mournful to behold or more wholesome in example and fruit.

units.la: Propos. Contemplare stupens proditionem & captivitatem, intuere pavens examen & condemnationem, deplora lugens execution​em, in ludibrio, coronatione, abductione, crucifixione innocentissimi servatoris.
units.tr: Propositio. Behold in amazement the betrayal and the captivity; look on in fear the trial and the condemnation; lament with mourning the execution, the mockery, the crowning, the leading away and the crucifixion of the most innocent Saviour.

units.la: Expositio. Membri I. videl. Proditionis & Captivitatis.
units.tr: Exposition. Member I, namely, of the betrayal and the captivity.

units.la: I. Proponatur breviter cum suis circumstantiis, & scemate admirationis, quòd ille qui ad liberandum captivos venerat, a Juda in horto proditus, & a Judæis captivus ductus sit Hierosolymam.
units.tr: I. Let it be set forth briefly with its circumstances, and with a figure of admiration, that he who had come to free captives was betrayed by Judas in the garden and led captive by the Jews to Jerusalem.

units.la: II. Exaggerentur omnia
units.tr: II. Let everything be magnified.

units.la: a. Christus a Juda: Deus Magister, pius, beneficus, a proditore discipulo, ingrato, obstinato, sub specie osculi. Figuretur Apostrophe ad Judam; amplificetur inductione bonitatis Christi, & comparatione cum aliis ingratis, v. g. Doego adversus Davidem. Ps. 55. Concludatur conciliatione absurdorum; scilicet osculo sub specie charitatis prodendus erat, quem sola charitas ad moriendum impulerat.
units.tr: a. Christ by Judas: God as Teacher, the pious, the beneficent, betrayed by a disciple, ingrate and obstinate, under the appearance of a kiss. Let an apostrophe to Judas be formed; let it be amplified by the enumeration of Christ's goodness and by comparison with other ingrates, for example Doeg against David, Ps. 55. Let it be concluded by the reconciling of absurdities: namely, he had to be betrayed by a kiss under the appearance of love, he whom love alone had driven to die.

units.la: b. In horto, ubi negotium redemtionis per preces ac luctam cruentam agitabat cum Patre. Exaggeretur hæc lucta a fœditate causæ quam in se suscéperat; a severitate judicis; ab insultatione Dæmonis, qui ipsi tanquam sponsori instabat. Amplificetur Apostrophe ad Adamum, qui in horto voluptatis tentationi voluptatis succubuerat. Christus contra &c. c. Ajudæis: populo proprio, tot beneficiis affectopræ reliquis gentibus: amplificetur ab inductione beneficiorum inde ab antiquo, & comparatione desiderii ac spei antiquorum, cum ingratitudine posterorum. Concludatur solatio ex conspirantibus vaticiniis Zach. Vulnera in domo amantium me.
units.tr: b. In the garden, where he was transacting the business of redemption with the Father through prayers and a bloody struggle. Let this struggle be magnified by the foulness of the cause he had undertaken; by the severity of the judge; by the taunting of the Devil, who pressed him as if he were his surety. Let an apostrophe to Adam be amplified, who in the garden of pleasure had succumbed to the temptation of pleasure. Christ, on the contrary, [did otherwise]. c. Among the Jews: his own people, honoured with so many benefits above the other nations. Let it be amplified by the enumeration of benefits from of old, and by comparing the desire and hope of the ancients with the ingratitude of their descendants. Let it be concluded with consolation from the agreeing prophecies of Zechariah: I was wounded in the house of my friends.

units.la: d. Hierolymam ducitur captivus, quæ custos esse debebat, Legis, asylum oppressorum: eo ducitur captivus, ubi libere docuerat, quæ gratulabunda pridie intrantem exceperat, qui colligere satagebat filios ejus, ligatur indigne. Amplificentur hæc porro oppositorum comparatione figurata, apostrophe, prosopopoeia ipsius Christi. Sic iniquitas, ingratitudo, odium, iniquitas, prævaluit pietati, gratitudini, charitati, justitiæ.
units.tr: d. He is led captive to Jerusalem, which ought to have been the guardian of the Law, the refuge of the oppressed. He is led captive there where he had taught freely, the city which had joyfully received him the day before when he entered, and he who had striven to gather its children is shamefully bound.
