Let these things be further amplified by the comparison of opposites, by apostrophe and by prosopopoeia of Christ himself. Thus iniquity, ingratitude, hatred, iniquity prevailed over piety, gratitude, love and justice.

units.la: Membrum II. de Examine & condemnatione.
units.tr: Member II. Concerning the examination and condemnation.

units.la: Hic facta transitione a minori ad majus: a præludio scilicet ad theatrum sanguine, sputo, flagris, spinis fœdum.
units.tr: Here a transition is made from the lesser to the greater: from the prelude, that is, to the theatre foul with blood, spittle, scourges and thorns.

units.la: I. Breviter referantur gesta in judicio sacro, & Politico. Scilicet in utroque per falsos testes accusatur affectati regni, motæ rebellionis, blasphemiæ; damnatur mortis; contumelia, verberibus, sputo oneratur. Negatur a Petro, innocens flagellatur.
units.tr: I. Let the deeds done in the sacred and in the civil judgment be briefly related. Namely, in each, false witnesses accuse him of aspiring to a kingdom, of stirring up rebellion, of blasphemy; he is condemned to death; he is burdened with insult, blows and spitting. He is denied by Peter; the innocent man is scourged.

units.la: II. Exaggerentur hæc per partes
units.tr: II. Let these things be magnified part by part.

units.la: a. Mendacium hic prævalet veritati, nec contradicenti etiam.
units.tr: a. Here lying prevails over truth, and even over one who contradicts it.

units.la: b. Regnum affectavit scilicet; qui humilitatis autor erat, qui regnum suum de hoc sæculo esse negabat, qui servus factus.
units.tr: b. He is charged with aspiring to a kingdom, he who was the author of humility, who declared that his kingdom was not of this world, who was made a servant.

units.la: c. Rebellionis arguitur, omnis ordinis fons.
units.tr: c. He is accused of rebellion, the source of every order.

units.la: d. Blasphemia imputatur illi, qui non suam, sed patris quæsivit gloriam, qui gloriæ, veritatis, justitiæ, bonitatis divinæ unicus vindex erat.
units.tr: d. Blasphemy is imputed to him who sought not his own glory but the Father's, who was the sole avenger of the glory, truth, justice and goodness of God.

units.la: e. Contumelia afficitur, Dominus gloriæ; verberibus, innocentiæ & pacis autor. sputo, pulcherrimus omnium. Flagellatur, a Pilato innocens declaratus. Exaggerentur hæc omnia in genere, ab interveniente gravissimo Petri lapsu, cujus majorem, quam sui curam habuit.
units.tr: e. He is subjected to insult, he the Lord of glory; to blows, he the author of innocence and peace; to spitting, he the most beautiful of all. He is scourged though Pilate had declared him innocent. Let all these things be magnified in general, from the serious fall of Peter, for whom he had a greater care than for himself.

units.la: Membrum III. de executione.
units.tr: Member III. Concerning the execution.

units.la: I. Prævia transitione pathetica, recensentur breviter factum per hypotypofin, videl. traditur militibus, qui ipsi illudunt, vestes detrahunt, verberant, spinis coronant, deducunt, crucifigunt, occidunt.
units.tr: I. After a pathetic transition, the deed is briefly rehearsed by hypotyposis: he is delivered to the soldiers, who mock him, strip off his garments, beat him, crown him with thorns, lead him away, crucify him, kill him.

units.la: II. Ponderentur & exaggerentur singula.
units.tr: II. Let each thing be weighed and magnified.

units.la: a. Illuditur illi, coram quo contremiscit orbis: per ludibrium rex salutatur, rex regum.
units.tr: a. He is mocked, he before whom the world trembles: by mockery he is saluted as king, King of kings.

units.la: b. Exuitur ille cujus justitia tecti coram Deo comparere possumus.
units.tr: b. He is stripped, he by whose righteousness we can appear clothed before God.

units.la: c. Verberatur, pacis autor, cujus tumices, fanatio nobis.
units.tr: c. He is beaten, the author of peace, by whose wounds we are healed.

units.la: d. Spinis coronatur, ex cujus capite omnis benedictio manat.
units.tr: d. He is crowned with thorns, from whose head every blessing flows.

units.la: e. Deducitur ad supplicium, qui nos ab inferis reduxit,
units.tr: e. He is led to punishment, he who brought us back from the dead.

units.la: f. Crucifigitur tanquam maledictus, autor benedictionis. Exaggeretur crudelitas supplicii hujus cum aliis. Hæc per hypotyposin.
units.tr: f. He is crucified as one accursed, he the author of blessing. Let the cruelty of this punishment be magnified in comparison with others. These things by hypotyposis.

units.la: g. Occiditur, vitæ autor.
units.tr: g. He is killed, the author of life.

units.la: Subjungatur pathos, de potestate tenebrarum, occupante Judæos, Pilatum, cunctos, ita ut solem justitiæ aversarentur.
units.tr: Let a pathos be added concerning the power of darkness, taking possession of the Jews, of Pilate, of all, so that they turned away from the Sun of righteousness.

units.la: Illustretur 1. comparatione Martyrum, Deciorum pro patria occumbentium à manu hostili. Marci Reguli, qui exquisitissimis cruciatib’ affectus a Carthaginiensi. Samsonis qui vexatus satis ab hostibus sua morte mortem intulit hostibus: Ita Christus.
units.tr: Let it be illustrated, first, by comparison with martyrs, the Decii who died for their country at the hand of the enemy; with Marcus Regulus, who was subjected to the most exquisite torments by the Carthaginians; with Samson, who, having been sufficiently harassed by his enemies, brought death upon them by his own death. So Christ.

units.la: 2. Ab effectis, in Pilato. Ecce homo; latrone, cœlo & terra denique, quæ obscuritate & tremore indignationem testata sunt. Apostrophe adsaxea corda hominum.
units.tr: Second, from the effects, in Pilate: "Behold the man"; in the robber; in heaven and earth finally, which bore witness by darkness and trembling to their indignation. An apostrophe to the stony hearts of men.

units.la: 3. A causa efficiente ex parte nostri, quæ est peccatum; Ef. 43.24. cujus hic exaggeretur fœditas. &c.
units.tr: Third, from the efficient cause on our part, which is sin, Ef. 43.24, whose foulness is to be magnified here, etc.

units.la: 4. A causa finali. Ex parte Dei & ipsi’ servatoris est satisfactio justitiæ divinæ, impletio veritatis prædictionum & figurarum, abolitio peccati, condemnatio diaboli & enervatio potestatis ac regni tenebrarum.
units.tr: Fourth, from the final cause. On God's part and on the part of the Saviour himself, there is the satisfaction of divine justice, the fulfilment of the truth of the predictions and figures, the abolition of sin, the condemnation of the devil and the weakening of the power and kingdom of darkness.

units.la: D. Explosio sententiæ Judæorum, qui per sanguinem victimarum; peccata elui posse credunt; & Samosatenianorum ac Sociniano-rum, qui non nisi in exemplum hæc passum esse Christum statuunt.
units.tr: D. An outburst against the opinion of the Jews, who believe that sins can be washed away by the blood of victims, and against the Samosatenians and Socinians, who hold that Christ suffered these things only as an example.

units.la: At cara nimis est redemtio animarum, quam ut sanguine hircotum parari queat.
units.tr: But the redemption of souls is too precious to be procured by the blood of goats.

units.la: Non defuere exempla patientiæ, si nil nisi exemplum requirebatur. Nec tali opus fuisset lucta servatoris, ut, tanquam maledictio, extensus in cruce, vociferari necesse habuerit, Deus mi Deus mi, quare me deseruisti. Exaggerentur hæc verba, & per defectum veluti virium vox sistatur. Denique sententia Pontificiorum explodatur, quasi addendæ adhuc sint passiones sanctorum.
units.tr: Examples of patience were not lacking, if nothing more than an example was required. Nor would the Saviour's struggle have been needed, such that, stretched on the cross as if accursed, he was obliged to cry out, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Let these words be magnified, and let the voice be halted, as if by the failing of strength. Finally, the opinion of the Papists is to be refuted, as if the sufferings of the saints still had to be added.

units.la: E. Conclusio. Revocationem animi habeat, ex eo quod sic moriendo, non vincatur, sed vincat servator, & morte sua mortis aboleat imperium, & paradisum gloriæ referet, omnibus confugientibus ad ipsum, qui extensis ulnis in cruce omnes veluti ad se invitat.
units.tr: Conclusio. Let him have a restoration of the spirit from this, that by dying thus the Saviour is not overcome but conquers, and by his death abolishes the empire of death, and brings back the paradise of glory, all taking refuge in him, who with arms stretched out on the cross invites all to himself.

units.la: V. DE GLORIA COELI.
units.tr: V. CONCERNING THE GLORY OF HEAVEN.

units.la: A. Exord. A dicto Apostoli Phil. 3. 20. πολίτευμα ἡμῶν ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει, ἐξ οὗ καὶ σωτῆρα ἀπεκδεχόμεθα κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the saying of the Apostle, Phil. 3:20: "Our citizenship is in heaven [πολίτευμα ἡμῶν ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει], from which we also await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ [ἐξ οὗ καὶ σωτῆρα ἀπεκδεχόμεθα κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν]."

units.la: Hoc dictum
units.tr: This saying.

units.la: I. Proponatur.
units.tr: I. To be set forth.

units.la: II. Illustretur paraphrasi; videlicet hoc velle Apostolum: rempublicam, cujus nos cives sumus, non esse hic in terris, sed in cœlis, ubi & caput ac redemtor noster sit, qui ad similem gloriam suos extollet.
units.tr: II. To be illustrated by paraphrase, namely that the Apostle means that the commonwealth of which we are citizens is not here on earth but in heaven, where our head and redeemer also is, who will raise his own to a like glory.

units.la: III. Addatur causa: quia homo non est conditus ad hanc vitam; quippe cujus anima cœlestis originis, semper anhelet originem & sedem stabilem ac perennem.
units.tr: III. The reason is to be added: man was not made for this life, since his soul, being of heavenly origin, always longs for its origin and for a stable and everlasting seat.

units.la: IV. Illustretur a contrario: videlicet a rerum terrestrium vanitate, ita ut merito cœleste ac stabile hoc habitaculum, quo Apostolus nos remittit ad prægustum præli-bandum sit. Addatur simile, a desiderio patriæ, quo tenemur in peregrinia.
units.tr: IV. To be illustrated by contrast, namely from the vanity of earthly things, so that this heavenly and stable dwelling, to which the Apostle sends us, is rightly to be tasted beforehand. A comparison is to be added from the longing for one's homeland, which holds us while we are abroad.

units.la: B. Propof. Cum præmissa virium extenuatione: videlicet. Quamvis vero materiæ hujus tantum sit pondus, ut ipse Apostolus non nisi cum exstasi illa meditari, Esaias vero nec visam oculis, nec perceptam auribus, nec cogitationibus penetrabilem dicat, te tamen conniventibus oculis, stupescente animo ac balbutiente lingua gloriam cœlestis hujus civitatis, tanquam solem, veluti carbone, adumbraturum; rogare vero Auditores, ut, illa quæ ἀρρήτα ipsi Apostolo, dicere conantem favore sublevare velint; admirantes potius ea quæ dicuntur.
units.tr: B. Propositio. With a preliminary admission of our weakness, namely: although the weight of this matter is so great that the Apostle himself says he can meditate on it only in ecstasy, and Isaiah says it is neither seen by the eyes, nor heard by the ears, nor penetrated by thought, yet I, with eyes half-closed, a dazed mind and a stammering tongue, shall try to shadow forth the glory of this heavenly city, as one would depict the sun with charcoal. I ask the hearers to be willing to support with their favour one who attempts to speak of the unspeakable things [ἀρρήτα] of which the Apostle himself spoke, and rather to marvel at what is said.

units.la: C. Tractatio habeat
units.tr: C. Tractatio should contain:

units.la: I. Παράγωγον, qua probetur dari talem gloriam cœlestem futuram post hanc vitam. 1. Ab idea, indeque enato naturali desiderio, quo mens humana, non satiata caducis hisce anhelat sedem stabilem, & felicitatem majorem illa, quæ in terris contingit.
units.tr: I. Derivation [Παράγωγον], by which it is proved that such a heavenly glory is given after this life. 1. From the idea, and from the natural desire arising from it, by which the human mind, not satisfied with these perishable things, longs for a stable seat and a greater happiness than what is found on earth.

units.la: 2. Probetur exemplo gentium, quæ de futura animæ felicitate sollicitæ sunt.
units.tr: 2. It is proved by the example of the Gentiles, who were anxious about the future happiness of the soul.

units.la: 3. Inquietudine animi, etiam in summa felicitate terrena. Hinc enim enatas esse differentes istas sententias de summo bono; quas brevi enumeratione exponat; ostendatque nullam esse, quæ animum satiare potuerit.
units.tr: 3. From the restlessness of the mind even in the greatest earthly happiness. For from this have arisen those differing opinions about the highest good, which he should set out in a brief enumeration, and show that none of them has been able to satisfy the mind.

units.la: 4. Testimonio S. Scripturarum, quæ in omnibus capitibus huc manuducant: quod ostendendum nervose & breviter. Quia vocant ad æterna insuper habitis caducis. Quia communionem cum æterno Deo docent. 3. Quia expresse hoc dicunt passim.
units.tr: 4. By the testimony of the Holy Scriptures, which in every chapter lead us to this; this is to be shown forcefully and briefly. Because they call us to eternal things, counting perishable things as nothing. Because they teach communion with the eternal God. 3. Because they say this expressly, everywhere.

units.la: 5. Concludatur; merito igitur quærendum esse illud bonum, in quo animus tuto acquiescat.
units.tr: 5. Conclusion: therefore that good is rightly to be sought in which the mind may rest securely.

units.la: II. Ἐξήγησις seu expositionem.
units.tr: II. Exegesis, or exposition.

units.la: 1. Excusét mentis hebetudinem & linguæ tarditatem quæ nec capere, nec eloqui queat illa, quæ Apostolus ἀρρήτα dicit: cujus solo prægustu raptus David, Petrus, caduca omnia insuper habuerunt. Illustret hæc similibus v. gr. quasi embrio utero clausus, de vitæ amœnitate, cæcus de cœlorum varietate differere velit. Quasi quis carbone solem depingere satagat.
units.tr: 1. Let him excuse the dullness of his mind and the slowness of his tongue, which can neither grasp nor utter those things the Apostle calls unspeakable [ἀρρήτα], by the foretaste of which alone David and Peter counted all perishable things as nothing. Let him illustrate this with comparisons: as one enclosed in the womb, an embryo, might try to speak of the pleasantness of life, or a blind man of the variety of the heavens, or as one might strive to paint the sun with charcoal.

units.la: 2. Explicet gentilium de conditione piorum opinionem, qui in insulis fortunatis, in campis Elysiis, inter sidera requiem, festivitatem, gloriam sibi imaginati sunt. Vide Cic. in somnio Scipionis. Pind. Od. I. &c.
units.tr: 2. Let him explain the Gentile opinion about the condition of the pious, who imagined for themselves rest, festivity and glory among the stars, in the Fortunate Isles and the Elysian Fields. See Cicero, in the Dream of Scipio; Pindar, Odes I, etc.

units.la: 3. Exponat similia, & emblemata, quibus Scriptura Sacra cœlorum gloriam ac felicitatem nobis depingit. v. g. sub imagine, convivii, nuptiarum perpetuarum, horti fructibus, fontibusque amœni, Templi & Palatii magnifici, hæreditatis amplæ, & repositæ, regni ac triumphi perpetui: quod expoliatur & exigua tantum umbra esse dicantur gloriæ revelandæ in cœlis.
units.tr: 3. Let him set out similar images and emblems by which Holy Scripture paints for us the glory and happiness of heaven: under the image of a banquet, of perpetual marriage, of a garden with fruits and pleasant fountains, of a magnificent temple and palace, of an ample inheritance laid up in reserve, of a perpetual kingdom and triumph. These are to be polished, and it is to be said that they are only a small shadow of the glory to be revealed in heaven.

units.la: 4. Enarret illam per partes: quales sunt.
units.tr: 4. Let him relate it part by part, as follows:

units.la: 1. Intuitus Dei, t. lucis itius in exhaustæ; quam intuentes in eandem imaginem transformamur. 1.Cor.13. non secus ac oculus, & speculum, soli oppositum. Abreptum hic se dicat cat sola cogitatione ejus claritatis, ad quam hic mens hebescat contemplando, ut frustra sint scholastici, qui modum mensuramque hujus intuitus definire satagunt: cum per visibilis lucis naturam, visusq; circa illam operationem describere queant. Interim talis futura est, qua non imaginem & diminutam speciem, sed ipsam Dei essentiam, proprietates & personas, modo hic incomprehensibili, contemplaturi sumus. Pf.17. 1. Cor. 13. 3. Joh. v.2. 1.Cor.3. v.14. &c.
units.tr: 1. The sight of God, the inexhaustible light of him, into which we, beholding it, are transformed into the same image (1 Cor. 13), just as the eye and a mirror are set against the sun. Here let him say that he is carried away by the mere thought of that brightness, at which the mind here grows dim when it contemplates; so the scholastics labour in vain who strive to define the mode and measure of this sight, since they can describe it only through the nature of visible light and the operation of sight upon it. Meanwhile, such will be the sight that we shall contemplate not an image or a diminished likeness, but the very essence of God, his properties and persons, in a mode that is incomprehensible here. Ps. 17. 1 Cor. 13. 3. Joh. v.2. 1 Cor. 3. v.14, etc.

units.la: II. Fruitio bonitatis ipsius infinitae; quae cum immensa sit, nunquam exhauriri potest, & quo plus inde haurit homo, eo plus semper restat. Hinc semper saturitas, & nunquam fastidium, quia cum totum & perfectum semper inde percipient pii, nunquam tamen omnia capient, quippe infinitum semper restat.
units.tr: II. The enjoyment of his infinite goodness, which, since it is immense, can never be exhausted; and the more a person draws from it, the more always remains. Hence there is always satisfaction and never weariness, because although the godly always receive from it the whole and the perfect, they will never take in everything, since the infinite always remains.

units.la: III. Rectificatio omnium defectuum, corporis, & animae. 1.Cor.15. Resurget incorruptibile &c: Apoc.21.4. & Phil.3.20.
units.tr: III. The restoration of all defects, of body and soul. 1 Cor. 15: it will rise incorruptible, etc.; Rev. 21:4; and Phil. 3:20.

units.la: IV. Enascens inde gaudium solidum ex re scilicet minime evanida; & perfectum ex re infinita & aeterna Pf.36. 9. 1.Cor.2. v.9. Comparetur cum gaudio ex rebus caducis, quod breve & conjunctum vel cum tristitia vel metu saltem mutationis.
units.tr: IV. The joy arising from it is solid, since it comes from a thing by no means fading, and perfect, since it comes from a thing infinite and eternal. Ps. 36:9; 1 Cor. 2:9. It is to be compared with the joy from perishable things, which is brief and mixed either with sadness or at least with fear of change.

units.la: Exaggeretur ex circumstantia Loci; caeli scilicet supremi, ubi thronus Dei: & sodales, Christus, Patriarchae, Prophetae, Apostoli, Angeli, Amici: quos cognoscemus, quibuscum de gratia Dei & felicitate colloquemur. Non attinet disputare de modo loquelae, certe lingua & forsan Hebraica: argumento. Act.26. 14. Nec dubitandum de notitia, invicem illuminata mente. Licet cognitio & intuitus Dei absorbebit & complectetur ac satiabit omnes perfecte tanquam lux inexhausta & abyssus infinita. Illustretur comparatione facis, quae licet videatur splendente sole, tamen veluti obtenebrescit. Ita &c. Hic revocet semetipsum Orator, quasi nimium progressus in abdita divinitatis, & obrutus lumine incomprehensibili, quod adorandum potius, quam scrutandum.
units.tr: It is to be enlarged upon from the circumstance of the place: namely the highest heaven, where the throne of God is; and the companions: Christ, the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, angels, friends, whom we shall know, and with whom we shall converse about the grace of God and our happiness. It is not worth disputing about the mode of speech, certainly a language perhaps Hebrew; the argument is Acts 26:14. Nor should we doubt about knowledge, with minds mutually enlightened, although the knowledge and sight of God will absorb, embrace and satisfy all perfectly, like an inexhaustible light and an infinite abyss. Let it be illustrated by the comparison of a torch, which, although it seems to be dimmed when the sun shines, is in fact as it were darkened. And so on. Here the orator should recall himself, as if he had gone too far into the hidden things of the Godhead and been overwhelmed by an incomprehensible light, which is to be adored rather than searched out.

units.la: V. Detestatio sententiae Epicureorum & Atheorum, qui porcorum instar, gratia Dei fruantur, at non respiciant autorem, qui instar lumbricorum, instar talparum, in terra se laginent, lucis veraeignari, cum voto ut vel minima scintilla hujus lucis ipsorum mens tingatur.
units.tr: V. Condemnation of the opinion of the Epicureans and Atheists, who, like pigs, enjoy the grace of God but do not look to its author, and who, like earthworms and moles, wallow in the earth, ignorant of the true light, with the wish that at least the smallest spark of this light might tinge their minds.

units.la: Conclusio. Habeat votum fruendæ cito istius felicitatis, quam nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor cujusquam venit, &c.
units.tr: Conclusio. Let him have the wish to enjoy soon that happiness which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of anyone, etc.

units.la: VI. DE GLORIA REGNI CHRISTI.
units.tr: VI. Concerning the Glory of the Kingdom of Christ.

units.la: Exord. Ab Emblemate Colossi Danielis. Hoc
units.tr: Exordium. From the emblem of Daniel's colossus. This:

units.la: 1. Proponatur
units.tr: 1. Let it be set forth.

units.la: 2. Significatio ejus explicetur videl. notari præcipua regna mundi eorumque gloriam, per lapidem vero regnum Christi omnem istam gloriam obscurans & confundens, ut ipsum illud solùm emineat, & dominus solus regnet.
units.tr: 2. Its meaning is to be explained, namely that the chief kingdoms of the world and their glory are signified; but by the stone the kingdom of Christ is meant, obscuring and confounding all that glory, so that it alone stands out and the Lord alone reigns.

units.la: 3. Hujus regni gloriam in spiritu vidisse & admiratum fuisse Esaiam cap. 6. Davidem Psal. 93. Psal 96. 97. &c.
units.tr: 3. That Isaiah in the Spirit saw the glory of this kingdom and was struck with wonder at it (Isa. 6); likewise David (Ps. 93; Ps. 96, 97, etc.).

units.la: 4. Meritò & nos qui subditi sumus, prædicare gloriam regis & regni hujus, maximè hoc tempore quo memoria ascensionis, qua regnum hoc occupavit Christus, solennis est Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 4. Rightly also we who are its subjects should proclaim the glory of this King and kingdom, especially at this time, when the memory of the ascension, by which Christ took possession of this kingdom, is solemn to the Church.

units.la: Propos. Quis scopus hujus orationis. videl. ut felicitatem nostram intelligamu. Captetur benevolentia & attentio.
units.tr: Propositio. The aim of this discourse is that we may understand our happiness. Goodwill and attention are to be sought.

units.la: Tractatio sit bimembris
units.tr: Tractatio is to be in two parts.

units.la: A. De Regni Christi Constitutione; ubi
units.tr: A. On the Constitution of Christ's Kingdom, where

units.la: 1. In genere ostendat gloriam regni mundani consistere tum in Majestate & virtutibus regentis, tum in amplitudine territorii & bonis regni, tum denique in bono regimine. Hoc
units.tr: 1. In general he shows that the glory of an earthly kingdom consists both in the majesty and virtues of the ruler, and in the extent of its territory and the goods of the realm, and finally in good government. This:

units.la: 2. In specie applicet ad regnum Christi facta subinde pro re nata comparatione cum Monarchiis eximiis. Itaque
units.tr: 2. In particular he applies to the kingdom of Christ, making from time to time, as the occasion arises, comparisons with outstanding monarchies. Thus:

units.la: 1. Prædicet regis.
units.tr: 1. He proclaims the King.

units.la: a. Personam: quòd non homo tantum ex illustri prosapia sed simul verus Deus, cujus nutu contremiscit orbis. Hinc toties inculcare Davidem & excitare populum quòd Deus regnet. O beata gens. &c.
units.tr: a. His person: that he is not merely a man of illustrious lineage but at the same time the true God, at whose nod the world trembles. Hence he repeatedly impresses on the hearers, and stirs up the people, that God reigns. O blessed nation, etc.

units.la: b. Jus regnandi videl. 1. datum à Deo Ps. 2.
units.tr: b. His right to reign, namely (1) given by God (Ps. 2).

units.la: 2. Acquisitum proprio sanguine contra hostem diabolum. Breviter explicetur jus à Diabolo acquisitum ex peccato & vindicatio per Christi mortem & resurrectionem.
units.tr: (2) Acquired by his own blood against the enemy, the devil. The right acquired from the devil through sin, and its vindication through Christ's death and resurrection, is briefly explained.

units.la: c. Majestatem & gloriam regis, qua post victoriam cruentam triumphabundus in cœlum ascendit constitutus ad dexteram Dei vid. Eph. 2. v. 9. & seq. Illustretur triumphorum Romanorum comparatione. Claudatur haec pars ephipho-nemate, qua majestas Christi omni mundanae majestati praeferatur, quantum solis fulgor nocturnae faci praeferendus est.
units.tr: c. The majesty and glory of the King, by which, after a bloody victory, he ascended triumphantly into heaven and was set at the right hand of God (see Eph. 2:9ff.). Let this be illustrated by comparison with Roman triumphs. Let this part be closed with an epiphonema, by which the majesty of Christ is preferred to all worldly majesty as far as the sun's brightness is to be preferred to a night torch.

units.la: 2. Agat de subditis; tum in genere uti sunt, omnes creaturae Pf. 103. v. 19. & Pf. 104. ipliusque hostes Pf. 110. tum in specie, uti sunt fideles ab aeterno electi, & qui sunt lux mundi, sal terrae, justi & sancti. Exaggeretur comparatione cum aliorum regum subditis, qui pauci, & promiscue boni & mali. Opponatur contra cursus & amplitudo regni Christi, per conversionem gentium in utroque orbe.
units.tr: 2. He treats of the subjects: first in general, as they are, namely all creatures (Ps. 103:19; Ps. 104) and his enemies too (Ps. 110); then in particular, as they are the faithful, chosen from eternity, who are the light of the world, the salt of the earth, the righteous and holy. Let this be magnified by comparison with the subjects of other kings, who are few and in whom good and bad are mixed. Set against this the course and extent of Christ's kingdom through the conversion of the nations in both hemispheres.

units.la: 3. Agat de bonis & privilegiis regni hujus. Videl. alia regna jactant privilegia & opes, regnum Christi non est de hoc mundo, sed bona habet praestantiora, videl. remissionem peccatorum, justitiam & haereditatem coeli Zach. 9. &c. quibus quid excellentius? &c. Exaggeres comparatione, & digrediaris in deplorationem caecitatis mundanae, quae deserto hoc rege ad mundum & diabolum deficit
units.tr: 3. He treats of the goods and privileges of this kingdom. Other kingdoms boast of privileges and wealth; the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, but has better goods, namely forgiveness of sins, righteousness and the inheritance of heaven (Zech. 9, etc.). What is more excellent than these? etc. Let this be magnified by comparison, and let him digress into a lament over the blindness of the world, which, forsaking this King, falls away to the world and the devil.

units.la: B. De Regni hujus administratione,
units.tr: B. On the Administration of this Kingdom,

units.la: I. In gubernatione subditorum.
units.tr: I. In the governance of the subjects.

units.la: 1. Per jus illud vere regium Legis scil. & Evangelii: illius legis lauda primo sanctitatem, comparatione cum aliis legibus. Hinc iplam legislationem in Sina explica, & usum ejus in Vet. & Nov. Test. ostende, vide Catech. hujus Evangelii revelationem & summam efficaciam in conversione mundi expone. Illustret comparatione cum aliis regnis, ubi justitia sed sine gratia obtinet.
units.tr: 1. By that truly royal law, namely of the Law and of the Gospel. Let him first praise the holiness of that law by comparison with other laws. Hence let him explain the legislation itself at Sinai, and show its use in the Old and New Testaments (see the Catechism); let him set out the revelation of this Gospel and its supreme efficacy in the conversion of the world. Let him illustrate it by comparison with other kingdoms, where justice holds sway but without grace.

units.la: 2. Per Spiritum sanctum, flectentem corda & inscribentem cordibus legem. Illustra comparatione cum aliis legislatoribus, quijus suum exigunt, perficiendi facultatem non largiuntur.
units.tr: 2. By the Holy Spirit, bending hearts and writing the law on hearts. Illustrate by comparison with other lawgivers, who exact their own obedience but do not bestow the ability to perform it.

units.la: Digrediatur in locum de effusione Sp. S. ex ejusdem operationibus in fidelibus, & hinc porro ostende praerogativam populi Dei, seu Ecclesiae pro reliquis cunctis gentibus, quarum miseram conditionem per inductionem ostende, ut Christianorum appareat felicitas.
units.tr: Let him digress into a place on the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and his operations in the faithful, and from this further show the preeminence of the people of God, or of the Church, over all the other nations, whose wretched condition is shown by induction, so that the happiness of Christians may appear.

units.la: II. In repressione hostium, Satanae & mundi, seu haereticorum seu tyrannorum, quorum furorem & insidias explica ex historia Ecclesiastica praesertim, & insuperabilem virtutem ac defensionem sionem Christi oppone, cui jus invicto robore subsistet semper ecclesia Matth. 16. Fiat apostrophe ad Christum ad dextram Dei exaltatum & ipsi ascribatur Ecclesiae contra hostium furores conservatio.
units.tr: II. In the repression of enemies, of Satan and of the world, whether heretics or tyrants, whose rage and snares are to be explained chiefly from ecclesiastical history; and the invincible power and defence of Christ is to be set against them, on whose strength the Church shall always stand firm (Matt. 16). Let there be an apostrophe to Christ exalted at the right hand of God, and let the preservation of the Church against the rage of its enemies be ascribed to him.

units.la: Conclusionis loco. 1. Fiat paraenesis ad fideles regni hujus subditos, ut mitissimo Christi sceptro colla submittant, & ruentibus in mutua arma Orientis & Occidentis regibus labantibus regnis in hujus regis potentia & cura confidant & in regni hujus bonis & spe acquiescant.
units.tr: By way of conclusion: 1. Let there be an exhortation to the faithful subjects of this kingdom, that they bow their necks to Christ's most gentle sceptre, and, while the kings of East and West rush into mutual arms and their kingdoms totter, trust in the power and care of this King and rest in the goods and hope of this kingdom.

units.la: 2. Addat votum pro successu regni Christi, ut quemadmodum illud ipsum lapidis instar totum mundum occupet, quo Satanae potestas in gentes aboleatur & Dominus solus regnet.
units.tr: 2. Let him add a prayer for the success of Christ's kingdom, that, as that very stone, like a mountain, fills the whole world, the power of Satan may be abolished among the nations and the Lord alone may reign.

units.la: VII. COMMENDATIO CONCORDIAE.
units.tr: VII. Commendation of Concord

units.la: Exord. A suavissima imagine concordiae naturae, quam proponit. Hos. 2. 21. 22. Ego exaudiam coelos, &c. Addatur illustrior paraphrasis, videl. notari suavissimam harmoniam, qua omnia creata mutuo amore revinciuntur & uniuntur Deo tanquam causae primae; ex qua per medias causas omnia bona tandem derivantur in hominem totius creaturae dominum & compendium. Scil. in natura ipsa posuisse Deum semina virtutum omnium. Hanc disciplinam in multis sectatos fuisse Stoicos: qui semina virtutum ex natura eruerunt. Ostendatur inductione quadam. Illustretur prolepsi videl. Licet corrupta sit natura humana, tamen vestigia pristinae rectitudinis in illa adhuc esse reliqua; ex quibus egregia illa monita ac Leges, quibus resp. colligatae sint, enata. Accedatur ad hypothesin; videl. praetermissis in praesentiarum aliis, te Concordiae semina ac argumenta ex naturae principiis depromturum; ut ejus amor ac studium in omnibus excitetur.
units.tr: Exord. Begin with the most lovely image of concord in nature, which he sets forth at Hos. 2:21-22: "I will hear the heavens," etc. Let a fuller paraphrase be added, namely that one notes the sweetest harmony by which all created things are bound together and united in mutual love, with God as their first cause. From this, through intermediate causes, all good things are at last derived into man, the lord and summary of all creation. That is, God placed in nature itself the seeds of all virtues. The Stoics, who drew the seeds of virtue out of nature, pursued this teaching in many respects. Let it be shown by a certain induction. Let it be illustrated by prolepsis, namely: although human nature is corrupted, traces of its original rectitude still remain in it, and from these arose those excellent admonitions and laws by which commonwealths are held together. Let the hypothesis be approached: setting aside for the present other matters, you will draw the seeds and arguments of concord from the principles of nature, so that love and zeal for it may be stirred up in everyone.

units.la: Propos. Scil. Concordiam commendaturum, te concors omnium auditorum votum sperare & benevolam petere auscultationem.
units.tr: Propos. Namely, that you will commend concord, hoping for the agreement of all your hearers and asking for their kindly attention.

units.la: Tractatio. Praemissa nominis consideratione per praeteritionem quod vel a conspiratione cordium vel cordarum dicatur, unde Graecis ὁμόνοια & συμφωνία; cum mente, corde ac voce in unum conspirant plures.
units.tr: Tractatio. Having first considered the name, by passing over whether it is derived from the conspiring of hearts or of strings, whence the Greeks have homonoia [ὁμόνοια] and symphonia [συμφωνία], since several people breathe together in one mind, heart and voice.

units.la: I. Fontem explicet: Hanc scil. perfectissimam esse in Deo, in quo uti una essentia, ita una voluntas, & concordans verbi divini consonantia. Hinc omnis tum in natura, tum in Ecclesia consensus & concordia. Deum scil. uti ipse amor est, ita mutui amoris ac <bl>συμπαθείας</bl> semina indidit naturae; & constanti Lege adstrinxit Ecclesiam. Hinc admiretur ac praedicet felicem rerum statum & Ecclesiae & universi, quamdiu in hac harmonia perseverat.
units.tr: I. Let him explain the source: this concord is most perfect in God, in whom, as there is one essence, so there is one will, and a harmony in agreement with the divine Word. Hence comes all agreement and concord, both in nature and in the Church. God, who is love itself, has implanted in nature the seeds of mutual love and <bl>sympathy [συμπαθείας]</bl>, and has bound the Church by a constant law. Hence let him marvel at and proclaim the happy state of things, both of the Church and of the whole universe, for as long as they persist in this harmony.

units.la: II. Ostendat concordiam in natura per inductionem vide Cic. in Laelio.
units.tr: II. Let him show concord in nature by induction; see Cicero in the Laelius.

units.la: 1. Corporum coelestium, solis & astrorum, quorum sine aemulatione ac ambitu quaelibet suum orbem ac ordinem servant, mutua luce se collustrant, & suavissimo consensu ac influxu haec inferiora illuminant, vegetant ac conservant. Hanc esse harmoniam illam Pythagoricam, de qua vide Macrob. ad Somn. Scip. Illustretur a contrario, si vel ad momentum turbaretur hic ordo, mundus periturus esset.
units.tr: 1. Of the heavenly bodies, the sun and the stars, which keep their own orbit and order without rivalry or ambition, shine upon one another with mutual light, and by most sweet agreement and influence illuminate, quicken and preserve these lower things. This is that Pythagorean harmony, on which see Macrobius on the Dream of Scipio. Let it be illustrated by the contrary: if this order were disturbed even for a moment, the world would perish.

units.la: 2. Corporum sublunarium. Hic. 1. per prolepsin proponas contrarietatem 4. Elementorum. 2. Exponas illorum concordiam, dum amice coeunt & temperantur ad productionem rerum compositarum: unde amica rerum sympathia & utilis antipathia. Exponas hic rerum generationem & conservationem. videl. calor attenuat & attrahit humores, frigus rursus condensat, unde ros & pluvia, quibus foecundatur terra, & producit germina, quibus nutriuntur animantia, ut cedant in alimentum hominis; qui hinc reducitur ad amandam & praedicandam bonitatem Domini. vide Ps. 104. Hinc merito exclamet cum Davide: Domine bonitate tua plena est terra; tu stabili pace revincis omnia.
units.tr: 2. Of the sublunary bodies. Here, first, by prolepsis, you may set forth the contrariety of the four elements. Second, you may explain their concord, as they come together amicably and are tempered to produce composite things; whence come the friendly sympathy and useful antipathy of things. Here you may explain the generation and preservation of things: namely, heat thins and draws up moisture, cold in turn condenses it, whence come dew and rain, by which the earth is made fruitful and produces the shoots on which living creatures feed, so that they serve as food for man. He is thereby led back to love and proclaim the goodness of the Lord; see Ps. 104. Hence let him justly exclaim with David: "The earth is full of your goodness, O Lord; you bind all things together with a steadfast peace."

units.la: 3. Ipsius hominis. Hinc exponas 1. mirabilem structuram corporis (dum membra singula in medio, bina ad latera in aequali honore constituta sunt) & membrorum concordiam ad salutem totius hominis, vide 1. Corinth. 12. v. 12. seqq. 2. amicam conjunctionem animae & corporis, licet diversae sint originis & diversi ordinis. 3. Consensum facultatum animae, intellectus scil. & voluntatis. Sed 4. deploret reluctantes hisce affectus, qui natura subditi, rationis imperium sæpe detrectant: Unde omnis discordiæ ac confusionis origo. Comparetur cum gigantomachia Ovidiana. Nec tamen rationem expugnare potuerunt, Hinc transeat, ac
units.tr: 3. Of man himself. Here you may explain 1. the wonderful structure of the body (the single members are placed in the middle and the paired ones at the sides with equal honour), and the concord of the members for the health of the whole man; see 1 Cor. 12:12ff. 2. The friendly union of soul and body, although they are of different origin and different order. 3. The agreement of the faculties of the soul, namely of the intellect and the will. But 4. he should lament that these affections, subject to nature, are often unwilling and refuse the rule of reason; hence comes the origin of all discord and confusion. Let it be compared with Ovid's battle of the giants. Yet they could not overcome reason. Let him therefore pass on, and

units.la: III. Laudet concordiam in vita
units.tr: III. He praises concord in life

units.la: 1. Oeconomica; quæ per concordiam parentum & liberorum dominorum & servorum, floret & conservatur.
units.tr: 1. In the household, which flourishes and is preserved through the concord of parents and children, masters and servants.

units.la: 2. Politica; quæ i.coiit per consensum in Leges certas ac Magistratum, cum antea vagi ac discordes ferrentur more ferarum bestiarum homines. 2. Conservatur & floret per concordiâ, dum omnes ad Reip. augmentum, ornamentum & defensionem conspirant. Illustretur exemplis Græcorum & Romanorum, Germanorum.
units.tr: 2. In the commonwealth, which came together by agreement upon certain laws and a magistracy, whereas before, men were carried about wandering and quarrelling like wild beasts. 2. It is preserved and flourishes through concord, while all conspire for the growth, adornment and defence of the commonwealth. Let it be illustrated with examples from the Greeks, the Romans and the Germans.

units.la: 3. Ecclesiastica; quippe quæ legibus ipsius Christi ad pacem ad fraternitatem, ad paritatem, ad mutuam submissionem, remissionem injuriarum stabilita est: ubi sine ambitione, sine æmulatione pro Christi gloria, pace conscientiæ & regno cœlesti concorditer certatur: uti Templum Hierosolymitanum olim sine strepitu constructum fuit.
units.tr: 3. In the Church, which indeed has been established by the laws of Christ himself upon peace, brotherhood, equality, mutual submission and the forgiveness of injuries; where, without ambition and without rivalry, people strive in harmony for the glory of Christ, for peace of conscience and for the heavenly kingdom, just as the Temple at Jerusalem was once built without noise.

units.la: Claudatur epiphonemate per μακαρισμὸν felicissimi status in omnibus vitæ ordinibus, si, uti in cœlis & in natura universa; ita & in domo, politia & Ecclesia pax est & concordia.
units.tr: Let it be closed with an epiphonema, by a blessing (makarismos) on the most happy state in all orders of life, if, as in the heavens and in all nature, so also in the household, the commonwealth and the Church there is peace and concord.

units.la: IV. Illustret superiora omnia oppositis malis discordiæ.
units.tr: IV. Let all the foregoing be illustrated by the evils opposed to discord.

units.la: 1. In Oeconomia, si liberi parentibus, servi dominis se opponant: uti in Cainitis ante diluvium.
units.tr: 1. In the household: if children set themselves against parents and servants against masters, as among the Cainites before the flood.

units.la: 2. In Politia; si subditi magistratibus, cives civibus reluctentur: vide exempla apud Palear. Orat. 6. de concord.Civium. pag.187.
units.tr: 2. In the state: if subjects resist magistrates and citizens struggle against citizens; see the examples in Palearius, Oration 6, On the Concord of Citizens, p. 187.

units.la: 3. In Ecclesia; si auditores pastoribus, & hi invicem ambitione & æmulatione opponantur. Hinc schismata, hæreses, exitium. Illustretur exemplo Ecclesiarum Orientalium, quæ hisce malis laceratæ Turcica tyrannide oppressæ jacent.
units.tr: 3. In the Church: if the hearers oppose the ministers, and the ministers in turn oppose one another through ambition and rivalry. Hence schisms, heresies and ruin. Let this be illustrated by the example of the Eastern Churches, which, torn by these evils, lie oppressed under Turkish tyranny.

units.la: 4. In natura; si vapores crassi & maligni nimis altè se elevent, tonitrua, fulgura aliæque tempestates inde oriuntur; contra si venti terræ motus inde existunt.
units.tr: 4. In nature: if thick and noxious vapours rise too high, thunders, lightnings and other storms arise from them; on the other hand, if winds are shut up, earthquakes come into being.

units.la: Si exhalationes malignæ aëris in supremam regionem extollantur, rerum concordia turbatur, & bella cruenta inter gentes ac regna consequuntur. Et tandem, dem, quando ipse stellarum ordo turbabitur, ipsa mundi compages dissolvetur; soluto scil. concordiae vinculo, qua omnia in hoc mundo continentur.
units.tr: If noxious exhalations of the air are lifted up into the highest region, the harmony of things is disturbed, and bloody wars follow between peoples and kingdoms. And finally, when the very order of the stars is thrown into confusion, the very framework of the world will be dissolved, namely, the bond of concord by which all things in this world are held together being loosed.

units.la: Conclusio. Repetitis nervose argumentorum summis 1. Concordiam ac pacem praedicet, & 2. eandem a Deo pacis ac concordiae autore exoptet.
units.tr: Conclusion. Having briefly repeated the heads of the arguments, let him (1) commend concord and peace, and (2) pray earnestly that they be granted by God, the author of peace and concord.

units.la: VIII. DE RESTITUTA PACE ET REDIVIVA GLORIA ROMANI IMPERII.
units.tr: VIII. ON THE RESTORED PEACE AND THE REVIVED GLORY OF THE ROMAN EMPIRE.

units.la: Exord. A comparatione minoris: annua scilicet laetitia tempore Veris. Haec
units.tr: Exordium. From comparison with the lesser: namely, the yearly joy of springtime. This

units.la: I. Proponatur illustrata contrario tempore hyemis. v. g. cum post exacta ingratae hyemis taedia & horrentia brumae frigora, atrocesque coeli minas ac tempestates, blandi succedunt Zephyri & grata cunctis veris viridantis amoenitas, quis non laetatur? quis non exultat? quid est in natura universa quod non veluti revivescat & redeuntem post nubila Phoebum cum tripudio veluti ac applausu excipiat & amplectatur?
units.tr: I. Let it be set forth, illustrated by the contrary season of winter: for example, when, after the wearisome tedium of unwelcome winter, the bristling cold of midwinter and the fierce threats and storms of the sky are past, mild west winds follow, and the welcome pleasantness of green spring returns. Who does not rejoice? Who does not exult? What is there in all nature that does not, as it were, revive, and welcome and embrace the sun returning after the clouds, with dancing and applause?

units.la: II. Expoliatur collatione specialiori molestiarum hyemis & amoenitatum vernarum. vide descriptiones Authorum.
units.tr: II. Let it be refined by a more particular comparison of the discomforts of winter and the delights of spring. See the descriptions in the authors.

units.la: III. Applicetur ad propositum: videl. eandem merito videri rationem praesentis status Imperii, imo Europae universae cum statu anni praeteriti collatam: ubi invasio hostis immanissimi, ceu tempestas brumalis obruit Hungariam vicinasque provincias, toti Germaniae, imo Europae minax: Verum derepente uti ex tenebris lux, ita ex bello pax optata emicuit, imbuitque laetitia inopinata imperium universum. Quis hic non exultet, si praeteriti animi motus minaces cum praesenti hac tranquillitate conferat.
units.tr: III. Let it be applied to the purpose: namely, that the same reasoning rightly holds when the present state of the Empire, indeed of all Europe, is compared with the state of last year. Then the invasion of a most savage enemy, like a wintry tempest, overwhelmed Hungary and the neighbouring provinces and threatened all Germany, indeed Europe. But suddenly, as light breaks out of darkness, so out of war the longed-for peace has shone forth, and an unexpected joy has filled the whole Empire. Who here would not exult, if he compares the threatening emotions of the past with this present tranquillity?

units.la: Propos. Nullius tantum esse flumen ingenii, quod hocce Dei optimi Maximi beneficium, & paternam tuam, Caesar augustissime, curam digne praedicare queat. vide Orat. Cic. pro Marcell. Haud ingratum fore speret, ad exiguum momentum oblectare se meditatione tanti boni illos, quos procul dubio communis belli metus perpessa aliis clades sæpius habuere sollicitos ; eosdemque excu-saturos imparem tantis rebus prædicandis facundiam, &c.
units.tr: Proposition. No one's flow of talent is so great that he could worthily proclaim this benefit of God, the best and greatest, and your paternal care, most august Emperor. See Cicero's oration for Marcellus. Let him hope it will not be unwelcome for those people, whom the common fear of war and the calamities it has brought have doubtless often troubled, to take delight for a brief moment in meditating on so great a good; and let him ask them to excuse his eloquence, which is unequal to proclaiming such great things, etc.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Development.

units.la: I. Abominetur opinionem pestiferam illorum, qui pacem hanc vel tanquam minus gloriosam, vel emolumentosam imperio, aut alias nimis præproperam improbant. Ignorare hosce aut potius dissimulare; quid intersit inter pacem & bellum. Hinc in genere incommoda belli, commoda pacis paucis & nervosè repræsentet, adductis utrobique Autorum sententiis efficacio-ribus, vide Locum Communem de pace & bello. Inferat inde, non Germaniæ aut imperii saluti, nec Ecclesiæ incolumita-ti, sed propriæ utilitati illos nimium addictos. Maximè cum bello Turcico nihil orbi Christiano infestius; ubi non corpo-rum modò, sed & animarum servitus, interitus, &c. Claudatur opposito horum affectui perverso publico omnium bonorum gaudio : cujus rationes jam porrò expendendæ paulo peni-tius. Hinc
units.tr: I. Let him denounce the pernicious opinion of those who disapprove of this peace, either as less glorious, or as not profitable to the Empire, or otherwise as too hasty. Let him say that these men either do not know, or rather pretend not to know, what the difference is between peace and war. Hence, in general, let him present briefly and forcefully the disadvantages of war and the advantages of peace, citing on both sides the more effective opinions of authors; see the common place on peace and war. Let him infer from this that these men are too devoted to private advantage, and not to the safety of Germany or the Empire, nor to the welfare of the Church. Especially since, with the Turkish war, nothing is more hostile to the Christian world, where there is slavery and destruction not only of bodies but also of souls, etc. Let him close by setting against this perverse feeling the public joy of all good men, whose grounds must now be weighed a little more deeply. Hence

units.la: II. Exponat rationes publici gaudii: & quidem à pacis hujus
units.tr: II. Let him set out the reasons for public joy, and indeed those arising from the necessity of this peace:

units.la: 1. Necessitate: quam arguat
units.tr: 1. Necessity, which he should argue

units.la: a. Ab imminenti belli hujus mole : idque propter multitudi-nem, potentiam & truculentiam hostis, quam breviter repræsentet. Illustret comparatione aliorum bello-rum inter Christianos, & Turcicum bellum longè gra-vius ostendat, quippe a. exitiale bonis, terris, cor-poribus, animabus. b. Raro terminatum sine jactura provin-ciarum. Hinc paucis referat, quid amissum bellis superio-ribus; vide Chartam Hungariæ recentem. c. Destitutum spe recuperandi ablata, propter legem Alcorani.
units.tr: a. From the weight of the imminent war, on account of the multitude, power and savagery of the enemy, which he should briefly describe. Let him illustrate it by comparison with other wars among Christians, and show that the Turkish war is far more grievous, being deadly to goods, lands, bodies and souls. b. Seldom ended without the loss of provinces. Hence let him briefly recount what was lost in earlier wars; see the recent charter of Hungary. c. Deprived of hope of recovering what has been taken, on account of the law of the Koran.

units.la: b. A virium oppositarum incertitudine. Hic a. prædicet ze-lum & concordiam Procerum Imperii & exterorum Regum, in submittendis auxiliis, uti adversus communem hostem, adversus publicum latronem, vel incendium oportet. b. Expen-dat contrà varios facilesque casus ad revocanda aut non con-tinuanda auxilia, si in propriis regnis aut cum vicinis bellum exardescat: uti jam tum inter Papam & Gallum, Polonum & Moscum; Venetas & Turcam; ubi quisque suis tantum, aut præcipuè intentus est rebus, & post inter Gallum & Africanos, Anglos & Belgas, & quis novit, quam partem reliqui Monarchæ electuri sint? Alludatur Loco Communi de intuto auxilio aliorum, vide Silhon Minist. d' Estat.
units.tr: b. From the uncertainty of the opposing forces. Here let him a. proclaim the zeal and concord of the princes of the Empire and of foreign kings in sending aid, as one must against a common enemy, a public robber or a fire. b. On the other hand, let him weigh the various and easy occasions for recalling or not continuing aid, if war breaks out in their own kingdoms or with their neighbours. This has already happened between the Pope and the Frenchman, the Pole and the Muscovite, the Venetians and the Turk, where each is intent only, or chiefly, on his own affairs; and afterwards between the French and the Africans, and the English and the Belgians. And who knows what part the remaining monarchs will choose? Allude to the common place on the unsafe aid of others; see Silhon, Ministre d'Estat.

units.la: A dubiis animis Hungarorum, qui suspensi neutram partem eligere valuerunt, victori forsan accessuri. Idem de Transylvano judicium. Quàm periculosum bellum cum hoste potente, cùm nec domi tranquilla satis res est, hodie Polonus, ante hac Gallus expertus est.
units.tr: From the doubtful minds of the Hungarians, who, hesitating, were unable to choose either side and might perhaps go over to the victor. The same judgement applies to the Transylvanian. How dangerous war with a powerful enemy is, when affairs at home are not even calm enough, the Pole has experienced today and the Frenchman formerly.

units.la: A metuendis motibus in ipsa Germania; ubi necdum consolidata aut tranquilla omnia post funestum illud bellum superiorum temporum: & jamdum in ipso meditullio peregrina Galli arma emicuere. Quid futurum si bellum Turcicum continuatum & magis exasperatum fuisset? Quis igitur non exultet, prudentia Cæsaris gloriosissimi arma ac ulteriora incendia averså fuisse?
units.tr: From the feared movements in Germany itself, where not everything is yet consolidated or calm after that deadly war of former times, and where foreign French arms have already flashed out in the very heart of the land. What would have happened if the Turkish war had continued and grown more bitter? Who then would not exult that, by the prudence of the most glorious Emperor, the arms and further conflagrations were turned away?

units.la: A dubio semper Martis exitu. Quid futurum si exercitus Imperii & Christianorum stratus, provinciæ imperii direptæ & spoliatæ fuissent? &c.
units.tr: From the always doubtful outcome of Mars. What would have happened if the army of the Empire and of the Christians had been struck down, and the provinces of the Empire plundered and despoiled? etc.

units.la: A pacis hujus utilitate: quæ elucet.
units.tr: From the usefulness of this peace, which is plain.

units.la: In adversis ulterioribus cladibus, tum Christiani sanguinis, quo nihil cordato duci preciosius: tum vastitatis provinciarum per cædes & incendia: tum jacturæ opum ac urbium. Hæc enim semper comitantur bellum Turcicum, propter immensas copias. Illustrentur ab oppositio; si Christiani perrumpant, cladem esse disparem; fundi quippe sanguinem vilem barbarorum: deinde vix sentire cladem Turcas propter amplitudinem copiamque provinciarum. At arctius conservanda imperii membra, utpote jam latis distracta ac mutilata, præ pristina imperii amplitudine.
units.tr: In the avoidance of further disasters: of Christian blood, than which nothing is more precious to a sensible leader; of the devastation of provinces through slaughter and fire; and of the loss of wealth and cities. For these always accompany the Turkish war, on account of its immense forces. Let them be illustrated by contrast: if the Christians should be broken, the loss would be unequal, since the blood of barbarians is cheap to spill; moreover, the Turks would hardly feel the loss, because of the vastness and abundance of their provinces. But the limbs of the Empire must be preserved more tightly, since they are already torn and mutilated by wide dismemberment, compared with its former greatness.

units.la: In conditionibus pacis factæ æquis; quæ proinde paucis expendantur.
units.tr: In the terms of the peace made, which are fair; these are therefore to be weighed briefly.

units.la: A pacis hujus opportunitate:
units.tr: From the opportuneness of this peace:

units.la: a. Post exiguâ Christianorū & imperii jacturâ, quæ specificetur.
units.tr: a. After a small loss to the Christians and the Empire, which should be specified.

units.la: b. Post obtentam a Christianis victoriam illustrem:
units.tr: b. After the illustrious victory won by the Christians:

units.la: α. Repræsentetur ex re gesta.
units.tr: α. Let it be presented from the deed done.

units.la: β. Exaggeretur a commodis inde redundantibus; videlicet quod de hinc, 1. Turcæ diffidere didicerint suis viribus bus, & vinci fe posse adhuc a Germanis. 2. Quod jam metuant robur & virtutem Germanorum. 3. Quod viderint Christianorum concordiam adversus hostem hæreditarium, adeoque non facile rursus irritaturi sint illos. 4. Quod sic conservatum reliquum robur imperii, ne in ejus debilitate sperare queant æmuli. 5. Quod sic imperium non necesse habuerit se arctius obstringere exteris &c.
units.tr: β. Let it be magnified by the advantages flowing from it, namely that henceforth: 1. The Turks have learned to distrust their own strength, and that they can still be conquered by the Germans. 2. They now fear the strength and valour of the Germans. 3. They have seen the concord of the Christians against the hereditary enemy, and so will not easily provoke them again. 4. The remaining strength of the Empire is thus preserved, so that its rivals cannot hope for its weakness. 5. The Empire has thus not needed to bind itself more tightly to outsiders, etc.

units.la: Hinc concludat jam hanc partem, videlicet. Quis igitur exorta rursus hac pacis aurora, & reduce veluti luce non lætetur? & exultet: utpote quæ una triumphis in numeris potior &c.
units.tr: Hence let him conclude this part: who then, with this dawn of peace risen again, and with light, as it were, returned, would not rejoice and exult? For this alone is worth more than triumphs in number, etc.

units.la: Conclus. 1. Prædicet providam curam ac pacificum animum Cæsaris, qui in ipso potius victoriarum cursu, quàm post cladem perpessam, pacem tam necessariam, emolumentosam & opportunam reddere imperio & Europæ voluit. 2. Gratias agat Deo pro eximio hoc pacis bono, dum alibi adhuc bellum ex bello nascitur 3. Voveat diuturnam ejus possessionem & fructum saluberrimum ex fine pf. 85
units.tr: Conclusion. 1. Let him proclaim the provident care and peaceful mind of the Emperor, who, at the very height of his victories rather than after a defeat suffered, wished to make peace so necessary, profitable and opportune for the Empire and for Europe. 2. Let him give thanks to God for this outstanding gift of peace, while elsewhere war still springs from war. 3. Let him vow its lasting possession and its most wholesome fruit, from the end of pf. 85.

units.la: IX. TRIUMPHUS FIDEI: Materia carminis. Ad imitationem Petrarchæ & Salustii.
units.tr: IX. THE TRIUMPH OF FAITH: Subject of the poem. In imitation of Petrarch and Sallust.

units.la: Propos. Cantent alii arma virosque virtute claros: cantent victorias ac triumphos, & stantes in curribus Æmilianos &c. At ego te diva fides canam; quæ mundo superior, mundum, carnem, satanam vincis & triumphas de morte & portis inferorum.
units.tr: Proposition. Let others sing of arms and men famous for valour: let them sing of victories and triumphs, and of the Aemilii standing in their chariots, etc. But I will sing of you, divine Faith, who are superior to the world, and who conquer the world, the flesh and Satan, and triumph over death and the gates of hell.

units.la: Invocatio: Spiritus alme dispelle tenebras cæcæ rationis, largire mihi fidem, qua supra mundana omnia evectus, cœlestia videam: frustra enim sine fide canere aggredior.
units.tr: Invocation: Kindly Spirit, dispel the darkness of blind reason, and grant me faith, by which, raised above all worldly things, I may see heavenly things. For I attempt to sing in vain without faith.

units.la: Stipulatio attentionis. Scio, quod nimis sublimia tento, & impossibilia occipio: Scio oculum humanum hic cæcutire, aurem obsurdescere, sensus nihil capere: sed fides reddet impossibilia possibilia: & vester, ô Proceres ac Musarum fautores, favor me faciet superare juga Pindi & bibere de sacro Pieridum fonte. &c.
units.tr: Request for attention. I know that I attempt things too lofty and begin things impossible. I know that the human eye grows blind here, the ear grows deaf, and the senses grasp nothing. But faith will make the impossible possible, and your favour, O nobles and patrons of the Muses, will enable me to surmount the heights of Pindus and drink from the sacred fountain of the Pierides, etc.

units.la: Tractatio: habeat
units.tr: Treatment: let it have

units.la: 1. Descriptionem fidei, tanquam victricis insidentis currui nitenti, ti, tracto vérsus cœlum ab aquila; at habentis corpus totum plenum oculis, os plenum linguis, humeros alatos & caput coronatum. Vexillum ejus veritas: latera cingunt Zelus, constantia, patientia, charitas, ípes, humilitas cæteraque turba virtutum.
units.tr: 1. A description of Faith, as a victorious figure seated on a chariot that is drawn up to heaven by an eagle; and she has a body entirely full of eyes, a mouth full of tongues, winged shoulders and a crowned head. Her standard is Truth. Zeal, Constancy, Patience, Charity, Hope, Humility and the rest of the crowd of virtues surround her sides.

units.la: II. Repræsentationem 1. rationis humanæ, tanquam fœminæ captivæ quæ præcedat currum: quam describat, tanquam specie formosam, sed sucatam variis pigmentis & figmentis: plenam quidem oculis instar fidei, sed non ferentibus lucem; plenam linguis, sed deceptricibus: habentem alas, sed cereas, quæ liquefactæ sint a sole veritatis. 2. Plurimorum principum, & tyrannorum qui inducti ab hac deceptrice ratione, opposuerunt se fidei ac cœlesti veritati: quorum præcipuos enumeret, inde a Caino usque ad Julianum Apostatam, qui omnes vincti currum præcedant. Vide Hist. Eccles. De hinc Mahumetem reliquosque Turcarum imperatores repræsentet veluti in tabulis depictos frustra & sine effectu, fidei ferrum ac flammas intentantes.
units.tr: II. Representation: 1. of human reason, as a captive woman walking before the chariot. He should describe her as beautiful in appearance but daubed with various paints and fictions: full of eyes like Faith, but not bearing light; full of tongues, but deceptive; having wings, but waxen, which the sun of truth has melted. 2. Of the many princes and tyrants who, led on by this deceitful reason, set themselves against faith and heavenly truth. He should list the chief of them, from Cain down to Julian the Apostate, all of them bound and walking before the chariot. See Church History. Then he should represent Mahomet and the other Turkish emperors, as if painted in pictures, vainly and without effect, threatening the sword and flames against the faith.

units.la: 3. Philosophorum gentilium vinctorum, qui veritati ac fidei sese opposuerunt; quorum præcipuos aliquot enumeret, demisso vultu incedentes. Vide Diog. Laertium.
units.tr: 3. Of the bound heathen philosophers who opposed themselves to truth and faith. He should list a few of the chief of them, advancing with downcast faces. See Diogenes Laertius.

units.la: 4. Hæreticorum classe: qui fidem occulta proditione subvertere voluerunt: quorum occultas machinationes sub vexillis fidei, & deinde illorum præcipuos aliquot enarret, detectos & nudos incedentes, qui ante sub pelle agnina latebant. Vid. Hist. Eccles. Parei.
units.tr: 4. The class of heretics, who sought to overthrow the faith by secret treachery. He should describe their hidden machinations under the banners of faith, and then recount a few of their chief men, exposed and naked, advancing, who had before lain hidden beneath a sheep's skin. See Church History, Parens.

units.la: 5. AntiChristi patefacti. Hic repræsentet longum ordinem in pontificalibus incedentium, & triplici corona redimitorum, itemque splendidam fœminam insidentem Draconi, cum præunte præcone: Ecce magna meretrix, quæ poculo suo venenato dementavit totum mundum.
units.tr: 5. The Antichrists revealed. Here he should represent a long line of men walking in pontifical vestments and crowned with a triple crown, and likewise a splendid woman seated on a dragon, with a herald going before: Behold the great harlot, who has maddened the whole world with her poisoned cup.

units.la: III. Repræsentationem militum & ducum fidei, qui sequantur currum triumphalem, galeas salutis gestantes in capitibus & gladium spiritus in manibus & thorace justitiæ indutos. Hi enumerentur per inductionem: videlicet Abrahamus, Josua, Simson, Jephta, David, Josaphat, Ezechias, Zerubabel, Esdra, Judas Maccabæus, Constantinus, Theodosii, Carolus Magnus; quos suis proprietatibus & gestis breviter & nervosè describat & introducat. De hinc Martyres aliquot introducat, stola candida indutos,coronas laureas gestantes in capitibus & palmas in manibus suis: videlicet Abelem, Johannem, Stephanum, & mille alios, qui fide sua & morte triumphum obtinuerunt de morte & furore tyrannorum.
units.tr: III. Representation of the soldiers and leaders of the faith, who follow the triumphal chariot, wearing helmets of salvation on their heads, carrying the sword of the Spirit in their hands, and clad in the breastplate of righteousness. These should be enumerated by induction: namely Abraham, Joshua, Samson, Jephthah, David, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Zerubbabel, Ezra, Judas Maccabaeus, Constantine, the Theodosiuses, Charlemagne. He should describe and introduce each briefly and vigorously by their characteristics and deeds. Next he should introduce a few martyrs, clothed in white robes, wearing laurel crowns on their heads and palms in their hands: namely Abel, John, Stephen, and a thousand others, who by their faith and death obtained triumph over death and the rage of tyrants.

units.la: IV. Ostentationem tabularum pictarum, quæ portentur ante currum triumphalem de præcipuis præliis ac victoriis fidei. 1. Recolligat se, quasi oblitus sit. 2. Exponat seriem victoriarum depictarum; videl. Fide divisas aquas maris rubri & jordanis. Fide dejectos muros Hierichuntis, expugnatam Cananæam &c. repressam a Daniele rabiem leonum, restinctas flammas. Vide. Heb.11.Fide resuscitatus mortuus Lazarus,aliique in historia Euangelica sanati.
units.tr: IV. A display of painted tablets, carried before the triumphal chariot, depicting the chief battles and victories of faith. 1. He should gather himself up, as if he had forgotten. 2. He should set out the series of depicted victories, namely: by faith the waters of the Red Sea and the Jordan were divided; by faith the walls of Jericho fell, the Canaanite woman was overcome, the raging of the lions was restrained by Daniel, the flames were quenched. See Heb. 11. By faith the dead Lazarus was raised, and others healed in the Gospel history.

units.la: V. Expressionè præconum seu quatuor Euangelistarum,qui versus 4. mundi plagas triumphum fidei intimabant; quos secuti 12. tubicines Apostoli: qui tanta vehementia publicabant victoriam fidei; ut ex omnibus orbis angulis ad pompam hanc occurrant sequaces.
units.tr: V. The expression of the heralds, that is, of the four Evangelists, who proclaimed the triumph of faith to the four quarters of the world; followed by the twelve trumpeters, the Apostles, who published the victory of faith with such vehemence that from every corner of the world followers would come running to this procession.

units.la: Concluf. Habeat votum, ut sonitus hic pertingat usque ad finem orbis, ur Judæi, Turcæ, gentes infideles submittant animos fidei: ut ita gloriâ Domini repleatur tota terra.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him express the wish that this sound may reach to the ends of the earth, so that Jews, Turks and unbelieving nations may submit their minds to the faith, and so the whole earth may be filled with the glory of the Lord.

units.la: X. LAUS MILITIÆ.
units.tr: X. The Praise of the Military Life

units.la: Exord. Ab extenuatione virium.
units.tr: Exord. From the weakness of one's own powers.

units.la: Propositio. In magnis voluisse satis: audendum igitur, ne dum omnes pacem, vitam togatam, artes laudant, militia deserta aut destituta suis laudibus videatur.
units.tr: Propositio. To have meant well is enough in great matters. We must therefore dare to speak, lest, while everyone praises peace, the civilian life and the liberal arts, the military life should seem deserted or left without its praises.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: I. a dignitate. Prob. 1. ab authore Deo vid. Deut. 20. Qui hinc se ipsum vocat dominum Exercituum.Objeƈt. reconde gladium Resp. privatis dictum, 2. Ab antiquitate ante diluvium viri illustres fuere: post diluvium Nimroth, imò Abraham miles. De hinc Moses, Josua, Judices, Reges. Quid de gentibus dicamus: scilicet nullum exercitium antiquius, 3. a virtutibus,quæ in belljs elucent, & quidem
units.tr: I. From its dignity. Proof. 1. From its author, God; see Deut. 20., where he calls himself the Lord of Hosts. Objection: "Put up your sword." Answer: that was said to private persons. 2. From its antiquity. There were illustrious men before the flood; after the flood there was Nimrod, and indeed Abraham was a soldier. From there come Moses, Joshua, the Judges and the kings. What shall we say of the nations? Surely no exercise is older. 3. From the virtues which shine forth in war, and indeed:

units.la: a. Pietas, hanc ostende in Davide, Ezechia, Jofia, Constantino Magno, Theodosiis, Carolo M. & compara illos cum philosophis, ICtis, tanquam probiores. Illustretur a causa: quia pugnant pro Ecclesia, lege, grege: quia singulis momentis veluti in termino vitæ versantur. Objectio: nulla fides pietasque &c. Refp. poetam sic putare. Contrarium probare experientiam. Objectio 2. occupantur in cæde. Refp. ad justam vindictam, ut magistratus, ut Chirurgi.
units.tr: a. Piety. Show this in David, Hezekiah, Josiah, Constantine the Great, the Theodosiuses and Charles the Great, and compare them with the philosophers and the jurisconsults, who were the more upright. Let it be illustrated from the cause: they fight for the Church, the law and the flock, and at every moment they stand, as it were, at the edge of life. Objection: no faith or piety, etc. Answer: the poet thinks so; experience proves the contrary. Objection 2: they are occupied in slaughter. Answer: it is for just vengeance, as with the magistrate and the surgeon.

units.la: b. Fortitudo: Verbis crepant illam philosophi, ad minimum sæpe dolorem reformidant: contra milites re præstant contra strictos gladios, contra tormentorum ictus intrepide nituntur. Illi muri sunt urbibus: comparentur munimenta, si heroibus destituta, scilicet receptacula & præmia sunt hostium.
units.tr: b. Courage. The philosophers boast of it in words, and often shrink from even the slightest pain. Soldiers, on the contrary, show it in deed: they face drawn swords and press on fearlessly under the blows of artillery. They are the walls of cities. Let fortifications be compared: if they are without heroes, they are only storehouses and prizes for the enemy.

units.la: c. Temperantia. Ubi illa nisi in bello? Conferatur aula, Respubl. schola, ubi luxus, compotationes aut disputationes: in campo & castris res ipsa. Exponatur per hypothesin dura paupertas in villis desertis, sub dio requiritur vestis unica. Frustra leges sumptuariæ feruntur in oppidis, huc huc venite delicatuli tanquam ad veram scholam temperantiæ &c.
units.tr: c. Temperance. Where is it, if not in war? Compare the court, the commonwealth, the school, where there is luxury, drinking parties or disputations; in the field and the camp the thing itself is found. Let hard poverty be set forth by way of supposition in deserted farmsteads, where a single garment is needed under the open sky. In vain are sumptuary laws passed in the towns. Come here, come here, you pampered fellows, as to a true school of temperance, etc.

units.la: d. Modestia: quippe ubi virtute metienda omnia, sub eodem tecto die scilicet princeps & miles cubat, nulla hic generis jactatio, sed sua quamque virtus probat. Hic vera virtutis, non inanis generis præmia.
units.tr: d. Modesty. Indeed, where everything must be measured by virtue, the prince and the soldier sleep under the same roof. Here there is no boasting of birth; each man's own virtue proves itself. Here are the true rewards of virtue, not empty rewards of birth.

units.la: e. Prudentia, in explorandis consiliis hostium, in struendis insidiis, & stratagematibus. vide Frontinum de stratagemat. Liv. & Plut. passim: Hic captanda momenta singula, quippe ubi non licet bis peccare. Comparetur jactata illa prudentia togata; ubi sæpe fœminæ & plebei inveniunt errata gravissima; quippe ubi nulla imprudentiæ ac temeritatis poena: secus in bello,
units.tr: e. Prudence, in exploring the enemy's plans, in laying ambushes and in stratagems. See Frontinus on stratagems, and Livy and Plutarch passim. Here every moment must be seized, for here it is not permitted to err twice. Let that vaunted civilian prudence be compared, where women and common people often make the gravest mistakes, and where there is no penalty for imprudence and rashness. It is otherwise in war.

units.la: II, Ab utilitate belli, publica, privata: Publica, quia vel patria sic defenditur ab hostibus, pax servatur; vel ablata vindicantur, provinciæ acquiruntur. Illustretur exemplis veteribus modernis. Privata, in dignitatibus & honoribus: nota; hinc fons nobilitatis omnis: In divitiis, quæ raræ togatis, crebræ & auctiores sagatis &c. III. A necessitate: quia imbelles omnium prædæ sunt; armis contra tranquillitas retinetur: hunc doce esse finem & scopum armorum. Ipsa religio sine armis defendi nequit, illustretur exemplo in asserenda superiori seculo religione Euangelica. Vide Sleidanum de statu religionis.
units.tr: II. From the utility of war, public and private. Public: because either the fatherland is thus defended from its enemies and peace is preserved, or what was taken away is reclaimed and provinces are acquired. Let this be illustrated by examples, ancient and modern. Private: in dignities and honours, which are well known; hence comes the source of all nobility. In riches, which are rare among civilians but frequent and greater among the soldiers, etc. III. From necessity: because the unwarlike are everyone's prey, whereas by arms tranquillity is kept. Teach that this is the aim and goal of arms. Religion itself cannot be defended without arms; let this be illustrated by the example of the defence of the evangelical religion in the last century. See Sleidan on the state of religion.

units.la: Conclusio. Collatis aliis vitæ generibus militiam tanquam exercitum omnium virtutum prædicet.
units.tr: Conclusio. Having compared the other ways of life, let him proclaim the military life as the training-ground of all virtues.

units.la: XI. COMMENDATIO AUSCULTATIONIS.
units.tr: XI. THE COMMENDATION OF LISTENING

units.la: Ex tractatu Plut. περὶ τῆς ἀκοῆς, seu de auscultatione.
units.tr: From Plutarch's treatise On Hearing [περὶ τῆς ἀκοῆς], or on listening.

units.la: Exord. Alleget laudetque effatum Servatoris, quo verbum Dei semini, mentè hominis agro comparat. Suavissima hæc comparatio; quod 1. ostendatur expositione similitudinis in protasi & apodosi. 2. Extendatur ad omnia homini scitu necessaria, quæ sermone ac institutione præcipue acquirantur. 3. Probetur 1. ratione: quia juxta Arist. mens hominis instar tabulæ rasæ, in naturalibus; & oblitteratæ in spiritualibus. Quæ proinde bona institutione, ceu bona semine conseranda. 2. Autoritate Plutarchi; qui proinde interalios egregios tractatus, de Auscultatione quoque libellum erudltum posteritati reliquit.
units.tr: Exordium. He should cite and praise the Saviour's saying, in which the word of God is compared to seed and the mind of man to a field. This is a most pleasing comparison, and it may be shown (1) by explaining the likeness in protasis and apodosis; (2) by extending it to everything a man needs to know, which is acquired chiefly through speech and instruction; (3) by proof: (1) by reason, since according to Aristotle the mind of man is like a blank tablet in natural matters, and like an erased one in spiritual matters, and so must be sown with good instruction as with good seed; (2) by the authority of Plutarch, who, among his other excellent treatises, also left to posterity a learned little book On Listening.

units.la: Propofit. Cujus vestigia secutum te ad studiosæ juventutis & propriam tui excitationem de auscultionis necessitate ac utilitate acturum; quam ad rem benevolam auscultationem ad exiguum monumentum petat.
units.tr: Proposition. Following his footsteps, you will speak of the necessity and usefulness of listening, both to stir up studious youth and to stir up yourself. For this purpose he asks a kindly hearing for this small monument.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. Occurrat tacitæ objectioni τῶν αὐτοδιδάκτων, qui solam lectionem sufficere ad eruditionem ac bonam mentem existimant. Hic 1. concedat egregiam lectionis utilitatem, cujus solius beneficio magna quædam ingenia ad eruditionem pervenerint. Hinc per concessionem utilitates lectionis sedulæ & attentæ exponat, & recenseat exempla quædam illorum, qui sola lectione docti evasere, ut Heraclitus, Virgilius ipsequeAugustinus, qui nullo doctore libros Logicos ac Rhetoricos Arist. sese intellexisse fatetur. 2. Refellat rationes pro autodidactis militantes; videlicet. 1. Certius judicari posse de lectis, quam auditis, ubi autoritas dicentis plus sæpe spectatur, quam ratio. Resp. non excludi lectionem cum auscultatio commendatur. Imò lectione assidua auscultationem fovendam esse. 2. Firmius imprimi posse lecta, quam audita. Resp. Contrarium potius verum esse, uti postea patebit. 3. Quolibet tempore patere nobis libros praestantissimorum virorum, quorum quidam enumerandi. Resp. Ideo tanto magis utendum esse facultate & occasione audiendi doctos, ut exploremus profectus nostros. Item auscultationem nos manuducere ad lectionem. Hinc explicet mentem Plutarchi, quod minime auscultationem lectioni opponat, sed utramq; conjungendam censeat discendi cupido. Addatur ratio ab insigni lectionis praestantia, cujus beneficio antiquissimorum doctissimorumque v. g. Mosis &c. (fiat inductio quaedam praecipuorum scriptorum) cogitationes exquisitissimas & inventa intueri nobis licet; hinc in Academia Platonis, in Peripato Aristotelis, in Stoa Zenonis &c, versari nobis licet. Hinc facta transitione
units.tr: I. Let him meet the silent objection of the self-taught (αὐτοδίδακτοι), who think that reading alone is enough for learning and a good mind. Here he should first concede the outstanding usefulness of reading, by whose benefit alone certain great minds have attained learning. By way of concession, he should then set out the advantages of diligent and attentive reading, and list some examples of those who became learned by reading alone, such as Heraclitus, Virgil, and Augustine, who confesses that without any teacher he understood the Logic and Rhetoric of Aristotle. (2) He should refute the arguments put forward for the self-taught, namely: (1) that what is read can be judged more surely than what is heard, since the authority of the speaker often counts for more than reason.
