Reply: reading is not excluded when listening is commended; indeed, listening should be fostered by constant reading. (2) That what is read can be impressed more firmly than what is heard. Reply: the opposite is rather true, as will become clear later. (3) That the books of the most outstanding men lie open to us at all times, some of whom should be listed. Reply: for that very reason we ought all the more to use the opportunity and occasion of hearing learned men, so that we may test our progress. Also, listening leads us by the hand to reading. Here he should explain Plutarch's meaning: he does not set listening against reading at all, but thinks that a desire for learning should join the two. Add the argument from the remarkable excellence of reading, by whose benefit we may look upon the most exquisite thoughts and discoveries of the most ancient and most learned men, such as Moses and others (some survey of the chief writers should be made). Thus we may dwell in Plato's Academy, in Aristotle's Peripatos, in Zeno's Stoa, and so on. With this transition made,

units.la: II. Auscultationem commendet.
units.tr: II. He commends listening.

units.la: 1. Ab antiquitate ejusdem. Hic ostendat auscultationem antiquissimam esse rationem instituendi per duo millia annorum usitatam ipsi Deo & patriarchis, ubi viva voce, sine scriptis peritiores rudiores informarunt. Deinde lata lege Mosis & extante scriptura, non defuit viva institutio, ut hac ratione veritas menti inculcaretur. Et antiquissimis Philosophis institutio oralis usitata fuit. v. g. Socrati, cujus praecepta nobis per Platonem demum scriptis relicta sunt: Pythagorae, cujus pauca carmina tantum superstitant. Claudatur hoc argumentum epiphonemate de auscultationis praestantia.
units.tr: 1. From its antiquity. Here he should show that listening is the oldest method of instruction, used for two thousand years by God himself and by the patriarchs, when the more skilled instructed the less skilled by the living voice, without writings. Then, after the law of Moses was given and Scripture existed, living instruction was not lacking, so that by this means the truth might be impressed on the mind. Oral instruction was also customary among the most ancient philosophers, for example Socrates, whose precepts were left to us in writing only later, by Plato; and Pythagoras, of whom only a few poems survive. Let this argument be closed with an epiphonema on the excellence of listening.

units.la: 2. Ab ejusdem utilitate; 1. Ad faciliorem intelligentiam; cum docentes auditorum captui & profectui se accommodent. Illustretur comparatione cum libris, qui omnibus eodem modo loquuntur, proindeque interpretatione ut plurimum indigent. Hinc non qui multos habet aut legit libros illico eruditus est; sed qui multos bonosque audivit Doctores semper inde melior evadit. Illustretur exemplo Nonni, de quo Suidas, quod licet sexies Demosthenem perlegisset, non tamen os aperire, aut verbum proferre ausus fuerit.
units.tr: 2. From its usefulness: (1) for easier understanding, since teachers accommodate themselves to the capacity and progress of their hearers. Illustrate this by comparison with books, which speak to all in the same way and therefore mostly need interpretation. Hence a man who owns or has read many books is not at once learned; but he who has heard many good teachers always becomes better. Illustrate with the example of Nonnus, of whom Suidas writes that although he had read Demosthenes through six times, he did not dare to open his mouth or utter a word.

units.la: 2. Ad delectum majorem. Multi enim multa legunt, vel inutilia, utilia, vel curiosa & nova, praeteritis illis, quae usum habent. Fiat digressio de perversitate discentium, qui jucunda potius quam salubria tractant. Hinc Aristippus cuidam jactanti, quòd nihil non legisset, respondit, uti non illi, qui plurimum comedunt melius valent iis, qui quantum opus est capiunt, ita non qui plurima, sed qui utilia legerunt, eruditi habendi. Secus fit in auscultatione, ubi non nisi illa proponuntur, quae publico judicio auscultatione digna habentur. 3. Ad firmiorem memoriam. Hic laudetur vis vivae vocis in penetrando ad animum audientis, multò efficacius, quam quae leguntur, cùm & autoritas & affectus dicentis accesserit. Hinc Plinius altius in animo sedere dixit quae pronunciatio, vultus, habitus, gestus etiam dicentis juvat. Hinc magnam partem deesse dicit Quintilianus Demosthenis scriptis, quia illum dicentem non audiamus.
units.tr: (2) For greater choice. Many read many things, some useless, some useful, some curious and new, passing over those that have practical value. Here make a digression on the perversity of learners, who handle pleasant things rather than wholesome ones. Hence Aristippus, when a certain man boasted that he had read everything, replied that just as those who eat the most are not healthier than those who take what is needed, so those who have read the most are not to be counted learned, but those who have read useful things. It is otherwise with listening, where only those things are offered which by public judgment are deemed worthy of being heard. (3) For a firmer memory. Here praise the power of the living voice in penetrating the mind of the hearer, far more effectively than what is read, since the authority and feeling of the speaker are added. Hence Pliny said that what the speaker's delivery, face, bearing, and gesture contribute sits deeper in the mind. Hence Quintilian says that a great part of Demosthenes is missing from his writings, because we do not hear him speaking.

units.la: 3. Ab ejus necessitate. Quia sine illa nemo eruditus evasit. Hinc merito auditu disciplinae sensum Aristoteles aliique Philosophi dixerunt; cujus praestantia proinde praedicetur & praeferatur reliquis sensibus per comparationem cum iisdem. Et hinc duabus auribus instruxit natura hominem & eas multis ambagibus instruxit, ne audita illico elabantur. Caeci multi, at surdus nemo ad rerum notitiam pervenit. Imò Democritus oculos sibi eruit, tanquam obstacula meditationum; nemo aures obturavit, quia necessaria ad eruditionem & bonam mentem organa. Hinc Cyclopum resp. auditu destituta à poëtis fingitur. Ubi ἀδὲς ἀδευὸς ἀκύει ἐν ἀδευί, nemo alterum ullam in re audit. Latius ostende necessitatem auditus: hinc in regnis ac rebuspubl. quae uti voce, ita non sine auditu, reguntur: itemque in Ecclesia, quae solo auditu verbi divini regitur: hinc fides, justitia & salus &c.
units.tr: 3. From its necessity, since no one has become learned without it. Hence Aristotle and other philosophers rightly called hearing the sense of learning; its excellence should therefore be proclaimed and set above the other senses by comparison with them. And hence nature furnished man with two ears and surrounded them with many windings, so that what is heard does not slip away at once. Many are blind, yet no one who is deaf has come to knowledge of things. Indeed Democritus put out his own eyes as obstacles to meditation; no one has stopped up his ears, because these are the organs necessary for learning and a good mind. Hence the poets feign the Cyclopes, who lack hearing, to be a race in which no one hears another in anything [ἀδὲς ἀδευὸς ἀκύει ἐν ἀδευί]. Show the necessity of hearing more widely: hence in kingdoms and commonwealths, which are governed by the voice and so not without hearing; likewise in the Church, which is governed solely by the hearing of the divine Word; hence faith, righteousness, salvation, and so on.

units.la: 4. Ab exemplis omnium gentium excultarum; ubi ἀκροατήρια & Academiae erectae sunt, ubi omnis erudita quotidie loquitur antiquitas. Hoc publico orbis testimonio auscultatio stabilita est.
units.tr: 4. From the examples of all cultivated nations, where lecture halls [ἀκροατήρια] and academies have been established, and where all learned antiquity speaks daily. By this public testimony of the world, listening has been established.

units.la: Conclusio. 1. Breviter & nervosè repetat summam superiorum, indeque 2. inferat adhortationem ad diligentem auscultationem; addita nova ratione ab insigni jucunditate, cùm illa, quae viri docti studio magno meditati sunt, & didicerunt cum labore & molestia, brevi temporis spacio, percipere sine labore nobis liceat, &c.
units.tr: Conclusion. (1) He should briefly and forcefully repeat the sum of what has gone before, and (2) from this draw an exhortation to diligent listening, adding a new argument from its remarkable pleasantness: that we may be allowed to grasp in a short space of time, without labour, what learned men have pondered with great effort and learned with toil and trouble.

units.la: XII. DISPOSITIO DE PACE.
units.tr: XII. THE DISPOSITION ON PEACE.

units.la: Exord. Laudetur dictum Silii Italici Pax optima rerum &c. Hoc I. Exponatur cum breviss. encomio Auctoris & dicti, cujus sensus paraphrasi explicetur paucis.
units.tr: Exordium. Let the saying of Silius Italicus be praised: "Peace is the best of things," etc. Here, in the first point, it is to be set out with a very brief encomium of the author and of the saying, whose sense is to be explained briefly by a paraphrase.

units.la: II. Ratio addatur: quia pax praestantissimum Dei donum est, sine qua alia mundi bona parum prosunt. Uti sine valetudine integra cibi parum sapiunt, saepissime etiam nocent. Ita sublata ex republica pace.
units.tr: II. Add the reason: because peace is the most excellent gift of God, without which the other goods of the world profit little. As food tastes of little relish without sound health, and very often even does harm, so is the world's good things when peace is taken away from the commonwealth.

units.la: III. Illustretur simili. Etenim quod valitudo est in corpore, hoc pax in rep: bellum contra affligit omnes ordines, ceu morbus periculosus & capitalis.
units.tr: III. Illustrate it by a comparison. For as health is in the body, so is peace in the commonwealth: war afflicts all orders, like a dangerous and deadly disease.

units.la: Propos it. Si alii de culice, pulice, febri quartana; nos meliori jure fructuque ingens hoc coeli donum perpendimus, quae jam aliquot annis extorris ex Europa, Dei bonitate nobis reddita est; ne tanti beneficii immemores, ingrati & illo indigni deprehendamur.
units.tr: Propositio. If others weigh gnats, fleas and quartan fever, we, with better right and greater profit, should weigh this immense gift of heaven, which, after being driven out of Europe for some years, has been restored to us by the goodness of God; lest we be found forgetful of so great a benefit, ungrateful and unworthy of it.

units.la: Tractatio. Praemissa descriptione pacis methaphorica. (videlicet. Qui pacem dicit, omnium reip. partium statum rectum ac incolumem dicit, omniumque rerum abundantiam ac optatum usum & fructum suavissimum. &c.)
units.tr: Treatment. Once a metaphorical description of peace has been given (namely: he who speaks of peace speaks of the right and sound condition of all parts of the commonwealth, and of the abundance of all things and the desired use and most sweet fruit of them, etc.).

units.la: I. Pacis originem authoremq; Deum inquirat. Hinc 1. ostendat praedicetque beatam pacem in qua degit S.S. Trinitas. 2. Fluentem hinc pacem naturae universae. 3. Nascentem exinde divinam in omnibus benedictionem. Hanc per Adamum primitus turbatam, per Christum restitutam esse: Turbari quidem saepius tum in natura, per turbines, tempestates, unde noxae plurimae; tum per turbas ac seditiones & bella, in republica. At divina bonitate redigi in ordinem, sedari tempestates, sopiri bella. vide Psalm. 46. &c. O donum vere coeleste pacis ac concordiae. Quis hoc agnoscit, nisi postquam deperditum est? Et quis satis laborat pro restitutione amissae pacis.
units.tr: I. Let him inquire into the origin and author of peace, namely God. Hence (1) let him show and proclaim that blessed peace in which the Holy Trinity dwells; (2) from this flows peace for all creation; (3) from that arises the divine blessing upon all things. This was first disturbed through Adam and restored through Christ. It is indeed disturbed rather often, both in nature, by whirlwinds and storms, whence come very many harms, and in the commonwealth, by tumults, seditions and wars. But by divine goodness it is brought back into order, the storms are calmed, the wars are lulled. See Psalm 46, etc. O truly heavenly gift of peace and concord! Who recognises it unless after it has been lost? And who labours enough for the restoration of lost peace?

units.la: II. Praedicet pacis utilitatem in tota vita & omnibus ordinibus; & quidem in 1. Politico: ubi a. concordiam stabilit inter magistratum & subditos, qua quid salutarius? b. Inter cives invicem qua quid suavius? &c. Inter vicinos qua quid optatius? O quam beata civitas, ubi fratres unum sunt. Illustretur à contrario bello, ubi & disruptio ordinis politici. Vide exempla sub Salomone; sub Augusto.
units.tr: II. Let him proclaim the usefulness of peace in the whole of life and in all orders; and indeed (1) in the political sphere, where (a) it establishes concord between the magistrate and the subjects: what is more wholesome? (b) Among citizens one with another: what is sweeter? etc. Among neighbours: what is more desirable? O how blessed is the city where brothers are one! Let it be illustrated by the contrary, war, where the political order is also broken up. See examples under Solomon and under Augustus.

units.la: 2. Domestico: ubi cultus in omni arte œconomica domi, foris & in agro: quæ pacis artes. At bello ferocit juventus, tradit se ocio, furtis, rapinis. Quanta inde scelera, quanta mala! &c.
units.tr: (2) In the domestic sphere, where there is cultivation in every economic art at home, abroad and in the field: these are the arts of peace. But in war the youth grow fierce, give themselves over to idleness, theft and plunder. What great crimes and what great evils come from this! etc.

units.la: 3. Ecclesiastico: ubi vigente pace; 1. Florent literæ & scientiæ ad vitæ cultum; 2. Sonat verbi præconium. 3. Excoluntur virtutes omnes &c. Unde laudata vita & omnis opulentia; & ex pace terrena transitus ad pacem & gloriam cœlestem. Hujus præludium esse pacem externam.
units.tr: (3) In the ecclesiastical sphere, where, while peace prevails: (1) letters and sciences flourish for the cultivation of life; (2) the proclamation of the Word resounds; (3) all virtues are cultivated, etc. Whence life is praised and all abundance; and from earthly peace there is a passage to the heavenly peace and glory. External peace is the prelude to this.

units.la: III. Deploret contra belli incommoda. Non in thesi hæc te exaggeraturum, quæ fœcunda nimis materia; sed revocaturum te in memoriam perpessa & superiori & præsenti bello Germaniæ mala, vicinarumque provinciarum & regnorum. Hæc exponat καὶ ἰσ-μονὴν & figuram communicationis: Quis nescit? Percurrat hic pathetice mala illa, quæ Germania, Gallia, Anglia, Dania, Suecia, Belgia perpessa novissimis hisce bellis. Hosce scilicet esse bellorum fructus. &c. Ipsa elementa conspirasse una in exitium, incendiis, eluvionibus, tempestatibus.
units.tr: III. Let him lament, on the other hand, the evils of war. You will not, in a thesis, exaggerate these things, since the matter is too fruitful; but you will recall to memory the sufferings of Germany, and of the neighbouring provinces and kingdoms, in the former and the present war. Let him set these out with καὶ ἰσμονή and the figure of communication: who does not know? Let him here run through pathetically those evils which Germany, France, England, Denmark, Sweden and Belgium have suffered in these latest wars. These, of course, are the fruits of wars, etc. The very elements have conspired together for ruin: by fires, floods and storms.

units.la: IV. Præsagium inde capiat secuturæ felicitatis, cum tot reges hactenus armis intenti infestique, conspiraturi sunt,
units.tr: IV. From this let him take an omen of the happiness that is to follow, when so many kings, hitherto intent upon and hostile in arms, are about to unite,

units.la: 1. In salutarem legum constitutionem & salutem subditorum. Has esse dignas regibus principibusque curas, hoc officium divinitus ipsis commissum. &c. Sic vere Deos dici. &c.
units.tr: (1) in the wholesome establishment of laws and the welfare of their subjects. That these are the cares worthy of kings and princes, this office committed to them by God, etc. Thus indeed they are truly called gods, etc.

units.la: 2. In agrorum commerciorumque cultum & augmentum. Fundum inexhaustum esse agrum, sed requirere culturam: satis divites esse provincias ac regiones, diversis abundantes copiis, si mutuis commerciis juventur; hic hasce, istic alias vigere artes, per commercia omnibus communicandas; si tuta per pacem fiant itinera, tuta maria. Quantas opes Vulcano, Oceano superioribus annis immolatas fuisse, eximio emolumento impositerum futuras. &c.
units.tr: (2) in the cultivation and increase of fields and commerce. The field is inexhaustible, but it requires cultivation; provinces and regions, abundant in various resources, are rich enough if they are aided by mutual trade; here these arts flourish, there others, to be shared with all through commerce; if journeys are made safe by peace, and seas safe. How great the wealth sacrificed to Vulcan and to Ocean in the years past will, in the future, bring an excellent profit, etc.

units.la: 3. In cultum sacrum & religionis. Tempore belli ferocire ingenia humana, ut ipsa sacra vilipendant. At pace restituta, reddi & cultum Numinis, & manuduci mentem ad gratitudinem erga Deum. Imo ipsa arma & belli necessitates junxisse in foedus dissidentes hactenus in religione, ad mutuam conversatio-nem, ad foedera, ad connubia: Quidni ulteriorem inde spe-raremus conjunctionem animorum: Ita futurum, ut ex Chri-stianorum concordia, efflorescat conversio judaeorum, & Turcorum gentiumque &c.
units.tr: (3) in the worship and the sacred things of religion. In time of war human minds grow fierce, so that they despise sacred things themselves. But with peace restored, both the worship of the Deity is restored and the mind is led to gratitude towards God. Indeed, arms and the necessities of war have joined in covenant those who until now were at odds in religion, to mutual conversation, to alliances, to marriages: why should we not from this hope for a further union of minds? Thus it will come to pass that, from the concord of Christians, the conversion of the Jews, of the Turks and of the nations, will flourish, etc.

units.la: Concluf. I. Gratias agat Deo pro reddita Christianis pace.
units.tr: Conclusio. I. Let him give thanks to God for the peace restored to the Christians.

units.la: II. Optet ut perpetua ac salutaris illa sit Ecclesiae Christi, vergat-que in conversionem infidelium, & salutem animarum. &c.
units.tr: II. Let him pray that this peace may be perpetual and salutary for the Church of Christ, and that it may tend towards the conversion of unbelievers and the salvation of souls, etc.

units.la: XIII. PRAECONIUM DIVINAE BONITATIS IN NOVO ANNO.
units.tr: XIII. A PRAISE OF THE DIVINE GOODNESS IN THE NEW YEAR.

units.la: Exord. A dicto Isocratis, quo ex factis judicium fieri jubet de faciendis. Tractetur breviter instar Chriae & applica ad praesens tempus, anni scilicet initium, ubi meminisse oportet anni praeteriti & prospicere futurum. Hoc voluisse veteres, cum Janum bifrontem pinxerint.
units.tr: Exordium. Begin from the saying of Isocrates, by which he bids judgment be made about things to be done from things already done. Let it be treated briefly in the manner of a chreia, and applied to the present time, namely the beginning of the year, when it is fitting to remember the past year and to look ahead to the future. The ancients meant this when they painted Janus with two faces.

units.la: Propof. Idem & noster scopus hic: videlicet meditari divinam boni-tatem anno elapso, & vovere felicem successum in futurum.
units.tr: Propositio. Our aim here is the same: namely, to meditate on the divine goodness during the year now past, and to wish for a happy outcome in the year to come.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Tractatio.

units.la: I. Bimembris recolat anni elapsi commoda: Hic 1. deploret epi-demia passim vitia, videl. verbi divini contemtum, neglectum justitiae in omnibus vitae ordinibus, luxum & fastum praevalen-tes. Exaggeret haec comparatione cum aureis seculis majorum, ipsorumq; gentilium. 2. Exemplaria Dei judicia, qua passim bellis, & peste animadvertit in plerasque nationes; Amplificentur in-ductione praecipuorum bellorum & cladium, quae hoc anno con-tigerunt. 3. Divinam bonitatem a. in avertendis malis. b. In exhibendis bonis in statu Ecclesiastico, Politico, Oeconomico, & praesertim in scholastico: cujus emolumenta exaggerentur, & illustrentur comparatione cum aliis regnis & rebuspublicis.
units.tr: I. Let him recall the blessings of the past year in two parts. Here (1) he should lament the epidemic of vices everywhere: the contempt of the divine Word, the neglect of justice in all walks of life, and the prevailing luxury and pride. Let him magnify these by comparison with the golden ages of our ancestors and even of the Gentiles. (2) Let him set forth God's judgments, which he has everywhere visited upon most nations with wars and plague. Let these be amplified by the enumeration of the chief wars and calamities that have befallen in this year. (3) Let him set forth the divine goodness: (a) in averting evils; (b) in bestowing blessings in the ecclesiastical, political, and domestic spheres, and especially in the scholastic one. Let its advantages be magnified and illustrated by comparison with other kingdoms and commonwealths.

units.la: II. Ex hac Dei indulgentia porro colligat voveatque anni instan-tis felicitatem.
units.tr: II. From this indulgence of God let him further draw conclusions and wish for the happiness of the coming year.

units.la: 1. Ut Deus bellum, & clades omnes in suos & Ecclesiae hostes convertat ad eversionem regni AntiChristi & Mahumetis. Amplif. ab effectis, videl. hinc futurum, ut crescat amplitudo & gloria regni Christi & redeant priscina secula. 2. Ut pacem reddat Germaniæ vicinisque regnis: quo vires vertant adversus hostes imminentes.
units.tr: 1. That God may turn all wars and calamities against his own people and the enemies of the Church, to the overthrow of the kingdom of Antichrist and of Mahomet. Amplify from the effects: namely, that from this it will follow that the greatness and glory of Christ's kingdom will grow and the former ages return. (2) That he may restore peace to Germany and the neighbouring kingdoms, so that their strength may be turned against the enemies who threaten.

units.la: 3. Ut Ecclesiam servet & scholas; quò ad vitam piam & honestam instruantur,' & ex mundi & mortalitatis civibus cœli & beatæ immortalitatis cives efficiantur omnes.
units.tr: 3. That he may preserve the Church and the schools, so that all may be instructed toward a pious and honourable life, and be made citizens of heaven and of blessed immortality rather than citizens of the world and of mortality.

units.la: Conclus. In hoc voto finiat.
units.tr: Conclusio. Let him end with this wish.

units.la: DISPOSITIONUM GENERIS DEMONSTRATIVI. PARS III.
units.tr: DISPOSITIONS OF THE DEMONSTRATIVE KIND. PART III.

units.la: CONTINENS LAUDES ET VITUPERIA FACTORUM. I. LAUS FACTI ABRAHAMI IMMOLATURI FILIUM.
units.tr: CONTAINING PRAISES AND BLAME OF DEEDS. I. PRAISE OF ABRAHAM'S DEED IN OFFERING UP HIS SON.

units.la: A. EXord. Ab Elogio scripturæ, quo Abrahamum dicit patrem credentium. Explicetur a causa 1. quia secutus est Deum in peregrinitatem.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the commendation in Scripture, where it calls Abraham the father of believers. It is explained from the cause: 1. because he followed God into a strange land.

units.la: 2. Ibidem ambulavit coram Deo.
units.tr: 2. Because he walked before God in the same place.

units.la: 3. Fidit Deo promittenti semen benedictum, contra spem.
units.tr: 3. Because he trusted God, who promised a blessed seed, against hope.

units.la: 4. Non desperavit de promissione, etiam cum immolare debebat filium.
units.tr: 4. Because he did not despair of the promise, even when he had to sacrifice his son.

units.la: B. Narratio, breviter factum explanet.
units.tr: B. Narration: briefly explain the deed.

units.la: C. Propositio. Egregium hoc facinus exornabo, ut simili fidei constantiâ patrem fidelium imitari discamus.
units.tr: C. Proposition: I shall set forth this outstanding deed, so that we may learn to imitate the father of the faithful in the like constancy of faith.

units.la: D. Expositio.
units.tr: D. Exposition.

units.la: I, A difficili, quod ostendatur.
units.tr: I. From what is difficult, which is to be shown.

units.la: a. Ex circumstantiis.
units.tr: a. From the circumstances.

units.la: 1. Pater debebat mactare & immolare filium. Quod adver-sum rationi, legibus.
units.tr: 1. The father had to slay and sacrifice his son, which is contrary to reason and to the laws.

units.la: 2. Occidere debebat filium unicum in senectute natum, dile-ctum. Illustretur a disparatis, difficile si ex pluribus unum,
units.tr: 2. He had to kill his only son, born in old age and beloved. Let it be illustrated by comparisons: it is hard when one is taken from many, but here the only one.

units.la: 3. Mactare illum debebat inscia matre. Exaggeretur, quo-modo ab illa accipiendus fuisset homicida filii communis.
units.tr: 3. He had to slay him without the knowledge of the mother. Let it be magnified how she would have had to receive as a murderer of her common son the one who had killed him.

units.la: 4. Illum filium, in cujus vita & posteritate ipsius & mundi spes erat reposita.
units.tr: 4. That son, in whose life and posterity the hope of himself and of the world was placed.

units.la: b. A justa dubitatione. Hic
units.tr: b. From a just doubt. Here:

units.la: a. Exponatur promissio divina.
units.tr: α. The divine promise is set forth.

units.la: β. Expendatur mandatum hoc adversum & inimicum,
units.tr: β. This hostile and contrary command is weighed.

units.la: γ. Inferatur dubitatio, quae subnasci potuisset, mandatum hoc utpote praecepto & promissioni divinae contrarium, non ab eodem Deo, sed forte a spiritu maligno proficisci: unde justa excusatio & detractatio obedientiae. At vicit haec omnia. Claudatur hoc argumentum exclamatione admirante constantiam. Transeatur ad alterum argumentum.
units.tr: γ. The doubt is inferred that could have arisen: that this command, being contrary to the precept and promise of God, did not proceed from the same God but perhaps from an evil spirit; whence there was a just excuse and a refusal of obedience. But he overcame all these things. Let this argument be closed with an exclamation admiring his constancy. Let us pass to the second argument.

units.la: II. Ab honesto. Quod probetur,
units.tr: II. From what is honourable. Which is proved:

units.la: a. A causa, Deo imperante, cui homo sine disceptatione obsequitur omni jure. Locus Communis de autoritate creatoris & subjectione creaturae.
units.tr: a. From the cause, God commanding, to whom man yields obedience without dispute by every right. Common place on the authority of the Creator and the subjection of the creature.

units.la: b. Ab aequitate mandati videlicet, 1. ut Deo redderet eum, qui a Deo datus erat: 2. qui potens erat ex pulvere ipsum resuscitare; 3. qui proprium filium daturus erat.
units.tr: b. From the fairness of the command, namely: 1. that he should give back to God the one who had been given by God; 2. the one who was able to raise him up again from the dust; 3. the one who was about to give his own Son.

units.la: III. Ab utili.
units.tr: III. From what is useful.

units.la: a. Hinc fides ejus approbata a Deo, celebrata per mundum, & ipse pater credentium factus est.
units.tr: a. Hence his faith was approved by God, celebrated throughout the world, and he himself was made the father of believers.

units.la: b. Benedictio Dei temporalis & aeterna ipsum consecuta est,
units.tr: b. The temporal and eternal blessing of God followed him.

units.la: E. Conclusio. In admirationem desinens & ad imitationem cohortans.
units.tr: E. Conclusion: ending in admiration and exhorting to imitation.

units.la: II. VITUPERATIO FRATRICIDII CAINI.
units.tr: II. A Denunciation of Cain's Fratricide.

units.la: A Exord. a comparatis: si omne scelus abominandum, tum maxime illud quod primum est, quia illud sine exemplo committitur. RaRatio 1. Quia illud viam aperit aliis. 2. Applicetur ad præsens factum, quod proinde breviter narretur.
units.tr: A. Exordium, from comparisons: if every crime is to be abhorred, then most of all that which comes first, because it was committed without precedent. Reasons: (1) because it opens the way for others; (2) it is applied to the present deed, which is therefore to be narrated briefly.

units.la: B. Propof. Hujus itaque detestabor fœditatem.
units.tr: B. Proposition: I will therefore detest the foulness of this deed.

units.la: C. Expositio.
units.tr: C. Exposition.

units.la: I. Ab inhonesto: quod probetur
units.tr: I. From dishonour, which is to be proved:

units.la: a. Ex Lege naturæ, quæ illustranda inductione brutorum animalium, quæ in suo genere probe degunt. Exaggeranda a præstantia hominis cujus vita preciosior, sævitia abominabilior, utpote rationi contraria. Claudatur invectiva in homicidas & in specie Cainum qui pejor brutis.
units.tr: a. From the law of nature, which is to be illustrated by the example of brute animals, which live decently in their own kind. It is to be magnified from the excellence of man, whose life is more precious and whose cruelty is more hateful, as being contrary to reason. The invective is to close against murderers and, in particular, against Cain, who is worse than the brutes.

units.la: b. A Lege Dei, quæ prohibet homicidia, & gravissima pœna ulciscitur. Exaggeretur hæc lex ab antiquitate: inter primas quippe, quas Judæi Leges gentium vocant.
units.tr: b. From the law of God, which forbids murder and punishes it most severely. This law is to be magnified by its antiquity: for it is among the first which the Jews call the laws of the nations.

units.la: c. A jure quo tenebatur
units.tr: c. From the right by which he was bound:

units.la: 1. Fratri, cui debebat amorem, auxilium, defensionem. Exaggeretur jus fraternitatis; & opponatur contra crudelitas fratricidii.
units.tr: 1. To his brother, to whom he owed love, help and defence. The right of brotherhood is to be magnified, and the cruelty of fratricide set against it.

units.la: 2. Parentibus; quibus debebat honorem, obsequium, auxilium in promovenda re familiari. Exaggeretur obligatio filialis & fœditas facti, mœrorem loco gaudii exhibentis parentibus.
units.tr: 2. To his parents, to whom he owed honour, obedience and help in advancing the family's fortunes. The filial obligation is to be magnified, and the foulness of the deed, which brought grief instead of joy to the parents.

units.la: d. A circumstantiis in quibus quod occiderit fratrem unicum innocentem, sacris intentum, itemque nulla injuria provocantem, sed ex sola invidia.
units.tr: d. From the circumstances: that he killed his only brother, who was innocent, intent on sacred things, and who provoked him by no injury, but out of mere envy.

units.la: II. Ab inutili: quia a. ipse non evasurus erat melior, licet meliorem occiderat. b. Quia sic cumulabat profanitatem parricidio. c. violabat jura omnia societatis & obnoxium se reddebat pœnis, uti eventus docuit: Nam fugit pavidus.
units.tr: II. From what is useless: because (a) he himself was not going to become better, although he had killed a better man; (b) because in this way he piled profanity upon parricide; (c) he violated all the laws of society and made himself liable to punishments, as the outcome taught: for he fled in fear.

units.la: 1. A facie Dei. 2. A communione Ecclesiæ. 3. Convertit se ad mundana, auctor defectionis omnibus posteris.
units.tr: (1) from the face of God; (2) from the communion of the Church; (3) he turned himself to worldly things, and became the author of apostasy for all his posterity.

units.la: D. Conclusio factum detestetur, & ut primum, ita perpetua abominatione dignum arguat.
units.tr: D. Conclusion: let him detest the deed, and let him show that it is worthy of perpetual abhorrence, as it was the first.

units.la: III. DETESTATIO FACTI, VIDELICET CONJURATIONIS CATILINARIÆ.
units.tr: III. THE DETESTATION OF THE DEED, NAMELY OF CATILINE'S CONSPIRACY.

units.la: Exord. A dicto JCtorum: Interest reip. ne crimina maneant impunita; nita; Tractetur paucis instar Chriae & applicetur ad institutum, non tantum puniri malefacta poenis viventum, led & justo vituperio post mortem, ut alii deterreantur.
units.tr: Exordium. From the saying of the lawyers: it is in the interest of the commonwealth that crimes not remain unpunished. This is to be treated briefly, in the manner of a chreia, and applied to the matter in hand: that wicked deeds should be punished not only with penalties upon the living, but also with just censure after death, so that others may be deterred.

units.la: Propos. In praesentiarum, foedam illam Catilinae conjurationem detestandam esse, ut à simili foedere alii abstinere dicant.
units.tr: Proposition. At present, that foul conspiracy of Catiline is to be detested, so that others may be said to abstain from a similar compact.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Ex loco generis: quia omnis conjuratio pessima, cum non ipse solum autor peccet, sed & alios ad peccandum induc it: & quidem non modo exemplo, quod pessimum; sed & instigatione ac hortatu. &c.
units.tr: Treatment. I. From the topic of the genus: because every conspiracy is most wicked, since not only its author sins but he also induces others to sin, and that not only by example, which is the worst, but also by incitement and exhortation, etc.

units.la: II. In ipecie ex facti hujus circumstantiis:
units.tr: II. Specifically, from the circumstances of this deed:

units.la: 1. Autore: qui homo patricius ; in quo conspicuum magis scelus, & tota familia dehonestatur.
units.tr: 1. From the author: who was a man of patrician rank; in whom the crime is more conspicuous, and the whole family is dishonoured.

units.la: 2. Ab sociis, quos legit; videl. viros ac juvenes nobilissimos pariter & corruptam Reip. secem. Tot scil. familias honestas infecit hac scabie.
units.tr: 2. From his associates, whom he chose, namely men and young men of the highest nobility, and at the same time corrupters of the commonwealth. He infected so many honourable families with this scab.

units.la: 3. Ab objecto: proditione patriae, quae charissima esse debuisset: caede consulum & Senatus, qui honorandi.
units.tr: 3. From the object: the betrayal of the fatherland, which ought to have been most dear; the slaughter of the consuls and of the Senate, who ought to have been honoured.

units.la: 4. A fine: direptione & incendio urbis, ut habeat luxus instrumenta, si salutem & vindicias Reip. intendisset, via haec mala fuisset: quid, cum perniciem Reip.?
units.tr: 4. From the end: the plundering and burning of the city, so that they might have the instruments of luxury. If he had aimed at the safety and protection of the commonwealth, this would have been an evil way; how much more, then, when his aim was the ruin of the commonwealth?

units.la: III. Ex praesenti periculo: cum scil. urbs milite destituta facile everti potuisset.
units.tr: III. From the present danger: since the city, stripped of its soldiers, could easily have been overthrown.

units.la: Conclus. Aver(i)etur factum tanquam barbarum & ipsi naturae adversum, proindeque uti morte complicum, ita per petua detestatione merito notandum.
units.tr: Conclusion. The deed is to be abhorred as barbarous and contrary to nature itself, and therefore, just as the accomplices were put to death, so it deserves to be marked with a perpetual detestation.

units.la: IV. LAUS FACTI, QUO POPULUS ROMANUS CICERONI LICET HOMINI NOVO CONSULATUM MANDAVIT.
units.tr: IV. THE PRAISE OF THE ACT BY WHICH THE ROMAN PEOPLE ENTRUSTED THE CONSULSHIP TO CICERO, A NEW MAN.

units.la: Exord. A necessaria cautione in eligendis magistratibus. Ratio quia fata Reip. ab imperantibus dependent: ut salus navis a gubernatione tempore tempestatis. Si aliquando sub malis imperantibus sarta tecta maneat Resp. felicitatis est singularis, non prudentiae.
units.tr: Exord. On the necessary caution in choosing magistrates. The reason is that the fortunes of the state depend on those who rule, as the safety of a ship depends on the steering in a storm. If sometimes the commonwealth remains intact under bad rulers, that is a singular good fortune, not prudence.

units.la: Propos. Ideoque hac hora factum Populi Romani tanquam aequissimum
units.tr: Propos. Therefore this deed of the Roman people is to be praised as most fair

units.la: Dd simum & Reip. salub errimum laudandum esse, ut exemplo sapere discamus.
units.tr: and most beneficial to the commonwealth, so that by its example we may learn wisdom.

units.la: Confirm. I. Exponat difficultates oppositas 1. quia insolitum hoc 2. quia odiosum proferre exterum indigenæ. 3. quia erant viri egregii patricii, in quorum hoc vergebat ignominiam. 4. quia Cicero homo forensis, causis agendis potius, quam regendæ Reip. assuetus.
units.tr: Confirm. I. Let him set out the objections: (1) because this was unusual; (2) because it was invidious to prefer an outsider to natives; (3) because they were distinguished patricians, to whom it brought disgrace; (4) because Cicero was a man of the forum, accustomed to pleading causes rather than governing the state.

units.la: II. Nihilominum laudandum hoc factum populi.
units.tr: II. Nevertheless, this deed of the people is to be praised.

units.la: 1. Tanquam honestum & æquissimum a. propter virtutes Ciceronis quas prædicet: & talibus deberi Rempubl. dicat. Hinc refellat rationes oppositas. b. propter pericula Reip. ubi potius habilitas personæ, quam mores Reipubl. spectandi, si salvam illam velimus. Hinc respondeat ad rationem primam & secundâ c. propter factiones patriciorum, qui vel cognati vel socii Catilinæ. Hinc refellat rationem tertiam d. propter exempla in ipso rege Numa, qui exterus fuit.
units.tr: 1. As honourable and most fair: (a) on account of Cicero's virtues, which he should extol, and on the ground that the commonwealth is owed to such men; from this he should refute the opposing arguments. (b) On account of the dangers to the commonwealth, where the suitability of the person, rather than the character of the commonwealth, should be considered if we wish it to be preserved; from this he should answer the first and second objections. (c) On account of the factions of the patricians, who were either kinsmen or allies of Catiline; from this he should refute the third objection. (d) On account of examples, in King Numa himself, who was a foreigner.

units.la: 2. Tanquam salutare Reipubl. quod arguat a. à vigilantia & animositate Ciceronis vide Salust. b. Ab effecto, conservatione Reip. ipsi soli debita.
units.tr: 2. As salutary for the commonwealth, which is shown: (a) from Cicero's vigilance and spirit; see Sallust. (b) from its effect, the preservation of the commonwealth, which is owed to him alone.

units.la: Concluf. Explodat sententiam contrariam. 2. Factum populi tanquam sapientissimum & saluberrimum prædicet.
units.tr: Concluf. He should refute the contrary opinion. 2. He should proclaim the people's deed as most wise and most salutary.

units.la: V. LAUS FACTI VIDELICET, CONSULTATIONUM VETERUM GERMANORUM INTER POCULA.
units.tr: V. PRAISE OF THE PRACTICE, NAMELY OF THE ANCIENT GERMANS' DELIBERATIONS OVER THEIR CUPS.

units.la: Ex Tacito de moribus German.
units.tr: From Tacitus, On the Manners of the Germans.

units.la: Exord. Cum magna laus vetustatis, tum præ cæteris veteresGermanos laudandos esse. Ratio: quia juxta Tacitum nemo ibi vitia risit. Illustretur comparatione cum luxu aliarum gentiū. Accedatur ad propositionē de consultatione ipsorū inter pocula merito dubitari.
units.tr: Exordium. Ancient things deserve great praise, and the ancient Germans deserve to be praised above all others. Reason: according to Tacitus, no one there laughed at vices. Let this be illustrated by comparison with the luxury of other peoples. Then approach the proposition: it may rightly be doubted whether they deliberated over their cups.

units.la: Propof. Tibi probandum morem videri.
units.tr: Proposition. You are to be shown that the custom seems good.

units.la: Confirm. I. Prædicet in genere convivia. 1. Ut salubria corpori ac animo ad recreationem. 2. ut utilia ad amorum conjunctionem seu amicitiam juratam veluti ad Bacchi aras.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. Commend drinking parties in general: 1. as wholesome for the body and mind, for recreation; 2. as useful for strengthening friendship and a sworn fellowship, as it were at the altars of Bacchus.

units.la: II. In specie consultationes hæ commendentur tanquā. 1. expeditiores, quippe ubi a. animi cerevisiā incaluerunt, quod necessariū ingeniis tardioribus in locis hisce frigidis: Secus ac in calidis locis, ubi potus generat furorem, hic vigorem. b. metus exulat, unde lenta, perplexa, irrita consilia. Potus vero onus eximit animo, ac docet artes. &c. 2. Liberiores, a. Illustretur a contraria simulatione, quae adeo profunde animis mortalium insita: b. opponatur sinceritas in compotatione. Unde & Tiberius amavit consiliarios bibaces. 3. honestas: quod non de rebus iudicris aut lascivis, sed de seriis egerint inter pocula: ubi redarguantur lascivia & nugae compotantium.
units.tr: II. In particular, these deliberations are to be commended as: 1. more expeditious, since (a) when their spirits have been warmed by beer, which is needful for slower wits in these cold regions (unlike hot regions, where drink produces frenzy, here vigour), and (b) fear is banished, whence come slow, tangled and fruitless counsels; drink indeed lifts the burden from the mind and teaches the arts, etc. 2. more free: (a) let this be illustrated by the contrary, namely pretence, which is so deeply implanted in the minds of mortals; (b) set against it the sincerity shown in drinking together. Hence Tiberius too loved counsellors who were fond of drink. 3. more honourable, since they discussed not trivial or wanton matters but serious ones over their cups; there the wantonness and trifling of drinkers are refuted.

units.la: III. Addantur retractationes matutinae; tanquam 1. utiles propter ingenii humani imbecillitate. 2. necessariae, ob hesteru compotione. 3. opportunae, ante executione, quae illico decreto addita.
units.tr: III. Add the morning reconsiderations, as (1) useful, because of the weakness of human understanding; (2) necessary, on account of the previous day's drinking; (3) opportune, since they came before execution, being added to the decision at once.

units.la: Conclus. Recollecta breviter argumentorum summa, propositionem inculcet.
units.tr: Conclusion. Having briefly recollected the sum of the arguments, let him press home the proposition.

units.la: VI. VITUPERATIO FACTI.
units.tr: VI. Censure of the Deed.

units.la: Veterum Germanorum inter pocula deliberantium & mane retractantium.
units.tr: Of the ancient Germans, who deliberated over their cups and reconsidered in the morning.

units.la: Exord. A necessaria cautione in aemulatione vetustatis. Ratio: quia & veteres suos habuere naevos. Illustretur oppositione illorum, qui omnia vetera laudanda putant: unde & antecessor veterem Germanorum morem laudare voluerit.
units.tr: Exordium. The necessity of caution in emulating antiquity. The reason: because even the ancients had their blemishes. Let it be illustrated by the opposition of those who think that everything ancient is to be praised; whence the predecessor too has wished to praise the old custom of the Germans.

units.la: Propos. Tibi morem illum deliberandi, ut turpem, ut noxium maxime improbandum videri.
units.tr: Proposition. That custom of deliberating (in that manner) is to be judged as wholly deserving of rejection, as shameful and above all harmful.

units.la: Confirmatio. 1. Quia turpis: quod probetur 1. ex ebrietatis & compotationum dedecore, utpote quae omnibus politis gentibus detestatae, Thracibus propriae. 2. ex consultationum sanctitate: utpote in quibus agitur de summa rerum, proindeque magna circumspectione & prudentia, sine vesania, sine ira, sine impetu tractandae. Hinc inter cordatos semper matutino tempore consilia publica semper agitata fuisse exemplo Graeciae, Romae. Hosce potius, quam barbaros mores imitandos.
units.tr: Confirmation. 1. Because it is shameful: which is proved (a) from the disgrace of drunkenness and drinking bouts, which are detested by all civilised peoples and are peculiar to the Thracians; (b) from the sanctity of consultations: since they concern the highest affairs of state, and must therefore be handled with great circumspection and prudence, without frenzy, without anger, without rashness. Hence among sensible men public counsels have always been held in the morning, as the examples of Greece and Rome show. These customs, rather than barbarian ones, are to be imitated.

units.la: II. Quia noxius 1. propter comitem ebrietatis mentis stuporem, praecipitantiam, temeritatem, impetum, obstinationem, inconstantiam: quae omnia sanis consiliis adversae: probetur exemplo Bessi & Alexandri ex Curtio. Hinc refellat quae pro consultationibus istis argumento II. praecedentis orationis dicta sunt. 2. propter facilem arcanorum revelationem; cum ebrius cor in lingua habeat. Quod perniciosissimum in consultationibus Hinc refutet quod num. II. dictum.
units.tr: II. Because it is harmful: (a) on account of the dullness of mind that accompanies drunkenness, its headlong haste, rashness, impetuosity, obstinacy and inconstancy, all of which are opposed to sound counsel; this is proved by the example of the Bessi and of Alexander from Curtius. Hence let him refute what was said in support of these consultations in the argument of the second point of the preceding speech. (b) on account of the easy revelation of secrets, since a drunk man has his heart on his tongue; this is most destructive in consultations. Hence let him refute what was said in the second point.

units.la: III. Quia retractatio sobria corrigere haud potuit errores inter pocula commissos: ob pertinaciam plurimorum, qui turpe putant, recedere à sententia semel placita.
units.tr: III. Because sober reconsideration could not correct the errors committed over wine, on account of the obstinacy of many, who think it shameful to depart from an opinion once adopted.

units.la: Conclus. Concedat convivia familiaria & sermones convivales de rebus minus seriis; ut consultationes de Rep. à conviviis & compotationibus removeat: cum mens sicca semper sapientissima.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him concede family dinners and table talk about less serious matters; but let him remove deliberations on the commonwealth from banquets and drinking bouts, since a sober mind is always the wiser.

units.la: VII. VITUPERATIO FACTI APPII CLAUDII QUO LIBIDINE FURENS FILIAM VERGINII IN SERVITUTEM ASSERI VOLUIT, vide Liv.
units.tr: VII. Censure of the deed of Appius Claudius, who, raging with lust, wished to have Verginius's daughter claimed as a slave; see Livy.

units.la: Exord. Ex Loco Communi de praemiis ac poenis: videl. ut illa virtutibus, ita hasce sceleribus deberi: & vel praecipue consistere in laude recte & vituperio male factorum, etiam apud posteros.
units.tr: Exord. From the common topic of rewards and punishments: namely, that as the former are due to virtues, so the latter are due to crimes; and that especially they consist in praise of right deeds and censure of wicked ones, even among posterity.

units.la: Propos. Factum Appii Claudii hac vice detestandum.
units.tr: Propos. The deed of Appius Claudius is to be detested on this occasion.

units.la: Narratio. Factum breviter exponat.
units.tr: Narratio. Let him set out the deed briefly.

units.la: Confirmatio. Illud vituperet
units.tr: Confirmatio. Let him censure it:

units.la: I. Tanquam turpe 1. ortum quippe ex libidine vitio foedissimo: idque adversus sponsam alterius.
units.tr: I. As shameful: 1. arising, to be sure, from lust, a most foul vice; and that against the betrothed of another man.

units.la: 2. Commissum ab ipso Judice, animo deliberato.
units.tr: 2. Committed by the judge himself, with deliberate intent.

units.la: 3. Sub specie justitiae; qua turpiter abutebatur ad oppressionem innocentis.
units.tr: 3. Under the appearance of justice, which he shamefully abused for the oppression of an innocent woman.

units.la: II. Tanquam noxium 1. Virgini, quae ex justo dolore peremta à patre. 2. civitati, quae ad tumultum concitata. 3. Ipsi Appio, qui depositus. 4. toti ordini magistratus, qui sic remotus fuit & restituti Consules.
units.tr: II. As harmful: 1. to the virgin, who, slain by her father out of just grief; 2. to the state, which was stirred up to tumult; 3. to Appius himself, who was deposed; 4. to the whole order of magistrates, which was thus removed, and the consuls restored.

units.la: Conclus. Damnet ipsum perpetuae infamiae 1. libidinem tanquam regnorum vastatricem detestetur.
units.tr: Conclus. Let him condemn him to perpetual infamy: 1. let him detest lust as the destroyer of kingdoms.

units.la: VIII. LAUS FACTI MOSIS QUOD ESERTA AULA PHARAONIS AD FRATRES SUOS ISRAELITAS REDIIT, Ex Heb. XI.
units.tr: VIII. IN PRAISE OF THE DEED OF MOSES, WHO, WHEN THE COURT OF PHARAOH WAS FORSAKEN, WENT BACK TO HIS BROTHERS THE ISRAELITES, from Heb. XI.

units.la: Exord. Ab exemplo gentilium, qui facta heroum suorum laudarint: & merito, ut virtuti constaret sua laus & alii excitarentur ad imitationem Majori jure Christianis illustria facta sacrorū heroū celebrari : quæ non ex ambitione sed ex fide & pietate fluunt, & ad Dei gloriam tendunt. Merito igitur præeunte Apostolo laudamus factum Mosis, &c.
units.tr: Exord. From the example of the Gentiles, who praised the deeds of their heroes: and rightly so, that their praise might stand firm as virtue and others might be stirred to imitate it. With greater right, the illustrious deeds of the sacred heroes should be celebrated among Christians, since these flow not from ambition but from faith and piety, and tend to the glory of God. Rightly, therefore, following the Apostle, we praise the deed of Moses, etc.

units.la: Propos. Hoc igitur in præsenti oratione exornandum esse.
units.tr: Propos. This, therefore, is what is to be set forth in the present oration.

units.la: Tractatio. Factum prædicet
units.tr: Tractatio. The deed is to be commended:

units.la: I. Ab honesto & pio. Hoc ostendatur comparatione aulæ Pharaonis, idololatria, injustitia luxu ac fastu refertæ, & conditionis Israelitarum miseræ quidem & abjectæ, attamen melioris : quia habebant verum Deum, & promissionem de regno Canaan & de venturo Messia, inque ipso spe fundata vitæ æternæ. Quis non præferet hæc istis? &c.
units.tr: I. From what is honourable and pious. This is to be shown by a comparison of the court of Pharaoh, filled with idolatry, injustice, luxury and pride, with the condition of the Israelites, which was indeed wretched and abject, yet better: because they had the true God, and the promise concerning the kingdom of Canaan and the coming Messiah, and in him was founded the hope of eternal life. Who would not prefer these things to those? etc.

units.la: II. A difficili: videl. pulchrum hoc quidem, verùm arduum: Hic 1. contendat aulæ delicias ac magnificentiam & spem successionis in regno lautissimo, & miseriam ac contemtū Israelitarum 2. virtutis esse dicat niti perardua, spernere voluptates; ac fidei: spectare non præsentia, sed futura. Illustret exemplis sacris profanis, illorum, qui nihil difficile putarunt, quod honestum.
units.tr: II. From what is difficult: namely, that this is indeed noble, but arduous. Here he should, first, set out the delights and magnificence of the court and the hope of succession to a most sumptuous kingdom, and the misery and contempt of the Israelites; second, he should say that virtue requires strenuous effort and the spurning of pleasures, and faith requires looking not at present things but at future ones. Let him illustrate this with examples, sacred and profane, of those who thought nothing difficult that was honourable.

units.la: III. Ab utili. Hic 1. concedat, ipsum variis incommodis se objecisse, quæ exponendæ: 2. Opponat vera commoda, non tantum temporalia, cum liberator, dux, Legislator Israelitarum factus; sed æterna præsertim, quòd Deo charus, dictator veluti perpetuus per Legem latam, & hæres cœli factus. Quàm breve gaudium Pharaonis, huic felicitati collatum.
units.tr: III. From what is useful. Here he should, first, concede that Moses exposed himself to various inconveniences, which are to be set out; second, he should set against them the true advantages, not merely temporal ones, since he became the liberator, leader and lawgiver of the Israelites, but especially eternal ones, in that he was dear to God, became a perpetual dictator, as it were, through the Law he gave, and an heir of heaven. How brief was the joy of Pharaoh, compared with this happiness!

units.la: Concluf. Prædicet Mosis fidem & constantiam, & ad ejus imitationem cohortetur.
units.tr: Concluf. He should commend the faith and constancy of Moses, and exhort his hearers to imitate him.

units.la: IX. VITUPERATIO FACTI MARCI CATONIS, CUM COGNITA CÆSARIS VICTORIA MORTEM SIBI INTULIT.
units.tr: IX. The blame of the deed of Marcus Cato, who, when he learned of Caesar's victory, brought death upon himself.

units.la: Vide Flor. lib. 4. c. 2.
units.tr: See Florus, book 4, chapter 2.

units.la: Exord. A periculo, si vitia sub specie virtutis obrepant. Probetur: quia tunc non solùm non vituperari, sed & laudari, & ab aliis patrari consueverint. Applicetur tum in genere ad virtutes gentilium, quas proinde splendida vitia dixerit Augustinus; tum in specie ad factum hoc Catonis: quod proinde breviter referatur, & malè laudari à Cicerone Floro aliisque dicatur. Propof. Tibi vero omni ratione vituperandum videri, tanquam pie-tati ac honestati contrarium.
units.tr: Exordium. There is danger when vices creep in under the appearance of virtue. This is proved, because such things are usually not only not blamed but even praised and committed by others. It is applied in general to the virtues of the Gentiles, which Augustine therefore called splendid vices; and in particular to this deed of Cato, which is therefore briefly related, and said to have been wrongly praised by Cicero, Florus and others. Proposition. But to you it ought to seem in every way deserving of blame, as contrary to piety and honesty.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. Ab impio: quia est contra Deum vitæ & stationis nostræ autorem. vide Cic. in Somnio Scipionis. Illustretur simili à milite in custodia constituto, cui deserere illam non licet.
units.tr: I. From the impious: because it is against God, the author of our life and of our station. See Cicero in the Dream of Scipio. Let it be illustrated by a simile of a soldier posted on guard, who is not permitted to desert his post.

units.la: II. Ab inhonesto, quia contra officium boni ducis, qui deserere exercitum non debet, uti hic fecit Cato. vide Florum. 1. contra fortitudinem, quæ vincere animum docet & terribilem esse hostibus, non sibi. 3. ex philautia profectum, qua turpe sibi putabat, venire supplicem ad Cæsarem. Hic per apostrophum urgenda ipsius conscientia, non ex pusillanimitate, ex mœrore & desperatione & vana gloria manus sibi intulerit, ut fortis videretur posteris.
units.tr: II. From the dishonourable: because it is contrary to the duty of a good commander, who ought not to desert his army, as Cato did here. See Florus, book 1, against fortitude, which teaches a man to conquer his own spirit and to be terrible to enemies, not to himself. Third, it arose from self-love, by which he thought it shameful to come as a suppliant to Caesar. Here, by an apostrophe, his own conscience is to be pressed: that he did not lay hands on himself out of pusillanimity, but out of grief, despair and vainglory, so that he might appear brave to posterity.

units.la: III. Ab inutili: quia sic prodidit causam & copias sibi commissas; prodidit patriam, pro qua pugnare usque ad mortem debuisset. Nec enim jam tum perditam fuisse. Illustretur comparatione illorum, qui pro patria fortiter morti se objecere & occubuere, ut Regulus, Fabii, Horatii &c. cum ipse contra veluti transfuga causam prodiderit.
units.tr: III. From the useless: because in this way he betrayed the cause and the forces entrusted to him; he betrayed his country, for which he ought to have fought even unto death. For the cause was not yet lost at that time. Let it be illustrated by a comparison with those who bravely offered themselves to death for their country and fell, such as Regulus, the Fabii, Horatius, etc., whereas he himself, like a deserter, betrayed the cause.

units.la: Concluf. Detestetur 1. factum hoc. 2. perniciosum dogma Stoicorum, qui autocheiriam impie probabant.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him detest first this deed, and second the pernicious doctrine of the Stoics, who impiously approved self-slaughter.

units.la: X. LAUS FACTI ABRAHAMI FILIUM DEO OBLATURI. Gen. 22.
units.tr: X. THE PRAISE OF THE DEED OF ABRAHAM, WHO WAS ABOUT TO OFFER HIS SON TO GOD. Gen. 22.

units.la: Exord. Ab encomio fidei, ex dicto 1. Joh. 5:4. Fides nostra victoria est, quæ vicit mundum. Hoc 1. proponatur cum encomio & illustretur paraphrasi. 2. Probetur ratione: quia fides unice inhæret divinæ promissioni, 3. Illustretur exemplis ex cap. 11. Heb. & nominatim Abrahami facto hoc.
units.tr: Exordium. From the praise of faith, from the saying in 1 John 5:4: "Our faith is the victory which has overcome the world." This is to be set forth first with praise and illustrated with a paraphrase; secondly, it is to be proved by reason, because faith clings solely to the divine promise; thirdly, it is to be illustrated by examples from Hebrews 11, and especially by this deed of Abraham.

units.la: Propof. Hoc proinde debitis laudibus evehendum, ut imitemur fidem ejus.
units.tr: Propositio. Therefore this must be raised up with due praises, so that we may imitate his faith.

units.la: Confirm. I. A difficultate facti hujus: Primò ex consideratione filii, 1. quia filius unicus. 2. Singulariter dilectus. 3. Serò tandem multis precibus obtentus. 4. Innocens. 5. Fundamentum omnium promissionum divinarum: quippe unde ampla posteritas, & ipse MesMessias oriturus erat. O igitur robustam fidem, quæ hæc obstacu- la superavit. Secundo ex consideratione facti: quod mactandus, immolandus; idque inscia matre, in deserto, manibus ipsius parentis tanquam parricidæ & tigride immanioris. Tertio ex consideratione Dei: qui videri poterat crudelis, sibi contrarius, forte alius, spiritus illusor. At superavit hæc omnia fides victrix mundi, sui ipsius, imo Dei tentantis.
units.tr: Confirmatio. I. From the difficulty of this deed. First, from consideration of the son: (1) because he was an only son; (2) he was singularly loved; (3) he had at last been obtained late, after many prayers; (4) he was innocent; (5) he was the foundation of all the divine promises, since from him came a great posterity, and the Messiah himself was to arise. O what a robust faith, which overcame these obstacles! Secondly, from consideration of the deed: that he was to be slain and sacrificed, and this without the knowledge of his mother, in the wilderness, by the hands of his own father, like a parricide and more savage than a tigress. Thirdly, from consideration of God: who could seem cruel, contrary to himself, perhaps another spirit, a deceiver of spirits. Yet faith, the conqueror of the world, overcame all these things, and even its own self, indeed God himself who was testing him.

units.la: II. A præstantia: quòd non carni aut propriis affectibus sed soli Deo obsecutus sit: qui Dominus vitæ & bonorum solus meretur obsequiū. Illustretur comparatione cum aliis dominis: si illis; multo magis Deo parem, Confer exempla Noachi, Moisis &c.
units.tr: II. From its excellence: that he obeyed not the flesh or his own affections, but God alone, who alone deserves the obedience of the Lord of life and of all goods. Let it be illustrated by comparison with other lords: if obedience is owed to them, much more is it owed to God, who is equal to none. Compare the examples of Noah, Moses, etc.

units.la: III. Ab utilitate: 1. Sic probatus fuit Abraham. 2. Recepit filium majori cum lætitia. 3, Ampliores accepit promissiones & pater credentium factus.
units.tr: III. From its usefulness: (1) Abraham was thus proved; (2) he received back his son with greater joy; (3) he received greater promises and became the father of believers.

units.la: Conclusio. Merito proinde hanc fidem prædicandam & fidelibus omnibus, tanquam exemplar, imitandam.
units.tr: Conclusio. Therefore this faith deservedly is to be proclaimed and, as an example, to be imitated by all the faithful.

units.la: XI. LAUS FACTI IMPERATORIS JUSTINIANI IN EMENDATIONE LEGUM ROMANARUM.
units.tr: XI. PRAISE OF THE DEED OF THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN IN THE EMENDATION OF THE ROMAN LAWS.

units.la: Exord. A dicto Imperii Justiniani: Imperatoriam majestatem non solùm armis decoratam, sed & Legibus oportet esse armatam. Additur ratio ab officio imperatoris tempore belli & pacis. Illustretur a contrario alterutrius defectu. Concludatur, merito igitur & Justinianum initio imperii emendando juri operam impendisse.
units.tr: Exordium. From the saying of Justinian's rule: the imperial majesty ought to be adorned not only with arms but also armed with laws. The reason is added from the duty of an emperor in time of war and in time of peace. Let it be illustrated from the lack of each of the two. Let it be concluded that Justinian rightly devoted effort at the beginning of his reign to emending the law.

units.la: Propos. Hoc ipsius institutum perpetuis laudibus dignum & prædicandum esse.
units.tr: Proposition. That this undertaking of his is worthy of, and ought to be proclaimed with, perpetual praise.

units.la: Confirm. I. A necessario: quod probetur 1. a juris usque ad illa tempora confusione & contrarietate: dū tot leges, Edicta, Senatus Consulta, plebiscita, Principum placita & Responsaprudentum, sibi invicem contrariebantur. 2. a conatu Julii Cæsaris, Gregorii & Hermogenis, tandemque Theodosii; qui irrito conatu opus illud tentarunt. Hoc tandem Justinianus perficiendum judicavit. Illustretur ex Loco Communi de legum necessitate, & periculosa earundem dissonantia.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From necessity: which is proved (1) from the confusion and contrariety of the law up to those times, when so many laws, edicts, decrees of the Senate, plebiscites, decisions of the princes and opinions of the jurists contradicted one another; (2) from the attempts of Julius Caesar, of Gregory and Hermogenes, and finally of Theodosius, who tried that work in vain. Justinian at last judged that this had to be carried through. Let it be illustrated from the common topic on the necessity of laws and the perilous discord among them.

units.la: II. A difficili. Probetur 1. à ruinosa legum antiquitate, quæ inde a temporibus Romuli requirendæ fuere, 2. à multiplici illarum mutamutatione facta a diversis, indeque nata pugnantia, quae concilianda fuit. 1. à multitudine librorum 2000. scilicet, ex quibus leges eruendae fuere. Exaggeretur a brevitate temporis, quo omnia confecta: videlicet spacio 5. annorum & a causa instrumentali, Triboniano scilicet una cum 16. solummodo JCtis.
units.tr: II. From difficulty. Let it be proved (1) from the ruinous antiquity of the laws, which had to be sought out from the times of Romulus onward; (2) from the manifold changes made to them by various men, and the resulting conflicts, which had to be reconciled. (1) from the multitude of books, namely two thousand, from which the laws had to be extracted. Let it be magnified by the brevity of time in which everything was completed, namely a span of five years, and by the instrumental cause, namely Tribonian together with only sixteen jurists.

units.la: III. A pulcherrimo ordine & harmonia; dum 50. digestorum libris omne jus vetus; 12. libris Cod. omnes principum constitutiones complexus est, & brevissima arte omnia comprehendit quatuor Institutionum libris, & quidem ita, ut nihil dissonum, nihil frustraneum aut iteratum. Exaggerentur omnia 1 ab effectis, quod hic omnia jura, antiquitates, ipsaque Latinitas vindicata ab interitu. 2. Comparatione studiorum bellicorum, quae longe inferiora. vid. Orat. pro Marcello.
units.tr: III. From the most beautiful order and harmony, since in fifty books of the Digest he embraced all the old law, in twelve books of the Code all the constitutions of the princes, and in four books of the Institutes he comprehended everything with the briefest art, and indeed in such a way that nothing is discordant, nothing superfluous or repeated. Let all these things be magnified (1) from their effects, since here all the laws, antiquities, and Latinity itself were rescued from destruction; (2) by comparison with the studies of war, which are far inferior. See the Oration for Marcellus.

units.la: Concluf. Desinat in laudes Justiniani, & veluti perpetuum juris dictatorem inter tot gentes hodieque illum extollat.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let it end in praises of Justinian, and let it extol him, as the perpetual lawgiver, among so many nations even today.

units.la: XII. LAUS FACTI ALEXANDRI MAGNI.
units.tr: XII. THE PRAISE OF ALEXANDER THE GREAT'S DEED.

units.la: Quo victor virgines regias excellentis formae, ut ait Curtius, tam sanctè habuit, quam si eodem, quo ipse, patre genitae forent. vide Curt. lib. 3. cap. 12.
units.tr: By this victory he treated the royal virgins, who were of outstanding beauty, as Curtius says, so chastely that it was as if they had been born of the same father as himself. See Curt. book 3, chapter 12.

units.la: Exord. A dicto Livii, lib. 1. initio: hoc est illud eximium, omnis ævi documenta intueri: unde quid tibi, quid Reip. utile capere liceat. Hoc 1. proponatur. 2. explicetur: videl. indigitari structum historiae, &c. 3. Verissimè: historiam enim esse speculum; cum veteres illi nobis in exemplum vixerint.
units.tr: Exordium. Taking his cue from the saying of Livy at the beginning of book 1: this is that outstanding benefit, to look upon the examples of every age, and from them to take whatever may be useful to you and to the Commonwealth. (1) Let this be proposed. (2) Let it be explained, namely, that the framework of history is pointed out, etc. (3) Most truly: for history is a mirror, since those ancients lived as an example for us.

units.la: Propofit. Hinc in praesentiarum factum illud Alexandri repraesentandum & commendandum esse, ut cupiditatum juvenilium continentiam inde discamus.
units.tr: Proposition. Hence it is at present to be set forth and commended, that deed of Alexander's, so that we may learn from it restraint of youthful desires.

units.la: Tractatio. 1. Paucis referat rem ex Curtio.
units.tr: Treatment. (1) Let him briefly relate the matter from Curtius.

units.la: II. Extollat illud 1. ab excellentia virtutis continentiae: quippe quae cohibet affectus vehementissimos irae, ambitionis, libidinis: quartum exponat, primo vehementiam, secundo, contrariam virtutis, quae tantos aestus cohibet intra terminos. Vide Ethicam & Locos Communes. Tertio comparet cum aliis virtutibus, fortitudine & justitia, tanquam minus arduis: quia facilius est minis resistere, quam blanditiis; uti postea apparuit in ipso Alexanlexandro. Sed quanto fortior, tantò felicior hîc fuisti Alexander &c.
units.tr: II. Let him extol it, first, for the excellence of the virtue of continence, since it restrains the most violent passions of anger, ambition and lust. Let him then set out, first, the violence of these passions and, second, the opposing virtue, which holds such fervour within its limits. See the Ethics and the Common Places. Third, let him compare it with other virtues, fortitude and justice, as less demanding, because it is easier to resist threats than flattery, as later appeared in Alexander himself. But the stronger you were, Alexander, the happier you were here, etc.

units.la: 2. Exaggeret factum hoc a. à personaAlexandri, qui juvenis, victor: Quàm insolens est victoria, quàm ferociens juventus &c, Sed vicisti Alexander fervorem juventæ, & ipsam victoriam. b. a conditione foeminarum, quae reginae erant, pulcherrimae, in victoris potestate. Quis verò hodie inter milites Christianos tali continentia; quis non potius crudelitate & libidine in subjectas grassatur? &c. Illustret porrò comparatione aliorum, & hoisce superasse Alexandrum ostendat. Vide Val. Max. lib.6. c.1. & lib.4. c.1. &c.
units.tr: (2) Let him amplify this deed: (a) from the person of Alexander, who was young and victorious. How insolent victory is, how wild youth is, etc. But you conquered, Alexander, both the ardour of youth and victory itself. (b) From the condition of the women, who were queens, most beautiful, and in the victor's power. Who among Christian soldiers today shows such continence? Who does not rather rage against the conquered with cruelty and lust? etc. Let him further illustrate this by comparison with others, and show that Alexander surpassed them in this. See Val. Max. book 6, chapter 1, and book 4, chapter 1, etc.

units.la: Conclus. Optet ut non principes modò, sed & privati, juvenes, senes, talia exempla imitentur. Hunc enim esse fructum historiarum & monumentorum veterum.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him wish that not only princes but also private persons, young and old, may imitate such examples, for this is the fruit of histories and the ancient records.

units.la: XIII. LAUS FACTI MILTIADIS DUCIS ATHENIENSIUM. quo cum 10. millibus 600. mille Persarum fudit.
units.tr: XIII. THE PRAISE OF THE DEED OF MILTIADES, GENERAL OF THE ATHENIANS, BY WHOM WITH 10,000 MEN HE PUT TO FLIGHT 600,000 PERSIANS.

units.la: Exord. A laude nationis Graecae, tum ob literarum cultum, tum ob virtutem belli: quibus ista natio omnibus aliis palmam praeripuit. Alias enim singulis, Graecos omnibus virtutibus excelluisse:
units.tr: Exordium. The praise of the Greek nation, both for its cultivation of letters and for its courage in war, in which this nation surpassed all others. For while each of the others excelled in single virtues, the Greeks excelled in all of them.

units.la: Propos. In praesentiarum factum Miltiadis clarissimum considerandum, ut quid patriae quisque debeat, inde pateat.
units.tr: Proposition. At present the most famous deed of Miltiades is to be considered, so that it may become clear from this what each person owes to his country.

units.la: Narratio. Factum referat ex Justin. 1. 2. c.9.
units.tr: Narration. Let him relate the deed from Justin, book 2, chapter 9.

units.la: Tractatio. Praedicet illud
units.tr: Treatment. Let him set forth that deed:

units.la: I. A necessitate: quòd non provocarit hostem temere; sed incumbentem patriae tantis copiis nec metuerit. Hanc scilicet naturam esse verae fortitudinis. &c.
units.tr: I. From necessity: because he did not rashly provoke the enemy, but did not fear even though such great forces were bearing down upon his country. Clearly this is the nature of true fortitude, etc.

units.la: II. A difficultate 1. quod tantillis copiis tantam multitudinem aggressus, 2. Quod impeditis religione Lacedaemoniis non trepidarit. Scilicet virtus per ardua nititur.
units.tr: II. From difficulty: (1) because he attacked so great a multitude with so tiny a force; (2) because, with the Lacedaemonians hindered by religious scruple, he did not lose heart. Clearly virtue strives through difficult things.

units.la: III. Ab honestate: 1. quia pro patria; quae iniquo bello petebatur, quid justius? 2. Quia non invito, sed alacri animo factum. Vide Justinum.
units.tr: III. From honour: (1) because he fought for his country, and what could be more just than a war waged against an unjust attack? (2) because he acted not reluctantly but with a willing spirit. See Justin.

units.la: IV. Ab utilitate: quòd sic fugati Persae, & primus impetus Darii factus, & secuta morte Darii Graecia à tanto bello liberata fuit.
units.tr: IV. From usefulness: because the Persians were so put to flight, and the first assault of Darius was made, and after Darius's death Greece was freed from so great a war.

units.la: Conclus. Ingeminet istius facti laudes, & similes civibus optet animos contra alieni invasores.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him repeat the praises of that deed, and wish that citizens may have similar spirits against the invaders of foreign lands.

units.la: XIV. VITUPERIUM ET DETESTATIO TENTATÆ PRODITIONIS a Bruti liberis.
units.tr: XIV. Censure and detestation of the attempted betrayal, in the speech against the sons of Brutus.

units.la: Exord. Verissimam dicat Orationem Bruti, & consule dignam. Ratio 1. quid enim melius, quid suavius libertate. 2. Quid dignum magis consule, quàm consulere dignitati ac saluti reip. quæ in sola licertate ejusque custodia est.
units.tr: Exord. He says that Brutus's speech is most true and worthy of a consul. Reasons: (1) for what is better or sweeter than liberty? (2) What is more worthy of a consul than to consult the dignity and safety of the commonwealth, which lies in liberty alone and in its preservation?

units.la: Propos. Quò magis detestanda machinatio maleferiatorum, imò tuorum, Brute, liberorum, qui de prodenda Tarquiniis urbe consilia agitant.
units.tr: Propos. All the more detestable is the plotting of the wicked men, indeed of your sons, Brutus, who are planning to betray the city to the Tarquins.

units.la: Confirmatio. I. Exaggeret crimen 1. tanquam turpissimum: a. ægenere.
units.tr: Confirmatio. I. Let him magnify the crime: (1) as most shameful: (a) from the kind of crime,

units.la: 1. criminis, quòd sit proditio patriæ. Exaggeret hîc a. proditionem, comparatione cum aliis sceleribus tanquam levioribus. β. Proditionem patriæ, quæ charissima esse debet. b. à personis proditorum: quod juvenes, patricii, bene educati, exemplo parentis rectius edocti. Deinde a persona cui? scilicet tyranno superbissimo, ob scelera foedissima ejecto. c. a causa impellente: quæ nulla alia, quàm licentia libidinis, luxus & scelerum sub tyranno. Orem auditu foedam, &c. d. à causa prohibente, lege sanctissima, qua ejurata est regia dominatio.
units.tr: (1) because it is a betrayal of the fatherland. Here he magnifies (a) the betrayal, by comparison with other crimes, as lighter ones; (β) the betrayal of the fatherland, which ought to be most dear. (b) From the persons of the traitors: that they are young men, patricians, well brought up, and more rightly taught by the example of a parent. Next, from the person to whom they betray it, namely a most arrogant tyrant, cast out for most foul crimes. (c) From the impelling cause: which is none other than the licence of lust, luxury and crimes under a tyrant. He calls it a thing foul to hear, etc. (d) From the forbidding cause, the most sacred law, by which regal domination was abjured.

units.la: 2. Tanquam nocentissimum. a. Ob futuram sævitiem tyranni reducis, quem grassaturum dicat in fortunas, pudicitiam, vitam omnium, etiam proximorum, ipsiusque parentis Bruti. Hæc non movisse juvenes feroces &c. b. Ob servitutem reip. perpetuam, si Tarquinii reversi fuerint. Ita scilicet lucturam patriam innoxiam.
units.tr: (2) As most harmful. (a) On account of the future cruelty of the returning tyrant, whom he says will rage against the fortunes, chastity and lives of all, even of their own kin, and of Brutus their very father. That these fierce young men were not moved by these things, etc. (b) On account of the perpetual servitude of the commonwealth, if the Tarquins should return. Thus, of course, the innocent fatherland would be made to suffer.

units.la: II. Convincat facti nefarii juvenes per apostrophen.
units.tr: II. Let him convict the guilty young men of the wicked deed by apostrophe.

units.la: 1. Ex clandestinis cum legatis Tarquinii colloquiis.
units.tr: (1) From the secret conversations with the envoys of Tarquin.

units.la: 2. Ex interceptis literis. Quid horum negare poteritis? &c.
units.tr: (2) From the intercepted letters. Which of these things will you be able to deny? etc.

units.la: Conclus. Avertat Orat. ad Patrem Brutum, & nefarii facti vindictam justam ipsi committat, si majorem patriæ & officii, quàm liberorum habeat.
units.tr: Conclus. Let him turn the speech to the father Brutus, and commit to him the just vengeance for the wicked deed, if he holds the duty to the fatherland and to office greater than that owed to his sons.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: LAUS FACTI, QUO BRUTUS ET COMPLICES JULIUM CÆSAREM OCCIDERUNT.
units.tr: PRAISE OF THE DEED BY WHICH BRUTUS AND HIS ACCOMPLICES KILLED JULIUS CAESAR

units.la: Exord. Ex abrupto per apostrophen ad Brutum: videl, vindicasti tandem oppressam libertatem, sustulisti tyrannum: Amplif. ab enumeratione incommodorum ex oppressione reip. emanantium. scilicet prostratæ libertatis, concultatæ autoritatis Senatus, magistratum, legum, &c.
units.tr: Exordium. Abruptly, by apostrophe to Brutus: you have at last avenged oppressed liberty and removed the tyrant. Amplification from the enumeration of the evils flowing from the oppression of the commonwealth: namely, liberty trodden down, the authority of the Senate shaken, the magistrates, the laws, and so on.

units.la: Propos. Quæ digna tibi laus, quæ par tibi gratia referri potest ?
units.tr: Proposition. What praise can be paid to you, what thanks can match you?

units.la: Confirm. I. A justo: 1. quia Cæsar tyrannus fuit. Hic exponatur qua vi, qua arte invaserit imperium, ita ut in omnibus iniquitas elucescat. Quis ergo juste interfectum negabit? Addatur ratio seu major. Quia tyrannum licet occidere. Vid. Locum Communem & Politicos. 2. Quia à Senatu hostis declaratus, & aperto Marte adversus Cæsarem pugnatum fuerat. Jam adversus hostem æterna autoritas est. 3. Quia omnem potestatem ad se trahebat, relicta tantum umbra veteris reip. Atqui patriæ assertio licita est omnibus. 4. Quia Brutus & socii non privati, sed ex Senatu fuere. Quis igitur vindex reip. nisi illi? &c.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From what is just: (1) because Caesar was a tyrant. Here let it be set out by what force and what craft he seized power, so that his wickedness shines forth in every respect. Who, then, will deny that he was justly killed? Add the reason, or major premise: that it is lawful to kill a tyrant. See the common place and the political writers. (2) Because he was declared an enemy by the Senate, and war was waged against Caesar in open battle. Now there is eternal authority against an enemy. (3) Because he drew all power to himself, leaving only the shadow of the old commonwealth. But the defence of the fatherland is lawful for all. (4) Because Brutus and his companions were not private persons but members of the Senate. Who, then, was the avenger of the commonwealth if not they? And so on.

units.la: II. Ab utili:quod probetur 1. quia sic restituta libertas, qua nullum majus bonum: pro qua omnia egerunt semper viri cordati.
