Adducatur Locus Communis de libertatis defensione & illustretur a contraria servitutis fœditate, in quam imperans regibus respubl. prolapsa erat. 2. Quia sine bello, idque in uno capite liberata fuit a tyranno patria. Illustretur à periculo, si justo bello aggrediendus fuisset Cæsar. Potius in uno capite expiandum nefas.
units.tr: II. From what is useful; this is proved (1) because thus liberty was restored, which is no greater good, and for which men of sound judgement have always acted. Let the common place on the defence of liberty be brought in and illustrated by the contrary foulness of slavery, into which the commonwealth, once ruled by kings, had fallen. (2) Because the fatherland was freed from a tyrant without war, and that by the removal of a single head. Let it be illustrated by the danger there would have been had Caesar to be attacked in a just war. Rather, a crime is to be atoned for in one head.

units.la: III. Ab exemplis illorum, qui tyrannos occiderunt: uti Ehud qui Eglonem regem Moabitarum trucidavit. Judic.3. &c. Arbacis & Phulbelochi, qui Nabucodonozarę, &c. Atheniensium, aliorum qui præmium tyrannicidis constituerunt. Et iniquum esset Bruto quod aliis laudabile? &c.
units.tr: III. From the examples of those who killed tyrants: such as Ehud, who slew Eglon, king of the Moabites (Judges 3, etc.); of Arbaces and Phulbelochus, who [overthrew] Nebuchadnezzar, and so on; of the Athenians, and of others who set a reward for the killers of tyrants. And would it be unfair for Brutus what is praiseworthy for others? And so on.

units.la: Conclus. Prædicet ipsum tanquam tyrannicidam, libertatis vindicem, & ultorem Romanorum.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him be proclaimed as a tyrant-slayer, the champion of liberty, and the avenger of the Romans.

units.la: XVI. VITUPERATIO EJUSDEM FACTI.
units.tr: XVI. Censure of the same deed.

units.la: Exord.Itidem ex abrupto ab ipsa propositione. Et inventus tandé est, qui pessimum factum laudare audeat,&c. Amplificetur recensione facti hujus pathetica.
units.tr: Exordium. Likewise, abruptly from the proposition itself: "And at last someone has been found who dares to praise the most wicked deed," etc. Let the deed be amplified by a moving recital of it.

units.la: Tractatio factum detestetur
units.tr: Tractatio: let him detest the deed.

units.la: I. Ab injusto; quia non tyrannicidium, sed parricidium est.
units.tr: I. From its injustice: because it was not a tyrannicide but a parricide.

units.la: 1. Ratio : à persona Cæsaris : licet enim armis primò oppresserit remp. Cæsar, tamen a. deinceps recognitus est princeps à Senatu populoque Rom. Illustretur ex Loco Communi de inviolabili semper majestate, & fœditate rebellionis eorum qui se opponunt. b. Clemens fuit & benignus erga omnes: ipsos etiam adversarios & bene meritos de rep.
units.tr: 1. Argument from the person of Caesar: for although Caesar first oppressed the republic by arms, nevertheless a. he was afterwards acknowledged as prince by the Senate and the Roman people. Let this be illustrated from the common place concerning the always inviolable majesty of rulers and the foulness of rebellion in those who set themselves against them. b. He was merciful and kind toward all, even toward his adversaries and those who had deserved well of the republic.

units.la: 2. A persona percussorum: qui privati, non senatus consilio egerunt. At privati non habent jus gladii, multò minus adversus principem. Quis dubitet igitur parricidas fuisse pessimos. &c. Exaggeretur comparatione illius, qui Saulem moribundum & petentem occidit, qui parricida judicatus fuit à Davide: quanto magis Brutus hic. Refellat hinc argumentum I.
units.tr: 2. From the person of the assassins: they acted as private individuals, not on the counsel of the Senate. But private persons have no right of the sword, much less against a prince. Who then could doubt that they were the most wicked parricides, etc.? Let this be amplified by comparison with the man who slew Saul as he lay dying and begging for death, and who was judged a parricide by David: how much more so is this Brutus. Let him refute the first argument with this.

units.la: II. A detrimento so: quia
units.tr: II. From the harm to the commonwealth: because

units.la: 1. Ita minimè restituta libertas; sed major ac perpetua attracta servitus sub Augusto & Tiberio. &c.
units.tr: 1. Liberty was in no way restored; rather a greater and perpetual servitude was brought upon the state under Augustus and Tiberius, etc.

units.la: 2. Turbata publica pax ac tranquillitas & invectus triumviratus nocentissimus. Hasce clades exaggeret ex historia; & quamlibet etiam iniquam pacem justo bello meliorem asserat.
units.tr: 2. Public peace and tranquillity were disturbed, and the most harmful triumvirate was introduced. Let him amplify these calamities from history, and let him assert that even an unjust peace is better than a just war.

units.la: III. A justa nemesi divina: qua Brutus, Cassius, reliqui conjurati plerique eodem pugione quo Cæsarem occiderant, ceciderunt. Exaggeretur ex Loco Communi de conscientia scelerum. Vide Orat. in Pison.
units.tr: III. From the just retribution of God: by which Brutus, Cassius, and most of the other conspirators perished by the same dagger with which they had slain Caesar. Let this be amplified from the common place concerning the conscience of crimes. See the Oration against Piso.

units.la: Conclus. Factum detestetur tanquam justitiæ ac saluti reip. ipsique Deo adversum; meritoque autoribus ipsis perniciosum.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him detest the deed as contrary to justice, to the safety of the commonwealth, and to God himself, and as rightly ruinous to its very authors.

units.la: DISPOSITIONES ORATORIÆ.
units.tr: DISPOSITIONES ORATORIAE.

units.la: IN GENERE DELIBERATIVO. THEMA I. CONSULTATIO DE BELLO PUNICO SUSCIPIENDO.
units.tr: ON THE DELIBERATIVE KIND. THEME I. A CONSULTATION ON UNDERTAKING THE PUNIC WAR.

units.la: Ex Liv. lib. 21,
units.tr: From Livy, book 21,

units.la: I. Saguntini Romam mittunt petitum auxilium.
units.tr: I. The Saguntines send to Rome to request aid.

units.la: Exord. Excusationem habeat molestiarum. videl. quamquam hoc egerint semper Saguntini, ut utiles potius, quam oneri. Esse sociis Romanis, tamen præsente necessitatem aliud imperare: Amplif. a fine societatum, quæ est mutuum adjumentum & auxilium.
units.tr: Exordium. Let him begin with an apology for the trouble: namely, although the Saguntines have always aimed to be useful rather than a burden, the Romans being allies, nevertheless the present necessity commands something else. Amplification from the purpose of alliances, which is mutual help and assistance.

units.la: Narratio. Exponat 1. adventum ducis juvenis Hannibalis in Hispaniam: cujus ingenium paucis describat ex Livio. 2. invasionem in fines Olcadum transiberum, ac deditionem gentium transiberanorum exceptis Saguntinis, 3. Præsens periculum belli, ni Romani auxilio sint.
units.tr: Narration. Let him set out: 1. the arrival of the young leader Hannibal in Spain, whose character he should describe briefly from Livy; 2. his invasion of the territory of the Olcades beyond the Tagus, and the surrender of the peoples beyond the Tagus, except the Saguntines; 3. the present danger of war, unless the Romans give aid.

units.la: Propos. Petat auxilium vel per legationem vel per arma.
units.tr: Proposition. Let him ask for aid, either by an embassy or by arms.

units.la: Confirm. I. A justo, propter fœdus cum Saguntinis: unde auxilium ipsis ferre teneantur exemplo majorum suorum: illustretur ex Loco Communi de causa belli, si pugnandum profociis.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From what is just, on account of the treaty with the Saguntines, whereby they are bound to bring aid to them, following the example of their ancestors; let this be illustrated from the common topic concerning the cause of war, whether war is to be waged on behalf of allies.

units.la: II. A necessario: quia imminet ipsis periculum, quod astruat tum à feroci natura Annibalis, tum ab exemplo vicinorum subactorum, tum ab imparibus viribus Saguntinorum contra copias Annibalis.
units.tr: II. From necessity: because danger threatens them, which he shows both from the fierce nature of Hannibal, from the example of neighbouring peoples already subdued, and from the unequal strength of the Saguntines against the forces of Hannibal.

units.la: III. A facili: quoniam 1. terribiles Pœnis Romani ob memoriam superioris belli, 2. juvenis Hannibal, qui cedet si serio rem agi videat. Sperasse impunitatem juvenem ferocem & juris ac fœderum nescium.
units.tr: III. From ease: since 1. the Romans are dreaded by the Carthaginians on account of the memory of the previous war, and 2. the young Hannibal will give way if he sees the matter taken up in earnest. He had hoped for impunity, being a fierce young man ignorant of law and treaties.

units.la: Conclus. Petat, ut pro sua prudentia statuant Romani quid facto opus, urgeatque festinationem.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him ask that the Romans, in their wisdom, decide what must be done, and let him press for haste.

units.la: EVENTUS.
units.tr: Outcome.

units.la: Decreta fuit legatio ad res sociorum inspiciendas; quibus si videretur digna causa, Annibali denunciarent, ut abstineret à Saguntinis & in Africam trajiceret: & Saguntinorum querimonias deferrent ad Remp.
units.tr: A commission was decreed to inquire into the affairs of the allies; if they judged the cause worthy, they were to denounce to Hannibal that he should refrain from Saguntum and cross into Africa; and they were to carry the complaints of the Saguntines to the state.

units.la: II. Legati Saguntini de oppugnatione urbis interea certiores facti, illud Senatui exponunt.
units.tr: II. The Saguntine envoys, meanwhile informed of the siege of the city, set this before the Senate.

units.la: I. Repetunt gratiarum actionem pro decreta legatione: id quod & Dominis suis renunciaverint: & exponant quid de oppugnatione Sagunti interea acceperint, exhibitis simul literis Senatus Saguntini.
units.tr: I. They repeat their thanks for the commission decreed; which they have also reported to their masters; and they set out what they have learned in the meantime about the siege of Saguntum, showing at the same time the letters of the Saguntine Senate.

units.la: II. Explicent justum metum suum, ne Annibal succeßu ferociens Legatos repudiet aut extrahat, donec urbem subegerit.
units.tr: II. They explain their just fear, lest Hannibal, growing proud in his success, should reject the envoys or delay them until he has subdued the city.

units.la: III. Petant ut quàm ocissimè unâ cum Legatis copiæ transmittantur. Addito 1. certos se esse, Saguntinos extrema passuros antequam dedant se hosti. 2. Ea esse urbis munimenta, ut impetum per aliquod tempus sustinere valeant. 3. sperare se visis Aquilis Romanis & serio rem geri, hæsiturum Annibalem; utpote qui sine Senatus Carthaginensis consensu violare pacem cum Romanis non sit ausurus.
units.tr: III. They ask that troops be sent across with the envoys as quickly as possible. Adding: (1) that they are certain the Saguntines will suffer the utmost before they surrender to the enemy; (2) that the city's defences are such that it can withstand the assault for some time; (3) that they hope, now that the Roman eagles are seen and the matter is being pursued in earnest, Hannibal will hold back, since he would not dare to violate the peace with the Romans without the consent of the Carthaginian Senate.

units.la: IV. Repetant petitum: addito, interesse gloriæ Romanorum, ut socii non derelicti videantur.
units.tr: IV. They repeat their request, adding that it concerns the glory of the Romans that the allies should not seem abandoned.

units.la: III. Senatus Romanus it in suffragia, & primus Senator cum sequacibus censet in Hispania & Africa terra marique rem gerendam.
units.tr: III. The Roman Senate goes to a vote, and the first senator, with his followers, proposes that war be waged in Spain and Africa, by land and by sea.

units.la: Exordium. A præsenti rerum statu, ubi non prolixis deliberationibus, sed manu res gerenda videatur. Hinc breviter repræsentet, quo loco res sint Saguntinorum.
units.tr: Exordium. From the present state of affairs, where the matter seems to call for action by hand rather than for lengthy deliberation. Hence he briefly sets out the situation of the Saguntines.

units.la: Propos. Consulibus decernendam Hispaniam pariter & Africam, & terra marique gerendum bellum adversus Carthaginenses & turbonem Hannibalem:
units.tr: Proposition. That Spain and likewise Africa be assigned to the consuls, and that war be waged by land and sea against the Carthaginians and the fierce Hannibal.

units.la: Confirm. I. A justo: quia satis magna belli causa est, cum confederata civitas oppugnatur. Hinc 1. ostendat jura federum & sociorum & 2. contra præsumat furorem Hannibalis: qui non auditurus sit legatos, sed urfurus propositum, fi junctas videat copias. Urgea- tur Locus Communis: Inter arma silent leges. Qui ausus violare fedus, non auditurus est exprobratores perfidiæ.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From what is just: because the cause of war is great enough when a confederate state is attacked. Hence (1) he should show the rights of the treaties and of the allies, and (2) then anticipate the madness of Hannibal, who will not hear the envoys but will press on with his purpose if he sees the forces joined. Here the commonplace is to be pressed: amid arms the laws are silent. He who dared to violate a treaty will not listen to those who reproach him with treachery.

units.la: II. Ab exemplis majorum, qui honestissimam belli causam semper existimarint, si socii læderentur. vide Orationem pro Lege Manil.
units.tr: II. From the examples of our ancestors, who always judged a war most honourable when the allies were injured. See the speech for the Manilian Law.

units.la: III. A possibili: hinc 1. comparet Romanorum vires cum Carthagi- nensibus, tum ratione copiarū, tum ratione Ducum, tum ratione sedis belli, quod in Africam translatum vires Carthaginensium afflicturum sit. 2. ex priori bello Punico argumentum capiat, ubi ad æquas conditiones redacti sint Carthaginenses.
units.tr: III. From what is possible: hence (1) he should compare the strength of the Romans with that of the Carthaginians, both in respect of numbers of troops, of the commanders, and of the seat of the war, which, once transferred to Africa, will wear down the strength of the Carthaginians. (2) He should draw an argument from the former Punic war, where the Carthaginians were reduced to equal terms.

units.la: IV. A necessario: ne socii opprimantur sine auxilio: unde jactura & detrimentum maximum Romanis & audacia Pœno.
units.tr: IV. From necessity: lest the allies be crushed without aid; whence the greatest loss and damage to the Romans and boldness to the Carthaginian.

units.la: Conclus. Urgeat propositionem & festinandum suadeat; ne, dum Romæ deliberatur, Saguntus expugnetur.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him press the proposal and urge that haste be made, lest, while the matter is debated at Rome, Saguntum be taken.

units.la: IV. Secundus Senator cum complicibus censet in Hispaniam tantùm mittendas copias ad liberandam Saguntum.
units.tr: IV. The second senator, with his associates, proposes that troops be sent only into Spain, to free Saguntum.

units.la: Exord. Comprobetilla, quæ collegæ pro sua prudentia ac studio in Remp. censuere: addita ratione, quia adversus fœdifragos & turbulentum ac perjurum & adversus Romanos devotum caput Annibalem jus sit fundatissimum.
units.tr: Exordium. He approves what his colleague, in his prudence and zeal for the state, has proposed, adding the reason that the right is most well-founded against a breaker of treaties, a turbulent and perjured man, and Hannibal, a head devoted to the Romans.

units.la: Propos. Interim moderatius agendum initio, & copias solummodo in Hispaniam ablegandas ad liberandum ab obsidione socios.
units.tr: Proposition. Meanwhile matters should be handled more moderately at the outset, and troops should be sent only into Spain, to free the allies from siege.

units.la: Confirm. I. Quia ibi maximum periculum, cui totis viribus occurren- dum. Distahi illas, si illico & Africa armis petatur. Insuper plus requiri temporis ad colligendas copias; & interea Saguntum periclitari posse.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. Because the greatest danger is there, and it must be met with all our strength. Those forces would be distracted if Africa were attacked by arms at once. Moreover, more time is required to gather troops; and in the meantime Saguntum could be imperilled.

units.la: II. Quia dubium utrum jussu aut etiam scitu Senatus Carthagi- nensis Saguntum oppugnet. Saltem prætexturos Carthagi- nenses, se insciis hoc fieri, & Romanos securis & ignorantibus intulisse bellum sine denunciatione. Hinc famam sinistram Romanis; qui justitiæ in bello non minus, quam in pace studiosi fuerint. Cavendam esse hanc maculam nomini Romano.
units.tr: II. Because it is doubtful whether the Carthaginians besiege Saguntum by order or even with the knowledge of their Senate. At least the Carthaginians will pretend that it is done without their knowledge, and that the Romans, careless and unaware, have brought war upon them without a declaration. Hence a bad reputation for the Romans, who have been as zealous for justice in war as in peace. This stain must be guarded against in the Roman name.

units.la: III. Quia probabile Annibalem juvenem temerarium & juratum hostem, ausum fuisse oppugnare Saguntum, laudem, si res successerit, si secus, excusationem facile apud suos inventurum.
units.tr: III. Because it is probable that Hannibal, a young, rash man and a sworn enemy, dared to attack Saguntum, and if the affair succeeds he will easily find praise among his own people, and if not, an excuse.

units.la: VI. Tutissimum hoc esse. Ita enim Saguntum posse liberari. Annibale debellari, & interim servari pacem cum Republ. Carthaginensium. Qui haud ægre ferent, ducem juveniliter ferocientem, multatum esse.
units.tr: VI. This is the safest course. For thus Saguntum can be freed, Hannibal can be subdued, and in the meantime the peace with the Carthaginian state can be kept. They will not take it hard that a youthful and fiery general has been punished.

units.la: Concluf. Propositionem repetat, addatque, maturandum omnino antequam urbs obsessa extrema patiatur.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him repeat the proposal and add that it must be hastened altogether, before the besieged city suffers the last extremity.

units.la: V. Tertius Senator cum sequacibus non temere movendam rem tantam censent, sed mittendos prius Legatos ad Annibalem, & in eventum Carthaginem.
units.tr: V. The third senator, with his followers, judges that so great a matter should not be rashly moved, but that envoys should first be sent to Hannibal, and, if the outcome is unfavourable, to Carthage.

units.la: Exord. Breviter repetitis quæ præcedentes collegæ statuerint, scil. armis agendum; veretur, ne suffragiis victus, aut etiam timidior videatur, si moderatiora suadeat, dicendum tamen pro Rep. quid ex re videatur quocunque etiam eventu.
units.tr: Exordium. Having briefly repeated what the preceding colleagues have decided, namely that action must be taken by arms, he fears that, defeated by the votes, or even seeming more timid, if he urges more moderate measures; yet he must speak for the state what seems expedient from the matter, whatever the outcome.

units.la: Propos. Videri sibi præproperè nimis decerni bellum grave & diuturnum, antequam mitiora remedia tentata fuerint.
units.tr: Proposition. It seems to him that too hastily a grave and lasting war is being decreed, before milder remedies have been tried.

units.la: Confirm. I. A justo, jure feciali scil. quod denunciationem tanquam mitissimum remedium primò exigat. Hujus legis æquitatem urgeat: quia scil. frustra armis agitur, ubi verbis & legationibus res expediri potest. Hinc 1. ostendat, quàm funestum sit decretum belli, videl. de tot millium vita ac fortunis ferri sententiam. Hanc causam esse, cur omnia prius tentanda, quàm arma sumenda majores voluerint. Si jam occupata urbs, primus restitutionem urgendam tamen esse. 2. Infamiam rupti fœderis Romanis imputatum iri à Carthag. si illico armis irruant. Nihil præcipitanter agendum, maxime in re ardua.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From what is just, namely by the fecial law, which demands a declaration first, as the mildest remedy. Let him press the fairness of this law: because, namely, it is vain to act by arms where the matter can be settled by words and embassies. Hence (1) he should show how deadly a decree of war is, namely that a sentence is pronounced on the lives and fortunes of so many thousands. This is the reason why the ancestors wished that everything be tried before arms are taken up. Even if the city is already occupied, restitution is nonetheless to be pressed first. (2) That the infamy of a broken treaty will be imputed to the Romans by the Carthaginians if they rush upon them at once with arms. Nothing should be done rashly, especially in a difficult matter.

units.la: II. A Tuto: quod arguat 1. quia ordinaria via sit per legationem prævia. 2. quia frustrata legatione semper adhuc arma sumi queant; at suscepto semel bello, finis est in arbitrio victoris.
units.tr: II. From what is safe: which he argues (1) because the ordinary way is by a prior embassy; (2) because, once an embassy has failed, arms can still be taken up at any time; but once war has been begun, the end lies in the hands of the victor.

units.la: III. Impossibili contrariæ sententiæ, 1. quia justus exercitus ita subito conscribi nequeat, tumultuarius nil proficiat contra vires Annibalis 150. millium. Rumpi tamen fœdus, periculo exponi exercitu, debilitari vires Romanorum & nihil effici. 2. Quia naves, commeatus aliaque ad tantum bellum necessaria necdum in promtu, nec tam subito parari queant.
units.tr: III. From the impossibility of the opposing view: (1) because a proper army cannot be raised so suddenly, and a hastily gathered mob would accomplish nothing against the forces of Hannibal, which number 150,000. Yet the treaty would be broken, the army exposed to danger, the strength of the Romans weakened, and nothing achieved. (2) Because ships, supplies, and other things necessary for so great a war are not yet ready, nor can they be got ready so suddenly.

units.la: Concluf. Ex dictis rationibus statuat mittendos legatos ad Annibalem, & si nihil obtineant, ad Senatum Carthaginensem, ne temere ad bellum proruisse Romani videantur.
units.tr: Conclusion. From these reasons let him propose that envoys be sent to Hannibal and, if they obtain nothing, to the Carthaginian Senate, so that the Romans may not seem to have rushed headlong into war.

units.la: Decretum.
units.tr: Decree.

units.la: Hæc sententia utpote tutissima vicit, legatique eo maturius missi ad Annibalem, atque inde Carthaginem, si non absisteretur bello, ad ducem ipsum in poenam foederis rupti deposcendum.
units.tr: This opinion, being the safest, prevailed; and the envoys were sent with all speed to Hannibal, and from there to Carthage, to demand that the general himself be surrendered for punishment of the broken treaty, unless he desisted from the war.

units.la: Eventus.
units.tr: Outcome.

units.la: Annibal Saguntum oppugnans, cognito appulsu Legatorum, misit obviam & infesta milite itinera causatus audiri illos inter occupationes bellicas non posse nunciavit: Ita Carthaginem trajecerunt. Hannibal interim scribit ad Principes suae factionis.
units.tr: Hannibal, who was besieging Saguntum, learned of the envoys' arrival, sent to meet them, and, pleading that the roads were beset by hostile soldiers, announced that they could not be heard amid the business of war. Thus they crossed over to Carthage. Meanwhile Hannibal writes to the leaders of his faction.

units.la: VI. Litera Annibalis ad principes factionis Barchinae.
units.tr: VI. Letter of Hannibal to the leaders of the Barcine faction.

units.la: I. Nunciet quid ipse egerit cum Legatis Romanis quos propediem Carthagne futuros putet, de oppugnatione Sagunti & repulsae questuros.
units.tr: I. He should report what he himself has done with the Roman envoys, whom he thinks will soon be at Carthage, and that they will complain about the siege of Saguntum and their rejection.

units.la: II. Significandum hoc ipsis fuisse, ut mature complices disponant, ne quid contra se in favorem Romanorum statuatur.
units.tr: II. He should make clear to them that it was necessary that they arrange their allies in good time, so that nothing be decided against him in favour of the Romans.

units.la: III. Exponat statum rerum in obsidione Sagunti vide Liv. cap. 9. lib. 21., & spem de subigenda brevi Sagunto, pariterque exaggeret emolumenta ex hac victoria: videl. 1. quod sic tota Hispania potentissima provincia juris sit Carthaginensis, unde ingens accessio Carthagini 2. Hanc ingentem utilitatem compensare & tegere iniquitatem armorum & foederis violationem. 3. Capta Sagunto, nil metuendum a Romanis. Facile excusare factum potentiores.
units.tr: III. He should set out the state of affairs in the siege of Saguntum (see Livy, book 21, chapter 9), and express hope of subduing Saguntum shortly, and likewise magnify the advantages of this victory, namely: (1) that thus the whole of Spain, a very powerful province, would be under the jurisdiction of Carthage, whence a great increase for Carthage; (2) that this great advantage would compensate for and cover the injustice of the arms and the violation of the treaty; (3) that once Saguntum is taken, nothing is to be feared from the Romans; the deed can easily be excused by the more powerful.

units.la: IV. Hortetur potentiores, ut dextre rem gerant, caveantque ne quid contra ipsum statuatur.
units.tr: IV. He should urge the more powerful men to conduct the affair skilfully, and to take care that nothing be decided against him.

units.la: VII. Acta Carthagini, Legati Romani de rupto foedere queruntur, dedi Annibalem petunt.
units.tr: VII. Proceedings at Carthage: the Roman envoys complain of the broken treaty and demand that Hannibal be given up.

units.la: Exord. Gratias agunt nomine Romanorum, pro concessa facultate exponendi, quae a Senatu populoque Romano in mandatis habent.
units.tr: Exordium. They give thanks in the name of the Romans for the granted opportunity of setting forth what they have in their instructions from the Senate and people of Rome.

units.la: Narratio. Rerum statum exponant. videl.
units.tr: Narration. They should set out the state of affairs, namely:

units.la: I. Justam querelam Legatorum Saguntinorum de invasione hostili Annibalis in regionem Transiberinam.
units.tr: I. The just complaint of the Saguntine envoys concerning the hostile invasion by Hannibal of the region beyond the Ebro.

units.la: II. Decretum Senatus Romani de mittendis Legatis ad Annibalem & Carthaginenses.
units.tr: II. The decree of the Roman Senate concerning the sending of envoys to Hannibal and the Carthaginians.

units.la: III. Oppugnationem Sagunti per Annibalem, & repulsam passam ab eodem.
units.tr: III. The siege of Saguntum by Hannibal, and the rebuff suffered from him.

units.la: IV. Impositam sibi necessitatem adeundi Senatum Carthaginensem Evictio iniquitatis in facto Annibalis:
units.tr: IV. The necessity imposed on them of approaching the Carthaginian Senate. Proof of the injustice in Hannibal's deed:

units.la: I. Quia contra fedus egerit, transiens hostiliter Iberum & oppugpugnans sociam Civitatem. Amplif. ex Loco Communi de sanctitate foederum.
units.tr: I. Because he acted against the treaty, crossing the Ebro in hostile fashion and attacking an allied city. Amplification from the commonplace on the sanctity of treaties.

units.la: II. Quod bellum inchoaverit sine indictione praevia, sine qua nullum legitimum bellum contra foederatos & pacificos : quales Romani.
units.tr: II. Because he began the war without a prior declaration, without which no war is lawful against allies and those at peace, such as the Romans are.

units.la: III. Quod repulsam dederit Legatis Romanis, quod est contra jus gentium, quo sancti & inviolabiles legati, etiam ab hostibus missi. Adducatur Locus Communis de jure legatorum.
units.tr: III. Because he rebuffed the Roman envoys, which is contrary to the law of nations, by which envoys are holy and inviolable, even when sent by enemies. Let the commonplace on the law of envoys be adduced.

units.la: Conclus. Petant, ut Carthaginenses mittant, qui ulteriore belli impetum inhibeant: & Annibalem omnia jura violante dedant Romanis. Addant rationem ab aequitate & continuanda fide ac pace ex parte Romanorum.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let them ask that the Carthaginians send men who will check the further onset of war, and that they hand over to the Romans Hannibal, who violates all laws. Let them add an argument from fairness, and from the continuing of faith and peace on the Roman side.

units.la: THEMA II. DELIBERATIO ISRAELITARUM DE MITIGANDIS ONERIBUS ISRAELITARUM POST MORTEM SALOMONIS.
units.tr: THEMA II. THE DELIBERATION OF THE ISRAELITES ON EASING THE BURDENS OF THE ISRAELITES AFTER THE DEATH OF SOLOMON.

units.la: I. Populus per deputatos rem Rehabeamo proponit.
units.tr: I. The people put the matter to Rehoboam through their deputies.

units.la: Exord. 1. Populi nomine missos se, ut justum dolorem contestentur ob mortem Regis Salomonis: cujus memoria tanto venerabilior ipsis, quo majoribus dotibus praeditus, regnum in culmine felicitatis constituit (quam paucis exponant) 2. Optandum fuisse vitam diuturniorem, ut jam stabilito regno, recreare etiam subditos potuerit. Sed aliter visum Deo, cujus voluntati acquiescendum. 3. Gratulari sibi populum de successore filio, cui prospera omnia foveant, a quo omnia fausta expectare se dicant.
units.tr: Exordium. 1. Sent in the name of the people, they attest their just grief at the death of King Solomon, whose memory is all the more venerable to them because he, endowed with greater gifts, established the kingdom at the height of happiness (which they briefly set out). 2. It would have been desirable for his life to last longer, so that, the kingdom now being settled, he could also refresh his subjects. But God had decided otherwise, and his will must be accepted. 3. The people congratulate themselves on a successor who is a son, whom all prosperous things favour, and from whom they say they expect every blessing.

units.la: Narratio Exponat I. Notam omnibus Salomonis magnificentiam in aedificiis, familitiis, satellitibus, equitatu. Et sane ita requisivisse stupendam ipsius sapientiam, ob quam exterae crebrae legationes ad ipsum missae: quas pari pompa excipiendas fuisse dicat. Scilicet praeludium quoddam in ipso fuisse gloriae venturi Messiae.
units.tr: Narratio. Let them set out: I. Solomon's magnificence in buildings, household, attendants and cavalry is known to all. Indeed, his stupendous wisdom required it, and on account of it frequent foreign embassies were sent to him, which, they say, must be received with equal pomp. Clearly there was in him a certain prelude to the glory of the coming Messiah.

units.la: II. Imposita hinc onera extraordinaria, quae libenter tolerarit populus; sperans illa propediem mitiganda.
units.tr: II. Extraordinary burdens were imposed as a result, which the people bore willingly, hoping that they would soon be eased.

units.la: III. Extremam interim inopiam populi, unde ruina regni metuenda, nisi prospiciatur.
units.tr: III. Meanwhile there is the people's extreme poverty, from which the ruin of the kingdom is to be feared unless provision is made.

units.la: Propos. Haec propter missos se a populo, ut mitigationem onerum supplices petant.
units.tr: Propositio. These things are said because they have been sent by the people to petition humbly for the easing of the burdens.

units.la: Confirm. I. Amoliantur suspicionem seditionis: videl. non impulsos se cupiditate novitatis, aut vilipendio juventutis regiæ, quasi sub initio regni aliquid novi moliantur. Procul hoc esse à se. &c. qui pari fide Rehabeamo atque Salomoni & Davidi obtemperaturi sint.
units.tr: Confirmatio. I. Let them remove any suspicion of sedition: namely, that they were not driven by a desire for novelty, or by contempt for the royal youth, as if they were plotting something new at the beginning of the reign. Far be this from them, etc., who will obey Rehoboam with the same loyalty as Solomon and David.

units.la: II. Rationes petiti exponant.
units.tr: II. Let them set out the reasons for their request.

units.la: 1. A necessario: extrema scil. populi paupertate: quam probet à causa: videl. perpetua militia sub Davide, structuris & magnificentia Salomonis: unde onera cumulata populo supra modum.
units.tr: 1. From necessity: namely the extreme poverty of the people, which they prove from its cause: the perpetual warfare under David, and the building works and magnificence of Solomon, whence burdens were heaped upon the people beyond measure.

units.la: 2. A pio: quia Deus prohibuerit pompam & equitium amplum regibus Deut.17. 14.seq. contra vero in poenam datum Saulé. 1. Sam. 8. gravem futurum fuisse fratribus. Absit, ut hunc potius, quam Dei præceptum sequatur novus rex.
units.tr: 2. From piety: because God forbade kings pomp and a large horse-establishment (Deut. 17. 14ff.), whereas it was given to Saul as a punishment (1 Sam. 8), and it would have been burdensome to his brothers. Far be it that the new king should follow this rather than God's precept.

units.la: 3. Ab utili: quia remittendo onera obsequentem habiturus sit populum: quos fratres esse cogitabit & Dei populum.
units.tr: 3. From advantage: because by remitting the burdens he will have a obedient people, whom he will reckon as brothers and as God's people.

units.la: Concluf. Petant itaque, ut annuat rex æquis hisce petitis, & obedientiam ac fidem, ac Dei benedictionem ipondeant.
units.tr: Conclusio. Let them therefore ask that the king grant these fair requests, and pledge obedience and loyalty, and God's blessing.

units.la: II. Rex petitum populi proponit Consilio Seniorum.
units.tr: II. The king lays the people's request before the council of elders.

units.la: I. Refert se ad petitionem populi, videl. audivisse illos, quid populus petierit. Rem videri maximi momenti, unde dependet regis authoritas & regni quies: ideo veluisse se sententiam ipsorum ea de re prius cognoscere, antequam populo respondeat.
units.tr: I. He refers to the people's petition, namely that he has heard what the people asked. The matter seems to be of the greatest moment, since on it the authority of the king and the peace of the kingdom depend; therefore he wished to learn their opinion on the matter before answering the people.

units.la: II. Expendat paucis rationes,
units.tr: II. Let him briefly weigh the reasons,

units.la: 1. A populo propositas: videl. a. verum esse populum exhaustum esse. b. Deum prohibuisse rigidam dominationem in fratres. c. Metuendam esse offensam populi & rebellionem.
units.tr: 1. Those put forward by the people: namely a. that it is true the people are exhausted; b. that God forbade harsh domination over brothers; c. that the offence and rebellion of the people is to be feared.

units.la: 2. Rationes in contrarium: videl. a. indignum esse rege, cedere postulatis populi, maxime sub regni initio: quasi metuat plebem, aut precarium habeat regnum. b. Gravari sic famam patris Salomonis; quasi iniquis exactionibus oppresserit populum. c. Intutum esse cedere petitis populi, qui fluminis instar semper ulterius progreditur, si priora obtinuerit.
units.tr: 2. Reasons to the contrary: namely a. that it is unworthy of a king to yield to the demands of the people, especially at the beginning of his reign, as if he feared the commons or held his kingdom on sufferance; b. that the reputation of his father Solomon would thus be harmed, as if he had oppressed the people with unjust exactions; c. that it is unsafe to yield to the requests of the people, who, like a river, always advance further once they have obtained the earlier things.

units.la: III. Sed malle se audire suffragia Senatus, quorum ætatem, prudentiam & fidem verbo laudet.
units.tr: III. But he prefers to hear the votes of the Senate, whose age, prudence and loyalty he praises in words.

units.la: III. Primus Seniorum suadet mitigationem onerum.
units.tr: III. The first of the elders advises the easing of the burdens.

units.la: Exord. Cum propositione generali à momento deliberationis, videl. gravissimam esse deliberationem, quam rex proposuit, ex qua regni salus, ipsiusque regiæ domus pendeat incolumitas. Optare se, ut rex pro sua prudentia in hac re statuat. Ita ipsum rationes ab utraque parte cordate expendisse, ut nihil addere queant. Interim quia & Senatus consilium audire malit, se memores officii, si non ad placitum, certe ad salutem regni arbitraturum: penes regem esse eligere.
units.tr: Exordium. With a general proposition on the weight of the deliberation: it is a most serious deliberation which the king has proposed, on which the safety of the kingdom and the security of the royal house itself depend. He prays that the king, in his prudence, will decide the matter. He himself has weighed the reasons on both sides so carefully that he can add nothing. Meanwhile, since the king prefers to hear the counsel of the Senate, he, mindful of his duty, will give his judgement, if not to the king's liking, at least for the safety of the kingdom; it rests with the king to choose.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Exponat regni statum: 1. Quod negari nequeat multis oneribus tum ob bella continua Davidis contra hostes ab omni latere gesta, tum ob structuras sumptuosas, tum ob aulam amplam Regis Salomonis, qualem famosa ipsius sapientia requisiverit ex haustum esse regnum.
units.tr: Tractatio. I. Let him set out the state of the kingdom: 1. It cannot be denied that it has been drained by many burdens, both because of David's continual wars waged against enemies on every side, and because of costly buildings, and because of the ample court of King Solomon, such as his famous wisdom required.

units.la: II. Laudet populi obsequium ultra vires: quo magis cavendum, ne de regia bonitate frustra sperent. Equos sponcaneos nimio onere solere fatiscere.
units.tr: II. Let him praise the people's obedience, which goes beyond their strength: so much the more must one beware lest they hope in vain for royal kindness. Horses that are driven beyond their strength are wont to collapse under excessive load.

units.la: III. Proponat periculum interregni & sub rege novo; ubi spes novitatis, & pauperū ac maleseriatorum, spes turbarum. Vide Salust. initio belli Catilin. quibus omni modo obviam eundum, & concedendum potius initio, deinde adstringi rursus posse frænum.
units.tr: III. Let him set forth the danger of an interregnum and of a new king, where the hope of novelty is the hope of the poor and the discontented, and the hope of disturbances. See Sallust at the beginning of the Catilinarian war. Such people must be met in every way, and it is better to concede at the beginning; afterwards the bridle can be drawn tight again.

units.la: IV. Explicet bonum sperandum ex indulgentia: videl. 1. Eludi sic machinationes malevolorum & hostium. 2. Populum obstringi sic fortius novo regi majori amore, qui fortissimum vinculum regnorum. Non sic fulgentia tela, quam tutatur amor, &c.
units.tr: IV. Let him explain the good to be hoped for from indulgence: namely 1. that in this way the schemes of malevolent men and enemies are frustrated; 2. that the people are bound more firmly to the new king by greater love, which is the strongest bond of kingdoms. Gleaming weapons are not so secure as love, which protects, etc.

units.la: Conclus. Hæc maturius perpendenda videri regi: qui initio regni non tam ad autoritatem regiam, quam ad demerendum populi amorem spectare debere videtur. Nil habere se, quod præscribant regi, sed hæc ratione officii humillime monenda fuisse. Rogare se Deum, ut pro sua prudentia ad Dei gloriam & regni salutem eligat.
units.tr: Conclusio. These things seem to be weighed more carefully by the king, who at the beginning of his reign ought to aim not so much at royal authority as at winning the love of the people. He has nothing to prescribe to the king, but these things were to be advised most humbly by reason of his duty. He asks God that the king choose, in his prudence, for the glory of God and the safety of the kingdom.

units.la: IV. Reliqui Seniores modeste examinat rationes regis contrarias.
units.tr: IV. The remaining elders modestly examine the king's opposing arguments.

units.la: Exord. A prolepsi videl. Licet satis a rege & collega expensa sint, quæ ad gravissimam hanc deliberationem facere queant, tamen officii ratione, volente sicRege, paucis se ponderaturos, quæ rex in contrarium afferre voluerit. Propof. Maximi esse illa momenti, sed nescire se utrum prioris rationibus praeponderare queant.
units.tr: Exordium, by anticipation, namely: although the king and his colleague have already weighed everything that could bear on this most serious deliberation, nevertheless, out of a sense of duty and with the king's leave, they will briefly consider the arguments the king wished to advance to the contrary. Proposition: those arguments are of the greatest weight, but they do not know whether they can outweigh the reasons of the former side.

units.la: Examen I. Indignum videri regem cedere populo: Resp. si scilicet coactus hoc faciat. Aliud esse si gratiam faciat supplicantibus: similem sic Deo esse, a quo precibus omne bonum impetramus. Maxime initio regni salutarem esse clementiam, propriam virtutem imperantium.
units.tr: Examen I. It seems unworthy for the king to yield to the people: the reply is, that this is so only if he does it under compulsion. It is otherwise if he grants a favour to those who beg for it; in that he is like God, from whom we obtain every good by prayer. At the beginning of a reign, clemency is most beneficial, being the proper virtue of those who rule.

units.la: II. Nec videri gravari famam Salomonis. Quia 1. ipse allegat populus causas, structuram scilicet & famosam Salomonis sapientiam. Diversa tempora diversos requirere sumptus. Clementiae esse, si remittat rex, quod jure exigere posset, & videri omnino minuendos esse sumptus aulae laxioris.
units.tr: II. Nor does the fame of Solomon seem to be harmed. For 1. the people themselves give the reasons: namely, the building works and Solomon's famous wisdom. Different times require different expenditures. It is an act of clemency if the king remits what he could lawfully exact, and it seems altogether right that the expenses of a more relaxed court be reduced.

units.la: III. Nec videri intutum hoc; sed in contraria negatione esse periculum, ne turbones populum concitent. In amore civium tutissimum regi praesidium & regni firmamentum esse.
units.tr: III. Nor does this seem unsafe; rather, the danger lies in refusing, lest they stir up the people to disturbances. In the affection of the citizens lies the surest protection of the king and the firmest foundation of the kingdom.

units.la: Concluf. Videri igitur & gloriosam & salutarem regi & regno esse hoc tempore clementiam, ad quam natura etiam propensus videtur rex &c.
units.tr: Conclusion: clemency at this time therefore seems both glorious and salutary for the king and the kingdom, a quality to which the king himself appears naturally inclined, etc.

units.la: V. Rex laudata ipsorum fide, de hac re ulterius deliberaturum se ait.
units.tr: V. The king, having praised their loyalty, says he will deliberate further on this matter.

units.la: I. Audivisse se dicat, quae pro sua prudentia ac fide, qua regi regnoque obstricti, in medium protulere. Hinc repetat summam sententiae ipsorum.
units.tr: I. He says he has heard what they have put forward, with their prudence and the loyalty by which they are bound to the king and the kingdom. Hence he repeats the substance of their opinion.

units.la: II. Laudet paucis ipsorum moderationem, qua convenienter officio & aetati suae ea censuere, quae ad regis amorem, & regni quietem facere videntur. Hanc cynosuram esse unicam, quo consilia omnia referenda sunt.
units.tr: II. He praises in a few words their moderation, by which they have given counsel fitting to their duty and their age, counsel that seems to promote both the king's affection and the quiet of the kingdom. This is the one cynosure to which all counsels must be referred.

units.la: III. Rem esse maximi momenti: idcirco se porro de ea cogitaturum, quibus terminis populo respondendum sit, ut amor subditorum & regia dignitas larta tecta conservetur.
units.tr: III. The matter is of the greatest importance: therefore he will further consider in what terms the people must be answered, so that the love of the subjects and the royal dignity may be preserved unimpaired.

units.la: VI. Rex junioribus causam proponit.
units.tr: VI. The king lays the matter before the younger men.

units.la: I. Referat petitum populi tanquam ipsis satis cognitum: videl: scire ipsos, quid populus nuper petierit, videl: onerum relaxationem.
units.tr: I. He reports the people's petition as something already well known to them, namely that they know what the people lately asked for, namely the relief of their burdens.

units.la: II. Audivisse se desuper seniores ex consilio regio, utpote quibus patris sui Salomonis acta & consilia magis cognita fuerint. Verum non satis placere sibi ipsorum consilium tanquam parum decorum & sibi & Patri Salomoni. Unde & ipsorum sententiam audiendam judicarit.
units.tr: II. He has heard from the elders of his council above, since the acts and counsels of his father Solomon are better known to them. But their counsel does not altogether please him, as too little fitting either to himself or to his father Solomon. For this reason he has judged that their opinion should be heard too.

units.la: III. Jubet itaque ut libere mentem suam aperiant, quid populo novaturienti respondendum censeant; ut honori regis regnique consulatur.
units.tr: III. He therefore bids them openly declare their mind, what they think should be answered to the people who are eager for novelty, so that the honour of the king and the kingdom may be looked after.

units.la: VII. Juniores suadent rigorem.
units.tr: VII. The younger men urge severity.

units.la: Exord. A proverbio: Cadente arbore quilibet ligna colligit. Scilicet Verisimum dictum esse: Cadente &c. Scilicet unde umbram habuerant immemores spoliare accolas. Applicetur ad regem Salomonem & populum onera incusantem sub rege optimo. Miratos se regis patientiam, qui non illico repulerit importunum hoc petitum. Quandoquidem igitur placuerit regi, audire ipsorum sententiam, pro fide debita se illam sine ambagibus prolaturos.
units.tr: Exordium, from a proverb: when a tree falls, everyone gathers wood. Namely, it is a most true saying: when a tree falls, etc. Namely, those who had enjoyed its shade forget themselves and despoil its neighbours. Let it be applied to King Solomon and to a people complaining of burdens under the best of kings. They have been amazed at the king's patience, in that he did not at once drive away this importunate petition. Since therefore it has pleased the king to hear their opinion, they will state it without circumlocution, out of the loyalty they owe.

units.la: Propof. Videri omnino importunitatem populi lascivientis severa repulsa compescendam.
units.tr: Proposition: the importunity of a wanton people must surely be checked by a stern rebuff.

units.la: Confirm. I. Ab honesto: Videl. regem pro sua prudentia in sua propositione innuisse, versari hic honorem Patris Salomonis & ipsius regis; cujus maxima ratio habenda imperantibus. Eo enim luxato solvi vim regnandi. Amplif. ex Loco Communi de authoritate imperantium. &c. Jam quis nesciat? 1. sic tacite sugillari regimen Salomonis, tanquam durum nimis. 2. Regem vilipendi; quasi ipsi facere audeant, quod non licuit sub Salomone. 3. Populum sic arrogare sibi potestatem praescribendi regi: quod indignum &c.
units.tr: Confirmation: I. From what is honourable: the king, in his prudence, has hinted in his proposition that the honour of Father Solomon and of the king himself is at stake here; the greatest regard for this must be had by those who rule, for once it is broken the force of ruling is dissolved. Amplified from the common topic on the authority of rulers, etc. Who does not already know this? 1. In this way the government of Solomon would be tacitly disparaged as too harsh. 2. The king would be made cheap, as if they dared to do what was not allowed under Solomon. 3. The people would thus arrogate to themselves the power of prescribing to the king, which is unworthy, etc.

units.la: II. A periculoso: 1. quia periculum, si hoc obtinuerint, ulteriora mox petituros. Populum enim insatiabilem esse, instar fluminis, quod si aggerem ruperit, vagatur sine termino. Ita & populum, cui regia voluntas pro termino esse debet. 2. Metuendum esse, ne provinciae & populi subacti, Ammonitae, Idumaei hoc exemplo irritentur ad excutiendum jugum regum. Amplif. ex Loco Communi de natura populorum.
units.tr: II. From what is dangerous: 1. because there is a danger that, if they obtain this, they will soon ask for more. For the people are insatiable, like a river which, once it has broken its embankment, wanders without limit. So the people must have the king's will as its limit. 2. It is to be feared that the subject provinces and peoples, the Ammonites and the Edomites, may be provoked by this example to throw off the yoke of kings. Amplified from the common topic on the nature of peoples.

units.la: III. Ab impossibili: quia regni onera alias sustineri nequeunt. Hinc exaggerent amplitudinem regni, & hostium vicinorum potentiam: quae praesidia & militem paratum requirunt.
units.tr: III. From what is impossible: because the burdens of the kingdom cannot otherwise be sustained. Hence they should stress the extent of the kingdom and the power of the neighbouring enemies, which require garrisons and a ready soldiery.

units.la: Conclusio. Regem itaque duro responso ferocientem populum repellere debere: ut sic constet sibi authoritas regia. &c.
units.tr: Conclusion: therefore the king ought to repel the people, who are growing fierce, with a harsh reply, so that the royal authority may stand consistent with itself, etc.

units.la: VIII. Cancellarius nomine Regis respondet populo ex consilio juniorum.
units.tr: VIII. The chancellor, in the king's name and on the counsel of the younger men, answers the people.

units.la: I. Accessus a repetitione actorum: videlicet 1. postquam visum sit Deo, avocare regem Salomonem gloriosae recordationis & regnum ad filium Rehabeamum devolvere, nihil aliud iperasse regem, quam quàm gratam memoriam erga defunctum, & paratam obedientiam erga filium. Sed proh-dolor contrarium patescere. &c.
units.tr: I. The approach is by recalling what has been done: namely, 1. after it pleased God to take away King Solomon of glorious memory and to hand the kingdom down to his son Rehoboam, the king has ordered nothing else than a grateful remembrance of the dead and a ready obedience to his son. But, alas, the contrary is becoming evident, etc.

units.la: 2. Inivisse regem consilium super petito populi, & re mature deliberata, mandasse sibi, ut suo nomine populo respondeat.
units.tr: 2. The king has entered upon a plan concerning the people's petition, and, having deliberated on the matter maturely, has charged me to answer the people in his name.

units.la: II. Videlicet.
units.tr: II. Namely:

units.la: 1. Grave fuisse regi, intelligere populi gravamina super regimine Salomonis, eujus laudes & fama apud exteros nervose inculcet hic. Non sperasse se populum tam ingratum, ut defuncti memoriam sugillet. Non intelligere populum consilia regum, & quid requirant regni onera. Violari regimen, si populo de omnibus reddenda ratio sit. Caveant igitur ne famam tanti regis lacerent.
units.tr: 1. It has been grievous to the king to learn of the people's complaints about Solomon's government, whose praises and fame among foreigners he here urges with vigour. He had not hoped that the people would be so ungrateful as to disparage the memory of the dead. He does not understand the people's understanding of the counsels of kings, or what the burdens of the kingdom require. The government would be violated if an account had to be rendered to the people of everything. Let them therefore take care not to tear apart the reputation of so great a king.

units.la: 2. Displicere regi, quod initio regiminis turbas hasce moverint, ubi satis curarum regi, ad custodiam regni inter hostes siti. Nec posse sibi imaginari populum tam impium, nisi quod turbonibus quibusdam autem praebeant: quos moneat desistere, nisi poenam incurrere velint majestatis. Non esse regem tam socordem, ut hosce metuat.
units.tr: 2. It displeases the king that they have stirred up these disturbances at the start of his reign, when he has enough cares, being set among enemies, for the guarding of the kingdom. Nor can he imagine the people to be so impious, unless they are giving encouragement to certain troublemakers; he warns them to desist, unless they wish to incur the penalty of treason. The king is not so careless as to fear these men.

units.la: 3. Rem esse periculosi exempli, quod populus arbitrium sibi sumat de expensis regni, & invadere sic jus regium quod quanto pere Deo displiceat, ex Lege regia praescripta a Samuele. 1. Reg. 8. facile intelligere queant.
units.tr: 3. It is a matter of dangerous precedent that the people should assume to themselves a judgement on the expenses of the kingdom and so invade the royal right; how greatly this displeases God, they can easily understand from the royal law prescribed by Samuel, 1 Sam. 8.

units.la: III. Mentem regis aperiat. videl. 1. velle regem, ut populus desistat ab iniquo ac periculoso hoc petito. 2. Ut agnoscat justum Zelum suum ac offensam pro gloria Parentis & regni, se duplicaturum onera parentis. vide 1. Sam. 12. donec agnoscat errorem, & regiae curae se suaque committere discat.
units.tr: III. He declares the king's mind, namely: 1. that the king wills the people to desist from this unjust and dangerous petition. 2. That they should acknowledge his just zeal and his displeasure for the glory of the father and the kingdom; he will double the burdens his father laid on them, see 1 Sam. 12., until they acknowledge their error and learn to commit themselves and their affairs to the royal care.

units.la: IX. Adoram missus a rege Rehabeamo invectus in rebelles ad concordiam hortatur.
units.tr: IX. Adoram, sent by King Rehoboam, rebukes the rebels and urges them toward concord.

units.la: Exord. Ex abrupto, a facti foeditate, improbet populi machinationes. Quis hic furor ô Viri Israelitæ? Itane discessum paratis a domo Davidis? Itane subditi a rege vestro deficietis? An etiam cogitatis, rebellionem esse, Deo hominibuique exosam? &c.
units.tr: Exordium. Abruptly, from the vileness of the deed, he condemns the people's plots. "What madness is this, O men of Israel? Are you really preparing to depart from the house of David? Will you really revolt from your king? Or do you even consider that rebellion is hateful to God and to men?" etc.

units.la: Propof. Huc missum a rege venire se, ne scelere novo se maculent; petere, ut patienter sana monentem audiant.
units.tr: Proposition. He says that he has been sent by the king to come here, so that they may not stain themselves with a new crime; he asks that they listen patiently to his wholesome admonitions.

units.la: Confirm. I. a jure regio; quod non ex populi electione, sed successione legitima descendat. Hinc exponat, a Deo ortum regnum Davidi & omnibus posteris suis: unde & ipse Messias suo tempore oriturus sit. Huic domui promissam benedictionem ac pacem: & hanc deseretis?
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From the royal right, which descends not from the people's election but from lawful succession. Here he sets out that the kingdom was given by God to David and to all his descendants, whence the Messiah himself was to arise in due time. Will you forsake this house, to which the blessing and peace were promised?

units.la: II. A foeditate rebellionis; quae Deo adversa & omnium scelerum ac calamitatis origo. Absit ut sanctus Deo populus tali flagitio se contaminet.
units.tr: II. From the vileness of rebellion, which is opposed to God and is the origin of all crimes and calamity. Far be it that a people holy to God should defile itself with such a shameful act.

units.la: III. A periculo profanitatis, uti idololatriae. Videlicet deseri sic Templum & Arcam foederis, quae Hierosolymis collocata. Scilicet hanc si deserant, vel profanos, vel Idololatras futuros. Omnia deserenda potius, quam Deum & Dei cultum ac sacra praesentiae divinae symbola.
units.tr: III. From the danger of profanity, such as idolatry. Clearly, if the Temple and the Ark of the covenant, which are placed at Jerusalem, are thus abandoned, they will become either profane or idolaters. Everything should rather be abandoned than God, the worship of God, and the sacred symbols of the divine presence.

units.la: IV. A secuturis poenis, si armis, quae jam parari dicat a rege, redigendi ad obsequium.
units.tr: IV. From the punishments that will follow if they are not brought back to obedience by the arms which he says are already being prepared by the king.

units.la: Conclus. Offerri adhuc gratiam mature ad officium redeuntibus; reliquis certissimas paratas esse poenas.
units.tr: Conclusion. Grace is still offered to those who return to their duty without delay; for the rest, the most certain punishments are prepared.

units.la: Eventus. Lapidatus a populo fuit Adoram & Rex electus Jaroboamus frustra parante arma Rehabeamo.
units.tr: Outcome. Adoram was stoned by the people, and Jeroboam was chosen king, while Rehoboam vainly prepared arms.

units.la: THEMA III. CONSULTATIO THEBANORUM DE BELLI DUCE ELIGENDO ADVERSUS PHOCENSES.
units.tr: THEMA III. THE THEBANS' CONSULTATION ON CHOOSING A LEADER OF THE WAR AGAINST THE PHOCIANS.

units.la: I. Praeses causam proponit.
units.tr: I. The President sets out the case.

units.la: Exord. A praesenti rerum statu, quem breviter exponat: videlicet 1. cladem recens perpessam a Phocensibus, 2. animositatem illorum ad urgendum bellum sub novo duce Onomarcho. 3. Periculum in quo versentur res Thebanorum nisi idoneo duce instructi sint.
units.tr: Exord. He should briefly explain the present state of affairs: namely, 1. the recent defeat suffered at the hands of the Phocians; 2. their eagerness to press the war under their new leader Onomarchus; 3. the danger in which the affairs of the Thebans stand unless they are equipped with a suitable leader.

units.la: Propos. Deliberandum itaque & dispiciendum de duce idoneo.
units.tr: Propos. Therefore it must be deliberated and considered who would be a suitable leader.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Ostendat 1. in genere, momentum quod est in duce idoneo: quia inde dependet consilium & robur totius exercitus. Illustret simili a nauclero, a capite; comprobetque exemplo ipsorum Thebanorum quondam sub Epaminonda. Vid. sub finem. lib. 7. Justinum & vide Politicios & Locum Communem de belli duce. 2. In specie hoc tempore, ubi cladem perpessi Thebani, & duce novo aucti Phocenses.
units.tr: Tractatio. I. He should first show, in general, how much depends on a suitable leader, since the counsel and strength of the whole army rest on him. Let him illustrate this by the comparison with a ship's captain and with the head, and confirm it by the example of the Thebans themselves under Epaminondas in former times. See Justin at the end of book 7, and see the political writers and the common place on the leader in war. 2. In particular, at this time, when the Thebans have been defeated and the Phocians have been strengthened by a new leader.

units.la: II. Proponat vias diversas: videlicet
units.tr: II. He should set out the different ways, namely:

units.la: 1. Utrum legendus ex civibus? quorum laudet quidem virtutem; tem; sed a. opponat periculum, si vincat; videlicet ne opprimat libertatem. Exaggeretur ex Loco Communi de periculosa nimia unius ex civibus potestate. b. Metuat, ne auxiliares copiae Lacedaemon. & Athenienlium, detrectent obedire civi Thebano, ex aemulatione.
units.tr: 1. Whether the leader should be chosen from among the citizens? He should indeed praise their virtue, but a. set against it the danger, if he wins, that he may crush liberty. Let this be amplified from the common place on the perilous excessive power of one citizen. b. Let him fear that the auxiliary forces of the Lacedaemonians and Athenians may refuse, out of rivalry, to obey a Theban citizen.

units.la: 2. An vero accersendus peregrinus? & quis? In hanc sententiam inclinet, 1. quia sic evitari queant incommoda illa, quae ex cive metuenda. 2. Quia ille nihil juris habeat, nisi quantum conceditur, adeo lege vinciri queat.
units.tr: 2. Or rather should a foreigner be summoned, and if so, who? Let him incline to this view: 1. because the inconveniences to be feared from a citizen can thus be avoided; 2. because a foreigner has no rights except those that are granted to him, and so can be bound by law.

units.la: Conclus. 1. Abrumpat, quasi nemini praescribere velit, 2. petat ut rem serio secum expendant; & quid videatur in medium consulent.
units.tr: Conclus. 1. Let him break off, as if he wishes to prescribe to no one; 2. let him ask them to weigh the matter seriously among themselves, and to put forward what seems best.

units.la: II. Senator primus suadet eligendum ducem ex civibus.
units.tr: II. The first senator urges that the leader be chosen from the citizens.

units.la: Exord. 1. breviter resumat, quae de statu rerum, de momento quod est in duce, & de diversis viis eligendi vel civem vel peregrinum, pro sua prudentia Praeses propoluit. 2. Dubium se offendat, quid statuendum, maxime cum praelidem in peregrinum inclinare videat.
units.tr: Exord. 1. He should briefly resume what the President, in his wisdom, has set out about the state of affairs, the importance of the leader, and the different ways of choosing either a citizen or a foreigner. 2. He should present himself as uncertain what is to be decided, especially since he sees the President inclining towards a foreigner.

units.la: Propof Praemissa exculatione modesta, videri sibi eligendum civem dicat.
units.tr: Propof With a modest apology first, he says that it seems to him a citizen should be chosen.

units.la: Confirm. 1. a periculo quod est a peregrino, per dilemma, si imbellem eligant, metuendum contemtum & jacturam; si potentem, metuendam oppreflionem civitatis post victoriam. Quod probet ab insolentia victorum: & universali experientia, quae docet & victos & adjutos a victoribus oppressos fuisse. Illustret apologo equi, qui imploraverat auxilium hominis. Hoc minime metuendum a cive; cui vires desunt, & obstat invidia concivium.
units.tr: Confirm. 1. From the danger that comes from a foreigner, by means of a dilemma: if they choose a weak man, contempt and loss are to be feared; if a powerful one, the oppression of the state after victory is to be feared. Let him prove this from the insolence of victors and from universal experience, which teaches that both the defeated and those who were helped have been oppressed by their victors. Let him illustrate this with the fable of the horse which had sought help from a man. This is in no way to be feared from a citizen, whose strength is lacking and who is held back by the envy of his fellow citizens.

units.la: II. A commodo sperando a duce cive:
units.tr: II. From the advantage to be hoped for from a citizen leader:

units.la: 1. Quod ille fidus sit patriae: cujus amor omnibus insitus, ubi habet fratres, propinquos, liberos; pro quibus acrius pugnabit.
units.tr: 1. That he is faithful to the fatherland, whose love is implanted in all, and where he has brothers, relatives and children, for whom he will fight more fiercely.

units.la: 2. Quod gloriosius, civi committere remp. quam peregrino. Et ita usitatum esse omnibus gentibus.
units.tr: 2. That it is more glorious to entrust the commonwealth to a citizen than to a foreigner, and that this is customary among all peoples.

units.la: 3. Quod cives ipsi promtius pareant, quam peregrino; tum propter amorem, tum propter fiduciam. Nec Lacedaemonios ac Athenienses hoc detrectare queant.
units.tr: 3. That the citizens themselves will obey more readily than a foreigner, both from affection and from trust. Nor can the Lacedaemonians and Athenians refuse this.

units.la: III. A defectu peregrini, praeterquam Macedone: in quo etiam nulla fides: quippe qui Graeciae libertati insidietur.
units.tr: III. From the lack of anyone but a foreigner, except a Macedonian, and in him there is no trust either, since he lays snares for the liberty of Greece.

units.la: Conclus. Recollectis breviter rationibus, suadeat eligendum ducem ex civibus, ne plus fiduciae in peregrinis, quam propriis civibus habere videantur.
units.tr: Conclus. Having briefly recalled the reasons, he should urge that the leader be chosen from among the citizens, lest they seem to put more trust in foreigners than in their own citizens.

units.la: III. Secundus Senator censet Philippum Macedonem esse eligen- dum, cui reliqui accedunt.
units.tr: III. The second senator judges that Philip the Macedonian should be chosen, and the rest agree.

units.la: Exord. A scopo publicarum consultationum, qui esse debeat salus Reip. quæ proinde tanquam helice & cynosura semper intuenda in deliberationibus; secus facile aberraturis. Hoc posito, nec sibi tam quid populariBus, quid antecessori gratum forte, sed quid rei Thebaicæ in præsenti rerum statu ubi armis committenda Resp. expediat, spectandum videri.
units.tr: Exord. From the aim of public deliberations, which must be the safety of the commonwealth, and which therefore must always be kept in view in deliberations as a helm and a guiding star; otherwise men will easily go astray. This being laid down, he thinks he must look not at what is pleasing to the common people, or perhaps to his predecessor, but at what is expedient for the Theban cause in the present state of affairs, when the commonwealth is to be entrusted to arms.

units.la: Examen sententiæ antecessoris. Et quidem
units.tr: Examination of the opinion of his predecessor. And indeed:

units.la: I. Argumenti prioris à periculo quod metuendum à peregrino. Invertendo illud; vid: multo magis hoc à cive metuendum: qui non facile autoritatem nisi per tyrrannidem obtinet. Quod & indigitarit præses. Illustretur ex thesi; nihil concive in concives imperante esse insolentius: & ex contrario, peregrino principe, cui gloria sufficit, domi habens quibus imperet. Alludatur Loco Communi de gloria pabulo generosarum mentium.
units.tr: I. Concerning the first argument, from the danger to be feared from a foreigner: turn it around, namely, that this is much more to be feared from a citizen, who does not easily gain authority except by tyranny. The President also hinted at this. Let it be illustrated by the thesis that nothing is more insolent than a citizen ruling over his fellow citizens; and, on the other hand, a foreign prince, for whom glory is enough, who has at home people to rule over. Let an allusion be made to the common place on glory as the food of noble minds.

units.la: II. Argumenti posterioris à commodo sperando à cive:
units.tr: II. Concerning the second argument, from the advantage to be hoped for from a citizen:

units.la: Resp. ad 1. fidem non origine, sed ex animo metiendam esse.
units.tr: Resp. To 1: fidelity is to be measured not by origin but by disposition of mind.

units.la: ad 2. potius quid securum, quam quid gloriosum spectandum, imo nec gloriosam esse servire concivi.
units.tr: To 2: one should look to what is safe rather than to what is glorious; indeed, it is not glorious to serve a fellow citizen.

units.la: ad 3. contrarium verum esse: ob simultates & æmulationes inter cives.
units.tr: To 3: the opposite is true, because of the feuds and rivalries among citizens.

units.la: Propositio: Sibi itaque videri eligendum extraneum, & quidem Philippum Macedon.
units.tr: Propositio: Therefore it seems to him that a foreigner should be chosen, and indeed Philip the Macedonian.

units.la: Confirm. I. Quia tutius hoc 1. ad victoriam: idque ob potentiam, scientiam rei militaris, virtutem ac felicitatem Philippi: quem proinde commendet ad imit. Cic. pro L. Manil. sed breviter. 2. ad retinendam libertatem reip. ne à cive victore illa opprimatur, exemplo plerorumque regum per totum Orientem: ubi cives potentia aucti oppresserint civitatem.
units.tr: Confirm. I. Because this course is safer: 1. for victory; and this on account of Philip's power, his knowledge of military affairs, his virtue and his good fortune, which he therefore commends for imitation. Cicero, for Lucius Manilius, but briefly. 2. For retaining the liberty of the commonwealth, lest it be oppressed by a victorious citizen, by the example of most kings throughout the East, where citizens, grown powerful, have oppressed their states.

units.la: II. 3. Ad vitandam æmulationem inter cives. Quia gloriosius hoc, habere regem ducem, quam civem; etiam apud socios Laced. & Athen.
units.tr: II. 3. For avoiding rivalry among the citizens. Because it is more glorious to have a king as leader than a citizen, and this is also so among the allies of the Lacedaemonians and Athenians.

units.la: Concluf. Repetat propositionem: submittens suffragium rectius sententibus.
units.tr: Concluf. He repeats his proposal, submitting his vote to those who judge more rightly.

units.la: IV. Præses consultationem concludit.
units.tr: IV. The president concludes the consultation.

units.la: I. Libenter percepisse dicat quæ utrinque sollicite graviterque tum pro cive, tum pro extraneo & quidem in specie Philippo dicta sint: uti neminem in gravissima hac deliberatione ex privati affectibus, sed ex Reip. salute censuisse credat, ita haud levibus rationibus utramque subnixam videri.
units.tr: I. Let him say that he has gladly heard what has been said on both sides, carefully and weightily, both on behalf of a citizen and of a foreigner, and in particular on behalf of Philip; so that, while he believes no one in this most serious deliberation has voted from private feelings but from the safety of the commonwealth, both sides appear to rest on no slight reasons.

units.la: II. Ex suffragiorum pluralitate Philippum Maced. designatum ducem ostendat: quem proinde ut potentem & rebus gestis gloriosissimum, ita dignissimum violatæ à Phocensibus religionis, & rei Thebanæ vindicem commendet: voveatque ut Deus faustam & salutarem velit esse electionem hanc Reip.
units.tr: II. From the plurality of votes let him declare Philip of Macedon designated as leader, whom he should then commend as powerful and most glorious in his achievements, and therefore most worthy to avenge the religion violated by the Phocians and the Theban cause; and let him pray that God may will this choice to be fortunate and salutary for the commonwealth.

units.la: III. Mittendos esse censeat ex Senatu, qui Philippo electionem hanc nuncient, supremum militiæ imperium ipsi deferant, & submisse rogent, ut saventer illud acceptare & expeditionem maturare velit.
units.tr: III. Let him judge that ministers should be sent from the Senate to announce this choice to Philip, to offer him the supreme command of the army, and to ask humbly that he be willing to accept it kindly and hasten the expedition.

units.la: V. Legati offerunt Philippo imperium.
units.tr: V. The envoys offer Philip the command.

units.la: Exord. Habeat faustam gratulationem nomine procerum populique Thebani, de victoriolis regis armis & læta regni pace: addito voto perpetuitatis.
units.tr: Exord. Let them offer a happy congratulation, in the name of the nobles and people of Thebes, on the king's victories in arms and the joyful peace of his realm, adding a wish for its perpetuity.

units.la: Narratio. Occasionem legationis exponat: videl. 1. enatū contra Phocenses sacrilegos bellum, & recens comissum præliū, ac submissum à sociis auxilium, 2. defectum ducis idonei & consensum in Philippum: 3. decretam legationem hanc:
units.tr: Narratio. Let them explain the occasion of the embassy, namely: 1. that a war has been begun against the sacrilegious Phocians, that a battle was recently fought, and that aid was sent by the allies; 2. that a suitable leader is lacking, and that consent has been given to Philip; 3. that this embassy has been decreed.

units.la: Propos. Orare se itaque nomine Thebanorum suppliciter, ut supremum regimen militiæ contra Phocenses suscipere ne gravetur.
units.tr: Propos. Accordingly they ask, in the name of the Thebans, humbly, that he not be reluctant to take up the supreme direction of the army against the Phocians.

units.la: Confirm Brevis sit.
units.tr: Confirm Let it be brief.

units.la: 1. Ab enixo Thebanorum voto; quod regi tam generoso, prudenti, forti ac felici parere, omnes vires conferre velint; ipsius ductum secuturi per omnia.
units.tr: 1. From the earnest wish of the Thebans, who are willing to contribute all their strength to obey a king so generous, prudent, brave and fortunate, and who will follow his leadership in all things.

units.la: II. Ab honesto: justitia causæ scil. Thebanorum, contra Phocenses, qui Boetiam vastarint, & spoliato templo Delphico bellum inferant. Nunquam laudabilius bellum quam pro Deo geri, vide lib. 8. just. ab init.
units.tr: II. From the honourable character of the cause, namely the justice of the Theban cause against the Phocians, who have laid waste Boeotia and make war after plundering the temple at Delphi. No war was ever more praiseworthy than one waged for God; see Justin, book 8, at the beginning.

units.la: Conclus. Petant ut sine mora suscipere bellum hoc & principatum Thebanum, & quam celerrime se Thebas conferre velit.
units.tr: Conclus. Let them ask that he take up this war and the leadership of Thebes without delay, and that he be willing to betake himself to Thebes as quickly as possible.

units.la: Epicrisis.
units.tr: Epicrisis.

units.la: Bene quidem factum à Thebanis ad obtinendam victoriam contra hostes Phocenses, sed imprudenter pro patriæ libertate, quàm victor Philippus, uti ordinarie potentes adjutores oppressunt.
units.tr: The Thebans acted well in seeking victory over the Phocian enemy, but imprudently with respect to the liberty of their fatherland, since Philip, the victor, oppresses such powerful helpers as is customary.

units.la: THEMA IV.
units.tr: THEMA IV.

units.la: CONSULTATIO DE COMPRIMENDA SEDITIONE.
units.tr: CONSULTATION ON SUPPRESSING SEDITION.

units.la: I. Appius Claudius Consul, vi agendum existimat contra plebem tumultuantem.
units.tr: I. Appius Claudius, the consul, thinks force must be used against the rioting plebs.

units.la: Exord. Patheticum & increpatorium: quo exprobrat Senatui metum præposterum, in exorbitante plebis furore: cui nisi magno animo obviam eatur, rempubl. eversum iri.
units.tr: Exord. Emotional and reproachful. He rebukes the Senate for its misplaced fear in the face of the plebs' excessive fury, and says that unless it is met with great courage, the commonwealth will be overthrown.

units.la: Propos. Imperio itaque consulari agendum, & in autores severe animadvertendum esse.
units.tr: Propos. Therefore action must be taken by consular authority, and the instigators must be punished severely.

units.la: Confirm. I. A necessario: quia 1. ipsa respublica periclitetur. 2. furor populi crescat lenitate ac metu Senatus. Amplif. à natura populi, qui terret nisi terreatur; instar fluvii qui cedendo irritatur. 3. in extremis malis extremis utendum remediis; exemplo medicorum.
units.tr: Confirm. I. From necessity: (1) the commonwealth itself is in danger; (2) the people's fury grows through the leniency and fear of the Senate. Amplified from the nature of the people, which terrifies unless it is itself terrified, like a river that rages the more it is yielded to; (3) in extreme evils one must use extreme remedies, as with physicians.

units.la: II. A justo: 1. quia leges ipsæ ferro compescendam rebellionem statuant. Lege agendum igitur, 2. quia patribus ipsis metuendum, ni animos ac vim opponant. Hinc exaggeret plebis importunitatem, ac minas. Quid æquius, quam ferro comprimere talia?
units.tr: II. From justice: (1) the laws themselves prescribe that rebellion be put down by the sword, so the law must be enforced; (2) the fathers themselves have cause to fear unless they oppose spirit and force to it. Here he dwells on the plebs' insolence and threats. What could be fairer than to suppress such things by the sword?

units.la: III. Ab utili: quia uno aut altero arrepto quieturi sint reliqui. Hinc explicet naturam plebis, quæ instar ferventis ollæ initio facile reprimitur vi opposita: secus, si caput habere ceperit.
units.tr: III. From expediency: if one or two are seized, the rest will be quiet. Here he explains the nature of the plebs, which, like a boiling pot, is easily held down at first by opposing force; otherwise, if it begins to have a head, it cannot be checked.

units.la: Concluf. Propositionem, inculcatis verbo rationibus, inferat.
units.tr: Concl. He draws the proposal to a close, driving home the reasons with repeated words.

units.la: II. Publ. Servilius lenibus remediis agendum censet.
units.tr: II. Publius Servilius thinks the rage must be calmed with gentle remedies.

units.la: Exord. A dicto: Malus diuturnitatis custos metus. Probetur: quia odium parit subditorum: Illustretur contrario amore, unde stabile imperium: 2. exemplo regis ultimi expulsi ob truculentiam: & substitutum mite imperium consulare. Iis artibus servari imperium, quibus partum est.
units.tr: Exord. From a saying: fear is a bad guardian of long duration. It is proved because it breeds the hatred of subjects, and is illustrated by the contrary, love, whence comes a stable rule. (2) By the example of the last king, expelled for his savagery, and the mild consular government that replaced him. A rule is preserved by the same arts by which it was won.

units.la: Propos. Videri sibi itaque lenibus remediis sedandos esse plebis irritatæ animos.
units.tr: Propos. Therefore he thinks the minds of the roused plebs should be calmed by gentle remedies.

units.la: Confirm. I. A contrario rigore; quo irritentur animi. Probetur à natura plebis, qui instar bestiæ multorum capitum, si unum amputes, exacerbari reliqua. Hinc refellat argumentum 3. Resp. in paucorum tumultu hoc procedere; secus, ubi tota sævit multitudo. do. Et hinc refellat porrò argumentum 2. Resp. multa jure fieri posse, quæ facere prohibet prudentia : quæ moderatrix est omnium reliquarum virtutum.
units.tr: Confirm. I. From the contrary, harshness, by which minds are provoked. It is proved from the nature of the plebs, which, like a many-headed beast, grows fiercer in the others if you cut off one. Here he refutes the third argument: the answer is that this holds in a riot of a few, but not where the whole multitude rages. And here he further refutes the second argument: the answer is that many things may be lawful which prudence forbids, and prudence is the moderator of all the other virtues.
