units.la: II. Ab effectis lenitatis : utpote quæ placat irritatos & excutit ferrum è manibus : peragit tranquilla potestas; quod violenta nequit. Hac ulos majores, Brutum & Valerium conditores imperii consularis. Hinc refellat argumentum 1.
units.tr: II. From the effects of leniency: it soothes the provoked and shakes the sword from their hands; a calm authority accomplishes what violence cannot. He appeals to our ancestors, Brutus and Valerius, the founders of the consular government. Here he refutes the first argument.

units.la: III. A circumstantia temporis : ubi hostes Volsci invadunt Remp. ubi periculum ne patres deserantur a civibus, si asperiori imperio agant, & urbs prodatur hostibus. Dum pastores inter se certant, lupis prodi gregem.
units.tr: III. From the circumstances of the time: when the Volscian enemy attacks the commonwealth, there is the danger that the fathers will be deserted by the citizens if they govern more harshly, and the city will be betrayed to the enemy. While the shepherds quarrel among themselves, the flock is betrayed to the wolves.

units.la: Conclus. Cedendum furori, & aliquid indulgendum plebi, si Remp. salvam velint.
units.tr: Concl. One must yield to the fury and grant the plebs something, if they wish the commonwealth to be saved.

units.la: Decretum, ut Servilius, cui populare magis ac mite ingenium, videat, quomodo expediat Remp.
units.tr: It is decreed that Servilius, whose temperament is more popular and mild, shall see how best to serve the commonwealth.

units.la: III. Oratio Servilii ad plebem placatoria. vid. Liv. p. 65.
units.tr: III. Servilius' speech to the plebs, conciliatory. See Livy, p. 65.

units.la: Exord. Doleat plebis perversitatem, quod hoste appropinquante detrectent militiam, lætentur periculo & interitu civitatis : Addita causa, quod neutra pars civitatis affligi queat sine ruina totius: exemplo membrorum corporis.
units.tr: Exord. He laments the perversity of the plebs, who refuse military service when the enemy is approaching and rejoice in the danger and ruin of the state. He adds the reason that neither part of the state can be harmed without the ruin of the whole, as with the members of the body.

units.la: Propos. Non esse causam diffidendi a Senatu.
units.tr: Propos. There is no cause for the plebs to distrust the Senate.

units.la: Confirm. 1. Quia paratus sit, ad abolenda gravamina. Ratio : quia in salute plebis & civitatis, & suam existimet Senatus. Illustretur a prolepsi: Cur igitur non emendent? Resp. illico non posse emendari omnia. Circumspecte curanda vetera vulnera: quæ jam cara sit Senatus.
units.tr: Confirm. (1) Because the Senate is ready to remove the grievances. The reason is that the Senate considers the welfare of the plebs and of the state to be its own. This is illustrated by an anticipated objection: why then do they not correct them? The answer is that not everything can be corrected at once; old wounds must be treated with care, and the Senate already holds them dear.

units.la: II. Quia probrosum plebi extorquere aliquid velle in præsenti periculo, cui prius eundum sit obviam : ne vel respubl. negligatur, vel vi extortum remedium videatur, quod probrosum plebi & patribus.
units.tr: II. Because it is shameful for the plebs to wish to extort something in the present danger, which must first be met head on, lest either the commonwealth be neglected or the remedy seem to have been wrested by force, which is shameful for both the plebs and the fathers.

units.la: III. Quia hosti ludibrio erunt, si diffidentes subigantur.
units.tr: III. Because they will be a laughingstock to the enemy if, distrusting one another, they are brought under subjection.

units.la: IV. Quia jam facto ipso solvi velit Senatus nexos, & in castris absentium bona possideri vendive nolit. Reliqua peracto bello emendanda, &c.
units.tr: IV. Because the Senate now wishes to release the bound debtors by that very act, and does not wish the goods of absent soldiers in the camp to be seized or sold. The remaining matters are to be corrected once the war is over, and so on.

units.la: Conclus. Meminerint igitur avitæ virtutis & nomina profiteantur, ut junctis viribus hosti ire queant obviam. Sopita sic seditio & certatim sacramentum dederunt militiæ, ac hostis repulsus fuit.
units.tr: Concl. Let them therefore remember their ancestral virtue and profess the name of Romans, so that with united strength they may go out to meet the enemy. The sedition was thus quelled, and they vied with one another in taking the military oath, and the enemy was repulsed.

units.la: THEMA V.
units.tr: THEMA V.

units.la: SUASIO LEGIS CENSORIÆ, UT QUISQUE QUOTANNIS RATIONEM REDDAT VITÆ VICTUSQUE.
units.tr: A SPEECH PROPOSING THE CENSORIAN LAW, THAT EACH PERSON RENDER AN ACCOUNT OF HIS LIFE AND LIVELIHOOD EVERY YEAR.

units.la: I. Consul Rom. populo proponat.
units.tr: I. The Roman consul proposes it to the people.

units.la: Exord. Laudet frequentem populi ad intimationem Senatus confluxum: addita 1. ratione, quia in eo se ostendant. a. vere cives. b. boni publici studiosos. 2. declaratione paterni affectus sui totiusque senatus pro civibus & Rep.
units.tr: Exordium. He should praise the people's numerous assembly in answer to the Senate's summons, adding (1) the reason, that in it they show themselves (a) to be true citizens and (b) keen on the public good; and (2) a declaration of his own fatherly affection, and that of the whole Senate, toward the citizens and the Republic.

units.la: Narratio. Exponat hinc 1. sollicitudinem Senatus pro salute Civium. 2. Animadversam dissolutionem maleferiatorum nonnullorum, qui nulli arti aut officio addicti, bona paterna dilapident. 3. Frequentem ac sollicitam sæpe deliberationem Senatus 4. Decretam medelam per legem censoriam: quæ sic habet: Cives Romani universi quotannis coram Censoribus vitæ victusq; rationem reddunto.
units.tr: Narration. He should set out here (1) the Senate's concern for the safety of the citizens; (2) the noticed collapse of some idlers who, attached to no craft or office, squander their paternal estates; (3) the Senate's frequent and anxious deliberation; (4) the remedy decreed through the censorial law, which runs thus: All Roman citizens are to render an account of their life and livelihood each year before the Censors.

units.la: Propos. Hanc legem proponi populo, quam ratam habendam velint jubeant.
units.tr: Proposition. This law is to be put before the people, and they are to order it to be held valid.

units.la: Confirm. Commendet legem
units.tr: Confirmation. He should commend the law.

units.la: I. A necessitate, propter copiam ociosorum, qui nulli arti addicti, vitiis malisque artibus se tradant. Unde mali mores, perversa œconomia, tandem everso civitatis: causam esse publicam vivendi licentiam, Illustret comparatione priscæ disciplinæ Servii Tulli, qui populum juxta opes & functiones in classes retulit: & necessariæ disciplinæ domesticæ, si domus salva esse debeat.
units.tr: I. From necessity: because of the abundance of idlers who, attached to no craft, give themselves over to vices and wicked arts. Hence bad morals, disordered household management, and at last the overthrow of the state; the cause of this is public license to live as one pleases. He should illustrate this by comparison with the old discipline of Servius Tullius, who divided the people into classes according to their wealth and functions, and by the necessary discipline of the household, if the household is to be kept safe.

units.la: II. Ab utilitate: vid: 1. sic laudem publicam futuram bene rem suam gerentibus. 2. opprobrio maleferiatis. Illustretur ex thesi, de necessitate præmiorum & pœnarum in Rep. 3. Averti sic posse paupertatem a civibus & ærario.
units.tr: II. From usefulness: (1) thus public praise will follow those who manage their affairs well; (2) disgrace will fall on the idlers. This should be illustrated from the thesis on the necessity of rewards and punishments in the Republic. (3) In this way poverty can be turned away from the citizens and the treasury.

units.la: III. A facili: quia boni amant in apricum venire, & reliqui assuescent ferre lucem.
units.tr: III. From ease: because good men love to come into the sunlight, and the rest grow accustomed to bearing the light.

units.la: Conclus. 1. Spem concipiat de assensu bonorum.'2. Eam ad rem solitum spacium trinundini ad deliberandum, suadendam, aut dissuadendam legem, populo concedat.
units.tr: Conclusion. (1) He should express hope of the assent of good men. (2) For this purpose he should grant the people the customary interval of three market-days to deliberate on the law, and to argue for or against it.

units.la: II. Tribunus plebis Legem dissuadeat.
units.tr: II. The tribune of the plebs argues against the law.

units.la: Exord. Quod semper periculosam novitatem existimarit in Rep. Licet enim speciosa videantur multa, tamen plura latere incommoda, quae non nisi tempore emergunt. Moribus antiquis stare rem Rom. Unde suspectam sibi Legem a Consule nuper rogatam.
units.tr: Exordium. He has always judged novelty in the Republic to be dangerous. For although many things may seem attractive, more disadvantages lie hidden, which emerge only with time. The Roman state rests on ancient customs. Hence the law recently proposed by the consul seems suspect to him.

units.la: Propos. Hanc causam esse dicat, cur prodeat pro libertate & disciplina prisca dicturus.
units.tr: Proposition. He says this is the reason why he comes forward to speak on behalf of liberty and the ancient discipline.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Examinet quae pro lege dixerat Consul 1. concedendo copiam maleferiatorum, & necessariam coercitionem; sed sub hoc praetextu non esse jugum imponendum insontibus. Veteres arcuisse otiosos, non serviliter coegisse cives. 2. Proemia & poenas necessaria quidem esse; sed citra servitutis impositionem. 3. Neminem vereri lucem; dummodo absit servilis coactio, hactenus Romae insueta. Ita bona promovenda, ut ne mala graviora invehantur.
units.tr: Treatment. I. He examines what the consul had said in favour of the law: (1) granting that there is a crowd of idlers and that some compulsion is necessary, but insisting that under this pretext no yoke should be laid on the innocent. The ancients kept off the idle; they did not force citizens like slaves. (2) Rewards and punishments are indeed necessary, but without imposing servitude. (3) No one fears the light, provided that servile compulsion, hitherto unknown at Rome, is absent. Good things should be promoted in such a way that worse evils are not introduced.

units.la: II. Impugnet Legem 1. quia probrosa civibus: quorum gloriam praedicet in subactione orbis. Quid igitur turpius, quam illos domi sub ferula esse & cogi ad laborem, servorum instar. Omnino discrimen esse ingenui & servi. Hoc agi scil. ut victor populus, domi serviat. Claudatur apostrophe ad cineres tumulosque majorum. 2. quia iniqua: patriciis scil. lascivam & ocium indulgens, plebem ad labores adigens. Neque enim hanc intentionem esse, ut divites cogantur, sed tenuiores. Leges omnibus aequaliter ferendas, si salva esse debeat libertas. 3. quia noxia: excitura quippe discordiam & invidiam inter Cives: unde seditiones, turbae. Notam esse vulgi naturam ac ferociam. Exemplo praeire debere patricios in virtute, labore; sic secutu-ram plebem.
units.tr: II. He attacks the law: (1) because it is shameful for citizens, whose glory he extols in the conquest of the world. What then could be more disgraceful than that they should be under the rod at home and be forced to labour like slaves? Clearly there is a difference between freeborn and slave. This is what is being done, namely that the victorious people should be enslaved at home. Here he should break into an apostrophe to the ashes and tombs of the ancestors. (2) Because it is unjust: it indulges the patricians in luxury and idleness, while driving the plebs to labour. For the intention is not that the rich should be compelled, but the poorer. Laws must be borne equally by all, if liberty is to be kept safe. (3) Because it is harmful: it will stir up discord and ill will among the citizens, whence come seditions and tumults. The nature and wildness of the common crowd are well known. The patricians ought to lead by example in virtue and labour; thus the plebs will follow.

units.la: Conclus. Hasce rationes esse, quare legem hanc abrogandam, servandam disciplinam veterum & libertatem esse statuat, in civitate quae armis illam acquisivit.
units.tr: Conclusion. He should lay down that these are the reasons why this law must be repealed, and that the discipline of the ancients and liberty must be preserved, in a state which won that liberty by arms.

units.la: III. Civis Roman. suadeat legem.
units.tr: III. A Roman citizen urges the law.

units.la: Exord. Gratuletur Reip. de paterna cura magistratus pro Rep. Rationem tionem addat ab effecto, quia speranda hinc meliora tempora. Illustretur simili à cura patris in ordinanda familia: unde ejusdem salus. Unde miretur contradictum salubri tali legi.
units.tr: Exordium. He should congratulate the Republic on the magistrate's paternal care for it. He adds a reason from the outcome: from this better times are to be hoped for. This is illustrated by a comparison with a father's care in ordering his household, on which the household's own safety depends. He should then wonder at anyone who contradicts so wholesome a law.

units.la: Propof. Hanc causam esse, cur ipse suadendi illam partes sibi sumserit: quod facile existimet apud Romanos laboris & virtutis studiosos.
units.tr: Proposition. He says this is the reason why he has taken upon himself the role of urging it, since he thinks it will easily be accepted among the Romans, who are keen on labour and virtue.

units.la: Confirmatio. I. Breviter per praeteritionem repetitis illis, quae de necessitate & utilitate legis dixit Confulrationem addat à justo & aequo; quia fcil. divinae & humanae leges laborem imperent hominibus: ocium vero improbent. Hinc & naturam universam & omnes cives in bene instituta Rep. operosos esse. Illustretur à membris corporis humani.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. Briefly, by way of preterition, repeating those things which the consul had said about the necessity and usefulness of the law, he adds an argument from what is just and fair: because divine and human laws both enjoin labour upon men and condemn idleness. Hence the whole of nature, and all citizens in a well-ordered Republic, are industrious. This is illustrated from the members of the human body.

units.la: II. Ab incommodo contrarii ocii multorum: unde non tantum vitia invehantur in civitatem; verum etiam egestas apud plurimos: qui deinceps oneri sint reliquis civibus. Hanc averti hac lege.
units.tr: II. From the harm of the contrary idleness of many: whence not only vices are introduced into the state, but also want among most people, who afterwards become a burden to the other citizens. This is averted by this law.

units.la: Confutat. Refellat argumenta contraria. 1. Non esse coactionem servilem, sed directionem salutarem ac monelam de officio, uti liberis opus assignatur a parentibus: veram libertatem, non in licentia ocii ac vitiorum, sed in obedientia & virtute consistere. 2. aequaliter omnibus ferri hanc legem. 3. Ideoque non metuendum hinc discordiam.
units.tr: Refutation. He refutes the contrary arguments. (1) There is no servile compulsion, but a salutary direction and reminder of duty, just as children are assigned tasks by their parents. True liberty consists not in the license of idleness and vices, but in obedience and virtue. (2) This law is borne equally by all. (3) Therefore discord should not be feared from it.

units.la: Conclus. Non dubitare fe itaque, quin omnes boni salutarem hanc Senatus curam agnituri, & hinc legi unde omnis prosperitas civitati, lubentes subscripturi sint. Nemini metuendum hinc nisi fucis,
units.tr: Conclusion. He does not doubt, therefore, that all good men will recognise this salutary care of the Senate, and will gladly subscribe to the law from which all prosperity comes to the state. No one, he says, should fear anything from it except the drones.

units.la: IV. Consul breviter resumat approbetq;, quae Civis pro lege dixit, expositaque porro legisfententia, illam publicet.
units.tr: IV. The consul briefly takes up again and approves what the citizen said in favour of the law, and then, having set out the sense of the law, he promulgates it.

units.la: Exord. Non mirandum dicat, à maleferiatis quibusdam oppugnatam fuisse Legem. Ratio: quia nihil tam salutare, quod non in malam partem trahi possit: nulla lex i. tis commoda omnibus. Non dubitare fe, quin cum Cive illo faciat incerior pars populi.
units.tr: Exordium. He says it is not to be wondered at that the law has been attacked by certain idlers. The reason: nothing is so salutary that it cannot be twisted to a bad end; no law is advantageous to all in the same way. He does not doubt that the less reliable part of the people will side with that citizen.

units.la: Propof. Ideoque fe paucis legis mentem explicaturum: hac ipse fretum, neminem fore, qui contradicturus fit instituto tam salutari.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore he will briefly explain the intention of the law, relying on this himself: that there will be no one who will contradict so salutary an institution.

units.la: Tractatio I. Per ἀπίφασιν neget fe repetiturum quae pro lege à fe & à Cive dicta: quae interim paucis repetat.
units.tr: Treatment. I. By aposiopesis he says he will not repeat what was said for the law by himself and by the citizen; he briefly recalls these things in the meantime.

units.la: II. Mentem legis exponat: videl. 1. Non intendere servilem coactionem civium, sed salutarem ordinem, qualis in singulis oeconomiis, conomiis, in ipso corpore, & tota natura, ubi nihil ociosum. Adeoque non ipectare sponte sua agentes, sed malè sibi suisque consulentes. Veram libertatem esse bonis legibus obedire, uti recte civis expositerit. Sed 2. esse paternam curam ac monelam de officio.
units.tr: II. He sets out the intention of the law, namely: (1) that it does not aim at servile compulsion of the citizens, but at a salutary order, such as exists in each household, in the body itself, and in the whole of nature, where nothing is idle. Accordingly it does not punish those who act of their own accord, but those who look badly to themselves and their own. True liberty is obedience to good laws, as the citizen rightly explained. But (2) it is a paternal care and a reminder of duty.

units.la: III. Censuram nemini molestam esse posse. a. quia deliguntur ad illam viri meritis in Remp. graves. b. amantes civium adeoque ipsis grati. 3. Ætate & consilio eximii, qui veluti publici civitatis patres sint, consilium potius unicuique suggesturi, quam acerbe imperaturi. Quid salubrius itaque civibus, quam horum res suas gerere consilio.
units.tr: III. The censorship can be a burden to no one. (a) Because men weighty in merit toward the Republic are chosen for it. (b) They love the citizens and are therefore pleasing to them. (3) They are outstanding in age and counsel, and as it were the fathers of the state, who will offer advice to each person rather than command harshly. What, then, is more wholesome for citizens than to have their affairs managed by such men's counsel?

units.la: Concluf. Hortetur ut, quid videatur, velint jubeantque ratam esse legem.
units.tr: Conclusion. He urges the people to declare what they think, and to order the law to be held valid.

units.la: V. Publicatio Legis.
units.tr: V. Publication of the law.

units.la: 1. Acceptato applausu populi, laudet ipsorum obsequium, & optime speret de flore civitatis. Hinc 2. quod felix faustumque voveat, Legem tanquam Senatus autoritate & consensu plebis ratificatam recitet, & concionem dimittat.
units.tr: (1) Having received the people's applause, he praises their compliance and hopes the best for the prosperity of the state. Then (2) he prays that it may be happy and fortunate, reads out the law as ratified by the authority of the Senate and the assent of the plebs, and dismisses the assembly.

units.la: THEMA VI. CONSULTATIO PTOLOMÆI UTRUM RECIPIENDUS POMPEJUS PROFUGUS.
units.tr: THEMA VI. THE CONSULTATION OF PTOLEMY, WHETHER POMPEY, A FUGITIVE, IS TO BE RECEIVED.

units.la: Rex causam proponit.
units.tr: The King sets out the case.

units.la: Exord. 1. Explicet causam deliberationis, referens rem notam: videl. cladem Pompeji & petitione protectionis adversus Cæsare. 2. Pondus rei; unde ipsorum sententiam cognoscendam judicarit.
units.tr: Exord. 1. He explains the cause of the deliberation, recalling a matter already known, namely the defeat of Pompey and his request for protection against Caesar. 2. The weight of the matter; for which reason he judges that their opinion ought to be known.

units.la: Propof. Deliberandum utrum recipiendus, an rejiciendus Pompejus; aut quid secus agendum.
units.tr: Propof. It is to be deliberated whether Pompey is to be received or rejected, or what else is to be done.

units.la: Tractatio. Exponat breviter rationes dubitandi.
units.tr: Tractatio. He should briefly set out the reasons for doubt.

units.la: I. Pro receptione, ut est: 1. autoritas tanti ducis, qui acie quidem victus, non bello, adeoque recolliget copias. 2. autoritas Senatus, qui est à partibus Pompeji. Hunc rejici sive rejiciatur Pompejus. 3. Beneficium Dionysio patri præstitum, quem in regnum restituerit.
units.tr: I. For receiving him: 1. the authority of so great a leader, who was defeated in the field but not in the war, and so will gather his forces again. 2. The authority of the Senate, which is on Pompey's side; if he is rejected, it too is rejected. 3. The benefit conferred on his father Dionysius, whom he restored to the kingdom.

units.la: II. Pro rejectione: 1. Periculum regni, propter potentiam & receneentem victoriam Cæsaris. 2. Onus regni, quod facile sic bello implicabitur. 3. Nullum contra emolumentum ex afflicti principis hospitio & patrocinio.
units.tr: II. For rejecting him: 1. The danger to the kingdom, on account of the power and the recent victory of Caesar. 2. The burden on the kingdom, which would easily be drawn into war by such a guest. 3. No corresponding advantage from the hospitality and patronage of a fallen prince.

units.la: Conclus. Hæc dubium ipsum habere : ut nesciat quid statuendum in causa hac ardua : Unde ad serio deliberandum hortetur.
units.tr: Conclus. These are the king's own doubts, so that he does not know what to decide in this difficult case; whence he urges them to deliberate seriously.

units.la: 1. Achoreus consiliarius senior Regis censet recipiendum Pompejum.
units.tr: 1. Achoreus, the senior counsellor of the King, advises that Pompey be received.

units.la: Exord. Agnoscit cum Rege pondus præsentis deliberationis: 1. propter personas Pompeji & Cæsaris, quorum neuter facile offendendus. 2. propter causam, quæ ambigua, 3. propter eventum dubium.
units.tr: Exord. He acknowledges with the King the weight of the present deliberation: 1. on account of the persons of Pompey and Caesar, neither of whom is to be offended easily. 2. On account of the cause, which is ambiguous. 3. On account of the uncertain outcome.

units.la: Propos. Interim statuendum e vestigio ; quia jam portum subiit Pompejus : id quod illa fide agere velit, qua Regi obstrictus.
units.tr: Propos. A decision must be made at once, since Pompey has already entered the harbour; and he wishes to act with that good faith by which he is bound to the King.

units.la: Tractatio. 1. Dubium se dicat propter rationes in utramque partem graviter a Rege allegatas. Maluisse se, regem aperuisse suam sententiam, ut haberet, quod sequatur. Dubium enim esse eventum consiliorum.
units.tr: Tractatio. 1. He says he is in doubt because of the arguments on both sides seriously advanced by the King. He would have preferred the King to state his own opinion, so that he would have something to follow; for the outcome of plans is uncertain.

units.la: II. Concedat rationes pro rejectione Pompej allegatas, tanquam ponderosas si utilitatem apparentem respicere velit Rex. Repetat hinc rationes allatas.
units.tr: II. He grants the arguments alleged for rejecting Pompey as weighty, if the King wishes to regard apparent advantage. He then repeats the arguments advanced.

units.la: III. Attamen majoris ponderis videri, quod pro receptione allegatum a Rege; nimirum 1. beneficium patri ipsius præstitum. Hoc exaggeret tanquam ingens meritum erga se & patrem cujus memoriæ debeatur gratitudo. 2. Autoritatem Senatus & Reip. quæ non morietur. 3. Quod non sit periculum a Cæsare: quia regnum satis robustum ad resistendum. Aliquid audendum pro tanto amico.
units.tr: III. Nevertheless, what was alleged by the King for receiving him seems of greater weight; namely: 1. the benefit conferred on his father. He magnifies this as an immense service towards himself and his father, to whose memory gratitude is owed. 2. The authority of the Senate and of the Commonwealth, which will not die. 3. That there is no danger from Caesar, since the kingdom is strong enough to resist. Something must be ventured for so great a friend.

units.la: Conluf. Recipiendum & fovendum Pompejum esse hinc inferat: addita ratione : quia adhuc dubius belli eventus.
units.tr: Conclus. He concludes from this that Pompey is to be received and cherished, adding the reason: because the outcome of the war is still doubtful.

units.la: Photinus statuit rejiciendum esse.
units.tr: Photinus decides that he is to be rejected.

units.la: Exord. A Regula recepta: Salus Reip. suprema lex est. Hanc 1. proponat, 2. probet a scopo imperantium, & simili navarchæ, qui omnia dirigit ad salutem navis. 3. Inferat & hanc præcipue hic spectandam esse.
units.tr: Exord. From a received rule: the safety of the Commonwealth is the supreme law. He 1. sets this forth, 2. proves it from the aim of rulers, and from the likeness of a ship's master, who directs everything to the safety of the ship. 3. He adds that this is to be looked to above all here.

units.la: Propos. Salubrius rutiusque esse Ægypto, si se huic bello non misceat.
units.tr: Propos. It is more wholesome for Egypt, on either side, that it not mingle itself in this war.

units.la: Confirm. I. Abintuta receptione: 1. quia Pompejus miser & ex acie profugus, qui cladem secum ferat. Felices colendos esse: vide LucaLucanum. 2. Quia potens Cæsar victor, qui bello petet Ægyptum. Nec esse satis præsidii adversus tantum heroem, recenti victoria ferocientem.
units.tr: Confirm. I. Against receiving him: 1. because Pompey is wretched and a fugitive from the field, and carries the ruin with him; the unfortunate are to be cultivated: see Lucan. 2. Because Caesar, powerful and victorious, will make war on Egypt; and there is not sufficient protection against so great a hero, made fierce by recent victory.

units.la: II. A facili repulsa Pompeji, 1. quia solus, non stipatus copiis. 2. Quia non convalescent rursus ipsius res, ob potentiam ac alacritatem Cæsaris.
units.tr: II. From the easy rejection of Pompey: 1. because he is alone, not surrounded by troops. 2. Because his affairs will not recover again, on account of the power and eagerness of Caesar.

units.la: III. A non necessario, quia rationes antecessoris non stringant in re tam momentosa. Hinc illas examinet.
units.tr: III. From the lack of necessity: because the arguments of his predecessor do not bind in a matter so momentous. Hence he examines them.

units.la: Conclus. Securiorem viam eligendam esse; & mittendum qui sub specie honoris obtruncet illum. Non esse consultum ob salutem unius periculo exponere publicam.
units.tr: Conclus. A safer course is to be chosen; and someone is to be sent who, under the pretext of honour, will cut him down. It is not wise to expose the public welfare to danger for the safety of one man.

units.la: EVENTUS.
units.tr: THE OUTCOME.

units.la: Placuit hoc consilium, licet nefarium nec Ægypto salutare.
units.tr: This plan pleased, although it was wicked and not beneficial to Egypt.

units.la: THEMA VII. UTRUM IN SCHOLIS PRÆLEGENDI SINT COMICI, PLAUTUS, TERENTIUS SIMILESQUE.
units.tr: THEME VII. WHETHER COMIC WRITERS, PLAUTUS, TERENCE AND THE LIKE, ARE TO BE READ IN SCHOOLS.

units.la: I. Dicat pro sententia negativa.
units.tr: I. Let him argue for the negative position.

units.la: Exord. A vi antiquæ consuetudinis, quæ legis instar habetur licet mala. Unde fieri solet, ut mala vetusta raro emendentur.
units.tr: Exordium. From the force of ancient custom, which is held to be as good as law, even when it is bad. Hence it commonly happens that old evils are seldom corrected.

units.la: Applicetur ad hypothesin: idem obtinere in Scholis, ubi inter Autores Classicos ex antiquo more Comici non sine detrimento morum retineantur; adeo ut apud multos nefas etiam habeatur, hoc velle vocare in dubium.
units.tr: Let this be applied to the hypothesis: the same holds in the schools, where among the Classical authors the comic writers are retained, by ancient custom, not without loss to morals; so much so that among many it is even thought wicked to call this into question.

units.la: Propos. Tibi vero minime probandam hanc consuetudinem videri, licet usu invaluerit; sed Comicos ex classibus removendos.
units.tr: Proposition. To you indeed this custom seems by no means to be approved, although it has gained strength through use; but the comic writers ought to be removed from the classes.

units.la: Confirm.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. A noxio: quia corrumpant mores juventutis scurrilitate, contumacia & libidine. Hic præmittatur quanta cura juventus educari debeat, Deinde probetur, quomodo per Comicos corrumpatur.
units.tr: I. From the harmful effect: because they corrupt the morals of youth by scurrility, insolence and lust. Here let it first be set out how great care youth ought to be educated with; then let it be shown how they are corrupted through the comic writers.

units.la: 1. Scurrilitate: Hic a. ostende in thesi quantum malum juventuti à pravis & vernilibus colloquiis Deo hominibusque exosis. b. Argue illa in Plauto & Terentio, ubi insulsi sales lenonum, meretricum & mancipiorum repræsentantur. Si itaque cum talibus conversari nolimus juniores;cur legere illa permittemus ?
units.tr: 1. Scurrility. Here (a) show in general how great an evil it is for youth to be exposed to base and servile conversation, hateful to God and men. (b) Argue this from Plautus and Terence, where the vapid jests of pimps, harlots and slaves are presented. If therefore we are unwilling that the young should associate with such people, why shall we permit them to read those things?

units.la: 2. Contumacia. Hic introduc adolescentes Plautinos & Terentianos, qui scortorum,famulorum, lenonum consilia, voluntati parentum praeferunt,senibus illudunt. Discit haec juventus dum legit, maxime cum haud male cessisse contumaciam videt. At quanta contra pietate honorari parentes voluit Deus.
units.tr: 2. Insolence. Here introduce the Plautine and Terentian young men, who prefer the counsels of prostitutes, servants and pimps to the will of their parents, and mock their elders. Youth learns these things while it reads, especially when it sees that such insolence has turned out not badly. Yet how great is the piety with which God willed that parents be honoured!

units.la: 3. Libidine. Hic a. doce inductione nullum aliud fere argumentum, aut condimentum comoediarum, quam furtivos amores,b. ostende quam noxia haec animis juniorum,ad pessima natura inclinantum, quam extenuentur in scenis: & quam enorme vitium sit libidinis.
units.tr: 3. Lust. Here (a) show by induction that there is hardly any other subject or seasoning of the comedies than secret love affairs; (b) show how harmful these things are to the minds of the young, who are inclined to the worst by nature, when they are softened up on the stage; and how monstrous a vice lust is.

units.la: Claudatur argumentum exclamatione ironica, hanc scil. utilitatem esse, quae speranda ex comoedia.
units.tr: Let the argument be closed with an ironic exclamation: that this, namely, is the benefit to be hoped for from comedy.

units.la: II. A non necessario. Hic 1. Praeoccupet rationes pro Comicis legendis. 2. refutet easdem respondendo a. Linguam Latinam ex aliis autoribus disci posse. b. Formulas Terentio peculiares inde excerpi posse c. Majorem rationem habendam esse morum, quam Latinitatis. d. Melius esse non nominari talia inter Christianos, juxta praeceptum Apostoli, quam ut cum cura discantur; videl. scortationum, pejerationum, convitiorum formulas.
units.tr: II. From the unnecessary. Here (1) anticipate the arguments for reading the comic writers; (2) refute the same by replying: (a) that the Latin tongue can be learned from other authors; (b) that the phrases peculiar to Terence can be extracted from elsewhere; (c) that more regard must be had to morals than to Latinity; (d) that it is better that such things not be named among Christians, according to the precept of the Apostle, than that they be learned with care, namely the formulas of fornication, perjury and reproach.

units.la: Concluf. 1. Excusset quod receptae scholarum consuetudini contradicat. 2. ex iis quae dicta & breviter hic repetenda sunt, prudentioribus judicium relinquat, sibi majorem morum, quam literarum habendam videri rationem.
units.tr: Conclusion. 1. He should excuse himself for contradicting the accepted custom of the schools. 2. From what has been said, and what must briefly be repeated here, he should leave the judgment to the wiser, while holding that more regard is due to morals than to letters.

units.la: 11. Stet pro sententia affirmativa.
units.tr: II. Let him stand for the affirmative position.

units.la: Exord. Non immerito vetustam consuetudinem pro lege haberi. Ratio: quia quod multis diu placuit, raro malum esse potest: cum sapientum judicio nitatur. Unde mirari antecessorem niti contra Comicos, tanto consensu eruditorum hactenus approbatos: scil. juvenis tot viris sapientibus se opponit.
units.tr: Exordium. It is not without reason that ancient custom is held to be law. The reason: because what has long pleased many can rarely be evil, since it rests on the judgment of the wise. Hence it is a wonder that our predecessor takes a stand against the comic writers, who have hitherto been approved by such a consensus of the learned; namely, a young man sets himself against so many wise men.

units.la: Propof. Tibi igitur veterem Scholarum consuetudinem merito vindicandam esse.
units.tr: Proposition. To you, therefore, the old custom of the schools is rightly to be defended.

units.la: Confutatio. Examinet & refutet rationem priorem antecessoris.vide Plutarch. & Chrys. de Legendis Poetis. Summa huc redit: vitia quiquidem proponi, sed in personis vitiosis, quæ non imitandæ sed vitandæ proponuntur, uti fit etiam in historia, & in Ethicis vitiorum doctrina; non ut ea faciamus, sed vitemus.
units.tr: Refutation. Let him examine and refute the former argument of his predecessor; see Plutarch and Chrysostom, on reading the poets. The sum of it comes to this: vices are indeed set forth, but in vicious persons, who are presented not to be imitated but to be avoided; this is done also in history, and in ethics the teaching about vices is given, not that we may do them, but that we may avoid them.

units.la: Rationes alleget pro Comicis, ab eorundem utilitate.
units.tr: Let him allege reasons for the comic writers from their usefulness.

units.la: Ad Latinam Linguam. Hic digredere in laudem Plauti, Terentii, quod terse, quod proprie, quod de rebus variis, de quibus non invenimus apud alios autores loquantur. Atque hinc refellat rationem posteriorem à non necessario.
units.tr: As to the Latin tongue. Here let him digress in praise of Plautus and Terence: that they are polished, that they are precise, that they speak of various matters about which we do not find things in other authors. And from this let him refute the latter argument, from the unnecessary.

units.la: Ad cautionem: quia istic repræsentantur mores diversorum hominum, cum quibus sæpe junioribus etiam invitis versandum est. Hoc ostendas per inductionem præcipuorum, v. g. modo cum avaris senibus, modò cum fallacibus gnatonibus, modo cum corruptis famulis, modo cum luxuriosis adolescentibus: Imò sæpe cum seductoribus & lenonibus maximè in peregrinatione: ubi bonum est ad cautionem talium mores ante habere prospectos. Hinc Theophrastum, aliosque vitiosorum mores & characteres descripsisse. Spartanos ebrios servos liberis contemplandos proposuisse. Hic digredere in tractationem de scopo Comicorum & poetarum, ingenere, juxta illud Hor. Delectare volunt simul & prodesse poetæ. Vitæ scil. fabulam repræsentari in vita.
units.tr: As to caution: because there are represented the characters of various kinds of men, with whom the young must often associate even against their will. Show this by an induction of the principal types, for example, now with avaricious old men, now with deceitful flatterers, now with corrupt slaves, now with luxurious young men; indeed often with seducers and pimps, especially when travelling, where it is good to have the characters of such men set before one's eyes in advance for caution. Hence Theophrastus and others described the characters and manners of vicious men; the Spartans displayed drunken slaves to their free sons to be looked upon. Here let him digress into a treatment of the aim of the comic writers and poets in general, according to that saying of Horace: poets wish to delight and at the same time to benefit; namely, the story of life is represented in life.

units.la: Ex repetitis breviter argumentis, Comicos retinendos in Scholis statuat, & novatorum studia perstringat.
units.tr: From the arguments briefly repeated, let him establish that the comic writers are to be retained in the schools, and let him censure the zeal of the innovators.

units.la: THEMA VIII. UTRUM HIEME NAVIGANDUM.
units.tr: THESIS VIII. WHETHER ONE SHOULD SAIL IN WINTER.

units.la: I. Affirmatè.
units.tr: I. Affirmatively.

units.la: A sententia Horat. Oda 3. qua miratur audaciam nautarum: Merito: á periculis maris. At illis hyeme non navigabatur. Quid diceret de nostrorum nautarum sive virtute, sive temeritate.
units.tr: From the opinion of Horace, Ode 3, in which he marvels at the boldness of sailors: rightly so, given the dangers of the sea. Yet in those days they did not sail in winter. What would he say of the courage or the recklessness of our sailors?

units.la: Dubium videri, utrum hyeme navigandum, placere tibi affirmativam.
units.tr: The question seems doubtful, whether one should sail in winter; you hold the affirmative.

units.la: I. Ab honesto seu licito. Hoc ostendat a primo rei nauticæ autore Deo, qui Noachum hiemari in mari fecit: qui mare commerciis destinavit æque ac terram: nec prohibuit hieme navigare. Frustra ergo metui tempestates.
units.tr: I. From what is honourable or lawful. This is shown from God, the first author of seafaring, who made Noah spend the winter at sea; who destined the sea for commerce just as much as the land, and did not forbid sailing in winter. Therefore the fear of storms is groundless.

units.la: Ab utili: 1. quia lecus dimidia parte anni feriandum illi generi neri hominum. 2. quia major spes lucri hyeme, quibusdam cessantibus. 3. quia plus emolumenti ex navigatione hiemali, quam damni.
units.tr: From what is useful: (1) it is unfitting that that class of men should be idle for half the year; (2) there is greater hope of gain in winter, when some others are idle; (3) more advantage comes from winter navigation than loss.

units.la: III. A facili: quod probetur 1. ex mole navium, quæ fluctus hyemales sustinere queunt: secus ac temporibus antiquis. 2. A mappis exactioribus, exploratis maribus, & beneficio acus nauticæ repertæ: unde tenebræ parum obsunt, acu signante viam, ad lucernam: Unde peritia rei nauticæ longè major, quam pristinis seculis.
units.tr: III. From what is easy, which is proved (1) from the build of ships, which can withstand winter waves, unlike in ancient times; (2) from more exact charts, seas that have been explored, and the benefit of the magnetic compass, by which the darkness does little harm, since the compass marks the way and a lantern serves. Hence skill in seamanship is far greater than in earlier centuries.

units.la: IV. A necessario, si succurrendum obsessis, si in remotiora loca & alterum orbem migrandum.
units.tr: IV. From necessity: if the besieged must be relieved, or if one must migrate to more distant places and another hemisphere.

units.la: V. Ab exemplis veteribus, modernis.
units.tr: V. From examples, ancient and modern.

units.la: Conclus. Non igitur morandos timidiusculos, sed utendum occasione lucri dum affulget: æque in placido ac turbido mari periculum esse.
units.tr: Conclusion. Therefore timid people should not be held back, but the opportunity of gain should be seized while it shines; the danger is the same on a calm sea as on a rough one.

units.la: II. Negatè.
units.tr: II. Negatively.

units.la: Exord. A vituperio avaritiæ: utpote quæ mater omnium malorum: ostendatur 1. inductione quadam scelerum inde nascentium: 2. in specie quod vitam hominis lucro postponat, quod probetur exemplo hyemalis navigationis: quæ hisce temporibus invaluit: secus ac olim.
units.tr: Exordium. From the censure of avarice, which is the mother of all evils. This is shown (1) by a kind of induction of the crimes that arise from it; (2) specifically, that it puts human life after gain, which is proved by the example of winter navigation, which has prevailed in these times, unlike in former ages.

units.la: Propos. Quam cum antecessor probarit, tibi improbandam ac vitandam videri.
units.tr: Proposition. Since your predecessor has proved this, it seems to you that it must be condemned and avoided.

units.la: Confirm. I. Quia Deus vices rerum esse voluit: v.g. dierum, noctium; æstatis, hyemis. Eundem & flumina glacie, maria tempestatibus veluti obsignasse & infesta reddidisse. Hinc ordini non sine temeritate oblucari mortales. Resp. hinc argumento 1. Noachi proinde exemplum, ut extraordinarium, huc non quadrare: & 2. velle Deum rerum vices, & quietem moderatam: huc hiemes, huc Sabbata, festa spectasse.
units.tr: Confirmation. (1) Because God willed that things should have their changes: for example, of days and nights, of summer and winter. The same God is said to have sealed rivers with ice and seas with tempests, and made them hostile. Hence mortals, not without rashness, struggle against this order. Reply: to this argument, first, the example of Noah, being extraordinary, does not fit here; and second, God willed the changes of things and moderate rest; to this end he looked at winters, Sabbaths and festivals.

units.la: II. A difficili ac periculoso. Quod ostendatur 1. à periculo navigationis in genere. 2. in specie hyberno tempore, ubi infestum mare ob aquarum incrementa, tempestates, tenebras & noctes longissimas. Hinc refellat argumentum. 3. A crebris naufragiis & damnis.
units.tr: II. From what is difficult and dangerous. This is shown (1) from the danger of navigation in general; (2) specifically in the winter season, when the sea is hostile because of rising waters, storms, darkness and the very long nights. Hence he refutes the argument; (3) from frequent shipwrecks and losses.

units.la: III. Ab exemplis priscorum, qui hyberno tempore mare non opportunum judicarunt. Avaritiam nonnullorum mutasse mores antiquorum. Superiora illustrentur prolepsi à necessario, si v. g. succurrendum obsessis, si ad remotiora loca navigandum. Respon. Necessitatem carere lege. Hic vero sermonem esse & captato privatorum lucro, ob quod hominum vita manifesto periculo non objicienda.
units.tr: III. From the examples of the ancients, who judged the sea unsuitable in the winter season. The avarice of some has changed the morals of the ancients. The above points are illustrated by a prolepsis from necessity: if, for example, the besieged must be relieved, or if one must sail to more distant places. Reply: necessity is not bound by law. But here the discussion concerns gain sought by private persons, for the sake of which human life must not be exposed to manifest danger.

units.la: Melius itaque intermitti navigationes hybernas more veterum, ne ob vile lucrum rerum ordinem turbari, & sævienti Neptuno nequicquam reluctari videamur.
units.tr: It is therefore better that winter voyages be discontinued after the manner of the ancients, lest for paltry gain we seem to disturb the order of things and to struggle in vain against raging Neptune.

units.la: THEMA IX.
units.tr: THEMA IX.

units.la: ACTUS LEGISLATORIUS. Ex Liv. lib. 3. dec. 1.
units.tr: THE LEGISLATIVE ACT. From Livy, book 3, decade 1.

units.la: I. Tribunorum plebis Oratio ad Senatum, pro condendis Legibus.
units.tr: I. Speech of the tribunes of the plebs to the Senate, in favour of enacting laws.

units.la: Ab opportunitate, quia jam quies sit ab hostibus: ideoque constituendam Remp. ut domi tuto vivere queant, qui armis contra hostes se tutati sunt.
units.tr: From opportunity: since there is now quiet from the enemies, and it is therefore right to settle the Republic so that those who have defended themselves with arms against the enemy may also live safely at home.

units.la: Quandoquidem jam legati Athenis redierint, cum legibus Solonis, conscribendas esse Leges ex æquitate, quibus omnes subjecti sint.
units.tr: Since the envoys have now returned from Athens with the laws of Solon, laws should be drawn up on the principle of equity, by which all the subjects are bound.

units.la: I. A necessario: quia jus ex arbitrio & favore Senatus redditum afflixerit plebem & civitatem: Unde enata varia dissidia & metuendum porrò rebellionem & exitium civitatis; nisi iniquitas hæc corrigatur: quod non nisi per jus æquale ac leges fieri queat.
units.tr: I. From necessity: because law dispensed at the discretion and favour of the Senate has afflicted the plebs and the state. From this various dissensions have arisen, and there is further reason to fear rebellion and the ruin of the state, unless this injustice is corrected; and this cannot be done except through equal law and statutes.

units.la: II. Ab utili: videl. 1. jure certo & æquabili. 2. vindicatione oppressorum ab potentibus 3. concordia inter patres ac plebem; indeque secutura confusione hostium, qui discordia Romanorum animantur.
units.tr: II. From usefulness, namely: (1) through a fixed and even-handed law; (2) through the protection of the oppressed against the powerful; (3) through concord between the patricians and the plebs, and the consequent confusion of the enemies, who are emboldened by the discord of the Romans.

units.la: III. Ab exemplis aliorum populorum, quorum per leges salutares Resp. coaluerit & conservata sit. Uti sint præceteris Lacedæmonii ac Athenienses: quorum proinde celebret resp. & Legibus felicitatem illorum adscribat.
units.tr: III. From the examples of other peoples, whose commonwealths have grown strong and been preserved through salutary laws. Among these, let the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians stand before the rest; the commonwealth should therefore praise them and ascribe their prosperity to their laws.

units.la: IV. A facili, quia jam exemplar Legum Solonis attulerint Legati reduces, ad quarum exemplum leges conscribendæ sint.
units.tr: IV. From ease: since the envoys returning have already brought back the model of Solon's laws, after whose pattern the laws may be drawn up.

units.la: Omnino igitur tandem accedendum esse ad opus tam salutare: & si ita visum creandos X. viros sine provocatione, qui leges conscribant, ab omnibus approbandas.
units.tr: Therefore it is wholly fitting at last to proceed to so salutary a work; and, if it seems good, ten men should be appointed, without appeal, to draw up the laws, which are to be approved by all.

units.la: II. Consul nomine Senatus consentit in leges condendas, sed vel a Senatu, vel X. viris ex Senatu creandis conscribendas esse.
units.tr: II. The consul, in the name of the Senate, agrees to the enactment of laws, but says they should be drawn up either by the Senate itself or by ten men to be chosen from the Senate.

units.la: I. Exponat studium Senatus in Rempubl. per comparationem, videl. uti nunquam illum adversum fuisse Reip. emolumentis: ita nec adversari legibus quas & utiles & necessarias civitati facile concedat. Illustretur ab adversativa, videl. unde miretur, cur tanta initantia ac importunitate urgeant tribuni, ad quod sua sponte pronus sit Senatus: & corrigat hanc diffidentiam monela, ne de Senatu secus quid statuant, quam quod patriae patribus decet.
units.tr: I. Let him set forth the Senate's zeal for the Republic by comparison, namely that the Senate has never been opposed to the advantages of the Republic, and so it should not readily oppose laws that are both useful and necessary to the state. Let him illustrate this by way of contrast: he is astonished why the tribunes press so insistently and importunately for something to which the Senate is of its own accord inclined; and let him correct this distrust by a warning that they should not decide anything about the Senate otherwise than befits the fathers of the fatherland.

units.la: II. Doceat Legum terendarum difficultatem ac momentum.
units.tr: II. Let him show the difficulty and the weight of drafting laws.

units.la: 1. A natura Legum: quae explicetur.
units.tr: 1. From the nature of laws, which is to be explained:

units.la: a. Ab autore Legum: qui non tantum debeat esse vir prudens, qui aequitatem omnesq; circumstantias personarum, quibus, & rerum, de quibus leges terendae sunt bene perspectas habeat: sed etiam autoritate pollens, quod probetur a causa finali; ne leges latae temere contemnantur & antiquentur. Illustrentur haec exemplis celebriorum in diversis rebus p. Legislatorum.
units.tr: a. From the author of laws, who ought not only to be a prudent man, who has thoroughly grasped equity and all the circumstances of the persons and things for which laws are to be drawn up, but also one who holds authority, which is shown from the final cause: so that enacted laws are not rashly despised and abrogated. Let these points be illustrated by examples of the more famous lawgivers in different matters.

units.la: b. Ab objecto legum; quae sint personae ac res universae totius reipubl. in toga ac sago, in contractibus & delictis; fiat inductio quaedam praecipuarum: idque non modo praesentes, sed & futurae, quae praevidendae sint legislatori, ne subinde opus sit mutatione: utpote quae uti in omnibus, ita praecipue in Legibus periculosae. vide Polit. loco de Legibus.
units.tr: b. From the object of laws: what are the persons and things of the whole commonwealth, in peace and war, in contracts and offences. Let a certain induction of the chief matters be made, and not only of present matters but also of future ones, which must be foreseen by the lawgiver, lest there be need of change from time to time; for change is as dangerous in laws as in everything else. See Politian, in his place on laws.

units.la: c. A forma legum; quae est aequitas, quae difficilis inventu: adeo ut & prudentissimos saepe exerceat.
units.tr: c. From the form of laws, which is equity, and which is difficult to discover, so much so that it often exercises even the most prudent men.

units.la: 2. A fine Legum, quae est salus universorum ac reip. Hanc facile per interesse privatum removeri ab oculis.
units.tr: 2. From the end of laws, which is the welfare of all and of the commonwealth. This is easily removed from sight through private interest.

units.la: Haec illustrentur prolepsi ab allatis legibus Solonis: Respon. 1. magnum quidem esse hic subsidium; sed 2. requiri multam prudentiam in applicatione ad remp. Rom. Non omnibus easdem quadrare Leges.
units.tr: These points are to be illustrated by a prolepsis drawn from the laws of Solon. Reply: (1) indeed this is a great help here; but (2) much prudence is required in applying it to the Roman Republic; not the same laws suit everyone.

units.la: III. Inferat hinc consilium suum: nimirum negocium hoc committendum Senatui, cui res & arcana civitatis jam nota sint: aut vero si placeat id fieri per Decemviros, nec repugnare Senatum, natu, dummodo ob dictas supra rationes ex ipsorum corpore deligantur, qui rei tam arduae praeficiantur.
units.tr: III. Let him draw his counsel from this: namely that this business should be entrusted to the Senate, to which the affairs and secrets of the state are already known; or, if it pleases that it be done by decemvirs, the Senate does not oppose this, provided that, for the reasons stated above, they are chosen from its own body, and are placed in charge of so weighty a matter.

units.la: III. Tribuni nituntur pro Decemviris ex patribus & plebe creandis.
units.tr: III. The tribunes argue that the Decemvirs should be chosen from both the patricians and the plebs.

units.la: Exord. A statu causae; in quo conveniunt, in quo discrepant. Hinc laetari se dicant, quod patres cum plebe de condendis Legibus consentiant. Facile vicissim concedere se Legum conscribendarum difficultatem; & quod virorum prudentium, ac publica auctoritate instructorum hoc opus sit: uti Consul pro sua prudentia uberius edisseruerit. 2. differentiam tantum esse nonnullam, a quibus in specie leges ferendae.
units.tr: Exord. From the state of the case, showing where they agree and where they differ. They say they are glad that the patricians agree with the plebs about enacting laws. In turn they readily grant the difficulty of drafting laws, and that this task needs men of prudence, equipped with public authority, as the Consul has explained more fully in his wisdom. (2) There is only some difference, concerning from which orders the laws are to be proposed.

units.la: Propos. Consultum videri, eligi ex utroque ordine Decemviros huic rei aptissimos cui haec provincia committatur.
units.tr: Propos. It seems advisable that the Decemvirs best suited to this business be chosen from each order, and that the charge be committed to them.

units.la: Confirm. I. Ab aequo: quia par sit, ut quod omnes tangit, ab omnibus approbetur. Hic 1. tractet minorem: videl. leges ferendas esse, quae jus reddant aequaliter omnibus, tam superioribus, quam inferioribus. 2. Majorem: aequum igitur esse, ut ab omnibus probentur: Illustretur a contrario, si ab una tantum parte ferantur, facile alterum laedi.
units.tr: Confirm. (I) From equity: because it is right that what concerns all be approved by all. Here (1) take the minor premise: namely, that laws should be enacted which render justice equally to all, superiors and inferiors alike. (2) The major premise: it is therefore fair that they be approved by all. Let this be illustrated from the contrary: if they are enacted by one party only, the other is easily harmed.

units.la: II. Ab utili: 1. quia sic obviam iri poterit suspicioni ac diffidentiae inter patricios ac plebem: quae diu satis laceraverit patriam & hostibus aperuerit. 2. quia sic minus graves erunt populo semper ringenti contra novas leges.
units.tr: (II) From usefulness: (1) because in this way suspicion and distrust between the patricians and the plebs can be countered, which has for a long time torn the country apart and laid it open to enemies; (2) because in this way the laws will be less burdensome to the people, who always resist new laws.

units.la: III. A facili, & congruo: quoniam sic commodissime satisfieri queat requisitis legislatoris a Consule praescriptis: quippe 1. ex utroque ordine legendos prudentissimos, eosque 2. instruendos esse publica auctoritate; & injugendum ut nihil aliud spectent, quam publicam salutem ac tranquillitatem.
units.tr: (III) From ease and fitness: since in this way the requirements of a lawgiver prescribed by the Consul can be most conveniently met. Indeed (1) the most prudent men should be chosen from each order, and (2) they should be equipped with public authority, and enjoined to aim at nothing but the public safety and tranquillity.

units.la: Occurrat hinc tacitae objectioni, quasi Lycurgus in Spartana Solon in Atheniensi rep. foli leges tulerint. Respond. id placuisse tunc istis civitatibus; Romae alia rationem esse, & populu scissum in patricios & plebejos: utrique ordini sua jura tuenda esse: quod fieri nequeat, nisi ex utroque ordine Decemviri legantur.
units.tr: Let an unspoken objection be met here: as if Lycurgus at Sparta and Solon at Athens had enacted laws alone. Reply: that suited those states at that time; at Rome the situation is different, and the people is divided into patricians and plebeians. Each order must protect its own rights, and this cannot be done unless Decemvirs are chosen from each order.

units.la: Conclus. Ex repetitis breviter argumentis propositionem inferat, & ab ulteriori mora dehortetur, addito: utrique ordini suos esse magistratus; neutiquam praetereundos.
units.tr: Conclus. From the arguments briefly repeated, he should draw the proposition, and dissuade them from further delay, adding that each order has its own magistrates, which must by no means be passed over.

units.la: IV. Consultat & pronunciat pro Decemviris ex Senatu & patriciis creandis.
units.tr: IV. He deliberates and pronounces in favour of the creation of decemvirs from the Senate and the patricians.

units.la: I. Exord. A spe Senatus, fore scil. ut tribuni facilitate Senatus, qua in omnia hactenus populi vota consenserit, acquiescerent. Sed elucere fere contrarium, ut quo plura conceduntur, eo plura petant: instar fluvii rapacis. Hinc accedat ad hypothesin exponens, quomodo Senatus autoritatem omnem convellere satagant, dum leges ab illo ferri nolunt.
units.tr: I. Exordium. The Senate hopes, namely, that the tribunes will acquiesce because of the Senate's readiness, by which it has so far consented to all the wishes of the people. But the opposite appears nearly certain: the more is conceded, the more they ask, like a greedy river. Hence he proceeds to the hypothesis, explaining how they strive to overthrow all the authority of the Senate, while they refuse to have laws proposed by it.

units.la: II. Confutatio. Rationis I. Concedendo omnia: videl. etiam approbari debere leges non modo à tribunis, sed à plebe universa. Conscribere vero leges obligantes ipsos patricios & Senatum, eorum esse, qui in regimine sunt. Hunc ordinem non convellendum, si salva esse debeat Respublica.
units.tr: II. Refutation. First argument: by conceding everything, namely that the laws ought to be approved not only by the tribunes but by the whole plebs. But to draw up binding laws for the patricians and the Senate themselves belongs to those who are in government. This order must not be overturned, if the commonwealth is to remain safe.

units.la: Rationis II. Non esse causam suspicionis & diffidentiæ, nisi quam ipsi tribuni moveant. Nec graves esse posse leges ex æquitate conscriptas & ab ipsa plebe approbatas & receptas. Hinc digrediatur in lamentationem de discordia, quæ seritur ab invidis inter plebem & Senatum: præscindendam ansam esse; ita melius actum iri in republica.
units.tr: Second argument: there is no cause for suspicion and distrust, except that which the tribunes themselves stir up. Nor can laws drawn up in fairness, and approved and accepted by the plebs themselves, be burdensome. Hence he should digress into a lament over the discord which the envious sow between the plebs and the Senate: that occasion must be cut off; in this way things will go better in the commonwealth.

units.la: Rationis. III. Inter requisita Legislatoris esse, ut sit persona publica pollens autoritate & reip. peritus; hoc nemini magis saltem competere, quàm illis, qui in magistratu sunt. Ita actum esse semper in bene constitutis rebusp. ad quas frustra provocent Tribuni.
units.tr: Third argument: among the requisites of a lawgiver is that he be a public person of weight and experienced in affairs of state; this qualification belongs to no one more than to those who hold office. So it has always been in well-ordered commonwealths, to which the tribunes appeal in vain.

units.la: Conclus. Seu consilium: Ut omnis ulterior altercatio præscindatur, confirmandos esse Decem illos, qui leges Solonis attulerunt, ut illi leges ex æquo conscribant, & publicè proponant, ut ex voluntate populi universi corrigantur, rogentur vel abrogentur. Additur ratio: hanc esse Senatus sententiam, ulterius nihil concedi posse. Cavendum jam ne inani dissensione tempus teratur, & turbæ sine causa concitentur.
units.tr: Conclusion, or counsel: that, so that all further dispute may be cut off, those ten men who brought the laws of Solon should be confirmed, so that they may draw up laws on equal terms and publish them publicly, to be corrected, enacted or repealed at the will of the whole people. The reason is added: that this is the Senate's judgment, that nothing further can be conceded. Care must now be taken that time is not wasted in empty dissension, and that tumults are not stirred up without cause.

units.la: V. Populus habita deliberatione consentit in Decemviros ex patribus, sub certis conditionibus, creandos.
units.tr: V. The people, after deliberation, agree to the creation of decemvirs from among the fathers, under certain conditions.

units.la: I. Exord. Præ se ferat Πάθος doloris, ob opinionem Patrum, quasi putent tribunos turbas ex turbis quærere. Contra testentur de suæ intentionis sinceritate, pro quiete ac salute publica.
units.tr: I. Exordium. Let him display an emotion of grief, because of the opinion of the Fathers, as if they thought the tribunes sought tumults out of tumults. On the contrary, let him call witnesses to the sincerity of his intention, for the public peace and welfare.

units.la: II. Nō-
units.tr: II. Narration.

units.la: II. Narratio. Resumat præcipua capita declarationis Senatus per præ- sidem propositæ: videl.
units.tr: II. Narration. Let him recall the principal heads of the Senate's declaration, proposed through the president, namely:

units.la: 1. Non examinaturum se ea quæ contra rationes à populo prola- tas regesta sint à consule. Frustra enim disputationibus teri tem- pus, ubi agendum est.
units.tr: 1. That he himself will not examine those things which were said by the consul in reply to the arguments put forward by the people. For time is wasted in disputes where action is needed.

units.la: 2. Acceptare populum, quæ dixit Consul
units.tr: 2. That the people accept what the consul said:

units.la: a. De ferendis legibus ex æquitate, obligantibus omnes æqua- liter.
units.tr: a. concerning the bringing in of laws in fairness, binding all equally;

units.la: b. De censura legum & approbatione permittenda omnibus.
units.tr: b. concerning the censure of the laws and approval being allowed to all;

units.la: c. De studio concordiæ: quod ipse vicissim de tribunis & popu- lo repromittat.
units.tr: c. concerning zeal for harmony, which he himself in turn promises on behalf of the tribunes and the people.

units.la: III. Propof. Decretum populi proponat: videl. Hisce præsuppositis, habita deliberatione
units.tr: III. Proposition. Let him set out the decree of the people, namely: with these premises having been considered,

units.la: 1. Consentire populum in confirmationem Decemvirorum ad conscribendas legem.
units.tr: 1. the people consent to the confirmation of the decemvirs to draw up the laws;

units.la: 2. Sed non esse derogandum Legi Aciliæ de Aventino aliisque le- gibus sacratis.
units.tr: 2. but the Lex Acilia concerning the Aventine and the other sacred laws are not to be repealed.

units.la: IV. Confirm. Rationem addat: hisce enim legibus innixam esse po- puli libertatem, reip. quietem: nec permissurum illum ullo tem- pore, quicquam ex hisce derogari.
units.tr: IV. Confirmation. Let him add the reason: for the liberty of the people and the quiet of the commonwealth rest upon these laws, and he will never allow any of them to be taken away.

units.la: V. Concludat voto, felicis successus, ut cedat ad reip. salutem & per- petuitatem.
units.tr: V. Let him conclude with a wish for a happy outcome, that it may tend to the safety and perpetuity of the commonwealth.

units.la: VI. Appius Claudius Leges X. tabulis consignatas populo proponit. vide Liv. lib. 3. c. 34. hortans ad revisionem & concordiam.
units.tr: VI. Appius Claudius proposes to the people the laws sealed on the ten tables. See Livy, book 3, chapter 34, exhorting them to revision and concord.

units.la: Exord. A re gesta: ubi breviter referat, 1. quod populus decemviris legumlationem commiserit. 2. quod ipsi omni studio commissum negocium executi sint, Solonis leges Romanæ reip. applicando.
units.tr: Exordium. From the event: where he briefly relates, 1. that the people committed the legislation to the decemvirs; 2. that they themselves carried out the commissioned business with all zeal, applying the laws of Solon to the Roman commonwealth.

units.la: Propof. Præmisso voto proponat Leges publice in tabulis, jubeat ire populum, legere, corrigere pro lubitu.
units.tr: Proposition. After prefacing with a wish, let him publish the laws on tables, and bid the people go and read them and correct them as they please.

units.la: Confirm. I. Provocet ad fidem sinceritatem & decemvirorum, qua in hoc negocio versati sint, ad æqualitatem juris inter omnes: excusetque si cubi lapsi humanitus; decem omnia prævidere non posse, in tanta rerum varietate.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. Let him appeal to the good faith and sincerity of the decemvirs, with which they have engaged in this business, towards equality of right among all; and let him excuse them if they have slipped in any place through human frailty: they cannot foresee everything in such variety of affairs.

units.la: II. Proponi hinc populo dicat leges: Nam 1. æquum esse, ut ab omnibus approbetur, quod omnes tangit: 2. Plus enim pollere mulmultorum ingenia, 3. populo nota esse gravamina civium. 4. tolli sic omnem suspicionem inter Senatum ac plebem. 5. praescindi sic omnem discordiarum materiam, quae diu satis vexaverit populum Romanum. Hinc
units.tr: II. Let him then tell the people that the laws are to be put forward: for 1. it is fair that what touches all be approved by all; 2. for the wits of many have greater weight; 3. the grievances of citizens are known to the people; 4. in this way all suspicion between the Senate and the plebs is removed; 5. in this way all material of discord, which has long troubled the Roman people, is cut off. Hence

units.la: III. Digrediatur in hortationem ad concordiam: utpote quae 1. nutrix rerumpubl. dum conservat pacem cum hoste, tranquillitatem inter cives, benevolentiam inter omnes ordines, 2. verum illud coelitus demissum Palladium est, quo salvo salva semper erit respublica. 3. illa sublata pessum iri omnia.
units.tr: III. He digresses into an exhortation to concord: which is 1. the nurse of the commonwealth, since while it preserves peace with the enemy, it preserves tranquillity among the citizens and goodwill among all orders; 2. it is that true Palladium sent down from heaven, with which safe, the commonwealth will always be safe; 3. with it removed, all things will go to ruin.

units.la: Conclus. Repetita propositione paratos decem viros dicat, ad mutandum, addendum, & detrahendum ex populi voto: hinc concludat voto feliciis auspicii ac successus.
units.tr: Conclusion. Having repeated the proposition, let him say that the decemvirs are ready to change, add to and remove from the will of the people; hence let him conclude with a wish for a happy beginning and outcome.

units.la: X. CONSULTATIO DE VITAE GENERE ELIGENDO.
units.tr: X. A CONSULTATION ON CHOOSING THE KIND OF LIFE

units.la: I. Pro vita privata & theoretica.
units.tr: I. For the private and contemplative life.

units.la: Exord. A difficultate praesentis deliberationis. Ratio 1. quia de totius vitae cursu statuendum. 2. quia statuendum in aetate minus provida. 3. quia mutari consilium sine damno nequit. Illustretur exemplo Herculis Prodici, ex 3. offic. Cic. Concludatur: Ergo merito sollicite de vitae genere deliberandum.
units.tr: Exordium: On the difficulty of the present deliberation. Reasons: (1) because a decision must be made about the whole course of life; (2) because the decision must be made at an age less far-sighted; (3) because a change of plan cannot be made without loss. Let this be illustrated by the example of Hercules in Prodicus, from Cic. Off. 3. Conclusion: therefore it is rightly necessary to deliberate carefully about the kind of life.

units.la: Propof. Te igitur, salvo aliorum judicio statuere praeferendam esse vitam theoreticam & privatam: id quod breviter evincendum.
units.tr: Proposition: Therefore, saving the judgment of others, you will maintain that the private and contemplative life is to be preferred. This is to be demonstrated briefly.

units.la: Confirm.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. Amoliatur suspicionem, quasi vel vitam ociosam, Epicuraeam ac monasticam probet, utpote beluinam ocio superstitione ac vitiis plurimis scatentem, omnibus bonis detestabilem, vel vitam practicam & negociosam improbet, uti enim illa perfugienda, ita hanc merito colendam esse, ne demus & respublicae intereant, &c.
units.tr: I. Let him remove the suspicion that he approves an idle, Epicurean and monastic life, as bestial, teeming with superstition and many vices, and detestable to all good men; or that he disapproves the practical and busy life. For just as the former is to be shunned, so the latter is rightly to be cultivated, lest we give up and commonwealths perish, etc.

units.la: II. Sententiam exponat, roboretque rationibus a commodis vitae privatae.
units.tr: II. Let him set out his opinion and strengthen it with arguments drawn from the advantages of private life.

units.la: 1. Quia praebet tranquillitatem animi, liberam ab affectibus, qui turbant vitam publicam. Haec tranquillitas supra caduca omnia effert hominem, & Deo similem reddit, sine hac nihil jucundum, vide Sen. de tranquill. animi. Illustretur comparatione vitae publ. 2.
units.tr: 1. Because it provides tranquillity of mind, free from the passions that disturb public life. This tranquillity raises a man above all perishable things and makes him like God; without it nothing is pleasant. See Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind. Let this be illustrated by comparison with public life.

units.la: 3. Quia vita privata mater est virtutum omnium, videl. σωφροσύνης, temperantiæ, justitiæ, sapientiæ, quibus nihil majus in vita.
units.tr: 2. Because private life is the mother of all the virtues, namely sophrosynē [σωφροσύνη], temperance, justice and wisdom, than which nothing is greater in life.

units.la: 3. Quia vacua est à molestiis & ærumnis, quibus subjecta vita activa. Hic exaggeret curas & labores vitæ activæ in aula, curia, foro, bello; & comparet suavitatem vitæ privatæ.
units.tr: 3. Because it is free from troubles and hardships, to which the active life is subject. Here he should magnify the cares and labours of the active life at court, in the senate, in the forum and in war, and set against them the sweetness of private life.

units.la: 4. Quia secura est ab iis casibus, quibus vita actuosa subjecta est. Quorum unum atque alterum proponat.
units.tr: 4. Because it is safe from those chances to which the active life is subject. Let him set forth one or two of them.

units.la: 5. Quia Patriarchis & Sapientibus, Socrati, Pythag. Platoni, Arist, frequentata salubriter; imò viri maximi ex rep. ad hanc redierunt, Sylla, Cicero, Dioclet. Carolus V. ideoque & prædicata Sapientibus. vide Sen. de tranquillitate animi.
units.tr: 5. Because it has been pursued profitably by the patriarchs and the wise: Socrates, Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle. Indeed the greatest men have returned to this life from the commonwealth: Sulla, Cicero, Diocletian, Charles V. Therefore it has also been commended by the wise. See Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind.

units.la: Conclus. Repetita breviter rationum summa, ad hanc adhortetur; occurrens simul objectioni: si minus splendida, etiam minus periculosa est.
units.tr: Conclusion: Having briefly repeated the sum of the reasons, let him exhort to this life, meeting at the same time the objection: if it is less splendid, it is also less dangerous.

units.la: II. Pro vita publica & actuosa.
units.tr: II. For the public and active life.

units.la: Exord. Ab emblemate psittaci: illum solum inter aves cavea delectari, cum reliquæ omnes libertatem ament. Tales videri tibi & homines illos, qui spretis vitæ negotiis domi suæ se abdunt cum Diogene. Accedatur ad propositum. Ex illis etiam videri tibi antecessorem, qui vitam privatam & theor. commendavit. Non invidere te illi suum otiū; dumodo aliis suadere hoc ne lategisset.
units.tr: Exordium: From the emblem of the parrot, which alone among birds delights in its cage, while all the others love liberty. Such, it seems to you, are those men who, scorning the business of life, shut themselves away at home like Diogenes. Let us come to the proposition. From them you may also see your predecessor, who commended the private and contemplative life. Do not begrudge him his leisure, provided he had not tried to persuade others of it.

units.la: Propos. Te igitur ipsius sententiam breviter examinaturum & meliori jure vitam publicam & actuosam sapienti præferendam esse evicturum.
units.tr: Proposition: Therefore you will briefly examine his opinion and, with the better right, prove that the public and active life is to be preferred by the wise.

units.la: Confutatio. Rationum antecessoris. Hic
units.tr: Refutation of the arguments of the predecessor. Here

units.la: I. Acceptet utiliter, quod otiosam vitam ipse improbarit, probárit contra actuosam; inferatque tanto meliorem esse vitam, quanto longius ab otio recedit, nihil enim naturæ adversum magis, quam otium.
units.tr: I. Let him usefully accept that the predecessor condemned the idle life but approved the active one, and let him infer that life is so much better the further it withdraws from idleness, for nothing is more contrary to nature than idleness.

units.la: II. Examinat rationes antecessoris, respondendo ad
units.tr: II. He examines the arguments of the predecessor, replying to them:

units.la: 1. Tranquillitatem animi non in otio, sed in honesto negotio quærendam esse, Dei exemplo.
units.tr: 1. That tranquillity of mind is to be sought not in leisure but in honourable business, by the example of God.

units.la: 2. Virtutem semper actuosam esse, & ex honestis nasci actionibus.
units.tr: 2. That virtue is always active and springs from honourable actions.

units.la: 3. Labores & molestias non fugiendas, sed virtute superandas esse.
units.tr: 3. That labours and troubles are not to be fled from but overcome by virtue.

units.la: 4. Nec solitariam vitam vacuam esse à casibus tragicis.
units.tr: 4. That the solitary life is not free from tragic chances.

units.la: 5. Optimos quosque minimè ociosos fuisse: nec ipse Plato, Arist. Cic. aulam & remp. detrectarunt, qui redierunt ad vitam contemplativam, vel tædio senectæ, & laborum, vel ob eversam remp.
units.tr: 5. That the best men were by no means idle; nor did Plato, Aristotle and Cicero reject the court and the commonwealth, though they returned to the contemplative life, either from the weariness of old age and of toils, or because the commonwealth had been overthrown.

units.la: Claudatur hæc pars & transeatur ad Confirm. Rationes afferat pro vita publica & actuosa.
units.tr: Let this part be closed and let us pass to the confirmation. Let him bring arguments for the public and active life.

units.la: I. Ab honesto, quod ostendatur exemplo ipsius Dei, mundum gubernantis: tum ipsius naturæ, ubi nihil ociosum, probetur inductione. Tum ipsius hominis, qui ad societatem inclinat, animal politicum juxta Arist.
units.tr: I. From the honourable: let this be shown by the example of God himself governing the world; then from nature itself, where nothing is idle, let it be proved by induction; and then from man himself, who inclines to society, a political animal according to Aristotle.

units.la: II. A necessario, quod probetur a natura societatis humanæ, quæ absque præfectura esse nequeat. Illustretur a contrario si omnes remp. desererent.
units.tr: II. From the necessary: let this be proved from the nature of human society, which cannot exist without government. Let it be illustrated by the contrary case, if all men were to desert the commonwealth.

units.la: III. Ab utili redundante, tum ad publ. in Ecclesia, Politia, Schola, tum ad hominem politicum ipsum, qui est honor & gloria &c. ubi comparentur heroes, cum tenebrione Diogene Tigimone, &c.
units.tr: III. From the useful, which overflows both to the public, in Church, polity and school, and to the political man himself, who is honour and glory, etc. Here heroes are to be compared with the skulking Diogenes and with Timon.

units.la: Concluf. Inculcata breviter argumentorum summa, vitam publicam longe præferendam privatæ, & sapienti amplectendam esse.
units.tr: Conclusion: Having impressed briefly the sum of the arguments, namely that the public life is far to be preferred to the private and is to be embraced by the wise.

units.la: XI. UTRUM PEREGRINI EXCLUDENDI SINT A DIGNITATIBUS ET REGIMINE REIP.
units.tr: XI. Whether foreigners should be excluded from offices and from the government of the commonwealth.

units.la: A. Affirmatè.
units.tr: A. In the affirmative.

units.la: Exord. Ab administrationis Reip. momento ac pondere.
units.tr: Exordium: From the importance and weight of administering the commonwealth.

units.la: Prop. Confitentur omnes, uti arduum, ita maximè momentosum esse, gerere rempubl.
units.tr: Proposition: Everyone admits that governing the commonwealth is as difficult as it is most important.

units.la: Ratio. Quia hinc dependet salus perniciesve Civitatis, omniumque subditorum; quæ cum regimine bono floret; cum malo corrumpitur peritque.
units.tr: Reason: Because the safety or ruin of the state and of all its subjects depends on it. These flourish under good government and are corrupted and perish under bad.

units.la: Exerg. A simil, desumta ab anima malè habente, quæ secum trahit perniciem corporis: imperito nauclero, qui perdit navem.
units.tr: Exergasia: From a simile of a sick soul, which drags the ruin of the body along with it, and of an inexperienced pilot, who loses the ship.

units.la: A testimonio Plat. qui beatas prædicat Civitates quibus sapientes imperant: Illustretur contrario, ubi imperiti rerum potiuntur. Addatur testimonium Esa. væ tibi terra &c. Exemplis omnium seculorum.
units.tr: From the testimony of Plato, who calls blessed those states ruled by wise men. Let this be illustrated by the contrary case, where the unskilled hold power. Add the testimony of Isaiah, "Woe to you, land," etc. Add examples from all ages.

units.la: Concl. Quare maximopere vigilandum, quales rectores reip. præficiantur.
units.tr: Conclusion: Therefore we must take the greatest care what kind of rulers are set over the commonwealth.

units.la: Propos. Cumque non exigua usque in hodiernum diem semper fuerit de Regentum personis disceptatio; nos in praesentiarum de admissione vel exclusione peregrinorum à republ. disquiremus. Vos interim Aud.
