units.tr: Propos. Since the debate about the persons of rulers has never been small, down to the present day, we shall for now inquire into the admission or exclusion of foreigners from the commonwealth. Meanwhile, listen.

units.la: Confirm. 1. A defectu requisitorum in Regente; uti sunt
units.tr: Confirm. 1. From the lack of the requisites in a ruler, such as:

units.la: α. Intima notitia arcanorum reip. videl. redituum, federum, simultatum cum exteris, vicinis; inclinationis civium, magistratus; commerciorum; rerum gestarum.
units.tr: α. Intimate knowledge of the secrets of the commonwealth, namely its revenues, treaties, enmities with foreign and neighbouring powers, the inclinations of citizens and magistrates, commerce, and the deeds done.

units.la: β. Amoris Civium activi, passivi: qui major inter συμπολίτας.
units.tr: β. Love of the active and passive citizens, which is greater among fellow citizens [συμπολίτας].

units.la: γ. Autoritatis; quippe quae nascitur ex notitia meritisque maiorum, vitae actae, propinquorum.
units.tr: γ. Authority; which arises from the knowledge and merits of ancestors, one's past life, and one's relatives.

units.la: Omnia haec desiderantur, aut saltem praesumuntur desiderari in peregrino; quod ostendatur rationibus, testimoniis, exemplis, vindicetur à contradictione per prolepsin.
units.tr: All these are lacking, or at least presumed to be lacking, in a foreigner. This should be shown by reasons, testimonies and examples, and defended against objection by prolepsis.

units.la: 2. A periculo, ne offensus forte prodat patriam. Mercenarius enim est. Exempla vetera, moderna. Aut ne cum suis patriotis incautius communicet; aut à Patria salarium habeat. Item ne suos post se trahat, peregrinis patriam oppleat, cives excludat, novos mores invehat; ne si oboriantur difficultates, concitetur seditio, omnibus in exterorum gubernationem culpam conferentibus.
units.tr: 2. From danger: lest, offended, he perhaps betray the fatherland, for he is a mercenary. Ancient and modern examples. Either he will communicate too carelessly with his fellow countrymen, or he receives his salary from the fatherland. Likewise, he will draw his own after him, overwhelm the fatherland with foreigners, exclude the citizens, and introduce new customs; and if difficulties arise, sedition will be stirred up, everyone laying the blame on the government of foreigners.

units.la: 3. A probro, quod inde redundat in patriam, quasi non alat ingenia, quae regendae patriae sufficiant, ut alium de accersi debeant. Unde neglectus literarum, & odium in patriam penes cordatiores.
units.tr: 3. From disgrace, which flows back onto the fatherland, as if it did not nurture talents sufficient to govern it, so that others must be summoned from abroad. Hence comes neglect of letters, and hatred of the fatherland among the more discerning.

units.la: 4. Ab exemplo cum praxi statutisque omnium regnorum, populorum, quibus exteri fere à magistratu arcentur: fiat inductio. Vindicentur per prolepsin, ea quae a praxi plurimorum principum objici queunt: scil. illos infringere leges populorum, plus curare amplificationem suae potestatis, quam salutem communem.
units.tr: 4. From the example, practice and statutes of all kingdoms and peoples, by which foreigners are almost everywhere kept away from magistracy. Let an induction be made. Let there be defended by prolepsis what may be objected from the practice of many princes: namely, that they break the laws of their peoples and care more for the enlargement of their own power than for the common welfare.

units.la: 5. Referri à Politicis inter notas tyranni, cooptare ministros extraneos. Addantur testimonia diversorum; ut Platonis, &c.
units.tr: 5. Politicians count among the marks of a tyrant that he co-opts foreign ministers. Add the testimonies of various writers, such as Plato, etc.

units.la: Conclus. Propositionem repetens cum praecipuis argumentis, addita adhortatione ad juventam patriam, ut dignam se reddat praebeatque cui reip. habenae committantur, ne opus sit, aliunde vocare, quos tecum habere queas.
units.tr: Conclus. Repeating the proposition with the chief arguments, with an added exhortation to the youth of the fatherland to make themselves worthy and fit to be entrusted with the reins of the commonwealth, so that there is no need to call from elsewhere those whom you could have with you.

units.la: B. Affirmatè.
units.tr: B. In the affirmative.

units.la: Exord. A salubritate consilii illorum, qui ad unionem hortantur.
units.tr: Exord. From the wholesomeness of the counsel of those who urge union.

units.la: Προβολή. Saluberrimè suadunt, qui sepolita omni factiositate humanam societatem ex hominis natura arcessunt; adeóque ex orbe veluti urbem efficere satagunt.
units.tr: Prolepsis. Those advise most wholesomely who, having buried all factiousness, derive human society from the nature of man, and therefore strive, as it were, to make a single city of the world.

units.la: Αιτιολογία. Illi enim quam maximè Dei imitantur naturam, exomnibus ad regnum suum admittentis, & eandem omnibus naturam, ad societatem propensam communicantis.
units.tr: Aetiology. For they most closely imitate the nature of God, who admits all to his kingdom and communicates the same nature, inclined to society, to all.

units.la: Εξήγησις. Unde culpandi semper illi vili sunt, qui propriæ genti plus æquo addicti, humanæ societatis jura solvunt. Ἐπιτέγημα. Non quod omnis arctior conjunctio uniusgentis, populi, civitatis tollenda; sed quod hæc in præjudicium societatis humanæ non nimium extendenda sit. Qualis videtur sententia illorum, qui ob solam gentis differentiam, virtutem ac eruditionem aspernandas censent.
units.tr: Explanation. Hence those who, devoted to their own nation beyond measure, violate the rights of human society, are always rightly condemned as base. Epitegma. Not that every closer bond within one race, people or state is to be abolished, but that it should not be extended too far to the prejudice of human society. Such seems the opinion of those who think that virtue and learning are to be spurned merely on account of difference of nation.

units.la: Propos. In hac sententia cum & A. esse videatur, qui exteros à magistratu ac dignitatibus arcendos judicat, agedum nos contrarium afferere non dubitamus: sperantes illum haud molestè laturum, quod uti ille, ita & ego arbitrandi libertatem hic mihi sumam.
units.tr: Propos. Since in this opinion A also seems to be included, who judges that foreigners should be kept away from magistracy and dignities, let us not hesitate to maintain the contrary, hoping that he will not take it badly that, just as he has, so I too claim here the liberty of judgement.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: 1. A Necessitate, quia contingere potest, ut patria idoneis careat subjectis, aut saltem, ut magis idonea inveniantur in peregrinis. Illustretur à difficultate regiminis, quod licet ab omnibus fere ambiatur, tamen non omnium quadrat humeris.
units.tr: 1. From necessity: because it can happen that the fatherland lacks suitable subjects, or at least that more suitable ones are found among foreigners. Let it be illustrated from the difficulty of government, which, although almost everyone seeks it, does not fit everyone's shoulders.

units.la: 2. Ab utilitate: quæ ostenditur. Quia hac ratione conciliantur peregrini vicini, si ex illorum numero in nostram assumantur remp. qui eidem præsint, illi enim suos habent propinquos in sua patria, per quos multum ibidem possunt. β. Quia sic egregiæ ingenia aliis eripiuntur, nobis acquiruntur; unde accessio nostræ reip. Afferantur exempla regnorum, rerump. qui sic creverunt. Illustretur contrariis exemplis, & ratione, quod nemo facile in alienam commigraturus sit civitatem, nisi uti onerum ita & honorum ibidem sit particeps. Unde exitium tandem reip,
units.tr: 2. From utility, which is shown thus. By this method neighbouring foreigners are won over, if some of their number are taken into our commonwealth and set over it, for they have kinsmen in their own country through whom they can accomplish much there. β. Because in this way outstanding talents are snatched from others and gained for us, whence comes an increase to our commonwealth. Let examples of kingdoms and commonwealths that grew in this way be cited. Let it be illustrated by contrary examples and by reason: no one will easily migrate to a foreign state unless he shares there in its honours as well as its burdens. Hence, at last, the ruin of the commonwealth.

units.la: 3. Ab æquitate. Noftrates cupimus alibi honestè haberi, & emergere, fiat itaque reciprocum. Virtuti debetur præmium, ubiabicunque invenitur. Æquum est, ut honorum sint capaces, qui cives facti onera reip. subeunt.
units.tr: 3. From equity. We ourselves wish to be honourably treated and to rise elsewhere; let there therefore be reciprocity. Reward is owed to virtue wherever it is found. It is fair that those who have become citizens and undertake the burdens of the commonwealth should be capable of its honours.

units.la: 4. A similibus: In familiam cooptatus, juris filiorum fit particeps: In Ecclesiae communionem concedens, omnibus ejusdem gaudet privilegiis & beneficiis: quid ni in civitate eodem modo?
units.tr: 4. From similar cases: one adopted into a family becomes a sharer in the rights of the children; one admitted into the communion of the Church enjoys all its privileges and benefits. Why not in the state in the same way?

units.la: Confutat. I. Proponantur summatim argumenta contraria. At inquis desunt necessaria requisita exteris, periculum est proditionis, dedecus hoc est indigenis; exempla, praxis ac statuta sunt in contrarium; tyrannorum nota est vocare peregrinos.
units.tr: Confutat. I. Let the contrary arguments be set out briefly. But you say that foreigners lack the necessary requisites, that there is danger of betrayal, that it is a disgrace to the natives; that examples, practice and statutes are against it; and that calling in foreigners is a mark of tyrants.

units.la: II. Refutentur sigillatim.
units.tr: II. Each objection is answered in turn.

units.la: 1. a. Non norunt intima reip. Resp. Imo tales eligendi, qui apti sunt. Et vero quis nescit, exteros aliquando linceos esse, ubi cives talpae sunt in rebus propriis.
units.tr: 1. They do not know the inner workings of the commonwealth. Answer: on the contrary, such men should be chosen as are fit. And indeed, who does not know that foreigners are sometimes lynx-eyed where citizens are moles in their own affairs?

units.la: b. Deest amor mutuus? Resp. Eligendi, qui virtute & eruditione amorem civium sibi conciliarunt, aut conciliare queunt. Quin imo saepe aemulatio est inter συμπλίτας, quae minime inter peregrinos.
units.tr: b. Is mutual love lacking? Answer: those should be chosen who by virtue and learning have won, or are able to win, the affection of the citizens. Indeed, rivalry is often found among fellow citizens [συμπολίτας], which is by no means so common among foreigners.

units.la: c. Deest autoritas? Imo contra, plus ordinarie exteros admiramur, quam indigenas, quos aut invidia premit aut vilipendium.
units.tr: c. Is authority lacking? On the contrary, we ordinarily admire foreigners more than natives, whom either envy or contempt weighs down.

units.la: 2. Periculosum est. Resp. Viri vitae probatae eligendi, non levesaut incogniti. Et vero, quis tam vecors erit, ut prodat locum, qui honoribus ipsum cumulavit, ubi rerum suarum posuit domicilium.
units.tr: 2. It is dangerous. Answer: men of proven life should be chosen, not the careless or the unknown. And indeed, who would be so mad as to betray the place which has heaped honours upon him and where he has set up his home?

units.la: 3. Probrosum civibus. Resp. Praestat probrum hoc, quam proditio patriae; acuet juventam ut dignum se faciat. Imo gloriae est civitati, quae optima ac florem aliunde legit, ut ornetur Respubl.
units.tr: 3. It is disgraceful to the citizens. Answer: this disgrace is better than betrayal of the fatherland, and it will spur the young to make themselves worthy. Indeed, it is a glory to a city that chooses the best and the flower of talent from elsewhere, so that the commonwealth may be adorned.

units.la: 4. Obstat praxis, statuta plerorumque populorum. Resp. illa non universalia, & intelligenda sunt, si adsint idonea aeque subjecta. Apud plurimos videmus negligi discrimen suo cum emolumento; unde cadit proprium hoc tyrannorum esse. Non enim hoc volumus excludendos indigenas, studio accersendos peregrinos, quod tyranni solent, sed si idonei satis haberi non queant in patria, quaerendos esse in peregrinia; id quodrationes allatae, quarum fiat brevis repetitio, suadent.
units.tr: 4. Practice and the statutes of most peoples stand in the way. Answer: those are not universal rules, and must be understood as applying where suitable men of equal qualification are available. Among very many peoples we see the distinction neglected for the sake of their own advantage, whence it follows that this is not the peculiar mark of tyrants. For we do not wish natives to be excluded and foreigners eagerly summoned, as tyrants are wont to do; rather, if suitable men cannot be had in sufficient number at home, they should be sought abroad. The reasons adduced, of which a brief repetition may be made, persuade us of this.

units.la: Concluf. Propositionem inferens, addito pondere, de aestimanda virtute, ejusque praemio inter cunctos.
units.tr: Conclusion. Drawing the proposition together, with added weight, concerning the valuing of virtue and its reward among all.

units.la: THEMA XII. ELECTIO CICERONIS IN CONSULEM.
units.tr: THEME XII. THE ELECTION OF CICERO AS CONSUL.

units.la: I. Tribunus commendat Ciceronem pro rostris. vide Orat. pro L. Manil.
units.tr: I. A tribune recommends Cicero from the Rostra. See the oration for L. Manilius.

units.la: Exord. Allegatis silentii diuturni causis, amore quietis & cura rerum suarum; rationes dicendi jam exponit, tum praesens periculum reip.tum erroneam sententiam nonnullorum, qua patria & natales obstent Ciceronis consulatui. vide Exord pro L. Manil.
units.tr: Exord. Having given the reasons for his long silence, his love of quiet and his care for his own affairs, he now sets out his reasons for speaking: first the present danger to the commonwealth, then the mistaken opinion of some that Cicero's country and birth stand in the way of his consulship. See the exordium of the speech for L. Manilius.

units.la: Propos. Necessario huic opinioni obviam eundum; ne dum affectibus indulgemus, negligatur salus publica.
units.tr: Propos. This opinion must necessarily be opposed, lest, while we indulge our feelings, the public safety be neglected.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Repraesentet periculum reip. ob machinationem pessimorum, qui summa imis pervertere satagant; Hanc patescere indies magis magisque & jam constare penitus.
units.tr: Tractatio. I. He sets out the danger to the commonwealth from the schemes of the worst men, who strive to overturn the highest things from the lowest; and he shows that this is becoming clearer every day and is now fully established.

units.la: II. Exponat qualis requiratur Consul: videl. 1. non suspectus, multo minus particeps conjurationis. 2. vigilans ad omnes casus. 3. Magnanimus: qui tantis turbis par sit, & obviam ire audeat.
units.tr: II. He describes what sort of consul is required: namely (1) one who is not suspected, much less a party to the conspiracy; (2) one who is watchful against every contingency; (3) one who is magnanimous, equal to such great disturbances and bold enough to meet them.

units.la: III. Talem pro caeteris esse Ciceronem, cujus proinde praedicet 1. Studium pro rep. ex vita anteacta. 2. Vigilantiam, quippe qui arcana conjurat: jam expiscatus sit. 3. Magnanimitatem negociis parem: utpote qui nullis amicitiis implicitus famam quaerat ex recte factis.
units.tr: III. That Cicero is such a man beyond all others. He therefore points out (1) his zeal for the commonwealth, shown in his past life; (2) his vigilance, since he has already uncovered the secret conspiracy; (3) his magnanimity, equal to the business, since, entangled in no friendships, he seeks his fame from right deeds.

units.la: Conclus. Huncigitur ex dictis rationibus eligendum videri. Potius enim esse ut prospectum sit reip. quam ambitioni patriciorum.
units.tr: Conclus. Therefore it seems that he should be chosen on the grounds stated. For it is better that provision be made for the commonwealth than for the ambition of the patricians.

units.la: II. Alius Tribunus dissuadet electionem Ciceronis.
units.tr: II. Another tribune argues against electing Cicero.

units.la: Exord. Amoliatur suspicionem siniistram malevolentiae ergaCiceronem & ignorantiae publici vel privati comodi: videl. non eu se esse, qui Ciceroni adversus sit, aut ignoret pericula reip. vel qui privatam hic suam suorumque utilitatem spectet, multo minus Catilinae faveat. Interim tamen pro publica salute dicendum se existimare quae sentiat.
units.tr: Exord. He removes the sinister suspicion of ill will towards Cicero, and of ignorance of public or private advantage: namely, that he is not one who opposes Cicero, or who is unaware of the dangers to the commonwealth, or who looks here to his own and his family's advantage, much less that he favours Catiline. Meanwhile, he says, he must speak for the public safety what he thinks.

units.la: Propos. Non videre se consultum esse, ut hoc tempore Cicero eligatur.
units.tr: Propos. He does not see that it is advisable for Cicero to be elected at this time.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Concedat ipsi notitiam juris, vigilantiam, dexteritatem & eloquentiam in causis agendis; uti & studium pro rep. & integrigritatem in dignitatibus, quibus præfuit hactenus: at majus quid à consule requiri: videl. affectum paternum erga remp.
units.tr: Tractatio. I. He grants Cicero knowledge of the law, vigilance, skill and eloquence in conducting cases, as well as zeal for the commonwealth and integrity in the offices he has held so far; but something greater is required of a consul, namely a fatherly affection towards the republic.

units.la: II. Desideret in ipso
units.tr: II. He desires the following in him:

units.la: 1. Natales & patriciatum. Hic a. exponat antiquam consuetudinem, quæ non facile mutanda, utpote ratione subnixam. b. Statum Ciceronis. c. Periculum exinde, si extraneus contra patricios acerbius statuere velit.
units.tr: 1. Birth and patrician status. Here he should set out the ancient custom, which is not easily changed, being grounded in reason. b. Cicero's own status. c. The danger that would follow if an outsider wished to rule more harshly against the patricians.

units.la: 2. Notitiam status reip. 1. quia careat documentis, monitis & exemplis majorum 2. quia in privatorum causis omne tempus posuit. Aliud vero esse jura novisse, aliud gubernandi rationem. Male ex jure Titii & Mævii judicari causas regnorum ac rerump.
units.tr: 2. Knowledge of the state of the commonwealth: (1) because he lacks the teachings, warnings and examples of his ancestors; (2) because he has spent all his time on private causes. But knowing the law is one thing, and knowing how to govern is another. It is wrong to judge the causes of kingdoms and commonwealths by the law of Titius and Maevius.

units.la: 3. Affectum paternum adversus remp. utpote qui extraneus: Illustretur simili à vitrico aut noverca & vero patre aut matre.
units.tr: 3. A fatherly affection towards the commonwealth, since he is an outsider. Let this be illustrated by a stepfather or stepmother compared with a true father or mother.

units.la: Concluf. Videri itaque hoc præsertim tempore prætereundum Ciceronem, & ex indigenis ac patriciis aliquem eligendum.
units.tr: Concl. It seems therefore that, especially at this time, Cicero should be passed over and someone from the native patricians chosen.

units.la: III. Consul examinatis breviter orationibus Tribunorum, Ciceronem eligendum suadeat.
units.tr: III. The consul, having briefly examined the speeches of the tribunes, urges that Cicero be chosen.

units.la: Exord. Paucis referat, quæ pro & contra Ciceronem dicta à Tribunis. Laudet studium utriusque, quod in præsenti periculo solliciti pro republ. Omnino libertatem & amorem patriæ hoc requirere, ut voces & suffragia libera sint.
units.tr: Exord. He briefly recounts what was said by the tribunes for and against Cicero. He praises the zeal of both, that they are anxious for the republic in the present danger. Altogether, freedom and love of country require this: that voices and votes be free.

units.la: Propos. Ideoque & se rationes allatas examinaturum, ut sic eatur in suffragia.
units.tr: Propos. And therefore he himself will examine the reasons given, so that they may proceed to the vote.

units.la: Tractatio. I. Gratuletur Ciceroni, quod uterque Tribunus amplissimarum virtutum laudes ipsi concedat tribuatque. Omnino innocentiæ ac probitatis indicium esse, non ab amicis modo, sed ab adversariis laudari. Macte ista virtute tua Tulli &c. Hinc provocet ad conscientiam omnium, qui talem revera agnoscant Ciceronem.
units.tr: Tractatio. I. He congratulates Cicero, because both tribunes grant and attribute to him the praises of the most distinguished virtues. Altogether it is a sign of innocence and uprightness to be praised not only by friends but also by adversaries. "Well done, Tullius, in that virtue of yours," and so on. Hence he appeals to the conscience of all who truly recognise such a Cicero.

units.la: II. Examinet rationes secundi Tribuni contra Ciceronem, resp. ad 1. Ciceronem federati municipii civem esse, adeoque non extraneum sed Civem habendum, qui & pridem domum Romam transtulerit. Patriciatum non requiri, cum jam pridem plebs, nedum equites, honorum capaces facti sint rep. Vinculum hoc esse concordiæ. &c. ad 2. Notitiam quantam ipse habeat reip. tum ex actionibus forensibus, tum ex gestis dignitatibus quæsturæ & præturæ satis patescere. Notitiam juris civilis non quidem sufficere ad regendam remp. sed tamen nec officere, imò requiri.
units.tr: II. He examines the reasons of the second tribune against Cicero, answering them. To 1: Cicero is a citizen of an allied municipality, and so he is to be regarded not as an outsider but as a citizen, who also long ago transferred his home to Rome. Patrician status is not required, since for some time the plebs, and much more the equites, have been made capable of the offices of the republic. This is a bond of concord, and so on. To 2: how great a knowledge of the commonwealth he himself has is sufficiently clear, both from his forensic activities and from the offices he has held, the quaestorship and the praetorship. Knowledge of civil law is indeed not enough to govern the commonwealth, but nevertheless it is no hindrance; rather it is required.

units.la: ad 3. Quam sincerus affectus sit Cic. pro rep. multis constare documentis.
units.tr: To 3: how sincere Cicero's affection for the republic is has been established by many proofs.

units.la: Concluf Hæc habuisse se monenda, unde pateat nihil obstare Consulatui Ciceronis: Proindeque jam eant in suffragia & statuant ex conscientia, non ex affectibus privatis, quid consultum judicent reip.
units.tr: Concl. He has said these things so that it may be plain that nothing stands in the way of Cicero's consulship. Therefore let them now proceed to the votes and decide from conscience, not from private feelings, what they judge advisable for the commonwealth.

units.la: XIII. ACTA IN SENATU POST DETECTA CATILINÆ. CONSILIA.
units.tr: XIII. THE PROCEEDINGS IN THE SENATE AFTER CATILINE'S PLOT WAS DISCOVERED. THE OPINIONS.

units.la: I. Cicero refert de Catilinæ Machinationibus.
units.tr: I. Cicero reports on Catiline's machinations.

units.la: Præfatur in genere de sua sollicitudine pro rep., postquam consulatus ipsi commissus. Rationem addit à comparatione civis & magistratus, cum illi nihil prius patria, multo minus huic esse debere, utpote qui custos constitutus omnium, &c.
units.tr: He begins in general with his own anxiety for the republic, now that the consulship has been entrusted to him. He adds a reason drawn from the comparison of a citizen and a magistrate: for the citizen nothing should come before the fatherland, and still less should it come before this for the magistrate, who has been appointed the guardian of all.

units.la: II. Refert in specie 1. de publica fama conjurationis Catilinariæ 11. de consilio suo, videl. 1. non modo præsidio tueri se & rempublicam contra oppressionem, verum 2. de exploratoribus omnium arcanorum maribus, fœminis, ut intima consilia expiscaretur. 3. de compertis machinationibus Mallii in Hetruria. vide Sal. 4. de detecto proposito præterita nocte trucidandi Ciceronis vide Sal.
units.tr: II. He reports, specifically, (1) the public rumour of the Catilinarian conspiracy; (2) his own plan, namely (a) to protect himself and the republic from oppression by armed force, and (b) to have spies, both men and women, on all secrets, so that he might draw out the innermost plans; (3) the plots of Mallius in Etruria that had been discovered (see Sallust); (4) the plan, detected the previous night, to slaughter Cicero (see Sallust).

units.la: III. Aperit consilium suum 1. in genere de referendo rem ad Senatu ut in re ardua communi consensu statuatur, 2. in specie consultum videri sibi, ut excedere jubeantur, & complices vel una excedere jubeantur, vel si nolint in carcerem conjiciantur, aut etiam pro re nata plectantur.
units.tr: III. He sets out his own opinion: (1) in general, that the matter should be referred to the Senate, so that in a grave business a decision may be reached by common consent; (2) specifically, that it seems right to him that they be ordered to leave the city, and that the accomplices either be ordered to leave together with them, or, if they refuse, be thrown into prison, or even be punished as the situation requires.

units.la: IV. Hortatur, ut in re ardua statuant quisque pro fide, quam debent reip.
units.tr: IV. He urges them each to decide in a grave matter according to the loyalty they owe the republic.

units.la: II. Nonnulli statuunt caute agendum in re hac maximi momenti.
units.tr: II. Some hold that caution must be used in this matter of the greatest moment.

units.la: Exord. Referat se ad propositionem Consulis paucis summa capitas resumens, & momentum rei agnoscens.
units.tr: Exordium. He refers to the proposal of the Consul, briefly sums up the main points, and acknowledges the weight of the matter.

units.la: Propof. Videri sibi caute agendum, donec res plenius patescat.
units.tr: Proposition. It seems to him that caution must be used until the matter is more fully disclosed.

units.la: Confirm. I. Quia res maximi momenti & multos etiam ex optimatibus concernens: contra quos si praecipitanter decernatur, tumultus metuendus sit. Secus si intra paucos sisteret conjuratio.
units.tr: Confirmation. (1) Because the matter is of the greatest moment and concerns many, even among the optimates; if a decision is made rashly against them, a tumult is to be feared. It would be otherwise if the conspiracy were confined to a few.

units.la: II. Quia non sat judicii sit in occultis exploratoribus: utpote 1. contra quos excipient tanquam emptos mercede & promissis, conjurati. Quid 2. si ipsi negent testes metu perculsi? In crimine tam atroci probationes requiri luce clariores. Imo 3. illis sine dubio silentium promissum à Cicerone. Num igitur fallenda fides data?
units.tr: (2) Because there is not sufficient judgment in secret informers, since (a) the conspirators will object that they were bought with money and promises; and what if the witnesses themselves deny it, struck with fear? In a crime so atrocious, proofs must be clearer than light. Indeed (b) they were without doubt promised silence by Cicero. Must faith given then be broken?

units.la: III. Quia vel propria poenitentia, vel lenitate forte reduci queant ad officium: sic parci civili sanguine, cui semper parcendum judicarint majores.
units.tr: (3) Because they may perhaps be brought back to their duty either by their own repentance or by leniency; and so civil blood should be spared, which the ancestors always judged should be spared.

units.la: Concluf. Videri igitur proposito Edicto monendos esse cives, ut si qui sint, desistant à perniciosis consiliis, sub poena capitis aut relegationis.
units.tr: Conclusion. It seems therefore that, by a proclaimed edict, the citizens, if there are any, should be warned to abandon their pernicious plans, under pain of death or banishment.

units.la: III. Reliqui unanimes decernunt committendam remp. Consulibus solenni formula.
units.tr: III. The others unanimously decide that the republic should be entrusted to the Consuls in the customary formula.

units.la: Exord. Non opus esse dicat, repetere illa, quae à Consule pro sua prudentia de conjuratione Catil. ejusque detectione proposita sint. Proindeque gratias agat pro vigilantia & cura publicae salutis. Audisse se etiam, quae à nonnullis de circumspectione dicta sint.
units.tr: Exordium. He says there is no need to repeat those things which the Consul, in his prudence, has proposed concerning the Catilinarian conspiracy and its discovery. He therefore gives thanks for his vigilance and care for the public safety. He has also heard what has been said by some about caution.

units.la: Propof. Quorum sententiae licet alias haud levibus rationibus nixa videatur, omnino obviam eundum.
units.tr: Proposition. Although their opinions seem to rest on reasons that are by no means slight, they must nevertheless be opposed altogether.

units.la: Confutatio Examinet rationes allatas, respondendo
units.tr: Refutation. He examines the arguments advanced, replying:

units.la: ad I. Tanto magis maturandum, ne hi plebem reliquam in partes trahant. Magnae factioni masculè obviam eundum nec agendum segniter.
units.tr: To the first: all the more must it be hastened, lest these men draw the rest of the common people into their party. A great faction must be resisted manfully, and nothing should be done sluggishly.

units.la: ad II. Indicii satis esse, utpote 1. ex ipsis conjuratis. 2. tormentis compelli posse ad fatendum confessa. 3. Silentium promissum ad ipsorum securitatem, quae praestanda illis. Nullam fidem obstringere contra officium & patriam.
units.tr: To the second: there is evidence enough, namely (1) from the conspirators themselves; (2) they can be compelled by torture to confess what they have admitted; (3) the silence promised is for their own security, which must be guaranteed to them. A promise does not bind one against duty and the fatherland.

units.la: ad III. Frustra sperari poenitentiam à conjuratis, qui lenitate corrumpuntur magis. Parcendum civili sanguine, si absque exitio patriae fieri queat.
units.tr: To the third: it is vainly hoped that repentance will come from the conspirators, who are rather corrupted by leniency. Civil blood must be spared, if this can be done without the ruin of the fatherland.

units.la: Ergo procedendum acriter : ideoque remp. Consulibus absolute committendam esse, videant illi, ne quid resp. detrimenti capiat.
units.tr: Therefore one must proceed sharply; and so the republic should be entrusted absolutely to the Consuls, who are to see to it that the republic take no harm.

units.la: THEMA XIV. DE COMOEDIIS ET LUDIS SCENICIS UTRUM ADMITTENDÆ IN REP. CHRISTIANA.
units.tr: THESIS XIV. ON COMEDIES AND STAGE PLAYS: WHETHER THEY ARE TO BE ADMITTED IN THE CHRISTIAN COMMONWEALTH.

units.la: I. Affirmate.
units.tr: I. In the affirmative.

units.la: Rectè distingui vitam humanam in otium & negotium; quia 1. Deus sic ordinavit, 2. necessitas humana requirit.
units.tr: Human life is rightly divided into leisure and business, because (1) God has so ordained it, and (2) human necessity requires it.

units.la: A Difficultate rectè collocandi ocium : probetur induction excessuum ab ociosis commissorum.
units.tr: On the difficulty of rightly placing leisure: this is to be proved by induction from the excesses committed by idlers.

units.la: Quæri de Comoediis & ludis scenicis, utrum ocium in iis rectè collocetur Christianis.
units.tr: The question is about comedies and stage plays: whether leisure is rightly spent on them by Christians.

units.la: Videri quod sic.
units.tr: The view is that it is.

units.la: I. Distinguat 1. comoedias in moratiores & lasciviores. 2. Tempora in prosperá & luctuosa, indifferentia. Ttempore luctuoso, & sacris destinato, imprimisque Ecclesiastis merito improbari dicat.
units.tr: I. Let him distinguish: (1) comedies into the more moral and the more wanton; (2) times into prosperous, sorrowful and indifferent. He should say that in a time of sorrow, and one set apart for sacred purposes, they are rightly disapproved, especially for ecclesiastics.

units.la: II. Probet Priores illas tanquam.
units.tr: II. Let him prove that the former are: (as follows)

units.la: 1. Honestas: quoniam a. nihil habent pietati & honestati Christianæ adversum, nisi quod ipsa vita humana, cujus comoedia imago est, & repræsentatio, hoc ostendatur ex natura comoediæ, qua actiones vitæ repræsentantur. b. Si quid in illa mali, illud reprehenditur & exagitatur: ostendatur per inductionem v.g. seniles sordes, juveniles amores, serviles nequitiæ, meretriciæ fraudes, quæ fugiendæ proponuntur, non laudantur.
units.tr: 1. Honourable, since (a) they contain nothing opposed to Christian piety and honour, unless this is shown from the nature of comedy, in which the actions of life are represented, and comedy is an image and representation of human life; (b) if anything evil appears in them, it is rebuked and lashed. This is shown by induction, for example: senile meanness, youthful loves, servile wickedness, and the deceits of prostitutes, which are set forth to be shunned, not praised.

units.la: 2. Utiles a. ad doctrinam virtutum & fugam vitiorum, quæ hic proponuntur cum laude, vituperio & eventu læto, tristi. Ostentur inductione aliqua. Et quidem tanto efficacius, in comoediis, quæ vivis coloribus hic repræsentantur. b. ad vocandum homines ab illicitis lusibus, compotationibus, ocio segni. c. ad exercitium facundiæ & parrhesias in variis argumentis
units.tr: 2. Useful: (a) for teaching the virtues and shunning vices, which are here set forth with praise, blame, and a happy or sad outcome. Let this be shown by some induction, and all the more effectively in comedies, which are here represented in lively colours; (b) for calling men away from unlawful amusements, drinking parties, and idle sloth; (c) for the exercise of eloquence and frankness of speech on various subjects.

units.la: 3. Usu publicè receptas, tum inter veteres, Græcos, Romanos, gengentes excultas moribus & literis, tum inter modernos, Italos, Gallos, Hisp. Anglos, ipsos Germanos: quos aberrare à vero non est verisimile. Imo ipsos Judæos sua habuisse dramata, utpatet ex Iobo & Cant. cant. Saltem igitur Comœdias sacri argumenti licitas esse, id quod viri eruditi exemplo probarunt in Terent. Christiano.
units.tr: 3. They are publicly received in practice: both among the ancients, the Greeks and Romans, nations refined in manners and letters, and among the moderns, the Italians, French, Spaniards, English, and the Germans themselves, who it is not likely have gone astray from the truth. Indeed, the Jews themselves had their own dramas, as is evident from Job and the Song of Songs. At least, therefore, comedies on a sacred subject are lawful, which learned men have proved by the example of the Christian Terence.

units.la: Conclus. 1. Arguat morosos Catones, & 2. ex repetitis brev. argumentis propositionem inferat.
units.tr: Conclusion. 1. Let him refute the censorious Catos; and 2. let him draw the proposition from the arguments briefly repeated.

units.la: II. Pro Sententia Negativa.
units.tr: II. In favour of the negative opinion.

units.la: I. Exord. A gravissima dehortatione Apostoli: Ne conformamini mundo huic. Explicetur vis vocis, q.d. ne eundem habitum induite, vel in eandem constellationem venite cum hominibus mundo deditis. Addatur ratio: quia mundus & Deus contrarii: hinc à communione impiorum & irrisorum seu mimorum dehortari Davidem. Applicetur ad hypoth. quo magis mirum videri queat antecessorem comœdias tanquam licitas Christianis defendisse, ubi mundus in theatrum adducitur & spectatur cum voluptate, repræsentatur cum studio æmulandi.
units.tr: I. Exordium. Begin with the most serious warning of the Apostle: "Be not conformed to this world" (Rom. 12). Let the force of the word be explained, as if to say: do not put on the same habit, or come into the same constellation, as men given over to the world. Add the reason: because the world and God are opposed; hence David warned against associating with the impious and the scornful, or mimes. Apply this to the hypothesis, so that it may seem all the more strange that the predecessor defended comedies as lawful for Christians, when the world is brought into the theatre and watched with pleasure, and represented with eagerness to imitate it.

units.la: II. Propos. In contraria penitus te esse sententia; quam proinde pace antecessoris adstruere velis, & remota cortina, turpitudinem scenæ propalaturum.
units.tr: II. Proposition. You are wholly of the contrary opinion; which, therefore, with the predecessor's leave, you would wish to maintain, and, the curtain removed, you will expose the baseness of the stage.

units.la: III. Confirm. 1. A requisita sanctitate & gravitate vitæ Christianæ. Hic describat hominem Christianum, ex sacris, qualis intus & extus esse debeat, & opponat histriones, & illum qui hisce delectatur.
units.tr: III. Confirmation. 1. From the holiness and seriousness of Christian life, which is required. Here let him describe the Christian man, from the sacred writings, what he ought to be inwardly and outwardly, and set against him the stage players and the man who delights in them.

units.la: II. A materia Comœdiarum 1. profanarum, ubi licet quædam utilia, illa tamen vitiari levitate, quæ Comœdiarum; aut scelerибus, quæ tragœdiarum ordinaria materia. Fiat inductio veteris scenæ ex Plaut. Terent. 2. sacrarum; ubi rerum gravitas futilitate agyrtarum deturpatur. Salubrius ex concionibus & lectione scripturæ illa hauriri: quod vivum & efficax Heb. 4.
units.tr: II. From the subject matter of comedies: 1. profane ones, where, though some things may be useful, they are nevertheless tainted by the levity that is characteristic of comedies, or by the crimes that are the usual matter of tragedies. Let there be an induction from the old stage, from Plautus and Terence. 2. Sacred ones, where the gravity of the subjects is disfigured by the frivolity of the mountebanks. It is more wholesome to draw these things from sermons and the reading of Scripture, which is "living and effective" (Heb. 4).

units.la: III. Ab adjunctis scenæ: quæ sunt scurrilitas, turpiloquia, stultorum repræsentatio, ulus larvarum, mutatio sexus in vestitu, saltationes obscenæ & similia, ipsis gentibus, nedum Christianis turpia & vetita.
units.tr: III. From the accompaniments of the stage: which are buffoonery, obscene speech, the representation of fools, the use of masks, a change of sex in dress, obscene dances and the like, which are shameful and forbidden even among the heathen nations, let alone among Christians.

units.la: IV. Ab effectis: jactura temporis & numis qui ab Agyrtis exportantur ad exteros: & proclivi seductione juventutis: quibus nihil noxium magis reip. V. A judicio antiquitatis. Hic doce 1. Histriones jure Romano infames & saepe urbe pulsos. vid. Tac. lib. 2. annal. Cic. 4. Tusc. 2. ab Ecclesia excommunicatos. 3. Antiquos Christianos debuisse renunciare pompis & spectaculis. Salv. lib.6. de prov. Tertull. de spect. c. 4.
units.tr: IV. From its effects: the loss of time and of money, which is carried off by the mountebanks to foreigners, and the ready seduction of the young, of whom nothing is more harmful to the commonwealth. V. From the judgment of antiquity. Here teach: 1. that stage players were infamous under Roman law and were often expelled from the city (see Tacitus, Annals book 2; Cicero, Tusculan Disputations book 4). 2. That they were excommunicated by the Church. 3. That the ancient Christians ought to have renounced the pomps and spectacles (Salvian, On the Government of God, book 6; Tertullian, On Spectacles, ch. 4).

units.la: V. Confutatio. Examinet argumenta antecessoris,
units.tr: V. Refutation. Let him examine the arguments of the predecessor.

units.la: 1. Concedendo differentiam comoediarum & temporum, personarum: attamen omnes omnibus temporibus Christianis illicitas, saltem vanas ac periculosas ocioforum esse illecebras, uti supra patuit.
units.tr: 1. Granting the difference of comedies, times, and persons, nevertheless all of them are unlawful for Christians at all times, or at least they are vain and dangerous enticements to idlers, as has been shown above.

units.la: 2. Refellendo rationes allatas: respondendo ad a. non omnes vitae actiones honestas esse, multo minus in scenam produci debere. Deinde melius esse velari scurrilitates, quam cum jucunditate repraesentari. Ad b. concedendo aliquam utilitatem, at majus esse periculum, quod inde metuendum, & utilitatem aliunde sine periculo haberi posse. ad c. exempla 1. esse & contraria, 2. gentilium exempla haud excusare Christianos, quia ut gentiles mundo dediti, ita Christiani eidem renunciare tenentur. Atque hic digrediatur in lamentationem, quod Christianorum vita nimium sapiat gentilimum.
units.tr: 2. By refuting the reasons advanced: answering to (a) that not all actions of life are honourable, much less should they be brought onto the stage; and that it is better for buffooneries to be veiled than to be represented with enjoyment. To (b) by granting some usefulness, but that the danger to be feared from it is greater, and that the same usefulness can be had elsewhere without danger. To (c) the examples: first, that they are also contrary; second, that the examples of the heathen do not excuse Christians, because, just as the heathen were given over to the world, so Christians are bound to renounce it. And here he may digress into lamentation that the life of Christians savours too much of the Gentiles.

units.la: V. Perorationem recollecta rei summa, Christianos a scena dehortetur, & ad vitam seriam ac Christianam excitet; argumento: ne gentes moratiores nos damnent in ultimo judicio.
units.tr: V. Peroration: gathering up the sum of the matter, let him dissuade Christians from the stage and rouse them to a serious and Christian life, with this argument: lest the more moral Gentiles condemn us at the last judgment.

units.la: THEMA XV. CONSULTATIO DE REPRIMENDO LUXU. Ex 3. An. Taciti, per C. Bibulum.
units.tr: THEME XV. A CONSULTATION ON RESTRAINING LUXURY. From the 3rd year of Tacitus, by C. Bibulus.

units.la: 1. Ædiles causam in Senatu proponunt, & in luxum invehuntur.
units.tr: 1. The aediles lay the matter before the Senate and inveigh against luxury.

units.la: Exord. Captet benevolentium Laudando morem patriae, quo salubriter constitutum, ut functiones inter plures dispertirentur. Illustret comparat, uti Principi totius reip. Senatui legum atque justitiae, ita Aedilibus aedium & ludorum & publicae honestatis & curam commissam: cui pro virili incubuerint hactenus.
units.tr: Exordium. He should win the goodwill of his hearers by praising the custom of the fatherland, under which it was wisely ordained that duties be divided among several officials. He should illustrate by comparison that, just as the Prince, the Senate and the laws and justice are entrusted to the whole commonwealth, so the care of buildings, of the games and of public decency has been entrusted to the aediles, who have so far applied themselves to it as well as they could.

units.la: Narratio. Exponat 1. quid prohdolor deprehenderint in luxus exuberantia. 2. Quid speraverint, scil. priscinas leges, reducendas esse; id quod ante paucos annos tentatum est, Hatterio Consulari autore.3. Frustra omnia, crescente indies luxu: ut non nisi fortiori manu comprimi posse videatur.
units.tr: Narratio. He should set out: (1) what, to their grief, they have found in the excess of luxury; (2) what they had hoped for, namely that the old laws would be brought back, which was attempted a few years ago on the advice of the consular Hatterius; (3) that all efforts are in vain, since luxury grows daily, so that it seems it can be checked only by a stronger hand.

units.la: Propos. Sui itaque officii judicasse Ædiles, causam hanc ad Senatum deferre: ut ipsius prudentia tanto malo obviam eatur.
units.tr: Propositio. Therefore the aediles judged it their duty to refer this cause to the Senate, so that by its wisdom this great evil might be met.

units.la: Confirm.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: I. A necessario. Hici. praemittat votum ipsorum, scilicet ne opus habuissent occupationes Senatus turbare. 2. Exaggeret notorium omnibus Excessum hujus vitii per hypotypolin & μετριότητα, quomodo modum excesserint in cibo & potu, vestibus, suppellectili aliisque preciosis vide Epist. Tib. lib. 3. & Senec. Ep. 3. & pass. Gell. 15. c. 8. Liv. 39. c. 6, Tac. lib. 2. Plin. lib. 33. c. 3. 9 11. 12. 3. Concluf. hinc cogitandum omnino de remedio.
units.tr: I. From what is necessary. Here he should first state their wish, namely that they would not have needed to disturb the business of the Senate. 2. He should magnify, by vivid description and moderation [μετριότητα], a fact notorious to all: how the vice has exceeded all bounds in food and drink, clothing, furniture and other costly things. See the Epistles of Tiberius, book 3, and Seneca, Ep. 3 and passim; Gellius 15, ch. 8; Livy 39, ch. 6; Tacitus, book 2; Pliny, book 33, ch. 3, 9, 11, 12. 3. Conclusion: from this it must be thought over thoroughly how to find a remedy.

units.la: II. A damno & periculo quod a luxu immineat, videl. ruina familiarum, & tandem reip. cum sic pecunia exportetur, peregrinis mores invehantur, fortitudo exstinguatur. Illustretur exemplo Sibaritarum aliorumque & ipsius Romae, ex quo Asiam & Corinthum expugnavit. Comparari possunt e contrario tempora pristina frugalitate illustria.
units.tr: II. From the damage and danger that hang over us from luxury, namely the ruin of families and at last of the commonwealth: money is thus carried out of the country, foreign customs are brought in, and courage is extinguished. Let it be illustrated by the example of the Sybarites and others, and of Rome itself, which after it had conquered Asia and Corinth was corrupted by the same vice. On the other hand, the earlier times, distinguished for their frugality, can be set against this.

units.la: III. Ab exemplo 1. majorum: qui lege Oppia, aliisque sumptuariis legibus luxum compresserint. vide Liv. lib. 24. Valer. M. lib. 2. c. 5. 2. Catonis, qui vehementissime contra luxum egerit. vide Liv. lib. 34. init. 3. Hatterii Consularis qui nuper licet frustra illud tentarit, contranitentibus luxuriae patronis. Hanc causam merito & sibi resumendam fuisse.
units.tr: III. From the example 1. of our ancestors, who checked luxury by the Oppian law and other sumptuary laws; see Livy, book 24; Valerius Maximus, book 2, ch. 5. 2. of Cato, who opposed luxury most vehemently; see Livy, book 34, at the beginning. 3. of the consular Hatterius, who lately attempted it, though in vain, while the patrons of luxury resisted; this cause, too, was rightly to be taken up again by them.

units.la: Concluf. I. Hortetur Consules & Senatum, ut rei tam necessariae exemplo majorum mederi velint: ne exitii, quod luxurianti reip. immineat, rei videantur: 2. Excusent suum factum, qui iram Deorum avertere a cervicibus, si non civitatis, suis saltem voluerint.
units.tr: Conclusio. I. He should exhort the consuls and the Senate to be willing to remedy so necessary a matter by the example of our ancestors, lest they seem to be guilty of the ruin that hangs over the commonwealth as it grows luxurious. 2. Let them excuse their own action, since they wished to turn the anger of the gods from the necks of the citizens, if not of the state, at least of their own.

units.la: II. C. Sulpitius Conf. respondet & causam Patribus proponit.
units.tr: II. C. Sulpitius, the consul, replies and lays the matter before the Fathers.

units.la: I. Praefatione. 1. Breviter reassumat summam propositionis factae ab Ædilibus. 2. Laudet ipsorum industriam & ad ulteriorem diligentiam cohortetur.
units.tr: I. Preface. 1. He briefly takes up again the substance of the proposal made by the aediles. 2. He praises their diligence and urges them to further care.

units.la: II. Respondeat
units.tr: II. He replies:

units.la: 1. Approbando rationes, quas prudenter contra luxum attulerint; cum addito voto optati successus, & promissione operae suae.
units.tr: 1. By approving the reasons which they have prudently brought against luxury, adding a wish for the desired success and a promise of his own help.

units.la: 2. Innuendo difficultatem exsecutionis, ob vitii vetustatem & amplitudinem.
units.tr: 2. By hinting at the difficulty of carrying it out, because of the age and extent of the vice.

units.la: III. Concludat: quoniam causa sit magni momenti, quae plurimos etiam magnates concernat, serio deliberandum; ideoque Senatorum sententias desuper exaudiendas esse. Quos re diligenter expensa proinde ire in suffragia hortetur.
units.tr: III. He concludes: since the matter is of great importance and concerns very many, even great men, it must be deliberated seriously; therefore the opinions of the senators must be heard on it. He urges them, after weighing the matter carefully, to proceed accordingly to a vote.

units.la: III. Primus Senator & sequaces approbant propositum Ædilium.
units.tr: III. The first senator and his followers approve the proposal of the aediles.

units.la: Exord. 1. Supervacuum esse dicat repetere quod ab Ædilibus propositum & a Consule responsum sit. 2. Agnoscat & commendet causae momentum ex dictis ab Ædil. & Consule rationibus. 3. Officii sui esse liberè, quid è rep. exist-imet, proferre.
units.tr: Exordium. 1. He says it is superfluous to repeat what was proposed by the aediles and answered by the consul. 2. He acknowledges and commends the weight of the cause, on the reasons stated by the aediles and the consul. 3. It is his duty to state freely what he thinks is for the good of the commonwealth.

units.la: Propos. Videri sibi audiendos Ædiles & medelam adhibendam esse luxui.
units.tr: Propositio. It seems to him that the aediles should be heard and a remedy applied to luxury.

units.la: Confirm.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: I. Ex rationibus ab Ædilibus rectè allatis: & non sine magna ratione approbatis à Consule; quibus repetendis nolit tempus terere.
units.tr: I. From the reasons rightly brought forward by the aediles and not without good reason approved by the consul; he is unwilling to waste time by repeating them.

units.la: II. A facili. Hic 1. per prolepsin moveat difficultatem ex vitii vetustate & frequentia apud omnes ordines. 2. At sanari posse legibus, si exemplo praeeant magnates: cujus vis apud populum exaggeretur. Addatur ratio; quia tum divites, tum pauperes, hi quidem necessitate, illi fastidio, destituri sint, sublata per legem & exemplum magnatum aemulatione. vid. Epist. Tib. apud Tac.
units.tr: II. From what is easy. Here, 1. by anticipating an objection, he should raise the difficulty arising from the age of the vice and its frequency among all classes. 2. But it can be cured by laws, if the great men lead by example; the force of this should be magnified before the people. Let the reason be added: since the rich and the poor, the latter from necessity and the former from disdain, will give it up once rivalry is removed by law and by the example of the great men. See the Epistle of Tiberius quoted by Tacitus.

units.la: III. Ab emolumentis contrariae frugalitatis & modestiae. Exaggeretur ab effectis publicè, privatim. Hinc digrediatur in admirationem pristinorum temporum, quando sub Curiis, Fabriciis, Fabiis, floruit resp. Antiquis moribus stare remp.
units.tr: III. From the advantages of the opposite frugality and moderation. These should be magnified as to their effects, both public and private. Hence he should digress into admiration of the earlier times, when the commonwealth flourished under the Curii, the Fabricii and the Fabii, and when the state stood by its ancient customs.

units.la: Conclus. Ex dictis rationibus statuere se, manum praebendam esse Ædilibus: & severa lege & exemplo obviam eundum.
units.tr: Conclusio. From the reasons stated he decides that his hand should be lent to the aediles, and that luxury should be met with a strict law and by example.

units.la: IV. Secundus Senator improbat sententiam Ædilium & Collegae.
units.tr: IV. The second senator disapproves the opinion of the aediles and their colleague.

units.la: Exord. 1. Amolitur suspicionem, quòd luxui faveat. Hinc protestatur de sua à luxu aversatione & immunitate: utpote, quem norit pestem publicam & privatam. 2. Astipulari se omnibus, quae ab Ædilibus & Collega graviter dicta sint. 3. Nec tamen placere sibi, ut legibus contra luxum agatur.
units.tr: Exordium. 1. He removes the suspicion that he favours luxury. Hence he protests his own aversion to luxury and his freedom from it, since he knows it to be a public and private plague. 2. He agrees with everything that was said weightily by the aediles and their colleague. 3. Yet it does not please him that the law should proceed against luxury.

units.la: Propos. Petere se veniam à Collega & Ædilibus, quorum honestis desideriis obniti cogatur.
units.tr: Propositio. He asks pardon of his colleague and the aediles, whose honourable wishes he is compelled to oppose.

units.la: Confirmatio. Habeat votum talium temporum, ubi sanis consiliis locus, ubi autoritas Magistratus salva. Contra digrediatur in deplorationem temporum, ubi mutata rep. mutati mores.
units.tr: Confirmatio. He should express a wish for such times, when sound counsels have their place and the authority of the magistrate is safe. On the contrary, he should digress into lamentation over the times, in which, with the commonwealth changed, the morals have changed.

units.la: II. Præsumat hinc efficiendi difficultatem; eamque probet
units.tr: II. He should next raise the difficulty of carrying it out, and prove it:

units.la: 1. A Vitii hujus frequentia & vetustate uti ipsi Ædiles falli sint. Talia difficulter sanari. Illustretur simili à morbis inveteratis. Tales mitigari, non vero tolli posse sine periculo corporis. Applicetur ad remp. Exaggeretur à magnatum cum hoc vitio participatione. vid. Epist. Tib. lib. 3. Tac.
units.tr: 1. Because of the frequency and age of this vice, the aediles themselves are deceived. Such evils are hardly cured. Let it be illustrated by a similar case of long-standing diseases: such can be mitigated, but not removed, without danger to the body. It is to be applied to the commonwealth. It should be magnified by the participation of the great men in this vice. See the Epistles of Tiberius, book 3; Tacitus.

units.la: 2. Ab exemplis majorum: qui frustra legibus compescere luxum sategerint. vide Epist. Tib. apud Tacit. Et superiorum annorum, ubi contradicentis emendationi Asinii Galli sententiæ, princeps subscripserit.
units.tr: 2. From the examples of our ancestors, who strove in vain to restrain luxury by laws. See the Epistles of Tiberius in Tacitus; and of recent years, when the prince subscribed to the opinion of Asinius Gallus opposing the amendment.

units.la: III. Refellat argumentum à facili: scil. frustra sperari cessaturam per legem æmulationem; cum nec divites, nec pauperes cessuri sint. Exempla parum profutura; cum rari sint, qui præire velint. Imò magnates primos semper fuisse, qui bonas majorum, & proprias leges violaverint. Frustra esse leges, ubi animus vitiis æger.
units.tr: III. He refutes the argument from what is easy: namely, that it is vainly hoped that rivalry will cease through the law, since neither the rich nor the poor will give it up. Examples will do little good, since there are few who want to lead the way. Indeed, it has always been the great men who first violated the good customs of our ancestors and their own laws. Laws are in vain where the mind is sick with vices.

units.la: Conclus. 1. Consultius sibi videri, non tangere ulcus, quod sanari nequeat. In omnem eventum, nihil hic inconsulto principe agendum.
units.tr: Conclusio. 1. It seems to him more prudent not to touch an ulcer that cannot be healed. In any event, nothing should be done here without the prince's knowledge.

units.la: V. Tertius Senator contrarius utrique Senatus autoritatem urgens, non audiendos Ædiles censet.
units.tr: V. The third senator, opposing both sides and insisting on the authority of the Senate, judges that the Aediles should not be heard.

units.la: Exord. 1. Præfatur de studio suo in remp. cui tum per nativitatem, tum per juramentum obstrictus sit. Verum illius salutem, cùm in incolumitate subditorum & autoritate Senatus consistere reputet, non videre se, quomodo vel Ædiles audiendi, vel, quod innuat antecessor, causa hæc ad Principem referenda sit.
units.tr: Introduction. He speaks first of his own zeal for the commonwealth, to which he is bound both by birth and by oath. Since he judges that the safety of the commonwealth rests on the welfare of the subjects and the authority of the Senate, he does not see how the Aediles could be heard, or how this matter could be referred to the Prince, as the previous speaker suggested.

units.la: Propos. Se itaque bona pace ab utrisque aliquantulum discedere, & rejiciendam petitionem Ædilium censere.
units.tr: Proposition. He therefore says that, with good will toward both sides, he parts somewhat from both, and judges that the petition of the Aediles should be rejected.

units.la: Confirm.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: 1. Concedat omnia quæ hactenus de luxus exuberantia, necessitate medelæ, de laudibus parsimoniæ; & contra de difficultate remedii modò dicta sint. Omnia ista bene dici quidem, at nescire se, numquid majus aliquid considerandum.
units.tr: 1. Let them grant everything said so far about the excess of luxury, the need for a remedy, and the praise of thrift; and, on the other hand, about the difficulty of the remedy. All of this has been said well, but he does not know whether anything greater must be considered.

units.la: II. Ostendat modum agendi vergere in praejudicium Senatus.
units.tr: II. Let him show that the manner of proceeding tends to the prejudice of the Senate.

units.la: 1. Quia Ædiles jus reformandi sibi arrogent. Hic itaque a. disserat de autoritate Senatus ab antiquo. b. Illam minui ostendat hac interpellatione, quod Senatus non sit functus officio: quasi Ædiles inspectores Senatus constituti sint, quorum officium eo usque se haud extendat. Hoc quam perniciosum fuerit ostendat exemplis tribunorum: quantae inde turbae in rep. vide Flor. lib. 1. sub sin.; at populo & inferioribus magistratibus minime cedendum, &c. nisi tandem exsecutor alienae libidinis esse velit.
units.tr: 1. Because the Aediles claim for themselves the right of reform. Here he should, a. discuss the authority of the Senate from antiquity; b. show that this authority is diminished by this interference, on the ground that the Senate has not performed its office, as if the Aediles had been appointed as overseers of the Senate, whose office does not extend so far. Let him show how harmful this would be by the examples of the tribunes: see the great disturbances this caused in the state, Florus, book 1, at the end; but one must by no means yield to the people or to the lesser magistrates, and so on, unless one wishes at last to be the instrument of another's lust.

units.la: 2. Quoniam antecessor cautum ad Principem referendam sub finem censuit. At cogitent quantum decessurum Senatui. Notum esse, quantum jamdudum per adulationes nonnullorum deperditum sit: cavendum, ne perdant quod adhuc reliquum.&c.
units.tr: 2. Because the previous speaker proposed, near the end, a cautious referral to the Prince. But let them consider how much this would cost the Senate. It is well known how much has already been lost through the flattery of some; care must be taken lest they lose what still remains, etc.

units.la: Conclus. Sibi igitur videri potius rejiciendam esse Ædilium petitionem: addita ratione, ne scil. & populum offendant, & quod reliquum est autoritatis porro disperdant, Se semper pro autoritate Ordinis staturum.
units.tr: Conclusion. It seems to him, therefore, that the petition of the Aediles should rather be rejected, with the added reason that they would both offend the people and further squander the authority that remains; and he will always stand by the authority of the Order.

units.la: VII. Quartus senator luxum felicitate temporum excusans, minus necessariam medelam statuit. vid. Orat. Asinii Galli lib. 2.
units.tr: VII. The fourth senator, excusing luxury by the happiness of the times, proposes a less necessary remedy. See the speech of Asinius Gallus, book 2.

units.la: Exord. Ex Orat. antecessoris: videl. vel tacitè concedere se posse in ejus sententiam, videl. rejiciendos Ædiles, nisi nova ratione ejus muniendam adhuc sententiam existimassēt.
units.tr: Introduction. From the speech of the previous speaker: namely, that he may tacitly concede that he can agree with that opinion, namely, that the Aediles should be rejected, unless they thought the opinion had to be fortified by some new argument.

units.la: Propos. Videl. haud necessarium sibi videri illam, quae tanta cum difficultate conjuncta videtur reformatio.
units.tr: Proposition. Namely, that reform, which seems bound up with such great difficulty, does not seem to him necessary.

units.la: Confirm. Hic
units.tr: Confirmation. Here:

units.la: I. Excuset se à suspicione quòd luxui faveat, & provocet ad familiam, in qua nemo quippiam jure reprehendere queat. Addita ratione quod nec sibi ignotafint illa quae contra luxum dicta sint dicive queant. Tamen non videri sibi necessarium, ut tali severitate agatur.
units.tr: I. Let him excuse himself from the suspicion that he favors luxury, and appeal to his family, against which no one could rightly find fault. Adding the reason that the arguments that have been or can be made against luxury are not unknown to him. Nevertheless, it does not seem necessary to him that the matter be handled with such severity.

units.la: II. Rationem afferat
units.tr: II. Let him offer a reason:

units.la: 1. A felicitate temporum, ubi creverint & publicae & privatae opes. Hinc instituat comparationem temporum pristinorum Curii, Fabricii, Scipionum cum populus pauper cum nova Roma fuit ; & præsentium, ubi tot provinciis ac regnis aucta res Rom. Ipsam urbem jam marmoream: quid mirum, si & cives lautius se gerant, splendorem crescere & adolescere cum civitatibus.
units.tr: 1. From the happiness of the times, when both public and private wealth have grown. Hence he should draw a comparison between the earlier times of Curius, Fabricius and the Scipios, when the people were poor and Rome was new, and the present, when the Roman state has been enlarged by so many provinces and kingdoms, and the city itself is now of marble. What wonder if the citizens also live more lavishly, since splendor grows and matures along with the states.

units.la: 2. A mutatione, quam tempus ipsum afferat: videl. a. exhaustum iri opes superfluas, & facietatem apud ditiores modum facturam. b. Orbem esse rerum omnium, uti jam luxus, ita succedente tempore parsimoniam prævaliturum. Illustret à morbis periculosis, quæ tempus sanet.
units.tr: 2. From the change which time itself brings, namely: a. superfluous wealth will be exhausted, and moderation will be brought about among the richer by necessity; b. luxury, as it now prevails, so in the course of time thrift will prevail, as with all things in the world. Let him illustrate this from dangerous diseases, which time heals.

units.la: Conclus. Non igitur opus esse, ut periculosam tentent curam, quam ipsum tempus afferre poterit. Maxime si ipsi Proceres laudabili exemplo præcessuri sint: Solam penulam Tiberii usum preciosorum palliorum sustulisse: quid si omnes?
units.tr: Conclusion. It is therefore not necessary to attempt a dangerous cure, which time itself will be able to bring. Especially if the leaders themselves are going to lead the way with a praiseworthy example: Tiberius alone, by abandoning the use of costly cloaks, removed only the penula; what if all did so?

units.la: VII. Consul repetitis breviter suffragiis singulorum causam ad Principem remittendam censet.
units.tr: VII. The consul, briefly repeating the votes of each, judges that the matter should be referred to the Prince.

units.la: I. Præfatur, se audivisse libenter, quæ de propositā ab Ædilibus causa prudenter censuerint.
units.tr: I. He introduces by saying that he has listened gladly to what the senators have wisely judged about the matter proposed by the Aediles.

units.la: II. Loco propositionis agnoscat momentum causæ hujus, quæ rarò feliciter tractata sit.
units.tr: II. In place of the proposition, let him acknowledge the weight of this matter, which has seldom been handled with success.

units.la: III. Loco confirmationis, 1. generatim ponderet & examinet rationes allatas, sigillatim: 2. Non ita expeditum esse dicat, quid agendum sit; ubique militare rationes graves, & haud leviora obstacula.
units.tr: III. In place of the confirmation: 1. let him generally weigh and examine the reasons given, one by one; 2. let him say that it is not so clear what should be done; everywhere there are serious reasons and no less serious obstacles.

units.la: IV. Concludat itaque videri sibi causam hanc arduam & perplexam indeterminatam ad Principem mittendam esse, maximè quoniam & ipsius in suffragiis facta sit mentio. Melius esse ipsius prudentia & autoritate rem determinari, quam ut patres omnium in se invitent odia.
units.tr: IV. He concludes, therefore, that it seems to him that this difficult and perplexing matter should be sent to the Prince without a decision, especially since mention has been made of him in the votes. It is better for the matter to be determined by his prudence and authority, than for the fathers to draw upon themselves the hatred of all.

units.la: VIII. Epistola, qua causa ad Principem remittitur.
units.tr: VIII. Letter by which the matter is referred to the Prince.

units.la: I. Exord. Captet benevolentiam 1. exponendo voluntatem Senatus pro ipsius salute & præsentia; quo in rebus gravissimis ipsius consilio uti possint. 2. Quæ causa sit, cur in re magni momenti ipsius judicio utendum censuerit.
units.tr: I. Opening. Let him win goodwill: 1. by setting out the will of the Senate for his safety and presence, so that in the most serious matters they may make use of his counsel; 2. by stating the reason why they have judged that in a matter of great moment his judgment should be used.

units.la: II. Narratio. Exponat factum prout hactenus gestum est.
units.tr: II. Narration. Let him set out the matter as it has been carried out so far.

units.la: III. Conclus. 1. Causam in integram Principi committat. 2. Senatum commendet Principi cum sponsione obsequii.
units.tr: III. Conclusion. 1. He entrusts the cause, entire, to the Prince. 2. He commends the Senate to the Prince with a pledge of obedience.

units.la: THEMA XVI.
units.tr: THEMA XVI.

units.la: MATERIÆ IN GENERE DELIBERATIVO.
units.tr: MATERIÆ IN GENERE DELIBERATIVO.

units.la: 1. Utrum ad religionem cogi quis debeat. Affirmatè ex sent. Pontif.
units.tr: 1. Whether a person ought to be compelled to religion. Affirmed from the opinion of the Papists.

units.la: Exord. 1. A pondere hujus quæstionis: videl, cum nihil præstantius sit rebusp. tum nihil in ipså republ. preciosius esse religione. Ratio quia per hanc Deo obligatur mortalis, unde omnis ordinis ac imperii origo Confect. Hinc principibus summæ semper curæ fuit, tum inter gentes, tum inter Christianos. Utrum cogi ad illam subditi debeant disquiri.
units.tr: Exordium. 1. From the weight of this question: since nothing is more excellent among human affairs, and nothing in the commonwealth itself is more precious than religion. The reason is that through religion mortal man is bound to God, and from this comes the origin of all order and government. Hence rulers have always held it of the highest concern, both among the nations and among Christians. Let it be inquired whether subjects ought to be compelled to it.

units.la: Propositio. Probari tibi affirmativam, quam clero Romano probatam & utiliter usurpatam videas.
units.tr: Proposition. Let him prove the affirmative, which you may see approved and usefully employed by the Roman clergy.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. Ab utili. Concordia scil. in rep. quam confervare in rep Magistratus teneatur. Hanc v. sine consensu religionis obtineri non posse. Amplif. hoc exaggeratione malorum ex religionis dissidio passim inter Christianos ortorum. Hæc averti non posse, nisi una religio imperetur, & si aliter fieri non posset armis introducatur. Hinc Leges 12. tabularum & gentes passim prohibuisse Deos alienos.
units.tr: I. From utility. Namely, concord in the commonwealth, which the magistrate is bound to preserve. This cannot be obtained without agreement in religion. Let this be amplified by the exaggeration of the evils that arise everywhere among Christians from dissension in religion. These cannot be averted unless one religion is imposed, and if this cannot be done otherwise, it is introduced by arms. Hence the Laws of the Twelve Tables and the nations everywhere forbade foreign gods.

units.la: II. A Legitimo: quod probatur
units.tr: II. From lawfulness, which is proved:

units.la: 1. Ab exemplo seu Mandato Dei, qui unum Templum in unam religionem esse voluit in V.T. Deut. 13. 17. Exod. 22. & Pseudo prophetas jubet occidi. Ergo & hæreticos Illustretur exemplis regnum Asæ, Jehu, Josiæ, Eliæ; qui idololatrias excide-rint. Et Christi ejicientis numularios è templo, Petri occidentis Ananiam, Pauli occæcantis Elymam magum.
units.tr: 1. From the example and command of God, who in the Old Testament willed one temple and one religion (Deut. 13, 17; Exod. 22), and orders false prophets to be put to death. Therefore also heretics. Let it be illustrated by the examples of the reigns of Asa, Jehu, Josiah and Elijah, who destroyed idolatries; and of Christ driving the money-changers out of the temple, Peter slaying Ananias, and Paul blinding the magician Elymas.

units.la: 2. A natura hæreticorum, qui in scriptura comparantur eupis, furibus, latronibus & adulteris; Hos verò magistratus non tolerat in republ. Ergo, vide Cofterum in Enchir. c. 2. & Sciopi clasf. sacrum.
units.tr: 2. From the nature of heretics, who in Scripture are compared to thieves, robbers and adulterers; magistrates do not tolerate these in the commonwealth. Therefore see Costerus in the Enchiridion, chapter 2, and Sciopius, Classis sacra.

units.la: III. A necessario:
units.tr: III. From necessity:

units.la: 1. Ab unitate religionis veræ. Hanc igitur tuendam esse magistratui, & secus sentientes pellendos vel plectendos. Illustretur simili à legibus politicis, quæ non admittuntur, nisi à legitimo Magistratu Catæ sint. Multo minus falsa religio.
units.tr: 1. From the unity of the true religion. This therefore is to be guarded by the magistrate, and those who think otherwise are to be driven out or punished. Let it be illustrated by a likeness from political laws, which are not admitted unless they are enacted by a lawful magistrate. Much less so false religion.

units.la: 2. A periculo autonomiæ: quia sic pluralitas religionum, libertas errorum, adeoque Atheismus inveheretur.
units.tr: 2. From the danger of lawlessness: for thus a plurality of religions, freedom of error, and so atheism would be introduced.

units.la: IV. Ab exemplis laudatissimis Imperatorum & regum veterum, Constantini, Theodos. Valentin. Martiani, qui in hæreticos legibus statuerunt.
units.tr: IV. From the most praised examples of the ancient emperors and kings, Constantine, Theodosius, Valentinian and Martian, who enacted laws against heretics.

units.la: Conclus. Repetitis breviter rationibus propositionem inculcet addito pondere; videl. optimo jure sic vindicari posse tot regna & provincias Ecclesiæ ereptas, ex quo religionis libertas defendi coepit.
units.tr: Conclusion. Having briefly repeated the arguments, let him press the proposition again with added weight: namely, that the many kingdoms and provinces torn from the Church since liberty of religion began to be defended could rightly be reclaimed by this means.

units.la: II. Negate ex sententia Evangel.
units.tr: II. Denied from the sentiment of the Gospel.

units.la: Exord. Probet quod de pondere quæstionis asseruit antecessor, videlicet esse quæstionem, quæ multo sanguine elapso & præsenti seculo in Ital. Gallia, Germ. Belg. agitata sit. Addat rationem a confusione utriusque potestatis sacræ & politicæ. Applicetur ad institutum: videl. inde & natam assertionem antecessoris,
units.tr: Exordium. Let him prove what the predecessor asserted about the weight of the question, namely that it is a question which has been debated in Italy, France, Germany and Belgium with much blood shed, and in the present age. Let him add the reason from the confusion of the two powers, sacred and political. Let it be applied to the subject: namely, that from this also arose the assertion of the predecessor.

units.la: Propos. Cui proinde contradicendum & conscientiæ libertatem contra iniquam coactionem asserendam esse. Addatur commendatio materiæ & petitio attentioni
units.tr: Proposition. To this one must therefore contradict, and liberty of conscience must be asserted against unjust compulsion. Let a commendation of the matter and a request for attention be added.

units.la: Confirmatio habeat
units.tr: Confirmation should contain:

units.la: I. Præparationem, quæ diluat suspicionem, quasi curam sacrorum adimere magistratui velit: cujus proinde partes circa religionem explicet: videl. quod custos utriusque tabulæ, quoad externum ordinem, qui pars administrationis politicæ. Huc facere illa, quæ ab antecessore de mandato Dei & exemplis regum dicta sint, non ut cogant conscientias.
units.tr: I. A preparation, which dissolves the suspicion that he wishes to take from the magistrate the care of sacred things. Let him therefore explain the magistrate's parts concerning religion: namely, that he is guardian of both tables of the Law as to external order, which is a part of political administration. Those things said by the predecessor about God's command and the examples of kings bear on this, but not in order to compel consciences.

units.la: II. Rationes a legitimo, quod probetur
units.tr: II. Reasons from lawfulness, which are to be proved:

units.la: 1. A natura religionis, quæ suadendo, non cogendo tradi debeat. Ratio: quia in corde ac voluntate sedem habeat: cujus solus Deus Dominus est. Magistratus vero corporibus tantum imperant armis & vi externa. Contra arma Ecclesiæ spiritualia sunt 2. Cor. 10. 4. Heb. 4. 12.
units.tr: 1. From the nature of religion, which ought to be delivered by persuading, not by compelling. The reason is that it has its seat in the heart and will, of which God alone is Lord. The magistrate, however, rules only bodies, by arms and external force. Against this the spiritual weapons of the Church are (2 Cor. 10:4; Heb. 4:12).

units.la: 2. Ab exemplo Dei in V.T. & Apostolorum in N T, qui instituendo ad religionem converterunt gentes sine coactione. Regum item & principum: v.g. Constantii Imperatoris, Caroli Magni & Caroli V. Maximil. II. qui tyrannidem dixit, velle conscientiis imperare. Stephani Batori regis Pol. qui tria sibi reservasse Deum dixit: ex nihilo aliquid facere, scire futura & dominari conscientiis. Quantum ab hisce discedunt, qui cogere ad religionem satagunt. 3. Ab inutili coactione: videl. hinc haereticos reputari vel martyres, si pertinaces sint; vel fieri hypocritas si sint molles uti Vandali in Africa, Gothi in Italia. Hinc frustra tentata superiori seculo coactio, &c. vide praefat. Thuani
units.tr: 2. From the example of God in the Old Testament and of the Apostles in the New, who converted the nations to religion without compulsion. Likewise of kings and princes: for example, of the Emperor Constantius, Charlemagne and Charles V; of Maximilian II, who said that tyranny wishes to rule over consciences; and of Stephen Báthory, king of Poland, who said that God reserved three things to himself: to make something out of nothing, to know the future, and to rule over consciences. How far from these do those depart who strive to compel people to religion! 3. From useless compulsion: namely, that thence heretics are regarded as martyrs if they are stubborn, or made into hypocrites if they are soft, as the Vandals in Africa and the Goths in Italy were. Hence the compulsion tried in the previous century was in vain, etc. See the preface of Thuanus.

units.la: 4. A non necessaria coactione. Quia Deus diversas religiones & haereses tolerari vult in Ecclesia, ut probentur vere fideles: 1. Cor. 11.19. & populus spontaneus ipsi serviat Pf. 110. Frustra igitur rigidior homo est Deo.
units.tr: 4. From unnecessary compulsion. Because God wills that diverse religions and heresies be tolerated in the Church, so that the truly faithful may be proved (1 Cor. 11:19), and so that a willing people may serve him (Pf. 110). It is therefore in vain for man to be harsher than God.

units.la: III. Praemisso voto de unitate religionis, claudat hanc partem, videl. tolerandum quod mutari nequeat.
units.tr: III. Having premised the wish for unity of religion, let him close this part: namely, that what cannot be changed must be tolerated.

units.la: Confutatio. Examinet & refellat rationes antecessoris. Interim.
units.tr: Refutation. Let him examine and refute the arguments of the predecessor. Meanwhile:

units.la: Concluf. 1. Damnet inquisitionem & carnificinam conscientiarum.
units.tr: Conclusion. 1. Let him condemn the inquisition and the butchery of consciences.

units.la: 2. Ad mutuam aedificationem & tolerantiam cohortetur Christianos.
units.tr: 2. Let him exhort Christians to mutual edification and tolerance.

units.la: THEMA XVII. CONSULTATIO SUPER PETITIONE CAMPANORUM. Ex Liv. lib. 7. c. 29. 30. 31.
units.tr: THEME XVII. CONSULTATION CONCERNING THE CAMPANIANS' PETITION. From Livy, book 7, chapters 29, 30, 31.

units.la: I. Legati Campanorum petunt auxilium Roman. contra Samnites eorundem federatos.
units.tr: I. The envoys of the Campanians ask the Romans for help against the Samnites, their allies.

units.la: Exord. 1. Verbo allegent autoritatem publicam: a Senatu Populoque Campano se missos, quod ex literis publicae fidei Romani intellexerint. Exponant breviter statum Campanorum, videl. ob defensos Sidicinos se implicitos bello cum Samnitibus, cui gerendo proimpares sint, nisi succurratur.
units.tr: Exordium 1. They should first cite public authority: that they have been sent by the Senate and People of Campania, as the Romans learned from the public letters of alliance. They should briefly set out the state of the Campanians, namely that, having defended the Sidicinians, they have been drawn into war with the Samnites, which they are too weak to wage unless help is given.
