units.la: Propof. Missos se igitur ut Populi Rom. opem implorent, ideoque gratias se agere, quod audire illos dignati sint in causa urgentissima.
units.tr: Proposition Therefore they have been sent to implore the help of the Roman People; and they thank the Romans for deigning to hear them in so urgent a matter.

units.la: Confirm.
units.tr: Confirmation

units.la: I. A necessario. Quia aliquoties siniftre conflixerint, & jam intra moenia compulsi sint, certo expugnandi, nisi Romani suppetias ferant. Hac necessitate pressos se venire, ut majori beneficio affecti arctiori nexu Romanis se jungant. vide Liv. initio.
units.tr: I. From necessity. Because they have several times fought unsuccessfully and have now been driven within the walls, they are certain to be overrun unless the Romans bring aid. They come pressed by this necessity, so that, having received a greater benefit, they may join themselves to the Romans by a closer bond. See Livy at the beginning.

units.la: II. Ab honesto: quod ostendatur: 1. quia bellum Campanorum justum est, quippe pro sociis Sidicinis. Samnitum contra injustum & crudele. vide Liv. 2. Quia Romanos Deus evexerit ad illud culmen, ut miseris & inique pressis succurrant, quod & fecerint hactenus. Hac justitiæ gloriâ auctum iri rem Rom. 3. Quia nulla re prohibeantur. Hic diluatur tacita objectio, quod Samnites priores sint in fœdere Roman. Resp. hoc fœdere non excludi alios, sed gradu tantum priores esse Samnites.
units.tr: II. From honour, which is shown: 1. because the Campanians' war is just, since it is waged for their allies the Sidicinians, whereas that of the Samnites is unjust and cruel. See Livy. 2. Because God has raised the Romans to such a height that they may succour the wretched and unjustly oppressed, as they have done hitherto; the Roman cause will be increased by this glory of justice. 3. Because they are prevented by no matter. Here the tacit objection is to be refuted, that the Samnites are prior in the Roman covenant. Answer: this covenant does not exclude others; the Samnites are only prior in rank.

units.la: III. Ab utili: quod evincatur 1.a reditibus ex ubertate Campaniæ. 2. emolumento in bellis contra Æquos & Volscos præsertim, si Campani Romanis accesserint. Illustretur à contrario, secus Samnitibus hæc emolumenta accessura esse. vide Liv.
units.tr: III. From advantage, which is proven 1. from the revenues of the fertile Campania; 2. from the gain in wars, especially against the Aequi and Volsci, if the Campanians join the Romans. It is illustrated by the contrary: otherwise these advantages would accrue to the Samnites. See Livy.

units.la: IV. A facili. Quia vel sine bello solo terrore nominis Roman. repelli Samnites queant. Nec enim si Campanis nimia felicitate fractis terribiles sint, se etiam Romanis latè victoribus futuros.
units.tr: IV. From ease. Because the Samnites can be repelled, even without war, by the terror of the Roman name alone. For even if they are terrible to the Campanians, who have been broken by excessive good fortune, they will not be so to the Romans, who are widely victorious.

units.la: Concluf. Inculcatis breviter argumentis urgeat maturum auxilium, addita ratione 1.ab enixo voto & plenaria deditione Campanorum per hypothesin, anhelantis responsum Civitatis 2. à collatione utilitatis & jacturæ Samnitnm & Romanorum, quod pendeat ex hoc momento.
units.tr: Conclusion Having briefly pressed the arguments, they should urge prompt help, adding the reasons: 1. from the eager wish and full surrender of the Campanians, supposed by hypothesis, who long for the State's answer; 2. from the comparison of the advantage and loss of the Samnites and the Romans, which depends on this moment.

units.la: II. Primus Senator audiendos dicit Campanos.
units.tr: II. The first senator says the Campanians should be heard.

units.la: Exord. 1. In genere ab officio Senatoris, quod sit studere amplificationi reip. Illustretur exemplo majorum: quorum vestigiis ipse semper insistendum exi-stimarit.
units.tr: Exordium 1. In general, from the duty of a senator, which is to strive for the enlargement of the commonwealth. It is illustrated by the example of the ancestors, in whose footsteps he has always thought he himself must tread.

units.la: 2, In specie accedatur ad hypoth. Lautas offerri à Campanis conditiones, quæ utrum acceptandæ an recusandæ sint, disquirendum.
units.tr: 2. In particular, he comes to the hypothesis: generous conditions are offered by the Campanians, and it must be inquired whether they are to be accepted or refused.

units.la: Propos. Quanquam res ardua sit, in qua aliorum sententias audire malit, quam dicere suam, tamen, quia ætatis ac ordinis ratio primas ipsi deferat, se liberè dicturum: videri sibi tam optatam occasionem amplificandi remp. minime negligendam esse.
units.tr: Proposition Although the matter is difficult, and he would rather hear others' opinions than state his own, nevertheless, since the reason of age and rank gives him the first place, he will speak freely: it seems to him that so desired an opportunity of enlarging the commonwealth is by no means to be neglected.

units.la: Confirm. I. Probet partim rationibus, quæ à Legatis Campanorum allatæ sunt videl. 1. neminem dubitare neque de summa utilitate, neque de facilitate rei conficendæ, & hic inculcet illud; Salus reip. summa lex est. 2. Maxime cum necessitas extrema urgeat. videl. in eo res statu esse, ut Campani subigantur à Samnitibus. Hic exponat, quanta hinc accessio futura sit Samnitibus, qui semper infesti fuerint & futuri sint Romanis, licet pro tempore federati. Facile rumpi fœdera à profectioribus. Exaggeret hic pericula à Samnitibus imminentia, si Campania ditissima potiti fuerint.
units.tr: Confirmation I. He proves partly by the reasons brought forward by the Campanian envoys, namely 1. that no one doubts either the very great advantage or the ease of accomplishing the matter; and here he should press that saying: the safety of the commonwealth is the highest law. 2. Especially since extreme necessity presses, namely that the Campanians are in such a state that they will be subdued by the Samnites. Here he should set out how great an accession will accrue to the Samnites from this, who have always been hostile to the Romans and will be so, although allies for the time being. Covenants are easily broken by those who are more advanced. Here he should exaggerate the dangers hanging over from the Samnites, if they had gained possession of very rich Campania.

units.la: II. Examinet argumentum ab honesto. Hic 1. dicat nolle se dispu- tare dejustitia causæ vel Campanorum vel Samnitum, alteros merito defendisse socios, alteros merito bellum, inferre adjuto- ribus. 2. Æquum esse dicat succurrere afflictis contra poten- tiorem, ut servetur æquilibrium inter vicinas resp. Sic egisse Philippum Macedonem, &c. 3. Nec priori fidere cum Samniti- bus Romanos excludi à defendendis oppressis. Hoc probet a. A natura foederis, quod sit fedus pacis, non mutui auxilii b. A modo auxilii præstandi; videl. interpositione, tanquam pro novis sociis rem forte confici sine armis: non auferos Samnites resi- stere petitis Romanorum c. A comparatione offensæ & in- gentis utilitatis; hanc præponderare. Rationem status excu- sare ista posse: eventu & felicitate æstimari consilia. Omnia re- gna & resp. crevisse non sine aliqua violatione æquitatis.
units.tr: II. He should examine the argument from honour. Here 1. he should say that he is unwilling to dispute about the justice of the cause, whether of the Campanians or of the Samnites: the former rightly defended their allies, the latter rightly make war on those who bring help to them. 2. He should say it is fair to succour the afflicted against the more powerful, so that the balance between neighbouring commonwealths is kept; so Philip of Macedon acted, etc. 3. Nor should it be trusted that the Romans are excluded from defending the oppressed by the earlier covenant with the Samnites. He should prove this a. from the nature of the covenant, which is a treaty of peace, not of mutual aid; b. from the manner of giving aid, namely by intervention, as on behalf of new allies, when the matter might perhaps be accomplished without arms, the Samnites not being so fierce as to resist the Romans' request; c. from the comparison of offence and very great advantage: the latter outweighs the former. The reason of state can excuse these things: counsels are judged by their outcome and good fortune. All kingdoms and commonwealths have grown not without some violation of equity.

units.la: Concluf. Hortetur ut arridentem fortunam amplectantur, & primo per Legationem, si illa minus succedat per arma supplices Campa- nos vindicent, & tueantur: Addita nova ratione; futurum sic ut oppressi omnes ad Romanos tanquam asylum confugiant; unde augmentum reip. certissimum.
units.tr: Conclusion He should urge them to embrace the smiling fortune, and first by embassy; if that should succeed less well, then by arms they should protect and defend the suppliant Campanians. Adding a new reason: thus it will come about that all the oppressed flee to the Romans as to a refuge, whence the increase of the commonwealth is most certain.

units.la: III. Secundus Senator contra statuit, non esse audiendos.
units.tr: III. The second senator, on the contrary, decides that they should not be heard.

units.la: Exord. A difficultate præsentis deliberationis. Hæc 1. Proponatur. 2. probetur: quia utilitas & honestas imo ipsa fi- des Deorum contendere inter se videantur, 3. Explicetur brevi repetitione factæ propositionis Campanorum, & suffragio Collegæ. 4. Concludatur. Et se igitur pro illa fide, qua Patriæ ob- strictus, sententiam dicturum, excutiendum, si religione Deorum à collega dissentiat, & apparenti reip. utilitati refragari videatur.
units.tr: Exord. From the difficulty of the present deliberation. Here: (1) it is to be set forth; (2) it is to be proved, because usefulness and honour, indeed the very faith owed to the gods, seem to contend with one another; (3) it is to be explained by a brief repetition of the proposal of the Campanians and the vote of the colleague; (4) a conclusion is to be drawn. And so he says he will give his opinion mindful of that loyalty by which he is bound to the fatherland, and that he must examine whether he differs from his colleague on religious grounds and seems to oppose the apparent advantage of the commonwealth.

units.la: Propof. Putare se, Campanos non esse audiendos in hac sua peti- tione.
units.tr: Propof. He thinks that the Campanians should not be heard in this their petition.

units.la: Confirm. I. Concedat apparentem utilitatem ex repetitis breviter Campanorum & collegæ rationibus. Quis enim nescit Campaniæ ubertatem &c. Nec dubium esse, quin illa cessura sit Samnitibus, ob inertiam Campanorum luxu corruptorum. Luxum enim pes- simum diuturnitatis custodem.
units.tr: Confirm. I. Let him grant the apparent advantage, from the reasons of the Campanians and of his colleague briefly repeated. For who does not know the fertility of Campania, etc.? Nor is there doubt that it will fall to the Samnites, because of the sloth of the Campanians, corrupted by luxury. For luxury is the worst guardian of long duration.

units.la: II. Opponat honestatem, quæ tantæ utilitati repugnet. Hic 1. Differat in genere de pugna honesti & utilis, quo casu majot honestatis, quam utilitatis habenda sit ratio; nec esse utile nisi quod honestum. Ita visum semper Romanis priscis, probetur exemplis. vide Cic. in 3. offic.
units.tr: II. Let him set honour against so great an advantage, which opposes it. Here: (1) let him discuss in general the contest between the honourable and the useful, in which case greater regard must be paid to honour than to advantage; and that nothing is useful unless it is honourable. This was always the view of the early Romans, let it be proved by examples. See Cicero, On Duties, book 3.

units.la: 2. Ostendat in hypothesi petitum Campanorum pugnare cum honestate:
units.tr: (2) Let him show that, in the present case, the petition of the Campanians is at odds with honour:

units.la: a. Quia sit contra fedus cum Samnitibus Deo teste initum, si hostes ipsorum juvent Romani. Disserat hic de foederum inviolabilitate, sine qua consistere nequeat humana societas.
units.tr: a. Because it is against the covenant entered into with the Samnites under God as witness, if the Romans assist their enemies. Let him discourse here on the inviolability of covenants, without which human society cannot stand.

units.la: b. Quia sit contra juramentum, cujus religio sacrosanctum semper habita sit, quippe cujus vindex Deus sit, qui temporalibus & sempiternis suppliciis mactabit temeratores & perjuros, &c.
units.tr: b. Because it is against an oath, whose sanctity has always been held sacred, since God is its avenger, who will punish violators and perjurers with temporal and eternal punishments, etc.

units.la: c. Quia sit contra famam Romanorum, qui fedifragi, perjuri, avari audient apud omnes & feram posteritatem; unde plus detrimenti rei Romanae futurum sit, quam emolumenti in praesens. Claudat Epiphon. Nihil, utile esse posse, quod ab honestate, quod a pietate dissidet.
units.tr: c. Because it is against the reputation of the Romans, who will be heard among all men and in distant posterity as covenant-breakers, perjurers, and greedy; so that more harm will come to the Roman state than advantage for the present. Let him close with the epiphonema: nothing can be useful which dissents from honour and from piety.

units.la: Confutatio. Examinet rationes Campanorum & Collegae.
units.tr: Confutatio. Let him examine the reasons of the Campanians and of the colleague.

units.la: 1. Excuset errorem, quod amore patriae & splendida oratione Legatorum Collega abreptus sit, ut honestatem utilitati praetulerit.
units.tr: 1. Let him excuse the error: that the colleague, carried away by love of country and by the splendid speech of the envoys, preferred honour to advantage.

units.la: 2. Refellat rationes.
units.tr: 2. Let him refute the reasons.

units.la: a. Salutem patriae supremam legem esse: videl. quamdiu honestis mediis salvari & juvari queat. Illa enim tantum nos posse, quae honeste possumus.
units.tr: a. That the safety of the fatherland is the supreme law: namely, so long as it can be saved and aided by honourable means. For we can only do those things which we can do honourably.

units.la: b. Necessitatem etiam summam, non excusare scelera.
units.tr: b. That even the greatest necessity does not excuse crimes.

units.la: c. Succurrendum afflictis, videl. si honeste possimus. Contra Deum saepe punire faustum & luxu, ut juvari nolit. Et talem videri conditionem Campanorum, in quorum insolentiam & luxum breviter invehatur.
units.tr: c. That the afflicted must be succoured, namely if we can do so honourably. God often punishes by good fortune and luxury, so that He is unwilling to be aided. And such appears to be the condition of the Campanians, against whose insolence and luxury he briefly inveighs.

units.la: d. Licet fedus cum Samnitibus non sit mutui auxilii, tamen illud prohibere mutuas offensiones.
units.tr: d. Although the covenant with the Samnites is not one of mutual aid, nevertheless it forbids mutual injuries.

units.la: e. Rationem status inventum esse priscis Romanis incognitum, qui religione & honestate omnia metiri consueverint; Deo adversum, patriae exitiale, quae virtute & patrocinio Deorum, non scelere asserenda sit. f. Animadvertere hoc ipsum collegam, qui sola interpositione sperer rem confici posse: Quod nec sibi displiceat.
units.tr: e. The principle of state-reason was unknown to the early Romans, who were accustomed to measure all things by religion and honour; it is hostile to God and destructive to the fatherland, which must be maintained by virtue and the protection of the gods, not by crime. f. Let him note that his colleague himself hopes the matter can be accomplished by mere intervention alone; and that this does not displease him.

units.la: Concluf. 1. Auxilium itaque Deum prius quam homines violaturum Campanis esse negandum. 2. Mittendos Legatos, ad Samnites socios, qui concordiam tentent. 3, Obtestetur patres, ut bene consideren t, utrum Deum & fidem famamque potius, quam Campanos offendere velint, sibi nullum, nisi in virtute ac pietate reip. videri emolumentum.
units.tr: Concluf. 1. Therefore it must be denied to the Campanians that aid should be given, since God will be violated before men. 2. Envoys are to be sent to the Samnites, allies, who should attempt concord. 3. Let him entreat the fathers to consider carefully whether they wish rather to offend God, faith and reputation than the Campanians, since to them there seems no advantage except in the virtue and piety of the commonwealth.

units.la: THEMA XVIII.
units.tr: THEME XVIII.

units.la: DE HISTRIONIBUS PELLENDIS ITALIA
units.tr: ON THE EXPULSION OF ACTORS FROM ITALY

units.la: Ex Tacit. lib.4. c.14. vide & lib.1. c.77. & Liv.pass.
units.tr: From Tacitus, Annals book 4, ch. 14; see also book 1, ch. 77, and Livy passim.

units.la: Tiberius rem patribus proponit, pellendos statuens
units.tr: Tiberius lays the matter before the senators, resolving that the actors be expelled

units.la: Exord. 1. Praefatur de sua lenitate erga omnes: 2. in specie etiam erga Histriones in honorem Augusti, qui illos toleraverit semper. 3. queritur de ipsorum immodestia, qua adversus omnes utuntur.
units.tr: Exordium 1. He speaks first of his own mildness towards all. 2. He speaks in particular of his mildness towards the actors, out of honour to Augustus, who always tolerated them. 3. He complains of their immodesty, with which they behave towards everyone.

units.la: Propof. Unde in contrariam sententiam fere inclinare incipiat, ideoque de iis referendum ad Senatum judicarit.
units.tr: Proposition: whence he begins to incline almost to the contrary opinion, and therefore judged that the matter should be referred to the Senate.

units.la: Confirm. I. Breviter concedat aliquem illorum usum. 1. in redarguendis vitiis popularibus: unde multi metuunt censuram. 2. in demulcendo populi ocio: qui alias ad illicita magis flectant. Unde & Augustus iis faverit. &c. Verum majora incommoda exinde esse.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. He briefly concedes some use of them: 1. in rebuking popular vices, whence many fear censure; 2. in soothing the idleness of the people, who otherwise are more inclined to illicit things. Whence Augustus also favoured them, etc. But greater inconveniences arise from this.

units.la: II. Exaggeret incommoda inde emergentia: uti est. 1. nimia licentia oris, qua passim optimos, imo ipsum principem perstringunt· 2. scurrilitates noxiae reip. 3. quod turbae & seditio saepe per hosce concitantur. vid. lib.1. 4. scelera & foeda multa quae per hosce homines leves & infames seminantur. 5. corruptela juventutis.
units.tr: II. He exaggerates the inconveniences that arise from them, namely: 1. their excessive licence of speech, by which they everywhere lash the best men, even the prince himself; 2. buffooneries harmful to the commonwealth; 3. that tumults and sedition are often stirred up through these men (see book 1); 4. the many crimes and foul deeds that are sown by these light and infamous men; 5. the corruption of youth.

units.la: III. Refellat praetensam recreationem ex talibus, ut insulsam & barbaris olim adamatam. Alia jam tempora esse, ubi publica honestatis cura.
units.tr: III. He refutes the alleged recreation to be had from such things, as insipid and once loved by barbarians. The times are now different, when there is public concern for decency.

units.la: Concluf. Quia magis magisque crescat haec licentia, autoritate patrum coercendum videri; siquidem ita ipsis visum fuerit. Quae de re ipsorum explorare sententiam voluerit.
units.tr: Conclusion. Since this licence grows more and more, it seems it should be restrained by the authority of the senators, if indeed it seems so to them. He wishes to learn their opinion on this matter.

units.la: Hatte.
units.tr: Hatterius.

units.la: Exord. Prædicet curam Tiberii in omnibus reipubl. partibus. Ratoinem addat ab officio principis, qui in sublimi veluti speculâ constitutus ceu vigil omnia prospicere debeat, Merito proinde & scenæ licentiam ipsum notasse & histrionum causam in consilium adduxisse, & inclinare in relegationem.
units.tr: Exordium. He extols Tiberius's care for every part of the commonwealth. He adds a reason from the office of a prince, who, placed as on a lofty watchtower, ought to watch over everything like a sentinel. Rightly, therefore, he has noted the licence of the stage and brought the cause of the actors before the council, and he inclines towards banishment.

units.la: Propos. Cum igitur & Patrum sententiam desuper audire voluerit: excusét Princeps, si ab ipso dissentiat.
units.tr: Proposition. Since he also wished to hear the opinion of the Fathers on this matter, let the Emperor be excused if he dissents from them.

units.la: Confirm. I. Ex rationibus ab ipso Tiberio allatis, quas repetat, expoliatque: & primam quidem: quia felicius per ludicra & jocum, quam per leges (e veriores corrigantur vitia popularia. Leges enim cogere invitos & reluctantes: satyram vero verecundia & pudore volentes corrigere &c. Alteram repræsentando & exaggerando scelera, quæ ex ignavo ocio nasci consueverint. Rectius illud ludicris, hujusmodi impendi. Nec posse plebem semper labori & seriis intentam esse.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From the reasons Tiberius himself advanced, which the speaker repeats and polishes. The first is that popular vices are corrected more happily through plays and jesting than through laws. Laws compel the unwilling and the resistant, whereas satire corrects those who are willing, through shame and modesty, and so on. The second is that by presenting and magnifying the crimes which usually arise from idle leisure, one makes better use of such light entertainments. Nor can the common people always be kept at labour and serious pursuits.

units.la: II. Ab exemplo Græcorum majorum, qui non obstantibus studiis & gravissimis bellis histriones admittendos censuerint. Hinc tot theatra erecta tanto sumptu. Non temere discedendum ab statutis majorum.
units.tr: II. From the example of the great Greeks, who, despite their studies and most serious wars, thought actors should be admitted. Hence so many theatres were erected at such great expense. One should not lightly depart from the statutes of our ancestors.

units.la: III. Ab exemplo ipsius Augusti, principis longe prudentissimi, qui illos foverit & præmiis suaque præsentia honoraverit. Non posse Tiberium discedere ab ipsius institutis, in quæ juraverit.
units.tr: III. From the example of Augustus himself, by far the most prudent of princes, who fostered actors and honoured them with rewards and his own presence. Tiberius cannot depart from his predecessor's institutions, to which he has sworn.

units.la: Conclus. Ex dictis rationibus retinendos & Legibus arctioribus nimiam licentiam constrigendam esse. Neque enim omnia incommoda tolli posse ex rep. &c.
units.tr: Conclusion. From the reasons given, actors should be retained, and excessive licence should be checked by stricter laws. For not all the inconveniences of the commonwealth can be removed, and so on.

units.la: Afinius Gallus Senator refutat Hatterium.
units.tr: Asinius Gallus, a senator, refutes Hatterius.

units.la: Exord. A natura verae clementiae, quæ bonis benigna, malis aspera est: Secus vecordia & lentitudo futura & sceleribus viam patefactura. Applicetur ad Tiberium contra Hatterium.
units.tr: Exordium. From the nature of true clemency, which is kind to good men and harsh to bad; otherwise folly and sloth will follow, and open the way to crimes. Let this be applied to Tiberius against Hatterius.

units.la: Propos. Non probare sibi, quæ pro Histrionibus a Collega allata sunt.
units.tr: Proposition. It does not please him that the arguments put forward for actors by his colleague should be accepted.

units.la: Confirm. I. Vindicet mentem Tiberii imper. videl per concessionem quandam ex mente dissentientium illa dicta esse. Interim revera 1. melius censoria gravitate, quam scurrilitate histrionum redargui-vitia. Nemo vitia ridere debet: bonos sponte parere legibus, malos cogendos; secus gratis leges imperant. 2. Idem & de ocio statuentuendum, legibus censoriis compescendum illud, non fovendum ludicris. Alia exercitia esse, qualia campus Martius suggerit; aut philosophia.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. Let him vindicate the mind of the Emperor Tiberius, namely by granting that those words were spoken from the standpoint of those who dissent. Meanwhile, in truth: (1) vices are better refuted by censorial gravity than by the buffoonery of actors. No one ought to laugh at vices; good men obey laws of their own accord, bad men must be compelled, otherwise laws are issued in vain. (2) The same must be decided about leisure: it should be restrained by censorial laws, not fostered by plays. There are other exercises, such as those the Campus Martius supplies, or philosophy.

units.la: II. Ad exempla respondeat, quod non exemplis, sed legibus judicandum. Alia tempora, alios requirere mores. Olim rudem populum oblectamentis puerilibus demulcendum fuisse: jam melioribus studiis in toga & sago tempus, sumptus theatrorum, melius collocari posse. Non facile discedendum ab institutis majorum; nisi gravia aut noxia esse incipiant.
units.tr: II. To the examples he answers that judgement must be based not on examples but on laws. Different times require different morals. Formerly the rude populace had to be soothed with childish amusements; now the time for better studies, in the toga and the military cloak, and the expense of theatres can be better spent. One should not readily depart from the institutions of our ancestors, unless they begin to be grave or harmful.

units.la: III. Ad exemplum Augusti respond. sic tulisse ipsius ingenium maxime post funesta illa tempora, ubi recreationibus refocillandum fuerit. Gratulandum jam reip. quod princeps laboribus par, & aversus ab illecebris vitiorum, qualis scena, uti illud princeps satis ostenderit.
units.tr: III. To the example of Augustus he replies that such was his disposition, especially after those disastrous times when he needed refreshing with recreations. It is now a matter for congratulation for the commonwealth that the Prince is equal to his labours and averse to the allurements of vice, such as the stage; the Prince has shown this sufficiently.

units.la: Concluf. Non dubitet; quin ipse Hatterius, haec altius perpendens, sic sensurus fit. Ideoque inhaerendum sententiae Tiberii.
units.tr: Conclusion. He does not doubt that Hatterius himself, weighing these matters more deeply, will think in the same way. Therefore one must adhere to the opinion of Tiberius.

units.la: Tiberius summam recolligens concludit pellendos esse.
units.tr: Tiberius, gathering up the sum, concludes that they must be expelled.

units.la: I. Referat fe ad illa quae pro sua fide & diligentia senatores in utramque partem attulerint. Uti sane haud facile fit adulta vitia exstirpare, nec facile mutandum quid in rep. quae causa fuerit, quod sine consilio patrum nihil hic agere voluerit.
units.tr: I. He refers himself to those things which the senators have brought forward on either side, according to their faith and diligence. Indeed, it is not easy to root out vices once grown, nor easy to change anything in the commonwealth that has long been in place, which he did not wish to do here without the counsel of the Fathers.

units.la: II. Conferat & examinet paucis quae pro histrionibus contra suas rationes ab Hatterio allata: quae cum ab ipso jam praevisa & tacta sint in propositione, nec refutata ab Hatterio, e contrario illa quae prolata ab Hatterio solide infracta sint per Asinium Gallum: insuperque nihil allatum ab Hatterio aut ullo alio contra rationes suas, ab incommodis ab hiftrionia & scena in remp. redundantibus, non videri se, quare discedere debeat a sua sententia.
units.tr: II. He compares and briefly examines the arguments advanced by Hatterius on behalf of the actors against his own reasons. Since these have already been anticipated and touched upon by him in his proposal and not refuted by Hatterius, while on the contrary those things advanced by Hatterius have been solidly overturned by Asinius Gallus; and moreover, since Hatterius, or anyone else, has brought forward nothing against his reasons concerning the inconveniences that flow from the stage and theatre into the commonwealth, he does not see why he should depart from his opinion.

units.la: III. Concludat publico S. decreto histriones omnesque scenae ministros, tanquam perniciosos reip: & bonis moribus & felicitati temporum suorum adversos in perpetuum ex rep. relegandos esse: ut honestis exercitiis quisque vitam tolerare discat.
units.tr: III. He concludes that, by a public decree of the Senate, actors and all the ministers of the stage, as dangerous to the commonwealth and hostile to good morals and to the welfare of his times, are to be banished from the commonwealth for ever, so that each may learn to endure life by honourable pursuits.

units.la: THEMA XIX. CONSULTATIO DE REFORMANDA POLITIA
units.tr: THEME XIX. A CONSULTATION ON REFORMING THE COMMONWEALTH

units.la: Ex I. Sam. 8. & seqq.
units.tr: From 1 Sam. 8 and following.

units.la: I. Præses Synedrii causam collegio proponit: videl. Cogitandum de reformat. Reip.
units.tr: I. The president of the Synedrium lays the case before the assembly: namely, that they must consider the reform of the commonwealth.

units.la: Exord. I. Gratias agat, quod ad suam convocationem frequentes convenerint.
units.tr: Exordium. I. He should thank them for coming in good numbers to his summons.

units.la: II. Amplificat. hoc 1. à causa vid. quod memores fuerint officii divinitus ipsis comissi, quo populi gerunt personam, cujus curà Deus ipsis commiserit, 2. à circumstantia temporis: quo omnia in pejus ruant, adeo ut de matura emendatione serio cogitandum, quæ causa hujus conventus: ad cujus successum benignum Numen exoptet.
units.tr: II. He amplifies this (1) from the cause, namely that they have remembered the office divinely committed to them, by which they bear the person of the people, whose care God has entrusted to them; and (2) from the circumstances of the time, when all things are collapsing for the worse, so that a timely reform must be seriously considered. This is the purpose of the present gathering, and he should pray that the gracious Deity grant it success.

units.la: Narrat. Statum rerum exponat: videl. 1. Senium Samuelis, quem laudet a fidelitate. 2. Substitutionem filiorum suorum, & spem conceptam, ipsos exemplum patris imitaturos. 3. Ipsorum degenerationem dum sacra & profana, libidine, avaritia, & injustitia corruperint:
units.tr: Narration. He sets out the state of affairs, namely: (1) Samuel's old age, which he should praise for his fidelity; (2) the appointment of his sons as successors, and the hope conceived that they would imitate their father's example; (3) their degeneracy, since they have corrupted both sacred and profane things with lust, greed and injustice.

units.la: Propofit. Ipsorum officium esse, serio cogitare de emendatione & providere ne resp. detrimentum capiat:
units.tr: Proposition. It is their duty to think seriously about amendment and to take care that the commonwealth does not suffer harm.

units.la: Confirm. I. à justo: autoritate scilicet legis Dei Deut. 17. v. 1. seq. ubi officium judicum describitur, & simul populo potestas datur constituendi sibi magistratum, imò & regem: uti & jura gentium ferant, ut populus liber statuere queat de forma regiminis. Illustretur prolepsi à potestate Samueli omnibusque magistratibus divinitus concessa. Resp. quod senior & impar imperio Samuel. 2. Quod resp. non sit hæreditaria. 3. Quod filii ipsius à populo non approbati. 4. Quod in tali casu seniorum officium sit rebus prospicere. Locus Communis de Ephoris & Senioribus regnorum ac rerumps: maximè vacante, uti hic, repub):
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From what is just, namely from the authority of the law of God in Deut. 17:1 and following, where the office of judges is described, and at the same time power is given to the people to appoint for themselves a magistrate, even a king, as the laws of nations also allow, so that a free people may decide on the form of government. Let this be illustrated by anticipation from the power granted by God to Samuel and to all magistrates. Reply: that Samuel was old and unequal to the command. (2) That the commonwealth is not hereditary. (3) That his sons were not approved by the people. (4) That in such a case it is the office of the elders to provide for the affairs of state. A common place about Ephors and elders of kingdoms and commonwealths, especially when the commonwealth is vacant, as here.

units.la: II. A necessario: quod probetur recensione pleniori & exaggeratione damnorum iniquitatis filiorum Samuelis. 2. ab invalescentibus passim querelis, quæ minimè negligendæ senioribus. 3. à metuenda profanitate in cultu & confusione in rep.
units.tr: II. From necessity, which is proved by a fuller enumeration and exaggeration of the damage done by the iniquity of Samuel's sons; (2) from the complaints growing everywhere, which the elders must by no means neglect; (3) from the fearful profanity in worship and the confusion in the commonwealth.

units.la: Concluf. 1. Moneat illos officii. 2. Hortetur ut in medium delibe-rent, statuantque quid ex rep. existiment.
units.tr: Conclusion. (1) He should remind them of their office; (2) he should urge them to deliberate in the open and to decide what they think should be done for the commonwealth.

units.la: II. Primus Senior statuit monendum prius esse Samuelem; nec ipso in-scio quicquam innovandum.
units.tr: II. The first elder rules that Samuel must be admonished first, and nothing should be changed without his knowledge.

units.la: Exord. I. Assumta & approbata Præsidis propositione, eidem gra-tias agat pro sollicitudine. II. Fateatur corruptionem regiminis & necessariam emendationé. III. De mediis salutaribus deliberandum.
units.tr: Exordium. I. Having taken up and approved the president's proposal, he should thank him for his concern. II. He should admit the corruption of the government and the need for reform. III. The means of salvation must be deliberated on.

units.la: Propos. Optet præsidem aperuisse mentem suam; interim quia or-do ipsum moneat officii, videri sibi tentandam esse viam lenissi-mam, & tum Samuelem, tum filios ipsius per deputatos monen-dos esse officii.
units.tr: Proposition. He hopes the president has made his mind plain; meanwhile, since the order of business reminds him of their office, it seems to him that the gentlest way must be tried, and that Samuel and his sons must be admonished of their duty through deputies.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. Examinet modestè argumenta præsidis; quæ inclinare tacite vi-deantur, ad remotionē Samuelis & liberorū, ac mutationem re-giminis: Sed 1. locum Deut. 17. loqui de casu vacantiæ reip. jam vero vivere adhuc Samuelem: Opponat aliam legem de obe-diendo magistratibus, & punita rebellione, probetur exemplo Coræ. 2. Samuelem divinitus constitutum esse, & bene præ-fuisse. Hunc non posse removeri, sine offensa Dei constituentis ipsum. 3. Multo minus ob delictum liberorum. 4. Minimè ve-ro non auditum. Hinc
units.tr: I. He should modestly examine the president's arguments, which seem tacitly to lean towards the removal of Samuel and his sons and a change of government. But (1) the passage in Deut. 17 speaks of a case of a vacant commonwealth, whereas Samuel is still alive. He should set against it another law about obeying magistrates, and show by the example of Korah that rebellion is punished. (2) Samuel was appointed by God and has governed well. He cannot be removed without offence to God who appointed him. (3) Much less on account of his sons' fault. (4) Yet he must by no means be left unheard. Hence:

units.la: II. Repetat & confirmet propositionem suam.
units.tr: II. He should repeat and confirm his proposal.

units.la: 1. A tuto si moneatur: a. ab indole Samuelis quia senex placi-dus ac reip. studiosus boni consulet admonitionem. b. A con-trarii periculo si removeatur: videlicet ipsum vindicem in-vocaturum Deum: Filios de rebellione conclamaturos, unde metuendæ turbæ & ἀναςχία. c. Si non prosit admonitio sem-per patere viam ad remedia asperiora. Illustretur exemplo medici, ad extrema remedia non nisi extrema necessitate ac-cedentis.
units.tr: 1. It is safe if he is admonished: a. from Samuel's character, since as a mild old man who cares for the commonwealth he will take the admonition well. b. From the danger of the opposite course, if he is removed: namely, he would call on God as avenger, and the sons would cry out against rebellion, whence there is fear of tumult and anarchy. c. If admonition does not help, the way to harsher remedies always stays open, as with a physician who comes to extreme remedies only under extreme necessity.

units.la: 2. Ab utili, si scilicet status præsens retineri queat, nihil salu-brius reip. Illustretur a contraria mutatione, quæ uti semper, ita præcipue in rep. periculosa. Maximè si in regem con-sentiant, actum videri de libertate. vid. 1. Sam. 8. & hæc ve-luti præsagiat.
units.tr: 2. It is useful, namely if the present state can be kept: nothing is more wholesome for the commonwealth. This is shown by the contrary change, which is always harmful, and especially so in a perilous commonwealth. Above all, if they agree to a king, liberty will seem to be done for. See 1 Sam. 8; this is, as it were, a foreshadowing.

units.la: Concluf. Ex repetitis breviter rationibus, consultum sibi videri dicat, si mittantur deputati ad Samuelem, qui de corrigendis filiorum nævis ipsum cohortentur. Si incorrigibiles, exspectandam saltem mortem Samuelis antequam quippiam movetur.
units.tr: Conclusion. Having briefly gone over the reasons, he says it seems good to him that deputies be sent to Samuel to urge him to correct his sons' blemishes. If they prove incorrigible, they should at least wait for Samuel's death before anything is moved.

units.la: III. Secundus senior statuit indices in ordinem redigendos esse & subjiciendos Synedrio;
units.tr: III. The second elder rules that the judges must be brought into order and made subject to the Synedrium.

units.la: Exord. I. Approbet moderationem Collegæ: addita ratione, quia uti in mortis, ita & in rep. extrema non facile tentanda.
units.tr: Exordium. I. He approves his colleague's moderation, adding the reason that, as in death, so also in the state, extreme measures must not lightly be attempted.

units.la: II. Illustret hoc prolepsi, vid. magnam quidem esse corruptelam; attamen non talem, quæ sine mutatione reip. fieri nequeat.
units.tr: II. He illustrates this by anticipation: the corruption is indeed great, yet not of a kind that cannot be remedied without changing the commonwealth.

units.la: Propos. Proponat sententiam suam; vid. revocandam esse autoritatem Synedrii, illiqve subjiciendos judices.
units.tr: Proposition. He sets out his opinion: namely, that the authority of the Synedrium must be restored and the judges made subject to it.

units.la: Confutat. Sententia cessoris, Hinc
units.tr: Refutation. The opinion of the previous speaker. Hence:

units.la: I. Præmittat laudem ejus, approbetque rationes ipsius, quas contra depositionem, pro autoritate magistratus divinitus constituti adduxerit:
units.tr: I. He should first praise him, and approve the reasons he has brought forward against deposition, in defence of the authority of a magistrate divinely appointed.

units.la: II. Ostendat dissensum à sententia ipsius de prævia admonitione.
units.tr: II. He should show his disagreement with the previous speaker about prior admonition.

units.la: 1. Quia assueti regimini admonitiones subditorum ægre ferre, saltem contemnere solent; aut etiam animadvertere in autores.
units.tr: 1. Because men accustomed to government usually bear admonitions from subjects badly, at least they despise them, or even take vengeance on their authors.

units.la: 2. Quia ad stabiliendam autoritatem, sæpe exasperant imperium, illustretur exemplo Pharaonis.
units.tr: 2. Because in order to establish authority they often make the rule harsher; let this be illustrated by the example of Pharaoh.

units.la: 3. Quia parum spei sit apud illos, qui patrem, qui populi quæreelas, qui Dei legem insuper hactenus habuere.
units.tr: 3. Because there is little hope among those who have so far held the father, the people's complaints and God's law itself in contempt.

units.la: III. Concludat hinc, aliam rationem ineundam esse; nec videre se commodiorem, quam illam quam indigitaverit:
units.tr: III. He concludes from this that another course must be taken, and he sees none more convenient than the one he has pointed out.

units.la: Confirm. 1. A justo, quod probet à natura Synedrii (de quo exstat Exod. 18. & Num. 11.) cujus sit cognoscere de causis omnibus gravioribus. Hoc officium esse seniorum, qui Ephori constituti sunt in republica. Illustret hoc exemplis dissimilibus Mosis, Josuæ, aliorumque judicum & Samuelis, qui extraordinarie ab ipso Deo constituti sint, & bene præfuerint: sicut ac hi filii Samuelis; qui nequam, & in ordinem redigendi autoritate Synedrii. Non ad oppressionem, sed ad liberationem populi constitutos esse judices.
units.tr: Confirmation. 1. From what is just, which he proves from the nature of the Synedrium (of which we have Exod. 18 and Num. 11), whose office is to hear all the weightier cases. This is the office of the elders, who have been appointed as Ephors in the commonwealth. Let him illustrate this with examples unlike one another: Moses, Joshua and the other judges, and Samuel, who were appointed extraordinarily by God himself and governed well; but these sons of Samuel are worthless and must be brought into order by the authority of the Synedrium. Judges were appointed not for the oppression but for the liberation of the people.

units.la: II. Ab utili: æquabili justitiæ administratione inter summos & infimos. Amplificetur ex Loco Communi de commodis Aristocratiæ, vid. Polit. Maxime in populo Dei, inter quem nemo princeps nisi Deus, reliquos fratres esse omnes.
units.tr: II. From what is useful: the even administration of justice between high and low. This should be amplified from the common place about the advantages of aristocracy, see Aristotle's Politics. Especially among the people of God, among whom no one is prince but God, and all the rest are brothers.

units.la: III. A facili, quia jam senex Samuel, cujus filii tantum vices gerant: ordinarios vicarios esse Seniores ac proceres; qui etiam post mortem Josuæ, & subinde defuncto judice, remp. administraverint.
units.tr: III. From what is easy: since Samuel is now old and his sons only bear his place, the elders and nobles, who also governed the commonwealth after the death of Joshua and whenever a judge had died, are the ordinary deputies.

units.la: Conclus. Ergo convocandum synedrium, & Samuelem declarandum emeritum ac honorifice ab onere judicandi liberandum; & transferendum regimen ad synedrium, præteritis filiis Samuelis.
units.tr: Conclusion. Therefore the Synedrium must be convened, and Samuel declared emeritus and honourably freed from the burden of judging; and the government must be transferred to the Synedrium, Samuel's sons being passed over.

units.la: IV. Tertius Senior approbata aliquatenus sententia antecessoris inclinet in creationem ducis in militaribus.
units.tr: IV. The third elder, having partly approved his predecessor's opinion, inclines toward appointing a leader in military affairs.

units.la: Exord. A momento præsentis consultationis, unde dependeat salus vel interitus reip. Quod 1. proponat exemplo medici deliberantis in morbo ancipiti. 2. Exaggeret à discrepantibus collegarum sententiis, quas breviter resumat. 3. Applicet ad se, quod dubius hæreat, quid statuendum.
units.tr: Exordium. He reminds them that the safety or ruin of the commonwealth depends on the present deliberation. (1) He should compare himself to a physician deliberating over a doubtful illness. (2) He should stress the disagreement among his colleagues' opinions, which he briefly recalls. (3) He should apply the matter to himself, saying that he hesitates in doubt about what ought to be decided.

units.la: Propos. Generalis sit: vid. se hortante officio libere quid sentiat diceturum: addita ratione, quia pro rep. dicenti non metuenda offensa.
units.tr: Propositio. It should be general: under the urging of his office, he will freely say what he thinks, adding the reason that a speaker who serves the commonwealth need not fear giving offence.

units.la: Resumtio & examen suffragiorum præcedentium.
units.tr: Summary and examination of the preceding votes.

units.la: I. Concedat necessitatem reformationis assertam à præside, & jus competens proceribus: addita cautione; dummodo ex præscripto legis & juxta consuetudinem reip. hactenus ulitatæ fiat, Hinc probet argumentum. 2. Primi senatoris de periculo mutationis, & regiminis regii. Hinc
units.tr: I. He should concede the need for reform asserted by the president, and the right due to the nobles, adding a caution: provided it is done according to the prescription of the law and in keeping with the custom of the commonwealth hitherto in use. Hence he should prove the argument. (2) He should prove the first senator's point about the danger of change and of royal rule. Hence

units.la: II. Laudet primi Senioris lenitatem; sed non semper servari posse, rationes secundi senioris contra allatas, cui hac in parte consentire se dicat. Cujus porrò
units.tr: II. He should praise the mildness of the first elder, but say that it cannot always be maintained; and he should state the reasons of the second elder brought against it, saying that he agrees with him on this point. Moreover,

units.la: III. Resumat sententiam de stabilienda autoritate Synedrii: verum contra moneat. 1. Synedrium subordinatum fuisse Mosi, Josuæ, judicibus, ad quas à senioribus causæ devolutæ fuerint. 2. Tempore interregni, quidem administrasse remp. Verum sic semper prævaluisse hostes donec Deus vindicem & judicem rursus excitaverit, vid. hist. judic. 3. Ex senioribus istis neminem esse, qui bello præfici queat, si ab hostibus vicinis infestentur. Propof. Specialis seu ipsum suffragium ipsius: videl, videri sibi constituendum esse ducem ordinarium: qui praesit in militaribus, causas vero forenses remittendas esse ad Synedrium, una cum inspectione totius politiae.
units.tr: III. He should repeat the opinion about establishing the authority of the Sanhedrin, but warn against it as follows. (1) The Sanhedrin was subordinate to Moses and Joshua, and to the judges, to whom cases were referred by the elders. (2) In the time of the interregnum it indeed administered the commonwealth; but thus the enemies always prevailed, until God raised up again an avenger and judge; see the history of the Judges. (3) Among those elders there is no one who could be placed over the war if they were harassed by neighbouring enemies. Propositio. Specific, or his own vote: namely, that it seems to him that an ordinary leader must be appointed, who should preside over military affairs, while civil cases should be referred to the Sanhedrin, together with the oversight of the whole polity.

units.la: Confirm. Hujus sententiae. 1. quia sic conservatur libertas potius quam si uni omnia committantur. 2. quia sic consulitur securitati, contra irruptionem hostis, & internas seditiones. 3. quia mixtus hujusmodi status reip. ex monarchia & Aristocratia optimus. 4. quia conveniens ordini divinitus instituto, Exod. 18. Num. 11.
units.tr: Confirmatio. Of this opinion: (1) because in this way liberty is better preserved than if everything were committed to one man; (2) because in this way security is provided for, against invasion by an enemy and internal sedition; (3) because a mixed state of this kind, made up of monarchy and aristocracy, is the best; (4) because it agrees with the order instituted by God, Exod. 18, Num. 11.

units.la: Conclus. Submittat judicium suum aliis melius sentientibus.
units.tr: Conclusio. He should submit his own judgement to others who think better.

units.la: V. Quartus Senior statuat eligendum esse Regem.
units.tr: V. The fourth elder should decide that a king must be chosen.

units.la: Exord. 1. Laudet illa, quae moderate ac prudenter a Collegis ad causam praesentem allata sunt; causam addens ab ipsorum aetate, experientia, fide. 2. Quoniam v. dissentiant dubium esse cui potissimum accedere debeat, ideoque se suam sententiam sine amore alicujus aut odio propositurum: addita ratione; quia pro rep. liberum unicuique suffragium.
units.tr: Exordium. (1) He should praise those things that were said moderately and prudently by his colleagues on the present matter, adding the reason of their age, experience and loyalty. (2) Since their opinions differ, it is doubtful to which one he ought to adhere; therefore he will set forth his own opinion without love or hatred of anyone, adding the reason that in the commonwealth each person's vote is free.

units.la: Propof. Posita necessitate reformationis, quam concedunt omnes, videri sibi eligendum esse Regem, cui rei totius summa committatur.
units.tr: Propositio. Given the need for reform, which all concede, it seems to him that a king must be chosen, to whom the whole sum of the matter should be committed.

units.la: Confirm. I. Quia regium imperium receptum sit inter omnes gentes. Fiat inductio gentium antiquissimarum. vide Hist. Ratio addatur: quia ipsi naturae hoc maxime consentaneum; huic rationem praesse in homine, Deum in mundo: ipsa animalia ab uno duci. Quid igitur moramur &c.
units.tr: Confirmatio. I. Because royal rule has been received among all nations. Let there be an induction of the most ancient nations; see History. Let the reason be added: because this is most consonant with nature itself; reason rules in man, God in the world; the animals themselves are led by one. Why then do we delay, etc.?

units.la: II. Quia regium imperium optimum est; ob autoritatem in regimine perpetuum in bello, justitiae aequabilitatem erga omnes. vid. Polit. Illustretur comparatione aristocratiae aut democratiae, ubi omnia secus se habeant. Hinc examinet sententiam tertii Senioris & incommoda ex illa emersura ostendat; videl. autoritatem duci, vim Synedrio defuturam, contentiones inter utrosque futuram.
units.tr: II. Because royal rule is the best, on account of its authority in government, its constancy in war, and its evenness of justice towards all. See the Politics. Let it be illustrated by comparison with aristocracy or democracy, where everything is otherwise. Hence he should examine the opinion of the third elder and show the inconveniences that would arise from it; namely, that authority would be given to the leader, power would be lacking to the Sanhedrin, and conflicts would arise between the two.

units.la: III. Quia Deus ipse huc manuducat Deut 17: v. 19. Hujus loci vim ostendat, & vindicet contra difficultatem inde motam a Senio re primo num. 1. confirmatam. IV. Quia tutissimus hic modus: cum sic filii Samuelis facilius cessuri sint regi, nec opponere se illi audeant.
units.tr: III. Because God himself leads us to this, Deut. 17:19. He should show the force of this passage and defend it against the difficulty raised from it, which was confirmed by the first elder in number 1. IV. Because this is the safest method: since in this way the sons of Samuel will more easily yield to the king, and not dare to oppose him.

units.la: Conclus. 1. Expendendam hanc reliquat sententiam collegio. 2. Hortetur, ut sepositis affectibus, quid è rep. futurum existiment, statuant.
units.tr: Conclusio. 1. This remaining opinion is to be weighed by the assembly. 2. He should urge them to set aside their passions and decide what they think will be to the advantage of the commonwealth.

units.la: VI. Præses vota recolligat, & quarto seniori recedat, adeoque deputatos mittendos ad Samuelem statuat, qui decretum concilii ipsi intimént, & ad creandum regem hortentur.
units.tr: VI. The president should gather the votes and yield to the fourth elder, and so decide that deputies are to be sent to Samuel, who are to announce to him the decree of the council and urge him to create a king.

units.la: I. Gratias agat omnibus & singulis, quod serio secum causam hanc momentosam expenderint, & omnes rationes corrigendi detectum exposuerint. Hinc laudet illa, quæ prudenter ac salubriter à singulis monita sunt. Apparere ex iis, quanto zelo agant pro rep.
units.tr: I. He should thank all and each of them, because they have weighed this momentous matter seriously and set out all the reasons for correction. Hence he should praise those things which were prudently and wholesomely advised by each. It appears from these how zealously they act for the commonwealth.

units.la: II. Resumat ordine suffragia singulorum, probetque quæ in iis à Collegis prudenter ac moderatè notata ac desiderata sint. Optare se quidem unanimem omnium consensum: ut eo facilius statuere queat, qui jam dubius sit cui sententiæ accedere, quas rejicere debeat: ita omnes subnixas rationibus esse, quod brevi inductione ostendat.
units.tr: II. He should repeat the votes of each in order, and approve those points which his colleagues prudently and moderately noted in them, or desired. He himself wishes for a unanimous consent of all, so that he who is now doubtful to which opinion he should adhere, and which he ought to reject, could more easily decide; that all are supported by reasons, he shows by a brief induction.

units.la: III. Ultimæ sententiæ suum calculum addat, videl. eligendum regem, tum ob rationes à Collega allatas, quas approbet suo suffragio tum ob vaticinium Jacobi Gen.49. ubi omnino regnum promissum sit judæis, & ipium Messiam regem futurum: cui via paranda sit per regis constitutionem.
units.tr: III. He should add his own vote to the last opinion, namely that a king should be chosen: partly on account of the reasons brought by his colleague, which he approves by his vote; partly on account of the prophecy of Jacob, Gen. 49, where the kingdom is wholly promised to the Jews, and the Messiah himself is to be king; for whom the way is to be prepared through the establishment of a king.

units.la: IV. Proponat medium agendi: videl. deputandos esse ex ipsorum medio, qui allegato Samuelis senio & filiorum ipsius degeneratione, actis Samueli gratiis pro fideli administratione decretum Synedrii ipsi renuncient, & ad ungendum ipsis regem cohortentur.
units.tr: IV. He should propose a means of acting: namely, that deputies be chosen from their own number, who, alleging Samuel's old age and the degeneration of his sons, should give thanks to Samuel for his faithful administration and announce to him the decree of the council, and urge him to anoint a king for them.

units.la: VII. Oratio Deputatorum ad Samuelem.
units.tr: VII. Speech of the Deputies to Samuel.

units.la: Exord. Captent attentionem & benevolentiam.
units.tr: Exordium. Let them win his attention and goodwill.

units.la: I. Allegando autores deputationis, ipsorumque dolorem, quod absente, Samuele consultare necesse habuerint.
units.tr: I. By naming the authors of the deputation and their grief that they had to deliberate in Samuel's absence.

units.la: II. Exponendo rationem hujus coloris à fide ac prudentia Samuelis, qua ipse sacris ac profanis hactenus præfuerit, addita gratiarum actione, pariterque vovendo ulteriorem continuationem fieret hoc possibile.
units.tr: II. By setting out the reason for this approach from Samuel's faith and prudence, by which he has so far presided over sacred and profane affairs, adding thanksgiving and at the same time vowing that this may continue for as long as possible.

units.la: III. Explicando ipem Synedrii, quod saltem precibus ac voto reip. sit consulturus: quae causa sit hujus deputationis.
units.tr: III. By explaining the intention of the Synedrion, that it will at least consult the commonwealth through prayers and vows, and what the cause of this deputation is.

units.la: Narratio. Exponat
units.tr: Narratio. Let them set out:

units.la: 1. Spem conceptam a Senioribus de ipsius filiis, hactenus vices ipsius gerentibus.
units.tr: 1. The hope the elders had conceived concerning his sons, who have so far acted in his place.

units.la: II. Degenerationem inemendabilem & profanationem justitiae & Sacrorum: quod ipsi non dicturi fuisset, nisi publica populi querela illos accusaret, adeo ut metuenda plenaria dissolutio, nisi adhibeatur remedium.
units.tr: II. The incurable degeneration and profanation of justice and of the sacred things; which they would not have said unless the public complaint of the people accused those men, so that a complete collapse is to be feared unless a remedy is applied.

units.la: III. Consultationem & decretum Seniorum, de prospiciendo reip. & quidem per creationem regis.
units.tr: III. The consultation and decree of the elders, about providing for the commonwealth, namely by the creation of a king.

units.la: Propos. Hoc voluisse Seniores communicare cum Samuele, ut ipsius consilio ac voto juvet remp.
units.tr: Propositio. That the elders wished to share this with Samuel, so that by his counsel and vote he may help the commonwealth.

units.la: Confirm. I. Breviter argumenta pro regimine regio repetant ex Oratione quinti Senioris.
units.tr: Confirmatio. I. Briefly repeat the arguments for kingly rule, drawn from the speech of the fifth elder.

units.la: II. Occurrant tacita prolepsi displicentiae Samuelis: scil. displicere ipsi consilium non posse, utpote qui 1. ob senium regimen deposuerit, 2. Populi querelas audiat, 3. Remp. in sacris & profanis labentem videat, 4. Nihil charius habeat quam populi salutem, promotionem justitiae ac cultus sacri.
units.tr: II. Let them anticipate Samuel's tacit objection of displeasure: namely, that he cannot be displeased with the plan, since he 1. laid down the rule because of old age, 2. hears the complaints of the people, 3. sees the commonwealth sliding in sacred and profane affairs, and 4. holds nothing dearer than the welfare of the people and the advancement of justice and of sacred worship.

units.la: Conclusio: Nomine collegii populique universi petant, ut Deum consulat & Regem ex ejusdem voluntate ipsis praeficiat: addito argumento impellente, quod hoc maximum beneficium sit, quo populum in senectute beare queat: cujus nomine etiamnum Seniores per ipsorum os gratias ipsi agant pro fideli ac paterna hactenus cura pro patria.
units.tr: Conclusio: In the name of the college and of the whole people, let them beg him to consult God and to appoint for them a king according to God's will, adding the compelling argument that this is the greatest benefit by which he could bless the people in his old age; and in the name of this, the elders, through their own mouths, thank him for his faithful and fatherly care of the country up to now.

units.la: VIII. Samuel grandaevus debortetur Populum ab electione regis.
units.tr: VIII. Aged Samuel dissuades the people from electing a king.

units.la: Exord. A causa dicendi; quae non propria, sed Dei est; per comparationem utriusque
units.tr: Exordium. From the cause of speaking, which is not his own but God's; by a comparison of the two.

units.la: Ubi I. Protalis; vid: si me meosque solum concerneret quaestio, non contradicerem. Ratio: quia didicerit pati injuriam & solari se bona conscientia.
units.tr: Where I. The protasis: namely, if the question concerned only me and mine, I would not object. Reason: because he has learned to bear injury and to console himself with a good conscience.

units.la: II. Apodosis: vid: at cum jam Dei causa agitur, non silendum. Illustretur ab officio suo, quod sit loqui pro Deo, & non timere offensam: imò loqui pro populo etiam ingrato.
units.tr: II. The apodosis: namely, but since now the cause of God is being handled, it must not be passed over in silence. Let it be illustrated from his office, which is to speak for God and not to fear offence; indeed to speak for the people even when they are ungrateful.

units.la: Propos. Non posse se itaque, quin dehortetur serió ab hoc proposito, quo populus regem postulat: Quia nihil magis Deo, justitiæ ac ipsius populi saluti contrarium.
units.tr: Propositio. He therefore cannot but earnestly dissuade them from this plan by which the people demand a king, because nothing is more contrary to God, to justice, and to the very welfare of the people.

units.la: Confirm. singula propositionis membra persequatur.
units.tr: Confirmatio. He should go through the individual parts of the proposition.

units.la: I. Quia hæc petitio regis sit detrectatio imperii Dei: quippe qui 1. Samuelem ipsis dedit judicem; probetur ex regesta 1. Sam. 1. seqq. ipse vero se neutiquam ingesserit. 2. Leges ipsis dederit, juxta quas regimen exerceatur. Occurrat hinc objectioni de filiorum degeneratione, respond. illam corrigi posse juxta legem. 3. rebelles semper puniverit, exemplo Mirjam, itemque Coræ, Dathan & Abiram.
units.tr: I. Because this demand for a king is a repudiation of God's rule, since God 1. gave them Samuel as judge; let this be proved from the narrative in 1 Sam. 1 ff., while Samuel himself never pushed himself forward. 2. God gave them laws by which rule is to be exercised. Here he meets the objection about the degeneration of the sons: the answer is that it can be corrected according to the law. 3. God always punished rebels, as in the example of Miriam, and likewise of Korah, Dathan and Abiram.

units.la: II. Quia petitio hæc injusta & sine causa, quod probet 1. à sua innocentia vide 1. Sam. 12. 2. Excusatione filiorum; utpote qui a. ex rumore condemnantur, qui fallax. b. admonitione emendari queant. c. ob merita patris tolerari deberent. Illustretur prolepsine putent, se magis de filiis, quam de causa Dei ac populi esse sollicitum. Hinc transeat ad
units.tr: II. Because this request is unjust and without cause, which he proves 1. from his own innocence, see 1 Sam. 12; 2. from the excuse of the sons, since they a. are condemned on the basis of rumour, which is deceptive; b. can be amended by admonition; c. ought to be tolerated on account of the father's merits. Let it be illustrated that they may think he is more concerned about his sons than about the cause of God and the people. From here he passes to

units.la: III. Quia petitio hæc populo noxia: Probetur, quia 1. regimen regiu durissimum. vide 1. Sam. 8. 2. indeclinabile semel receptum. Hæc illustrentur comparatione a. cum præsenti regimine leni & facile emendabili. b. cum cæteris gentibus, quæ à Deo desertæ tyrannide premantur. Israelitæ vero assumpti in Dei populum, ipsius regantur legibus. Hinc examinet locum Deut. 17. videl. 1. illum dirigere tantum ipsorum prævisam contumaciam, non probare factum. 2. Comminari expresse poenam petentibus regem.
units.tr: III. Because this request is harmful to the people. Let it be proved, because 1. kingly rule is very harsh, see 1 Sam. 8; 2. once received, it cannot be turned aside. These points are illustrated by comparison a. with the present rule, which is mild and easily corrected, and b. with the other nations, which, deserted by God, are oppressed by tyranny, whereas the Israelites, taken up as God's people, are ruled by his laws. Hence he examines the passage Deut. 17, namely: 1. that it merely directs their foreseen stubbornness and does not approve the deed; 2. that it expressly threatens punishment to those who ask for a king.

units.la: Concluf. 1. Inculcet propositionem. 2. offerat se ad parendum populo, si perfistant, optans, ut melius cedat res, quàm ipsi petunt.
units.tr: Conclusio: 1. He presses the proposition home. 2. He offers himself to obey the people if they persist, wishing that the outcome be better than they ask.

units.la: 3. Avertat Orationem ad Deum, ut ipse cœlitus edito signo de sua innocentia ac hoc populi peccato contestetur.
units.tr: 3. He turns his speech to God, that God, by a sign sent from heaven, may bear witness to his own innocence and to this sin of the people.

units.la: IX. Novi regis introductio facta per Samuelem.
units.tr: IX. Introduction of the new king by Samuel.

units.la: Exord. 1. Ab ipsa propositione, videl. sisti hic regem, quem ad preces populi Deus ipsis præficere voluerit: quem ipsa staturæ majestas arguat. 2. ab allegatione officii Samuelis, quod est, ut regem populumque votis Deo consecret, officium ipsi committat, & mutui officii moneat, in solemni hac inauguratione.
units.tr: Exordium. 1. From the proposition itself: namely, that the king whom God wished to set over them at the people's prayers is here presented, and his stature and majesty bear witness to him. 2. From the statement of Samuel's office, which is to consecrate the king and the people to God by prayers; he entrusts this office to him in this solemn inauguration and reminds him of their mutual duties.

units.la: Tractatio. habeat
units.tr: Tractatio. habeat

units.la: I. Ipsum officii commissionem, qua ex auctoritate Dei, juxta votum universi populi sceptrum ipsi resignet. Amplif. 1. à causa Deo, scil. à quo omnis legitima potestas imperantibus, ut à sole lumen. Itemq; à virtutibus majestatis inde fluentibus videl. summa potestas in pace ac bello, ad regni securitatem & incolumitatem. 3. à curis concomitantibus sceptrum; videl. in custodia legis divinæ, conservatione sacri cultus, administratione justitiæ, præsidio oppressorum, defensione omnium contra hostes. Hæc scil. committere Deum regi, exspectare populum à rege.
units.tr: I. The commission of the office itself, by which, on the authority of God and according to the vote of the whole people, he resigns the sceptre to him. Amplification: (1) from the cause, namely God, from whom all lawful power comes to rulers, as light from the sun; likewise from the virtues of majesty flowing from this, namely supreme power in peace and in war, for the security and safety of the kingdom. (2) From the cares that accompany the sceptre, namely: in the keeping of the divine law, the preservation of sacred worship, the administration of justice, the protection of the oppressed, and the defence of all against enemies. In short, that God commits these things to the king, and that the people expect them from the king.

units.la: II. Populi ad obedientiam obligatione. Hoc 1. proponatur per apostrophen ad Populum. 2. Asstruatur 4. quia rex unctus Domini, in quem omnis populi potestas translata. b. quia ipsi talem habere voluerint, c. quia auxilium & spes populi jam in rege; uti olim in Mose & Josua.
units.tr: II. The obligation of the people to obedience. This may be set forth (1) by an apostrophe to the People; (2) and it may be asserted (a) because the king is the anointed of the Lord, upon whom all the power of the people has been transferred; (b) because they themselves have wished to have such a king; (c) because the help and hope of the people now rest in the king, as once they did in Moses and Joshua.

units.la: Illustrentur hæc ab imminente vindicta, si aut rex legem, aut populus regem deserat.
units.tr: Let these things be illustrated by the impending vengeance if either the king deserts the law or the people desert the king.

units.la: Conclus. Votum habeat, quo optet 1. regi omnem prosperitatem ac felix regimen. 2. populo pacem ac tranquillitatem, & ut sic regi obediant, ne Dei obliviscantur.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let there be a prayer by which we wish for the king every prosperity and a happy reign, and for the people peace and tranquillity, and that so they may obey the king and not forget God.

units.la: THEMA XX. BRUTUS CONSUL SUADET COLLEGÆ TARQUINIO COLLATINO UT ALIO MIGRET OBSUSPECTUM TARQUINII NOMEN.
units.tr: THEMA XX. BRUTUS THE CONSUL ADVISES HIS COLLEAGUE TARQUINIUS COLLATINUS TO DEPART ELSEWHERE, SINCE THE NAME OF TARQUIN IS UNDER SUSPICION.

units.la: Exord. Amoliatur à se suspicionem invidiæ. Hinc 1. optet vel alium dicere, vel de alio, quàm de Collega sibi optatissimo. 2. prætexat necessitatem tum officii, tum amoris patriæ. 3. Revocet illis memoriam ejurati regni; metumque populi à familia Tarquiniorum.
units.tr: Exordium. He removes from himself the suspicion of envy. Hence he (1) wishes to say either something else, or to speak of someone other than his colleague, who is most dear to him; (2) pleads the necessity both of his office and of his love for his country; (3) recalls to them the memory of the abolished kingship and the people's fear of the Tarquin family.

units.la: Propos. Ad Tarquinium, ut sua sponte migrans populum metu liberet.
units.tr: Proposition. To Tarquin: that, by departing of his own accord, he should free the people from fear.

units.la: Confirm. I. Ab honesto. Quia sic majus beneficium præstabit populo, quam cum ejecit reges. Quod proinde exaggeret tanquam maximum; at non minus alterum futurum esse.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From what is honourable: because in this way he will confer a greater benefit on the people than when they drove out the kings. He should magnify this as the greatest, yet the other will be no less.

units.la: II. A necessario: quia metus sit, ne ex gente Tarquinorum Romæ superstite existat qui regnum affectet. Licet ipse non faciat, posse aliquem ex liberis, ex nepotibus, qui deberi sibi regnum putent. Assuevisce Tarquinios regno.
units.tr: II. From necessity: because there is fear lest, while a member of the Tarquin race survives at Rome, someone should arise who aspires to the kingship. Although he himself does not do so, someone of his sons or grandsons may think the kingship is owed to him. The Tarquins are accustomed to kingship.

units.la: III. A facili: quia bona sua libere transferre queant alió, auctio-ra etiam munere Romanorum. Forti ubique patriam esse.
units.tr: III. From what is easy: because he can freely transfer his goods elsewhere, and will be all the more welcome even with the gift of Roman citizenship. For a brave man, every place is his country.

units.la: Conclus. Petat ut hoc vel inani metu liberet populum, & plena liber-tate beet. Addito argumento à gloriosó.
units.tr: Conclusion. He should ask that he free the people from this fear, even if it is empty, and grant them full liberty, adding an argument from glory.

units.la: Sp. Lucretius socer Collatini ad idem cohortatur.
units.tr: Spurius Lucretius, father-in-law of Collatinus, exhorts him to the same.

units.la: Exord. A justo timore Romanorum: videl.
units.tr: Exordium. From the people of Rome's just fear, namely:

units.la: I. Quod ill solent, qui ex magno periculo recens erepti sunt, ut etiam tuta timeant; hoc & usu venire populo Romano. Huc spectare quod Consul proposuerit: quod proinde paucis re-petat.
units.tr: I. It is the custom of those who have been lately rescued from great danger to fear even safe things; this happens also to the Roman people. The consul's proposal aims at this, which therefore he will briefly repeat.

units.la: Propos. Licet verò res non sibi minus, quàm ipsi genero suo gravis sit, tamen nescire se, quomodo Bruto assentiri cogatur.
units.tr: Proposition. Although the matter is no less grave for himself than for his son-in-law, nevertheless he does not know how he is compelled to assent to Brutus.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Treatment.

units.la: I. Rationes in contrarium præoccupet.
units.tr: I. He forestalls the arguments to the contrary.

units.la: a. Quasi sic reum, aut saltem suspectum se fateri videatur. Re-spond. Non hanc esse mentem Collegæ, qui hoc petat nomi-ne populi, non imperet. Qui vanum forte metum civium di-xerit.
units.tr: a. As if in this way he seemed to confess himself guilty, or at least suspect. Reply: this is not the intention of his colleague, who asks this in the name of the people, not commands it; who perhaps called the citizens' fear vain.

units.la: b. Quasi indignum sit non frui libertate per se parta. Resp. Cu-mulatius fore beneficium, si & metum amittendæ tollat civi-bus, qui sic novo beneficio se obstrictos judicaturi sint.
units.tr: b. As if it were unworthy not to enjoy a liberty won for oneself. Reply: the benefit will be greater if he also removes from the citizens the fear of losing it, since they will judge themselves bound by a new benefit.

units.la: II. Iis, quæ à consule dicta, addat argumentum ab utili & gloria: vid. sic majori cum gloria ipsum vivere posse apud exteros; quàm si suspectus civibus ob solum nomen & familiam Romæ degat. Hinc exaggeret quam grave futurum ipsi sit in publico odio aut suspicione omnium versari. Quanto gloriosius vivere alibi tan-quam vindex & lospitator patriæ. b. Ab exemplo Lycurgi si-miliumque, qui ob patriæ salutem exilium elegerint.
units.tr: II. To what the consul has said, he adds an argument from advantage and glory: namely, that he can live among foreigners with greater glory than if, suspected by the citizens merely because of his name and family, he lived at Rome. Hence he should magnify how grievous it would be for him to live under public hatred or suspicion of all. How much more gloriously he would live elsewhere, as the avenger and host of his country. b. From the example of Lycurgus and others like him, who chose exile for the safety of their country.

units.la: Conclus. Petat ut hæc considerans novo beneficio populum obliget qui sic absentis gloriam amplificaturus sit.
units.tr: Conclusion. He should ask that, considering these things, Tarquin bind the people by a new benefit, since in this way he will increase the glory of one who is absent.

units.la: II. Tarquinius ejectus Româ auxilium petit ab Hetruriæ populis Vejentibus.
units.tr: II. Tarquin, driven out of Rome, seeks aid from the peoples of Etruria, the Veientines.

units.la: Exord. A prolepsi: Quamquam difficile norit esse, in calamitate aliorum sollicitare opem; tamen certam fiduciam se concepisse de Vejentibus.
units.tr: Exordium. By prolepsis: although it may be difficult to seek help in another's calamity, nevertheless he has conceived a sure confidence in the Veientines.

units.la: Hinc paucis referat 1. fortunam suam. 2. tentatam restitutionem viis levioribus. 3. frustrationem. 4. fiduciam in armis & virtute Vejentium, reliquæque Hetruriæ, populi ad Italiæ vindicias nati.
units.tr: Hence he briefly relates (1) his own fortune; (2) his attempt at restoration by gentler ways; (3) its frustration; (4) his trust in the arms and valour of the Veientines and of the rest of Etruria, a people born for the defence of Italy.

units.la: Propof. Ipsum votum ipsius habeat, ut junctis armis ipsum restituant.
units.tr: Proposition. He should have his own wish, that with joined arms they restore him.

units.la: Confirm. I. Ab honesto: 1. quia ex sanguine Hetrusco genitus, Tarquinio Prisco. Cedere in gentis infamiam, si patiantur illam pelli regno: cum tota familia, idque ipsis videntibus hæc.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From what is honourable: (1) because he was born of Etruscan blood, from Tarquin the Elder. It would be a disgrace to their nation if they allowed him to be driven from the kingship, together with his whole family, and that before their very eyes.

units.la: II. A justo: 1. quia sine causâ pulsus sit, si filius deliquit: quid contra potest pater. 2. quia ex sola Bruti similiumque invidia & ambitione. 3. quia bona diripienda data, ne quis expers scelerís esset. 4. quia nihil petat, quam recuperationem regni aviti & bonorum suorum. 5. quia ipsi Hetrusci toties injuria affecti sint à Romanis.
units.tr: II. From what is just: (1) because he was expelled without cause, if the son has done wrong, what can the father do about it? (2) because it arises only from the envy and ambition of Brutus and others like him; (3) because the goods were given to be plundered, lest anyone should be free of crime; (4) because he seeks nothing but the recovery of his ancestral kingdom and his own goods; (5) because the Etruscans themselves have so often been wronged by the Romans.

units.la: III. A facili: quia 1. ipse multos socios habeat in civitate strenuissimos & 2. Vejentes sat virium.
units.tr: III. From what is easy: because (1) he himself has many very vigorous allies in the city, and (2) the Veientines have sufficient strength.

units.la: Concluf. Propositionem inculcet addita ratione à perpetua amicitia nascitura hinc inter utrumque populum.
units.tr: Conclusion. He should press the proposal, adding the reason that from it a perpetual friendship will arise between the two peoples.

units.la: Brutus secum disceptat, utrum gratiam facere liberis, an plectere debeat.
units.tr: Brutus debates with himself whether he ought to grant favour to his sons or to punish them.

units.la: Exord. A professione infelicitatis illorum, quorum officio privati se affectus opponunt. Verè infelices sunt: dum hi ad utile, illud ad honestum invitat.
units.tr: Exordium. From the profession of the unhappiness of those whose duty is opposed by private affections. They are truly unhappy: while the one invites to what is useful, the other to what is honourable.

units.la: Propof. Applicet hoc ad suam conditionem, ubi vel patria, vel filiorum amor abjiciendus: quod utrumque durum est.
units.tr: Proposition. He applies this to his own condition, where either his country or the love of his sons must be cast off: both of which are hard.

units.la: Tractatio. Adducat argumenta.
units.tr: Treatment. He adduces arguments.

units.la: I. Pro filiis 1. quod natura ipsa amorem eorum etiam brutis ingenerarit. 2. quod in iis spes familiæ. 3. quod frustra parta libertas, si fructum ejus suis eripere debeat. 4. quod crudele, sanguine liberorum maculare manus. 5. quod juventâ excusari possint.
units.tr: I. For the sons: (1) because nature itself has implanted their love even in brute beasts; (2) because in them lies the hope of the family; (3) because liberty, won in vain, would be useless if he must snatch its fruit from his own; (4) because it is cruel to stain one's hands with the blood of one's children; (5) because they may be excused by their youth.

units.la: II. Pro patria: scil. hisce rationibus opponere se 1. patriam omnibus præferenda. 2. libertatem, quia communis parens, quæ inæstimabilis. 3. votum omnium bonorum. III. Contra liberos: quod egerint. 1. contra libertatem recenter recuperatam. 2. contra patrem liberatorem. 3. contra eundem consulem. 4. contra senatum. 5. contra plebem. 6. quod conspiraverint cum hoste infestissimo.
units.tr: II. For the country, namely that against these reasons he sets: (1) the country to be preferred to all things; (2) liberty, as the common parent, which is beyond price; (3) the wish of all good men. III. Against the sons, because of what they have done: (1) against the liberty lately recovered; (2) against the liberating father; (3) against the same consul; (4) against the senate; (5) against the plebs; (6) because they have conspired with the most hostile enemy.

units.la: Concludat, agendum esse ex jure, vincendos affectus privatos, illi cui patria loco liberorum sit.
units.tr: He concludes that one must act according to right, and that private affections must be overcome by one for whom the country takes the place of children.

units.la: Tarquinii Porsenae implorant auxilium.
units.tr: Tarquin's Porsenna Implores Aid.
