units.la: Exord. Pathos moveat à sua ac Roman. persona: quod res exul alienum auxilium implorare cogatur, iniqueque habitus cum familia à Rom: præ fastu regimen regium fastidientibus.
units.tr: Exordium. Let the appeal move pathos from his own person and that of the Romans: that an exile is forced to beg for foreign help, and that he was treated unjustly along with his family by those who, out of pride, scorned royal rule.

units.la: Narrat. Exponat. 1. iniquam ejectionem. 2. studium suum reconciliandi animos per liberos magnatum. 3. malè habitos legatos suos, 4. tentata à searma & frustrationem.
units.tr: Narratio. He should set out: (1) the unjust expulsion; (2) his own effort to reconcile minds through the sons of the magnates; (3) the ill treatment of his envoys; (4) the attempts made by the senate and their frustration.

units.la: Propos. Petat ut misertus arma jungat.
units.tr: Propositio. Let him ask that Porsenna, moved by pity, join arms with him.

units.la: Confirm. 1. Ab honesto: quia ejusdem ipsi sanguinis sint. Cum igitur homo homini, rex regi, multo magis agnatum agnatis obstrictum. Juris hoc esse naturalis, ipsis animantibus insitum.
units.tr: Confirmatio. (1) From what is honourable: because they are of the same blood. Therefore, as man is bound to man and king to king, so much more is kinsman bound to kinsman. This is a law of nature, implanted in living creatures themselves.

units.la: II. A necessitate: ne invalescat mos pellendi reges. Hinc futurum, ut nullus princeps tutus sit. 1. omne enim imperium grave esse, & ut plurimum invitis imperari, qui amoliri jugum satagent, nisi sacram & inviolatam credat majestatem, & vindictam paratam si contra egerit. 2. libertatis magnam esse dulcedinem, si impune illa plebs potiri queat.
units.tr: II. From necessity: lest the custom of driving out kings should gain strength. From this it will follow that no prince is safe. (1) For every government is burdensome, and for the most part is imposed on unwilling subjects, who strive to throw off the yoke; unless they believe that majesty is sacred and inviolable, and that vengeance is ready if they act against it. (2) The sweetness of liberty is great, if that common people can seize it with impunity.

units.la: III. A justo: ne si impunis sit rebellio, omnis potestas convellatur & invehatur confusio in orbem. Amplif. demonstratione incommodorum hinc metuendorum, & contra pulchritudine regni ac imperii legitimi.
units.tr: III. From what is just: lest, if rebellion goes unpunished, all authority be overthrown and confusion be brought upon the world. Amplification by demonstrating the disadvantages to be feared from this, and by contrast the beauty of a lawful kingdom and government.

units.la: Concluf. Repetat petitum; addito unam hanc spem sibi reliquam, ut vel ad securitatem utriusque restituatur, vel cum certo periculo ac jactura utriusque deseratur.
units.tr: Conclusio. He repeats the request, adding that only this one hope remains to him: that either he be restored, for the security of both, or else be abandoned with certain danger and loss to both.

units.la: THEMA XXI. UTRUM CONDUCAT COLLEGIA ET SOCIETATES INSTITUERE ET FOVERE IN REPUBLICA.
units.tr: THEMA XXI. WHETHER IT IS EXPEDIENT TO ESTABLISH AND FOSTER COLLEGES AND SOCIETIES IN THE COMMONWEALTH.

units.la: I. Negatè contra Collegia.
units.tr: I. Negatively, against colleges.

units.la: Exord. Ex comparatis: vid. uti duci nihil magis cavendum, quàm seditio ditio, quippe per quam autoritas ducis convellitur, disciplina militaris solvitur &c. Ita magistratui nihil prius esse debere, quam cavere factiones civium & conjurationes. Hisce enim audaces reddi cives, & vilescere autoritatem magistratus. Hinc dubium videri, quod statuendum de collegiis & sociatibus civium, passim usitatis: quarum species praecipuas enarret. vid Tolosf.
units.tr: Exordium. From comparisons: as a commander must guard above all against sedition, since through it the authority of the commander is overthrown, military discipline dissolved, and so on, so the magistrate ought to make it his first concern to guard against factions and conspiracies among the citizens. For these make citizens bold and cheapen the authority of the magistrate. Hence it seems doubtful what should be decided about the colleges and societies of citizens that are commonly in use. Tolosanus sets out their principal kinds.

units.la: Propos. Videri tibi non necessarias, imo periculosas & noxias esse civitatibus.
units.tr: Proposition. They seem to you not necessary, indeed dangerous and harmful to states.

units.la: Confirm. I. Quia non necessariae. Hic praemittat majorem, vid. Nugas & non necessaria non agenda in rep. quia satis ibi quod agendum. Minorem probet: quia sufficit, cives communibus legibus civitates & reipublicae & invicem obstrictos esse. Quorsum igitur aliis legibus privatis illos obstringi?
units.tr: Confirmation. I. Because they are not necessary. Here he should first put the major premise, citing Nugae: what is not necessary should not be done in a commonwealth, since there is already enough that must be done. Let him prove the minor: because it is sufficient that citizens are bound to the states and to one another by the common laws. Why, then, bind them by other private laws?

units.la: II. Quia periculosae. Vid. Libenth. Rat.1.2.3. Hic minor tantum adstruatur rationibus & exemplis. Et addatur aliud periculum, quod saepe dissidium religionis se miscceat, & urgere soleant collegia exercitium suae religionis clam palam: quod periculosum uti patet ex quaest, 8. ratione negante 4. Concludatur: & putet quis collegia fovenda, unde tanta pericula. &c.
units.tr: II. Because they are dangerous. See Libenthal, Rat. 1, 2, 3. Here only the minor needs to be supported by reasons and examples. Let another danger be added: that the discord of religion often mixes itself in, and colleges are wont to press the exercise of their religion secretly and openly. This is dangerous, as is clear from question 8, the reason denying 4. Let him conclude: and one may think colleges should be fostered, when there are such great dangers? and so on.

units.la: III. Quia noxiae: Probetur itidem minor: 1. quia collegia illa exteros ut plurimum excludunt, per quos perfectiora reddi opificia & promoveri commercia possent. 2. quia sapiunt monopolium, dum nemini exercere artem libere licitum, nisi ex collegio sit & illorum placitis se accommodet. In rep. liberas debere esse artes, & foveri aemulationem honestam.
units.tr: III. Because they are harmful. Let the minor be proved likewise: 1. because those colleges mostly exclude foreigners, through whom crafts could be made more perfect and trade promoted. 2. Because they smack of monopoly, since no one is allowed to practise an art freely unless he belongs to a college and conforms to its decrees. In a commonwealth the arts ought to be free, and honest emulation fostered.

units.la: IV. Propter haec aliasque rationes ab Imperatoribus regibusque prohibitas saepe fuisse societates. vide Lib. & Tolos. d. l.3. c.3, 14. 19. 21. 22. 23.
units.tr: IV. For these and other reasons, societies have often been prohibited by emperors and kings. See Lib. and Tolos. ibid. c. 3, 14, 19, 21, 22, 23.

units.la: Conclus. Licet ratiunculae sint in contrarium, tutius tamen esse non instituere, aut invectas paulatim dissolvere societates. Communes civibus leges esse debere.
units.tr: Conclusion. Although there are little reasons to the contrary, it is nevertheless safer not to establish societies, or to dissolve gradually those that have crept in. Laws should be common to the citizens.

units.la: II. Affirmatè pro Collegiis & societatibus.
units.tr: II. Affirmatively, in favour of colleges and societies.

units.la: Exord. Ex Loco Communi de bono concordiae: scilicet nihil salubrius esse reip. Unde miretur quod conjurationem interpretatus sit antecessor societates & concordiam civium: quasi in dissensione securitas principi aut civitati: quod ex pernitiosis doctoris Hetrusci principiis. Concordia res parvas crescere juxta Salust.
units.tr: Exordium. From the common topic of the good of concord, namely that nothing is more wholesome for a commonwealth. Hence one may wonder that the opponent interpreted societies and the concord of citizens as conspiracy, as if security for a prince or a state lay in dissension. This follows from the pernicious principles of the Tuscan doctor. Concord makes small things grow, according to Sallust.

units.la: Propof. Itaque te rationes ipsius contra societates primo examinatu-rum fortiores pro & societatibus allaturum.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore you will first examine his reasons against societies, and then bring forward stronger ones in favour of them.

units.la: Confutat. Rat. 1. Resp. Leges communes non exclamere particulares, conditioni loci & personarum ac negotiationum accomodatas. Ad II. resp. pericula illa 1. imaginaria. 2. inspectione magistratus averti posse. 3. nihil tam sanctum, cujus non abusus esse queat: interim non tollendum usum. Ad III. Cives praestare posse, quod exteri; cum exteris & fraudes invehi. 2. Monopolium non esse omnibus quod permissum civibus. Ad IV. Prohibitas esse ex specialibus casibus. Alibi vero utiliter receptas esse, uti jam evincendum.
units.tr: Refutation. Reason 1. Reply: common laws do not exclude particular ones, which are adapted to the condition of place, of persons and of business. To II, reply: those dangers are 1. imaginary; 2. they can be averted by the oversight of the magistrate; 3. nothing is so holy that its abuse cannot occur, yet the use is not to be removed on that account. To III: citizens can supply what foreigners do, and frauds are introduced along with foreigners too. 2. A monopoly does not exist merely because something is permitted to all citizens. To IV: they were prohibited because of special cases. Elsewhere, however, they have been usefully received, as will now be shown.

units.la: Confirmat. 1. Distinguat Collegia in privata, quae periculosa vetita; & publica authoritate stabilita; qualia utilia censenda vid. Lib. in fine quaest.
units.tr: Confirmatio. 1. Distinguish colleges into private ones, which are dangerous and forbidden, and those established by public authority, such as are to be judged useful; see the book at the end of the question.

units.la: II. Rationes afferat ex Libenth. illasque oratorie adstruat, exemplis, rationibus & testimoniis. Not. ratione 3. pro tolerantur, legendum tollantur, Addat rationem 5. quia prohibet promiscuum affluxum peregrinorum, & cum illis novum luxum in cibis, vestibus, supellectili.
units.tr: II. Let him bring forward the reasons from Libenthal and build them up rhetorically with examples, reasons and testimonies. Note: in reason 3, "tolerantur" should be read as "tollantur". Let him add reason 5: because it prevents the promiscuous influx of foreigners, and with them new luxury in food, clothing and household goods.

units.la: Concluj. Fovendas itaque esse societates, nec facile concessa a majoribus privilegia abroganda esse.
units.tr: Conclusio. Therefore societies are to be fostered, and privileges granted by our ancestors should not easily be abrogated.

units.la: THEMA XXII. CONSULTATIO UTRUM PAX INIQUA JUSTO BELLO PRAEFERENDA.
units.tr: THESIS XXII. A CONSULTATION WHETHER AN UNJUST PEACE IS TO BE PREFERRED TO A JUST WAR.

units.la: I. Affirmative.
units.tr: I. Affirmative.

units.la: Exord. Ab ancipiti belli consilio. vid. si ullibi certe in bello debent Principes esse circumspecti Ratio. Quia 1. contra tot hominum vitas ac fortunas statuitur. 2. Semel coeptum non nisi arbitrio victoris finitur.
units.tr: Exordium. From the dangerous decision of war. See whether rulers ought to be circumspect anywhere, and especially in war. Reason: (1) it is decided against so many men's lives and fortunes; (2) once begun, it is ended only at the discretion of the victor.

units.la: Propof. Videri hinc pacem iniquam etiam bello praeferendam.
units.tr: Proposition. It seems from this that even an unjust peace is to be preferred to war.

units.la: Confirmatio, ubi
units.tr: Confirmation, where

units.la: I. Remotio non pertinentis: vid. non te facere cum illis, qui bellum penitus Christianis interdictum putant. Addatur breviter ratio una atque altera: vid. quia in Vetere Testamento fuerit licitum bellum, nec in Novo Testamento vetitum. 2. quia regnum Christi non tollit politias, quæ sine bello sæpe conscivari nequeunt. Unde exeant, qui contrarium tuentur.
units.tr: I. Removal of what does not pertain: see that you are not siding with those who think war is entirely forbidden to Christians. Add briefly one or two reasons: (1) in the Old Testament war was lawful, and in the New Testament it is not forbidden; (2) the kingdom of Christ does not abolish polities, which often cannot be maintained without war. Let those who hold the contrary explain how they get out of this.

units.la: II. Adstructio propositionis:
units.tr: II. Establishing the proposition:

units.la: 1. A pacis præstantia: quippe quæ maximum est Dei donum: quam tota natura, ipsaque corporis, imò totius hominis fabrica commendat. Ostendatur inductione quadam; & illustretur opposita naturæ ac membrorum nostrorum discordia; qua nihil tutius, nihil Deo hominibusque exosum magis. Inferatur propositio. Rem tam sanctam tam eximiam, quis dubitet, vel iniquis conditionibus redimere? Fiat transitio ad argumentum.
units.tr: 1. From the excellence of peace, which is the greatest gift of God, and which the whole of nature commends, indeed the very structure of the body and of the whole man. Let this be shown by a certain induction, and let the opposed discord of nature and of our members be illustrated: nothing is more unsafe, nothing more hateful to God and men. Let the proposition be inferred: who would doubt to redeem so holy and excellent a thing even on unfair terms? Make the transition to the next argument.

units.la: 2. A pacis utilitate: quam ostendat per μεσότητα in omnibus vitæ partibus; & illustret oppositis belli incommodis. Inferatq; propositionem per apostrophen ad pacem. Quis te non exoptet. Transeatur ad tertium argumentum. Sed devoranda essent belli mala, si semper bonus exitus.
units.tr: 2. From the utility of peace, which he should show through the mean (μεσότης) in all parts of life, and illustrate with the opposed inconveniences of war. Let him infer the proposition by an apostrophe to peace: who would not desire you? Pass to the third argument. But the evils of war would have to be swallowed up, if the outcome were always good.

units.la: 3. A dubia bellorum sorte; quæ non semper justiori causæ, nec parti numerosiori favet: Hoc illustretur exemplis Xerxis, Hannibalis, Græcorum aliorumque, quibus fortiores, justires sæpe occubuere: Maxime si quis spretis pacis conditionibus bellum præoptavit.
units.tr: 3. From the uncertain fortune of wars, which does not always favour the juster cause nor the more numerous side. This is illustrated by the examples of Xerxes, Hannibal, the Greeks and others, by whom the stronger and the more just have often fallen, especially if someone, having rejected the conditions of peace, preferred war.

units.la: 4. A conditione Christianorum; quibus pax, charitas tantopere commendata à Servatore.
units.tr: 4. From the condition of Christians, to whom peace and charity are so highly commended by the Saviour.

units.la: Conclus. Repetita argumentorum summa, ad amplectendam pacem etiam minus æquam & commodam cohortetur.
units.tr: Conclusion. Having repeated the sum of the arguments, he should urge them to embrace peace even if it is less fair and less convenient.

units.la: II. Negate.
units.tr: II. Negative.

units.la: Exord. Ab Orat. antecess. in qua
units.tr: Exordium. From the preceding speech, in which

units.la: 1. Probes, quod pacem commendaverit; addat breviter rationes: nec quemquam facile, nisi barbarum penitus, qui refragetur.
units.tr: 1. He should approve that it commended peace, briefly adding the reasons: hardly anyone, unless utterly barbarous, would object.

units.la: 2. Verum improbes, quod nimio pacis amore etiam iniquam probarit. Rationem dissensus sui addat, quia sæpe incidant tempora, ut ab ipsis quoque legibus porrigi gladius videatur.
units.tr: 2. But he should disapprove that, out of excessive love of peace, it also approved an unjust one. Let him add the reason for his dissent: times often arise when the sword seems to be drawn even by the laws themselves.

units.la: Propos. Ideoque bellum sæpissime pacis maximè iniquæ præferendum esse, nisi deserere patriam & oppressos velimus. Id quod pace antecess. adstruere velit.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore war is very often to be preferred to the most unjust peace, unless we wish to desert our country and the oppressed. This the previous speaker wished to establish in favour of peace.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. Acceptet in rem suam, quod antecessor, licet studiosus pacis, bella tamen illicita Christianis dicere non ausus sit. Inferat hinc. Ergo ipso fatente dari tempora, quibus bellum tuto geri queat, & quandoque debeat.
units.tr: I. Let him take for his own purpose that the predecessor, although eager for peace, did not dare to call wars unlawful for Christians. Let him infer from this: therefore, by the predecessor's own admission, there are times when war can safely be waged and sometimes ought to be.

units.la: II. Adducat argumenta.
units.tr: II. Let him bring forward arguments.

units.la: 1. A jure divino; quod non modo permiserit, verum etiam imperaverit judæis bellum contra hostes infestos. Allegari possunt exempla. Imò Deum improbasse pacem cum Amalakitis & Cananitis initam. Inferatur propositio per communicationem.
units.tr: 1. From divine law, which not only permitted but even commanded the Jews to wage war against hostile enemies. Examples may be cited. Indeed God disapproved of the peace made with the Amalekites and Canaanites. Let the proposition be inferred by communication.

units.la: 2. A jure naturali, quod 1. commendatur ex Orat. pro Milone. 2. adstruatur, tum ab exemplo ipsorum animantium, quæ vim vi repellant; tum omnium gentium; & maximè exculta-rum, v. g. Assyr. Persæ, Gr. Rom.
units.tr: 2. From natural law, which (1) is commended from the oration for Milo; (2) is to be established both from the example of the animals themselves, which repel force with force, and from all nations, and especially the most cultivated, such as the Assyrians, Persians, Greeks and Romans.

units.la: 3. A necessitate. 1. Fiat accessus per prolepsin: vid. fortassis concedet licitè aliquem bellum geri quidem posse; at consultius esse præferri pacem. 2. Adstruatur necessitas belli, suadente ipsa prudentia: vid. si hostis, bona, vitam, libertatem, religionem petat, aut fides data sociis hoc exigat. Hic utique extrema potius patienda, quàm in turpem pacem consentiendum. vid. Cic. 1. offic.
units.tr: 3. From necessity. (1) Make the approach by prolepsis: perhaps he will concede that some war may indeed be lawfully waged, but that it is more prudent to prefer peace. (2) Let the necessity of war be established, prudence itself urging it: if an enemy seeks goods, life, liberty or religion, or a pledge given to allies demands it. Here surely extreme sufferings are to be endured rather than consenting to a shameful peace. See Cicero, De Officiis, book 1.

units.la: 4. Ab exemplis optimorum: v. g. Davidis, Ezechiæ, Judæ Maccabæi Constantini M. Theodof. Caroli Magni Regum & Principum modernorum.
units.tr: 4. From the examples of the best: e.g. David, Hezekiah, Judas Maccabeus, Constantine the Great, Theodosius, Charlemagne, and the kings and princes of modern times.

units.la: III. Addat cautionem; videlicet 1. ne temere bella suscipiantur, sed tentata prius via pacis, 2. ut fortiter & absque crudelitate gerantur. 3. ut quam primum fieri possit, pace terminetur. Hunc enim finem esse bellorum.
units.tr: III. Let him add a caution, namely: (1) that wars not be undertaken rashly, but that the way of peace be tried first; (2) that they be waged bravely and without cruelty; (3) that they be ended by peace as soon as possible, for this is the end of wars.

units.la: Concluf. Licet igitur paci semper studendum, etiam in ipso bello; tamen cavendum, ne intempestivo ejus amore libertatem, socios, patriam, religionem prodamus.
units.tr: Conclusion. Therefore peace is always to be pursued, even in war itself; yet care must be taken lest, through an untimely love of it, we betray liberty, allies, country and religion.

units.la: THEMA XXIII.
units.tr: THEME XXIII.

units.la: SUASIO DETITIONIS. Ex 2. Sam 19. v. 18. 19. seqq.
units.tr: PERSUASION TO SURRENDER. From 2 Sam. 19. vv. 18, 19 and following.

units.la: Archipincerna Regis Sennacheribi suadet Ministris Hiskiæ deditionem.
units.tr: The chief cupbearer of King Sennacherib persuades the ministers of Hezekiah to surrender.

units.la: Exord. A potentia & clementia expertaSennacheribi. vid. non prima vice expertum esse Hiskiam potentia & clementia regis invictissimi Sennach. Probetur ex re gesta vide v. 13. & 14. Illustretur adversativa: Verum rem Assyriacam requirere plenariam deditionem: Quae causa sit, cur missus sit, ut gratiam Regis sui Hiskiae offerat.
units.tr: Exordium. From the power and clemency of Sennacherib as already experienced. Show that Hezekiah has not experienced the power and clemency of the most invincible king Sennacherib for the first time. Prove this from the deed done, see vv. 13 and 14. Illustrate the adversative: "But the Assyrian affair requires a full surrender." Explain the reason he was sent, namely to offer his king's grace to Hezekiah.

units.la: Propos. Mandatum igitur Regis sui esse, ut dedat urbem Hierosol. secus praedae futuram victoris.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore it is the command of his king that they surrender the city of Jerusalem, otherwise it will be plunder for the victor.

units.la: Confirm. I. A necessario: quod probet
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From necessity, which he proves:

units.la: 1. Ab impotentia Hiskiae, consilio & viribus destituto.
units.tr: 1. From the impotence of Hezekiah, who is deprived of counsel and strength.

units.la: 2. A defectu auxilii, ob infidelitatem Aegyptii: unde si maxime possit juvare, plus periculi: ut si quis baculo Arundineo inniti velit. Hinc insultet ipsi, frustra deliberare, cum necessitas imperat: Clementiam esse regis, qui petat quod imperare potest.
units.tr: 2. From the lack of help, because of the unfaithfulness of Egypt; so that even if it could help greatly, there is more danger, as if someone wished to lean on a reed staff. Hence he mocks them, saying it is pointless to deliberate when necessity commands, and that it is the king's clemency to ask for what he could command.

units.la: II. A justo; accessus fiat per prolepsin, verf. 22. quia sic velit Deus: quem peccatis offenderit Hiskias & populus judaicus; cujus instinctu venerit Sennacherib. Hic alleget subactam jam Samariam & Judaeam. Non esse quod resistant Deo.
units.tr: II. From what is just. The approach is made by prolepsis, v. 22: because God so wills it, whom Hezekiah and the Jewish people have offended by their sins, and at whose instigation Sennacherib has come. Here he adduces that Samaria and Judea are already subdued, so there is no reason to resist God.

units.la: III. Ab utili; sic parci posse sanguini innocentis populi: & impetrari conditiones aequiores.
units.tr: III. From what is useful: thus the blood of the innocent people can be spared, and more equitable conditions obtained.

units.la: Concluf. Hortetur ut agnoscat regis sui clementiam 2. ut sine cunctatione gratiam acceptet, antequam admotis, quas videant copiis, sero deplorent obstinationem.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him exhort them (1) to acknowledge the clemency of their king; (2) to accept the grace without delay, before, when the troops they see are brought up, they lament their obstinacy too late.

units.la: Ejusdem Oratio suasoria ad populum verf. 27. & seq. ditti cap.
units.tr: The same man's persuasive speech to the people, v. 27 and following of the said chapter.

units.la: Exord. A frustranea spe Hierosolym. in rege sua. Ratio, quia suae potius autoritati, quam saluti populi reges velificentur. Haec thesis applicetur ad Hiskiam, qui a Rege suo monitus deditionem recusat.
units.tr: Exordium. From the vain hope placed in their king by the people of Jerusalem. The reason: kings set their own authority above the safety of the people. This thesis is applied to Hezekiah, who, though admonished by his king, refuses to surrender.

units.la: Propos. Quocirca ex mandato regis se autorem esse populo, ut cunctante rege ipsi urbem dedant.
units.tr: Proposition. Wherefore, by the king's command, he becomes the author for the people that, while the king delays, they themselves surrender the city.

units.la: Confirm. I. Ab justo & honesto; jure scilicet populi. Illum quidem subjectum superioribus, quamdiu illi ad publicam salutem imperant: aliam rationem esse, si secum in perniciem trahere velint remp. & uti hic, propriae gloriae, non reip. intenti sint.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From what is just and honourable, namely the right of the people. They are indeed subject to their superiors as long as these rule for the public safety. There is another case if the rulers wish to drag the commonwealth with them into ruin, and, like this one, are intent on their own glory rather than the commonwealth's.

units.la: II. A necessario; quod probetur 1. comparatione dispari potentiae Magni regis Assyr. & impotentis Hiskiae. Illustret haec thesis: videl. tam diu durare obsequium, quamdiu durat patrocinium; eo deficiente, subditos merito sequi imperium victoris. III. Ab utili: videl. r. sic pacem redimi posse, ut quisque sub ficu & vinea sua maneat. 2. Traducendum esse populum mox in terram meliorem Assyriam scil. cujus fertilitas praedicetur prae terra judaica; bello maxime jam exhausta. Inculcet propositionem; videant ne negligant gratiam oblatam.
units.tr: II. From necessity, which is proved (1) by comparing the unequal power of the great king of Assyria with the powerless Hezekiah. This thesis illustrates that obedience lasts as long as protection lasts; when that fails, subjects rightly follow the victor's command. III. From what is useful: (1) that peace can thus be bought, so that each may remain under his own fig tree and vine; (2) that the people are soon to be transferred to a better land, namely Assyria, whose fertility is praised above the Jewish land, which is now much exhausted by war. He should press the proposition, so that they see to it they do not neglect the grace offered.

units.la: IV. Refellat spem populi in Dei auxilio 1. ab exemplis aliarum gentium, quasDii defendere non potuerint vide vers. 32. in sin. & seqq. 2. à provid. Dei in genere; quae coelum regat, terrâ regibus commiserit. Hos esse Joves, martes, hinc Dei pancratica regis Babyloniae & inspecie regis sui majestate loquatur, quibus orbis dominium concessum sit.
units.tr: IV. He should refute the people's hope in God's help: (1) from the examples of other nations, whose gods could not defend them, see v. 32 at the end and following; (2) from God's providence in general, who rules heaven and has committed the earth to kings. These are the Jove(s)... [obscure]; hence he speaks of the all-powerful God of the king of Babylon and, in the person of his own king, of the majesty to whom dominion over the world has been granted.

units.la: Concluf. Hortetur ad deditionem; inculcato argumento à momento, salute scil. aut ruina populi, quae in hac deliberatione versetur.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him exhort them to surrender, pressing the argument from the moment at stake, namely the safety or ruin of the people, which hangs on this deliberation.

units.la: Cancellarii regis Hiskiae Oratio ad populum hortatoria ad fiduciam.
units.tr: The Oration of King Hezekiah's Chancellor, Exhorting the People to Confidence.

units.la: Exord. A persona Archipincernae & populi.
units.tr: Exord. From the person of the chief cupbearer and the people.

units.la: 1. Exosum & suspectum ipsum reddat; quod cognita Hiskiae regis constantia, populi fidem labefactare voluerit. Illustretur à fine: videl. ut ad diffidentiam erga Deum, & perjurium adversus regem populum sollicitet.
units.tr: 1. He makes the chancellor hateful and suspect, since, having recognised King Hezekiah's constancy, he wished to shake the people's faith. Let this be illustrated from the end: namely, that he may stir the people to distrust of God and to perjury against the king.

units.la: 2. Laudet contra fidem populi, quam & Deo & regi probârit hactenus: vel hoc ipso facto, quod sine responso thrasonem dimiserit: id quod regi suo tanquam faustum omen relaturi & praedicaturi sint.
units.tr: 2. He praises the people's faith against him, which they have so far shown both to God and to the king, or at least by this very fact, that he dismissed the boaster without an answer. They are to report this to their king and proclaim it as a favourable omen.

units.la: Propos. Hortari se velle populum, ut in hac fide porrò continuet; nec in deditionem consentiat.
units.tr: Propos. He wishes to exhort the people to continue in this faith and not to consent to surrender.

units.la: Confirm.
units.tr: Confirm.

units.la: I. A spe liberationis divinae. Hanc roboret
units.tr: I. From the hope of divine deliverance. He strengthens this hope by:

units.la: 1. Promissione divina in genere omnibus fidentibus ipsi; in specie facta domui Davidis, & Hierosolymae, ubi templum & arca symbolum divinae praesentiae. Huic promissioni fidendum esse. Hinc refellat argumentum IV. & argumentum II. Orat. praecedentis.
units.tr: 1. The divine promise, given in general to all who trust in him and in particular made to the house of David and to Jerusalem, where the temple and the ark are the symbol of the divine presence. This promise must be trusted. Hence he is to refute argument IV and argument II of the preceding oration.

units.la: 2. Pietate regis Hiskiae; quam ex effectis praedicet; indeque fiduciam concipiat certae liberationis. Illustret illam porrò comparatione aliarum regum & urbium subactarum; qui ob imimpietatem puniti sint; & exemplo Mosis, ad cujus preces Deus sæpe toti populo pepercerit.
units.tr: 2. The piety of King Hezekiah, which he proclaims from its effects, and from which he should draw confidence of certain deliverance. He illustrates this further by comparison with other kings and conquered cities, which were punished for their impiety, and by the example of Moses, at whose prayers God often spared the whole people.

units.la: II. A profanitate regis Sennacheribi; utpote 1. Quem Deus certò puniturus sit: vide text. exemplo Goliathi, quem vel per puerum everterit Deus.
units.tr: II. From the profanity of King Sennacherib, namely: 1. God will surely punish him. See the text, with the example of Goliath, whom God overthrew even through a boy.

units.la: 2. Cui submittere se populus nequeat, nisi Deum majorum suorum, nisi fœdus deserere, & expositas in fœdere comminationes attrahere sibi velint. Hinc porrò refellat argumentum
units.tr: 2. The people cannot submit to him unless they wish to desert the God of their fathers and the covenant, and draw upon themselves the threats set out in the covenant. Hence he is further to refute argument III of the preceding oration,

units.la: III. Orat. præced. & exaggeret & detestetur Assyriorum idolomaniam duriori oneri futuram, quam olim servit. Ægypt.
units.tr: and to magnify and detest the Assyrians' idolatry, which will be a heavier burden than the servitude once endured in Egypt.

units.la: Conclus. Hortetur iterato ad constantiam, saltem eo usque dum consilium Prophetæ Esaiæ prius & divinum responsum desuper impetretur.
units.tr: Conclus. He should exhort them again to constancy, at least until the counsel of the prophet Isaiah has first been sought and a divine answer obtained from above.

units.la: Esaiæ Εὐχαριστία seu Oratio Eucharistica post urbis liberationem.
units.tr: Isaiah's Thanksgiving [Εὐχαριστία], or Eucharistic Oration after the Deliverance of the City.

units.la: Exord. Habeat expositionem lætitiæ & liberationem urbis: his partibus.
units.tr: Exord. Let it give an account of joy and of the deliverance of the city, in these parts.

units.la: I. Quod optavimus Hierosolymitani adepti sumus, inde: Ab initio.
units.tr: I. That we Jerusalemites have obtained what we hoped for. From this: Ab initio.

units.la: II. Ergo merito lætamur. Amplificetur comparata inductione illorum, quæ grata fuerant antea, & post liberationem gratiora visa sunt; uti sunt uxores & liberi, libertas, pax, religio. Inde: Etsi homini,
units.tr: II. Therefore we rightly rejoice. Let this be amplified by a comparative induction of those things which were pleasing before and seemed even more pleasing after the deliverance, such as wives and children, liberty, peace and religion. From this: Etsi homini,

units.la: Propos. Propterea dici hæc, ut magnitudo beneficii divini intelligatur. Inde: Quorsum igitur.
units.tr: Propos. Therefore these things are said so that the greatness of the divine benefit may be understood. From this: Quorsum igitur.

units.la: Confirm. Sit bimembris:
units.tr: Confirm. Let it have two parts:

units.la: I. Prædicet divinam liberationem 1. per comparationem minorum:
units.tr: I. Let him proclaim the divine deliverance, 1. by comparison with lesser things:

units.la: a. Cum beneficiis majorum, qui urbem illis reliquerunt. Inde: A parentibus.
units.tr: a. with the benefits of greater men, who left the city to them. From this: A parentibus.

units.la: b. Cum præced. regibus Judæis, qui per Syros, Ægyptios aliosque liberati, Hiskias per ipsum Deum. vide histor. præced. ad verb. Non enim pro meo redit. Exaggeretur hypothyposi potentiæ minarum Sennacheribi & opposita impotentia Judæorum. 2. per enumerationem illorum qui precibus juverunt, ut fuere cives omnes, propheta, Rex, in cujus pietatis ac constantiæ laudes digrediatur. Inde: Sed quemadmodum.
units.tr: b. with the earlier kings of Judah, who were delivered by the Syrians, the Egyptians and others, whereas Hezekiah was delivered by God himself. See the preceding history at the words "For not for my own sake..." Let this be magnified by a hypotyposis of the power of Sennacherib's threats and the opposing impotence of the Jews. 2. By enumerating those who helped by their prayers: all the citizens, the prophet, and the king, in whose praise for piety and constancy he digresses. From this: Sed quemadmodum.

units.la: II. Hortetur omnes ad gratitudinem adversus Deum; per 1. Gratam recordationem. Inde: En ego.
units.tr: II. Let him exhort everyone to gratitude towards God, by 1. a grateful remembrance. From this: En ego.

units.la: 2. Vitiorum emendationem. Quodsi quis.
units.tr: 2. The amendment of vices. Quodsi quis.

units.la: 3. Cultus divini instaurationem & sedulam frequentationem. Quanquam mihi major.
units.tr: 3. The restoration and diligent frequenting of divine worship. Quanquam mihi major.

units.la: Conclusio. Avertat se ad Deum, ipsque gratias agat & ulteriorem conservationem ac hostium confusionem imploret, Inde; Atque hæc cura.
units.tr: Conclusio. Let him turn himself to God, give thanks to him, and implore his further preservation and the confusion of the enemies. From this: Atque hæc cura.

units.la: THEMA XXIV. EXHORTATIO AD IMITANDUM CICERONEM.
units.tr: THEMA XXIV. AN EXHORTATION TO IMITATE CICERO.

units.la: Exord. A difficultate eloquentiæ: hisce partibus,
units.tr: Exordium: On the difficulty of eloquence; in these parts:

units.la: I. Mirandum, cum Eloquentia res sit pulcherrima, cur tamen pauci ad ejus perfectionem & laudem perveniant.
units.tr: I. It is remarkable that, although eloquence is a most excellent thing, yet few attain to its perfection and praise.

units.la: II. Causam vero esse. 1. quia multi rem facilem esse arbitrantur & segniter tractant. 2. alii difficultate abster reri se patiuntur. 3. alii non justa via aggrediuntur.
units.tr: II. The cause is this: (1) because many think the matter easy and handle it sluggishly; (2) others allow themselves to be deterred by its difficulty; (3) others approach it by no proper road.

units.la: III. At vero multa esse, quæ ad illam requiruntur: vid. præcepta, exercitationem, imitationem optimorum.
units.tr: III. Yet many things are required for it, namely the precepts, practice, and imitation of the best writers.

units.la: Propos. Hinc propositum tibi esse ad imitationem Ciceronem tanquam optimi magistri, cohortari: quod non ingratum aut inutile futurum auditoribus.
units.tr: Propositio: Hence it is your purpose to urge the imitation of Cicero as the best of teachers; this will not be unwelcome or unprofitable to the hearers.

units.la: Tractat. Habeat duas partes.
units.tr: Tractatio: It has two parts.

units.la: I. Imitationem esse necessariam & utilissimam. Hoc probetur.
units.tr: I. Imitation is necessary and most useful. This is to be proved.

units.la: 1. A causa: quia nemo perfectus ulla in re nascitur. Probetur inductione quadam v. gr. ambulationis, sermonis. Applicetur ad eloquentiam per comparationem minorum, quæ quia nemini natura data; utique per præcepta & imitationem disertorum discenda.
units.tr: 1. From cause: because no one is born perfect in any skill. This is to be proved by an induction, for example of walking and of speech. It is to be applied to eloquence by comparison with lesser things: since nature has given it to no one, it must be learned by precepts and by imitation of the skilled speakers.

units.la: 2. A simili, pictorum, statuariorum, & in specie Phidiæ, Apellis, Zeuxis, Policleti: Itemque hederæ ac vitis robustioribus arboribus se applicantium: applicetur ad apodosin.
units.tr: 2. From a likeness: of painters and sculptors, and especially Phidias, Apelles, Zeuxis and Polyclitus; likewise of ivy and the vine, which attach themselves to stronger trees. This is to be applied to the conclusion.

units.la: 3. Ab exemplis Demosthenis, Cic. Virgil. Horat. itemque testimoniis Cicer. Quintil. &c. Illustretur prolepsi Horat. qui servile pecus imitatores dicit: distinguendum inter imitationem servilem & ingenuam, quæ describatur & commendetur.
units.tr: 3. From the examples of Demosthenes, Cicero, Virgil and Horace, and likewise from the testimonies of Cicero, Quintilian, etc. It is to be illustrated by the prolepsis of Horace, who calls imitators a servile herd; a distinction must be drawn between servile and free imitation, which is to be described and commended.

units.la: II. Ciceronem præ cæteris imitandum esse.
units.tr: II. Cicero is to be imitated before all others.

units.la: 1. Quia ipse perfectissimus, in quo juxta Quintil. omne eloquentiæ vim natura exseruit. Illustretur comparatione dispari Demosthenis, Platonis, Isocratis aliorumque. Quis vero dubitet optimum imitandum esse.
units.tr: 1. Because he was himself most perfect, in whom, according to Quintilian, nature displayed the full power of eloquence. This is to be illustrated by a contrast with Demosthenes, Plato, Isocrates and others. Who, indeed, would doubt that the best is to be imitated?

units.la: 2. Quia in omni genere dicendi humili, mediocri, sublimi, exempla reliquit, fiat inductio scriptorum ejus. Hinc parens dictus, quia quod reliquis per partes, hoc Ciceroni omne datum est.
units.tr: 2. Because he left examples in every kind of style, low, middle and high; an induction is to be made from his writings. Hence he is called the parent, because what was given to the others piecemeal was all given to Cicero.

units.la: 3. A testimoniis & exemplis optimorum, qui ipsius lectione profecisse se dicunt.
units.tr: 3. From the testimonies and examples of the best men, who say that they have profited from reading him.

units.la: Conclus. Hortetur ad illum legendum & imitandum sedulo, addito testimonio Quint. Illum multum profecisse, cui Cicero placet.
units.tr: Conclusio: He is to be urged to read and imitate him diligently, adding the testimony of Quintilian: he has profited greatly to whom Cicero is pleasing.

units.la: THEMA XXV. ACTUS LEGISLATORIUS, DE NON TOLERANDIS OCIOSIS IN REPUBL.
units.tr: THEME 25. LEGISLATIVE ACT, ON NOT TOLERATING IDLERS IN THE COMMONWEALTH

units.la: I. Consul rem populo proponit.
units.tr: I. The consul lays the matter before the people.

units.la: Exord. 1. Laudet obsequium quod ad publicationem Senatus, tali frequentia convenerint. Amplif. ab officio boni civis, quod sit agnoscere curam Magistratus illumque ad alacritatem suo studio excitare, & consulere reip.
units.tr: Exordium. 1. He should praise the compliance of those who have assembled in such numbers for the Senate's deliberation. Amplification from the duty of a good citizen, which is to recognise the care of the magistrate, to rouse him to zeal by one's own eagerness, and to consult the commonwealth.

units.la: Narratio. Breviter exponat 1. in genere sollicitudinem Senatus in abrogandis abusibus. 2. in specie displicentiam ejusdem quod tot otiosis abundet resp. unde noxii effectus & periculum seditionis in rep. unde & moti Censores ad Senatum retulerint. 3. inventione remedii, ut scilicet lege certa otiosi a rep. arceantur.
units.tr: Narration. He should briefly set out: 1. in general, the Senate's concern to abolish abuses; 2. in particular, its displeasure that the commonwealth abounds in so many idlers, whence come harmful effects and the danger of sedition in the state, which is why the censors were also moved to bring the matter before the Senate; 3. the discovery of a remedy, namely that idlers be kept out of the commonwealth by a fixed law.

units.la: Propos. Hanc legem ex more proponendam populo, ut illam suis suffragiis comprobet.
units.tr: Proposition. That this law, as is customary, be put before the people, so that they may approve it by their votes.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. A necessario: Hoc probetur ex periculo, quod ab otiosis metuendum reip. dum 1. vitia varia inde nascuntur. 2. paupertas. 3. studium turbandi remp. Amplif. exemplo bonorum legislatorum, Lycurgi præsertim, qui laboribus occupatos voluerit cives & juventam: & primorum regum, qui populum in tribus dispescuerint & Censores instituerint, qui de singulorum moribus & unde viverent inquirerent, vide Halicarn. Illustretur a contrario. Hanc disciplinam paulatim callapsam instaurandam esse, ut moribus antiquis stet resp.
units.tr: I. From necessity. This is proved from the danger to the commonwealth that must be feared from idlers: (1) various vices arise from idleness; (2) poverty; (3) the desire to disturb the state. Amplification from the example of good lawgivers, especially Lycurgus, who wanted the citizens and the young to be occupied with labour; and of the first kings, who divided the people into tribes and appointed censors to inquire into the morals of each man and how he lived. See Halicarnassus. Let it be illustrated by the contrary. This discipline, now gradually fallen into disuse, must be restored, so that the commonwealth may stand by its ancient customs.

units.la: II. Ab utilitate hujus legis, quæ probetur ab effectis: videl. hinc
units.tr: II. From the usefulness of this law, which is proved from its effects, namely as follows:

units.la: 1. Averti pauperiem à civibus. Labor enim ditat.
units.tr: 1. Poverty is kept away from the citizens, for labour enriches.

units.la: 2. Stabiliri concordiam inter cives, dum quilibet operi intentus victum ab altero lucratur.
units.tr: 2. Harmony is established among the citizens, since each, busy with his work, earns his living without depending on another.

units.la: 3. Promoveri Commercia, etiam cum exteris.
units.tr: 3. Commerce is promoted, even with foreigners.

units.la: 4. Augeri fiscum: ut non opus sit ad capitationes & collectas confugere illico: quæ res turbas facile ciere soleat.
units.tr: 4. The treasury is increased, so that there is no need to resort at once to poll taxes and levies, which usually stir up disturbances easily.

units.la: Concluf. Consilium Senatus repetat, videl. hinc motum illum ad ferendam hanc legem, quæ proinde prælegatur videl. Nullus otiosus esto in rep. quod si inveniatur exul esto. II. Proponi illam, ut per trinundini spacium juxta morem populus deliberet, & per tribunos ad Senatum referat.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him repeat the Senate's counsel, namely that this motion was made to pass this law, which is therefore to be read out beforehand: No one shall be idle in the commonwealth; and if anyone is found to be, let him be exiled. II. That it be put forward, so that the people may deliberate for the customary space of three market-days, and that the tribunes report it back to the Senate.

units.la: II. Tribunus primus nomine plebis legem improbat: ad Concives.
units.tr: II. The first tribune, speaking for the plebs, disapproves of the law: to the citizens.

units.la: Exord. A scopo legum omnium, quæ est salus reip. 1. Proponatur hoc. 2. Probetur ex lege antiquissima: Salus populi suprema lex esto. 3. Amplit.à contrario videl. ideoq; minus ferendum si lex rogetur, quæ huic scopo adversetur. 4. Talem sibi videri illam legem quam proposuerit Consul contra otiosos.
units.tr: Exordium. From the aim of all laws, which is the safety of the commonwealth: (1) let this be put forward; (2) let it be proved from the most ancient law, "Let the safety of the people be the supreme law"; (3) an amplification from the contrary: the less should such a law be passed if it is proposed to oppose this aim; (4) the law the consul has proposed against the idle seems to me to be of this kind.

units.la: Propof. Hinc se motum ratione officii, loqui pro salute publica & populi Rom. libertate, quæ hac lege everti videatur, quod ostensurus sit.
units.tr: Propositio. Hence I am moved, by the duty of my office, to speak for the public safety and the liberty of the Roman people, which this law seems to overturn, as I shall show.

units.la: Confirmatio,
units.tr: Confirmatio,

units.la: I. A turpitudine hujus legis, 1. quia turpe sit cogere ad laborem Romanos cives. Hoc ostendatur à gloria Roman. qui armis orbem subegerint & late imperant populis. Quam indignum, hunc pœnis cogere ad laborem; instar mancipiorum. Frustra libertatem & dominium armis quæsitum esse, si domi serviat victor populus. Avertat orationem ad manes ac cineres majorum, ne patiantur inuri hanc maculam Romanis. 2. Quia famam sic perdet apud exteros, quam degenerarint ab avita virtute cum æterno dedecore nominis Romani, quod venerandum gentibus. Et hanc legem probaremus?
units.tr: I. From the baseness of this law: (1) it is shameful to compel Roman citizens to labour. This should be shown from the glory of the Romans, who by arms subdued the world and rule widely over the peoples. How unworthy it is to compel men to labour by punishments, like slaves. In vain was liberty and dominion won by arms, if at home the victorious people is enslaved. Let him turn his speech to the spirits and ashes of the ancestors, lest they suffer this stain to be branded on the Romans. (2) Because by this they will lose their reputation among foreigners, since they have degenerated from ancestral virtue, with eternal disgrace to the Roman name, which is venerable to the nations. And should we approve this law?

units.la: II. A noxio: 1. quia hinc contentiones futuræ inter divites & pauperes, nobiles & plebejos, quasi scil. si coacti sint laborare, ut reliqui lasciviant. 2. Neque enim divites ac nobiles pariturosle-gi: quod probetur aliis legibus, sumptuariis præsertim, quas potentes tentes minimè observent. Fiat digressio in Locũ Communem de impunitate potentiorum. Si verò cogendi sint & illi dissi-dium & bellum civile oriturum inter cives & magistratum. Con-cludatur argumentum cautione generali, videl. tales ferendas leges, quæ turbas minuant, non excitent.
units.tr: II. From its harmfulness: (1) because from this there will arise future quarrels between rich and poor, nobles and plebeians, as if, that is, some were compelled to labour so that the rest might indulge in luxury. (2) For the rich and the nobles will not obey the law; this may be proved from other laws, especially sumptuary ones, which the powerful by no means observe. Let a digression be made into the common place on the impunity of the powerful. But if they too are to be compelled, discord and civil war will arise between the citizens and the magistrate. Let the argument be concluded with a general caution: such laws should be enacted as diminish disturbances, not as stir them up.

units.la: III. Ab iniquo eum omnis laboris scopum esse, ut opes & quietem nobis paremus. Illustretur simili à bello quod geritur propter pacem. Si igitur pace frui licet, quid ni & opibus, in quiete honesta, & vita suaviori. Hic exaggeret labores & molestias vitæ generum, & frustra illas suscipi dicat, si requies legibus vetetur.
units.tr: III. From its injustice: the whole aim of labour is that we may procure wealth and quiet for ourselves. Let this be illustrated by a simile from war, which is waged for the sake of peace. If therefore it is allowed to enjoy peace, why not also wealth, in honest quiet and a more pleasant life? Here he should enlarge on the labours and troubles of life, and say that they are undertaken in vain if rest is forbidden by law.

units.la: Concluf. Ex dictis constare, iniquam esse legem: quibuscunque etiam coloribus a Consule pingatur; Proindeque caveant, ne fructum laboris, quietem civitatis, & gloriam populi Romani sub iniqua hac lege violari patiantur.
units.tr: Conclusio. From what has been said it is clear that the law is unjust, whatever colours the consul may paint it with; and therefore let the citizens take care not to suffer the fruit of their labour, the quiet of the state, and the glory of the Roman people to be violated under this unjust law.

units.la: III. Tribunus plebis secundus legem suadet.
units.tr: III. The second tribune of the plebs argues for the law.

units.la: Exord. A miseriis vitæ regentum, qui dum pro aliis vigilant censuris omnium maximè sunt expositi. Hinc diadema regum vix tollendum humo rectè dictum esse, si constet quantis calamitatibus conjunctum. Applicetur ad hypothefin, idem contingere consuli, cujus lex salu-berrima sugilletur & traducatur publice, invaluisse proh-dolor tem-pora, ut is se maximè virum credat, qui maxime adversum se pro-bet magistratui.
units.tr: Exord. From the miseries of life for rulers, who, while they watch over others, are most exposed to the censure of all. Hence the saying that a king's diadem can hardly be lifted from the ground is rightly spoken, if one considers how many calamities are joined to it. Applied to the present case, the same happens to the consul, whose most salutary law is publicly mocked and slandered. Alas, the times have so prevailed that the man who shows himself most hostile to the magistrate believes himself the most manly.

units.la: Propos. Se verò non posse non probare legem à Consule propositam: quæ causa sit, quare hortante officio, examinaturus quæ contra al-lata processerit.
units.tr: Propos. But he cannot fail to approve the law proposed by the consul. Since duty urges him, he will examine what has been brought forward against it.

units.la: Confutatio.
units.tr: Confutatio.

units.la: 1. Præstruat accessus, mirari se cum legis hujus satis à consule de-monstrata sit tuum necessitas, tum utilitas, tamen non defuisse, qui contradixerit: quasi probrosa, quasi noxia & iniqua. Huic merito obviam eundum!
units.tr: 1. First he should forestall the approach. He should wonder that, although the necessity and the usefulness of this law have been sufficiently demonstrated by the consul, there were nonetheless some who spoke against it, as if it were shameful, harmful and unjust. This must rightly be met head on!

units.la: 2. Examinet rationes tribuni ordine
units.tr: 2. Let him examine the tribune's arguments in order.

units.la: Ad 1. resp. non servitutem esse, sed libertatem parere legibus. Frustra orbem subactum, si ocio & vitiis succumbant Romani. Famam auctum iri per salutares constitutiones. Ad 2. resp. non metuenda dissidia ex labore injuncto, sed potius ex ocio: cujus damna explicentur. Legem obligare omnes æqualiter. Si leges sumptuariæ neglectæ hactenus, hoc vel incuriæ magistratus, vel injuriæ temporum adscribendum.
units.tr: To the first, reply that obeying laws is not slavery but freedom. It is in vain that the world has been subdued if the Romans succumb to idleness and vices. Their fame will be increased by wholesome constitutions. To the second, reply that the dissensions to be feared arise not from the labour imposed but rather from idleness, whose harms should be set out. The law binds all equally. If sumptuary laws have been neglected until now, this must be ascribed either to the carelessness of the magistrates or to the wrongs of the times.

units.la: Ad 3. resp. Quietem honestam non prohiberi hac lege, sed ignavum ocium, quod proinde describatur, & vituperetur ex effectis. Sic igitur patere, quam frivole & periculose lex hæc in suspicionem vocata; cujus æquitatem porrò offendendam esse.
units.tr: To the third, reply that honest rest is not forbidden by this law, but only lazy idleness, which should therefore be described and condemned by its effects. In this way it will be plain how frivolously and dangerously this law has been called into suspicion, and its fairness must further be defended.

units.la: Conclusio. Cum itaque non stringant rationes contra allatæ, merito stare rationes à Consule allatas: adeoque se calculum adjicere legi propositæ, tanquam maximè necessariæ & longè saluberrimæ.
units.tr: Conclusio. Since the arguments brought against it do not hold, the arguments brought by the consul rightly stand. He therefore adds his vote to the proposed law, as most necessary and by far most salutary.

units.la: IV. Tertius tribus adstipuletur secundo.
units.tr: IV. Let the third tribune support the second.

units.la: Exord. Resumat paucis actorum summam.
units.tr: Exord. He should briefly sum up what has been said.

units.la: Propos. Pauca adhuc pro lege propositā addenda videri: ut omnis scrupulus eximatur animis.
units.tr: Propos. A few more things still seem to need adding in favour of the proposed law, so that every doubt may be removed from minds.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: I. Ab honesto: quod probetur 1. à lege naturali, qua tota natura mancipata laboribus. 2. A legibus Civilibus, Lacedæm. & Athenienf. præsertim, quæ laborem imperent; unde & florue-rint resp. 3. à lege gentium, quæ probetur testimoniis autorum: In nascente rep Christianorum legem esse. Qui non vult laborare, ne comedat. Hæc commendetur & longe æquiorem adhuc esse dicat hanc legem à Consule propositam. 4. Ab exemplo ipsius Dei; qui minimè ociosus sit ut impius error Epicureorum statuit; sed regimini orbis semper intentum.
units.tr: I. From honesty, which is proved: 1. by the law of nature, by which all nature is bound to labours; 2. by the civil laws of the Lacedaemonians and especially the Athenians, which enjoin labour, whence their commonwealths also flourished; 3. by the law of nations, which is proved by the testimony of authors, that it was a law in the nascent Christian commonwealth: "If anyone will not work, neither let him eat." This should be commended, and he should say that the law now proposed by the consul is far fairer still; 4. from the example of God himself, who is by no means idle, as the impious error of the Epicureans held, but always intent on governing the world.

units.la: II. A facili; Hic ostendas 1. ocio nihil gravius esse, cum quis tempus terere non novit; unde moles & intemperies corporis & ægritudo animi; & vitiorum occupationem longe gravissimam. 2. Labore mitescere laborem, cum corpus vegetum, animus alacer agendo efficiatur. Probetur simili ab aqua mota & contra stagnante; item ab exemplo militum, qui labore confervantur. Ne metuant igitur tanquam onus, illud quod ad propriæ ipsorum salutem tendit.
units.tr: II. From ease. Here he should show: 1. that nothing is more grievous than idleness, when a man does not know how to pass his time; whence come sluggishness and disorder of the body, sickness of the mind, and the by far most grievous occupation with vices. 2. That labour makes labour lighter, since the body is made vigorous and the mind lively by action. This should be proved by the analogy of moving water and, on the contrary, stagnant water; likewise by the example of soldiers, who are preserved by labour. Let them therefore not fear it as a burden, since it tends to their own safety.

units.la: Concluf. Per revocationem sui frustra se prolixum in commendanda lege saluberrima, quæ apud omnes honestatis amantes applausum facile inveniet: Sperare se pristina rursus tempora, cum otio ejecto, virtuti ac laboribus mancipatum cernere licet populum Romanum.
units.tr: Concluf. By recalling his points, he says he has spoken at length in vain in commending this most salutary law, which will easily win applause among all lovers of honour. He hopes that the former times may return, when idleness has been cast out and the Roman people can be seen devoted to virtue and labours.

units.la: IV. Consul approbata sententia populi suffragiis subnixus Legem sancit.
units.tr: IV. The consul, his opinion approved and supported by the votes of the people, enacts the law.

units.la: Exord. Gratuletur civitati, quod plures boni reperti, qui paternam senatus curam agnoscentes, saluberrimae legi subscripserint.
units.tr: Exord. Let him congratulate the commonwealth that many good men have been found who, acknowledging the paternal care of the senate, have subscribed to this most salutary law.

units.la: Propos. Neque enim aliam vel Senatus vel suam esse intentionem, quam veram populi Rom. gloriam ac quietem hac lege afferre & aeternam facere.
units.tr: Propos. For neither the senate nor himself has any other intention than to bring about, and by this law to make eternal, the true glory and quiet of the Roman people.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmatio.

units.la: I. Explicet mentem legis: quae sit 1. non serviliter cogere ad opuscives, uti ociose a daemagogo obiectum; sed excitare omnes ad industriam & honestas artes: quibus Resp. Rom. hactenus creverit. Hinc veterum mores paucis & instituta repetat ac laudet. Illustret contrariis exemplis Sybaritarum aliarumque Rerump. quae inertia everse sint. 2. Non prohibere honestam requiem seu ocium liberale; quod vel in literis, vel in colendis praediis & curandis patrimoniis amplioribus ponitur: haec enim a majoribus culta fuisse, & salubria reip: literatos ut consilio, divites ut opibus juvent remp. sed prohiberi inertiam maleficiatorum, qui nihil aguntin rep. quam ut nova venentur theatra & scenas frequentent, symposia agitent, luxui indulgeant; unde maximum malum metuendum civitati. Hanc mentem legis, hanc senatus intentionem esse.
units.tr: I. He should explain the spirit of the law, namely: 1. that it does not compel the citizens in a servile manner, as the demagogue objected idly, but rouses everyone to industry and honourable arts, by which the Roman commonwealth has grown until now. Hence he should recall and praise in a few words the customs and institutions of the ancients. He should illustrate with contrary examples the Sybarites and other commonwealths overthrown by inertia. 2. That it does not forbid honest rest or liberal leisure, which lies in literary pursuits, or in cultivating estates and managing larger patrimonies; for these were cultivated by our ancestors, and it is useful to the commonwealth that men of letters should help it by counsel and the rich by their resources. What is forbidden is the idleness of wrongdoers, who do nothing in the commonwealth except hunt after new theatres and frequent the stage, hold drinking parties and indulge in luxury, whence the greatest evil is to be feared for the state. This is the spirit of the law, this the intention of the senate.

units.la: II. Gratuletur reip. quod patres & populus, saltem sincerior pars hac in parte conspirent, ut ignavi arceantur a rep. Hinc spem esse brevi remp. convaliturum. Illustretur simili apum, lucos arcentium; & corporis, nullum admittentis membrum ociosum aut mortuum. Applicetur ad hypothesin.
units.tr: II. He should congratulate the commonwealth that the fathers and the people, or at least the more sincere part of them in this matter, agree that the idle should be kept out of the commonwealth. Hence there is hope that the commonwealth will soon grow strong again. Let it be illustrated by the likeness of bees, who keep off drones from their hives, and of the body, which admits no idle or dead member. Let it be applied to the case in hand.

units.la: Conclus. 1. Horteturad hoc studium & concordiam universos. 2. Quod felix sausumque legem repetat, & ex decreto senatus, consensu populi ratam esse jubeat.
units.tr: Conclus. 1. He should exhort everyone to this zeal and concord. 2. He should, happily and fortunately, repeat the law and order that, by decree of the senate, it be ratified with the consent of the people.

units.la: THEMA XXVI. CONJURATIO ADONIÆ AD INVADENDUM REGNUM.
units.tr: THEMA XXVI. The conspiracy of Adonijah to seize the kingdom.

units.la: Ex 1. Reg. 1. v. 5. &seqq.
units.tr: From 1 Kings 1:5 and following.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Adonia filius regis natu maximus consilium suum aperit Joabo supremo momilitiæ & Abjatare sacrorum præfectis, de occupando regno vivente patre Davide.
units.tr: Adonijah, the eldest son of the king, opens his plan to Joab, the commander-in-chief, and Abiathar, the prefect of the sacred things, to seize the kingdom while his father David is still alive.

units.la: Exord. Benevolentiam captat.
units.tr: Exordium. He seeks their goodwill.

units.la: 1. Προβολὴ, qua spectatam illorum fidem ac dexteritatem in gerendis regni negotiis. Ea semper &c. prædicat.
units.tr: 1. Proboli [Προβολή], by which he praises their tested loyalty and skill in conducting the affairs of the kingdom. Ea semper etc. he proclaims.

units.la: 2. Ἐξηγασία, ab effectis in genere κατὰ μεζισμὸν, sive in sacris, sive profanis: & in specie in ultima machinatione Absolomi.
units.tr: 2. Exegasia [Ἐξηγασία], drawn from their achievements in general, kata mesismon [κατὰ μεσισμόν], whether in sacred or in secular matters, and in particular from the last scheme of Absalom.

units.la: 3. Πρόληψις ab effectu sperato quoque in futurum, subjectio a causis impedientibus, senio regis, metuendo imperio muliebri.
units.tr: 3. Prolepsis [Πρόληψις], drawn from the success hoped for in the future as well. Hypobolē [ὑποβολή] is drawn from the hindrances: the old age of the king, and the dreaded rule of a woman.

units.la: Explicatio causæ moventis ad hanc consultationem; vid.
units.tr: Explanation of the cause that moves him to this consultation; see:

units.la: I. Periculi imminentis
units.tr: I. Of the imminent danger:

units.la: a. A Recenti pellice, quæ penitus occupabit regis animum: Probatur verisimile:
units.tr: a. From the recent concubine, who will thoroughly take possession of the king's mind. This is shown to be likely:

units.la: 1. A forma excellenti. 2. ætate juvenili puellæ. 3. senio extremo regis: cujus adjunctum proprium esse soleat nimius & delirans in tales amor, supplere satagens defectum virium corporis. 4. Ab impudentia aut importunitate juvencularum amorem in tali casu in ambitionem aut avaritiam vertentium.
units.tr: 1. from her outstanding beauty; 2. from the youthful age of the girl; 3. from the extreme old age of the king, whose usual companion is an excessive and frenzied love for such a woman, striving to make up for the failing of his bodily strength; 4. from the shamelessness or importunity of young women who in such a case turn love into ambition or greed.

units.la: b. A Bathsheba, Exagg. ab ejusdem adjunctis ambitione, æmulatione, gratia qua polleat apud regem. Æmulatio amplificetur porrò 1. à causa, recenti pellice. 2. effectis, quod acrius instabit regi, ut filium Solomonem, pro forma scil. in effectu, se matrem sceptrum regium resignet. Explicetur porrò a causa adjuvante Nathane, qui fœminæ hujus oraculum domesticum sit: quique hoc aget omni conatu, ut ipse cum puero & fœmina, seu potius solus imperet.
units.tr: b. From Bathsheba. The danger is magnified by her attendant circumstances: her ambition, her rivalry, and the favour she enjoys with the king. The rivalry is further magnified (1) from its cause, the recent concubine; (2) from its effects, since she will press the king more keenly, so that she, as mother, may surrender the royal sceptre to her son Solomon, that is, in effect, to her own beauty. It is further explained from the contributing cause, Nathan, who is this woman's private oracle, and who will strive with every effort so that he himself may rule with the boy and the woman, or rather alone.

units.la: II. Æquitatis suadentis vigilantiam in hoc rerum statu.
units.tr: II. Of the fairness that urges vigilance in this state of affairs.

units.la: a. Quia primogenitus, ad quem uti defuncto parente successio, ita eodem civiliter mortuo administratio pertineat. Prob. 1. jure divino inde a patriarcharum tempore. 2. Jure naturali. 3. jure gentium seu praxi populorum.
units.tr: a. Because the firstborn, to whom the succession belongs when the parent dies, and to whom the administration belongs when the parent is civilly dead, is the rightful heir. This is proved (1) by divine law from the time of the patriarchs; (2) by natural law; (3) by the law of nations, or the practice of peoples.

units.la: b. Quia increbuerit fama successuri Solomonis, ob promissionem matri factam & juramento confirmatam. Probatur verisimile, 1. a causa fœminæ ambitu scil. 2. metu ne forte prolem rex adhuc suscipiat ex Abisai, quem senili & perverso amore ob gratiam matris sceptris forte destinet. c. Quia exitio involveretur regnum, si regi puero illud concrederetur. Probetur à causa, 1. hostibus intentis in omnem occasionem in regis novi successione. 2. Israelitis vixdum ex seditione Sebana pacatis, qui regis pueri & foeminae imperium detrectaturi sint. b. Ab effectis praesentibus, ubi passim jam querelae de mala justitia & remisso nimium regimine.
units.tr: b. Because the report has grown that Solomon will succeed, on account of the promise made to his mother and confirmed by oath. This is shown to be likely: (1) from the cause, namely the ambition of the woman; (2) from the fear that the king may still beget offspring by Abishag, whom in his senile and perverse love, because of his mother's favour, he may perhaps designate for the sceptre. c. Because the kingdom would be thrown into ruin if it were entrusted to a boy king. This is proved (1) from the cause: enemies are ready to seize any opportunity that arises at the succession of a new king; (2) from the Israelites, who have scarcely been pacified after the sedition of Sheba and who will refuse to submit to the rule of a boy and a woman. b. From the present effects: complaints of bad justice and of excessively lax government are already everywhere.

units.la: d. Quia ipsius regis huc inclinare videatur voluntas. Prob. quia regium indulserit sibi satellitium, non facturus, si regem esse nollet. Explicatur per prolepsin, Cur regnum non resignet: Resp. quia offendere nolit Bathsebam pro filio ambientem; Nullum esse dubium, occupatum illud velle regem à primogenito, quod denegare non audeat importunitati foeminae dilectae.
units.tr: d. Because the king's own will seems to lean this way. This is proved because he has granted himself a bodyguard, which he would not do if he did not wish to be king. It is explained by prolepsis, why he does not surrender the kingdom. Answer: because he is unwilling to offend Bathsheba, who is pleading for her son. There is no doubt that the king wishes the kingdom to be taken from the firstborn, something he dares not refuse to the importunity of his beloved woman.

units.la: Illatio propositi sui: scil. cupere itaque ut hi duo viri videant deliberentque quid in hoc rerum statu agendum sibi judicent.
units.tr: Inference of his proposal: namely, he desires that these two men see and judge what they think must be done in this state of affairs.

units.la: Numquid occupandum videatur regnum omni jure sibi debitum, & tantum non ad se devolutum.
units.tr: Whether the kingdom, owed to him by every right and almost fallen to him already, seems to be something to be seized.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Abjathar Sacerdos approbat Adoniae propositum gnatonicè.
units.tr: Abiathar the priest approves Adonijah's proposal with flattering obsequiousness.

units.la: Praefatio.
units.tr: Preface.

units.la: 1. De humillimo suo affectu comparatè cum suo debito. Si quantum, &c.
units.tr: 1. On his most humble feeling, compared with his duty. Si quantum, etc.

units.la: 2. Rationem dicendi sententiam suam arcessit tum à suo officio; tum à Domini Adoniae imperio.
units.tr: 2. He draws the ground for stating his opinion both from his office and from the command of his lord Adonijah.

units.la: 3. Se igitur utrique satisfacturum, & libere quid de re momentosa ipsi videatur editurum.
units.tr: 3. He will therefore satisfy both, and freely set out what seems to him on a matter of great moment.

units.la: Proponit sententiam suam, scil. jure regnum deberi Adoniae.
units.tr: He sets out his opinion, namely that by right the kingdom is owed to Adonijah.

units.la: Confirmatio. I. Ex jure naturae, gentium & sacro, uti sapienter & cordate ab Adonia allegatum. Expositio uberior juris sacri. 1. ab ipso mundi origine in Caino. 2. In contentione desuper Esavi & Jacobi. 3. In patriarcharum familiis, ubi primogenitus caput familiae, unde seniorum numerus. Illustratur prolepsi. Quod hactenus in Judicibus, Saulis familia nulla successio; Ratio quia judices electi extra ordinem, Saul vero cecidit Dei judicio & reprobatus divinitus cum familia, ne regeret.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From the law of nature, of nations, and of sacred law, as wisely and shrewdly alleged by Adonijah. A fuller exposition of sacred law: 1. from the very origin of the world, in Cain; 2. in the contention above between Esau and Jacob; 3. in the families of the patriarchs, where the firstborn is head of the family, whence the number of elders. Illustrated by prolepsis. As has been the case so far in Judges: Saul's family had no succession. The reason: the judges were chosen outside the ordinary order, but Saul fell by the judgment of God and was divinely rejected, with his family, so that he should not reign.

units.la: II. Ab absurdo: si inter nativitatem pares, dotibus necessariis inferior rior præferri deberet. Illustretur similibus, ut si liberi regere deberent parentes, servi dominos; indocti instruere peritiores, balbutientes ab ore esse facundis; cæcus dux videntium, claudus ductor recte incedentis. Applicetur.
units.tr: II. From the absurd: if among those equal by birth the one inferior in the necessary gifts should be preferred. Let it be illustrated by similar cases: as if children should rule their parents, or slaves their masters; the untaught should teach the more skilled; stammerers should be fluent speakers; a blind man should lead those who see, a lame man should guide one who walks straight. Let it be applied.

units.la: III. Ab incommodo scil. continuus contemptus jussorum istorum qui minus capaces; aut continua pugna contra debiliores. Ratio: quia spretos se videntmajores præ minoribus. Exemplum Esavi vitæ Jacobi hac propter insidiantis etiam in vita privata. Illustretur contrario bono ordine, si natu majores minoribus imperent.
units.tr: III. From inconvenience, namely the constant contempt of those who are commanded, being less capable, or constant fighting against the weaker. The reason: because the greater see themselves despised in comparison with the lesser. The example of Esau, and of Jacob's life, which for this reason was plotted against even in private life. Let it be illustrated by the contrary good order, if the elder by birth were to command the younger.

units.la: Solvit dubium quod movit Adonia; quasi David promiserit Bathsebæ successionem filii Solomonis. Ratio 1. Nimis sapiens est David. 2. Nimis provida Bathseba, quæ metuat sibi dubio oppositionem Adoniæ Viri cordati, & regio jam satellitio clari. Digreditur in laudem Adoniæ, qui ob egregias dotes & alia rege digna, jam rex habeatur à primariis ministris facile acclamatione excipiendus à toto populo; si vel minimo nutu voluntatem indicit.
units.tr: He resolves the doubt which Adonijah raised, as if David had promised Bathsheba the succession for her son Solomon. Reasons: 1. David is too wise. 2. Bathsheba is too provident, since she fears, not without reason, opposition from Adonijah, a man of sound judgment and already famous for his royal bodyguard. He digresses into praise of Adonijah, who, on account of his outstanding gifts and other qualities worthy of a king, is already regarded as king by the chief ministers, and would easily be received with acclamation by the whole people, if he were to signify his will by even the slightest nod.

units.la: Concludit 1. Regnum jure deberi post mortem Davidis Adoniæ. 2. Utrum jam gravi hac ætate patris præoccupandum, se prudentiæ regis & Jacobi, qui vires perficiendi magis perspectas habeant, relinquere dijudicandum.
units.tr: He concludes: 1. that by right the kingdom is owed to Adonijah after David's death; 2. whether it should be seized now, while his father is in such advanced age, he leaves to be decided by the prudence of the king and of Joab, who have a clearer view of the means of carrying it out.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Joab suo suffragio occupandum regnum statuit.
units.tr: Joab decides by his own vote that the kingdom should be seized.

units.la: Accessus, 1. ab imperio Adoniæ, cui sibi ministro obtemperandum. 2. A sua fidelitate, quam re, ubi opus melius præstiturus quam verbis declaraturus sit.
units.tr: The approach: 1. from the command of Adonijah, to whom, as his minister, he must obey; 2. from his loyalty, which he will show in deed rather than declare in words, since he will do the work better than he can explain it.

units.la: Propositio: Post auditam sententiam Abjatharis, qui de jure satis educuerit, nihil restare aliud, quam ut actu regnum occupet, quod jure ipsi debeatur.
units.tr: Proposition: After hearing the opinion of Abiathar, who has sufficiently brought out the right, nothing remains but that Adonijah seize the kingdom in act, since it is owed to him by right.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: I. Ab testimonio Abjatharis, qui haud obscure in fine hoc innuat, cum regis ac sui humillimi ministri judicio relinquat, utrum vires sufficiat. Confirm. comparatione juris & facti: ubi de eo constat, de hoc illico ineunda consilia.
units.tr: I. From the testimony of Abiathar, who at the close hints quite plainly that he leaves it to the judgment of the king and of his most humble minister whether his strength suffices. Confirmation by comparison of right and fact: where the right is established, the plans are to be entered upon at once.

units.la: II. A necessario. Quod prob. 1. à persona regis senio jam soluti, & apud juvenculam sponsam jam considentis securus de regno. 2. à molimine Bathsebæ & Nathanis, qui non negligent causam Solomonis hoc rerum cardine. Astruitur à juramento Bathsebæ facto de successione Solomonis. Non esse quod dubitet ea de re Abjathar. Hoc eludendum præventione.
units.tr: II. From necessity. Proved: 1. from the person of the king, now loosed from age and sitting with a young bride, secure about the kingdom; 2. from the schemes of Bathsheba and Nathan, who will not neglect Solomon's cause at this crucial turn of affairs. It is supported by the oath made by Bathsheba about Solomon's succession. Abiathar has no reason to doubt this matter. This must be countered by forestalling it.

units.la: III. Ab honesto; posse hoc fieri licite. Ratio à causa juramenti blanditiis scil. Bathsebæ, quibus regem eo pellexerit: 1. à conditione Solomonis, qui si rigide examinari quis velit ex damnato coitu natus; matre scil. quæ mortis rea fuerat ob commissum adulterium. 2. à præsumta voluntate Davidis, qui veluti pœnitens temerarii juramenti, non contradicat Adoniæ regali satellitio stipato; optans forte, ut ipse arripiat, quod dare non audet.
units.tr: III. From honour: that this can be done lawfully. The reason is drawn from the cause of the oath, namely the flatteries of Bathsheba, by which she enticed the king to it: 1. from the condition of Solomon, who, if one wishes to examine it strictly, was born of a condemned union, namely of a mother who had been liable to death for the adultery she had committed; 2. from the presumed will of David, who, like a man repenting of a rash oath, does not oppose Adonijah, surrounded by his royal guard, perhaps wishing that he himself would seize what he does not dare to give.

units.la: IV. A facili, Prob. 1. à satellitio numeroso & primariis, quos secum habeat Adonia regni ministris. 2. ab alienatione animorum Israelitarum à Davide & totius populi; levi momento inclinando. Ab exemplo Absalomi, Sebæ, nequiorum, quos tamen tam pronis statim animis secuti sint,
units.tr: IV. From ease. Proved: 1. from the numerous bodyguard and the chief ministers of the kingdom whom Adonijah has with him; 2. from the alienation of the minds of the Israelites and of the whole people from David, which would be turned by a slight impulse. From the example of Absalom and Sheba, worse men, whom nevertheless they followed at once with such ready minds.

units.la: Conclusio hortatoria, ut regem se declaret publicè & solemne convivium instituat. Addit pathos à causa corona & sceptro, quæ non contigunt facile sine aliquo discrimine.
units.tr: Exhortatory conclusion: that he should declare himself king publicly and hold a solemn banquet. He adds an emotional appeal from the matter of crown and sceptre, which are not easily obtained without some danger.

units.la: THEMA XXVII.
units.tr: THEMA XXVII.

units.la: 1. Icilius Tribunus ad populum rogationem pro Triumpho Consulum Valerii & Horat. ex Liv. l. III. c. 63. seqq.
units.tr: 1. Icilius the tribune to the people, proposing a triumph for the consuls Valerius and Horatius, from Livy, book 3, chapter 63 and following.

units.la: Exord. A laudabili consuetudine majorum, sua virtuti præmia decernentium. Merito: virtutis enim nutrimentum esse honorem, magnos animos magnis honoribus fieri. vide lib. 4. c. 36. & Cic. pro Arch.
units.tr: Exord. From the praiseworthy custom of our ancestors, who decreed rewards to virtue. Rightly so: for honour is the nourishment of virtue, and great honours make great spirits. See book 4, chapter 36, and Cicero, Pro Archia.

units.la: Narratio. Referat nervose 1. geminam à Consulibus de Sabinis reportatam victoriam. 2. invidiam Senatus vix popularem supplicationem uno die utrique Consuli decernentis, & detrectantis comitia in campo Martio loco ordinario à consulibus indicta. 3. iniquam Senatus denegationem meriti triumphi.
units.tr: Narratio. Set out vividly: (1) the twofold victory won over the Sabines by the consuls; (2) the jealousy of the Senate, which scarcely granted a thanksgiving to both consuls for one day and disliked the assembly in the Campus Martius, which the consuls had appointed in the usual place; (3) the unjust refusal by the Senate of the triumph they had earned.
