units.la: Præstructæ rationes pro triumpho 1. à more recepto in rep. Rom. ut deletis hostibus victoribus triumphus decernatur. Ratio hujus moris addatur: ut sic præmium illustre reddatur virtuti, quò alii excitarentur ad audendum pro patria in medio hostium sita. Tanto illustriorem hanc victoriam, quod de gente aemula Sabinorum reportata.
units.tr: The arguments prepared in favour of a triumph are: (1) the custom received in the Roman commonwealth that a triumph is granted when the enemy has been defeated and the commanders have won. The reason for this custom should be added: that such a reward may be a distinguished recognition of virtue, by which others may be stirred to dare everything for their country when placed in the midst of enemies. This victory is all the more distinguished because it was won over a people rivalling the Sabines.

units.la: II. A causa invidiae Senatus Contra consules, quia scil plebi faveant. Hisce talibus infestum esse Senatum, plebi semper adversum. At tanto magis nitendum plebi pro suis fautoribus. Ingratorum esse, deesse patronis.
units.tr: II. From the Senate's jealousy of the consuls, because they favour the plebs. The Senate is always hostile to such men and always opposed to the plebs. But for that very reason the plebs must strive all the more for their own champions. It is ungrateful to abandon one's patrons.

units.la: III. A facultate plebis; quae uti pericula obire necesse habet, ita & arbitrium habere debet praemiorum. Maxime cum Consules sint a suis partibus.
units.tr: III. From the power of the plebs: just as they are obliged to face dangers, so they ought also to have the judgment of rewards. Especially since the consuls belong to the other party.

units.la: Conclusio. Proponat rogationem, vid. velint jubeant Quirites, ut utrique Consuli solennis triumphus decernatur, quo ita egregia victoria digno praemio cohonestetur.
units.tr: Conclusio. Let him put the proposal to the vote, that the Quirites may vote and ordain that a solemn triumph be granted to each consul, so that so outstanding a victory may be honoured by a worthy reward.

units.la: II. C. Claudius Senator contra nititur dissuadens rogationem Icilii, quod munus Senatus invadat.
units.tr: II. Gaius Claudius, a senator, struggles against Icilius' proposal, arguing that it usurps the function of the Senate.

units.la: Exord. Ex Loco Communi de periculosa specie virtutis videl. Nihil magis metuendum, quam cum vitia sub specie virtutis surrexerit. Hoc 1. proponatur addita ratione a facili incautorum deceptione. 1. Applicetur ad Icilium, qui observans moris antiqui videri velit, ordinis antiqui eversor.
units.tr: Exord. From the common place concerning the dangerous appearance of virtue: nothing is more to be feared than when vices arise under the appearance of virtue. This is to be set forth first, with the added reason of how easily the unwary are deceived. (1) Apply it to Icilius, who, wishing to seem an observer of ancient custom, is in fact an overturner of the ancient order.

units.la: Propof. Perperam judicium de triumpho pro plebi deferri ab Icilio.
units.tr: Propositio. Icilius has wrongly referred the judgment about the triumph to the plebs.

units.la: Confirm. 1. Declinet suspitionem invidiae: concedere le laudem meritam Consulibus; nec Senatum ipsorum invidere virtuti; quippe qui supplicationem illis decreverit. Rationes habuisse non decreti triumphi, licet illas Icilio complicibusque non revelaverit.
units.tr: Confirmatio. (1) Let him avoid any suspicion of jealousy: let him concede the merited praise to the consuls, and let him deny that the Senate begrudges virtue, since it has decreed them a thanksgiving. He had reasons for not decreeing a triumph, although he did not disclose them to Icilius and his allies.

units.la: II. Rationes afferat contra rogationem Icilii.
units.tr: II. Let him bring forward reasons against Icilius' proposal.

units.la: 1. Quia non populi sed Senatus sit decernere honores, & triumphum obtinuisse hoc etiam tempore regum. Male igitur confundi jura omnium. Populum non posse judicare de meritis, sed duci affectibus, praesentationibus, precio & favore. Amplif. a natura vulgi mutabili.
units.tr: (1) Because it is the office of the Senate, not of the people, to decree honours, and even in the time of the kings a triumph had to be obtained in this way. It is therefore wrong to confound the rights of all. The people cannot judge of merits, but are led by passions, prejudices, bribery and favour. Amplify this from the changeable nature of the crowd.

units.la: 2. Quia non ex gratitudine erga victores, sed a. ex invidia profecta rogatio, ut triumphet tribunus de Senatu & Consulibus.
units.tr: (2) Because the proposal did not arise from gratitude towards the victors, but from (a) jealousy, that the tribune wishes to triumph over the Senate and the consuls.

units.la: b. ex privato beneficio Icilio facto, profectam hanc rogationem Illustretur ex Loco Communi quod pessimum sit, miscere emolumentum privatum cum publico, & detrimento publico adjutum velle suis amicis. Conclus. Increpet Icilium, quod Senatus officium invadat, ordinem ipsum sugillet, & confusionem invehat in omnes ordines. Ordine agenda omnia.
units.tr: (b) This proposal arose from a private favour done to Icilius. Illustrate this from the common place that it is the worst thing to mix private advantage with public, and to wish to help one's friends to the public's loss. Conclusio. Let him rebuke Icilius for usurping the office of the Senate, disparage the order itself, and bring confusion into all orders. Everything must be done in good order.

units.la: III. Alius Senator refutat rationes Icilii Tribuni.
units.tr: III. Another senator refutes the arguments of the tribune Icilius.

units.la: Exord. A simili falsi injusti haeredis, qui largus est in erogando, sciens non de suo se liberalem, sed de alieno. Proponatur in protasi & apotasi; ita & Icilium usurpatorem alienae potestatis munificum in decernendis triumphis, ideoque merito reprehensum à C. Claudio.
units.tr: Exord. From the likeness of a false and unjust heir, who is lavish in spending, knowing that he is generous not with his own but with another's property. Let this be set out in protasis and apodosis: so Icilius, a usurper of another's power, is lavish in decreeing triumphs, and therefore is rightly rebuked by Gaius Claudius.

units.la: Propos. Non opus esse ulteriori refutatione, nisi forte sint, qui in ipsius Icilii rationibus aliquid ponderis inesse putent, quas proinde paucis examinandas existimet.
units.tr: Propositio. There is no need for further refutation, unless there are some who think that any weight lies in Icilius' own arguments, which he thinks should therefore be examined briefly.

units.la: Refutatio. I. Concedat victoriam tanquam notam omnibus; at negat ex invidia decretam supplicationem: imo v. hoc usitatum, & debitum Diis immortalibus & satis honoris esse victoribus; quibus non sine ratione negatur triumphus.
units.tr: Refutatio. (1) Let him concede the victory as known to all; but let him deny that the thanksgiving was decreed out of jealousy. Indeed, this is customary and owed to the immortal gods, and is sufficient honour for the victors, to whom a triumph is refused not without reason.

units.la: II. Examinet rationem. 1. non omni victoriae decerni triumphos, diversa esse praemia judicio Senatus aestimanda. vide de triumphis. 2. negando invidiam Senatus. Esse hanc calumniam tribunitiam, qui semper sugillare solent actiones Senatus, quasi non faveat plebi. Amplif: expositione officii Senatus, scil. ut foveat totam Civitatem. Cic. 1. Offic. 3. aliud esse pugnare, aliud decernere praemia: illud plebis, hoc Senatus esse: uti Collega evicerit.
units.tr: II. Let him examine the argument. (1) Not every victory deserves a triumph; rewards are different and must be judged by the Senate's assessment. See on triumphs. (2) By denying the Senate's jealousy. This is a tribunician calumny; they are accustomed always to disparage the Senate's actions, as if the Senate did not favour the plebs. Amplify by setting out the duty of the Senate, namely to cherish the whole state. Cicero, On Duties, book 1, chapter 3: it is one thing to fight, another to decree rewards; the former belongs to the plebs, the latter to the Senate, as the colleague has won.

units.la: Conclus. Cum igitur nihil soliditatis sit in rationibus Icilii cavendum esse a novitate periculosa, & cuique sua curanda & relinquenda esse.
units.tr: Conclusio. Since therefore there is no solidity in Icilius' arguments, one must beware of the dangerous novelty, and each should look after and leave to others what is their own.

units.la: IV. Tribunus plebis refert de consensu tribunorum omnium in rogationem Icilii pro triumpho Consulum.
units.tr: IV. The tribune of the plebs reports the consent of all the tribunes to Icilius' proposal concerning the triumph of the consuls.

units.la: I. Referat paucis acta. Audivisse populum quae ab Icilio pro triumpho decernendo retulerit; quaeque contra a Senatoribus allata sint: & desuper ivisse in suffragia sine affectibus, amore ac odio, quorum causas procul habere dicant.
units.tr: I. Let him briefly report the proceedings: that the people have heard what Icilius put forward in favour of decreeing a triumph, and what the senators on the other side brought forward in reply; and that they went to the vote on this without emotion, love or hatred, the causes of which, they say, they keep far away.

units.la: II. Judicium ferant.
units.tr: II. Let him pass judgment.

units.la: 2. De examine rationum Icilii per secundum Senatorem: dixisse. xisse quidem ipsum aliquid, non selvisse argumenta Icilii ex consuetudine antiqua & ipsis fundamentis reip. deprompta, quorum proinde 1. & 2. paucis resumat & inculcet. Non facile mutandos veteres mores, aut minuendos favores. Ita urgendam esse authoritatem Senatus, ne populus opprimatur.
units.tr: 2. On the examination of Icilius' arguments by the second senator: he said something, indeed, but did not refute Icilius' arguments, which were drawn from ancient custom and from the very foundations of the commonwealth. Therefore he should briefly resume and press points 1 and 2. Ancient customs are not to be changed easily, nor favours diminished. Thus the authority of the Senate must be pressed, lest the people be oppressed.

units.la: 1. De rationibus primi Senatoris, respondendo ad a. non adimi Senatui jus, quando populus utitur suo jure. Sinistrè judicare ipsum de populo, quasi affectibus, prece, precio non judicio agere sciat. Etiam in populo viros cerdatos esse. respond. ad b. cavendam suspicionem invidiæ aut privati commodi. In causa publica, cavendos privatos affectus esse, &c.
units.tr: 1. On the arguments of the first senator, answering (a) that the right of the Senate is not taken away when the people use their own right; that he judges wrongly about the people, as if they acted from passion, entreaty or price rather than from judgment; and that there are also wise men among the people. Answering (b) that the suspicion of envy or private advantage must be guarded against: in a public cause, private affections must be set aside, and so on.

units.la: 2. Vide supra.
units.tr: 2. See above.

units.la: III. Decretum tribunum proferat, videl. accipere rogationem Icilii universas tribus, & placere ut solennis triumphus decernatur Consulibus victoribus, ne virtus defectu præmii languescat.
units.tr: III. Let the tribune propose the decree: namely, that Icilius' proposal is accepted by all the tribes, and that it is agreed a solemn triumph be decreed for the victorious consuls, so that virtue does not languish for lack of reward.

units.la: DISPOSITIONES ORATORIÆ GENERIS JUDICIALIS.
units.tr: Oratorical Dispositions of the Judicial Genus

units.la: THEMA I. REVISIO JUDICII, QUO INNOCENS SERVATOR FALSO ACCUSATUS ET INIQUE DAMNATUS FUIT.
units.tr: THEME I. A REVIEW OF THE TRIAL IN WHICH THE INNOCENT SAVIOUR WAS FALSELY ACCUSED AND UNJUSTLY CONDEMNED.

units.la: I. Examen falsæ criminationis in judicio Ecclesiastico.
units.tr: I. An examination of the false accusation in the ecclesiastical trial.

units.la: Exord. Patheticum à rei indignitate; quod veritas accusata à mendacio, justitia ab iniquitate, à servo Dominus, ab homine Deus. Quis non stuperet, quis non contradiceret? Exagger. exemplo minori, quo Josephus accusatus insons: item quo Susanna accusata à senioribus at vindicata à juvene Daniele. Applicetur ad hypoth. multò minus hic tacendum, ne calumnia de Christo triumphet.
units.tr: Exord. A pathetic appeal from the unworthiness of the deed: truth is accused by a lie, justice by iniquity, the Lord by a servant, God by a man. Who would not be astonished? Who would not protest? Amplify by a lesser example, as when Joseph, innocent, was accused, and when Susanna was accused by the elders but vindicated by the youth Daniel. Apply this to the hypothesis: it must all the less be kept silent here, lest calumny triumph over Christ.

units.la: Propos.Te igitur falsas judæorû criminationes sub examen vocaturû ut Christi innocentia & atrorum judæorum calumnia patescat.
units.tr: Propos. You will therefore submit the false accusations of the Jews to examination, so that the innocence of Christ and the calumny of the savage Jews may be laid open.

units.la: Examen ipsum criminationis; ubi A. antegressa criminationis.
units.tr: The examination of the accusation itself; here the preceding accusation is recalled.

units.la: I. Breviter exponat, quoniam in horto proditorie captus & ligatus, desertus a suis, tractus ad palatium Caiphæ noctu & examini subjectus. Arguat præposterum modum, quod clanculum noctu agunt illa, quæ meridianam lucem desiderabant. Scil. malos odisse lucem, in operibus tenebrarum.
units.tr: I. Briefly set out how, having been betrayed in the garden, he was seized and bound, deserted by his own, dragged by night to the palace of Caiaphas and subjected to examination. Denounce the perverse order: they act secretly at night, these men who desired the light of midday. That is, the evil hate the light, which is found in the works of darkness.

units.la: II. Interrogat de persona, doctrina. Admiretur summi sacerdotis ignorantiam, qui rogat de Messia, quem ex prophetis novisse doctrina ejus, qui publice docuerat. Itane functus es officio? Itane ignota doctrina ejus, qui tuos tuorumque errores publice reprehenderat. Recenseantur præcipua aliquot capita doctrinæ Christi. Hæc novisse decuit summum sacerd.
units.tr: II. He asks about the person and his teaching. Marvel at the ignorance of the high priest, who asks about the Messiah, whom the teaching of one who had taught publicly ought to have made known from the prophets. Have you so discharged your office? Is his teaching so unknown, of him who had publicly rebuked your errors and those of your people? Recount some of the chief heads of Christ's doctrine. The high priest ought to have known these things.

units.la: III. Falsos testes subornat: qui tales à limine removere; & etiam fonti patronum dare ex officio debuisset.
units.tr: III. He suborns false witnesses, whom he ought, by his office, to have removed from the threshold; and he ought also to have given the accused a defender.

units.la: B. Ipsa criminati accusatio: hic primo in genere ex antegressis iniquitatem colligas; adde causam scilicet potestas hæc tenebrarum, luci veritatis prævalentium; invectiva in calumniam.
units.tr: B. The accusation itself. Here, first, in general, from what has gone before, infer the iniquity: add that this power is of darkness, prevailing against the light of truth. An invective against the calumny.

units.la: In specie vero conficta crimina examinentur singula: vid.
units.tr: But in particular, let the invented charges be examined one by one, namely:

units.la: 1. Quod docuerit contraria Mosi & templo. Defendatur negando; sed quod finem venisse ceremoniarum & politiæ jud. docuerit; futurum fuisse à fine legis cerimonialis, qui sit manuductio ad Christum.
units.tr: 1. That he taught things contrary to Moses and the temple. Let it be defended by denial; but that he taught that the ceremonies and the Jewish polity had come to an end, and that the ceremonial law would cease at its purpose, which is to lead to Christ.

units.la: 2. Quod blasphemus fuerit, dicens se filium Dei. Resp. per invectivam in cæcitatem judæorum; qui propriam salutem ignoraverint: Coarguat in cæcitatem judæorum; Coarguat illos ex dicto uno atque altero V. T. de divinitate Christi. Scil. in quo salus vestra, illud in materiam condemnationis Messiæ vertitis, & laceres vestimentum Caiphe: at laceratum noris pontificatum tuum, dum verum pontificem abnegas &c.
units.tr: 2. That he was a blasphemer, in saying that he was the Son of God. Reply by an invective against the blindness of the Jews, who did not know their own salvation. Let him rebuke their blindness, convicting them from one or another saying of the Old Testament concerning the divinity of Christ: "In whom is your salvation" (cf. Isa. 28) you turn into matter for condemning the Messiah, and you tear your garments, Caiaphas. Yet you should know your priesthood is torn, while you deny the true high priest, etc.

units.la: 3. Quod seditiosus sit & turbarit plebem; Regem se dicendo. Refell. 1. à natura Euangelii, quod nuncium pacis, cujus proinde summa capita de remissione peccatorum & condonatione ac charitate, mutua, patientia, manuetudine, abnegatione sui & mundi breviter inculcentur. 2. Ab officio & professione ChriChristi, quem cœli regem esse, ex prophetis novisse debuissent, & regnum mundanum recusare norant, qui cæsari sua danda dixerat. Fiat invectiva in calumniam in genere & in specie Pharisæorum.
units.tr: 3. That he was seditious and stirred up the people by calling himself King. Refute it: (a) from the nature of the Gospel, which is a message of peace, whose chief heads, concerning the forgiveness of sins and pardon, and mutual charity, patience, meekness, self-denial and renunciation of the world, are to be briefly impressed. (b) From the office and profession of Christ, whom they ought to have known from the prophets to be King of heaven; and they knew how to refuse a worldly kingdom, since he had said that what is Caesar's is to be given to Caesar. Let there be an invective against the calumny, in general and in the particular case of the Pharisees.

units.la: 4. Quod præpostera criminatione gravatum, sputo, sannis & colaphis exceperint. Exaggeretur facti atrocitas 1. ex loco judicii ubi tutus esse debuit; fiat invectiva in impurum os, & parricidalem dexteram. 2. Ex personis: scil. læsa auctoritas sacerdotis videbatur veritate: at verum sacerdotem calumnia lædi quis cogitat?
units.tr: 4. That, weighed down by a preposterous accusation, they received him with spitting, mockery and blows. Let the atrocity of the deed be amplified: (a) from the place of judgment, where he ought to have been safe; let there be an invective against the impure mouth and the parricidal right hand. (b) From the persons: the authority of the priest seemed to be injured by the truth; but who thinks that the true priest is injured by calumny?

units.la: 5. Quod quasi convictum Pilato tanquam executori tradiderint, ipso etiam juda proditore, attestante de Christi innocentia. Improbetur hypocrysis. scil. frustra in Pilatum, in Judam sanguinis innocentis reatum devolvere satagis, Pharisæe, qui tua instigatione inducti, de Christi innocentia ad extremum testati sunt.
units.tr: 5. That, as if he were convicted, they handed him over to Pilate as to an executioner, Judas the betrayer himself also bearing witness to Christ's innocence. Let the hypocrisy be condemned. You Pharisees, in vain do you labour to roll the guilt of innocent blood upon Pilate and upon Judas, when, moved by your own instigation, they at last testified to Christ's innocence.

units.la: Conclus. 1. Devolvat sanguinem Christi in Judæos à Christo exterminandos, qui ipsum Servatorem rejecerunt. 2. Fructum innocentiæ Christi afferat fidelibus. ex Esa.53.
units.tr: Conclus. 1. Let him roll the blood of Christ upon the Jews, who are to be cut off by Christ, since they rejected the Saviour himself. 2. Let him bring the fruit of Christ's innocence to the faithful, from Isaiah 53.

units.la: II. Examen iniquæ Christi condemnationis coram judicio politico.
units.tr: II. An examination of the unjust condemnation of Christ before the civil court.

units.la: Exord. Pathetice attestetur solem & mundum universum, ad testandum de rei indignitate; quum mendacio veritas, vita morti succubuit, à creatura damnatus creator. Recenseat hic illa miracula, quæ in morte Christi contigere.
units.tr: Exord. Let him call upon the sun and the whole world as witnesses, pathetically, to bear witness to the unworthiness of the deed: since truth has yielded to a lie and life to death, the Creator has been condemned by his creature. Let him here recount those miracles which occurred at the death of Christ.

units.la: Propos. Causas tanti creaturæ stuporis te expositurum in insontis Christi condemnatione.
units.tr: Propos. You will set forth the causes of so great an astonishment of creation in the condemnation of the innocent Christ.

units.la: Tractatio habeat examen illorum, quæ in condemnatione occurrunt.
units.tr: Tractatio. Let it contain an examination of the things that occur in the condemnation.

units.la: Hic I. Per apostrophen evocet Pilatum, ut rationem reddat judicii. Hinc inculcet ipsi officium judicis, quod Dei vices gerant ad pœnam nocentium, patrocinium insontium. At quomodo hoc fecisti. &c.
units.tr: Here, I. by apostrophe let him summon Pilate to render an account of the judgment. Hence let him impress upon him the office of a judge: that judges act in God's place, to punish the guilty and to protect the innocent. But how have you done this, etc.?

units.la: II. Proponat Christi innocentiam ex omnibus circumstantiis & ipsius Judæ, & Herodis confessione; uxoris commonefactione, & ipsa Herodis conscientia & sententia: ad quam provocetur.
units.tr: II. Let him set forth the innocence of Christ from all the circumstances, and from the confession of Judas himself and of Herod; from the admonition of his wife, and from Herod's own conscience and judgment, to which appeal is to be made.

units.la: III. Opponat iniquam damnationem contra conscientiam propriam priam. Frustra aquâ abluis manus, contaminato corde, aquâ crimen haud purgatur. Remittat ipsum ad Judam sui ipsius carnificem: sistat ipsum futuro judicio coram tremendo judice, quem ipse insontem damnavit. Qui Cæsarem, qui Pharisæos, qui plebem metuit offendere: quod Deo respondebit, cujus judicium neglexit. &c.
units.tr: III. Let him set against the iniquitous condemnation Pilate's own conscience. In vain do you wash your hands with water; with a defiled heart, guilt is not purged by water. Let him send him back to Judas, his own executioner; let him bring him before the coming judgment, before the dreadful Judge whom he himself condemned as innocent. He who feared to offend Caesar, the Pharisees and the people: what will he answer to God, whose judgment he neglected? etc.

units.la: IV. Exagitet Pilati perplexitatem, qua dum semel ab officio & distamine justitiæ deflexisset, ulterius aberrat. Cur flagellas, quem innocentem noveras? cur tradis ludibrio militum, quem morti adjudicaveras; quem commiseratione, non exagitatione dignum noveras. Cur corona spinea lancinas caput, quod insons pronunciaverat, cur latronibus æquiparas, quem sanctum noveras. Cur morti, cur cruci tradis, quem nihil vita dignum commisisse fassus eras. Hic sistas ipsum divino judicio pavidum, & desperabundum, cum adhortatione ad judices ad justitiam.
units.tr: IV. Let him lay bare Pilate's perplexity, by which, once he had turned aside from the duty and rule of justice, he wandered further. Why did you scourge him whom you knew to be innocent? Why did you hand over to the mockery of soldiers him whom you had adjudged to death, whom you knew to deserve pity rather than harassment? Why do you pierce his head with a crown of thorns, him whom you had pronounced innocent? Why do you put on a level with robbers him whom you knew to be holy? Why do you hand him over to death, to the cross, whom you confessed had committed nothing worthy of life? Here set him before the divine judgment, trembling and in despair, with an exhortation to judges to justice.

units.la: Conclus. Erigat se ad judicium & decretum Dei, qui insontem damnari voluit Christum, ut nos à noxa redimeret. Ipse seditionis, majestatis damnatus, ut nos rebelles & violatores divinæ majestatis absolveremur. Flagellari, coronari, crucifigi, mori voluit, ut nos à flagellis iræ divinæ & tortura conscientiæ & crucis infamia & morte æterna liberaremur, coronari spinis voluit, ut de expugnato inferno, servatis civibus & merito triumpho certi, coronam gloriæ reportaremur:
units.tr: Conclus. Let him raise himself to the judgment and decree of God, who willed that Christ, the innocent, should be condemned, so that he might redeem us from guilt. He, condemned for sedition and treason, that we, rebels and violators of the divine majesty, might be absolved. He willed to be scourged, crowned, crucified and to die, that we might be freed from the scourges of divine wrath, from the torture of conscience, from the infamy of the cross and from eternal death. He willed to be crowned with thorns, so that, the hell being overcome and our fellow citizens saved, we might carry off with certainty the crown of glory and the merited triumph.

units.la: THEMA II. FISCALIS CONJURATIONIS CONTRA REGEM ALEXANDRUM ACCUSAT CORAM EXERCITU PHILOTAM.
units.tr: THEME II. A FISCAL ACCUSATION OF CONSPIRACY AGAINST KING ALEXANDER, BROUGHT BEFORE THE ARMY AGAINST PHILOTAS.

units.la: Ex Curt. lib.6.
units.tr: From Curtius, book 6.

units.la: Exord. Amorem conciliet ex persona regis, & odium ex persona Philotæ. vid. eò tandem rem rediisse, ut à suis vix tutus sit, cui hostium vis nocere non potuit &c: scil. insidias à Philota regi strui: quem tot beneficiis affecerit. Exponat facilitatem suam ad condonandum, nisi in suo capite totus exercitus periclitaretur & fructus tot victoriarum periret.
units.tr: Exordium. He should win affection by the person of the king and win hatred by the person of Philotas. He should show how the matter has come to this, that one who could not be harmed by the force of enemies is scarcely safe from his own men, namely that Philotas is laying plots against the king, whom he has loaded with so many benefits. He should set out the king's readiness to pardon, unless the whole army were endangered in his person and the fruit of so many victories were lost.

units.la: Propos. Hinc regem causam hanc ducibus & militibus exposituram, ut ipsi judicent; ne majestate oppressus videatur reus.
units.tr: Proposition. Hence the king will lay this cause before the commanders and soldiers, that they may judge it, lest he seem to be the accused, overborne by his majesty.

units.la: Tractatio. Colligat factum,
units.tr: Treatment. He should gather the facts,

units.la: I. Ex conjecturis.
units.tr: I. From conjectures.

units.la: 1. Voluntatis: videl. odio ac invidia adversus regem: quae pateant ex literis ad regem, quibus misereatur fortem illorum, qui subditi sint illi, qui se ipsum ignoret & Jovis filium se credat. Scil. Apollinis oraculum regi imputari ad invidiam, noxium maxime affectum.
units.tr: 1. Of will: namely hatred and envy against the king, which are evident from the letters to the king, in which he pities the lot of those who are subjects of a man who does not know himself and believes himself a son of Jove. Namely, the oracle of Apollo is imputed to the king as a cause of envy, a most harmful disposition.

units.la: a. Superbia hominis & ambitio: qui pessimi consiliarii sint. Auctam illam orbitate regis, inde spem regni concepe-rit facile. b. Exaggeret haec a bonitate regis, qui haec dissimularit, lenitate emendum sperans. Frustra praevalentibus affectibus in Philota. c. a spe successionis, cum ipse maxime potens fuerit.
units.tr: a. The pride and ambition of the man, who are the worst counsellors. He could easily conceive hope of the kingdom, which was increased by the king's childlessness. b. He should amplify this by the kindness of the king, who had overlooked these things, hoping to cure them by gentleness, but in vain, since the passions prevailed in Philotas. c. From hope of succession, since he himself was most powerful.

units.la: 2. Facultatis: quam probet. a. a favore militum. b. ab officio, quia equitatui praefectus: c. ab autoritate & potentia Patris Parmenionis, Mediae potentissimae praefecti. Moveat ποῦ ἀ conditione regum, qui saepe ad suum exitium honoribus & potentia augent amicos: qui deinceps propriae conditionis obliti in benefactorem saeviunt. Ipsos testes veluti faciat Parmenionem & Philotam, beneficia exaggerans.
units.tr: 2. Of ability, which he proves: a. from the favour of the soldiers; b. from his office, since he was prefect of the cavalry; c. from the authority and power of his father Parmenion, prefect of Media, a most powerful man. He should appeal to the condition of kings, who often, to their own destruction, advance friends with honours and power, and who afterwards, forgetting their own condition, rage against their benefactor. He should, as it were, make Parmenion and Philotas themselves witnesses, amplifying the benefits.

units.la: 3. Ex signis, videl. aversione animi a rege, & amicitia cum inimicis regis Amyta, Attalo. vid. Curt. Dissimulasse haec regem quidem hactenus; at cum alia testimonia accedant, non debere ipsum prodigum esse salutis suae. Hinc probet
units.tr: 3. From signs, namely the aversion of mind from the king, and friendship with the king's enemies Amyntas and Attalus. See Curtius. The king has indeed overlooked these things until now; but since other testimonies are added, he should not be prodigal of his own safety. Hence he should prove

units.la: II. Ex testimoniis. Ceballini, qui indicavit conjurationem; aliorumque complicum, Demetrii, Peucolai, & Dymni, qui conscientia criminis mortem sibi intulerint.
units.tr: II. From testimonies: of Ceballinus, who revealed the conspiracy, and of the other accomplices, Demetrius, Peucolaus, and Dymnus, who, conscious of the crime, brought death upon themselves.

units.la: III. Ex proprio facto Philotae, qui detectam ipsi conjurationem reticuit, quod capitale in crimine majestatis. Exaggeretur ab officio Philotae, qui in re gravissima nihil tutum existimare debuisset, nisi suspectum & participem se reddere voluisset.
units.tr: III. From Philotas' own act, since he kept silent about the conspiracy when it was disclosed to him, which is a capital crime of majesty. It should be amplified from Philotas' office: in so grave a matter he ought to have considered nothing safe, unless he wished to make himself suspect and a participant.

units.la: Conclus. Repetitis summatim rationibus, judicium ducibus & exercitui permittat, addito affectu a persona regis, qui vitae ac securitatis suae arbitrium militi committat, quem virtute non scelere delectari norit.
units.tr: Conclusion. Having briefly repeated the arguments, he should leave the judgement to the commanders and the army, adding an appeal from the person of the king, who should entrust the decision on his life and safety to a soldier whom he knows to delight in virtue, not crime.

units.la: Responsio Philotae.
units.tr: Reply of Philotas.

units.la: Exord. A difficultate hujus defensionis, tum quod contra regem; tum quod desertus ab omnibus; tum quod ad exercitum, praejudicio occupatum sibi dicendum. Spem tamen concipiat ex fiducia causae.
units.tr: Exordium. He should speak of the difficulty of this defence: both because it is against the king, and because he is deserted by all, and because he must speak to an army already occupied by prejudice. Yet he should take hope from the confidence of his cause.

units.la: Propos. Quam speret se cunctis approbaturum & a conjurationis suspicione se purgaturum.
units.tr: Proposition. That he hopes to win over everyone and to clear himself of the suspicion of conspiracy.

units.la: Refutatio argumentorum.
units.tr: Refutation of the arguments.

units.la: I. Ex proprio facto. Resp. 1. Rem non fuisse satis sibi cognitam, nec creditam sibi. 2. Regem non fuisse proclivem ad admittendas suspiciones, ostendat exemplo Parmenionis qui a medici veneno dehortatus frustra fuerat. 3. Regem si quid culpae hic jamdum condonasse, porrecta dextera. Forte ab invidis concitatum rursus regem.
units.tr: I. From his own act. Reply: 1. The matter was not sufficiently known to him, nor was it entrusted to him. 2. The king was not prone to admitting suspicions; let him show this by the example of Parmenion, who had in vain dissuaded the king from the physician's poison. 3. The king, if he had long since pardoned any fault in this matter, has extended his right hand; perhaps he was roused again against him by envious men.

units.la: II. Ex testimonio. Resp. 1. plurimos conjuratorum se non nominasse; non omissuros in tormentis, cum vel hinc spem concipere potuissent. 2. Ceballini solius testimonium haud sufficere, nec aliud testatum fuisse, quam ipsi indicatam fuisse. 3. Reos esse, illos, qui mortem sibi conscivere, quid ultra quaerant.
units.tr: II. From testimony. Reply: 1. Most of the conspirators he did not name, and they would not have failed to do so under torture, since from this they could have conceived hope. 2. The testimony of Ceballinus alone is not sufficient, nor was anything else attested than that the plot had been revealed to him by Ceballinus. 3. Those accused are the men who consciously brought death upon themselves; why do they seek anything further?

units.la: III. Ad argumentum. Resp. 1. removendo a se suspicionem superbiae & spe successionis alios se majores novisse. 2. Odii suspicionem tollat, quia literas scripsisset ad regem monendum. Loc' Communis de periculosa veritate in aula. 3. Facultatem se omnem habere & patrem a rege, & ipsius servitia. Malle se exui omnibus honoribus. 4. Amicitiam coluisse cum Amynta, tanquam amico regis, non constare sibi de regis aut Amyntae animo oculto. Si reus Amyntas, sibi non posse imputari.
units.tr: III. To the argument. Reply: 1. By removing from himself the suspicion of pride and of hope of succession, showing that he knew others to be greater. 2. Let him remove the suspicion of hatred, because he had written letters to the king to warn him; a common place on the dangerous truth at court. 3. He has every ability, both from his father and from the king, and from his own services. He would rather be stripped of all honours. 4. He cultivated friendship with Amyntas as a friend of the king; it is not clear to him what the secret intention of the king or of Amyntas was. If Amyntas is accused, this cannot be imputed to him.

units.la: Confirm. Argumenta innocentiae.
units.tr: Confirmation. Arguments of innocence.

units.la: I. Ab ipsius patrisque fidelibus servitiis hactenus praestitis, scilicet jam felicitatem suam suspectam esse, per quos rex felix.
units.tr: I. From the faithful services hitherto rendered by himself and his father; namely, that now his own good fortune is suspected, through whom the king is prosperous.

units.la: II. A contestatione supremi Numinis, cujus filius rex, quod conscium sit, quo animo servierit regi.
units.tr: II. From the calling of the supreme Deity to witness, whose son the king is, that he is conscious of the spirit in which he has served the king.

units.la: Concluf. Revocet se fidens bonae causae, quam ponderare petat exercitum: addito; se paratum mori pro rege, dummodo sine suspicione culpae hoc fieri possit.
units.tr: Conclusion. Trusting in his good cause, he calls the army to weigh it, adding that he is ready to die for the king, provided this can be done without suspicion of guilt.

units.la: THEMA III. CICERO ACCUSAT ANTONIUM CONSULEM MAJESTATIS.
units.tr: THEME III. CICERO ACCUSES ANTONY THE CONSUL OF TREASON (MAJESTAS).

units.la: Ex Orat. Philipp. præcipuè 2.3.4.5.6. & Dion. Cass. Lib.45 ad Senat. populumque Rom.
units.tr: From the Philippics, chiefly 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, and from Dio Cassius, book 45, to the Senate and the Roman people.

units.la: Exord. Gratuletur reip. quod ex turbis per Cæsarem & Pompejum concitatis emerse-t; & imminens nuper ex morte Cæsaris tempestas per amnem̄am sedata sit: quam proinde laudet tanquam saluberrimum in tali casu remedium.
units.tr: Exordium. He should congratulate the commonwealth that it has emerged from the disturbances stirred up by Caesar and Pompey, and that the storm which recently threatened after Caesar's death has been calmed by the amnesty. He should praise this as the most wholesome remedy in such a case.

units.la: Narrat. Exponat contrarias machinationes Antonii, qui contra decretum senatus vindicare velit necem Cæsaris: unde metuendæ novæ turbæ; maxime cum monitus à senatu non desistat.
units.tr: Narration. He should set out Antony's contrary schemes, since Antony wishes, against the decree of the Senate, to avenge the killing of Caesar. Hence come fears of new disturbances, especially since Antony, though warned by the Senate, does not desist.

units.la: Propos. Esse hoc contra remp. adeoque crimen majestatis.
units.tr: Proposition. That this is against the commonwealth and therefore a crime of treason.

units.la: Confirm. I. Quia contra decretum senatus suscepta hæc vindicta. Hic urgeat autoritatem senatus & senatus consultorum: quæ sine perturbatione reip. infringi nequeant à nemine; nedum à Consule, cujus officium proinde exponat in tuendis decretis non evertendis. Vid. Phil. 4 init. Exaggeret hic severitatem majorum in mature deliberando & severe exsequendo.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. Because this vengeance was undertaken against a decree of the Senate. Here he should press the authority of the Senate and of its decrees, which no one can infringe without disturbing the commonwealth, much less a consul, whose duty he should therefore set out as being to uphold decrees, not to overturn them. See Philippic 4, at the beginning. Here he should amplify the severity of our ancestors in deliberating maturely and enforcing decisions sternly.

units.la: II. Quia hostis sit omnium bonorum virorum dictis & factis infensus & crudelis. vid. Phil.;.
units.tr: II. Because Antony is hostile and cruel towards all good men, in words and deeds. See the Philippics.

units.la: III. Quia noxia foveat consilia, de stabilienda hac ratione sua potentia, opprimendis viris bonis & invadenda rep. quod probet ex ipsius largitionibus, legibus &c. vid. Phil.4.
units.tr: III. Because he fosters harmful plans to establish his power on this footing, to crush good men and to invade the commonwealth. He should prove this from Antony's own largesses, laws and so on. See Philippic 4.

units.la: IV. Quia arma sumserit contra remp: Quod ipsum crimen majestatis dicat, comparetque cum Tarquinio tanquam minus minaci.
units.tr: IV. Because he has taken up arms against the commonwealth. Cicero calls this itself the crime of treason, and compares Antony with Tarquin, as one less dangerous.

units.la: Conclus. Declarandum proinde reum majestatis & hostem reip. & opponenda arma, sine ulteriori tergiversatione.
units.tr: Conclusion. Therefore the accused should be declared guilty of treason and an enemy of the commonwealth, and arms should be opposed to him without further delay.

units.la: Antonius defendit se.
units.tr: Antony defends himself.

units.la: Exord. Pathos movet ab ingratitudine Ciceronis, qui spretis omnibus benefactis suis, majestatis ipsum accusat. Hinc enarret beneficta, vid. quod cesserit ipsi in petitione auguratus, quod pepercerit ipsius vitæ Brundusii: Et summam contra Cic. exaggeret ingragratitudinem & atrocem accusationem ob benefactum. vid. 2. Philip.
units.tr: Exordium. He should move pathos by Cicero's ingratitude, who, having disregarded all Antony's services, accuses him of treason. Hence he should recount the benefits: that Cicero yielded to him in the canvass for the augurship, and that he spared Cicero's life at Brundisium. He should magnify Cicero's great ingratitude and the atrocious accusation made in return for a kindness. See the Second Philippic.

units.la: Propof. Recte urgeri vindictam Caesaris, herois incomparabilis.
units.tr: Proposition. That the vengeance for Caesar, an incomparable hero, was rightly pursued.

units.la: Confirm. I. A persona & dignitate Caesaris. Quia civis Romanus, Consul, dictator, Princeps fuerit a Senatu populoque confirmatus: qualis sine crimine parricidii ac majestatis interfici nequeat. Urgeat hic jura civium Rom. legem de licariis ex Orat. Milon. & leg. Majestatis: & mansuetudinem Caesaris post victoriam. Vid. Orat. pro Marcell.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From the person and dignity of Caesar: he was a Roman citizen, consul, dictator and prince, confirmed by the Senate and people, and such a man cannot be killed without the crime of parricide and treason. Here he should press the rights of Roman citizens, the law concerning assassins from the Pro Milone, and the law of majesty, and Caesar's clemency after victory. See the Pro Marcello.

units.la: II. A persona interfectorum: qui 1. privati fuere. 2. conjurati. 3. conscientia criminis profugi: proindeque merito plectendi, ne remp. armis tentent.
units.tr: II. From the persons of those who were killed: (1) they were private men; (2) they were conspirators; (3) they were fugitives conscious of their crime, and therefore deservedly to be punished, lest they attempt the commonwealth with arms.

units.la: III. A circumstantia loci & modo agendi: quod 1. in curia, loco sancto & inviolabili. 2. in praesentia senatus, custodis libertatis ac reip. 3. quod non auditum, nedum convictum. 4. quod 23. vulneribus trucidarint.
units.tr: III. From the circumstances of place and manner of action: (1) they acted in the curia, a holy and inviolable place; (2) in the presence of the Senate, the guardian of liberty and of the commonwealth; (3) without being heard, much less convicted; (4) they butchered him with twenty-three wounds.

units.la: Et haec impunita sint? Quid non tentabunt alii? quis securus tandem?
units.tr: And are these deeds to go unpunished? What will others not attempt? Who will be safe at last?

units.la: IV. A persona sua: quod Consul sit, cui reip. salus & tranquillitas commissa. Majestatis reum, qui illi pro rep. agenti se opposuerit. Hinc insimulet Ciceronem conspirationis cum Pompejo antea, & jam cum Cassio & Bruto Caesaris interfectoribus.
units.tr: IV. From Antony's own person: he is consul, to whom the safety and tranquillity of the commonwealth have been entrusted. Cicero, who opposed him while he was acting for the commonwealth, is guilty of treason. Hence he should accuse Cicero of having conspired earlier with Pompey, and now with Cassius and Brutus, the murderers of Caesar.

units.la: Confutatio examinet rationes Ciceronis.
units.tr: Refutation. He should examine Cicero's arguments.

units.la: Primam. 1. concedendo autoritatem Senatus & officium Consulis. 2. explicando mentem Senatus in decernenda amnestia; scil. ad sedandum populum, pro tempore, non ad absolvendos parricidas factum esse; Quia interfit reip. ne crimina maneant impunita. &c.
units.tr: Against the first: (1) by conceding the authority of the Senate and the duty of the consul; (2) by explaining the intention of the Senate in decreeing the amnesty, namely that it was done to calm the people for the time being, not to absolve the parricides, because it is in the interest of the commonwealth that crimes should not remain unpunished, and so on.

units.la: Secundam negando & opponendo officium suum consulare. Esse crimen majestatis & seditionis Consulem dicere hostem sine legitima convictione
units.tr: Against the second, by denying it and setting his own consular duty against it. To call the consul an enemy without lawful conviction is treason and sedition.

units.la: Tertiam. Itidem negando. Hinc justificet suorum actiones, tanquam reip. saluti semper intentas. Contra arguat Cic. tanquam patronem parricidarum.
units.tr: Against the third, likewise by denial. Hence he should justify the actions of his own men as always aimed at the safety of the commonwealth. On the contrary, he should argue that Cicero is acting as patron of parricides.

units.la: Quartam, arma sumta 1. pro reipubl. salute. 2. contra conjuratos, qui jus civium perdidere; adeoque 3. ad sui defensionem & vindictam turbonum ac facinorosorum. Conclus. 1. Repetitis rationibus insontem se asserat. 2. Ex lege talionis reum majestatis & parricidarum patronum esse Ciceronem, & ut talem merito plectendum.
units.tr: The fourth: arms were taken (1) for the safety of the commonwealth; (2) against the conspirators, who forfeited the rights of citizens; and so (3) for the defence and vengeance of himself against riotous and wicked men. Conclusion: (1) by repeating his arguments he asserts his own innocence; (2) by the law of retaliation, Cicero is the guilty party of treason and patron of parricides, and as such is deservedly to be punished.

units.la: THEMA IV. ACCUSATIO HORATII DE OCCISA SORORE.
units.tr: THEME IV. THE ACCUSATION OF HORATIUS CONCERNING THE SISTER SLAIN.

units.la: Ex Flor. lib.1. c.3. Liv. lib.1.
units.tr: From Florus, book 1, chapter 3; Livy, book 1.

units.la: A. Exord. Excusat praesentem accusationem proleptica comparatione virtutis & commissi sceleris Horatii: cujus enormitas tanta sit, ut eximiam viri virtutem obfuscet; interesse vero reip. ne fortiter gesta licentiam praebeant vitiis.
units.tr: A. Exordium. He excuses the present accusation by a prolepsis, comparing the virtue of Horatius with the crime he committed: the enormity of the crime is so great that it obscures the outstanding virtue of the man; yet it is in the interest of the commonwealth that brave deeds should not furnish license for vices.

units.la: B. Propof. Hac propter se eundem illum, quem modo victorem admirati sint, victum a scelere, parricidii postulaturum.
units.tr: B. Proposition. For this reason he will demand that the same man, whom they have just admired as victor, be prosecuted for parricide, now that he is vanquished by his crime.

units.la: C. Narrat. Facti speciem breviter exponat, & propositionem repetat.
units.tr: C. Narration. He briefly sets out the appearance of the deed and repeats the proposition.

units.la: D. Confirmatio.
units.tr: D. Confirmation.

units.la: I. Facti rationem doceat, & quidem
units.tr: I. He should show the reason for the deed, and indeed:

units.la: 1. Ex conditione personae reae, quae privata, & ex causa impulsiva, vid. non forte fortuna, sed destinato & ira concitato animo, adeoque dolo facinus hoc commissum. Probetur porro
units.tr: 1. From the condition of the accused person, who is a private citizen, and from the impelling cause: namely, that this deed was committed not by chance, but with a purpose and with a mind stirred by anger, and so by deliberate malice. Let it further be proved

units.la: 2. Ex objecto: quia sororem innoxiam, plorantem tantum casum sponsi, quod humanitatis est, quamque consolari debuerat, obtruncarit.
units.tr: 2. From the object: because he struck down his innocent sister, who was only weeping over the misfortune of her betrothed, which is a natural human feeling, and whom he ought rather to have comforted.

units.la: 3. Ab eventu, foedatam hinc victoriam, & turbatam luctu laetitiam publicam.
units.tr: 3. From the outcome: the public victory was thereby disgraced, and the public joy disturbed by mourning.

units.la: II. Testimonia afferat.
units.tr: II. He should bring forward testimonies.

units.la: 1. A lege tum naturae, quae abominatur tam tetrum facinus, tum positiva, quae capite plecti velit homicidas, multo magis parricidas, contra quam nulla valere queat dispensatio.
units.tr: 1. From the law, both of nature, which abhors so foul a crime, and of positive law, which wishes murderers, and much more parricides, to be punished by death; against which no dispensation can prevail.

units.la: 2. Consuetudine omnium gentium, ipsorumque Romanorum, qui parricidium puniverint.
units.tr: 2. From the custom of all nations, and of the Romans themselves, who punished parricide.

units.la: E. Refutatio. Non posse hic allegari meritum recens: quippe quod facinus admissum non excusat, sed potius infamet: quod ille, qui hostem vicerit, animum vincere non potuerit. Digress. in Locum Communem de vera fortitudine, quae in animo obfirmando adversus vitia, non in robore corporis ac ferocia consistat. Conclusf. Poscat ipsum ad supplicium capitis, animetque judices ad justitiam inflexam, ut non justitiæ unius, quam fortitudinis gloria splendeat resp. Romana.
units.tr: E. Refutation. It cannot be alleged here that his recent merit counts for anything: for a deed once committed is not excused by it but rather branded with infamy; he who has conquered an enemy has not been able to conquer his own temper. Digression on the common theme of true courage, which consists in fortifying the mind against vices, not in bodily strength and ferocity. Conclusion. Let him demand that the man be put to death, and let him urge the judges to inflexible justice, so that the glory of the Roman commonwealth may shine not in the glory of justice alone, nor of courage alone.

units.la: Defensio Horatii in persona ipsius Horat. in Statu qual. absoluto & assumpto.
units.tr: Defence of Horatius, in the person of Horatius himself, in the absolute and assumed status.

units.la: A. Exord. Ab affectu indignationis: videlicet. Pro patria se pugnasse & triumphasse, ut ab eadem tanquam piaculum mactetur. Amplificetur apostrophe ad Fratres defunctos, quos felicius ab hoste occisos dicat, quam se servatum, scilicet ut manu carnificis pereat. Addatur revocatio sui, scilicet: Sed melius se sperare de æquitate judicum.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From a feeling of indignation: namely, that he fought and triumphed for his country, and is now to be slaughtered by that same country as an expiatory offering. Let an apostrophe be amplified to the brothers who have died, whom he says were more fortunately slain by the enemy than he himself was preserved, to perish by the hand of the executioner. Let a recalling of himself be added: namely, "But I hope better of the fairness of the judges."

units.la: B. Propof. Ideo se causam dicturum & sororem non sua, sed propria culpa periisse evicturum.
units.tr: B. Proposition. Therefore he will plead his cause and will prove that his sister perished not through his fault but through her own.

units.la: C. Confirmatio.
units.tr: C. Confirmation.

units.la: I. A causa impulsiva, quæ fuerit justa indignatio; quod soror
units.tr: I. From the impelling cause, which was a just indignation; because the sister

units.la: 1. Publicam lætitiam, intempestivo planctu turbarit. Amplif. à periculo, ex quo liberata sit per hanc victoriam patria. Unde proditionis rea soror videri potuerit; quæ potiorem privatæ domus, quam reip. curam habuerit.
units.tr: 1. disturbed public joy with untimely lamentation. Amplified from the danger from which the country had been freed by this victory. Whence the sister could seem guilty of treason, since she had regard for the private household rather than for the commonwealth.

units.la: 2. Quod potiorem rationem habuerit sponsi, quam duorum fratrum interfectorum; quod potius luxerit sponsum occisum, quam gavisa sit de fratre superstite; quem gaudio excipere debuerit.
units.tr: 2. because she had regard for her betrothed rather than for her two brothers who had been killed; because she mourned the betrothed slain rather than rejoicing over the brother who survived, whom she ought to have welcomed with joy.

units.la: II. Ab objecto. Videlicet sororem quidem fuisse, sed revera hostem patriæ, quæ cum hostibus noxios tractarit amores; potius sorsan proditura patriam, quam desertura sponsum. Cum tamen si Horatia familia digna esse voluerit, aliter affecta esse debuerit. Hinc se, licet privatum, in flagranti veluti delicto, justo zelo armatum fecisse illud, quod amor patriæ dictarit. Hanc scilicet esse legem omnibus legibus antiquiorem, ut patriæ saluti consulatur. Digress. in Locu Commune de zelo pro patria, quod etiam excusét perperam acta. Exemplo Romuli, occidentis fratrem, Patrum, discerpentium Romulum. Per correctionem dicat, se nec ut privatum considerandum, qui publico decreto pro universo populo certamen subierit. Hac nemesi inflammatum, se ultum esse sororem.
units.tr: II. From the object. Namely, that she was indeed his sister, but in truth an enemy of the country, who entertained harmful loves with the enemies; perhaps rather about to betray the country than to desert her betrothed. Yet if she had wished to be worthy of the Horatian family, she ought to have been disposed otherwise. Hence he, though a private man, caught as it were in the flagrant act of crime and armed with just zeal, did that which love of country prompted. This, namely, is the law older than all laws, that the safety of the country be consulted. Digression on the common theme of zeal for the country, which excuses even things wrongly done. By the example of Romulus, who killed his brother, and of the Fathers, who tore Romulus apart. By correction he says that he is not to be considered as a private man, since he undertook the contest by public decree on behalf of the whole people. Inflamed by this indignation, he avenged his sister.

units.la: D. Confutatio Testimoniorum: videl.
units.tr: D. Refutation of the testimonies, namely:

units.la: Leges punire homicidia dolo commissa, non illa, quae adversus personas capitaliter suspectas & in recenti crimine deprehensas ex justo zelo à patriae vindicibus committuntur. Naturam abominare crudelitatem in agnatos, sed patriam imperare vindictam adversus proditores. Hinc Codrum, Lycurgum &c. ut patriam servarent, vita & exilio semetipsos multasse.
units.tr: The laws punish homicides committed by deliberate malice, not those which are committed against persons under capital suspicion and caught in a recent crime, by the avengers of the country from just zeal. Nature abhors cruelty against kinsmen, but the country commands vengeance against traitors. Hence Codrus, Lycurgus, etc., who to save their country punished themselves with death and exile.

units.la: E. Conclusio;
units.tr: E. Conclusion;

units.la: Ad statum assumptum confugiat & ad deprecationem: videl. Licet purgare se à crimine porro queat, malle se tamen confugere ad aequitatem judicum, & ipsorum gratiae acceptum ferre, quod per justitiam obtinere forsan queat; ut per eosdem illos ipse vivat, qui sibi vitam & salutem patriae debeant.
units.tr: He takes refuge in the assumed status and in a plea for mercy, namely: although he is able to clear himself further of the crime, he would rather flee to the fairness of the judges and acknowledge as a gift of their favour what perhaps he could obtain by justice; so that by those same men he may live, who owe him life and safety for the country.

units.la: Ad hoc genus pertinent etiam
units.tr: To this kind also belong:

units.la: I. Objurgationes & reprehensiones, expostulationes; exprobat. Exempli loco introduci potest:
units.tr: I. Rebukes and reprimands, expostulations, reproaches. By way of example, the following may be introduced:

units.la: 1. Camillus objurgens Ludimagistrum urbis proditorem apud Faliscos 1. Flor. c.12.
units.tr: 1. Camillus rebuking the schoolmaster of the city, a traitor among the Faliscans. Florus, ch. 12.

units.la: 2. Senatus reprehendens Consules Veturium & Posthumium, quod turpiter cum Samnitibus transegerint. Flor. I. c.16.
units.tr: 2. The Senate reprimanding the consuls Veturius and Postumius, because they had shamefully made a treaty with the Samnites. Florus, book 1, ch. 16.

units.la: II. Excusationes & apologiae, exemplum potest esse in Persona Manlii excusantis pugnam adversus edictum patris Consulis commissam. Flor. lib.1, c.14. Liv. lib.8.
units.tr: II. Excuses and apologies; an example may be the person of Manlius excusing the battle fought against the edict of his consul father. Florus, book 1, ch. 14; Livy, book 8.

units.la: THEMA V. MARCUS MANLIUS CAPITOLINUS ACCUSATUR SEDITIONIS.
units.tr: THEME V. MARCUS MANLIUS CAPITOLINUS IS ACCUSED OF SEDITION.

units.la: Vid. Liv. lib.6.
units.tr: See Livy, book 6.

units.la: Exord. Ex regula: Salus reip. suprema lex est. Haec 1. breviter astruatur & 2. opponatur molitio Manlii, privatae potentiae studentis spreta salute publica, 3. Illustretur prolepsi à meritis ipsius, qua Capitolium à Gallis conservaverit; Resp. communi bono, non privatae potentiae servatam esse patriam.
units.tr: Exordium. From the rule: the safety of the state is the supreme law. This is first briefly established; second, it is set against the scheme of Manlius, who, scorning the public safety, pursues private power; third, it is illustrated by a prolepsis from his merits, namely that he saved the Capitol from the Gauls. The reply: the state was saved for the common good, not for private power.

units.la: Propof. Hanc eandem jam velle, ut seditionis arcessatur hic idem Manlius, ex vindice quondam oppressor reip.
units.tr: Proposition. That this same Manlius, once a champion of liberty and now an oppressor of the state, should be summoned on a charge of sedition.

units.la: Confirm. I. A praesumtionibus voluntatis: ubi ostendatur ipsius 1. insolensolentia ex fortuna & opibus. 2. contemtus reliquorum senato-rum, 3, æmulatio contra M. Furium. 4. jactantia de vindicato Capitolio per se solum. vid. Liv. Hinc colligat animum plus quàm civilia molientem, qualis haud ferendus in libera rep. Unde o-stracismo usus in rep. Athenienf.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. From presumptions of his intention, where it is shown: 1. his insolence, arising from his fortune and resources; 2. his contempt for the rest of the senators; 3. his rivalry with M. Furius; 4. his boasting that he alone saved the Capitol. See Livy. From this the accuser infers a mind aiming at more than civic power, such as cannot be tolerated in a free state. Hence ostracism was used in the Athenian state.

units.la: II. A factis ipsis: vid. 1. quod primus ex patribus popularis factus, patrum consilia communicet cum plebe, criminando patres, quod contra juramentum & fidem datam reip.
units.tr: II. From the deeds themselves: see 1. that, being the first of the patricians to become a popularis, he shares the counsels of the patricians with the plebs, slandering the patricians, which is contrary to his oath and the faith he pledged to the state.

units.la: 2. Quod leges agrarias jactet, quæ perpetua tribunis plebis seditionum materia.
units.tr: 2. That he boasts of agrarian laws, which are always a source of sedition for the tribunes of the plebs.

units.la: 3. Quod plebem ad se alliciat, regnum ambiens, promittendo liberationem ab ære alieno; quo plerique laborent; unde metuenda seditio: maximè durante bello Volsco, & recenti Latinorum & Hernicorum defectione.
units.tr: 3. That he wins the plebs over to himself, aspiring to kingship, by promising release from debt, which many are burdened with; whence sedition is to be feared, especially while the Volscian war lasts and with the recent revolt of the Latins and Hernici.

units.la: 4. Quod centurionem concitata turba judicio exemerit, & seditiosa concione plebem concitaverit. vid. Liv.
units.tr: 4. That he snatched a centurion from judgment by an excited mob and stirred up the plebs with a seditious harangue. See Livy.

units.la: 5. Quod criminetur patres, quasi pecuniam publicam occultent.
units.tr: 5. That he accuses the patricians, as if they were hiding public money.

units.la: Concluf. Petat ut in vincula ducatur, & tanquam reus majestatis ex saxo Tarpejo præcipitetur, ibidem prodendæ patriæ pœnam luituri, ubi servatæ quondam trophæa fixerat.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him ask to be led into chains and, as one guilty of treason, be hurled from the Tarpeian Rock, there to pay the penalty for betraying his country, where he had once set up trophies of its preservation.

units.la: M. Manlius Capitolinus defendit se.
units.tr: M. Manlius Capitolinus defends himself.

units.la: Exord. Per pathos indignationis eludat exordiù accusatoris; quod ipse vindex reip. prætextu publicæ salutis in discrimen capitis vocetur.
units.tr: Exordium. By a pathos of indignation he mocks the accuser's exordium: that he, the champion of the state, under the pretext of public safety, is being brought into peril of his life.

units.la: Amplif. ex thesi; quod salus reip. prætextus sit speciosus illis qui remp. pessundant. Remp. enim non esse magnates; sed populum, cui cum consultum eat ipse, odio se esse patribus.
units.tr: Amplification. From the thesis: the safety of the state is a specious pretext for those who ruin the commonwealth. For the state is not the magnates but the people, to whose good he himself attends, and for that very reason he is hated by the patricians.

units.la: Propof. Inique se accusari seditionis ac majestatis.
units.tr: Proposition. That he is unjustly accused of sedition and treason.

units.la: Confirm. 1. a studio suo pro rep. & civibus: quod probet à factis suis: videlicet.
units.tr: Confirmation. 1. From his zeal for the state and the citizens, which he proves from his deeds, namely:

units.la: 1. Quod popularis sit: hoc explicet quid sit: vid. qui utilitates quærit populi. Id quod invisum magnatibus, qui soli regnare velint.
units.tr: 1. That he is a popularis. He explains what this means: one who seeks the advantage of the people. This is hateful to the magnates, who alone wish to reign.

units.la: 2. Quod agrarias leges jactet: hoc ostendat, esse ex re populi & sic reip. utile. Frustra jactari remp. ubi populus, qui anima reip. opprimitur. II. A benefacto: quod ipse solus liberaverit Capitolium & remp. à Gallis. Nihil esse, quod hoc facto non meruerit: quod tamen nihil propterea ambiverit aut ambiat, sola gloria contentus. Hanc sibi causam esse invidiae apud patres.
units.tr: 2. That he boasts of agrarian laws. He shows that these serve the people's good and so are useful to the state. It is in vain to boast of the state where the people, which is the soul of the state, is oppressed. II. From a good deed: that he alone freed the Capitol and the state from the Gauls. There is nothing he has not deserved by this deed; yet he has aspired to nothing on that account and does not aspire, being content with glory alone. This, he says, is the cause of the patricians' hostility toward him.

units.la: Confutatio, Ex hisce refellat argumenta accusatoris ordine.
units.tr: Refutation. From these points he refutes the accuser's arguments in order.

units.la: Perorat. Petat se absolvi à falso intentatis criminibus, & ex poena talionis plecti accusatorem.
units.tr: Peroration. He asks to be absolved of the falsely alleged crimes, and that the accuser be punished by the law of retaliation.

units.la: THEMA VI.
units.tr: THEME VI.

units.la: I. Doëgus conjurationis accusat Abimelechum, ex 1. Sam. c. 22.
units.tr: I. Doeg accuses Abimelech of conspiracy, from 1. Sam. c. 22.

units.la: Exord. 1. Pathos moveat à periculis, quibus exposita vita regum. Videl. non immerito dixisse aliquem, diadema regium tot periculis conjunctum, ut humi jacens vix tolli mereatur.
units.tr: Introduction. 1. Let him stir the emotions by the dangers to which the lives of kings are exposed. Someone has rightly said that the royal diadem is so bound up with dangers that it hardly deserves to be lifted from the ground where it lies.

units.la: 2. Rationem addat ab inductione quadam periculorum diversorum.
units.tr: 2. Let him add an argument drawn from an induction of various dangers.

units.la: 3. Illustret prolepsi: videl constitutos quidem satellites, custodias, sed frustra, si & illi, à quibus nulla suspicio, qui orare pro regibus tenentur, hostes evadant.
units.tr: 3. Let him illustrate with a prolepsis: bodyguards and guards are indeed posted, but in vain, if those from whom no suspicion arises, who are bound to pray for kings, prove to be enemies.

units.la: 4. Applicat ad hypothesin, videl. obstupescitis: Ipse ego accusator & testis sum, Te Abimeleche illum esse, quem reum indigito. Pathos addat à suo officio; venerari se officium ipsius; sed & juramento obstrictum se esse regi.
units.tr: 4. He applies it to the case in hand: "Astonished as you are, I myself am the accuser and witness that you, Abimelech, are the one I point out as the defendant." Let him add emotion from his own office: he reveres that office, and he is also bound by oath to the king.

units.la: Propos. Ideo processisse se, ut conjurationis rerum agat Abimelechum Sacerdotem Domini, & quotquot cum ipso sint Nobae sacri ordinis.
units.tr: Proposition. Therefore he has come forward to charge Abimelech, priest of the Lord, and all who are with him of the sacred order of Nob, with conspiracy.

units.la: Narratio: factum exponat 1. quomodo ipse Nobae fuerit ad expiationem delicti. 2. David cum paucis pavidus ibi venerit. 3. Abimelech panes sacros & gladium Goliathi ipsi tradiderit. 4. Oraculum pro ipso consuluerit & cum benedictione dimiserit. Conclus. loco contestetur conscientiam Abimelechi & Levitarum, remita se habere.
units.tr: Narration: he sets out the facts: 1. how he himself came to Nob to make expiation for his offence; 2. how David came there with a few men, in fear; 3. how Abimelech gave him the holy bread and the sword of Goliath; 4. how he consulted the oracle for him and dismissed him with a blessing. Conclusion in place of this: let him call to witness the conscience of Abimelech and the Levites, and show that he himself is blameless.

units.la: Contentio: Conjurationem hinc arguens
units.tr: Argument: he proves the conspiracy from the following:

units.la: I. Ex praesumt. voluntatis. Hic 1. ab amore erga Davidem. Hic dicat se nolle examinare vitam ipsius Sacerdotis anteactam, qualiter erga legem affectus fuerit; sed amore singulari erga Davidem, ipsum semper habuisse. buisse:quod & hinc constet,quod panes sacros ipsi tradiderit contra præceptū Domini. Quid de illo sperandum regi, qui nec Deo fidus sit.2.ex ratiocinatione de ipsius intentione: videl.cur gladio ipsum instruxerit. Numquid colligere potuit, ipsum fugitivum, qui ex aula digressus sine gladio. An credibile, ipsum non examinasse Davidem, & Davidem occultasse hoc Sacerdoti. Cur gladium Goliathi? videl. ut habeat materiam jactandi se ex pristina victoria, & ex consensu Sacerdotis,qui hunc ipsi tradiderit, sperare ipsum lautiores reditus ex Davide, qui pietatem semper simulaverit: ut potiatur regno. Denique latere fugam non potuisse Sacerdoti, qui Deum consuluerit super Davide. Claudat hoc membrum epiphon. Nihil periculosius esse, quam cum sub velo pietatis se occultat proditio.
units.tr: I. From presumptions of will. Here 1. from love toward David. Here let him say that he does not wish to examine the priest's past life, how he has been disposed toward the law, but that he has always held him in singular love for David. This is also clear from the fact that he handed over the holy bread to him contrary to the Lord's command. What can be hoped from a king who is not even faithful to God? 2. From reasoning about his intention: namely, why he armed him with a sword. Could he not infer that David was a fugitive, who had left the court without a sword? Is it credible that he did not question David, and that David concealed this from the priest? Why Goliath's sword? Namely, so that he might have material for boasting of his former victory; and with the priest's consent, who handed it over to him, that he might hope for richer rewards from David, who has always feigned piety, so that he may gain the kingdom. Finally, the priest, who consulted God about David, could not have been unaware of the flight. Let him close this member with an epiphonema: nothing is more dangerous than when treachery hides itself beneath the veil of piety.

units.la: II. Ex præsumt. facultatis, 1. quia David facilè regno potiri queat, si faventes habeat Sacerdotes,quorum autoritas magna apud populum. 2. quia jam à Samuele unctus sit rex. 3.quia recenti victoria à Goliatho clarus sit. 4. Jonathanem filium regis & totum populum faventem habeat. 5. gener sit regis. 6. ad Moabitas confugerit, brevi manu armata reversurus. Addat pathos; scil. privata paucorum utilitate tantum malum parari regno, idque conspirante Sacerdote.
units.tr: II. From presumptions of ability: 1. because David could easily gain the kingdom if he had priests favouring him, whose authority is great among the people; 2. because he has already been anointed king by Samuel; 3. because he is famous for his recent victory over Goliath; 4. because he has the king's son Jonathan and the whole people on his side; 5. because he is the king's son-in-law; 6. because he has fled to the Moabites, to return shortly with an armed hand. Let him add emotion: that so great an evil is being prepared for the kingdom for the private advantage of a few, and that with the priest conspiring.

units.la: III. Ex signis,videl. 1. occultè multa agitasse Ahimelechum cum Davide. Hic urgeat Ahimelechum quid mussitarint; quid Oraculum sacrum ipsi renunciarit. 2. Enixa cum benedictione ipsum dimisisse pavidum & maturantem: scil. pro rege tunc eras sollicitus, qui ministrum profugum occultasti & viatico ac armis instruxisti.
units.tr: III. From signs, namely: 1. that Ahimelech has secretly discussed many things with David. Here let him press Ahimelech on what they muttered together, and what the sacred oracle announced to him. 2. that he dismissed him, frightened and hurrying, with an eager blessing. That is, he was anxious then for the king, since he had hidden the fugitive minister and equipped him with provisions and arms.

units.la: Conclus. Quoniam igitur conjurationis & majestatis reus sit, exemplariter ipsum & omnes Levitas ipsius, qui conscii rem non revelarint, puniendos esse. Nec reverendum sacrum munus & Ephod, quibus se indignos reddiderint. Vel se paratum inferre manus, si regi ita visum fuerit.
units.tr: Conclusion. Since he is therefore guilty of conspiracy and treason, he and all his Levites, who knew of the matter and did not reveal it, should be punished as an example. Nor should the sacred office and the ephod be respected, since they have made themselves unworthy of them. Or he is ready to lay hands on them himself, if it should seem good to the king.

units.la: II. Ahimelechus se purgat negando intentatum crimen.
units.tr: II. Ahimelech clears himself by denying the crime charged.

units.la: Exord. 1. Misericordiâ moveat à persona accusatorū; videl. in judicium capitis vocari Sacerdotē & Levitas, qui sacro muneri intenti nunquam in judiciis versati sint; qui crimina populi expiari consueverint, rint, illos atrocissimi criminis reos agi: idque per calumniam, quæ regi placere satagat, accusatione innocentum. Hic contestetur Doëgum atrocis calumniæ, ex Ps.64.
units.tr: Introduction. 1. Let him move pity by the character of the accusers: namely, that a priest and Levites, devoted to sacred office and never involved in judicial matters, who are accustomed to make expiation for the crimes of the people, are summoned to a capital trial and charged with the most atrocious crime; and this through calumny, which strives to please the king, by accusing the innocent. Here let him call Doeg a witness of atrocious calumny, from Ps. 64.

units.la: II. Soletur se in regis justitia & sua innocentia, qua sola fretus mendacia se velle refellere.
units.tr: II. Let him take comfort in the king's justice and in his own innocence, relying on which alone he wishes to refute the lies.

units.la: Propos. Se & Levitas ab intentato majestatis crimine prorsus immunes esse.
units.tr: Proposition. That he and the Levites are wholly free from the charged crime of treason.

units.la: Tractatio habeat
units.tr: Treatment should contain:

units.la: I. Confirmationem
units.tr: I. Confirmation

units.la: 1. Præsumtionum voluntatis. Hic 1. Contestetur de vitæ innocentia, qua Deo sacer aulæ & politicis negotiis nunquam se miscuerit. 2. fateatur se dilexisse Davidem, ut virum pium, & fidelem regis ministrum, & bello strenuum. 3. Panes sacros & gladium Goliathi dedisse tanquam regis legato in casu necessitatis. 4. calumnias esse, quod de intentione ratiocinetur Doëgus. Se credidisse Davidi allegantì regis mandatum, non suum esse examinare regios ministros secretam expeditionem allegantes, odisse se πολυπραγμοσύνην. 5. Latiorem conditionem se nunquam affectasse, nec à Davide sperare potuisse. Sacerdotum sortem Deum esse. Gnatonem se nunquam egisse. Invehatur in Gnatones aulicos, qui ut regis gratia potiantur, prodant innocentes. 4. Deum non omnia revelare Sacerdotibus; sed illa, quæ sint muneris ipsorum.
units.tr: 1. Of presumptions of will. Here 1. let him testify to the innocence of his life, by which, being sacred to God, he has never meddled in court or political affairs. 2. Let him confess that he loved David as a pious man, a faithful minister of the king, and valiant in war. 3. He gave the holy bread and the sword of Goliath as to the king's envoy, in a case of necessity. 4. It is calumny that Doeg reasons about his intention. He believed David, who alleged the king's command; it is not his place to examine royal ministers who allege a secret mission; he hates meddling [πολυπραγμοσύνην]. 5. He never aimed at a wider position, nor could he have hoped for one from David. The lot of priests is God's doing. He has never played the flatterer. Let him inveigh against court flatterers, who, in order to win the king's favour, betray the innocent. 4. God does not reveal everything to priests, but only those things that belong to their office.

units.la: 2. Præsumtionum facultatis. 1. Sacerdotum favorem parum posse ad regna, quæ vel à Deo dantur, vel ferro acquiruntur. Arma sua preces esse, quas semper pro rege fuderit. 2. Successione se reliquisse Dei arbitrio. Verum esse, Davidé multis prærogativis clarum; sed à rege ipso evectum, tanquam fidelem ministrum. In regis manu esse aliquè extollere & deprimere. Se secutū semper regis judicium. 3. Utrum ad Moabitas fugerit David, sibi non constare. Se hostem habiturum Davidem, si hostile quid contra regem, aut regnum moliatur. Didicisse se Deo & regi fidelem esse, in qua fide moriturus sit.
units.tr: 2. Of presumptions of ability. 1. The favour of priests can do little for kingdoms, which are either given by God or acquired by the sword. His weapons are the prayers he has always poured out for the king. 2. He has left the succession to God's judgment. It is true that David was distinguished by many prerogatives, but he was raised up by the king himself, as a faithful minister. It lies in the king's hand to raise up and to cast down. He has always followed the king's judgment. 3. He does not know whether David fled to the Moabites. He will regard David as an enemy if he plans anything hostile against the king or the kingdom. He has learned to be faithful to God and to the king, and in that faith he is prepared to die.

units.la: 3. Signorum 1. Occulte se nihil egisse cum Davide, nisi quod petenti panes & gladium dederit. Contestetur Doëgum, num viderit, se mussitasse aut quicquam egisse clanculum. Deum esse testem, sibi nihil constitisse de fuga Davidis. 2. Dimisisse illum cum benedictione, ut regium ministrum, & ut decet Sacerdotem. Pro rege se fuisse sollicitum, qui ministrum juvit & illi benedixit.
units.tr: 3. Of signs: 1. He did nothing in secret with David, except that he gave bread and the sword to one who asked for them. Let him call Doeg to witness whether he saw him muttering or doing anything furtively. God is witness that he knew nothing of David's flight. 2. He dismissed him with a blessing, as a royal minister, and as a priest should. He was anxious for the king, since he helped the minister and blessed him.

units.la: II. Confirmationem innocentiae.
units.tr: II. Confirmation of innocence.

units.la: 1. Ex praesumtionibus a. contrariae voluntatis: quia Sacerdos sit, cui persona regis sacrosancta sit, quique nullam causam habeat machinandi contra Saulem, à quo nunquam male habitus sit. b. facultatis: tum quia procul ab aula, nihil scire potuit de regis offensa: cum necipse Doegus, qui recens inde venerit quicquam de illa retulerit: vir caeteroquin rerum malarum cupidus, lingua procacissimus: tum quia ipse Nobae residens in urbe ignobili, parum autoritatis habeat apud populum, qui suum Sacerdotem & prophetas sequi merito soleat.
units.tr: 1. From presumptions: (a) of contrary will, because he is a priest, to whom the person of the king is sacrosanct, and who has no cause to plot against Saul, by whom he was never ill-treated. (b) Of opportunity: first, because being far from the court he could know nothing of the king's offence, since not even Doeg himself, who had just come from there, reported anything about it—a man otherwise eager for evil things and most insolent in his tongue; second, because he himself, residing at Nob, a humble city, has little authority among the people, who are wont rightly to follow their own priest and prophets.

units.la: 2. Ex signis: à quod sistat se regi irato, cum toto clero, signum esse evidens innocentiae: fugiturus ad Davidem, si male conscius esset. b. Quod Doegus non accusaverit ipsum, antequam rex mentionem injecerit. Unde ipse majestatis reus habendus sit; qui conjurationem non indicaverit, nisi interrogatus.
units.tr: 2. From signs: (a) that he presents himself to the angry king, together with the whole priesthood, is a clear sign of innocence; he would have fled to David if he had been conscious of guilt. (b) That Doeg did not accuse him before the king himself mentioned it. Hence he himself should be held guilty of treason, who did not disclose the conspiracy unless questioned.

units.la: Concluf. 1. Contestetur coram Deo innocentiam, 2. Petat justam absolutionem. 3. Postulet ut accusator ad poenas trahatur, tanquam calumniator, & dissimulator conjurationis, si qua fuerit. Sic stabilitum iri thronum regis justitia.
units.tr: Conclusion: 1. Let him call God to witness his innocence. 2. Let him ask for a just acquittal. 3. Let him demand that the accuser be dragged to punishment as a slanderer and a concealer of the conspiracy, if there was any. Thus the king's throne will be made firm by justice.

units.la: THEMA VII.
units.tr: THEME VII.

units.la: I. Vitellius coram Senatu accusat Pisonem quod Germanicum veneno sustulit. Ex Tac. l. 2. c. 55.
units.tr: I. Vitellius accuses Piso before the Senate of having poisoned Germanicus. From Tacitus, Annals, book 2, chapter 55.

units.la: Exord. Excuset quod praeter consuetudinem suam ad accusandum accedat: rationem afferat à publica omnium voce, quam ipse licet impar referat. Pathos moveat à persona Germanici defuncti, quem omnes boni & ipsa Principis domus defleat. Hinc odium concitet Pisoni, qui solus inter publicum luctum triumphet. vide cap. 9.
units.tr: Exordium. He should excuse himself for coming forward to accuse against his usual custom, and give as his reason the public voice of everyone, which he, though unequal to the task, reports. He should stir pathos by mentioning the person of the dead Germanicus, whom all good people and the Prince's own house mourn. From this he should stir up hatred against Piso, who alone among the public grief rejoices. See chapter 9.

units.la: Propof. Per apostrophen ad Pisonem: Te ego parricidam optimi principis & Caesaris ac reip. hostem rationibus convincam necessariis.
