units.tr: Propositio. By apostrophe to Piso: "You, parricide of the best prince, of Caesar and of the commonwealth, enemy of the state, I will convict by necessary arguments."

units.la: Confirm. Perpetua apostrophe illum urgeat.
units.tr: Confirmatio. He should press him with a continuous apostrophe.

units.la: I. Conjecturis
units.tr: I. By conjectures

units.la: 1. Voluntatis, quam probet a. ex moribus & vita anteaſta; quod homo ambitiosus, audax & uxoris affectibus serviens. b. ex odio adversus German, cujus argumenta collige ex Tac. lib. 2. c. ff. c. a spe successionis in praefectura belli, in quo adjutor Germanici fuerat.
units.tr: 1. Of will, which he proves a. from character and former life: that he is an ambitious, reckless man, a slave to his wife's passions; b. from hatred toward Germanicus, whose arguments you may gather from Tacitus, book 2, chapters ff. and c.; from hope of succession to the command of the war, in which he had been Germanicus's assistant.

units.la: 2. Facultatis: quam probet a. a studio militum, quod licentia ac largitionibus acquisiverat b. a mansuetudine & animo Germanici suspicionibus vacuo. c. ab occasione temporis & loci: vid. in Syria apud exercitum, cum omnes haberet favent es.
units.tr: 2. Of capacity, which he proves a. from Piso's zeal for the soldiers, which he had won by license and largesse; b. from the gentleness and mind of Germanicus, free of suspicion; c. from the opportunity of time and place: namely in Syria, among the army, where he had all the good will.

units.la: 3. Ex signis: a. antecedentibus, quod apud Athenienses acta Germanici perstrinxerit lib. 2. c. ff. quod maturaverit ad assequendum Germanicum, castra corruperit, & parentem legionum se dici passus sit, Germanico & ipsius amicis semper contrarius fuerit, vota pro ipsius valetudine suscepta turbaverit. b. concurrentibus; inventa carmina Magica in Germanicum lib. 2. c. 69. c. consequentibus videl. notis veneni in cadavere; metu Pisonis disluasione filii, ne rediret Romam.
units.tr: 3. From signs: a. preceding ones: that he disparaged Germanicus's acts among the Athenians (book 2, chapters ff.); that he hastened to overtake Germanicus, corrupted the camp, and allowed himself to be called the father of the legions; that he was always opposed to Germanicus and his friends, and disturbed the vows made for his health. b. accompanying ones: the magic spells found against Germanicus (book 2, chapter 69); c. following ones, namely the marks of poison on the corpse, and Piso's fear, and the dissuading of his son from returning to Rome.

units.la: II. Ex testimoniis videl. 1. Publico rumore, quod Piso Germanico venenum propinaverit, qui rumor pro publico testimonio bendus. 2. [psius defuncti querela, qui vindictam amicis commendarit. Hanc ultimam voluntatem merito exsequendam principi & reip. pro qua toties mortis periculo expoluerit. Conclusio hic per prosop. manium Germanici vindictam expoícat a Senatu.
units.tr: II. From testimonies, namely: 1. the public rumour that Piso gave Germanicus poison, which rumour is to be taken as public testimony. 2. The complaint of the dead man himself, who commended vengeance to his friends. This last wish should rightly be carried out by the Prince and the commonwealth, for which he had so often exposed himself to the danger of death. Here the conclusion is made by prosopopoeia: the shade of Germanicus asks the Senate for vengeance.

units.la: II. Piso diluat objectum parricidii crimen.
units.tr: II. Piso should refute the charge of parricide brought against him.

units.la: Exord. Misericordiam captet 1. a publico odio, quo calumnia suorum adversariorum gravatum se videat; 2. a facundia suorum adversariorum, qui meditata facundia ipsum urgeant certatim. 3. a sua persona, quod miles, quod imparatus; attamen bona conscientia fretus causam suam agere valit.
units.tr: Exordium. He should win pity: 1. from the public hatred, by which he sees himself burdened through the slanders of his adversaries; 2. from the eloquence of his adversaries, who press him with eloquence prepared in advance, each trying to outdo the other; 3. from his own person, that he is a soldier and unpractised in speech; yet, relying on a good conscience, he is able to plead his own cause.

units.la: Propos. Immunem se esse a caede Germanici.
units.tr: Propositio. That he is innocent of the death of Germanicus.

units.la: Tractatio. Refutet
units.tr: Tractatio. He should refute:

units.la: 1. Conjecturas t. voluntatis. ꝯ. videl. vitæ anteactæ se principem testem habere; odii non habuisse causas; successionem se non iperasse. Si quæ ænulatio in uxores fuerit, frustra illam allegari tanti sceleris causam.
units.tr: 1. The conjectures of will: namely, that he has the witness of his former life as the Prince himself; that he had no causes of hatred; that he did not aspire to the succession. If there was any rivalry over wives, it is in vain that this is alleged as the cause of so great a crime.

units.la: 2. Facultatis. ꝯ. officii sui fuisse conciliare sibi militum animos; qui tamen nunquam contra Germanicum quicquam tentaturi fuissent. Satis cautum fuisse Germanicum & sua cohorte prætoria semper custoditum.
units.tr: 2. Of capacity: that it was his duty to win over the minds of the soldiers, who nevertheless would never have attempted anything against Germanicus. That Germanicus was sufficiently guarded, and always protected by his praetorian cohort.

units.la: 3. Signa, solum imperatoris nomen venerabile esse debere in provinciis: si milites parentem ipsum dixerint, præter suam voluntatem esse: nasci sæpe dissensiones inter duces; si carmina magica inventa, num ipse propterea autor sit: non metuisse filium conscientia criminis, sed rumorem falsum: Imo ipsum reditum suum testari de bona conscientia.
units.tr: 3. The signs: that the name of the emperor alone ought to be venerated in the provinces; that if the soldiers called him their father, this was against his own will; that disagreements often arise between commanders; that if magic spells were found, he is not for that reason their author; that he did not fear his son's guilt of conscience but a false rumour; indeed, that his return itself bears witness to his good conscience.

units.la: II. Testimonia. 1. vulgi rumorem lubricum esse, per unum invidum facile excitari. Ipsum imperatorem conscium cædis dici.
units.tr: II. Testimonies: 1. That the rumour of the common people is slippery, and easily stirred up by one envious man. That the emperor himself is said to be privy to the murder.

units.la: 2. Nescire se, quid defunctus questus sit; forte muliebri odio inductum & vix sui compotem ipsum fuisse conquestum. Neminem tutum futurum, si morientium voces pro veritate habeantur. Alia testimonia ac indicia requiri, antequam contra famam ac vitam civis Romani statuatur. Sic ipsum imperatorem, ipsum Augustam forte reos argui posse.
units.tr: 2. That he does not know what the dead man complained of; perhaps he was moved by womanish hatred, and complained while scarcely in command of himself. That no one will be safe if the words of the dying are held to be true. That other testimonies and indications should be required before a judgment is made against the reputation and life of a Roman citizen. In this way the emperor himself, and perhaps the Augusta, could be accused as guilty.

units.la: Concluf. Quia nihil ab accusatoribus probatum sit, petat se absolvi, & exemplum statui in calumniatores.
units.tr: Conclusion: Since nothing has been proved by the accusers, he should ask to be acquitted, and that an example be made of the calumniators.

units.la: THEMA VIII. INVECTIVA IN JUDÆOS CHRISTUM FALSO ACCUSANTES ET CONDEMNANTES.
units.tr: THEME VIII. AN INVECTIVE AGAINST THE JEWS WHO FALSELY ACCUSE AND CONDEMN CHRIST.

units.la: Exord. Ex abrupto invehatur in pertinaciam. Quousque tandem sæviet vester furor: amplificetur 1. per Synonym. 2. per comparationem obstinatæ oppositionis contra Christum ab initio prædicationis ipsius, ubi tamen toties verbis & miraculis convicti sunt.
units.tr: Exordium. Let him launch straight into an attack on their obstinacy: "How long, pray, will your fury rage?" Let it be amplified (1) by synonyms, and (2) by comparison with the obstinate opposition to Christ from the beginning of his preaching, although they had been so often convicted by his words and miracles.

units.la: Propos. Sed hanc vim esse tenebrarum, quibus diabolus circumfudit mentes & corda ipsorum, ut contra innocentem sæviant: quod clare evincendum, ut vel jam demum posteri respiciant. Tractat. Refellat crimina intentata Christo. videl. Et quid tandem est, quod Christo objecistis, &c.
units.tr: Proposition. But this violence is the power of darkness, by which the devil has poured himself around their minds and hearts, so that they rage against the innocent; this must be clearly demonstrated, so that posterity may at last take note. Treatment. Let him refute the charges brought against Christ, namely: "And what, after all, is it that you have objected to Christ, etc.?"

units.la: 1. Quod blasphemus fuerit, Dei filium se dicens. Hoc r. proponatur. 2. Defendatur a. à vaticiniis Vet. Teft. de Christo ut Pfalm. 2. filius meus es tu. Pf. 110. sede ad dexteram. b. ab operibus per Christum peragendis, quæ solius Dei sunt: cæci vident &c. Hæc omnia in Jesu Nazar. completa ipsis testibus. Hic urgeantur inductione miraculorum & disputationum, quibus convicti sunt Matth. 22. &c. Claudatur increpatione pertinaciæ desperatæ.
units.tr: 1. That he was a blasphemer, in calling himself the Son of God. This should first be set out. 2. Let it be defended (a) from the prophecies of the Old Testament concerning Christ, as in Psalm 2: "You are my Son," and Psalm 110: "Sit at my right hand"; (b) from the works to be performed through Christ, which belong to God alone: "the blind see," etc. All these things were fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth, as the witnesses themselves testify. Here let them be pressed with the citation of the miracles and disputations by which they were convicted, Matt. 22, etc. Let it close with a rebuke of their desperate obstinacy.

units.la: II. Quòd seduxerit populum & contra Mosen docuerit. 1. Ponatur objectio. 2. Refellatur a. quia Moses ipse Deut. 18. 15. hunc Prophetam prædixerit. b. quia œconomia Mosaica Christum præfigurarit. c. quia cessare debuit. Nam Jer. 31. promittitur novum fedus: & Pf. 110. alius Sacerdos juxta ordinem non Aaronis, sed Melchised. vide Heb. 7. Non igitur zelum ipsorum fuisse pro lege, sed pro avaritia ipsorum; & ex odio vitiorum gravissimo censore.
units.tr: II. That he led the people astray and taught against Moses. 1. Let the objection be stated. 2. Let it be refuted (a) because Moses himself, in Deut. 18:15, foretold this Prophet; (b) because the Mosaic economy prefigured Christ; (c) because it was bound to cease. For Jer. 31 promises a new covenant, and Psalm 110 speaks of another priest, not after the order of Aaron but of Melchizedek; see Heb. 7. Therefore their zeal was not for the law but for their own greed, and their hatred of vices made him the most severe censor.

units.la: III. Quod crimen majestatis commiserit contra Cæsarem. 4. Negando 1. quia Christi regnum non est ex hoc mundo. Unde & ipse Herodes & Pilatus ipsum innocentem pronunciaverint. 2. quia contrarium docuerit: date Cæsari, &c. Et verò nulla doctrina sit, magis stabiliens ordinem politicum quam Christi doctrina, &c.
units.tr: III. That he committed the crime of treason against Caesar. 4. Let it be denied (1) because the kingdom of Christ is not of this world; whence Herod himself and Pilate pronounced him innocent. (2) Because he taught the contrary: "Render to Caesar," etc. Indeed there is no doctrine that establishes the political order more firmly than the doctrine of Christ, etc.

units.la: Conclus. Cum igitur fœda calumnia fuerit, qua Christus impetitus est à Pharisæis, hortetur judæos hodiernos, ut hunc regem tandem amplectantur.
units.tr: Conclusion. Since, therefore, the charge with which the Pharisees assailed Christ was a shameful calumny, let him exhort the Jews of today to at last embrace this King.

units.la: THEMA IX.
units.tr: THEME IX.

units.la: M. Horatius accusat decemviros Tyrannidis Liv. 3. 19.
units.tr: M. Horatius accuses the decemvirs of tyranny. Livy 3.19.

units.la: Exord. Excusat quod contra magistr. loquatur. Vid. Mirari forte nonnullos, quod contra decemviros dicere occipiat, ipse privatus contra magistratum: sed desituros mirari, si larvam imperii Appio complicibusque detraxerit. Vid. Exord. pro Roscio Amer.
units.tr: Exordium. He excuses himself for speaking against the magistrates. See: "Perhaps some may wonder that he, a private man, begins to speak against the decemvirs, against the magistracy; but they will cease to wonder if he strips Appius and his accomplices of the mask of power." See the exordium of the speech for Roscius of Ameria.

units.la: Propos. Se manifestæ tyrannidis convicturum decemviros.
units.tr: Propositio. He will prove that the decemvirs are manifest tyrants.

units.la: Confirm. I. Quia sibi arrogant potestatem regiam; scil. non nomen ejus. regis ejuratum esse, sed violentiam regiam. Regem se gerere non illum modo, qui regem se dicit. Sed qui regiam potestatem sibi arrogat. Hoc facere Appium & collegas; dum tyrannice multa agunt, libere loqui de rep. vetant. &c. vid. Liv.
units.tr: Confirmatio. I. Because they arrogate to themselves regal power; that is, the king's name has been renounced, but not regal violence. He is a king not only who calls himself king, but he who arrogates to himself royal power. Appius and his colleagues do this: while they act tyrannically in many matters, they forbid free speech about the commonwealth, etc. See Livy.

units.la: II. Quia privati dominium sibi arrogant: Hic r. exponat, quo consilio annui magistratus invecti fuerint. vid. Flor.9. & Liv.1. sub sin. 2. redarguat decemviros per apostrophen, quod exacto anno in regimine continuunt, sine jussu populi. Ergo esse illos non magistratum legitimum, sed usurpatores, nullo titulo imperantes vid. Liv. in quos populo libera potestas.
units.tr: II. Because they arrogate to themselves private dominion. Here he should explain with what purpose annual magistrates were introduced; see Florus 9 and Livy 1 near the end. He rebukes the decemvirs by apostrophe, because, the year having expired, they continue in government without the command of the people. Therefore they are not a lawful magistracy but usurpers, ruling without any title; see Livy, over whom the people have free power.

units.la: III. Quia creati tantum sint ad ferendas leges: ipsi vero malitiose protracto negotio illo, jus belli gerendi, & indicendi dilectus sine rogatione populi sibi arrogent. Hic suspectos illos reddat, quod armis opprimere satagant remp. si prius sacramento obstrictas habent sibi legiones. Has artes esse tyrannorum bella ex bellis serere, ut ipsi armati exhaustae viris bellicosis civitati jugum imponant.
units.tr: III. Because they were created only to bring forth laws, but they, maliciously prolonging that business, arrogate to themselves the right of waging war and proclaiming levies without the people's request. Here he should make them appear suspect, in that they strive to oppress the commonwealth by arms if they hold the legions bound to them first by oath. These arts are the tricks of tyrants: to sow wars out of wars, so that, themselves armed and the civic body drained of warlike men, they may impose the yoke.

units.la: Conclus. Hortetur, ut injustum imperium deponant & resignent in manus populi, secus jus fore populo, ereptam libertatem ferro vindicandi.
units.tr: Conclusio. He should urge them to lay down their unjust rule and surrender it into the hands of the people; otherwise the people will have the right to reclaim by force the liberty that has been snatched away.

units.la: II. Appius excusat decemviros a tyrannide.
units.tr: II. Appius excuses the decemvirs from tyranny.

units.la: Exord. A pessima intentione M. Horatii: nempe, hoc velle Horatium & complices, ut depósito magistratu a populo ipsis delatosalutare negotium perficiendarum legum impediatur, & ipse suique similes sine lege rursus dominentur. Illustretur ex Loco Communi de praetextu ambitionis: quae ordinarie sugillat magistratum & praetendit libertatem, ut se ipsam efferat. Hinc tyrannidis accusari decemviros innoxios, quam calumniam licet ferro compesci debeat, majori moderatione usus refutare necesse habeat.
units.tr: Exordium. From the worst intention of M. Horatius: namely, that Horatius and his companions want, once the magistracy has been laid down and handed back to the people, the salutary task of perfecting the laws to be hindered, and that he and those like him should rule again without law. Let this be illustrated by the common topic on the pretext of ambition: which ordinarily disparages the magistracy and puts forward liberty, so that it may exalt itself. Hence the decemvirs, being innocent, are accused of tyranny; a calumny which, although it ought to be checked by the sword, he must refute with greater moderation.

units.la: Propos. Falso accusari decemviros tyrannidis.
units.tr: Propositio. The decemvirs are falsely accused of tyranny.

units.la: Confutatio. argumenti
units.tr: Confutatio of the argument.

units.la: I. negando nec nomen, nec dominatum regium se affectasse. Reges enim suo jure absolute imperasse: decemviros vero agnoscere potestatem suam se habere a populo, & dirigere ad salutem reip. Hinc exponat curam suam in scribendis legibus & subjicienciendis illis censuræ populi. Reges dominos fuisse legum; se subjectos legibus &c.
units.tr: I. By denying that they have aspired either to the name or to the dominion of kings. For kings ruled absolutely by their own right; but the decemvirs acknowledge that they have their power from the people and are directed to the welfare of the commonwealth. Hence he should set out his care in writing laws and in subjecting them to the censure of the people. Kings were lords of the laws; they themselves are subject to the laws, etc.

units.la: II. Exponendo, quo consilio creati sint; scil. non in annum tantum, sed ad ferendas leges, & reformandum remp. Hoc egisse se fideliter. Sed nondum perfecisse. Hic disserat, de difficultate ferendarum legum, quibus in omnes casus prospectum sit, ne crebra opus mutatione: quæ adimit legibus auctoritatem, ut tandem evertantur omnes: quia nulla lex satis commoda omnibus. Atrocem injuriam esse, quod privatos, quod usurpatores ipsos vocet Horatius: Imperare se jussu populi, non invasisse imperium; nec patriciis, sed populo suo tempore reddituros.
units.tr: II. By explaining with what purpose they were created: namely, not for a single year only, but to bring forth laws and reform the commonwealth. This they have faithfully done, but have not yet completed. Here he should discourse on the difficulty of bringing forth laws which provide for all cases, lest there be frequent need of change; which takes away authority from laws, so that in the end all are overturned, since no law is sufficiently convenient for all. It is an atrocious injury that Horatius calls them private men, usurpers: to rule by command of the people is not to have seized dominion; and they will restore it to the people, not to the patricians, in due time.

units.la: III. Falsum arguendo, quod protrahant lationem legum, uti ex dictis pateat. Scil. assuetis regimini Horatio similibusque longum videri tempus, quo ipsi non imperant. Sperare illos ex bellis turbas, hinc impedire velle delectum. Hostes peti armis à decemviris, non remp. Hostem esse, qui arma capi contra hostes prohibet.
units.tr: III. He refutes falsely, by arguing that they prolong the proposing of laws, as is clear from what has been said. Namely, to Horatius and those like him, accustomed to rule, the time during which they do not rule seems long. They hope that disturbances will arise from wars, and therefore wish to hinder the levy. The decemvirs seek enemies by arms, not the commonwealth. He is the enemy who forbids arms to be taken against enemies.

units.la: Conclus. Moneat Horatium, ut cautius loquatur de magistratu caveatque ne turbet remp. & hostibus illam prodere velle videatur, secus sibi non deficere autoritatem & vires compescendi rebelles: licet ægre ad extrema hæc progredi malunt.
units.tr: Conclusio. He should admonish Horatius to speak more cautiously about the magistracy, and to beware lest he disturb the commonwealth and seem willing to betray it to enemies; otherwise the authority and strength to restrain rebels will not fail them, although they would rather proceed to these extremes with reluctance.

units.la: THEMA X. UTRUM MAJESTATI COMPETAT CURA ET ARBITRIUM SACRORUM.
units.tr: THEME X. WHETHER THE CARE AND DIRECTION OF SACRED MATTERS BELONGS TO THE MAJESTY (THE CIVIL MAGISTRATE).

units.la: I. Negatè ex sent. Pontific.
units.tr: I. Negatively, from the opinion of the Papists.

units.la: Exord. Ab exemplo hominis, qui duabus partibus constat, corpore & anima, optimè se habere rem si inter utrumque sit concordia. Amplif. encomio concordiæ tanquam conservatricis omnium rerum. Applicetur ad remp. & nominatim utramque potestatem Ecclesiasticam & politicam: utrique suas esse partes, & optimè agi si utraque suis fungatur, politica corporalia, Ecclesiastica spiritualia curet.
units.tr: Exordium. Begin from the example of a man, who consists of two parts, body and soul: a thing goes very well when there is harmony between the two. Amplify with a eulogy of concord as the preserver of all things. Apply this to the commonwealth, and specifically to both powers, the ecclesiastical and the political: each has its own part, and all goes well if each performs its own function, the political power attending to bodily matters and the ecclesiastical to spiritual ones.

units.la: Propos. Quæstionem proponat & negativam præferat.
units.tr: Proposition. Let him pose the question and put the negative first.

units.la: Confirmat. I. Concedat magistratui curam, sed ministerialem in promomovendis sacris, quatenus ab Ecclesiasticis determinatum. Hisce enim animarum curam commissam esse; uti porrò probandum.
units.tr: Confirmation. I. Let him grant the magistrate a care, but a ministerial one, in promoting sacred matters, insofar as this has been determined by the ecclesiastical authorities. For the care of souls has been committed to them, as will be proved further on.

units.la: II. Rationes afferat.
units.tr: II. Let him bring forward reasons.

units.la: 1. Quia magistratus politicus politica curare tantum debet: qualia recensentur; & illustretur ex Deut. 17. verf. 14. & seq. ubi inter functiones regis religionis cura non continetur. Et satis habere negocii principem in politiae ac justitiae cura. Unde & Josaphat Sacerdoti curam sacrorum commisit. 2.Chron.19,11.
units.tr: 1. Because the political magistrate ought to attend only to political matters, such as are enumerated; and let it be illustrated from Deut. 17, verse 14 and following, where care of religion is not included among the functions of the king. And the prince has enough business in the care of civil order and justice. Hence also Jehoshaphat committed the care of sacred matters to the priest. 2 Chron. 19:11.

units.la: 2. Quia religio non dependet ex autoritate magistratus, sed solius Dei: Ratio: quia solus Deus auctor esse potest, quomodo coli velit, improbans ἐπλοτεντσκείαν. Hinc in lege sua statuisse ipsum de cultu suo. At legis custodiam & interpretationem Sacerdoti commissam esse. Deut.17. v.8.9. Mal.2.7. Et verò Petro, non regi traditas claves regni coelorum. Matt.16.
units.tr: 2. Because religion does not depend on the authority of the magistrate, but on God alone. The reason: only God can be the author of how he wishes to be worshipped, rejecting self-devised worship [ἐθελοθρησκείαν]. Hence he himself laid down in his law concerning his own worship. But the keeping and interpretation of the law was committed to the priest: Deut. 17:8, 9; Mal. 2:7. And indeed the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to Peter, not to a king: Matt. 16.

units.la: 3. Quia sacra munia omnia Ephes.4.11. Ecclesiasticis committuntur, nulla regi: uti & Apostoli lites exortas composuerunt. Act.5.3.
units.tr: 3. Because all sacred offices are committed to ecclesiastical persons, none to the king: Eph. 4:11; just as the apostles settled the disputes that arose: Acts 5:3.

units.la: 4. Ab exemplo Azariae, qui punitus est lepra, cum sacerdotium invadere vellet.
units.tr: 4. From the example of Azariah, who was punished with leprosy when he wished to usurp the priesthood.

units.la: Conclus. Thema inferat; addens exemplum membrorum in corpore, ubi nullum alterius munus affectat.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him draw the theme to a close, adding the example of the members in the body, where none claims the function of another.

units.la: II. Affirmatè cum distinctione quo ad arbitrium religionis.
units.tr: II. Affirmatively, with a distinction as regards authority over religion.

units.la: Exord. Ab elogio magistratus: quando ab ipso Deo dii vocantur: dixi dii estis. Ps.82. 1.explicetur sensus, quod Dei in terris vicarii sint, & potestate ac honore Deo proximi. 2. addatur ratio: quia à Deo constituti, ut Dei gloriam & reip. pacem promoveant. 3. Inferatur consectarium; malè igitur Magistratum excludi à negocio religionis.
units.tr: Exordium. From the praise of the magistrate: since by God himself they are called gods: "I said, Ye are gods," Ps. 82:1. Let the sense be explained: that they are God's vicars on earth, and next to God in power and honour. 2. Add the reason: because they have been appointed by God to promote the glory of God and the peace of the commonwealth. 3. Let a consequence be drawn: it is therefore wrong to exclude the magistrate from the business of religion.

units.la: Propos. Hoc contra adversarium paucis evincendum esse.
units.tr: Proposition. That this must be demonstrated briefly against the opponent.

units.la: Tractatio. 1. Acceptet quod aliqua & ministerialis potestas concedatur Magistratui ab antecessore: sed illam non dependere a Clero seu Ecclesiasticis: quippe quorum & hic nulla autoritas nisi ministerialis ex S. Scriptura determinanda. Hanc unicam in dogmatibus normam esse. Hujus lectionem & notitiam & magistratui ac regi commendari. Deut.17.18. 2.Reg.11.12.
units.tr: Treatment. 1. Let him accept that some ministerial power is granted to the magistrate by the predecessor, but that it does not depend on the clergy or the ecclesiastical persons: indeed, their authority too is only ministerial, and is to be determined from Holy Scripture. This is the sole norm in matters of doctrine. The reading and knowledge of it are also commended to the magistrate and the king: Deut. 17:18; 2 Kings 11:12.

units.la: II. Rationes afferat pro sententia affirmante.
units.tr: II. Let him bring forward reasons in favour of the affirmative position.

units.la: 1. Quia reges debent esse nutricii & custodes Ecclesiæ Ef.49: 23. horum igitur officium inculcetur.
units.tr: 1. Because kings ought to be nursing fathers and guardians of the Church: Isa. 49:23. Let the duty of these men therefore be impressed.

units.la: 2. Quia regi & magistratui injungitur lectio legis divinæ assidua. Urgeatur hic scopus, scil. ut discat timere Deum, & legem Dei servet & imperet subditis.
units.tr: 2. Because the king and magistrate are enjoined to read the divine law constantly. Let the aim be stressed here, namely that he learn to fear God, and keep God's law and enforce it on his subjects.

units.la: 3. Quia sic fecerunt Moses & Reges pii in V. & Nov. Test. vid. Libent. diff. 13. q. 3. Secus facientes reges Israelis puniti sunt. Addi etiam possunt exempla gentilium, ubi cura sacrorum regibus commissa fuit, natura sic suadente.
units.tr: 3. Because Moses and the pious kings did so in the Old and New Testament; see Libent., diff. 13, q. 3. Kings of Israel who acted otherwise were punished. Examples of the Gentiles may also be added, where the care of sacred matters was committed to kings, nature itself so suggesting.

units.la: III. Refutentur rationes contrariæ.
units.tr: III. Let the contrary arguments be refuted.

units.la: Conclusio Decisionem habeat; videl. licet ex scriptura, & consilio Ecclesiasticorum statuendum sit de dogmatibus religionis; tamen neutiquam excludendum Magistratum; sed potius tanquam membrum eximium Ecclesiæ ipsius ductu & auctoritate omnia gerenda & stabilienda &c.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him give the decision: namely, that although matters of religious doctrine must be determined from Scripture and the counsel of the ecclesiastical men, the magistrate must by no means be excluded; rather, as an outstanding member of the Church, all things are to be managed and established under her guidance and authority, etc.

units.la: THEMA XI.
units.tr: THEMA XI.

units.la: I. Accusatio Ludimagistri Faliscorum, per Fiscalem. Ex Liv. 5. 27. Flor. 1. 12.
units.tr: I. Accusation of the schoolmaster of the Faliscans, brought by the prosecutor. From Livy 5.27; Florus 1.12.

units.la: Exord. A simili capitis, aut cordis ægrotantis; unde periculum toti corpori. Proponatur in protasi & apodosi, videl. ita & nihil nocentius, quàm si ille, qui aliis præpositus malo exemplo præeat.
units.tr: Exord. From the likeness of a diseased head or heart, whence danger comes to the whole body. Let it be put in protasis and apodosis, namely: thus, and nothing is more harmful than when he who is set over others goes before them with a bad example.

units.la: Narratio. Ex historia exponat. 1. qua fiducia magnates ipsi commiserint liberos. 2. quomodo subinde eduxerit veluti spaciatu. 3. quomodo tradiderit illos. 4. quomodo remissus à Camillo.
units.tr: Narratio. Let him set out from the history: (1) with what confidence the nobles entrusted their children to him; (2) how he then led them out, as it were for a walk; (3) how he handed them over; (4) how he was sent back by Camillus.

units.la: Propos. Capitis reum esse, ut exemplo sit aliis.
units.tr: Propos. That the accused deserves capital punishment, so that he may be an example to others.

units.la: Confirmat. I. Quia prodere sic voluit urbem, traditis magnatum liberis. Hic exaggeret crimen proditionis tanquam turpissimum & omnibus legibus divinis & humanis capitale. &c. crimen quippe majestatis esse.
units.tr: Confirmat. I. Because he wished to betray the city in this way, by handing over the children of the nobles. Here let him magnify the crime of treason as most shameful and capital by all divine and human laws, and so on, for it is indeed a crime against majesty.

units.la: II. Quia trucidandos, aut saltem in servitutem tradere voluit liberos Faliscorum, carissima pignora parentum: adeoque & plagii reum esse; jam vero plagium omnibus legibus capitale esse, vel in uno commissum. Quid in tam multis, iisque flore civitatis. III. Quia fefellit fidem datam; sine qua nulla societas esse potest. Igitur ex societate humana bestiam exturbandam esse.
units.tr: II. Because he wished to slaughter, or at least to hand over into slavery, the children of the Faliscans, the dearest pledges of their parents; and so he is also guilty of kidnapping (plagium). Now kidnapping is capital by all laws, even when committed against a single person. What then when it is committed against so many, and those the flower of the state? III. Because he broke the faith he had given, without which no society can exist. Therefore this beast must be driven out of human society.

units.la: IV. A praejudicio & exemplo, quod statuit in mastigiam istum Camillus; infamem sic declarans & ad justam poenam senatui Falisco remittens.
units.tr: IV. From the precedent and example which Camillus set against this schoolmaster, declaring him infamous and sending him back to the Falisci senate for just punishment.

units.la: Conclus. Ex repetitis summatim argumentis tot mortibus merito plectendum, quot pueros prodere voluit, exemplari supplicio mactandum censeat.
units.tr: Conclus. From the arguments briefly repeated, let him advise that he be put to death by an exemplary punishment, as many deaths as he wished to inflict by handing over the boys, since he deserves them.

units.la: II. Excusatio ipsius.
units.tr: II. His own excuse.

units.la: Exord. A facto Platonis, qui Rhetoricam tanquam incantandi artem ex sua rep. relegandam censuit. Vid. jam suo malo experiri se, non sine ratione sic statuisse Platonem virum sapientissimum.
units.tr: Exord. From the deed of Plato, who judged that Rhetoric, as an art of enchanting, should be banished from his commonwealth. Let him note that by his own cost he now experiences that Plato, a most wise man, decided this not without reason.

units.la: Applicetur ad hypothesin: Ita enim exaggerari factum suum, qua spaciatum eduxit discipulos, quasi proditor, parricida & majestatis Reus sit.
units.tr: Let it be applied to the case: his deed is thus exaggerated, in that he led the pupils out for a walk, as if he were a traitor, a parricide and guilty of majesty.

units.la: Propof. Petere se, ne perverso Camilli praejudicio damnetur, sed audiatur in justa sua excusatione.
units.tr: Propof. He asks that he not be condemned through Camillus' perverse prejudice, but be heard in his just excuse.

units.la: Confirm. 1. In statu qualitatis: neget dolo se fecisse ex praesumtionibus: 1. quia fecerit ratione officii; & quidé ut animi puerorum reficerentur & alacriores redderentur ad studia. Opus esse quiete & recreatione teneris annis: Deinde, ut ad memoriam castra hostium ostenderet & ipse exploraret. 2. quia fecerit spe immunitatis aetatis innoxiae, confisus generositate hostium Romanorum, ex praecedentibus belli s cognitam; innocentiam tutam ubique sperans, 3. quia jam aliquoties tuto egressus ita fuerit & redierit, hinc crevisse ipsi fiduciam; si prodere pueros voluerit prima vice potius facturus id fuisset. 4. quia stratagema Camilli credendum sit, quod ita ipsum remiserit; ut sic pelliciat illos ad deditionem.
units.tr: Confirm. 1. In the state of quality: he denies that he acted by deceit, and argues from presumptions: (1) because he acted by reason of his office, and indeed so that the boys' minds might be refreshed and made more eager for their studies, since tender years need rest and recreation; and then so that he might show them the enemy camp and explore it himself. (2) Because he acted in hope of immunity for innocent youth, trusting in the generosity of the Roman enemy, known from earlier wars, and hoping that innocence would be safe everywhere. (3) Because he had already several times gone out safely and returned, and so his confidence had grown; had he wished to betray the boys, he would have done it the first time. (4) Because Camillus' stratagem must be believed, in that he sent him back in this way, so as to lure the boys into surrender.

units.la: II. In statu definitivo: si maximè dolo fecisset, non tamen esse proditionem aut crimen Majestatis; 1. quia norit, propter paucos pueros non traditum iri urbem. 2. quia scire potuerit experientia, Romanos in imbellem aetatem non animadversuros. Atrocius itaque fieri, quod parricidii, proditionis insimuletur. 3. quia leges in mitiorem partem inclinant. Itaque si maximè malo animo fecisset, imprudentiam, avaritiam captandi praemium mium dici posse, scelus non posse. Cadere illud facile in genus hominum scholasticorum, quo nihil simplicius.
units.tr: II. In the definitive state: even if he had acted most deceitfully, it would still not be treason or the crime of majesty: (1) because he knew the city would not be handed over on account of a few boys; (2) because experience could have taught him that the Romans would not harm an age unfit for war, so what is charged as parricide and treason is made more atrocious than it is; (3) because the laws incline to the milder side. Therefore, even if he had acted with the worst intent, it could be called imprudence, or greed in seeking a reward, but it could not be called a crime. That easily falls to the class of scholastic men, than whom nothing is more simple.

units.la: Concluf. Petere se itaque, ut non finiitre de se credant, aut acerbius statuant; quippe quem expertæ fidei hactenus deprehenderit: si improvide, si temere fecerit, cautiorem se futurum imposterum.
units.tr: Concluf. He asks, therefore, that they not finally think the worst of him or decide more harshly, since he has hitherto shown himself of proven faith; if he has acted imprudently or rashly, he will be more cautious in future.

units.la: THEMA XII.
units.tr: THEMA XII.

units.la: I. Gentes coram Constantino M. accusant Christianos tanquam orbis turbatores. Arnobius defendit. Videatur Tertullianus, Justinus in Apolog. & Minucium Felicem.
units.tr: I. The Gentiles, before Constantine the Great, accuse the Christians as disturbers of the world. Arnobius defends them. See Tertullian, Justin in his Apology, and Minucius Felix.

units.la: Exord. Captet favorem judicis congratulatione victoriarum, & spe concepta de restitutione imperii diu afflicti. 2. causam turbarum alleget tum ambitionem, tum impietatem, qua passim cultus Deorum abrogatus. Maximè per novum hominum genus Christianos: qui Deorum spretores causa sint tot cladium.
units.tr: Exordium. He should win the judge's favour by congratulating him on his victories and on the hope conceived of restoring the long-afflicted empire. 2. He should attribute the causes of the disturbances both to ambition and to impiety, by which the worship of the gods has been abolished everywhere, and above all to the new race of men, the Christians, who, as scorners of the gods, are the cause of so many disasters.

units.la: Narrat. Odiosè exponat ipsorum ortum, incrementum passim, & doctrinam receptis ritibus, ac Diis omnibus adversam: unde nil nisi interitus orbis metuendus.
units.tr: Narratio. He should describe their origin, their growth everywhere, and their teaching, which is opposed to the accepted rites and to all the gods; from this nothing but the destruction of the world is to be feared.

units.la: Propof. De horum causa jam statuendum, utrum fovendi aut extirpandi sint, id quod pietas, justitia & publica orbis securitas exigere videtur.
units.tr: Propositio. The cause of these people must now be decided: whether they should be cherished or exterminated, which piety, justice, and the public safety of the world seem to require.

units.la: Contentio exstirpationem urgens
units.tr: Contentio, urging extermination:

units.la: I. Ab honesto seu pio. Quia injurii sint adversus Deos: quos tanta veneratione coluerint majores. Principis esse vindicare honorem Deorum, quorum vices gerat: illustretur a contrario neglectu Deorum; unde publicæ hæ clades orbis per 3. hæc secula.
units.tr: I. From what is honourable or pious: because they are wrongdoers against the gods, whom our ancestors worshipped with such great reverence. It is the prince's duty to avenge the honour of the gods whose place he holds. Let this be made clear by the contrary case of neglect of the gods, from which have come the public disasters of the world throughout these three centuries.

units.la: II. A justo: 1. quia rebelles sint magistratui, spernentes edicta principum. 2. judicia evertant, docentes non resistendum injuriis, non litigandum coram tribunalibus. Hæc exaggeret tanquam fontem scelerum, quæ legibus Romanis puniuntur. 3. Vitam agant cyclopicam, noctu in cryptis convenientes, & prætextu religionis forsan fœda perpetrantes.
units.tr: II. From what is just: 1. because they are rebels against the magistrate, scorning the edicts of princes. 2. because they subvert the courts, teaching that one must not resist injuries nor go to law before tribunals. He should magnify these things as the source of crimes, which are punished by Roman laws. 3. because they lead a Cyclopean life, meeting by night in crypts, and perhaps committing foul deeds under the pretext of religion.

units.la: III. A securo: quia ipsorum secta vigente, nec regnum ullum, nec familia subsistere queat. Probetur 1. quia ipsi novum regem, & novum regnum doceant, adeoque subditos a regibus suis avellant. 2. quia libertatem prædicent omnibus, unde ruina na familiarum. 3. quia obtentu hujus regni & libertatis spiri-tualis poenas, exilia, imò & mortem contemnant. Quantum hinc incommoda metuenda orbi.
units.tr: III. From what is safe: because, while their sect flourishes, no kingdom and no family can survive. Let it be proved: 1. because they teach a new king and a new kingdom, and so turn subjects away from their own kings. 2. because they proclaim liberty to all, whence comes the ruin of families. 3. because, under the pretext of this kingdom and of spiritual liberty, they despise penalties, exile, and even death. How great the inconveniences to be feared from this for the world!

units.la: IV. Ab exemplis superiorum imperatorum, qui severis edictis ac poenis in illos statuerunt, quarum praecipuae aliquot enumerandae ex historia. vide Sulpit.
units.tr: IV. From the examples of earlier emperors, who decreed against them with severe edicts and penalties; some of the chief of these are to be enumerated from history. See Sulpicius.

units.la: Epilogus. 1. Inculcata argumentorum summa, Imperatorem obtestetur, ne Christianis aurem praebeat.
units.tr: Epilogue. 1. Having driven home the sum of the arguments, he should entreat the emperor not to lend an ear to the Christians.

units.la: 2. Cohortetur ut priora edicta renovet & animose exsequatur, ita vero Augustum ipsum futurum, ita cultum Deorum, pacem & tranquillitatem imperii rediturum.
units.tr: 2. He should exhort him to renew the earlier edicts and to enforce them vigorously; thus the emperor himself will be augmented, the worship of the gods, peace and the tranquillity of the empire will return.

units.la: II. Arnobius defendit Christianos.
units.tr: II. Arnobius defends the Christians.

units.la: Exord. Conciliet sibi judicem 1. à persona reorum, qui calumniis hostium delati, indigna passi sint per tria secula, constantia tamen ac vitae probitate hactenus superarint furorem hostium. 2. à persona judicis; quem Deus ut Imperio, ita & Christianis asylum dedérit. 3. à rei ipsius aequitate, petere se patrocinium innocentiae & securitatem contra calumniatores ac delatores.
units.tr: Exordium. He should win the judge over: 1. from the persons of the accused, who, having been denounced by the calumnies of enemies, have suffered unworthy treatment for three centuries, yet have hitherto overcome the fury of their enemies by constancy and integrity of life. 2. from the person of the judge, whom God has given as a refuge both to the empire and to the Christians. 3. from the fairness of the matter itself, he should ask for the protection of innocence and for security against calumniators and informers.

units.la: Narratio. Breviter & verè exponat ortum, incrementum, doctrinam ac vitam Christianorum.
units.tr: Narratio. He should briefly and truthfully set out the origin, growth, teaching and life of the Christians.

units.la: Propos. Horum agi causam, utrum tanquam orbis purgamenta ferro, flammis exscindi, an potius tanquam lux mundi, sal terrae fovendi & asserendi sint: addat votum, ut tandem justam causam Deus asserat.
units.tr: Propositio. The question is whether these people are to be cut off with iron and fire as the refuse of the world, or rather cherished and vindicated as the light of the world and the salt of the earth. He should add a prayer that at last God may vindicate the just cause.

units.la: Confutatio. Refellat ordine calumnias ab accusatore objectas.
units.tr: Confutatio. He refutes in order the calumnies brought forward by the accuser.

units.la: ad I. Gentilium Deos exagitet: vide Minucium Felicem. Arnob. contra gentes: non horum neglectum, sed oppressionem innocentum causam esse publicarum cladium. Veri Dei honorem promovendum esse Principibus.
units.tr: To I. He attacks the gods of the Gentiles; see Minucius Felix and Arnobius Against the Gentiles. The cause of the public disasters is not the neglect of these gods but the oppression of the innocent. The honour of the true God is to be promoted by the princes.

units.la: ad II. Neget crimina objecta, & vitam ac doctrinam Christianorum asserat.
units.tr: To II. He denies the crimes charged, and vindicates the life and teaching of the Christians.

units.la: ad III. Exponat quale regnum, qualem libertatem Christiani doceant; unde maxima tranquillitas ac securitas orbi.
units.tr: To III. He sets out what kind of kingdom and what kind of liberty the Christians teach; whence comes the greatest tranquillity and security for the world.

units.la: ad IV. Calumnia adversariorum incitatos imperatores nonnullos persecutos fuisse Christianos: nec quicquam profecisse. Alios contra foviisse Christianos. Hinc transeat ad ConConfirmat. Videl. Christianos non modo non persequendos, sed tanquam lucem ac meliorem orbis partem fovendos esse.
units.tr: To IV. The calumny of the adversaries stirred up some emperors to persecute the Christians, and nothing was gained by it. Others, on the contrary, favoured the Christians. From this he passes to the Confirmation. That is, the Christians should not only not be persecuted, but cherished as the light and the better part of the world.

units.la: I. Quia ipsorum religio sanctissima : quod ostendatur inductione quadam praecipuorum dogmatum & collatione gentilium.
units.tr: I. Because their religion is most holy; this is to be shown by a certain survey of the chief doctrines and by comparison with the Gentile religion.

units.la: II. Quia vita ipsorum innocentissima. Probetur inductione praeceptorum practicorum.
units.tr: II. Because their life is most innocent; this is to be proved by a survey of the practical precepts.

units.la: III. Quia a Deo profecta haec religio. Hinc ostende, quomodo Deus se revelarit Judaeis : 2. quomodo hoc compleverit in Christo : qui Dominus dominantium, in cujus gloria omnis gloria regnorum.
units.tr: III. Because this religion has come from God. Here show: 1. how God revealed himself to the Jews; 2. how he fulfilled this in Christ, who is Lord of lords, in whose glory is all the glory of kingdoms.

units.la: Epilogus. 1. Apellet conscientiam imperatoris de veritate dictorum. 2. Hortetur, ut quemadmodum coepit, ita porro foveat causam Christianorum, quo tandem fallax daemonum cultus cesset, veri Dei gloria asseratur.
units.tr: Epilogue. 1. He calls on the emperor's conscience as to the truth of what has been said. 2. He exhorts him that, as he has begun, so he should continue to favour the cause of the Christians, so that at last the deceitful worship of demons may cease and the glory of the true God be vindicated.

units.la: THEMA XIII.
units.tr: THEMA XIII.

units.la: I. Examen iniquae accusationis Judaeorum adversus Christum institutae.
units.tr: I. An examination of the unjust accusation brought by the Jews against Christ.

units.la: Exord. Patheticum per concessionem obtenti voti : videl. jam tandem obtinuisti Judaeae, quod tanto zelo anhelasti &c. Amplif. ab effecto. videl. obtinuisti : at magno tuo malo. Ratio addatur: quia sanguis innocentis Christi adversus vos & liberos vestros clamat vindictam, multo magis, quam olim sanguis Abelis.
units.tr: Exordium. A pathetic opening, granting the wish obtained: "At last you have gained in Judea what you so eagerly longed for," etc. Amplification from the result: "you have gained it, but to your own great harm." Add the reason: the blood of the innocent Christ cries out for vengeance against you and your children, much more than the blood of Abel did of old.

units.la: Propos. Ut jam tandem facti iniquitatem agnoscant: cui fini sub examen illud revocandum ; ad ipsorum confusionem, & si fieri possit, ad poenitentiam. Vos saltem Aud. judicate.
units.tr: Propositio. That they may at last acknowledge the wickedness of the deed. To this end the trial is to be brought back for examination, for their confusion and, if possible, for their repentance. Let you, the hearers, be the judges.

units.la: Tractatio. Iniquitatem accusationis evincat:
units.tr: Tractatio. He proves the wickedness of the accusation:

units.la: I. A Christi innocentia. Et quid tandem o impie in Christo requiris &c.
units.tr: I. From the innocence of Christ: "And what, O impious one, do you require of Christ?" etc.

units.la: Probetur 1. quia doctrina ipsius sanctissima, ostendatur per inductionem praecipuorum capitum, & probetur ac concilietur cum lege Mosaica. 2. Quia vita ipsius innocentissima, quippe a. quam nullius peccati arguere potuerint etiam provocati. b. quae exemplar fuit virtutum omnium. c. quae beneficiis in aegros errantes fuit conspicua. Et hunc talem accusare audes.
units.tr: Let it be proved: (1) because his doctrine is most holy, shown by setting out its principal heads and by proving and reconciling it with the Mosaic law; (2) because his life was most innocent, for (a) they could not convict him of any sin, even when they challenged him; (b) it was a pattern of all virtues; (c) it was conspicuous for its benefits to the sick and the erring. And do you dare to accuse such a man?

units.la: Vindicetur ab objecto. 1. At turbavit plebem. ¤. At quomodo per Evangel. pacis, 2. At dixit se Deum ¤. a. multi Dii dicuntur in V. T. b. Novisse debuisses Messiam futurum esse Deum ex Pf. 110 & ex officio ipsius. Hinc invehatur in foedam ipsorum ignorantiam, qui Rabbi dicebantur. vide Rom. 2. obj. 3, At prohibet tributum Caesari dari. ʀ. Imo jussit dare Caesari, quae sunt Caesaris. Ipse solvit stateram. obj. 4. dixit se regem, adeoque est contra Caesarem ℞. At regem non hujus mundi. Talem se regem dixit, qualis Messias esse debebat. Vos vero illum Patribus desideratum, non agnovistis; imo contumaciter rejecistis, &c.
units.tr: Let it be defended against the objections. (1) "But he stirred up the people." Answer: but how, through the Gospel of peace? (2) "But he said that he was God." Answer: (a) many are called gods in the Old Testament; (b) you ought to have known that the Messiah would be God, from Psalm 110 and from his office. Here let him inveigh against the foul ignorance of the Jews, who were called Rabbis; see Rom. 2, obj. 3. (3) "But he forbade tribute to be given to Caesar." Answer: on the contrary, he bade them give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and he himself paid the tax-coin (stater). (4) "He said he was a king, and so is against Caesar." Answer: but his kingdom is not of this world. He called himself such a king as the Messiah ought to be. You, however, did not recognise him, whom the fathers had desired; nay, you obstinately rejected him, etc.

units.la: II. A defectu probationis. Sed ut malitia tua clarius elucescat, &c. Hinc 1. Exponatur Lex Dei de non dicendo falso testimonio, itemque de nemine condemnando nisi ex ore duorum. Hujus legis exaggeretur aequitas ac sanctitas. 2. opponatur praepostera judaeorum ratio; qua a. testes ipsi subornarunt. b. dissentientibus testibus, tamen damnarunt. Ita scil. observas legem o Pharisaee, qui clavem scientiae tibi arrogas.
units.tr: II. From the lack of proof. But that your malice may shine more clearly, etc. Hence: (1) let the law of God be set out, that one must not bear false witness, and that no one is to be condemned except on the word of two witnesses. Let the equity and holiness of this law be magnified. (2) Let the perverse reasoning of the Jews be set against it: (a) they themselves suborned the witnesses; (b) though the witnesses disagreed, they condemned him all the same. Thus, O Pharisee, you keep the law, you who claim the key of knowledge for yourself.

units.la: III. Ab extrema malitia accusantium Pharisaeorum; qui ipsi infensi erant, quia vitia ipsorum redarguebat. Hinc clandestinis conventibus in ipsius necem conspirarunt. Frustra praetextum quaeri sceleribus, Itane qui judices videri volebant juxta legem, qui oculus caeci, os muti, qui patroni oppressorum ac innocentum esse debebant, degenerarunt. vide Roman. 2.
units.tr: III. From the extreme malice of the accusing Pharisees, who were hostile to him because he rebuked their vices. Hence they conspired in secret meetings for his death. In vain is a pretext sought for crimes. Did those who wished to seem judges according to the law, who ought to have been the eyes of the blind, the mouths of the dumb, and the patrons of the oppressed and innocent, really degenerate so far? See Rom. 2.

units.la: Perorat. Quin potius agnoscis malitiam & fateris errorem ac ad gratiam confugis.
units.tr: Peroration. Rather, acknowledge your malice and confess your error, and flee to grace.

units.la: II. Examen iniqui judicii Pilati quo insontem Servatorem condemnavit.
units.tr: II. An examination of the unjust judgement of Pilate, by which he condemned the innocent Saviour.

units.la: Exord. A periculosa vitiorum sub nomine ac specie virtutum occultatione. Addatur ratio, quia sic incautis obrepunt & plus nocent: exemplo diaboli sub specie angeli lucis periculosius decipientis. Applicetur ad hypothes. videl. ita nullam iniquitatem nocentiorem, quam quae sub specie justitiae nocet; ut Pilatus sub persona judicis, Christum contra jus condemnans.
units.tr: Exordium. On the danger of concealing vices under the name and appearance of virtues. Add the reason: thus they creep upon the unwary and do more harm, as the devil does by example, deceiving more dangerously under the appearance of an angel of light. Apply this to the case: no injustice harms more than that which harms under the appearance of justice, as Pilate did when, in the character of judge, he condemned Christ against the law.

units.la: Propos. Qui proinde in judicium trahendus, ut rationem reddat latae sententiae; ut innocentia Christi ipsius iniquitas patescat.
units.tr: Propositio. He is therefore to be brought to trial, to give an account of the sentence pronounced, so that the innocence of Christ and the iniquity of Pilate himself may be made plain.

units.la: Tractatio.
units.tr: Tractatio.

units.la: I. Examinet ipsius judicium in ipsius iniqua condemnatione: quae probetur.
units.tr: I. Let his judgement be examined in his unjust condemnation, which is proved as follows:

units.la: Quod noverit ipsum ex odio accusari de criminibus, quae ficta sciebat quaeque non spectabant ad ipsius tribunal, sed censura Ecclesiae argui debuissent. Nonne igitur liberare debuisses innocentem ab oppressoribus. Exaggeretur ab officio judicum.
units.tr: That he knew the accusation against Christ was made out of hatred, concerning crimes which he knew to be fabricated, and which did not belong to his tribunal but should have been censured by the Church. Ought you not, then, to have freed the innocent from his oppressors? Let this be magnified from the duty of judges.

units.la: Quod in testibus & probatione defecerint. Nonne igitur accusatore non probante absolvere reum debuisses juxta leges Roman.
units.tr: That they failed in witnesses and in proof. Ought you not, then, since the accuser did not prove his case, to have acquitted the accused according to the Roman laws?

units.la: Quod contra testimonium Herodis, quod exploraverat, damnavit. Cur enim alba veste indutum remisit Herodes, nisi ut innocentem illum declararet. Cur non perstas in hac sententia? Scil. plebem metuebas. Hoc exaggera tanquam indignum judice. Adde admonitionem uxoris, quam spernere non debuit.
units.tr: That he condemned him against the testimony of Herod, whom he had examined. For why did Herod send him back clothed in a white robe, unless to declare him innocent? Why did you not persist in this sentence? Namely, you feared the people. Magnify this as unworthy of a judge. Add the admonition of his wife, which he ought not to have spurned.

units.la: Quod contra testim. ipsius proditoris; qui iniquam proditionem & innocentiam Christi proprio exitio testatus est. Hoc exaggeretur.
units.tr: That he acted against the testimony of the traitor himself, who, by his own destruction, bore witness to the wicked betrayal and to Christ's innocence. Let this be magnified.

units.la: Ab ipsius Pilati conscientia & confessione totics iterata. Cur non potius deponis personam judicis? Imo in judae exemplum judicii & poenam vides. Frustra speras aqua ablui crimina in perversa iniquae sententiae executione. Fiat transitio, sed quo te praecipitat vesania, &c.
units.tr: From Pilate's own conscience and confession, so often repeated. Why do you not rather lay aside the person of judge? Nay, in Judas you see an example of judgement and punishment. In vain do you hope to wash away your crimes with water in the perverse execution of an unjust sentence. Let there be a transition: but whither does madness hurl you, etc.

units.la: Dum tanquam facinorosum illum satagit dimittere. At sic innocentem reum declaras & judicium invido & imperito populo committis. Si innocens, cur non absolvis sententia juxta leges?
units.tr: While he strives to dismiss him as a criminal. But thus you declare the accused innocent, and commit the judgement to an envious and ignorant people. If he is innocent, why do you not acquit him by sentence, according to the laws?

units.la: Dum innocentem flagellari jubet. Haec quorsum, si reus mortis erat. Scilicet liberare voluisti illum hoc medio. At si insons cur ita tractas: Hic exagites sapientiam carnis, quae semel deserta recta via, gravius semper labitur.
units.tr: While he orders the innocent man to be scourged. To what purpose this, if he was liable to death? Clearly you wished to free him by this means. But if he was guiltless, why do you treat him thus? Here scourge the wisdom of the flesh, which, once it has deserted the straight way, always slips more heavily.

units.la: Dum sannis, ludibrio & saevitiae militum illum exponit. Ita scil. innocenti cumulas supplicium, etiam ultra falsi delicti meritum; & pluribus mortibus occidis. Contra jus iterum; quod in poena excedere prohibet.
units.tr: While he exposes him to jeering, ridicule and the savagery of the soldiers. Thus, clearly, you heap punishment upon the innocent, even beyond the deserts of the false charge, and you kill him with many deaths. Again this is against the law, which forbids exceeding the penalty.

units.la: II. Assurgat hinc ad judicium & consilium Dei: qui ita innocentem Servatorem damnari, ita iniquè tractari voluit, ut hoc sacrificio propitiatorio expiarentur peccata nostra. Hoc amplif. deductione per omnes iniqui hujus judicii partes. Conclus. Habeat votum gratiarum actionis ad Christum, qui insons pro nobis nocentibus condemnari voluit, ut nos à condemnatione æterna liberaret. Cui proinde nosmetipsos in vivam hostiam gratitudinis consecrare velimus.
units.tr: II. Let him rise from here to the judgement and counsel of God, who willed the innocent Saviour to be condemned and so unjustly treated, so that our sins might be expiated by this propitiatory sacrifice. Let this be amplified by going through every part of this unjust judgement. Conclusio. Let there be a vow of thanksgiving to Christ, who willed to be condemned as innocent on behalf of us the guilty, that he might free us from eternal condemnation. To him, therefore, let us wish to consecrate ourselves as a living sacrifice of gratitude.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Marefchallus Bironius accusatur criminis læsæ majestatis, quod contra regem & regnum Galliæ Henricum IV. cum Hispano & Sabaudo conspiraverit.
units.tr: Marshal Biron is accused of treason, namely that he conspired with the Spaniard and the Savoyard against King Henry IV and the kingdom of France.

units.la: A. Exord. Ab autoritate personæ rei, I. Προσωπολημψία, Tantam esse personæ hujus autoritatem & nomen, ut vix fidem inveniat, qui contra dicturus sit. II. Αἰτιολογία. Exponat ejus servitia pro rege, & præmia, quod ex Barone, Marefchallus, princeps, intimus regis evaserit. III. Ἐξεργασία per prolepsin: quamquam hæc ita se habeant, tamen non novum esse, quod viri magni magnos committant errores. IV. Conclusio. Idem & hic usu venire de personarei.
units.tr: A. Exordium. From the authority of the accused. I. Prosopolepsy [προσωπολημψία]: this man's authority and name are so great that hardly anyone will be found who will speak against him. II. Aetiology [αἰτιολογία]: let the speaker set out his services to the king and the rewards he received, how from a baron he became Marshal of France, a prince, and an intimate of the king. III. Exergasia [ἐξεργασία] through prolepsis: although these things are so, it is nonetheless not new for great men to commit great errors. IV. Conclusion: the same thing happens here, in the case of the person accused.

units.la: B. Narratio, quod oblitus bonitatis regiæ, spreta prima gratia, quam rex reo majestatis jam ante fecerat; ad eundem rursus impegerit lapidem; in Burgundia agens secreta tractans consilia cum rege Hisp. & duce Sabaudiæ, de dividendo regno Galliæ in plura regna; & exterminando sanguine regio, ac ipso rege tradendo captivo in manus hostis Hispan.
units.tr: B. Narration: that, forgetting the king's goodness and having spurned the first favour the king had already shown him as a man accused of treason, he again hurled the stone at the same person. While in Burgundy he held secret councils with the king of Spain and the duke of Savoy about dividing the kingdom of France into several kingdoms, exterminating the royal blood, and handing the king himself over as a captive into the hands of the Spanish enemy.

units.la: C. Propof. Hujus nefandi criminis te inficiantem audacter, hodie reum sistam, ac grate & justam nemesin implorabo.
units.tr: C. Proposition: I will today bring you before the court as a defendant, guilty of this nefarious crime which you deny so boldly, and I will earnestly call for just and fitting vengeance.

units.la: D. Confirmatio compellans pathetice conscientiam ducis, eundem convincere satagat. I. Præsumtionibus.
units.tr: D. Confirmation. Appealing pathetically to the duke's conscience, the prosecutor labours to convict him. I. By presumptions.

units.la: a. Ex signis videl. 1. negotiationibus secretis cum hostibus regis Sebaudo, & Comite de Fucates, illorumque secretariis. Urgeatur hoc signum tanquam minime fallax. 2. Judicio, quod ipse legatus in Angliam tulit. de comite Esfexio à regina decollato: videl. nunquam se permissurum, ut à carnifice caput sibi amputetur, sed vel laniaturum se illum, ut certando potius cadat. 3. recusatione mittendi secretarium ad regem. 4. Tergiversatione, qua bis terve à rege vocatus ex Burgundia Parisios, venire noluit. Scil. conscientia pavidus.
units.tr: a. From signs, namely: 1. his secret dealings with the king's enemies, the Savoyard and the Count de Fuentes, and with their secretaries. This sign is to be pressed as the least deceptive. 2. A judgement which the envoy himself brought back from England concerning Count Essex, who was beheaded by the queen: namely that Biron would never allow his own head to be cut off by the executioner, but would rather mangle the executioner, so that he might fall fighting. 3. His refusal to send a secretary to the king. 4. His evasion: when he was summoned twice or three times by the king from Burgundy to Paris, he refused to come. This is the mark of a man fearful in his conscience.

units.la: b. Voluntatis: quæ colliguntur.
units.tr: b. Of the will: the following points are gathered together.

units.la: 1. Ex affectibus impellentibus, videl. ira ac odio in regem: quæ probatur a. à causa, videl. Quia rex ipsius opera non fuit usus in expugnatione arcis Montismeliani : itemque præfecturam Civitatis Burgi, ipsi non commisit. β ab effectis, videl. querelis passim contra regem, quasi non compensat merita.
units.tr: 1. From impelling passions, namely anger and hatred towards the king. This is proved a. from the cause: the king did not use his services in the storming of the castle of Montmélian, and likewise did not entrust to him the governorship of the city of Bourg. β From the effects: complaints everywhere against the king, as if he did not repay Biron's merits.

units.la: 2. A moribus, videl. quod homo irrequietus, audax, ferax & superbus, qui & per aruspicem de regno spem sibi fieri passus sit, & conjugium cum filia Sabaudi ambiat.
units.tr: 2. From his character: he is a restless, reckless, ambitious and proud man, who also allowed himself to be given hope of the kingdom by a soothsayer, and who seeks a marriage with the daughter of the Savoyard.

units.la: 3. Ex spe, quam sibi facere potuit, de favore Hispani & Sabaudi, reliquorumque principum Catholicorum in Gallia, ob consensum in religione. Unde & ipse forsan regem sane sentientem aversetur.
units.tr: 3. From the hope he could have formed of favour from the Spaniard, the Savoyard, and the other Catholic princes in France, on account of agreement in religion. Hence perhaps he is alienated from the king, who indeed thinks otherwise in religion.

units.la: c. Facultatis. 1. quod vires habeat; autoritate pollens apud exercitus, & fultus sit auxilio Hisp. & Sabaudi. 2. Rex contra exosus plurimis ob religionem. 3. Occasionem habeat, Burgundiæ gubernamento præfectus, ubi in vicinia habeat Sabaudum, & Helvetios.
units.tr: c. Of capacity. 1. He has the means: he is powerful in authority among the armies, and is supported by the aid of the Spaniard and the Savoyard. 2. The king, on the other hand, is hated by very many on account of religion. 3. He has the opportunity: placed in charge of the government of Burgundy, where he has the Savoyard and the Swiss nearby.

units.la: II. Testimoniis a. Secretarii ipsius de la Fin, qui coram regi hoc confessus est, & veniam impetraverit ob indicium. b. Literis propria manu Bironii exaratis, quibus Secretarium informat, ut caute agat cum rege nec turbetur, si suspiciosum regem animadvertat. Exaggerentur hæc omnia, & talia esse dicantur, ut nil nisi propria confessio desideretur, quæ tortura elici posset, nisi personæ dignitas illum eximeret.
units.tr: II. By testimonies: a. of his secretary de la Fin, who confessed this before the king and obtained pardon in return for the information; b. by letters written in Biron's own hand, in which he instructs the secretary to act cautiously with the king and not to be disturbed if he notices the king is suspicious. Let all these things be magnified and presented as such that nothing but his own confession is lacking, which could be extracted by torture, were it not that the dignity of his person exempts him.

units.la: E. Concluf. Hortetur judices ut in re tanti momenti, statuant, nec patiantur periclitari amplius regem & regnum universum, nimia scrupulositate.
units.tr: E. Conclusion: let the prosecutor exhort the judges that, in a matter of such great moment, they should decide, and not allow the king and the whole kingdom to be endangered any longer through excessive scrupulosity.

units.la: Defensio Bironii.
units.tr: Defence of Biron.

units.la: A. Exord. A comparatione fœditatis criminis, & patrocinii debiti innocentiæ. Scil. tantam esse sceleris objecti gravitatem, ut nefas videatur ejus suscipere patrocinium, nisi innocentiæ debita defensio hoc imperaret, &c. Amplif. à personæ dignitate & meritis.
units.tr: A. Exordium: from the comparison between the foulness of the crime and the due defence of innocence. Namely, the gravity of the crime charged is so great that it seems wrong to undertake its defence, unless the due defence of innocence demanded it. Amplification from the dignity and merits of the person.

units.la: B. Propofit. Itaque confictam hanc à malevolis accusationem refel-lam, ad triumphum innocentiæ.
units.tr: B. Proposition: therefore I will refute this accusation, fabricated by malevolent men, for the triumph of innocence.

units.la: C. Refutatio.
units.tr: C. Refutation.

units.la: I. Præsumtionum in genere, scil. dolendum incertis conjecturis certa ipsius merita obfuscari. Locus de calumnia.
units.tr: I. Concerning presumptions in general: it is to be lamented that his certain merits are obscured by uncertain conjectures. Commonplace on calumny.

units.la: a. In specie refutatio signorum.
units.tr: a. In particular, refutation of the indications.

units.la: 1. Non esse hostem amplius Sabaudum; & nihil aliud cum illo tractatum nisi de matrimonio cum filia.
units.tr: 1. That the Savoyard is no longer an enemy, and that nothing was negotiated with him except a marriage to his daughter.

units.la: 2. Judicium unicuique suum liberum esse. Etiamnum se in eadem esse sententia.
units.tr: 2. That each person's judgment is his own to hold freely, and that he is still of the same opinion.

units.la: 3. & 4. Moram fuisse rationalem, non detrectationem obedientiæ, Disponenda prius fuisse negotia in provincia.
units.tr: 3. and 4. That the delay was a reasonable one, not a refusal of obedience, since his affairs in the province had first to be put in order.

units.la: b. Refutatio voluntatis.
units.tr: b. Refutation of the will.

units.la: 1. Et quidem sinistrorum affectuum.
units.tr: 1. Namely, of wrongful motives.

units.la: a. Ægre ducem tulisse, à malevolis suam personam suspectam redditam regi. Iram hinc concepisse, non contra regem; sed contra calumniatores.
units.tr: a. That the general took it badly that his person had been made suspect to the king by ill-wishers. That he conceived anger from this, not against the king, but against the calumniators.

units.la: β. Non se questum de rege, sed de adulatoribus. Contentum se præmiis largiter à rege datis. Non se animo mercenario esse.
units.tr: β. That he did not complain of the king, but of the flatterers. That he was content with the rewards generously given by the king, and that he is not of a mercenary mind.

units.la: 2. Calumniam esse, quod de moribus spargitur. Se adulationibus non quæsivisse gratiam regis, sed servitiis, quorum conscius sit rex & regnum.
units.tr: 2. That what is spread about his morals is a calumny. That he did not seek the king's favour by flattery but by services, of which the king and kingdom are aware.

units.la: 3. Religionis dissidium se Clericis permisisse hominem militarem à pueritia. Diversum loqui servitia sua regi præstita.
units.tr: 3. That, as a soldier from boyhood, he left the matter of religious dissension to the clergy. That his services rendered to the king speak otherwise.

units.la: c. Facultatis. 1. Si quid habeat autoritatis, illud meritis suis deberi, nunquam se illud contra regem usurpasse. Hispanum se hostem judicasse, non patronum. 2. Regem plures fautores, majores vires habere sua creatura; quam verbo destruere queat.
units.tr: c. Concerning ability. 1. If he has any authority, it is owed to his merits, and he never used it against the king. He judged the Spaniard an enemy, not a patron. 2. The king has more supporters and greater strength in his own creature than could be destroyed by a word.

units.la: II. Refutatio testimonii.
units.tr: II. Refutation of the testimony.

units.la: a. Se nondum credere posse Secretarium suum mentiri ausum contra se & veritatem. Si vero fecit, non audiendum esse ministrum male contentum, contra dominum. Servitia sua contrarium testari.
units.tr: a. That he cannot yet believe his secretary dared to lie against him and against the truth. But if he did, a discontented minister should not be heard against his master. His services bear witness to the contrary.

units.la: b. Literas se dedisse ad Secretarium, & hortatum esse, ut cautè moram excusét, & si suspicionem conceperit ex negotiationibus cum Sabaudo, causam, nuptias scil. exponat.
units.tr: b. That he wrote a letter to the secretary, urging him to excuse the delay cautiously, and, if he had conceived suspicion from the dealings with the Savoyard, to set out the cause, namely the marriage.

units.la: Eleventur jam omnes hujusmodi præsumtiones, quia incertæ & se& leves ; & exaggerentur porrò certa & maxima ipsius Marescalli servitia, quibus plus credendum, quam malevolorum calumniis.
units.tr: Let all presumptions of this kind now be set aside, since they are uncertain and often slight; and let the certain and very great services of the Marshal himself be further magnified, to which more credence is to be given than to the calumnies of ill-wishers.

units.la: D. Conclusio petens ut ab accusatione & judicio absolvatur, & ut nominentur sibi autores calumnarum, quò contra illos honorem ac famam suam vindicare queat.
units.tr: D. Conclusion, asking that he be absolved from the accusation and judgment, and that the authors of the calumnies be named to him, so that he may be able to vindicate his honour and reputation against them.

units.la: Decretum fuit decollatio.
units.tr: Decapitation was decreed.

units.la: THEMA XV.
units.tr: THEMA XV.

units.la: Accusatur Manlius Junior violatæ disciplinæ militaris. Ex Flor. c.14.
units.tr: Manlius the Younger is accused of violating military discipline. From Florus, chapter 14.

units.la: A. Exord. A contraria obedientia, quæ probatur necessaria, tum in omni regimine; tum præcipue in militari; utpote ubi in arena sæpe danda & expedienda mandata.
units.tr: A. Exordium. Obedience, the opposite of disobedience, is shown to be necessary in every form of government, and especially in the military, since commands must often be given and carried out in the heat of battle.

units.la: B. Narratio facti: Contra fecit Manlius Junior, pugnans contra imperium parentis imperatoris.
units.tr: B. Narratio facti: Manlius the Younger acted against this, fighting against the command of his father, the commander.

units.la: C. Propos. Hunc igitur posco ad supplicium.
units.tr: C. Propositio. I therefore demand that he be put to death.

units.la: D. Confirmatio.
units.tr: D. Confirmatio.

units.la: I. Quia inobediens fuit duci suo, pugnando contra imperium. Hoc ostendatur esse commissum contra sacramentum, quo duci juravit obsequium. Exaggeretur
units.tr: I. Because he was disobedient to his commander, fighting against the command. This should be shown to have been committed against the oath by which he swore obedience to the commander. Let it be amplified:

units.la: 1. A scopo juramenti, qui est, ut obstringat se duci.
units.tr: 1. From the aim of the oath, which is to bind him to the commander.

units.la: 2. A minori, si in omnibus servandum hoc, multò magis in pugnando; ubi vita tot militum Romanorum in discrimen adducit.
units.tr: 2. From the lesser case: if this must be observed in all things, much more must it be observed in fighting, where the lives of so many Roman soldiers are put at risk.

units.la: II. Quia violavit disciplinam militarem; quæ exigit, ut à duce pugnæ fiat initium. Exaggeretur 1. à momento, quod situm sit in captando tempore & loco idoneo. 2. à consequentia, quod si impunitum maneat, reliqui in exemplum facilè trahere queant. Unde luxatio disciplinæ.
units.tr: II. Because he violated military discipline, which requires that the battle be begun by the commander. Let it be amplified: (1) from its importance, since it lies in seizing the right time and place; (2) from its consequence, since if it remains unpunished, others can easily be drawn to follow the example. Hence the dislocation of discipline.

units.la: III. Quia periculo exposuit totum exercitium. Hoc probetur ex circumstantia præsentis belli, ubi cum Latinis, gente ejusdem linguæ consligendum suit; quæ causa mandati fuerit Imperatorii, ne scil. confusio oboriretur ex identitate Linguæ.
units.tr: III. Because he exposed the whole army to danger. This is proved from the circumstances of the present war, in which they had to fight the Latins, a people of the same language. The reason for the imperial command was that confusion might arise from the sameness of language.

units.la: E. Conclus. Ex brevi repetitione allegatarum rationum poscens Manlium ad ultimum supplicium. Addito pondere ne imperator in suo filio patiatur luxari disciplinam.
units.tr: E. Conclusio. From a brief repetition of the reasons alleged, I demand Manlius's ultimate punishment, with added weight: lest the commander suffer discipline to be dislocated in his own son.

units.la: De-
units.tr: Defence

units.la: Exord. Benevolentiam captat 1. à persona rei, qui non ob sceleus aliquot, quorum quædam militibus familiaria enumerentur; sed ob virtutem ac victoriam accusetur. 2. a persona judicis, qui vel ut judex rigidus condemnare, vel ut pater benignus absolvere filium queat.
units.tr: Exordium. He seeks goodwill: (1) from the person of the accused, who is charged not with some crimes, some of which are listed as familiar to soldiers, but for his valour and victory; (2) from the person of the judge, who may either condemn as a strict judge or acquit his son as a kindly father.

units.la: Propos. Posterius hoc ipsa justitia suadente evincam, innocentiæ ac virtutis patronus.
units.tr: Propositio. I will prove the latter, justice itself persuading me, as the defender of innocence and virtue.

units.la: Confutatio Rationis
units.tr: Refutation of the Argument

units.la: 1. Omnem pugnam contra Imperium Imperatoris, non esse illico inobedientiam: Hic
units.tr: 1. Not every fight against the commander's command is at once disobedience. Here:

units.la: a. Confitendum est factum, scilicet inhibitam fuisse pugnam & necessariam esse militi obedientiam.
units.tr: a. It must be conceded that the fact happened, namely that fighting was forbidden and that obedience is necessary for a soldier.

units.la: b. Negandam esse hanc inobedientiam, ex causa, cur pugnaverit 1. negatè, scil. non ex contemtu aut vilipendio mandati: 2. affirmatè; sed ex inopinata occasione, & provocatione facta à Genimio Metio, hostium Duce. Talia verò fatalia & divina existimanda esse. Nec posse honestè aut tutò recusari à viro forti. Tales casus exemtos esse legibus.
units.tr: b. This disobedience must be denied, on account of the reason he fought: (1) negatively, namely, not from contempt or disdain for the command; (2) affirmatively, but from an unexpected opportunity and challenge made by Geminius Metius, the enemy leader. Such things are to be regarded as fated and divine, and a brave man can neither honourably nor safely refuse them. Such cases are exempt from the laws.

units.la: II. Sic pugnando non violari disciplinam militarem. a. Quia causa mandati & pugnæ commissæ ipectanda. Quæ illa fuerit explicandum. b. Quia pugna fuerit tantum particularis, qualis à centurione pro re nata sine violatione disciplinæ committi aliquando queat ac debeat. c. proindeque non posse trahi in consequiti in simili casu.
units.tr: II. Thus, by fighting, military discipline is not violated. a. Because the reason for the command and the battle that was fought must be considered; what that reason was must be explained. b. Because the fight was only a particular one, such as a centurion may sometimes, and should, engage in on the spur of the moment without violating discipline. c. And therefore it cannot be drawn into precedent in a similar case.

units.la: III. Nec fuisse periculum, quia singulare veluti certamen tantum fuit; indeque nec metuendam confusionem, adeoque cessasse cautam legis. Qua cessante, legem ipsam cessare.
units.tr: III. Nor was there any danger, since it was only, as it were, a single combat. Hence no confusion was to be feared, and so the cause of the law ceased. With that cause ceasing, the law itself ceases.

units.la: Conclus. Absolvendum itaque Manlium, si non ex summo jure, saltem ex gratia Imperatoris, parentis. Idque eò magis, quia pugna hæc salutaris fuit, & veluti ab ipso Deo approbata per lætam victoriam.
